question: A summer insect pours out of the ground by the billions every 13 or 17 years and swarms the forests of the eastern United States. It has a shiny black body about the size of a thumb, two brilliant red compound eyes and clear wings with bright orange veins. Which insect wears this eerie red-eyed look?
answer: The periodical cicada
choices: The periodical cicada
The luna moth
The dog-day katydid
The box elder bug
context: The adult periodical cicada has two brilliant red compound eyes set in a black body with clear, orange-veined wings — the eerie look people remember when billions surface at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas

question: A brood of periodical cicadas crawls out of one forest's soil within the same few nights, billions strong, after 13 or 17 years as pale nymphs sucking sap from tree roots. For decades biologists wondered how insects buried so deep all know when to come out. What signal tells them the moment has come?
answer: The soil 8 inches down warming to about 64 degrees F
choices: The soil 8 inches down warming to about 64 degrees F
The first full moon after the spring equinox
The scent of new tree blossoms overhead
A sudden spring rain soaking the ground
context: A whole generation surfaces together when the soil 8 inches (20 cm) down warms to about 64°F (17.9°C). Because the cue is soil warmth, broods in the south surface weeks before broods in the north. Underground, the nymphs appear to 'count' the years by sensing seasonal changes in the tree's xylem sap, an internal calendar with no clock. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas

question: A male cicada crawls out of the dirt after 17 years underground and starts to sing. He is barely the size of a thumb, yet his song carries across the whole forest, one of the loudest calls any insect makes. His tymbals, ribbed membranes on his sides, buckle hundreds of times a second to make the clicks. What lets so small a body throw that sound so far?
answer: His hollow abdomen works as a resonating chamber that amplifies the clicks into a roar
choices: His hollow abdomen works as a resonating chamber that amplifies the clicks into a roar
His wing veins trap and re-release the sound like a second pair of drums
His stiffened outer shell rings like a bell each time a tymbal snaps
His crowd of neighbors all click in unison to stack the sound louder
context: Only male cicadas sing, using a tymbal, a stiff, ribbed membrane on each side of the hollow abdomen, snapped in and out by muscles so fast the clicks blur into a continuous song. The hollow abdomen acts as a resonating chamber, and a big chorus can reach about 100 decibels close by, among the loudest sounds in the insect world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas

question: After 17 years in the dark sipping sap from tree roots, a whole brood of periodical cicadas tunnels out in the same summer, sometimes more than 1.5 million to a single acre of forest. They do not sting, hide or run from a hungry bird. How does arriving in such staggering numbers keep the species going?
answer: Predators fill up long before the swarm runs out, so most cicadas survive to mate
choices: Predators fill up long before the swarm runs out, so most cicadas survive to mate
The dense swarm confuses hunting birds into striking each other instead
The crush of bodies buries and smothers most ground predators outright
The sheer noise of the chorus drives most predators out of the forest
context: They emerge at more than 1.5 million cicadas per acre (about 370 per square meter) — so many that predators simply cannot eat them all, and most survive to mate. Scientists call this 'predator satiation.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas

question: Broods of periodical cicadas wait 13 or 17 years underground before they surface, never 12, 15 or 18. Both numbers are prime, and Stephen Jay Gould made famous an idea about why. In that idea, what survival edge does such an odd wait give the cicadas?
answer: Predators on 2-, 3- or 4-year cycles rarely peak in an emergence year
choices: Predators on 2-, 3- or 4-year cycles rarely peak in an emergence year
The long wait starves out any predator that had specialized in eating cicadas
It lines their emergence up with the rare, extra-wet summers
The gap outlasts the memory any single predator can pass to its young
context: This is a leading hypothesis, not proven fact: a prime, indivisible cycle makes it nearly impossible for any predator with a shorter life cycle to line up and feast every time. It was first formally proposed by entomologists Monte Lloyd and Henry Dybas in a 1966 paper and later popularized by evolutionary biologist Stephen Jay Gould in a 1977 essay. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas

question: A cicada sucks sap from tree roots in total darkness for 13 or 17 years. Then one summer it tunnels up, splits out of its brown shell on the side of a tree, unfolds its wings and climbs into the sunlight, ready to sing and mate. How long does the winged adult live above ground?
answer: About four to six weeks
choices: About four to six weeks
About a single day
About two years
About three months
context: After 13 or 17 years underground, the emerged adults live only four to six weeks — just long enough to sing, mate, and lay eggs — and then die, and the cycle begins again. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical_cicadas

question: On the moonlit grasslands of Africa, a burrowing mammal shuffles out of its den at dusk. It has a pig-like snout, tall rabbit-like ears and a heavy tail like a kangaroo's. All night it rips open termite mounds and slurps up ants and termites. What is it?
answer: The aardvark
choices: The aardvark
The giant anteater
The pangolin
The armadillo
context: Orycteropus afer, the aardvark, is a mash-up of borrowed parts: a pig-like snout, long donkey- or rabbit-like ears, a heavy kangaroo-like tail, and spade-clawed digging feet. A big one weighs 60-80 kg and stretches over 2 metres including the tail. Its name is Afrikaans for 'earth pig,' and it is also called the antbear or Cape anteater. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aardvark

question: An aardvark noses through the African night with a pig-like snout, tall rabbit ears and a sticky, ropy tongue for lapping up ants and termites. It looks like an anteater wearing a pig's face, but its genes place it in Afrotheria, an ancient group of African mammals. Which familiar animals share that group with it?
answer: Elephants and manatees
choices: Elephants and manatees
Pigs and warthogs
Anteaters and pangolins
Armadillos and sloths
context: Despite the anteater-with-a-pig-snout look, the aardvark belongs to the African superorder Afrotheria, alongside elephants, manatees (sea cows) and hyraxes; within that group its very closest living relatives are the elephant shrews, tenrecs and golden moles. Its resemblance to South American anteaters is convergent evolution: the same ant-eating body plan arising independently in unrelated lineages, not shared ancestry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aardvark

question: An aardvark feeding on ants and termites carries teeth so strange that biologists named its whole order of mammals after them: Tubulidentata, 'tube-toothed.' Each tooth is a rootless column of as many as 1,500 thin, hexagonal tubes packed side by side. What do these tube-teeth completely lack?
answer: Enamel
choices: Enamel
Any nerves
A blood supply
A jaw socket
context: An aardvark tooth has no enamel at all; it is built from vasodentin, thin hexagonal tubes of dentine, and the largest tooth holds about 1,500 of them. Because the teeth are rootless, they never stop growing, wearing down at the top as they push up from below. This tube-tooth is what gives the order its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aardvark

question: An aardvark rips open a rock-hard termite mound with its shovel-like front claws, and the panicked insects flee deep into their tunnels. In a single night it can gather as many as 50,000 of them. What body part does it use to reach inside the tunnels and gather them up?
answer: A sticky, snakelike tongue
choices: A sticky, snakelike tongue
A thin, hooked probing finger
A narrow retractable snout-tube
A row of fine comb-like teeth
context: The aardvark feeds by breaking into ant and termite nests with its powerful spade-clawed feet, then slurping up the insects with a long, thin, snakelike, sticky tongue up to 30 centimetres (12 inches) long, enough to reach as many as 50,000 insects in a single night's foraging. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aardvark

question: An aardvark tears up the African savanna night after night, tunneling a yard in five minutes or so and carving fresh burrows wherever it feeds. Ecologists call it a keystone species of the savanna. Which effect of all that digging earns it the title?
answer: Its abandoned burrows shelter warthogs, hyenas, owls, and pythons
choices: Its abandoned burrows shelter warthogs, hyenas, owls, and pythons
Its digging exposes salt licks that the grazing herds visit
It eats enough termites to keep whole mounds from overrunning the plain
Its tunnels channel rainwater into pools the herds drink from
context: An aardvark can dig a yard of tunnel in roughly five minutes, and its main burrow can run 13 metres (43 feet) long. Abandoned burrows become shelters for a whole cast of animals: warthogs, hyenas, mongooses, hares, owls, pythons, lizards, ant-eating chats, and African wild dogs. Many would die in wildfire season without an aardvark hole to hide in, which makes the aardvark a keystone species. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aardvark

question: Camera traps in central Namibia watched seven kinds of mammal pass patches of the aardvark cucumber in a 2025 study. It is the only cucumber that pushes its fruit about a foot underground to ripen out of sight. What part did the aardvark play that no other mammal there could?
answer: It dug up the buried fruit and planted the seeds in its dung
choices: It dug up the buried fruit and planted the seeds in its dung
It pollinated the flowers and carried pollen to the next vine
It stored the melons in its burrow and let the seeds sprout there
It hid the melons in termite mounds, where the seeds sprouted
context: The aardvark cucumber grows its fruit about a foot underground and is the only cucumber species with buried fruit. The aardvark sniffs it out, digs it up for the moisture, and passes the seeds whole in its dung, replanting them with fertilizer. In the 2025 study (Johnson, Eichhoff & Midgley, Plants, People, Planet) the aardvark was the only one of seven mammals able to locate and reach the buried melons; porcupines ate the fruit only when it lay near the surface, and they destroyed the seeds. Source: https://botany.one/2025/07/unearthing-the-old-mystery-of-underground-melons/ ; https://news.mongabay.com/short-article/2025/02/study-confirms-that-ant-eating-aardvarks-have-a-craving-for-buried-melons/

question: A blue whale, longer than three school buses end to end, rolls up to the surface, and warm spray bursts from the blowhole on top of its head. Whales evolved from four-legged land mammals, and the blowhole is an ordinary body part that slowly moved there. Which body part is it?
answer: Its nostrils
choices: Its nostrils
Its gill slits
Its ear canals
Its throat pouch
context: Whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish: they breathe air with lungs and have no gills. Over evolution the nostrils migrated to the top of the head and became the blowhole, so the animal can breathe at the surface while the rest of the body stays underwater. Source: Wikipedia 'Blowhole (anatomy)'; Whale & Dolphin Conservation (us.whales.org).

question: A blue whale strains krill through comb-like plates in its mouth, so it is a baleen whale; a dolphin is a toothed whale. A whale-watcher can tell one kind from the other by its spout. How many blowholes does a baleen whale have?
answer: Two
choices: Two
One
Four
Three
context: Baleen whales (like the blue whale) have two blowholes; toothed whales (like dolphins) have just one. Neither has gills - both are air-breathing mammals. Source: Wikipedia 'Blowhole (anatomy)'; Whale & Dolphin Conservation (us.whales.org).

question: A long, brown, eel-shaped fish of the muddy swamps south of the Sahara looks like any other fish from the outside. Yet sealed in a tank of clean water, with no way to reach the surface, it will in time drown. What is strange about how it gets its oxygen?
answer: It has a true lung and gulps air
choices: It has a true lung and gulps air
It absorbs it through its scales
It filters it from mud, not water
It swallows air into its gut
context: The African lungfish (Protopterus) has a true lung and gulps air at the surface. It breathes air much as a land animal does instead of relying on gills like most fish, so with no access to air it drowns. Source: education.nationalgeographic.org 'West African lungfish'; Britannica 'lungfish'.

question: A betta, the Siamese fighting fish, lives in warm, stagnant puddles and rice paddies in Southeast Asia, where almost no oxygen dissolves in the still water. Other fish would soon suffocate there, but every few minutes the betta swims up, gulps air, and thrives. What organ in its head lets it breathe that way?
answer: A labyrinth organ that works like a lung
choices: A labyrinth organ that works like a lung
An extra set of high-efficiency gills
A swim bladder full of stored oxygen
A layer of oxygen-making algae on its skin
context: The betta has a labyrinth organ - a maze of folded, blood-rich tissue that works like a lung. That is why it gulps air at the surface and can survive warm, stagnant, low-oxygen water where other fish would suffocate. Source: Wikipedia 'Anabantoidei'; bettasource.com 'betta-labyrinth-organ'.

question: The electric eel of the Amazon stuns its prey with jolts of its own electricity, and it lives underwater on gills so feeble they are almost useless. It gets about 80 percent of the oxygen it needs from air gulped into a spongy lining in its mouth, and an eel kept from the surface drowns. About how often must it rise for a breath?
answer: About every two minutes
choices: About every two minutes
Once a day
Only when the water warms up
About once an hour
context: The electric eel is an obligate air-breather: it gets about 80% of its oxygen from air gulped into its mouth and must surface for a breath about every two minutes. Its gills are so poorly developed that trapped underwater with no air, it drowns. Source: Wikipedia 'Electric eel' ('About every two minutes, the fish takes in air through the mouth'); Johansen et al. 1968, Z. vergl. Physiol. 61:137 (doi 10.1007/BF00341112), free-swimming eels rarely went more than two minutes between breaths.

question: The great diving beetle, black and about the size of a fingernail, hunts tadpoles and small fish in ponds and slow streams. As it slips under, a bead of what looks like liquid silver clings to it and glints as it paddles along. The silver is not metal, and it is not decoration: it is what lets the beetle stay under so long. What is the silver bead?
answer: A trapped bubble of air held under its wing covers
choices: A trapped bubble of air held under its wing covers
A pocket of glowing bioluminescent slime
A polished shell that reflects like a mirror
A cloud of tiny gas-producing bacteria
context: When it dives, the diving beetle traps a shining silvery bubble of air beneath its hard wing covers (the elytra), held by water-repellent hairs. It carries its own scuba tank - the bubble looks like a bead of liquid silver underwater. Source: kqed.org 'Nature's scuba divers'; NC State (genent.cals.ncsu.edu).

question: The marine iguana of the Galapagos is the only lizard on Earth that feeds in the sea. It dives from black volcanic shores on a single breath to graze on algae growing on the rocks underwater. Like every lizard it is cold-blooded, and the cold Pacific drains its body heat fast. What must it do when it climbs back onto land?
answer: Bake on the black rocks in the sun
choices: Bake on the black rocks in the sun
Shiver until its muscles rewarm
Eat a second time to make heat
Dive again to escape the wind
context: The marine iguana dives around 15 meters (about 50 feet) on a single breath to graze underwater algae. Because it is cold-blooded, the cold ocean drains its heat, so afterward it must haul out onto black rocks to bake in the sun before it can move well again. Source: gogalapagos.com; everywherewild.com.

question: Europe's still ponds and slow streams are home to a small brown spider that spends almost its entire life underwater: resting, hunting insects, mating and laying its eggs, all beneath the surface. Yet like every spider, the diving-bell spider must breathe air, not water. How does it keep a supply of air down there?
answer: It builds a silk dome and fills it with air from the surface
choices: It builds a silk dome and fills it with air from the surface
It grows temporary gills for the underwater months
It breathes dissolved oxygen straight through its legs
It surfaces for every single breath, all day long
context: The diving bell spider (Argyroneta aquatica) builds a dome of silk anchored to water plants and fills it with air carried down from the surface - a shimmering underwater 'diving bell' where it lives its whole life below the water. Source: Wikipedia 'Diving bell spider'; wildlifetrusts.org 'water spider'.

question: When drought dries its swamp pool to cracked mud, a scaly African fish with long, snake-like fins burrows into the muck, curls back on itself and oozes so much mucus that a hard cocoon sets around its body. Sealed in the baked earth, it slows almost to a halt and waits for rain. Some have been dug up alive after how long in this buried, dried-out sleep?
answer: Up to four years
choices: Up to four years
About one week
Roughly two months
A single day
context: Sealed in its mud cocoon, the lungfish can wait out drought for months - and some have been documented surviving dried, buried, and dormant for up to four years, then waking and swimming away when the rains return. This months-long dormancy is called aestivation. Source: oxsci.org; the-scientist.com 'Lungfish cocoons are alive, sort of'.

question: Scientists call the diving beetle's silver bubble a physical gill, because it is more than a stored tank. As the beetle burns through the oxygen inside, the bubble partly refills on its own, so the beetle stays down far longer than the tank alone should allow. Where does that fresh oxygen come from?
answer: It diffuses IN from the surrounding water
choices: It diffuses IN from the surrounding water
The beetle's body chemically makes more
It leaks up from mud stirred below
Sunlight splits it out of the water
context: The bubble is a 'physical gill': as the beetle uses up the oxygen, more oxygen diffuses in from the surrounding water to refill it, so the water itself keeps topping up the tank. Field Museum scientist Crystal Maier: 'The relatively large surface area of the bubble allows it to exchange oxygen with the surrounding water.' Source: kqed.org 'Nature's scuba divers'.

question: The diving beetle's self-refilling bubble-gill sounds like an endless air supply, but it always fails and the beetle has to pop up for a fresh one. One gas the water can't wash away builds up inside the bubble faster than the oxygen can be replaced. Which gas ends the dive?
answer: Nitrogen
choices: Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide
Helium
Hydrogen
context: The bubble-gill has a catch: over time nitrogen builds up and concentrates in the bubble while oxygen is spent faster than the water can refill it. Eventually the beetle must release the old bubble and surface for a fresh one. Source: kqed.org 'Nature's scuba divers'.

question: Cuvier's beaked whale dives deeper and longer on one breath than any other mammal. One recorded dive lasted 3 hours and 42 minutes, all on a single lungful of air, beating even the sperm whale and the elephant seal. Roughly how deep did another of its record dives reach?
answer: Nearly 3 kilometers down
choices: Nearly 3 kilometers down
About 300 meters down
Around 50 meters down
Just past 1 kilometer down
context: Cuvier's beaked whale holds the mammal record: one dive lasted 222 minutes (3 hours 42 minutes) on a single breath, and another reached 2,992 meters - nearly 3 km, about 9,800 feet - beating even the sperm whale and elephant seal. Source: sciencenews.org 'Cuvier's beaked whale longest record dive'; Wikipedia.

question: A sperm whale dives a kilometer down on one breath, yet its lungs are small for its size, filling roughly 3 percent of the body cavity, far too little to hold the oxygen it needs. A clue sits in its dark flesh, stained by ten times the oxygen-binding protein packed into human tissue. Where does this whale actually stockpile the oxygen it dives on?
answer: Bound up inside its muscle
choices: Bound up inside its muscle
In an air sac behind the ribs
Dissolved through its blubber
In hollow, air-filled bones
context: The oxygen-binding protein is myoglobin - the same molecule that makes red meat red. Elite divers pack it into muscle roughly ten times denser than humans can, so about a third of the whale's whole-body oxygen store rides in muscle (with most of the rest in blood), and only a tiny fraction in the collapsing lungs. Mirceta et al. (2013, Science) found the trick: in deep divers the myoglobin molecule carries a strong positive electric charge on its surface, so the crowded copies repel each other like same-pole magnets instead of clumping and misfolding - a 'non-stick' charge that turns muscle itself into an oxygen tank, a molecular aqualung. Sources: Mirceta et al. 2013, Science (nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/130614-diving-mammal-myoglobin-oxygen-ocean-science); lung/oxygen-store fractions via uk.whales.org and orcaireland.org.

question: Scientists argued for a century over which living fish is the closest relative of every land animal with a backbone. Two rivals led the field: one survives droughts sealed in a mucus cocoon in the mud, and the other is a living fossil rediscovered in 1938. Which fish turned out to be the closer cousin?
answer: The lungfish
choices: The lungfish
The coelacanth
The bichir
The mudskipper
context: Whole-genome analysis put the question to rest: the lungfish, not the coelacanth, is the closest living relative of every land vertebrate - meaning the deepest fishy cousin of every four-legged animal, humans included, is the same air-gulping fish that survives droughts sealed in a mucus cocoon in the mud. The lungfish genome turned out to be a monster in its own right: the South American Lepidosiren paradoxa carries over 90 billion DNA base pairs, about thirty times the human genome and the largest of any animal yet sequenced, bloated by 'jumping genes' copying themselves. Sources: Amemiya et al. 2013, Nature 496:311 (nature.com/articles/nature12027) and Brinkmann/Takezaki nuclear-gene analyses; genome size via Schartl et al. 2024, Nature (uni-wuerzburg.de).

question: Out over the stormy Southern Ocean glides the wandering albatross, a huge white seabird that can ride the winds around the globe for weeks without ever flapping. From tip to tip its wingspan beats that of every other bird alive today. Roughly how wide is that span?
answer: About 11 to 12 feet
choices: About 11 to 12 feet
About 4 to 5 feet
About 20 to 22 feet
About 6 to 7 feet
context: The wandering albatross has the longest wingspan of any living bird, up to about 11-12 feet (3.5 m), with the largest ever recorded at 3.7 m (12.1 ft). Source: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution / National Geographic.

question: Gliding just above the waves, a wandering albatross hangs in the wind for hours over the open Southern Ocean without a single flap. An ordinary flying bird tires because its muscles must keep its wings held out, but a special tendon in the albatross's shoulder does that job for it. What does the tendon do?
answer: Locking the wing open with no muscle effort
choices: Locking the wing open with no muscle effort
Pumping warm blood into the wingtips
Snapping the wing shut between gusts
Storing fat to burn during the glide
context: A tendon in the albatross's shoulder mechanically locks the wing open in the extended position, so no muscle effort is needed to hold it out and the bird can glide for hours. Source: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, 'New Research Unlocks Clues About the Iconic Flight of the Wandering Albatross.'

question: The wind alone fuels a wandering albatross as it crosses whole oceans almost without flapping its enormous wings. Right at the surface, friction with the waves slows the wind, while a few dozen meters higher it races much faster, and the bird exploits that difference. What does an albatross physically do to steal energy from the wind?
answer: Climbs into the fast upper air, then dives into the slow surface air
choices: Climbs into the fast upper air, then dives into the slow surface air
Beats its wings hard only on the downwind stretches
Rides warm columns of air spiraling up off the sea
Coasts down the sloping face of each swell like a hill
context: Wind moves faster higher up and slower right at the sea surface. The albatross repeatedly climbs into the faster upper air and dives back into the slower air near the waves, harvesting energy from that difference over and over. This technique is called dynamic soaring. Source: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution; National Geographic, 'Albatross's Effortless Flight Decoded.'

question: Every bite of squid or small fish that a wandering albatross snatches from the open ocean comes with a gulp of seawater. Most animals that drank that much salt would die of salt poisoning within a day, but the albatross has a special gland tucked just above each eye that deals with the overload. What does that gland do with all the extra salt?
answer: Dripping concentrated brine out its nostrils
choices: Dripping concentrated brine out its nostrils
Storing the salt in hollow leg bones
Sweating it out through the feet
Coughing up salt crystals in a pellet
context: A special salt gland above the eyes concentrates the excess salt into a briny solution that drips out through the bird's tube-shaped nostrils and down its beak. Albatrosses belong to a group called 'tubenoses' named for exactly these tube-like nostrils. Source: Audubon, 'How Do Seabirds Drink Salt Water?'; Cordell Bank National Marine Sanctuary (NOAA).

question: Out hunting for food, a wandering albatross can cross the open sea day after day, barely flapping its wings and burning almost no energy as it rides the wind. In a single day of foraging, roughly how far can one bird travel?
answer: About 950 km
choices: About 950 km
About 120 km
About 300 km
About 60 km
context: A foraging wandering albatross can cover roughly 950 km (about 590 miles) in a single day, averaging around 40 km/h, and sustain it for days while spending almost no energy thanks to dynamic soaring. Source: British Antarctic Survey tracking data; WHOI research.

question: Croxall's team tagged grey-headed albatrosses, smaller cousins of the wandering albatross, on their nesting island of South Georgia and followed them between breeding seasons. Some flew right around the world over the Southern Ocean without touching land. How long did the fastest full circuit take?
answer: Just 46 days
choices: Just 46 days
Just over a year
Nearly 200 days
About one week
context: Croxall and colleagues (Science, 2005) tracked grey-headed albatrosses from South Georgia through the months between breeding seasons. Several circled the globe, some more than once, and the fastest made the trip, at least 22,000 km, in just 46 days. Source: Croxall et al. 2005, 'Global circumnavigations: tracking year-round ranges of nonbreeding albatrosses,' Science; https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna6822563

question: Biologists banded a female Laysan albatross, a smaller Pacific cousin of the wandering albatross, on Midway Atoll west of Hawaii in 1956, and they nicknamed her Wisdom. Nearly seventy years later she was still alive, still returning to the same atoll to raise chicks. What record does Wisdom hold?
answer: Oldest known wild bird in the world
choices: Oldest known wild bird in the world
Longest single migration ever tracked
Largest clutch ever laid by a seabird
Fastest bird over open water
context: Wisdom was first banded, as #Z333, by the biologist Chandler Robbins on Midway in 1956, when she was already thought to be about five years old. She was at least 74 in 2025, when she was seen back on Midway with her new mate, which makes her the oldest known wild bird in the world. She has hatched an estimated 30 or more chicks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisdom_(albatross); Grokipedia 'Wisdom (albatross)'.

question: A pair of wandering albatrosses mates for life, yet once their chick can fend for itself the two split up and roam the empty Southern Ocean alone for many months, hunting squid far apart. When at last both birds are back at the same nest site on a windswept island, they must recognize each other after all that time. What do the two birds do when they reunite?
answer: Perform an elaborate greeting dance
choices: Perform an elaborate greeting dance
Fight to win back the nest site
Feed each other regurgitated squid
Rebuild the nest from scratch
context: Albatrosses mate for life, and a reunited pair performs an elaborate greeting dance: sky-pointing, wing-spreading, and loud clucking calls. Source: KQED Science, 'Love Is an Albatross'; Marine Ornithology (courtship behaviour of the wandering albatross).

question: On a windswept island in the freezing Southern Ocean, a pair of wandering albatrosses lays a single egg on a mound of grass. The chick that hatches then sits in that nest, growing its enormous flight feathers, far longer than the young of nearly any other bird. About how long does it wait before its first flight?
answer: Around 278 days
choices: Around 278 days
Around 60 days
Around 120 days
Around 400 days
context: The wandering albatross has the longest incubation of any bird (about 78 days), and its single fluffy chick then sits in the nest for around 278 days, nearly nine months, before it can fly. Because raising one chick takes so long, a pair breeds only every other year. Source: Birdfact; Animal Diversity Web (Diomedea exulans).

question: A young wandering albatross that survives to adulthood can cruise the Southern Ocean decade after decade, returning to the same windswept nesting island every other year to raise a single chick with its lifelong mate. Out in the wild, about how long can a wandering albatross live?
answer: 50 to 60 years or more
choices: 50 to 60 years or more
10 to 15 years
25 to 30 years
Over 100 years
context: The albatross can live 50 to 60 years or more in the wild, one of the longest-lived of all birds. Source: Cornell Lab / British Antarctic Survey; Audubon.

question: Patches of squid and krill lie scattered across hundreds of miles of empty ocean, where nothing shows from the air above, and a wandering albatross must find them. When Gabrielle Nevitt's team tracked the birds by GPS in 2008, they caught them zig-zagging upwind toward their prey, tacking back and forth like a sailboat. What are the birds following?
answer: A chemical scent the sea releases where plankton are being grazed
choices: A chemical scent the sea releases where plankton are being grazed
The flash of sunlight glinting off shoals of fish near the surface
The low rumble that feeding whales send through the water
A drop in air pressure that marks where storms churn up prey
context: When krill graze on phytoplankton, the plankton release dimethyl sulfide (DMS) - the 'ocean' smell. The albatross catches this scent on the wind and works upwind in a zig-zag to the patchy prey. When Gabrielle Nevitt's team GPS-tagged 19 wandering albatrosses over the southern Indian Ocean, these upwind turning approaches accounted for 37% of daytime prey captures and 47% of nighttime captures - the first hard evidence that these seabirds smell their way to food across the open sea. Source: Nevitt, Losekoot & Weimerskirch 2008, 'Evidence for olfactory search in wandering albatross, Diomedea exulans,' PNAS 105(12); https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0709047105

question: Giant seabirds with 21-foot wingspans left their bones in the rocks of Antarctica, and their leg and foot bones matched an albatross's so closely that for decades they were filed as the largest albatrosses that ever lived. A closer look at their jaws overturned that. What were they really?
answer: A separate seabird lineage whose beaks bristled with tooth-like bony spikes
choices: A separate seabird lineage whose beaks bristled with tooth-like bony spikes
An early branch of the albatross family that later shrank down to modern sizes
A giant petrel cousin that lost the power of flight and dived for its food
A flightless diving bird convergent on penguins of the northern seas
context: The giant 'albatrosses' were pelagornithids - the 'bony-toothed' or pseudotooth birds, a lineage whose jaws bore tooth-like bony spikes. Convergent evolution had made their leg and foot bones nearly identical to an albatross, which is what fooled taxonomists. True fossil albatrosses were in fact modest: Aldiomedes angustirostris, from an almost-complete ~3-million-year-old Pliocene skull in New Zealand's Tangahoe Formation, reached only about 90% the size of today's smallest living albatross and had a slender, fish-eating beak. Sources: Berkeley News 2020, 'Antarctica yields oldest fossils of giant birds with 21-foot wingspans' (https://news.berkeley.edu/2020/10/27/antarctica-yields-oldest-fossils-of-giant-birds); Mayr & Tennyson 2019, Ibis (https://phys.org/news/2019-07-scientists-albatross-skull-pliocene-epoch.html)

question: A huge female sea turtle heaves herself out of the surf late at night and up a moonlit tropical beach. With her back flippers she digs a deep pit in the sand, lays roughly a hundred eggs and packs sand back over them to hide them from crabs and raccoons. What does she do once the eggs are buried?
answer: Drags herself back to the ocean and leaves forever
choices: Drags herself back to the ocean and leaves forever
Coils around the nest and guards it until they hatch
Fans cool water over the buried eggs each night
Carries the eggs one by one into a tidal pool
context: A female sea turtle digs a pit, lays roughly 80 to 120 eggs (up to about 200), buries them, and drags herself back to the ocean forever. The hatchlings dig themselves out weeks later and race to the sea with no parent present. This is the 'none' end of the spectrum. Source: NOAA Ocean Service, 'How do sea turtles hatch?'; FWC Sea Turtle FAQ.

question: A female giant Pacific octopus slips into a rocky den in the cold deep waters of the North Pacific to spawn, her arms sometimes spanning sixteen feet. She hangs tens of thousands of tiny rice-grain eggs from the ceiling in long, draping strands, then settles in to guard and clean them for roughly six months. What does she do about eating all that time?
answer: Nothing — she never eats, living on her own body fat
choices: Nothing — she never eats, living on her own body fat
Slips out briefly each night to snatch a passing crab
Nibbles the weakest eggs to fuel guarding the rest
Filters plankton from the water she blows over them
context: For roughly six months the mother giant Pacific octopus (Enteroctopus dofleini) never eats. She continuously blows water over her eggs and grooms off algae, living on her own body fat, and dies soon after the eggs hatch. The all-in extreme. Source: Wikipedia, Giant Pacific octopus.

question: A female ocean sunfish, Mola mola, drifts through open water and does the opposite of a guarding octopus mother: she gives her young no care at all and bets everything on sheer numbers. In a single spawning, how many eggs can she release?
answer: Up to about 300 million
choices: Up to about 300 million
Up to about 30 million
Up to about 3 million
Up to about 300,000
context: The female ocean sunfish (Mola mola) can release up to 300 million eggs at a time, more than any other known vertebrate, each only about 0.13 cm across, and gives no care at all. Nearly all are eaten; a few survive. Source: Wikipedia, Ocean sunfish; Animal Diversity Web, Mola mola.

question: A mother cichlid hovers over a cloud of her tiny newborn fry just above the sand of one of Africa's great freshwater lakes. When she spots a predator gliding toward them, the whole brood vanishes in a single second, darting into one hiding place no enemy can reach. Where do the fry hide?
answer: Back inside her own mouth
choices: Back inside her own mouth
Under a flat rock she guards
Under their father's fins
Beneath a raft of algae
context: In many mouthbrooding cichlids the mother scoops her fertilized eggs into her mouth and holds them — and later the hatched fry — for up to about two weeks, not eating the whole time, letting them dart back into her mouth when danger threatens. Source: Wikipedia, Mouthbrooder; Natural History Museum.

question: A male emperor penguin has kept the pair's single egg warm through two months of Antarctic winter while his mate hunted at sea. Now, as the polar sun returns, she waddles back across the ice fat and full of fish, and the two must pass the egg between them in a frantic few seconds. If it slips loose and lies bare on the ice for more than about two minutes, what happens to it?
answer: The embryo inside freezes and dies
choices: The embryo inside freezes and dies
The parents can no longer tell it apart from others
The shell cracks under the pressure of the wind
A skua swoops in and steals it away
context: When the female passes the egg to the male, they must complete the hand-off in seconds; if the egg is exposed to the polar air for more than about two minutes, the embryo freezes and dies. Source: penguinehub.com; Live Science, 'How Do Emperor Penguin Dads Stop Their Eggs From Freezing?'

question: A male cardinalfish, a small, big-eyed reef fish of tropical seas, scoops the whole clutch into his mouth as soon as the female lays her eggs and holds it there for two weeks or more. He cannot hunt or eat while that mass of eggs fills his jaws. Every two to three minutes he opens his mouth wide in what looks like a yawn. Why does the father yawn?
answer: To churn and re-aerate the eggs with fresh water
choices: To churn and re-aerate the eggs with fresh water
To count and reposition any egg that slipped loose
To warn off rivals with a threatening gape
To swallow the weakest eggs and thin the brood
context: In cardinalfish it is the father who mouthbroods: he holds the egg mass and every two to three minutes opens his jaws to churn and re-aerate the eggs, unable to feed the whole time. Source: Underwater Photography Guide, Mouthbrooding Cardinalfish; Wikipedia, Mouthbrooder.

question: A mother sea turtle lays about a hundred eggs in a pit on a moonlit beach, covers them and returns to the sea, never meeting her babies. Over her lifetime she may lay thousands of eggs this way, a bet that pays only in bulk. Of every 1,000 hatchlings, about how many reach adulthood?
answer: Around 1
choices: Around 1
Around 100
Around 500
Around 900
context: Only about 1 in 1,000 sea turtle hatchlings survives to adulthood; the 'make thousands, tend none' bet works only because so many are laid. Source: Loggerhead Marinelife Center; SEE Turtles life cycle.

question: The air around an emperor penguin father sits near -40°C through the Antarctic winter, yet he keeps his egg warm, and the fathers pack into tight huddles to defend their eggs. The egg is not just tucked under a flap of skin: it presses against one particular thing on his body. What keeps the egg alive?
answer: A bare, blood-rich patch of belly skin held near body heat
choices: A bare, blood-rich patch of belly skin held near body heat
A thick cushion of down feathers wrapped over the shell
A pouch of stored fat the father presses against the shell
A layer of warm oil the father smears across the shell
context: That featherless, blood-rich patch of skin is the brood patch, kept at about 36-37C -- a gap of roughly 75-80C over the -40C air outside. The father cannot feed for the whole two-month incubation, so the birds huddle together, with temperatures deep in the center of a huddle reaching about 37C, and shuffle positions so each takes a turn out of the wind. Source: Gilbert et al. (2006), 'Body temperature changes induced by huddling in breeding male emperor penguins,' Am. J. Physiology (journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajpregu.00912.2005).

question: An electric eel longer than a person glides through a muddy Amazon river, carrying a jolt that can knock a wading horse off its feet. For all its name, which two familiar fish are its closest cousins?
answer: Catfish and carp
choices: Catfish and carp
Moray and conger
Salmon and trout
Pike and perch
context: Despite the name, the electric eel (order Gymnotiformes) is a knifefish, far closer to catfish and carp than to true eels like the moray. Source: Wikipedia, Electric eel; Mongabay 2019.

question: Thousands of flat cells sit stacked end to end down each side of an electric eel's body, wired like batteries in a row, as it hunts the murky Amazon. Each one is a remodeled version of an ordinary kind of cell. Which kind of cell does the eel rebuild into these living batteries?
answer: A muscle cell
choices: A muscle cell
A nerve cell
A skin cell
A fat cell
context: These stacked cells, called electrocytes, are modified muscle cells. Roughly 6,000 sit end-to-end in a stack like batteries wired in series, with about 35 stacks in parallel down each side of the eel's long body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_eel

question: Like the electric eel, a torpedo ray fights with an electric jolt of its own, and the great torpedo can reach about 220 volts, enough to floor a person. Yet the ray stores its charge in a completely different place from the eel's long body. Where does the torpedo ray keep its two electric organs?
answer: Inside its broad pectoral 'wings'
choices: Inside its broad pectoral 'wings'
Coiled inside its whip-like tail
Behind its eyes in its skull
Lining the roof of its mouth
context: The torpedo ray makes its charge in two large kidney-shaped organs set inside its flat pectoral fins, each packed with hundreds to over a thousand electrocytes; the great torpedo (Torpedo nobiliana) can hit ~220 volts, enough to knock down a person. Source: Elasmo-research; Wikipedia, Electric organ (fish).

question: Volta's electric eel can fire a shock of more than 500 volts, far above a household wall socket. Yet the current in a full discharge peaks near just 1 amp, a tenth of what a wall outlet carries. What makes the eel's blast so dangerous?
answer: The high voltage drives current across a body in a rapid volley of pulses
choices: The high voltage drives current across a body in a rapid volley of pulses
It sustains one enormous unbroken current for several full seconds
It heats the surrounding water until the prey is scalded and stunned
It magnetizes the prey so later pulses strike with far more force
context: The eel's weapon is high VOLTAGE but low CURRENT: a full discharge peaks near ~1 ampere at ~500 volts, roughly 500 watts, yet only about a tenth the amperage of a household wall outlet (10-20 A). The danger is the high voltage driving that current across a body, delivered in bursts of up to ~500 pulses per second (500 Hz), each lasting only ~2 milliseconds. It's the voltage and the rapid volley, not a huge sustained current. Source: Wikipedia 'Electric eel' (~1 ampere at 500 V; up to 500 Hz; ~2 ms pulses) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_eel ; power/amperage comparison corroborated by Scientific American and a Fluke case study.

question: An elephantfish of African rivers and an electric eel of the Amazon both build electric organs, though their lineages split long before either had one. Such organs evolved at least six separate times in fishes. What did a 2014 study comparing the genes of three unrelated electric lineages find about how each built its organ?
answer: They drew on a similar set of genes and developmental pathways
choices: They drew on a similar set of genes and developmental pathways
They each borrowed the needed genes from prey they had eaten
Each invented its own unrelated genetic recipe from scratch
They pooled their genes by interbreeding across the lineages
context: The muscle-built electric organ is one of evolution's favorite reruns: it evolved independently at least six times in fishes. Gallant, Traeger and colleagues (Science, 2014) assembled the first electric-eel genome and compared electric organ with muscle in three lineages that evolved electric organs on their own, and found that each had leveraged similar transcription factors and developmental and cellular pathways to turn muscle into electrocytes. Source: Gallant et al. 2014, 'Genomic basis for the convergent evolution of electric organs,' Science 344:1522, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24970089/

question: A low, wide, four-legged plant-eater walked across ancient North America. Its whole back was covered in bony armor, and it stayed low to the ground like a tank. Which armored dinosaur was this?
answer: Ankylosaurus
choices: Ankylosaurus
Stegosaurus
Triceratops
Iguanodon
context: Ankylosaurus was the classic armored tank of the dinosaur world: low, broad, four-legged, and plated head to tail in bony armor as it grazed the Late Cretaceous of North America. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaurus).

question: On short, stumpy legs, Ankylosaurus plodded across western North America, its back plated in bony armor and its tail ending in a huge bony club. Nose to tail-tip, this squat plant-eater stretched 6 to 8 meters, roughly a school bus. How much did it weigh?
answer: As much as an elephant, 5 to 8 tonnes
choices: As much as an elephant, 5 to 8 tonnes
As much as a cow, under 1 tonne
As much as a blue whale, over 100 tonnes
As much as a rhino, about 2 tonnes
context: At 6 to 8 meters (20 to 26 feet) long and perhaps 5 to 8 tonnes, Ankylosaurus carried roughly an elephant's weight in body plus bony armor. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (6-8 m long, 4.8-8 t).

question: Bony plates sat right in the skin of Ankylosaurus as it lumbered across the Late Cretaceous plains of North America, from tiny pebble-sized knobs to armored tiles more than a foot long. It also carried one guard that almost no other dinosaur is known to have shared. Which surprising body part was armored too?
answer: Its eyes, shielded by bony eyelids
choices: Its eyes, shielded by bony eyelids
Its throat, sheathed in bony scutes
Its snout tip, capped with a bony guard
Its cheeks, plated in bony tiles
context: Ankylosaurus had bony eyelids formed from the palpebral bones, plates of bone that could shield the eyes, a protection almost no other dinosaur is known to have had. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (palpebral bones over the eyes); AMNH.

question: Ankylosaurus grazed its way across ancient North America, a walking fortress covered in bony plates from head to tail. Yet one region of its body carried no armor at all, and any predator that could reach that spot had a real chance of killing it. Which part of Ankylosaurus went bare?
answer: Its belly
choices: Its belly
Its snout
Its feet
Its throat
context: Ankylosaurus was armored on top but bare underneath, so it hugged the ground to keep that soft belly away from a predator's jaws. Its species name magniventris means 'great belly.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (magniventris = 'great belly'); AMNH.

question: At the end of its long, heavy tail, Ankylosaurus carried a knob of bone the size of a beach ball. When paleontologists studied its skeleton, they noticed something unusual about the last seven bones of that tail. What did they find?
answer: Fused into a single stiff handle
choices: Fused into a single stiff handle
Hollowed out to lighten the swing
Studded with backward-pointing spikes
Split into two independent lobes
context: The last seven tail vertebrae fused into a stiff handle, with knobs of bony armor welded over the tip; one known club measured 60 cm long and 49 cm wide. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (tail club 60 cm long, 49 cm wide; last seven caudal vertebrae form the handle).

question: Ankylosaurus carried a very wide skull tipped with a broad, flat beak, roughly the shape of a shovel rather than a deer's narrow, pointed snout. From that beak, paleontologists work out how the dinosaur most likely fed. How did Ankylosaurus eat?
answer: By cropping low plants without picking favorites
choices: By cropping low plants without picking favorites
By stripping tall trees of their top branches
By digging up roots with its clawed feet
By ambushing and swallowing small animals
context: Its wide, low skull ended in a beak used to crop low-growing ferns and shrubs, feeding by non-selective low browsing rather than picking choice leaves. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ankylosaurus' (wide low skull, beak for non-selective low-browse cropping).

question: In Euoplocephalus, a relative of Ankylosaurus, the airway inside the snout was no straight tube but a crazy-straw of loops and twists, running about 80 centimeters folded inside the skull. Researchers modeling its airflow found that the coiled passage did a specific job. What did all that looping accomplish?
answer: Recovering breath heat and cooling blood to the brain
choices: Recovering breath heat and cooling blood to the brain
Amplifying its calls into deep booming honks
Storing air for long underwater dives
Filtering out dust before it reached the lungs
context: In the relative Euoplocephalus the airway ran about 808 mm folded inside the snout and worked like a heat exchanger, recovering up to 84% of a breath's heat and cooling blood before it reached the small brain. Source: Bourke, Porter & Witmer (2018), 'Convoluted nasal passages function as efficient heat exchangers in ankylosaurs,' PLOS ONE.

question: Arbour and Snively modeled the blows of ankylosaur tail clubs to test a famous claim: that one swing could shatter the leg of a T. rex. The bone-breaking blow turned out to be real, but not something every ankylosaur could deliver. Which animals actually had the force to break a predator's bone?
answer: Only the biggest-clubbed adults, whose knobs cleared bone strength tenfold
choices: Only the biggest-clubbed adults, whose knobs cleared bone strength tenfold
Any adult, since the fused handle always multiplied the swing enough
Only the fastest swingers, whose whip-quick tails outran the bone limit
Only the oldest, whose brittle knobs cracked but still delivered the blow
context: In their finite-element study, Arbour and Snively found that only large knobs (wider than about 500 mm) generated bone-breaking force: roughly 364 to 718 MPa of impact stress, an order of magnitude past the ~64 to 84 MPa shear strength of cortical bone. Average knobs (48 to 101 MPa) and small knobs (29 to 56 MPa) fell short. So the leg-shattering feat was real, but it belonged to the biggest-clubbed adults, not to every ankylosaur. Source: Arbour & Snively 2009, PLOS ONE, 'Estimating Impact Forces of Tail Club Strikes by Ankylosaurid Dinosaurs' -- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2726940/

question: For an animal the size of an elephant, Ankylosaurus had almost comically tiny teeth, only millimeters tall, and jaws too weak to grind up the ferns it swallowed nearly whole. Its species name, magniventris, points to how it got nutrients from food it barely chewed. What did the work its teeth could not?
answer: Gut microbes fermenting the unchewed plants in a huge chambered belly
choices: Gut microbes fermenting the unchewed plants in a huge chambered belly
A gizzard of swallowed stones grinding the plants into paste
Acid strong enough to dissolve whole ferns before they reached the gut
A second row of hidden grinding teeth set deep in the throat
context: Adult Ankylosaurus teeth were only a few millimeters tall (juvenile teeth measured just 3.2 to 3.3 mm), and its jaws had low mechanical advantage, so it barely chewed. Its name magniventris means 'great belly,' and paleontologists infer it relied on hindgut fermentation in a huge, broad-ribbed gut, much like modern herbivorous lizards with enlarged, chambered colons: gut microbes, not teeth, broke down the tough unchewed plants. Source: Carpenter 2004 redescription and Arbour & Mallon 2017 (FACETS), via Wikipedia 'Ankylosaurus' -- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaurus

question: Anomalocaris prowled the Cambrian seas about 500 million years ago, long before dinosaurs or sharks, when most animals around it were no longer than a finger. Its squashed fossils turn up in the Burgess Shale of British Columbia, Canada. How long could its body grow?
answer: Up to about 38 centimeters
choices: Up to about 38 centimeters
Up to about 12 centimeters
Up to about 1.5 meters
Up to about 4 meters
context: Anomalocaris canadensis is estimated at about 34 to 38 cm long, not counting its grasping arms and tail fan; an older estimate of up to 1 meter is now thought unlikely. Most Cambrian animals were only a few centimeters long, so it was one of the giants of its world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomalocaris

question: A 500-million-year-old Anomalocaris lies flattened in the Burgess Shale of Canada, two spiny grasping arms at the front of its head and a round mouth ringed with plates. Down each side of its long body runs a row of sixteen matching structures, from just behind the head all the way to the tail. What were these sixteen structures on each side?
answer: Flexible flaps
choices: Flexible flaps
Armored plates
Suction discs
Jointed paddle-legs
context: Anomalocaris swam by rippling rows of flexible flaps down both sides of its body. One specimen shows sixteen lateral flaps whose overlapping, wave-like undulations pushed it through the open water, with a three-part tail fan for sharp turns while chasing prey. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale; Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomalocaris).

question: Anomalocaris reached out with two jointed grabbing limbs, each about fourteen segments long, that curled from the front of its head to seize prey and sweep it back toward its mouth. It was one of the largest hunters of the Cambrian seas, half a billion years ago. What lined the inner edge of those two front limbs?
answer: Rows of trident-like spikes
choices: Rows of trident-like spikes
A fringe of fine filtering hairs
A row of glowing light organs
Bands of sticky suction cups
context: In front of its mouth Anomalocaris had two spiny grasping arms (frontal appendages), jointed limbs of about fourteen segments each, lined with trident-like spikes it used to seize and hold prey and sweep it toward its mouth. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale (burgess-shale.rom.on.ca/fossils/anomalocaris-canadensis/).

question: A rare fossil of a whole Anomalocaris eye, pulled from the shale of South Australia in 2011, came out still perfectly preserved. When scientists counted the lenses packed onto that single eye, they realized its vision had already been as sharp as a modern dragonfly's half a billion years ago. Roughly how many lenses did that one eye hold?
answer: About 16,000
choices: About 16,000
About 160
About 8
About 40
context: Anomalocaris had big compound eyes on stalks with astonishingly sharp vision: a fossil eye from the Emu Bay Shale of Australia holds at least 16,000 tiny lenses, rivaling a modern dragonfly and making it one of the keenest-sighted hunters of its time. Source: Paterson et al. 2011, 'Acute vision in the giant Cambrian predator Anomalocaris', Nature 480:237-240 (nature.com/articles/nature10689).

question: A team of scientists built a digital model of an Anomalocaris grasping arm in 2023 and loaded it with stress, testing the century-old picture of the animal as a terror that pried open trilobites. Against mineralized armor, the thin gripping spines bent and snapped. What did the test conclude those arms were actually built to catch?
answer: Soft-bodied swimmers
choices: Soft-bodied swimmers
Armored trilobites
Buried burrowers
Shelled brachiopods
context: The old reputation wasn't baseless: Cameron Nedin's 1999 paper pointed to real clues, Cambrian trilobites with round and W-shaped healed bite wounds and large fossil fecal pellets stuffed with crushed shell, and proposed Anomalocaris rocked a trilobite back and forth in its mouth until the armor failed. But Bicknell et al. (2023, Proc. R. Soc. B 290:20230638) ran finite-element analysis on a 3D model of the frontal appendage and found the ventral gripping spines (endites) would suffer high stress and bend or break against a hard trilobite shell. With an oral cone of pliable, weakly hardened plates that could not close fully, the study concluded Anomalocaris canadensis was an agile open-water hunter of soft-bodied swimming prey, not a shell-crusher. Whether some radiodonts still tackled hard prey remains debated. Source: Bicknell et al. 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10320336/ ; Nedin 1999, Geology 27:987-990.

question: Anomalocaris hunted the Cambrian seas with stalked compound eyes, the kind that mark many of its cousins the arthropods. Yet one hallmark of every living arthropod, from crab to beetle, never appears anywhere on its body, which is why it sits just outside them. What did it never grow?
answer: Jointed trunk limbs
choices: Jointed trunk limbs
Sensory antennae
Grinding jaw plates
Paired book gills
context: Anomalocaris belongs to the extinct order Radiodonta, an early-diverging branch just outside the crown-group arthropods. It shows arthropod hallmarks such as stalked compound eyes and segmented frontal appendages, but lacks the defining feature of modern arthropods: jointed, two-branched (biramous) walking and swimming trunk limbs. Instead of legs, its trunk bore only soft, flexible swimming flaps with feathery setal blades (gills) above them. It likewise had no true sensory antennae, no chewing jaws (its disk-like oral cone was a soft suction mouth that couldn't bite hard), and no book gills. That has-it/lacks-it mix is exactly why paleontologists prize it as a snapshot of the arthropod body plan mid-assembly during the Cambrian explosion. Source: Wikipedia 'Anomalocaris' (Radiodonta lacking biramous trunk limbs; setal-blade gills; soft suction oral cone); Frontiers in Earth Science 2023 review, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/earth-science/articles/10.3389/feart.2023.1160285/full

question: Around Antarctica, a crocodile icefish glides through water so cold that most fish would die there. It is one of the very few backboned animals known to live as an adult with no hemoglobin, and its blood holds few red cells or none. What does that blood look like when a scientist draws a sample?
answer: Clear and white
choices: Clear and white
Bright red
Deep blue
Dark green
context: Crocodile icefishes (family Channichthyidae) live their adult lives without hemoglobin, the pigment that makes blood red; they were the only backboned animals known to do so until a 2025 study found the same loss in some Asian noodlefishes. Red blood cells are usually absent from icefish blood, or rare and defunct, so it runs clear and translucent white. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channichthyidae ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Channichthyidae ; https://news.northeastern.edu/2026/01/01/asian-noodlefish-red-blood-cells/

question: A notothenioid fish cruises the Antarctic sea at about minus 1.9°C, colder than the point where an ordinary fish's blood would freeze into slush. Its kin make up most of the fish in those icy waters, and none of them turns solid. When a tiny ice crystal sneaks into its blood, what do its antifreeze proteins do to it?
answer: Grip it so it can't grow
choices: Grip it so it can't grow
Melt it into water
Push it out through the gills
Wrap it in fat
context: These antifreeze glycoproteins latch onto any tiny ice crystal that gets inside and stop it from growing, so ice can't spread through the fish. Source: PMC8851421, 'Antifreeze Proteins: A Tale of Evolution'; PNAS 94(8):3811 (DeVries lab).

question: A little brown wood frog lies under the Canadian leaf litter through January with everything stopped: no heartbeat, no breath, no brain activity, its whole body frozen into a lump of ice for months. In April the warming soil finally thaws its blood, and the frog stirs back to life. Once thawed, roughly how long does it take to be hopping around and behaving normally again?
answer: About one day
choices: About one day
About a minute
About 10 days
About 10 weeks
context: The heart starts beating again even before the frog has fully thawed, but its leg muscles take more than five hours to regain some function, and it needs up to about a day to show normal posture and coordinated movement. Source: Wisconsin Wetlands Association, 'The Symphony of Spring' (https://www.wisconsinwetlands.org/updates/the-symphony-of-spring/); Storey Lab, wood frog freeze tolerance.

question: A fly larva spends the winter inside a round swelling on a goldenrod stem, with only a thin wall of plant tissue between it and the frost. In autumn it loads its body with glycerol, then adds a second protectant as the cold deepens. What do those chemicals let it do?
answer: Freeze solid and thaw again, over and over
choices: Freeze solid and thaw again, over and over
Stay liquid far below zero all winter
Burn sugar to keep its body warm
Dry out like a seed until spring
context: The goldenrod gall fly larva (Eurosta solidaginis) is freeze-tolerant: rather than staying liquid, it lets its body freeze, protected first by glycerol and then by sorbitol, surviving frozen down to about minus 40 C and thawing and refreezing all winter. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurosta_solidaginis ; Storey Lab, 'Goldenrod gall fly'; JEB 221(15):jeb177956.

question: Antifreeze proteins keep a notothenioid fish from freezing all its life in the icy seas around Antarctica. Evolution built that defense and never built it an off switch. What strange lifelong price does the fish pay for carrying that antifreeze?
answer: The trapped ice never melts, even in summer-warm water
choices: The trapped ice never melts, even in summer-warm water
The trapped ice slowly crowds and starves its cells
The thin blood can no longer carry any oxygen
The eggs it lays will not survive open water
context: The proteins grip the ice so tightly that trapped crystals refuse to melt even when summer sea-water warms above their normal melting point, so the fish can carry damaging ice inside its body for its whole life. Source: Cziko et al., PNAS 111(40):14583 (2014), 'Antifreeze protein-induced superheating of ice inside Antarctic notothenioid fishes'.

question: An icefish swims and hunts through the Antarctic seas with no hemoglobin, the red protein that lets most animals' blood carry oxygen, so each drop of its blood carries very little. Evolution made up for it by supersizing one organ far beyond a normal fish's. Which organ did the icefish enlarge?
answer: Its heart
choices: Its heart
Its liver
Its brain
Its stomach
context: The icefish grew an oversized heart that pumps four to five times more blood per body weight than a normal fish, plus up to about four times the blood volume and extra-wide vessels, so a large amount of thin, clear blood moves fast at low pressure. Source: Scientific American; Spacedaily.

question: Biologists tracing the gene behind the antifreeze of Antarctic notothenioid fish in 1997 found that it was not invented from scratch. It had been rebuilt from a gene the fish already carried for a completely different job. What was that borrowed gene originally for?
answer: A digestive enzyme that breaks down food in the gut
choices: A digestive enzyme that breaks down food in the gut
A tough structural protein that builds the scales
A sensor protein that detects water pressure
An oxygen-storing protein packed in the muscle
context: One of biology's clearest cases of a brand-new gene born from an old one. Chen, DeVries & Cheng (PNAS 94:3811, 1997) showed the antifreeze glycoprotein gene was assembled from a pancreatic trypsinogen gene -- a digestive-enzyme gene -- by keeping the old gene's front and back ends and copying a tiny nine-letter 'Thr-Ala-Ala' snippet over and over to grow the long ice-gripping backbone. They called it the first clear example of an old protein gene spawning an entirely new protein with a new function. The switch happened only about 5-14 million years ago, right when the Antarctic Ocean first froze. Source: Chen, DeVries & Cheng, 'Evolution of antifreeze glycoprotein gene from a trypsinogen gene in Antarctic notothenioid fish,' PNAS 94:3811 (1997) -- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC20523/

question: A crocodile icefish swims right beside its red-blooded cousins in the same Antarctic water, though its own blood carries barely a tenth of the oxygen theirs does. Biologists still argue over why it lost its red blood cells at all. Which explanation does Sidell and O'Brien's leading 2006 review defend?
answer: No measured benefit: a fluke that cold, oxygen-rich water let survive
choices: No measured benefit: a fluke that cold, oxygen-rich water let survive
Clear blood raised oxygen delivery in the thick, frigid Antarctic water
Thinner, cell-free blood cut the heart's pumping cost in the cold
Scrapping red cells freed up iron the fish reused in other tissues
context: A genuine, still-live scientific debate. Sidell & O'Brien's 2006 review argues there is no measured fitness advantage to being white-blooded: icefish live right alongside red-blooded cousins, and their clear blood carries only about 10 percent of the oxygen. The hemoglobin-loss mutation likely survived only because frigid, oxygen-rich Antarctic waters, emptied of many competitors, relaxed the pressure long enough for extreme compensations, an enormous heart, huge blood volume and scaleless skin that soaks oxygen straight from the water, to evolve and keep the fish alive. Whether the loss was ever adaptive at all is still argued. Source: Sidell & O'Brien, 'When bad things happen to good fish: the loss of hemoglobin and myoglobin expression in Antarctic icefishes,' J. Exp. Biol. 209:1791 (2006); https://www.scientificamerican.com/blog/brainwaves/how-the-antarctic-icefish-lost-its-red-blood-cells-but-survived-anyway/

question: A smooth, cone-shaped pit the size of a walnut sits in the loose, dry sand under a porch. Buried at its bottom, a small insect larva waits with only its huge curved jaws sticking up. An ant that strays over the crumbling rim tumbles straight into them. Which insect makes this trap?
answer: The antlion
choices: The antlion
The ambush bug
The dung beetle
The tiger beetle
context: The antlion larva (family Myrmeleontidae) buries its whole body at the bottom of the pit, leaving only its jaws exposed just below the surface. The sloped sand walls do the hunting: prey that touches the rim slides down into the waiting jaws. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antlion

question: An ant slides down the crumbling wall of an antlion's sand pit, then scrambles halfway back up and looks as if it might escape. The larva buried at the bottom, with only its wide jaws poking up, has a way to drag it back down. What does the antlion do?
answer: Flicks sand up at the ant to trigger tiny landslides
choices: Flicks sand up at the ant to trigger tiny landslides
Squirts a jet of sticky glue up the wall
Vibrates the whole pit like a drumhead
Lunges halfway up the wall to seize it
context: With violent jerks of its head the antlion showers the climbing ant with flung sand, setting off little avalanches that carry the ant back down into its jaws. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antlion

question: A young antlion crawls across dry sand hunting for a good spot to dig its pit, and it leaves squiggly, winding doodle-trails behind it. The way it moves is one of the oddest things about it. Which way does the larva walk?
answer: Backward, rear end first
choices: Backward, rear end first
Forward, jaws first
Sideways, like a crab
In tight, spinning circles
context: A pit-digging antlion larva walks backward. Wandering in reverse in search of a spot to dig, it leaves squiggly winding trails in the sand, which is why in North America it is nicknamed the 'doodlebug'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antlion

question: After years as a pit-digger buried in the sand, an antlion larva at last spins a silken cocoon below the surface and pupates. Out crawls a winged adult that looks nothing like the small sand-monster it came from. What does the grown-up antlion look like?
answer: A delicate, long-winged flier often mistaken for a damselfly
choices: A delicate, long-winged flier often mistaken for a damselfly
A stout, furry night-flier like a small moth
A hard-shelled beetle with a horned head
A hovering, striped insect resembling a wasp
context: The adult antlion has long, lacewing-like wings and looks so unlike its larva that it's frequently mistaken for a damselfly or dragonfly — and it no longer eats ants. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antlion

question: An antlion larva may sit at the bottom of one sand pit for years, draining ant after ant that tumbles into its jaws. In all that time it never once leaves a single dropping in the sand. What is the strange reason it never poops?
answer: It has no anus at all
choices: It has no anus at all
Its food leaves no solid waste behind
It sheds its whole gut with each molt
It sweats its waste out through its skin
context: The larva has no anus and cannot expel waste; everything from years of hunting is stored inside its body and only released after it becomes an adult. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antlion

question: A raven-sized Archaeopteryx lived 150 million years ago in what is now southern Germany, and it looked like two creatures glued together. It had true feathers and a wishbone like a bird, but also small pointed teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail. Which two great animal groups does this one fossil famously bridge?
answer: Dinosaurs and birds
choices: Dinosaurs and birds
Pterosaurs and birds
Lizards and birds
Crocodiles and birds
context: Birds ARE living dinosaurs, and Archaeopteryx sits on that road as a creature part dinosaur, part bird, preserved in the fine Solnhofen limestone of southern Germany. Source: UCMP Berkeley 'Archaeopteryx: An Early Bird'; National Geographic (2014); Britannica 'Archaeopteryx'.

question: An Archaeopteryx skeleton came out of the quarry with its feathers only faintly preserved, and the people who first examined it missed the feather marks altogether. They filed the fossil under the wrong animal entirely. What did they first catalog it as?
answer: A small bipedal dinosaur (a Compsognathus)
choices: A small bipedal dinosaur (a Compsognathus)
A lizard-like reptile (a Homoeosaurus)
A fossil fish (a Leedsichthys)
An early crocodile (a Goniopholis)
context: A real-world demonstration of how close the two groups are: with the feathers barely showing, the bird was taken for a small bipedal dinosaur, a Compsognathus. Source: UCMP Berkeley 'Archaeopteryx: An Early Bird'.

question: Archaeopteryx already had feathers and a wishbone, yet it still kept its teeth, its clawed hands and its long bony tail, all at the same time. What does this patchwork tell scientists about the pace of the change from dinosaur to bird?
answer: Evolution swapped one system at a time, not all at once
choices: Evolution swapped one system at a time, not all at once
The switch happened in a single dramatic generation
Dinosaurs and early birds traded traits by interbreeding
Each animal reshaped its own body as it grew
context: Because it mixes traits, the transition proceeded piecemeal: feathers and a wishbone arrived while teeth, clawed hands, and a bony tail were still hanging around. Source: NCBI/PMC5418581 'Mosaic evolution in an asymmetrically feathered troodontid'; Wikipedia 'Archaeopteryx'.

question: A beautifully preserved Archaeopteryx had feathers from head to foot, even long ones wrapping its legs like a pair of trousers. Feathers like these also grew on its dinosaur relatives that never flew. What were such feathers most likely first used for?
answer: Warmth or showing off
choices: Warmth or showing off
Rowing through shallow water
Netting insects out of the air
Steering during fast sprints
context: Paleontologist Oliver Rauhut: 'The only thing we can say with some certainty is that [feathers] did not primarily evolve for flight, as it was long believed.' The scientists summed up the sequence as 'First show off, then take-off.' Source: National Geographic (2014); ScienceDaily '140703091959' and 'First show off, then take-off' (2014).

question: Dennis Voeten fired synchrotron X-rays through the wing bones of Archaeopteryx to settle whether it truly flapped or merely glided. He read their inner architecture, thin walls threaded with dense blood-vessel channels, and matched it against living birds. Its bones plotted right on top of one particular kind of flier. Which one?
answer: Pheasants, which burst into short powered flights to clear obstacles
choices: Pheasants, which burst into short powered flights to clear obstacles
Albatrosses, which lock their wings and soar for days without a flap
Hummingbirds, which hover in place on a blur of beating wings
Penguins, whose stiffened wings row them through open water
context: In 2018 Dennis Voeten and colleagues used propagation phase-contrast synchrotron X-ray microtomography at the European Synchrotron to image the interior of Archaeopteryx wing bones. The thin, densely vascularized walls matched living birds that actively flap, not gliders or soarers, so Archaeopteryx was an active flapping flier, but its bones plotted closest to birds like pheasants that fly in short bursts to clear obstacles or escape predators, not to long-distance soarers. The twist: the wing bones showed flight adaptations while the shoulder girdle did not, so it could not raise its wing fully above its back for the modern high-lift flight stroke. It flew, but not the way any bird flies today, the live edge of the how-did-it-fly debate. Source: Voeten et al. 2018, Nature Communications, 'Wing bone geometry reveals active flight in Archaeopteryx' (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-03296-8, PMC5849612); Sci-News summary (https://www.sci.news/paleontology/archaeopteryx-active-flyer-05814.html).

question: Quarry workers at Solnhofen in southern Germany lifted a crow-sized creature out of the fine, pale limestone in 1861, an animal from 150 million years ago. Named Archaeopteryx, 'ancient wing,' it stunned the scientific world. What covered its body?
answer: A full coat of true feathers
choices: A full coat of true feathers
A shell of bony plates
Rows of spiny scales
A layer of thick fur
context: Archaeopteryx lived on a tropical archipelago of low islands that is now the Solnhofen region of southern Germany, in the Late Jurassic. It is one of the most famous 'transitional fossils' ever found. Source: UCMP Berkeley - Archaeopteryx: An Early Bird; Wikipedia - Archaeopteryx.

question: Archaeopteryx carried true feathers along its arms and long tail in what is now Germany, 150 million years ago, and it looked so bird-like that scientists crowned it the Urvogel, German for 'primeval bird.' Yet its jaws held a clear holdover from its reptile ancestors. What did its jaws hold?
answer: Rows of small sharp teeth
choices: Rows of small sharp teeth
A hard horny beak
A long sticky tongue
A pouch of stored seeds
context: Archaeopteryx had real feathers and wings like a bird, yet unlike any bird alive today its jaws were lined with small sharp teeth - a reptilian holdover. Source: UCMP Berkeley - Archaeopteryx: An Early Bird; Britannica - Archaeopteryx.

question: A modern robin, pigeon or eagle ends each wing in a smooth feathered tip. But Archaeopteryx, the 150-million-year-old feathered fossil animal from Germany, still carried something at each wingtip that robins and eagles lack. What did each wing of Archaeopteryx bear at its tip?
answer: Three clawed fingers
choices: Three clawed fingers
A single curved spur
A webbed flap of skin
A pad of blunt scales
context: On each wing Archaeopteryx kept three clawed fingers that no living bird has - claws that could have grasped prey or gripped tree branches. Source: UCMP Berkeley - Archaeopteryx; Fossilicious species profile.

question: The fine Solnhofen mud of southern Germany kept an Archaeopteryx feather so sharply that scientists could study its vane, the flat part along each side of the shaft. In a bird that flies, one side of the vane is wider than the other, a lopsided shape that helps the feather grip the air; an ostrich, which never flies, grows feathers with even sides. Which pattern did the 150-million-year-old feather match?
answer: Lopsided vanes, like a flying bird
choices: Lopsided vanes, like a flying bird
Even vanes, like an ostrich
Loose, hairlike barbs, like down
Twin shafts sharing one base
context: The Archaeopteryx flight feather had asymmetric vanes - narrow on one edge, wide on the other - the lopsided shape that in modern birds pushes air for lift, hinting the wing was built to fly, not just for show. Source: Feduccia & Tordoff, 'Feathers of Archaeopteryx: asymmetric vanes indicate aerodynamic function' (PubMed 17811125); NHM dino-directory.

question: Archaeopteryx spread feathered wings 150 million years ago, yet scientists still argue whether it truly flew or mostly glided from tree to tree. The doubt comes from its skeleton, which is missing a key part of a strong flier's engine room. What did the chest of Archaeopteryx lack?
answer: A deep keeled breastbone
choices: A deep keeled breastbone
A wishbone of any kind
A rib cage entirely
A set of hollow bones
context: Archaeopteryx lacked the deep keeled breastbone that anchors a modern bird's powerful flight muscles, so at best it managed weak, flappy flight - whether it flew or glided is still honestly debated. Source: UCMP Berkeley - Archaeopteryx (flat sternum); Wikipedia - Archaeopteryx (flight).

question: Archaeopteryx had an oddly long upper-arm bone, which opened a gap between its wing feathers and its body where air would leak through and spoil lift. The 2025 Chicago specimen finally showed how the animal sealed that gap. What did paleontologists find running along its upper arm?
answer: A row of long tertial feathers
choices: A row of long tertial feathers
A flap of bare gliding skin
A second short pair of wings
A cluster of short, fluffy down
context: The 14th Archaeopteryx skeleton, the 'Chicago specimen' at the Field Museum, was described in Nature in 2025 by Jingmai O'Connor and colleagues using UV light and CT scans. It preserved long tertial feathers on the upper arm for the first time in any Archaeopteryx. Because its humerus is unusually long, those tertials are exactly what fills the leak-prone gap between wing and body, letting the wing act as one continuous airfoil. Closely related feathered dinosaurs have wing feathers that stop at the elbow with no tertials, which is a big reason they could not fly and Archaeopteryx could.
