Source: https://www.sci.news/paleontology/chicago-archaeopteryx-13912.html ; https://www.fieldmuseum.org/about/press/uv-light-and-ct-scans-helped-scientists-unlock-hidden-details ; Nature 2025, s41586-025-08912-4.

question: Archaeopteryx had feathers, wings and a wishbone, so it should have reached adult size in weeks like a modern bird. Scientists cut thin slices of its bone, found dense tissue with few blood vessels, and counted the growth rings. Compared with a living bird its size, how did it grow?
answer: About three times slower
choices: About three times slower
About twice as fast
The same rate, but no yearly rings
Slower, but grown within one year
context: A 2009 study led by Gregory Erickson, with Mark Norell and others (PLOS ONE), thin-sectioned Archaeopteryx bone and found poorly vascularized, parallel-fibered 'reptilian-grade' tissue with growth lines (LAGs, annual rings) in the larger London and Solnhofen specimens. Those rings show it kept growing across the second and third years of life, pausing each year like a small non-avian dinosaur, at roughly three times slower than modern precocial birds of similar size (maximal rates of 1.87-2.2 g/day, about a third of the rate for extant precocial land birds). So despite its feathers and wings, its metabolism and growth were still dinosaur-like, not fully bird-like. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0007390 (Erickson et al., PLOS ONE, 2009); https://www.amnh.org/research/science-news/2009/archaeopteryx-lacked-rapid-bone-growth-the-hallmark-of-birds.

question: A slim, silver fish striped in black patrols a shallow mangrove creek in Southeast Asia. It eats crickets, ants and spiders perched on leaves above the water, insects it can never reach. How does it bring down a bug on a branch above the water?
answer: It spits a jet of water that knocks the bug into the creek
choices: It spits a jet of water that knocks the bug into the creek
It leaps and snatches the bug from the branch with its fins
It lures the bug down by wiggling like a floating seed
It waits for wind to shake the bug loose from the leaf
context: The archerfish (genus Toxotes) is one of the only animals that uses a projectile of water as a weapon, firing a precise jet from below the surface to knock insects off overhanging leaves and branches into the water, where it eats them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archerfish

question: From the shallows of a Southeast Asian mangrove swamp, an archerfish fixes its eyes on a beetle sitting on a leaf two feet above the water. It spits a fast jet of water, a real water-bullet, up at the leaf. What does the very first shot usually do?
answer: Hits the beetle dead-on and knocks it into the water
choices: Hits the beetle dead-on and knocks it into the water
Falls short, so the fish circles for a better angle
Splashes wide, warning the beetle to fly off
Startles the beetle into dropping on its own
context: An adult archerfish almost always hits on the very first shot; a well-practiced fish can score a near-100% hit rate on insects up to about 65 cm (2 ft) away, and its jet can reach prey as far as 3 metres (about 10 feet) overhead. Source: https://elifesciences.org/reviewed-preprints/92909v1 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archerfish

question: Insects perched on the leaves above a mangrove creek get knocked down by a tight jet of water an archerfish spits straight up at them. The fish has no hands and no tool, yet the jet fires as if it came from a squeezed nozzle. Where does it build the barrel that shapes and launches its watery bullet?
answer: Inside its own mouth, pressing its tongue into a grooved roof
choices: Inside its own mouth, pressing its tongue into a grooved roof
In its throat, where a ring of muscle squeezes the water out
Between its lips, which purse into a tight round hole
In a pouch behind its gills that fills and then bursts
context: The archerfish presses its tongue up against a deep groove in the roof of its mouth, turning the groove into a narrow tube exactly like the barrel of a gun, then snaps its gill covers shut to blast water down the barrel. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archerfish

question: An archerfish aims at a bug on a leaf from below the surface, and light bends where air meets water. To its eyes the bug sits in the wrong place, shifted by as much as 25 degrees from where it really is. Faced with a target its own eyes misplace, what does the archerfish do?
answer: Corrects for the bend and aims at the bug's true position
choices: Corrects for the bend and aims at the bug's true position
Aims straight at the image it sees and fires anyway
Rises to the surface so the water no longer distorts the view
Fires a spread of shots to cover every possible spot
context: The archerfish compensates for refraction, aiming at the insect's real location rather than the distorted position its eyes show it. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2982040/ ; https://elifesciences.org/reviewed-preprints/92909v1

question: A distant bug takes a hard-hitting blast from an archerfish, though the fish's mouth muscles are far too weak to fire a shot that strong. The punch is built in mid-air, after the water leaves its mouth. What makes the flying jet stronger than the fish that fired it?
answer: Water shot later catches up and bunches the jet into one slug
choices: Water shot later catches up and bunches the jet into one slug
The jet spins like a rifle bullet and drills through the air
A pocket of air behind the water pushes it faster as it flies
The jet freezes into a tiny bead that strikes like a pebble
context: Water shot later travels faster than the water shot first, so the back of the jet catches the front mid-flight and bunches into one compact, hard-hitting slug, by one calculated estimate about six times more powerful than the fish's mouth muscles alone could deliver, the same physics as a drop-on-demand inkjet printer. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0047867 (Vailati et al. 2012, PLOS ONE)

question: In Stefan Schuster's experiment, some archerfish sat out the whole training with not a single practice shot, yet the moment they were finally given a turn they nailed fast-flying targets almost as well as the trained experts. Where did their sharp aim come from?
answer: Copying the aim of trained fish purely by observation
choices: Copying the aim of trained fish purely by observation
A burst of instinct that switched on the first time they went hungry
A knack for the skill they were simply hatched already knowing
A chemical cue in the tank water that carried the trick between fish
context: In Schuster's 2006 study, archerfish that never fired during training suddenly shot almost as well as the experts once given a turn, learning to hit fast-flying targets purely by observing other fish. Source: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(06)01013-X (Schuster, Current Biology 2006)

question: The Arctic tern breeds near the North Pole and winters near the South Pole, a small seabird whose life stretches across the whole planet. For which record does this bird stand ahead of every other animal on Earth?
answer: The longest migration of any animal
choices: The longest migration of any animal
The fastest level flight of any bird
The most non-stop days aloft of any seabird
The highest-altitude migration of any bird
context: Egevang et al.'s 2010 tracking study was titled 'Tracking of Arctic terns reveals longest animal migration' — pole to pole, Arctic breeding grounds to Antarctica and back, every single year. Source: Egevang et al. 2010, PNAS.

question: An Arctic tern raises its chicks near the North Pole, then crosses the entire globe to spend the rest of the year near the South Pole. What does living at the two ends of the Earth this way give it that likely no other creature gets?
answer: Two summers and more daylight than any animal alive
choices: Two summers and more daylight than any animal alive
A warm climate but very little food
A shorter journey than flying straight south
Fewer predators at both ends
context: Because it lives in perpetual summer at both poles, the Arctic tern sees two summers a year and very likely more daylight than any other animal on Earth. Source: Wikipedia, Arctic tern; discoverwildlife.com. LEGEND.

question: A long life for an Arctic tern runs 30 years or more, and in every year of it the bird flies its full loop from the Arctic to Antarctica and back. Over a lifetime, one bird flies about 2.4 million km in all. What famous distance does that match?
answer: Roughly three round trips to the Moon and back
choices: Roughly three round trips to the Moon and back
Roughly one trip around the Earth
Roughly a trip to the Sun
Roughly a trip to the nearest star
context: Over a life of 30-plus years the bird flies roughly 2.4 million km — the equivalent of about three return journeys to the Moon. Source: Egevang et al. 2010, PNAS; National Geographic. LEGEND.

question: Riding the prevailing winds, an Arctic tern swings through a huge S-shaped loop that spirals down through the South Atlantic and back up through the North Atlantic, instead of beating straight across the ocean. Which way does its loop actually turn at each end?
answer: Counterclockwise around the South Atlantic, clockwise around the North Atlantic
choices: Counterclockwise around the South Atlantic, clockwise around the North Atlantic
Clockwise around the South Atlantic, counterclockwise around the North Atlantic
Clockwise around both the South and North Atlantic
Counterclockwise around both the South and North Atlantic
context: The tern's sigmoidal route runs counterclockwise around the South Atlantic gyre and clockwise around the North Atlantic gyre, riding each ocean's prevailing winds rather than fighting a straight-line crossing. Source: Egevang et al. 2010, PNAS.

question: A farmer named Guillermo Heredia noticed a huge object sticking out of his land near Plaza Huincul, Argentina, in 1987. He was sure of what it was and phoned the local museum. What did he think he had found?
answer: A petrified log
choices: A petrified log
A meteorite
A whale skull
A buried statue
context: The 'log' was a gigantic bone of Argentinosaurus, one of the largest land animals ever known. His call to the museum began the discovery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentinosaurus

question: A long-necked plant-eater walked what is now Argentina about 95 million years ago, and its huge bones suggest a body 30 to 35 meters long weighing 65 to 80 tons. Scientists compare the estimated weight of this Argentinosaurus to a whole herd of one familiar living animal. How many of what?
answer: A dozen elephants
choices: A dozen elephants
A hundred horses
Fifty cattle
A thousand dogs
context: At 65 to 80 tons, Argentinosaurus weighed more than a dozen African elephants and stretched nearly the length of a basketball court. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentinosaurus

question: Argentinosaurus lumbered across South America about 95 million years ago, stretching roughly 30 to 35 meters from snout to tail-tip, one of the largest animals that ever walked on land. Yet no one has dug up a whole skeleton, only a few pieces: some huge vertebrae from its back, part of its hips, a rib and a leg bone. How did paleontologists work out its total length from so little?
answer: They matched its bones to fuller skeletons of its kin
choices: They matched its bones to fuller skeletons of its kin
They counted the growth rings in its leg bone
They measured the stride length in a fossil trackway
They compared it to the largest living whale
context: Argentinosaurus is known from only a handful of bones: about seven back vertebrae, part of the hip, a piece of rib and a slender leg bone first taken for a shinbone. Its 30-35 m length and 70-plus-ton weight are reconstructed mostly by fitting those fragments to the fuller skeletons of related titanosaurs such as Saltasaurus and Futalognkosaurus, not measured from a whole skeleton. Honest paleontology flags the uncertainty. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentinosaurus

question: A full-grown Argentinosaurus could stretch about thirty meters from nose to tail, yet every one began life inside an egg small enough for a person to cradle in two hands. From hatchling to full size, a giant like this multiplied its length by roughly what factor?
answer: About 100 times longer
choices: About 100 times longer
About 5 times longer
About 20 times longer
About 1,000 times longer
context: A sauropod hatched from an egg only about the size of a cantaloupe to a basketball, then grew perhaps 100 times longer to reach adult size, an explosive growth spurt over decades. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-sauropod-dinosaurs-became-the-biggest-land-animals-again-and-again/

question: Across Patagonia, in southern Argentina, Argentinosaurus hauled 65 to 80 tons on four legs about 95 million years ago. When paleontologists looked inside its giant back and hip vertebrae, they found a feature that surprised them. What was inside those bones?
answer: Air-filled chambers
choices: Air-filled chambers
Solid marrow cores
Coiled cartilage bundles
Dense mineral crystals
context: Argentinosaurus's bones were internally lightened by a complex pattern of air-filled chambers, the same pneumatic trick modern birds use, letting the giant carry 70-plus tons without a crushingly heavy skeleton. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentinosaurus

question: To learn how a 65-to-80-ton titanosaur got around, Bill Sellers and colleagues built a digital muscle-and-bone model of Argentinosaurus and let a computer search for its most efficient possible gait. No matter how the software searched, the giant's motion topped out at one thing. What was the fastest way this enormous body could ever move?
answer: A slow walk of about 2 meters per second
choices: A slow walk of about 2 meters per second
A heavy pounding trot between trees
A brief charging run over short distances
A rocking gallop on all four legs
context: Sellers and colleagues (2013) ran forward-dynamic simulations of an 83-tonne Argentinosaurus in their GaitSym software, using a genetic algorithm to find the most efficient gait. The optimizer could only ever produce a slow walk, top speed roughly 2 m/s (about 5 mph), and never a run or gallop; the authors concluded that an 83-tonne body is 'approaching a functional limit' for a land animal. Source: Sellers et al. 2013, PLOS ONE, 'March of the Titans: The Locomotor Capabilities of Sauropod Dinosaurs' (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0078733).

question: Two colossal long-necked plant-eaters came out of the same dusty Patagonian badlands: Argentinosaurus, and Patagotitan, named in 2017. Both rank among the biggest dinosaurs known, each far longer than a school bus, and which one holds the record keeps flipping as fresh fossils come in. What decides which titan wins the crown?
answer: Which set of back bones the estimate is measured from
choices: Which set of back bones the estimate is measured from
Which one left the greater number of fossil eggs
Which was discovered and formally named first
Which came from the more complete adult skeleton
context: In 2017 Carballido and colleagues argued that Patagotitan (about 37 m, roughly 69 tonnes) edged out Argentinosaurus by about 10 percent, using the cross-sectional area of its front back-vertebrae. In 2019 Gregory Paul countered that Argentinosaurus was still larger because its dorsal (back-bone) column was considerably longer, and several later analyses again favor Argentinosaurus as the biggest known titanosaur. Which one ranks first genuinely flips depending on which bones are measured. Source: Wikipedia 'Argentinosaurus' and 'Patagotitan', citing Carballido et al. 2017 and Paul 2019 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentinosaurus); SV-POW analysis (https://svpow.com/2017/08/09/dont-believe-the-hype-patagotitan-was-not-bigger-than-argentinosaurus/).

question: A mongoose corners an armadillo girdled lizard on a rock in South Africa, far from any crack to hide in. The lizard is too slow to outrun it. What does it do?
answer: It grabs its own tail in its mouth and curls into a ring
choices: It grabs its own tail in its mouth and curls into a ring
It puffs up with air until it is too wide to swallow
It sheds its tail and skitters off on the stump
It flattens against the rock and plays dead
context: Frightened, the armadillo girdled lizard (Ouroborus cataphractus) bites its own tail and curls into a spiky loop, so its hard armored back and spined tail face outward and its soft belly is hidden inside the ring. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armadillo_girdled_lizard

question: A cornered armadillo girdled lizard bends its body into a loop, so its armored back and spined tail bristle outward on every side. The point is to hide one body part in the middle, where a predator's teeth cannot reach. Which part does the ring lock away in its center?
answer: Its soft, unarmored belly
choices: Its soft, unarmored belly
Its delicate ear openings
Its still-growing new tail tip
Its store of body fat for the dry season
context: When the armadillo girdled lizard curls into its tail-in-mouth ring, the hard armored back and spined tail face outward while the soft, vulnerable belly is hidden inside the loop - the one part predator teeth could pierce is tucked safely in the center. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armadillo_girdled_lizard

question: The armadillo girdled lizard of South Africa produces just one or two young a year, and the way they enter the world is rare among lizards. Even rarer, the mother may stay and tend them afterward. How do her young arrive?
answer: The female gives birth to live, wriggling babies
choices: The female gives birth to live, wriggling babies
The eggs are carried inside the mother's mouth
A single huge egg is buried and guarded for months
The young hatch from eggs glued under a rock ledge
context: Unlike most lizards, the armadillo girdled lizard does not lay eggs - the female gives birth to live young, usually just one or two at a time, after a gestation of about six to eight months. She is also one of the few lizards that may care for her offspring after birth. Source: https://www.sanbi.org/animal-of-the-week/armadillo-girdled-lizard/

question: An armadillo girdled lizard hunts insects by day among the rocks of South Africa's western coast and shelters in the cracks between the stones. Most lizards live alone, but this one does not. What does its living arrangement look like?
answer: A crowd of all ages packed into one crevice
choices: A crowd of all ages packed into one crevice
A bonded pair that shares one crevice for life
A loose band that moves to a new rock each night
A hunting pack that herds insects together
context: Instead of living alone like most lizards, the armadillo girdled lizard lives in social groups packed into rock cracks - colonies of up to 30 to 60 individuals of all ages sharing the same crevice, which is highly unusual for a reptile. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armadillo_girdled_lizard

question: A jackal charges a tortoise on open ground. The tortoise doesn't run for cover -- it just pulls its head, legs and tail out of sight and waits. How can it defend itself with no cover anywhere near?
answer: it carries its fortress on its back
choices: it carries its fortress on its back
it plays dead until the jackal leaves
it puffs up too big to bite
it squirts a foul warning spray
context: A tortoise defends itself by drawing its head, legs and tail inside the shell -- a fortress it carries everywhere, so it never needs a burrow or rock. Source: Mesker Park Zoo Turtle Facts (PDF); allturtles.com Turtle Anatomy 101.

question: A hermit crab lives inside a borrowed empty snail shell. When it outgrows one, it crawls out and walks over to a larger shell down the beach and slides in. A turtle can never move house that way — a turtle is stuck inside the same shell for its entire life. Why can no turtle, sea or land, ever leave the armor on its back?
answer: the shell is its own fused ribs and spine
choices: the shell is its own fused ribs and spine
the shell is glued on by tough skin
the shell regrows too slowly to shed
the shell is welded shut by muscle
context: A turtle's shell is not a house it borrows -- it is the turtle's own ribcage and backbone, fused and flattened into the dome, so it can never crawl out. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'A turtle's shell has a lot in common with your ribs'; Turtle shell -- Wikipedia.

question: An armadillo on the grasslands of South America usually meets danger by sprinting into a burrow, or digging one on the spot with its powerful claws. One small species has a very different trick: it snaps its whole armored body shut into a perfectly sealed ball, its head-plate and tail-plate meeting to lock the seam like a lid on a pot. Which armadillo does that?
answer: the three-banded armadillo
choices: the three-banded armadillo
the nine-banded armadillo
the giant armadillo
the pink fairy armadillo
context: The three-banded armadillo (genus Tolypeutes) is the only armadillo that curls into a complete sealed ball, its head-plate and tail-plate interlocking to lock the seam shut. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, La Plata three-banded armadillo; Brazilian three-banded armadillo -- Wikipedia.

question: A leopard grabs a pangolin, and the shy, ant-eating mammal curls into a tight ball of hard, overlapping scales. Its scientific order, Pholidota, is Greek for 'clad in scales.' As the pangolin flexes and jerks its body, those sharp scales do one more thing. What do they do?
answer: they work as slashing blades
choices: they work as slashing blades
they rattle out a warning
they lock its limbs in place
they soak up a snake's venom
context: The order Pholidota means 'clad in scales'; the sharp overlapping scales double as blades a pangolin can slash with by flexing its body. Source: Pangolin -- Wikipedia (order Pholidota).

question: A turtle builds its shell out of its own body, and the job shoves one bone into a spot that no other backboned animal uses. In a mouse or a whale, that bone lies outside the ribcage. Which bone ends up inside the ribs in a turtle?
answer: its shoulder blades
choices: its shoulder blades
its kneecaps
its collarbone
its breastbone
context: In every other backboned animal the shoulder blades sit outside the ribs; because a turtle's shell is its fused ribcage, its shoulder blades sit inside it. Source: Turtle shell -- Wikipedia; Nature Communications, 'The endoskeletal origin of the turtle carapace.'

question: A 220-million-year-old fossil turtle, Odontochelys, still had teeth and only broadened, half-grown ribs where a modern turtle's domed back-shell would be -- yet its underside was already sheathed in a complete, fully-formed bony sheet. Paleontologists say the fossil settles a long argument over the order the two halves of the shell evolved. Which half came first?
answer: the belly plate, before the back shell
choices: the belly plate, before the back shell
the neck bones, before the leg bones
the horny beak, before the true teeth
the tail club, before the domed back
context: Odontochelys semitestacea means 'toothed turtle with a half-shell.' Described in Nature in 2008 (Li, Wu, Rieppel & Wang), it had a fully ossified plastron (belly plate) but only broadened ribs and no finished carapace on top -- the exact layout of a modern turtle embryo caught mid-development. That resolved the long debate: the plastron evolved before the carapace. Odontochelys also still had teeth in its jaws, which every living turtle has since traded for a horny beak. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odontochelys ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turtle_shell ('The fossil showed that the plastron evolved before the carapace').

question: Deep in the rainforest, a colony of army ants marches all day and never keeps a permanent nest. When the colony stops marching at nightfall, the queen and the young still need shelter. What do the workers build it from?
answer: Their own bodies, hooked leg to leg
choices: Their own bodies, hooked leg to leg
Leaves stitched together with larval silk
Chewed wood pulp shaped into paper walls
Mud pellets packed into a hollow dome
context: Army ants have no fixed nest. The workers grip each other with hooked feet to form a temporary living nest, called a bivouac, that shelters the queen and brood inside. Source: Discover Magazine, 'How Army Ants Build City-Like Nests Using Their Own Bodies' / Nature Communications s41467-022-28773-z.

question: Blind or nearly blind workers steer each raid of the army ant Eciton burchellii, some two hundred thousand ants pouring across the forest floor. With no useful eyes to guide them, what does the swarm rely on to hold its shape and direction?
answer: Touch and chemical scent trails
choices: Touch and chemical scent trails
Wind direction on their antennae
Vibrations from a lead drummer ant
Magnetic sense in their antennae
context: Army ant workers are blind or nearly blind. They run the entire raid by touch and by pheromone trails they lay down with their own bodies. Source: The Conversation, 'Bridges, highways, scaffolds...' / Britannica, 'Eciton army ant'.

question: A raiding column of the army ant Eciton burchellii, hundreds of thousands strong, marches through the rainforest and comes to a gap it cannot go around: a broken twig, a hollow in the trail, a split between two leaves. The raid does not stop or even slow. Within seconds something appears across the gap, and the column pours straight over it. What have the ants made?
answer: A living bridge of their own bodies
choices: A living bridge of their own bodies
A rope of dried saliva
A raft of floating leaves
A tunnel dug under the gap
context: Army ants build living bridges from their own bodies, hooking together with tarsal claws so nestmates can cross rough ground without slowing. Source: Reid et al. 2015, PNAS 112:15113, 'Army ants dynamically adjust living bridges in response to a cost-benefit trade-off' (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1512241112) / AntWiki, 'The Ants Chapter 16'.

question: Scott Powell and Nigel Franks laid planks drilled with holes of many sizes across an army ant trail and watched the traffic. The workers didn't avoid the holes. Instead, each ant did something at a hole that let prey-laden nestmates sprint home at full speed. What did each ant do at a hole?
answer: Plugged a hole its body exactly fit
choices: Plugged a hole its body exactly fit
Dropped a pebble to fill it
Spun a silk patch across it
Widened it into a shortcut
context: Each ant selected a hole matching its own body size and flattened into it, filling potholes with living bodies so the column ran home at full speed. Source: Powell & Franks study, via ScienceBlogs 'Army ants plug potholes with their own bodies' (2009). (legend)

question: A colony of army ants spends the night in its bivouac, a temporary nest wrapped around the queen and her young. As the outside air heats and cools, the workers hold the core of that nest steady near 28.5 degrees Celsius. How do they manage it?
answer: Opening and closing air passages through the mass
choices: Opening and closing air passages through the mass
Fanning their wings to move air
Carrying the queen to cooler ground
Sealing the whole cluster shut at dawn
context: Even a nest made only of ants is thermoregulated: the colony opens and closes air passages to hold the core near 28.5 degrees C while outside temperatures swing. Source: Franks, 'Thermoregulation in army ant bivouacs' (1989), Physiological Entomology.

question: Arthropleura, a giant relative of the millipedes, scuttled across the floor of a Carboniferous coal-swamp forest 326 million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs. The biggest millipedes alive today stretch about a foot long. How long did the biggest Arthropleura grow?
answer: About 2.7 metres, the length of a small car
choices: About 2.7 metres, the length of a small car
About 40 centimetres, the length of a cat
About 1 metre, the length of a big dog
About 6 metres, the length of a van
context: Arthropleura is the largest land invertebrate ever known to have lived. The biggest reached about 2.6 to 2.7 metres (over 8 feet) long, roughly the length of a small car, and weighed around 50 kilograms. Source: University of Cambridge, 'Millipedes as big as cars once roamed England'; Natural History Museum (2021).

question: A big adult Arthropleura carried about 28 to 32 armored body segments from head to tail. Counting the legs on any one of those segments reveals the signature that marks it as a millipede relative. What did each segment carry?
answer: Two pairs of walking legs
choices: Two pairs of walking legs
A single pair of legs
One clawed grasping leg
No legs, just armour
context: Two pairs of legs per body segment is the millipede signature (centipedes carry one pair per segment). A big adult had roughly 28 to 32 segments, leaving it scuttling on dozens of legs. Source: Wikipedia 'Arthropleura' (body structure).

question: A block of sandstone cracked off a cliff in January 2018 and split open on the beach at Howick Bay in Northumberland, England. A former PhD student spotted giant Arthropleura remains inside, the find that finally pinned down its true size. But the 75-centimeter object was not what it first looked like. What had hardened in that rock over 300 million years?
answer: A shed skin the animal had outgrown
choices: A shed skin the animal had outgrown
A crushed complete skeleton
A fossilised clutch of eggs
A footprint pressed into mud
context: Dr Neil Davies called it 'a complete fluke of a discovery.' The fossil was a moulted piece of exoskeleton, about 75 cm long, that had filled with sand and hardened. Most Arthropleura fossils are these cast-off skins, not carcasses. Source: University of Cambridge giantmillipede story; Britannica 'Arthropleura'.

question: An armored, eight-foot Arthropleura sounds like the nightmare predator of the coal forests, yet it carried no venom fangs and no grabbing claws. Scientists now think it lived a very different life than its size suggests. How did it actually feed?
answer: Munching rotting logs, leaf litter, and seeds
choices: Munching rotting logs, leaf litter, and seeds
Grazing algae from the swamp's pools
Sucking sap from giant tree ferns
Filtering plankton from swamp water
context: Arthropleura is now thought to be a detritivore, eating rotting wood, leaf litter, and nuts and seeds like modern millipedes, not a hunter. Source: Natural History Museum (2021); Wikipedia 'Arthropleura' (diet).

question: Neil Davies studied Arthropleura fossils and took on the textbook story of the Carboniferous giants. That story credits the ancient air, extra rich in oxygen, for letting Arthropleura and the enormous dragonfly Meganeura balloon larger than anything alive today. Davies argued that oxygen 'cannot be the only explanation.' What did he point to instead?
answer: A rich, high-nutrient diet in the ancient forests
choices: A rich, high-nutrient diet in the ancient forests
A far weaker pull of ancient gravity
Warmer seas driving faster growth
A total absence of any predators
context: Scientists long credited high Carboniferous oxygen for insect and millipede gigantism, but Davies noted oxygen alone cannot explain it, pointing to the nutrient-rich food available in those forests. Source: University of Cambridge giantmillipede story (Dr Neil Davies quote).

question: An assassin bug does not chew its prey. It drives a curved beak into a captured insect and pumps in saliva that turns the victim's insides to soup. Then what does it do with that soup?
answer: Sucks it out through the beak like a milkshake
choices: Sucks it out through the beak like a milkshake
Spits it back out to attract more prey
Stores it in a pouch to feed its young
Lets it drip onto the ground as a scent trail
context: The saliva carries paralytic toxins and digestive enzymes that liquefy the victim's tissues OUTSIDE the body (called extraoral digestion); the bug then drinks the liquefied insides up through the same beak, the rostrum. The saliva is potent enough to dissolve prey much larger than the bug itself. Source: Reduviidae - Wikipedia; Britannica 'Assassin bug'.

question: The nymph of the assassin bug Acanthaspis petax drains ants dry, then does something ghoulish with the empty husks. It glues them together with sticky threads from its own belly into a walking pile it carries around. Where does that pile of dead ants ride?
answer: Heaped on top of its own back
choices: Heaped on top of its own back
Wedged inside its hollow beak
Slung beneath its belly
Strung along a silk line behind it
context: The nymph secretes sticky threads from special abdominal hairs and cements the drained ant carcasses into a heap on its back that can hold roughly a dozen or more bodies - a mound of its own victims worn as camouflage. Source: Acanthaspis petax - Wikipedia; Newsweek 'Assassin Bug Stacks Its Victims on Its Back'. (Legend-status wonder.)

question: Jackson and Pollard tested whether the Acanthaspis petax nymph's backpack of dead ants really protects it, or whether its movement saves it. They offered jumping spiders both stripped-down nymphs and corpse-wearing ones, even dead, preserved bugs. What did the test reveal?
answer: Spiders attacked bare nymphs about ten times more often
choices: Spiders attacked bare nymphs about ten times more often
Spiders ignored both kinds of nymph entirely
Spiders preferred the corpse-wearing nymphs
The backpack only helped while the nymph was moving
context: Jackson & Pollard (2007, Journal of Zoology) found jumping spiders struck bare nymphs about ten times as often as backpack-wearing ones - and because the effect held even for dead, motionless bugs, the disguise ITSELF fools the spider's vision, not any movement. Source: Jackson & Pollard 2007, 'Bugs with backpacks deter vision-guided predation by jumping spiders'; summarized National Geographic. (Legend-status wonder.)

question: The feather-legged assassin bug of Australia hunts jack jumper ants bigger than itself. A gland oozes an intoxicating secretion, and the bug waves a feathery hind leg at the ant. Why offer the ant that leg?
answer: The ant grabs and tastes it, and the bug twists to stab its neck
choices: The ant grabs and tastes it, and the bug twists to stab its neck
The leg squirts glue that pins the ant in place
The leg snaps off to distract the ant while the bug flees
The ant carries the leg home, poisoning its whole colony
context: Entomologists nicknamed it the 'fatal attraction' strategy: the trichome gland's secretion lures the ant into grabbing and tasting the feathery leg, whereupon the bug twists around and drives its beak into a soft spot at the ant's neck joint - the ant is drawn in by the very leg that leads it to its death. Source: Ptilocnemus lemur - Wikipedia; myrmician 'Ptilocnemus lemur: the ant assassin'. (Legend-status wonder.)

question: An atlas moth flutters through a Southeast Asian forest on wings so broad that people who glimpse it often mistake it for a bird. Held open, how wide can its wings span?
answer: Nearly a foot across
choices: Nearly a foot across
About four inches across
Nearly two feet across
About three feet across
context: An atlas moth's wingspan reaches about 25-30 cm - up to nearly a foot across - and by wing surface area it has more total wing than almost any insect on Earth. Source: Natural History Museum, London - Spotlight: the atlas moth.

question: When a hungry bird closes in on a resting atlas moth, the moth flaps and writhes. Its curved wingtips suddenly rear up and jerk at the attacker, and it flees. The pattern on those wingtips mimics the head of which dangerous animal?
answer: A cobra
choices: A cobra
A great owl
A scorpion
A wolf spider
context: The atlas moth's forewing tips are patterned to resemble a cobra's head; by flapping so the two 'snake heads' rear up, the moth scares off predators. Its Cantonese name even translates to 'snake's head moth.' Source: Natural History Museum, London; California Academy of Sciences - Atlas Moth. (Legend/defense wonder.)

question: From the moment an atlas moth crawls out of its cocoon in a Southeast Asian forest, its whole life is a race. The adult lives only about one or two weeks and spends every hour of that time searching for a mate. Why does it die so fast, however safely it hides from bats and birds?
answer: It has no working mouth and can never eat
choices: It has no working mouth and can never eat
It burns out its wings within days of flying
Its blood freezes the first cold night
It cannot see well enough to find food
context: The adult atlas moth has only a tiny, useless proboscis - it can never eat, and survives just a week or two on fat it stored as a caterpillar, existing only to mate and lay eggs. Source: Wikipedia - Attacus atlas; HowStuffWorks - The Atlas Moth Is a Behe-moth.

question: A female atlas moth barely moves after hatching - she clings near her old cocoon and releases a faint chemical scent into the night air. A male can find her from kilometers away across dark forest. What lets him track that scent from so far?
answer: Huge, feathery antennae on his head
choices: Huge, feathery antennae on his head
A long tongue that tastes the breeze
Taste sensors on the tips of his feet
Scent pits hidden along his wings
context: The male atlas moth has enormous, feathery antennae that detect a female's pheromones from kilometers away and home in on her. The female is larger and stays put near her cocoon, releasing scent, while the smaller male does the flying. Source: Animal Diversity Web / Wikipedia - Attacus atlas.

question: A small pink axolotl hangs almost motionless in the still water of a tank. Behind its head, a frilly crown of six feathery pink branches fans out into the water. What is that crown doing for the axolotl as it hangs there?
answer: Pulling oxygen straight from the water
choices: Pulling oxygen straight from the water
Sensing electric fields from prey
Storing fat for the dry season
Warning rivals to keep away
context: The axolotl's showy 'crown' is a set of six branched external gills; oxygen passes straight from the water into the blood flowing through them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl

question: An axolotl in a tank seems to smile up at anyone who peers in, its mouth curved in a cheerful little grin that never changes. What is really behind that permanent happy face?
answer: Just the upturned shape of its mouth
choices: Just the upturned shape of its mouth
A puff of air held in its cheeks
A ring of muscle it flexes at visitors
Rows of tiny teeth showing through
context: The pale-pink, black-eyed axolotl isn't feeling anything by its grin — the smile is simply the fixed upturned shape of its face. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl

question: An axolotl glides through the water looking like a salamander that never grew up: a feathery pink crown fans out behind its head, its body stays soft and larval, and it never sheds its tadpole-like tail fin. Yet it is no helpless juvenile. What can this eternal-baby body do that ordinary salamander larvae cannot?
answer: Breed and lay eggs while still in its larval form
choices: Breed and lay eggs while still in its larval form
Feed only on milk-like fluid from its mother
Survive on land for months between water spells
Change its sex once each breeding season
context: Staying a larva forever is called neoteny (or paedomorphosis): the axolotl keeps its feathery gills and larval body yet becomes sexually mature and breeds, never transforming into a land salamander. Legend among biologists as the classic case. Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2019.00237/full

question: Millions of pink axolotls swim in biology labs and home aquariums all over the world. Yet in nature the wild axolotl is critically endangered, clinging on in just a few scraps of water. Where do the last wild axolotls survive?
answer: The old lake canals of Mexico City
choices: The old lake canals of Mexico City
A hot spring in the Sierra Madre
The mouth of the Rio Grande
A flooded quarry near Veracruz
context: Pollution and sewage crashed the wild population by about 99% between 1998 and 2014; perhaps 50 to 1,000 adults survive, nearly all in the canals of Xochimilco in Mexico City, the last scrap of its old lakes, with a few confirmed in the city's Chapultepec park. An animal nearly extinct in nature is everywhere in captivity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl

question: A tankmate bites off an axolotl's leg. A human cut would seal fast with tough collagen that hardens into a scar, but the axolotl's stump first clears away the debris. Then its cells refuse to scar. What do those cells do instead?
answer: Switch back to the growth they used as an embryo
choices: Switch back to the growth they used as an embryo
Rest in a dormant standstill for many months
Harden into a bony knob that caps the stump
Turn into fat that pads the healed stump
context: Instead of scarring, the axolotl's wound pauses, clears the debris, and reverts to embryo-style growth — so it rebuilds the part perfectly with no scar. A biology legend. Source: https://siliconcanals.com/sc-c-axolotls-can-regrow-entire-limbs-parts-of-their-heart-sections-of-their-spinal-cord-and-even-portions-of-their-brain-and-they-do-it-without-forming-scar-tissue-which-is-why-labs-from-vienna-to-bo/

question: Scientists lift an eye, or even a piece of brain, from one axolotl and graft it onto another. When a human patient gets a donor heart or kidney, his immune system usually attacks it as foreign, and he needs special drugs for life to hold that off. What happens to the axolotl's graft instead?
answer: The alien organ settles in and works normally
choices: The alien organ settles in and works normally
The graft is walled off in a hard capsule
The host absorbs it within a few days
The tissue survives but never connects up
context: An axolotl's immune system doesn't reject transplants the way ours does; scientists have grafted eyes and pieces of another axolotl's brain onto one and had the foreign organs work normally. A biology legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl

question: A scientist doses an axolotl with thyroid hormone, the same hormone a human thyroid gland pumps out. Until now the axolotl has kept its baby form all its life, with feathery pink gills and a soft larval body. What does the hormone turn it into?
answer: A land-crawling salamander with no gills
choices: A land-crawling salamander with no gills
A giant twice its normal size
A blind, cave-dwelling drifter
A larger larva with even longer gills
context: Given thyroid hormone, the axolotl loses its gills, its tail fin shrinks, and it crawls onto land looking almost exactly like its cousin the tiger salamander. A biology legend. Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2019.00237/full

question: N. J. de Both, working with European laboratory axolotls, transplanted a whole head from one animal onto another's back and reported the result in the journal Science in 1968. Few animals would accept a graft like that. What became of the extra head?
answer: It grew and acted on its own, apart from its host
choices: It grew and acted on its own, apart from its host
It slowly shrank until the host absorbed it
Its brain fused into the host's own brain
It sprouted a third head from its base
context: In de Both's 1968 experiment ('Transplantation of Axolotl Heads,' Science 162:460), heads grafted onto the backs of other axolotls survived because the hosts showed no graft rejection; they grew rapidly, showed many of the reactions of a normal axolotl head, and behaved independently of the host animal. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.162.3852.460

question: Godwin, Pinto and Rosenthal stripped an axolotl of its macrophages, one kind of immune cell, in 2013 and then amputated one of its legs. Normally an axolotl rebuilds a lost leg perfectly, but this time the leg never regrew, even when the macrophages reappeared. What formed at the stump instead?
answer: A permanent scar of tough collagen
choices: A permanent scar of tough collagen
A cluster of the missing macrophages
A shrunken half-limb missing its foot
A blister that reopened the wound
context: This 2013 experiment (Godwin, Pinto & Rosenthal) pinned regeneration on the immune system: with macrophages depleted before amputation, the stump healed like a mammal wound, capping itself in thick mature type-I collagen instead of forming a blastema. The macrophages fully returned within about two weeks, but by then the window had closed and no limb grew. Their early inflammatory signals are the switch between scar-free regrowth and scarring. Source: Godwin, Pinto & Rosenthal, "Macrophages are required for adult salamander limb regeneration," PNAS 2013 (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1300290110).

question: Scientists who read the axolotl's genome in 2018 found the biggest animal genome anyone had assembled at the time, some 32 billion letters long, over ten times the size of a human's. It also held a shock about a gene long thought essential for building every other backboned animal. What had become of that gene?
answer: It was missing, and a cousin gene did its job
choices: It was missing, and a cousin gene did its job
It had been copied hundreds of times over
It worked only in the larva, then shut down
It was split in two across separate chromosomes
context: At about 32 gigabases, over ten times the human genome and the largest animal genome assembled at the time, the axolotl genome needed a purpose-built assembler (MARVEL). The find that stunned developmental biologists: Pax3, considered indispensable in all other vertebrates, is absent, and its close relative Pax7 has taken over its role. Mutating Pax7 in axolotls reproduces the very defects mice suffer when they lose Pax3. Source: Nowoshilow et al., 'The axolotl genome and the evolution of key tissue formation regulators,' Nature 2018 (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature25458); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl

question: A strange creature creeps through the Madagascar treetops after dark, with huge yellow eyes, big leathery ears that swivel toward the faintest sound, and one long, bony middle finger for tapping bark. It is the largest nocturnal primate on Earth. Which animal is it?
answer: the aye-aye
choices: the aye-aye
the slow loris
the tarsier
the mouse lemur
context: The aye-aye (Daubentonia madagascariensis) runs about 15 inches of body with a bushy tail even longer than that, weighing roughly 4-6 pounds. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: At night in a Madagascar rainforest, an aye-aye raps on a tree trunk with its skinny middle finger, up to eight times a second, then pauses with its head close to the bark. No other primate hunts this way. What is the aye-aye sensing beneath the bark as it taps?
answer: a hollow echo where a grub tunnel runs
choices: a hollow echo where a grub tunnel runs
sap rising through the trunk
the scent of insect eggs
the warmth of a hidden grub
context: Tap-scanning fills between 5 and 41 percent of the aye-aye's foraging time; it listens for the hollow echo that betrays a grub tunnel hidden under the bark. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: As an aye-aye taps along a branch, ridges lining the inside of each of its oversized, bat-like ears go to work on the faint sound coming back through the wood. What do those ridges do to that sound?
answer: focus it, the way a lens focuses light
choices: focus it, the way a lens focuses light
split it into two delayed signals
cancel out its own tapping noise
amplify only the highest frequencies
context: The ridges on the inner surface of the ear work like an acoustic lens, sharply focusing both the echo of the aye-aye's own taps and the faint sounds of larvae moving under the bark, so it can pinpoint prey it cannot see. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: Deep in a Madagascar forest, an aye-aye has tracked down a beetle grub hidden in a tree, and it gnaws through the hard bark toward it with its two long front teeth. Those incisors do something no other primate's front teeth do. What is strange about them?
answer: they never stop growing for its whole life
choices: they never stop growing for its whole life
they sit in a second row like a shark's
they close sideways like an insect's jaws
they fall out and regrow yearly
context: These rodent-like, ever-growing incisors are unique among primates and are the reason early naturalists mistook the aye-aye for a rodent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: Having gnawed a hole in a Madagascar branch, an aye-aye hooks a fat grub out of the wood with one thin, wiry finger. On other continents a very different creature does the same job with its beak. Why did a primate evolve to fill that role on Madagascar?
answer: the island has no woodpeckers
choices: the island has no woodpeckers
its grub prey burrow too deep for any beak
Madagascar's birds are all fruit-eaters
the island's woodpeckers went extinct long ago
context: Madagascar has no woodpeckers, so the aye-aye evolved to fill that empty niche, doing with a wiry middle finger the exact job a woodpecker's beak does elsewhere. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: An aye-aye's long, wiry middle finger slides into a grub's winding tunnel and probes around the bends for the fat larva. That finger can do its work because its knuckle carries a joint found in no other primate hand. Which kind of joint is it?
answer: a ball-and-socket joint
choices: a ball-and-socket joint
a fused rigid joint
a double-hinged joint
a sliding cartilage pad
context: The ball-and-socket knuckle joint is the only one of its kind in a primate hand, letting the middle finger rotate freely as it hooks a grub. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: Edwin Dickinson and Adam Hartstone-Rose solved a puzzle about the aye-aye in 2019. Its fingers are so specialized for fishing grubs out of bark that they grip a branch poorly, yet it climbs just fine. How does it hold on?
answer: a hidden extra thumb of bone and cartilage, with its own muscles
choices: a hidden extra thumb of bone and cartilage, with its own muscles
its long claws hook over the branch and lock in place
its long bushy tail coils around the branch like a fifth limb
its palms are padded with sticky, suction-cup-like skin
context: NC State researchers Adam Hartstone-Rose and Edwin Dickinson found the aye-aye has a hidden sixth digit, a 'pseudothumb' with its own fingerprint. Hartstone-Rose: 'It has both a bone and cartilaginous extension and three distinct muscles that move it.' Source: https://news.ncsu.edu/2019/10/aye-aye-extra-finger/

question: A near-hairless wild pig roams the Indonesian island of Sulawesi. Local people named it the pig-deer because the male's strange tusks reminded them of a deer's antlers. Which animal is this?
answer: the babirusa
choices: the babirusa
the warthog
the Malayan tapir
the collared peccary
context: 'Babirusa' comes straight from Indonesian 'babi rusa' — literally 'pig-deer.' It is a wild pig of Sulawesi and a few nearby islands (the Togian, Sula, and Buru islands), and its near-hairless grey body only adds to the odd look. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babirusa

question: A male babirusa, a nearly hairless wild pig, wallows in the mud of a swampy rainforest on Sulawesi. His upper canine tusks keep curving as he ages, and they do something no other pig's teeth do. Where do those upper tusks end up?
answer: piercing up through the skin on top of its snout
choices: piercing up through the skin on top of its snout
jutting sideways past its fleshy cheeks
curving down below its lower jaw
hooking forward out past the tip of its snout
context: The male's upper canines don't exit the mouth at all — they grow straight UP, pushing through the skin on top of the snout, then curve backward over the face toward the forehead. It is one of the strangest sets of teeth in the animal kingdom. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babirusa

question: A male babirusa trots through the Sulawesi rainforest, showing off the two famous upper tusks that star in most photos of him. Yet he carries four tusks in all. What is the second pair?
answer: a lower pair of canines that also curve upward
choices: a lower pair of canines that also curve upward
a hidden pair rooted deep in the throat
a spare pair that only grow in old age
a pair of flat grinding tusks at the back
context: The male has FOUR tusks: the famous upper pair that pierces the snout, plus a lower pair of canines that also sweep upward. In dominance fights the lower tusks work as offensive weapons while the snout-tusks act more like defensive guards. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babirusa

question: An old male babirusa noses through the Sulawesi forest with upper tusks that have grown all his life without stopping, for food does nothing to wear them down. In rare cases one of those unworn tusks does something grim. What does it do?
answer: it curls round and grows into the animal's own skull
choices: it curls round and grows into the animal's own skull
it snaps off and blinds one of its eyes
it locks the animal's jaw permanently shut
it splits the tip of the snout clean in two
context: Because the tusks never stop growing, an unworn one can, in rare cases, keep arcing until it curls round and penetrates the animal's own skull — a creature that literally grows its teeth through its face and, occasionally, back into its own head. Source: https://blogs.ucl.ac.uk/museums/2016/08/12/specimen-of-the-week-252-the-babirusa-skull/

question: In the deep ocean twilight, a small fish about 15 centimeters long hangs perfectly motionless. The whole top of its head is a transparent, fluid-filled dome, clear enough to see straight through. What is this fish called?
answer: The barreleye
choices: The barreleye
The blobfish
The anglerfish
The viperfish
context: The barreleye (Macropinna microstoma) has a see-through dome covering the top of its skull. Despite its otherworldly, alien-looking head, it is only about 15 cm (6 inches) long. Source: MBARI animal page (mbari.org/animal/barreleye-fish); Robison & Reisenbichler 2008, Copeia.

question: A barreleye hovers in the dark water, and inside its clear, glass-like dome glow two green tubes: its real eyes. A human's eyes look forward, but at rest the barreleye's tubes point in one surprising direction. Where do they aim?
answer: Straight up through the transparent skull
choices: Straight up through the transparent skull
Straight down toward the seafloor
Out to the left and right sides
Backward toward its own tail
context: The tubular green eyes point straight UP through the see-through skull to spot prey silhouetted against the faint light drifting down from far above. Source: MBARI news; Robison & Reisenbichler 2008.

question: Two dark spots sit on the front of a barreleye's face, right where a fish's eyes ought to be, and the first observers took them for eyes. The real eyes are the green tubes tucked inside its dome. What are the two dark spots?
answer: Nostrils — smell organs
choices: Nostrils — smell organs
A second pair of backup eyes
Light-producing lures
Openings to its gills
context: The two dark spots that look like eyes are actually nares — the fish's nostrils, its smell organs. The real eyes are the green tubes hidden inside the transparent dome. Source: MBARI animal page; Wikipedia (Macropinna).

question: Bruce Robison and Kim Reisenbichler watched a living barreleye feed, from robot submarines and in a lab tank. Its tubular eyes turned inside the clear dome in step with one particular move of its whole body. What was that move?
answer: Tipping its body from horizontal to vertical
choices: Tipping its body from horizontal to vertical
Beating its tail hard three times
Drifting into a shaft of brighter light
Pressing its snout against the prey
context: Robison and Reisenbichler saw the tubular eyes rotate inside the dome from pointing up to pointing forward as the fish tipped its body from horizontal to vertical to feed: the eyes swing like binoculars as the whole fish turns upright. Source: Wikipedia 'Macropinna microstoma' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macropinna_microstoma); Robison & Reisenbichler 2008, Copeia.

question: Deep in the ocean's twilight zone, 600 to 800 meters down, where sunlight fades toward total darkness, a barreleye barely swims at all. Instead it hangs almost perfectly still in the water. How does it hold its position so precisely?
answer: With large flat fins making tiny adjustments
choices: With large flat fins making tiny adjustments
By anchoring to rocks with a sticky foot
By filling a float sac with gas
By clinging to passing jellyfish
context: The barreleye hovers almost motionless around 600-800 meters (2,000-2,600 feet) down, using large flat fins to hold position with tiny, precise adjustments. Source: MBARI animal page; ScienceDaily 2009.

question: Researchers think the barreleye is a thief: it hovers beneath a siphonophore, a drifting colony trailing stinging tentacles over 10 meters long, and picks off small animals already snared there. Captured barreleyes have held jelly fragments in their guts. What is thought to let the fish raid those tentacles safely?
answer: The clear dome shields its eyes from the stinging cells
choices: The clear dome shields its eyes from the stinging cells
A slime coat that neutralizes the venom
It only strikes when the siphonophore sleeps
Thick scales armor-plate its whole body
context: Researchers think the barreleye hovers beneath a siphonophore and picks off small animals already trapped in its stinging tentacles; the transparent dome is thought to shield its delicate eyes from the stinging cells. Captured specimens had jelly fragments in their stomachs. Source: MBARI news; ScienceDaily 2009; Robison & Reisenbichler 2008.

question: W. M. Chapman described the barreleye in 1939, yet for 65 years every drawing of it left the top of the head blank — no artist had ever seen the transparent dome intact until MBARI (the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute) filmed a live one in 2004. Why did those decades of net-caught specimens never show the dome?
answer: The fragile dome collapsed or tore off as nets hauled the fish up
choices: The fragile dome collapsed or tore off as nets hauled the fish up
The dome turns cloudy and opaque the moment the fish dies
The dome dissolves in the preservative used to store specimens
The dome retracts inside the skull whenever the fish is startled
context: Described in 1939 by W. M. Chapman, the barreleye was known only from net-caught specimens whose fragile transparent dome arrived collapsed or torn away — so old drawings left it out entirely. MBARI's ROVs captured the first footage of a living barreleye with its dome intact in 2004, 65 years later. Source: Wikipedia (Macropinna); MBARI news; Robison & Reisenbichler 2008.

question: A slim green lizard rears up on its two back legs beside a Central American stream and dashes away across the surface of the water without sinking. Which lizard pulls off this famous escape?
answer: The basilisk
choices: The basilisk
The green iguana
The frilled lizard
The marine iguana
context: The basilisk (genus Basiliscus) of Central and South American rainforest streams dashes across the surface of a pond or stream on its hind legs without sinking, so it looks like it is running on top of the water — hence the 'Jesus Christ lizard' nickname. Source: National Geographic — Green basilisk lizard.

question: High above a Central American rainforest stream, a basilisk basks on a thin branch while a hunting snake slides silently up the trunk toward it. There is no other branch to leap to and no room left to back away. What does the cornered basilisk do to escape?
answer: drops straight down out of the tree into the water
choices: drops straight down out of the tree into the water
clamps flat and motionless against the bark
wedges itself into a hollow in the trunk
spreads its ribs into a gliding flap
context: A startled basilisk bolts for the nearest water — and it will even drop straight down out of a tree into the water below to flee, then sprint or swim away, leaving a land predator stranded. Source: Wikipedia — Common basilisk; National Geographic — Green basilisk lizard.

question: Basilisks of every age bolt across Central American streams on their hind legs to escape predators, but they do not all get equally far. Some get 10 to 20 meters over open water, while others sink within a few meters. Which basilisks run on water best?
answer: The small, light youngsters
choices: The small, light youngsters
Big adult males with long legs
Crested males with tall sail-backs
Long-tailed adults that balance best
context: Only the light young pull it off well: juvenile basilisks can sprint 10 to 20 m (33-66 ft) across open water, while heavy adults manage only a few meters before their weight breaks them through the surface and they sink. Source: Wikipedia — Common basilisk; Biology Insights.

question: A basilisk flees across a pond on its two hind legs, sprinting on top of the water. Water cannot hold up a lizard standing still, so the trick lies in how each foot strikes and leaves the surface. What keeps each foot from sinking?
answer: It slaps down and lifts away before the water closes over it
choices: It slaps down and lifts away before the water closes over it
Oil on its soles repels the water like a duck's feathers
Its hollow bones make it light enough to float
Its tail beats the water to push its body upward
context: Each foot slaps down hard, opening a pocket of air in the water, then strokes back and pulls free before that pocket can collapse over it; long, fringed hind toes widen each foot as it strikes. Source: National Geographic, Green basilisk lizard (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/green-basilisk-lizard); Glasheen & McMahon 1996, Journal of Experimental Biology.

question: Off the coast of Scotland, a diver hangs still in the green sea as a basking shark, the second-largest fish in the world, glides straight at him with its mouth hanging wide open. What does the shark do to him?
answer: Nothing: it is harmless to people
choices: Nothing: it is harmless to people
Delivers a crushing, bone-breaking bite
Swallows him whole in one gulp
Stings with venom-tipped fin spurs
context: The basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) is completely harmless to people; despite its huge size and gaping mouth it is a gentle, non-aggressive giant. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basking_shark

question: A basking shark cruises slowly through cold water, its enormous mouth held open like a scoop. It grows past 33 feet long and weighs several tons, and among fish only the whale shark is bigger. With a mouth that huge, what does it feed on?
answer: Tiny drifting plankton
choices: Tiny drifting plankton
Seals hauled out on rocks
Schools of tuna and mackerel
Other sharks its own size
context: For all its size, the basking shark eats nothing but tiny plankton -- straining out copepods and other minute animals from the seawater. Source: https://www.marlin.ac.uk/species/detail/1438

question: A single 5-meter basking shark strains up to 500 tons of seawater an hour to sieve out its food. A whale shark or a megamouth works its throat instead, pumping and gulping water over its filter. How does the basking shark drive all that water through its gills?
answer: It simply swims forward with its mouth open
choices: It simply swims forward with its mouth open
It gulps and spits water like a bellows
It suctions prey in with a piston throat
It fans water inward with its huge pectoral fins
context: The basking shark is a passive ram filter-feeder: unlike the megamouth and whale sharks it does no pumping or sucking, relying only on the water it forces through its gills just by swimming forward at about 2 knots. A single 5-metre shark can filter up to 500 tons of seawater an hour this way. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basking_shark

question: A basking shark cruises through cold water with its cavernous mouth wide open, and the sea pours in full of copepods, tiny drifting shrimp-like creatures. The copepods stay behind in its throat while the water streams on out through the gills. What piece of gear inside its mouth catches the food?
answer: Dark, bristle-like gill rakers
choices: Dark, bristle-like gill rakers
A sticky mucus net in the throat
Rows of small hooked teeth
A muscular grinding gizzard
context: The basking shark strains plankton with dark, comb-like gill rakers on its gill arches; they catch the food while the water passes on through the gills. Its actual teeth are tiny (5-6 mm), useless for feeding. Source: https://asknature.org/strategy/specialized-gills-filter-plankton/

question: The crew of the Japanese trawler Zuiyo-maru, fishing off New Zealand in 1977, hauled up a decaying body with a tiny head, a 1.5-meter neck and four flipper-like limbs, and took it for a plesiosaur. Tests on its tissue pointed instead to a decayed basking shark. How does a rotting basking shark come to look like a long-necked reptile?
answer: Its jaw and gills fall away first, leaving a thin neck
choices: Its jaw and gills fall away first, leaving a thin neck
Gas swells its belly into four limb-like lumps
Its tail curls forward over its back like a neck
Its skin shrinks tight over a reptile-like skull
context: A rotting basking shark loses its lower jaw, gill area and its dorsal and tail fins first, leaving the small skull and backbone looking like a head on a long neck, so decayed ones are repeatedly mistaken for plesiosaurs. Amino-acid tests on the saved Zuiyo-maru tissue pointed to a basking shark as the most likely identity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuiyo-maru_carcass

question: David Sims recalculated what filter-feeding really costs a basking shark and found the animal lives on a knife-edge. Naturalists had long believed it spent the lean winter hibernating on the seabed, its filter idle. What did his numbers show it does instead?
answer: Keeps feeding on any patch dense enough, and just abandons thin water
choices: Keeps feeding on any patch dense enough, and just abandons thin water
Buries itself deep in the seafloor sediment until the spring bloom returns
Switches to hunting and gulping small schooling fish once copepods thin out
Drops its whole metabolism near zero and coasts along on stored liver oil
context: Sims's threshold-foraging work put a real energy budget on the giant filter. Pushing that cavernous mouth through the water creates enormous drag, so filtering only pays off above a plankton density of roughly 0.5 grams per cubic metre; below that the shark burns more energy than it gains and stops feeding, moving on to hunt richer water. Because that break-even threshold is lower than anyone expected, the shark never needs to hibernate -- it can profit on plankton year-round wherever the water is thick enough. Source: Sims 1999 & Sims et al. 2003, 'Threshold foraging behaviour of basking sharks on zooplankton: life on an energetic knife-edge?' (PMC1690094); CORDIS/Nature, 'UK study disproves basking shark hibernation myth.'

question: Off County Clare, Ireland, drones filmed something no one had ever recorded for this species. Up to two dozen mature basking sharks slowly wheeled nose-to-tail, gently rolling belly-up and brushing fin to body as they turned. What were the sharks most likely doing in that stacked, doughnut-shaped ring?
answer: Courting -- each sizing up many possible mates at once
choices: Courting -- each sizing up many possible mates at once
Herding a drifting plankton swarm into one richer patch
Settling a dominance order by jostling for the ring's centre
Basking in the sun-warmed surface before a long deep dive
context: David Sims and colleagues assembled underwater and aerial footage from 2016 to 2021 to describe this 'torus': groups of 6 to 23 mature sharks, equal males and females, circling in a ring 17 to 39 metres across and stacked in layers down to about 16 metres deep, with gentle fin-to-body touching and belly-rolling. Sims called it a slow-motion speed-dating event, where each shark can assess many potential partners at once -- the first courtship behaviour ever documented for the basking shark. Source: Sims et al., Journal of Fish Biology, 2022, 'Circles in the sea' (PubMed 36073958; PMC9826005); phys.org, 'Mysterious circling behavior of basking sharks explained.'

question: On a rocky shore, a bald eagle drops from the air and pins a fresh-caught fish under its yellow talons. This big, dark-brown raptor with a snow-white head hunts fish for a living. What is the shape of the beak it tears the flesh with?
answer: A downward-curving hook
choices: A downward-curving hook
A flat sieve like a comb
A slim hollow straw
A hard chisel point
context: A raptor's hooked upper bill lets it tear flesh from prey the talons hold pinned — the shape follows a meat-eater's diet. Source: raptor.umn.edu/about-us/news/what-makes-raptor-part-1-hooked-beaks

question: A woodpecker props itself against a tree trunk on its stiff tail and hammers at the bark, listening for the faint chewing of grubs tunneling deep inside. To reach them, its bill must punch through solid wood without shattering. What is its bill shaped like?
answer: A hard, straight chisel
choices: A hard, straight chisel
A curved tearing hook
A flat scooping spoon
A stretchy fishing net
context: A woodpecker's straight, hard bill works like a chisel, drilling into wood to reach insects hidden under bark. Source: calacademy.org/explore-science/woodpecker-inspiration

question: In a summer garden, a hummingbird hovers before a long, tube-shaped flower on wings that beat dozens of times a second. It reaches deep inside to sip the nectar pooled at the very bottom. What is its bill shaped like to reach so far in?
answer: A slender needle
choices: A slender needle
A broad flat spoon
A hooked tearing blade
A blunt cracking wedge
context: A hummingbird's slender, needle-like bill is built to reach down inside deep tube-shaped flowers for nectar. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird

question: A brown pelican folds back its wings high above the sea and slams beak-first into the water after fish. The long, floppy pouch under its bill looks like a shabby afterthought, yet in one plunge it scoops up more water and fish than the whole bird weighs. About how much does the full pouch hold?
answer: About 3 gallons
choices: About 3 gallons
About 1 gallon
About 6 gallons
About a half gallon
context: The pelican's gular pouch can hold about 3 gallons (11 liters) of water and fish, then drains the water out before the bird swallows the catch. Source: seaworld.org/animals/facts/birds/brown-pelican/

question: A roseate spoonbill walks slowly through a cloudy lagoon, sweeping its flat bill, shaped like a soup spoon, steadily from side to side and held a little open under the water. The instant a shrimp brushes between the two halves, it snaps them shut. Which sense tells the spoonbill the exact moment to snap?
answer: Touch
choices: Touch
Sight
Smell
Hearing
context: The spoonbill holds its flat bill slightly open and sweeps it through mud, snapping shut the instant it feels a shrimp or small fish — it hunts by touch, not by sight. Source: nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/news/bold-bizarre-and-brilliant-8-fascinating-facts-about-roseate-spoonbill

question: In a northern pine forest, a small, stubby finch sets to work on a cone, after the seeds locked tight between its closed woody scales. It eats almost nothing but conifer seeds, yet an ordinary straight, pointed bill cannot force those scales apart at all. What is different about this finch's bill?
answer: Bill tips that cross past each other for leverage
choices: Bill tips that cross past each other for leverage
A hooked upper bill for tearing
A comb of ridges lining the bill
A pouch under the lower bill
context: The crossbill's upper and lower bill tips cross past each other; jammed between two cone scales, the crossed tips give the leverage to pry a scale apart, and the tongue lifts out the seed. Source: allaboutbirds.org/news/craig-benkmans-40-year-fascination-with-crossbills-and-conifers/

question: On one spruce tree in the northern woods, two different crossbill species can feed side by side and never compete for the same cones. Both are small forest finches that pry conifer cones open for their seeds. What single trait sorts each species onto its own kind of cones?
answer: The size of its bill
choices: The size of its bill
The color of its feathers
The time of day it feeds
The height it perches at
context: The small-billed white-winged crossbill works tiny spruce and tamarack cones, while the heavier-billed red crossbill breaks into big pine cones — bill size sorts the birds onto different cones on the same tree. Source: allaboutbirds.org/news/craig-benkmans-40-year-fascination-with-crossbills-and-conifers/

question: Charles Darwin, exploring the Galápagos Islands off Ecuador, found a group of closely related little birds, later called Darwin's finches. Their beaks came in wildly different shapes across the islands, from heavy and blunt to fine and pointed. What single thing does each bird's beak shape track?
answer: The food that bird eats
choices: The food that bird eats
The color of its mate
The island's rainfall
The song it sings
context: Give one island a dozen foods and evolution carves a dozen bills — Darwin's finches are closely related species whose bills scale from nut-cracker to insect-tweezer, with only about six genes explaining nearly half the variation in beak size. Source: news.ucsc.edu/2023/10/darwin-finches/

question: A peregrine falcon drops from high in the sky in a dive that can pass 200 miles an hour and slams into a bird in mid-air. With its prey knocked down, it uses a tool hawks and eagles lack: an extra sharp notch along the upper edge of its beak, the tomial tooth. It slots the prey's neck into that notch and bites down. What does the bite do?
answer: Severs the spinal cord for a fast kill
choices: Severs the spinal cord for a fast kill
Crushes the prey's skull
Punctures a lung to slow it
Snaps a wing so it cannot flee
context: The tomial tooth lets a falcon sever a prey's spinal cord for a quick kill — a feature hawks and eagles do not have. Source: birdsandblooms.com/birding/bird-species/birds-of-prey/falcon-vs-hawk/

question: On Daphne Major, a small volcanic islet in the Galápagos, Peter and Rosemary Grant spent decades measuring the beaks of every finch they could catch. A hard drought hit in 1977, and by the next year about 85 percent of the medium ground finches were dead, but not at random: the soft seeds ran out first, leaving only the toughest behind. Which beaks did the drought favor?
answer: The biggest, strongest beaks
choices: The biggest, strongest beaks
The smallest, lightest beaks
The most sharply hooked beaks
The most brightly colored beaks
context: The drought left mostly large, tough Tribulus seeds; birds with the biggest, strongest beaks could crack them and survived, so the survivors shared that one trait — natural selection acting in a single dry year. Source: knowledge.carolina.com/discipline/life-science/biology/evolution-of-the-galapagos-finch/

question: A second harsh drought hit Daphne Major in 2004, years after the drought of 1977 that Peter and Rosemary Grant had studied there. By then a bigger rival, the large ground finch, had arrived and was hogging the large seeds. Which beak did the surviving medium ground finches carry?
answer: The smallest beaks, better on the seeds left over
choices: The smallest beaks, better on the seeds left over
The widest beaks, for scooping up fallen fruit
The longest beaks, for probing cactus flowers
The most hooked beaks, for tearing tough husks
context: Same island, same species as the famous 1977 result -- but the OPPOSITE winner. A population of the much larger LARGE ground finch had colonized Daphne Major and monopolized the big, hard seeds, so during the 2004-2005 drought the medium ground finches with SMALLER beaks (better at the small seeds left over) survived and the big-beaked ones died. This is a textbook case of 'character displacement' caught in real time, and selection against the large-beak type was fierce (selection coefficient s = 0.59). Lamichhaney and colleagues later traced the shift to the HMGA2 gene: birds carrying two copies of the small-beak variant (HMGA2*S) survived far better. Source: Lamichhaney et al. 2016, 'A beak size locus in Darwin's finches facilitated character displacement during a drought,' Science, Apr 22 2016 (PubMed 27102486; Princeton/Uppsala/ScienceDaily coverage), corroborated across multiple outlets.

question: A red crossbill attacks a cone from one side only, for its bill is handed: the lower tip crosses either left or right, fixed for life. Craig Benkman found red crossbills split almost exactly 50-50 between the two kinds. What keeps that even balance?
answer: Whichever type is rarer finds more untouched cones, so it thrives
choices: Whichever type is rarer finds more untouched cones, so it thrives
Chicks copy the crossing direction of the parent that feeds them
The crossing direction flips to match each new cone crop
Left and right tips wear down at exactly the same rate
context: A crossbill's crossed tip is 'handed' -- it crosses either to the left ('sinistral') or the right ('dextral'), fixed for life, forcing the bird to attack cones from one direction. Lefties and righties literally walk around a cone in opposite directions and pry from opposite sides. Craig Benkman found red crossbills occur in a roughly 1:1 ratio and argued it is held there by negative frequency-dependent selection: whichever morph is rarer has more un-worked cones available, so it does better, which pulls the ratio back toward even. (White-winged crossbills are skewed ~3:1 toward right-crossing.) Source: Craig Benkman's work and Springer, 'Are the ratios of bill crossing morphs in crossbills the result of frequency-dependent selection?' (Evolutionary Ecology); Scottish Wildlife Trust, Montana Public Radio, Bootstrap Analysis coverage, corroborated across sources.

question: A beaver, a big flat-tailed rodent, gnaws through a tree trunk beside a stream it has dammed into a pond. Its two upper front teeth are enormous chisels, and a close look shows they are an unexpected color for a tooth. What color are they?
answer: Bright orange
choices: Bright orange
Pale white
Jet black
Dull gray
context: A beaver's incisors are famously orange because the outer enamel is packed with iron instead of the ordinary magnesium in most animal teeth. The iron makes them harder and more acid-resistant, so they resist decay without brushing. Source: https://scienceinsights.org/why-are-beaver-teeth-orange-its-iron-in-the-enamel/

question: At the edge of a woodland pond sits a lodge, a big dome of mud and sticks where a beaver family eats, sleeps and raises its kits. A fox prowls the bank, sniffing, but cannot get in. Where did the beavers put the front door?
answer: Underwater, entered by diving
choices: Underwater, entered by diving
On the roof, reached by climbing
Behind a wall of thorns
