Facing away, hidden in reeds
context: A beaver builds its lodge with an entrance underwater, so a fox or wolf cannot follow it inside. The dam floods a safe moat around the home, and the family enters by diving. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/articles/ecosystem-engineers-how-beavers-build-wetlands-that-help-fight-climate-change/

question: A beaver glides through the murky water of its pond with its eyes wide open. Mud and grit swirl all around, yet it still sees clearly and its eyes come to no harm. What piece of built-in gear lets it swim like that?
answer: A see-through third eyelid
choices: A see-through third eyelid
A ring of tiny scales
An oily protective film
A pair of bony eye-shields
context: A beaver has a transparent third eyelid that slides across each eye like built-in swim goggles, letting it see clearly underwater while keeping the water out. Source: https://forthriverstrust.org/mammals-week-anatomy-of-a-beaver/

question: A beaver is swimming quietly across its pond at dusk when a shadow passes overhead. In a flash it brings its broad, flat tail smacking down on the surface with a crack that echoes across the pond. The tail steers like a rudder, but what is that slap for?
answer: Warning the colony of danger
choices: Warning the colony of danger
Stunning fish to eat
Splashing mud onto the dam
Cooling itself in summer heat
context: A beaver's flat scaly tail is a Swiss-army tool: a rudder for steering while swimming, and an alarm. When danger appears, the beaver slaps it hard on the water with a loud crack to warn the whole colony. Source: https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/castoreum/

question: A beaver spends its autumn evenings dragging leafy branches to the bottom of its pond, stocking an underwater larder for winter. It clamps a branch tight in its huge incisors and dives, staying under for many minutes at a time, yet no water pours down its throat to drown it. What lets it work with its mouth full?
answer: Its lips close behind the front teeth
choices: Its lips close behind the front teeth
It breathes out bubbles to keep water out
Its cheeks hold a pocket of trapped air
Thick saliva plugs the back of its mouth
context: Before diving, a beaver seals itself shut: valve-like muscles clamp the nostrils and ears closed, and its lips close BEHIND the front teeth, so it can carry a branch underwater without swallowing water. It can stay under for about 15 minutes. Source: https://beaversinengland.com/beaver-biology/beaver-biology-2/

question: Deep in the wet boreal forest of Wood Buffalo National Park in northern Canada, generations of beaver families have stacked sticks and mud into a single dam so enormous that Jean Thie picked it out of satellite images in 2007. No bigger beaver dam is known. How long is it, end to end?
answer: About 800 meters, eight football fields
choices: About 800 meters, eight football fields
About 80 meters, one football field
About 8 kilometers across a valley
About 300 meters, three football fields
context: The largest known beaver dam stretches about 800 meters, the length of eight football fields, hidden in Wood Buffalo National Park. It was so big it showed up on satellite imagery in 2007. Source: https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/nt/woodbuffalo/nature/beaver_gallery

question: A shaggy, black mammal that weighs as much as a mid-sized dog prowls the rainforest canopy of South and Southeast Asia. It is often called the bearcat, though it is no bear and no cat but a cousin of the civets. What is this tree-dweller?
answer: The binturong
choices: The binturong
The red panda
The kinkajou
The fossa
context: The binturong (Arctictis binturong) is a viverrid — a relative of the civets — not a bear and not a cat, despite its 'bearcat' nickname. Its genus name Arctictis is Greek for 'bear-weasel.' It really does smell strongly of hot buttered popcorn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binturong ; https://today.duke.edu/2016/04/popcorn-scented-binturong

question: A zookeeper walking past a binturong, a shaggy tree-dweller of Southeast Asia, catches an odd smell, like something from a kitchen. A Duke University study in 2016 traced it to a molecule people smell at home all the time. Which foods share the binturong's scent molecule?
answer: Popcorn and cooked jasmine rice
choices: Popcorn and cooked jasmine rice
Fresh-cut cucumber and melon rind
Ripe banana and pear skin
Roasted coffee and dark chocolate
context: The compound is 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline (2-AP) — the very same molecule that makes popcorn and cooked jasmine rice smell the way they do. Greene et al. (2016) found it in every binturong urine sample they tested. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27056047/ ; https://today.duke.edu/2016/04/popcorn-scented-binturong

question: Christine Drea's team at Duke University found a molecule with a cooking smell in binturong urine. In popcorn it forms under high heat, when sugars and amino acids react together, so Drea asked how an animal could make a cooking smell without ever cooking. Where does her team think the compound comes from?
answer: Microbes on its skin, fur or gut make it as urine passes
choices: Microbes on its skin, fur or gut make it as urine passes
A special heat-producing gland warms the urine to 'cook' it
The animal eats fermenting fruit that already contains it
Its liver synthesizes the finished molecule directly
context: In popcorn, 2-AP forms through the Maillard reaction — sugars and amino acids reacting under high heat. A binturong never gets that hot, so Christine Drea asked, 'How does this animal make a cooking smell, but without cooking?' The team believes microbes on the binturong's skin, fur, or gut produce the compound as the urine passes. Source: https://today.duke.edu/2016/04/popcorn-scented-binturong

question: High in a Southeast Asian rainforest, a binturong climbs down from its tree headfirst, walking straight down the trunk without slipping. A cat coming down a tree usually has to back down or leap. What lets the binturong make a headfirst descent?
answer: Its hind ankles twist 180 degrees so the claws stay hooked
choices: Its hind ankles twist 180 degrees so the claws stay hooked
Suction pads on the soles of its feet grip the bark
It descends by hanging from its tail and letting go in stages
Backward-curving spines along its belly catch the trunk
context: The binturong can rotate its hind ankles a full 180 degrees, so its claws stay hooked into the bark even while it climbs down a trunk head-first. It also has a fully prehensile tail it uses as a fifth limb to anchor and balance in the trees. Source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Binturong (https://animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/binturong); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binturong

question: A female blanket octopus spreads a purple web between her arms and never once touches a rock or a grain of sand. Most octopuses shelter in rocky crevices of the reef by day and crawl the seafloor at night. Where does she live instead?
answer: Drifting in the open blue ocean, far above any bottom
choices: Drifting in the open blue ocean, far above any bottom
Clinging to floating rafts of drifting seaweed at the surface
Riding on the backs of large drifting jellyfish
Hovering in the warm water just above deep-sea vents
context: The blanket octopus is pelagic — it lives in the open ocean far from any reef or seafloor, drifting through tropical and subtropical waters from the surface down to about 250 meters. Most octopuses are bottom-dwellers, which makes this open-water lifestyle unusual. Source: https://octonation.com/octopedia/blanket-octopus/

question: A hungry tuna closes in on a female blanket octopus, a soft octopus with no shell, and she has only the sheets of iridescent purple webbing strung between her arms to save herself. What does she do with that webbing?
answer: Spreads it wide to look suddenly enormous
choices: Spreads it wide to look suddenly enormous
Wraps herself into a tight armored ball
Catches the current with it to outrun the tuna
Flashes it in pulses to dazzle the tuna
context: The female unfurls a huge iridescent 'blanket' — sheets of webbing strung between her arms — and spreads it so she suddenly looks enormous and scary, ballooning out to intimidate tuna, sailfish and even sharks. Source: https://octonation.com/fun-facts-about-the-female-blanket-octopus/

question: A blanket octopus swims right up to a Portuguese man o' war, a drifting jelly-like creature whose long trailing threads carry a sting that can put a swimmer in hospital. Rather than flee the danger, it rips pieces off. What does it do with the stolen venomous strands?
answer: Holds the stinging tentacles in its arms as venomous whips
choices: Holds the stinging tentacles in its arms as venomous whips
Eats them to absorb the venom into its own skin
Weaves them into its blanket for extra color
Uses them as bait to lure fish closer
context: Legendary. The blanket octopus tears pieces off the man o' war's deadly tentacles and holds them in its arms like whips, using the stolen stingers as weapons to attack prey and fend off predators. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanket_octopus

question: A full-grown female blanket octopus drifts through the warm sea, her shimmering web stretched about 2 meters across, roughly the height of a doorway. Few people have ever seen the male of the same species alive. How big is a grown male?
answer: About the size of a walnut
choices: About the size of a walnut
About the size of a dinner plate
About half her size
About the size of a house cat
context: Legendary. The blanket octopus shows one of the most extreme size gaps in the animal kingdom: the female can reach about 2 meters (6.6 ft), while the male is only about 2.4 cm — roughly the size of a walnut. Source: https://www.iflscience.com/the-blanket-octopus-has-the-most-extreme-sexual-dimorphism-in-the-animal-kingdom-80008

question: For much of the 1800s, naturalists turned up a wriggling thread inside female argonauts and blanket octopuses. Georges Cuvier named it Hectocotylus in 1829, taking it for a parasitic worm. Only in the early 1850s did naturalists work out what it really was. What was the thread?
answer: The dwarf male's own detachable arm, left behind after mating
choices: The dwarf male's own detachable arm, left behind after mating
A parasitic ribbon-worm that feeds on octopus eggs
A coiled string of the female's own unfertilized eggs
A stinging thread stripped from a Portuguese man o' war
context: One of biology's great mistaken-identity blunders. Cuvier described the severed hectocotylus as a parasitic worm; in the 1840s Albert von Kölliker, who found such threads in argonauts and blanket octopuses, took them for tiny degenerate males. In 1852-53 Jean-Baptiste Vérany and Carl Vogt, and Heinrich Müller, showed the 'worm' was really the male's own detached mating arm, the hectocotylus, which he packs with sperm and hands to the female; the male almost certainly dies shortly after. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectocotylus ; Darwin Correspondence Project note (https://darwin-editorial.darwinproject.ac.uk/view/letters/DCP-LETT-1435) ; Müller 1853, Zeitschrift für wissenschaftliche Zoologie 4.

question: A blanket octopus can tear a stinger from a Portuguese man o' war and carry it as a weapon, but no blanket octopus over about 7 centimeters long has ever been seen with one. The carriers are all tiny males or small young females. What is thought to stop a bigger octopus from carrying one?
answer: A bigger octopus's larger suckers can no longer grip the narrow stinger
choices: A bigger octopus's larger suckers can no longer grip the narrow stinger
Larger octopuses lose their immunity to the man o' war's venom as they mature
The stinger's venom breaks down too fast to be useful on a slow-moving adult
Bigger octopuses can no longer swim close enough to a man o' war to harvest one
context: Individuals longer than about 7 cm have never been seen carrying the tentacles -- their larger suckers likely can't grip the narrow stingers without injury. The borrowed weapon gives the small males a "size refuge," which researchers propose may itself have pushed females to grow enormous while males stayed miniature. Source: Norman, Paul, Finn & Tregenza 2002, "First encounter with a live male blanket octopus," NZ J. Marine & Freshwater Research 36:733-736; citing Jones 1963 and Thomas 1977.

question: A droopy pink blob with a permanent frown lies on a fishing boat's deck: a blobfish, known online as the saddest fish in the world. At home off Australia, about a kilometer down, it looks very different. What does a living blobfish look like there?
answer: a normal blunt-headed pink fish with big black eyes
choices: a normal blunt-headed pink fish with big black eyes
a translucent jelly with glowing blue veins
a spiny grey lump bristling with venom quills
a flat ribbon of skin with no eyes at all
context: The famous melted-face look only appears at the surface: built for crushing deep-sea pressure, the blobfish's body relaxes and collapses in our thin air 'much like a washed-up jellyfish.' At depth it is an ordinary-looking pink fish with feathery fins. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'The blobfish: a bloated guide to the world's ugliest animal' (sciencefocus.com).

question: A trawl net drags a blobfish up from the seabed a kilometer down off Australia, where the water pushes 60 to 120 times as hard as air does at the surface. On deck its body sags into the famous drooping mess. What change up here turned a firm deep-sea fish into slop?
answer: the crushing squeeze its body needed suddenly vanished
choices: the crushing squeeze its body needed suddenly vanished
the sunlight burned and blistered its skin
the warm surface water boiled its blood
the thin surface air poisoned its gills
context: At home the blobfish lives where water presses on it 60 to 120 times harder than air presses on us at the surface. A body engineered against that crushing squeeze simply falls apart once the pressure is gone. Source: Wikipedia, Psychrolutes marcidus (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychrolutes_marcidus).

question: A blobfish drifts above the seabed a kilometer down in the cold, dark water off Australia and New Zealand. Its body is mostly floppy jelly, with hardly any muscle and barely any bone, because chasing prey would burn energy the food-poor deep cannot spare. How does this lazy pink fish manage to eat at all?
answer: it gulps whatever edible scraps drift right past its mouth
choices: it gulps whatever edible scraps drift right past its mouth
it filters mud through long comb-like teeth
it lures prey with a glowing lure on its head
it scrapes algae off rocks with a rasping tongue
context: Strong bones and big muscles cost energy the food-poor deep can't spare, so the blobfish hovers nearly motionless and swallows small crustaceans, sea snails, and drifting scraps, 'whatever passes right in front of them.' As one expert put it, 'Being lazy is a survival strategy.' Source: BBC Science Focus (sciencefocus.com); Australian Museum, fathead / Mr Blobby page.

question: A blue dragon, a silver-and-blue sea slug no bigger than a grape, drifts on the open ocean far from any coast or seafloor. It has no shell and can barely swim, yet it lives its whole life at the surface. How does it ride there?
answer: Belly-up, floating upside down
choices: Belly-up, floating upside down
Clinging to a rock with one foot
Buried in the sandy seabed
Riding on a sea turtle's shell
context: The blue dragon floats upside down at the very surface, belly toward the sky, drifting at the mercy of the wind and currents with almost no power to swim on its own. Source: https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/fact-file/fact-file-blue-dragon-glaucus-atlanticus/

question: A blue dragon, a sea slug about three centimeters long, hunts a drifter more dangerous than itself: a jellyfish-like creature armed with venomous stinging cells. It eats its prey whole and keeps the stingers, still working. How bad can its sting be for a swimmer?
answer: Worse than the Portuguese man o' war it ate
choices: Worse than the Portuguese man o' war it ate
About the same as a mild mosquito bite
Like a bee sting, sharp but soon over
Only a faint tingle, barely noticed
context: Despite being smaller than a grape, the blue dragon can sting a human worse than the man o' war did, causing nausea, pain, and vomiting. It concentrates the venom it steals, so the thief becomes deadlier than its victim. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucus_atlanticus

question: A blue dragon drifts at the ocean surface, carried by wind and current, with hungry seabirds diving from above and hungry fish hunting from below. How is its small body colored to survive that double threat?
answer: Blue on one side, silver-grey on the other
choices: Blue on one side, silver-grey on the other
Bright red all over as a poison warning
See-through so light passes through it
A dull sandy brown, top and bottom alike
context: Its camouflage is counter-shaded in REVERSE: the side pointing up to the sky is brilliant blue to hide against the sea from above, and the side pointing down into the water is silver-grey to hide against the bright surface from below. Because the blue dragon floats upside down, this puts the blue on its belly. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucus_atlanticus

question: A blue dragon lives its whole life adrift in the thin sunlit layer at the top of the tropical ocean. It has no fins to speak of and can barely swim, yet it never sinks out of that layer. What keeps this little slug afloat?
answer: An air bubble it holds in its stomach
choices: An air bubble it holds in its stomach
Oil-filled fins that spread like a raft
A jelly float grown on its back
Beating thousands of tiny leg-paddles
context: The blue dragon stays afloat by swallowing and holding an air bubble in its stomach — a gas-filled sac in its belly acts like a built-in life-jacket, helped by the surface tension of the water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucus_atlanticus

question: A blue dragon, a little sea slug that eats the Portuguese man o' war and keeps its stingers, washes up dead and drying on a warm beach, a few centimeters of beautiful electric blue. A curious child reaches for the pretty shape. Why should the child not touch it?
answer: Its stolen stingers still fire on contact after it dies
choices: Its stolen stingers still fire on contact after it dies
Its drying body puffs out a cloud of toxic spores
Its skin turns acidic and burns whatever touches it
Its blue pigment soaks in and poisons through the skin
context: The blue dragon's venom stays active even after the slug is dead: a washed-up blue dragon on the beach can still sting a person, because the borrowed stinging cells fire on contact. Source: https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/fact-file/fact-file-blue-dragon-glaucus-atlanticus/

question: A blue dragon swallows the loaded stinging cells of a Portuguese man o' war whole, but however carefully it eats, a few of them always misfire inside its gut. How does its gut keep the ones that fire from harming the slug?
answer: Mucus quiets the stingers, and tough chitin plates in the gut soak up the ones that fire
choices: Mucus quiets the stingers, and tough chitin plates in the gut soak up the ones that fire
Heat from its stomach denatures the stingers and makes them fall limp before they fire
It fires each stinger into a sealed water sac that then vents harmlessly to the open sea
It starves itself for days so the loaded stingers slowly discharge on their own instead
context: The disarming is a two-part trick. First, the slug's mucus suppresses nematocyst discharge (in the related aeolid Aeolidia papillosa, mucus cut prey-stinger firing by roughly 60% below control). Second, a tough chitin cuticle plus granular-chitin discs called 'spindles' line the gut and act like biological sandbags, absorbing any stinger that still goes off. So swallowing a man o' war whole is not luck: it chemically quiets the weapons, then physically shields its own insides from the ones that fire anyway. Source: PMC review 'Acquisition and Use of Nematocysts by Cnidarian Predators' (PMC2783962), citing Aeolidia papillosa mucus-suppression and buccal chitin 'spindle' data.

question: A blue dragon in an aquarium tank went after a live small fish while cameras rolled for a 2025 study. Biologists had long seen it as a Portuguese man o' war specialist that killed with borrowed stings, and the film overturned that picture. How did it catch the fish?
answer: It grabbed and pinned it with its long front cerata, then bit down near the gills
choices: It grabbed and pinned it with its long front cerata, then bit down near the gills
It stunned the passing fish with a sudden burst of its stored stinging cells
It lured small fish in under its belly using its bright glowing blue underside
It snared it in sticky mucus threads it spun out from its muscular foot
context: Reared in aquaria, Glaucus atlanticus used its enlarged front cerata like ARMS, pinning live whitebait (Japanese anchovy) between them and biting near the gills. Histology found a well-developed muscle-fiber layer at the base of these front cerata, which are built longer than the rest 'like an arm,' giving the grip needed to seize fast prey. It fed as a generalist on several cnidarians plus fish, not as a man o' war specialist, and the stolen stingers were NOT observed doing the killing: capture was by physical grip and biting. The frilly cerata, long thought to be purely a defensive sting-battery, turned out to be grasping limbs too. Source: Yamamoto et al. 2025, Ecology, 'Blue angels have devil hands: Predatory behavior using cerata in Glaucus atlanticus' (PMC11912302 / doi:10.1002/ecy.70062).

question: A small octopus hunts along an Australian tide pool, its skin a drab, mottled gray-brown that blends into the rocks. Something disturbs it, and in a third of a second dozens of glowing blue rings erupt across its skin. What is this sudden flash?
answer: A warning display that says 'do not touch'
choices: A warning display that says 'do not touch'
A net it spreads to trap passing fish
A trail of light that lures prey closer
A glow it uses to see in dark water
context: The blue rings are aposematic — a 'do not touch' signal. When resting, the blue-ringed octopus (Hapalochlaena) is a drab grey-to-yellowish brown that camouflages into the rocks; the famous rings stay hidden until it is threatened. Source: Australian Geographic, 'Fact File: Blue-ringed octopus'; Natural History Museum (London).

question: A golf-ball-sized blue-ringed octopus creeps among the rocks of an Australian tide pool. It would much rather avoid a fight than start one. What is the one thing that makes it bite a person?
answer: Being grabbed or stepped on
choices: Being grabbed or stepped on
Swimming past it in open water
Shining a bright light at it
Making a loud noise nearby
context: The rings are a warning, not an attack — the octopus flashes rather than fights, and only bites if it is grabbed or stepped on. Source: Natural History Museum (London), 'The blue-ringed octopus: small, vibrant and exceptionally deadly'.

question: Arms and all, a blue-ringed octopus resting in an Australian tide pool is only 12 to 20 centimeters long, small enough to sit in a person's open hand. Yet a single one carries a great deal of venom. What is that venom enough to do?
answer: Kill more than twenty adult humans within minutes
choices: Kill more than twenty adult humans within minutes
Dissolve a crab's shell in seconds
Stun every fish in a small tide pool
Numb a diver's hand for an hour
context: The blue-ringed octopus is only about 12-20 cm including its arms, yet one carries enough venom to kill over 20 adults within minutes. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'.

question: Among the rocks of a Pacific tide pool, a blue-ringed octopus stalks small crabs and shrimp by ambush. It is far too small to crush a crab's armored shell, so it uses one hard body part to punch through the shell and inject a paralyzing venom. What is that tool?
answer: A hard, parrot-like beak
choices: A hard, parrot-like beak
A row of grinding teeth
A barbed, whip-like tail
A pair of pincer claws
context: The octopus uses a hard, parrot-like beak to pierce a crab's or shrimp's shell and inject venom, hunting small crabs, hermit crabs, and shrimp as an ambush predator. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; animals.net.

question: When a blue-ringed octopus bites, it injects tetrodotoxin, a poison with no known antidote, and the octopus is not the only animal that carries it. One notorious fish holds the very same poison, and in Japan chefs must earn a special license before they may prepare it. Which fish shares this exact poison?
answer: The pufferfish
choices: The pufferfish
The stonefish
The lionfish
The electric eel
context: The venom is tetrodotoxin (TTX), the same poison found in pufferfish (and in some poison dart frogs and newts). The blue-ringed octopus was the first animal known to use tetrodotoxin as a venom. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Science (1978).

question: A wader in an Australian tide pool steps on a blue-ringed octopus and gets a tiny, painless bite. The human body usually clears the octopus's tetrodotoxin within about a day, but within minutes the venom paralyzes something that cannot wait that long. What must a rescuer do for the victim in the meantime?
answer: Put the victim on a ventilator
choices: Put the victim on a ventilator
Warm the victim with blankets
Feed the victim sugar water
Keep the wound above the heart
context: The venom paralyzes the breathing muscles; a victim is kept alive by artificial respiration / a ventilator until the body clears the toxin on its own. Survive the first 24 hours on breathing support and recovery is usually complete. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Snopes citing Aquarium of the Pacific.

question: A blue-ringed octopus subdues a crab with one venom, but researchers have found that it stores a second, different venom in a separate gland. Each kind does its own job. Besides subduing prey, what job does the two-venom system handle?
answer: Fighting off predators
choices: Fighting off predators
Marking its den against rivals
Sealing the wound the beak makes
Coloring the warning rings blue
context: The blue-ringed octopus carries two different venoms in separate glands — one to subdue prey and a second used in defense against predators. Source: Great Barrier Reef Foundation, 'Blue-Ringed Octopus Facts'.

question: Disturbed in its tide pool, a blue-ringed octopus flashes 50 to 60 electric-blue rings across its skin in about one-third of a second, among the fastest color changes of any animal. Ordinary octopus color change relies on slow pigment cells the size of a grain of sand. How does the blue-ring flash so fast?
answer: Muscle-controlled skin pouches snap open over inert mirror cells
choices: Muscle-controlled skin pouches snap open over inert mirror cells
The mirror cells suddenly light up with a glow of their own
A rippling wave of blue pigment floods across the skin
The rings rise up on the skin as tiny inflating bumps
context: The blue iridophores are physiologically inert mirrors tucked into muscle-controlled skin pouches that snap open to reveal the flash, while surrounding brown cells darken for contrast — flashing 50-60 rings in about a third of a second. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology 215(21):3752, Mäthger et al.

question: A blue-ringed octopus carries tetrodotoxin in its bite, a poison that can paralyze a grown person, yet it never paralyzes itself. In 2019 researchers sequenced the octopus's own gene for the very protein the toxin latches onto. What keeps it from poisoning itself?
answer: Three swapped amino acids reshape the docking site so the toxin slips off
choices: Three swapped amino acids reshape the docking site so the toxin slips off
A thick mucus layer sheathes its nerves and soaks up the toxin first
It walls the toxin off in glands its own nerves never make contact with
Its blood runs a carrier protein that ferries the toxin safely away
context: Geffeney et al. (2019) sequenced the Greater Blue-ringed Octopus sodium-channel gene HlNaV1 and found three amino-acid substitutions in the tetrodotoxin-binding site that lower the channel's affinity for the toxin. The striking part is that pufferfish, newts and salamanders, and TTX-resistant snakes independently evolved the SAME kinds of substitutions to survive the SAME poison. That is convergent evolution at its clearest: unrelated animals, facing the identical problem of not killing themselves with their own weapon, arrived at the identical molecular fix. Source: Geffeney, Williams, Rosenthal, et al., 'Convergent and parallel evolution in a voltage-gated sodium channel underlies TTX-resistance in the Greater Blue-ringed Octopus: Hapalochlaena lunulata,' Toxicon (2019), https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10148497 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31550451/

question: A male blue-lined octopus, a close relative of the blue-ringed, creeps toward a female far bigger than he is off the coast of Australia. She will readily grab and eat any suitor that comes near, yet scientists filmed in 2025 how he mates with her for 40 minutes or more and lives. What is his trick?
answer: He bites her aorta at the back of her head and stops her breathing
choices: He bites her aorta at the back of her head and stops her breathing
He mates at arm's length, reaching in with a single specialized arm
He darts in, deposits sperm, and flees before she can turn on him
He mimics a female's coloring to slip past her guard unnoticed
context: Chung et al. (2025, Current Biology) documented the blue-lined octopus (Hapalochlaena fasciata) as the first known animal to weaponize venom for mating. The much smaller male bites the far larger female exactly over the aorta at the back of her head and injects tetrodotoxin; her breathing slows and stops after about eight minutes and her body goes pale, immobilizing her for the 40 to 75 minutes of mating so she cannot cannibalize him. It is a targeted, non-lethal dose delivered to precisely the right spot: she recovers fully afterward, resumes eating, and lays eggs days later. Source: Chung et al., Current Biology (March 2025), reported by Smithsonian Magazine https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/these-male-octopuses-use-venom-to-subdue-female-mates-and-avoid-being-eaten-after-sex-180986208/ and CNN https://www.cnn.com/2025/03/13/science/blue-lined-octopus-venom-mating-scli-intl

question: An African elephant, the biggest animal on land today, would look small beside Argentinosaurus, a long-necked dinosaur that was bigger still. Yet the largest animal known to have lived on Earth is not extinct: it is swimming in the open ocean right now. What is it?
answer: The blue whale
choices: The blue whale
Argentinosaurus
The African elephant
The great white shark
context: A blue whale can reach about 100 feet (30 m) long and weigh up to 200 tons — bigger and far heavier than any dinosaur that ever walked. Source: NOAA Fisheries — Blue Whale species profile (fisheries.noaa.gov/species/blue-whale); Smithsonian Ocean.

question: Argentinosaurus lumbered across prehistoric South America, a long-necked plant-eater over 30 meters long that weighed close to a hundred tons, one of the largest dinosaurs ever found. How does a blue whale, the largest animal alive today, compare with it in weight?
answer: It weighs more than twice as much
choices: It weighs more than twice as much
It weighs about the same
It weighs a little less
It weighs roughly a tenth as much
context: A blue whale can weigh up to 200 tons — as much as about 33 elephants — so even the largest known dinosaur weighed less than half a blue whale. Source: worldatlas.com 'Why the Blue Whale Might Not Be the Largest Animal in History'; Slate 'Whales or dinosaurs' (2014).

question: A blue whale glides through the open ocean, the largest animal ever known to have lived. One single part of its body weighs about three tons all on its own, as much as the biggest land animal alive today. Which body part is it?
answer: Its tongue
choices: Its tongue
Its eye
Its ear bone
Its blowhole
context: A blue whale's tongue can weigh around 3 tons (about 2.7 metric tonnes) — as heavy as a full-grown elephant. Source: AMNH Ology 'A Whale of a Tale'; howstuffworks 'This Is the Biggest Whale'.

question: Visitors to the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto can stand beside a preserved blue whale heart. Counting the aorta, the giant blood vessel above it, the heart stands nearly six and a half feet tall and weighs almost four hundred pounds. Museum staff joked that it was big enough to do what?
answer: Hold a person squeezed in, like a Smart car
choices: Hold a person squeezed in, like a Smart car
Fill an entire swimming pool
Pump a bathtub of blood each beat
Be lifted only by a forklift
context: The preserved heart weighs nearly 400 pounds and stands roughly six and a half feet tall with the aorta, and staff joked that a person could squeeze inside it as if into a Smart car. Source: Smithsonian Magazine 'The Painstaking Process of Preserving a 400-Pound Blue Whale Heart'; Royal Ontario Museum.

question: In storybooks, a child crawls right through a blue whale's aorta, the main artery that carries blood out of a heart weighing nearly 400 pounds. Roughly how wide across is the real aorta, the biggest blood vessel of any animal?
answer: About a dinner plate
choices: About a dinner plate
About a doorway
About a manhole cover
About a coffee mug
context: The blue whale's aorta is roughly 9 inches across — about the width of a dinner plate. That is huge for a blood vessel, but far too narrow for a child to crawl through. Source: funfactz.com 'Blue Whale Aorta Size'; whalefacts.org 'The Blue Whale's Heart'; ROM specimen reporting.

question: A hunting blue whale strains millions of krill, shrimp-like sea creatures barely as long as a finger, from mouthful after mouthful of ocean water, and it eats almost nothing else. About how much krill can one of the biggest blue whales pack away in a single day?
answer: Up to 6 tons
choices: Up to 6 tons
About 20 pounds
Roughly 200 pounds
Around half a ton
context: A big blue whale can eat up to about 6 tons of krill a day — millions of the tiny creatures. Source: NOAA Fisheries — Blue Whale species profile.

question: A blue whale moans across the sea at around 188 decibels, one of the loudest voices in the animal world. Because the sound travels so well through water, distant whales can hear one another across a remarkable distance. How far?
answer: Up to about 1,000 miles
choices: Up to about 1,000 miles
About 10 miles
Roughly 100 yards
A few dozen miles
context: Blue whale calls can be heard by other whales up to 1,000 miles away, letting them communicate across a whole sea. Source: NOAA Fisheries — Blue Whale profile; IFAW 'loudest animals on Earth'.  (Legend.)

question: A blue whale calls out to another whale far across the open ocean while a swimmer floats right beside it in the water. The swimmer may not hear a single sound of the conversation. Why do the calls slip past human ears?
answer: They are too low-pitched for people to hear
choices: They are too low-pitched for people to hear
They are too quiet to detect
They only travel downward, away from the surface
They are drowned out by the whale's heartbeat
context: Blue whale calls run around 10–40 Hz, below the range of human hearing — and low sounds scatter and fade less in water, so they travel far. Source: scienceinsights.org 'How Far Can Blue Whales Communicate Underwater'; NOAA Fisheries.

question: A blue whale mother carries her calf for nearly a full year and gives birth in warm tropical seas. The calf slides out already bigger than most land animals a kid can name. On its very first day of life, it already outweighs a full-grown what?
answer: Elephant
choices: Elephant
Hippopotamus
Giraffe
Bull rhinoceros
context: A newborn blue whale calf is about 23–25 feet long and weighs up to 3 tons at birth — bigger than a full-grown elephant on day one. Source: SeaWorld 'All About Baleen Whales — Birth & Care of Young'; Marine Mammal Center 'Blue Whale'.

question: A blue whale calf nurses on its mother's milk, which runs 35 to 50 percent fat, and grows at a nearly unbelievable pace. A human baby might gain a few ounces a day. About how much does the calf add each day?
answer: About 200 pounds
choices: About 200 pounds
About 5 pounds
About 40 pounds
About 1,000 pounds
context: A blue whale calf gains about 200 pounds (90 kg) every day — roughly 8 to 10 pounds an hour — on milk that is 35–50% fat. Source: SeaWorld 'Birth & Care of Young'; A-Z Animals 'Baby Blue Whale Facts'.

question: Slater, Goldbogen and Pyenson traced the fossil record of whales across an enormous span of prehistory to find out when the blue whale's giant body arose. A body that big might seem ancient. What did the record reveal about how this size came about?
answer: It leapt from about 10 m to 30 m only in the last few million years, on several branches at once
choices: It leapt from about 10 m to 30 m only in the last few million years, on several branches at once
It crept upward at a slow, steady pace across the whole thirty-million-year span
It was already near today’s length in the earliest baleen whales and simply held there
It shrank down from far larger ancestors and has been getting smaller ever since
context: For most of whale history the biggest baleen whales were only about 10 m long. The jump to today's ~30 m happened rapidly and independently on several branches of the family tree around 4.5 million years ago, when the first ice ages began concentrating krill into dense patches through wind-driven coastal upwelling — suddenly it paid to be a colossal filter feeder. The blue whale is the biggest animal ever, yet its body plan is evolutionarily recent and was reinvented more than once. Source: Slater, Goldbogen & Pyenson, 'Independent evolution of baleen whale gigantism linked to Plio-Pleistocene ocean dynamics,' Proceedings of the Royal Society B 284:20170546 (2017); Smithsonian Institution news release (2017).

question: Five thin antennae poke up from the sandy seabed like little fingers, and beneath them a bobbit worm lies buried, only its head showing. When a fish glides past, what are those antennae doing for the hidden worm?
answer: Acting as tripwires that a passing fish brushes
choices: Acting as tripwires that a passing fish brushes
Filtering plankton from the passing current
Soaking up sunlight to warm its buried body
Waving to attract a mate across the sand
context: The bobbit worm buries nearly its entire body and leaves only its head exposed, waiting motionless. When a fish brushes one of the five antennae, the worm strikes. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'What is a bobbit worm?' — https://www.sciencefocus.com/nature/what-is-a-bobbit-worm

question: Only the head of a bobbit worm shows above the sandy seabed; almost all of its body hides below. The longest one ever measured, stretched out flat, was about as long as what?
answer: A small car, nearly 10 feet
choices: A small car, nearly 10 feet
A dinner fork, about 8 inches
A garden snake, about 2 feet
A school bus, about 40 feet
context: The longest bobbit worm ever recorded measured 299 cm — nearly 10 feet — though its body averages only about 25 mm (one inch) wide, making it one of the longest worms in the ocean. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eunice aphroditois' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunice_aphroditois

question: A fish swims past a patch of seabed where a bobbit worm waits buried, and in a split second the worm strikes and yanks its catch down under the sand. What can its scissor-like jaws sometimes do to a fish in that strike?
answer: Slice it clean in two
choices: Slice it clean in two
Crush its skull in one bite
Tear off a chunk and let the rest flee
Pin it against the sand and swallow it whole
context: The strike comes so fast that the fish has no time to flee. The worm's razor-sharp jaws can sometimes slice the prey clean in two before dragging it down into the sand. Those jaws are paired mandibles and larger serrated, hooked maxillae that snap shut like scissors. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'What is a bobbit worm?' — https://www.sciencefocus.com/nature/what-is-a-bobbit-worm

question: A four-foot bobbit worm the staff named Barry turned up in a reef tank at the Blue Reef Aquarium in Newquay, England, though nobody there had ever bought or ordered him. He had been growing quietly in the tank for years. How did he first get in?
answer: He hitchhiked in as a tiny juvenile inside 'live rock'
choices: He hitchhiked in as a tiny juvenile inside 'live rock'
He crawled up a drainpipe from the sea outside
He arrived inside a delivery of frozen fish food
He hatched from eggs stuck to a new fish's fins
context: Barry had hitchhiked in as a tiny juvenile hidden inside a piece of 'live rock' the aquarium had bought, then grew undetected in the tank, possibly for years — one reason a bobbit worm can go unseen for so long is that it recoils and vanishes down its burrow whenever a bright light hits it. Source: BBC Science Focus + The Misfits Pair archive — https://themisfitspair.com/2009/04/01/barry-the-giant-sea-worm-discovered-by-aquarium-staff-after-mysterious-attacks-on-coral-reef/

question: In 20-million-year-old rock in Taiwan, Yu-Yen Pan's team found 319 fossils of ancient bobbit-type worms, yet not one worm's body was preserved. A soft, boneless worm almost never fossilizes, so the fossils record something else the worms left behind. What got fossilized instead?
answer: The L-shaped burrow the worm hunted from
choices: The L-shaped burrow the worm hunted from
A cast of the worm’s serrated jaws
A trail of its scattered bristles
A tangle of shed skins and molts
context: This is one of the rare cases where a predator's BEHAVIOR fossilized rather than its body. Yu-Yen Pan and colleagues named the trace fossil Pennichnus formosae from ~20-million-year-old Miocene rock (Taliao Formation) in northeast Taiwan: L-shaped burrows up to 2 m long and only 2-3 cm wide, the buried lair of an ancient bobbit-type worm. Near the top of each burrow, X-ray scans show an abrupt spike in iron: chemical residue of the worm's mucus, which fed bacteria that built iron minerals as the worm rebuilt and reinforced its lair after each violent strike. Repeated dragging of prey down the funnel left distinctive 'feather-like' collapse structures at the mouth. Bobbit-worm jaws do survive elsewhere as fossils called scolecodonts, but here only the burrow was preserved. Source: Pan et al., Scientific Reports 11:1174 (2021), via PMC7820589 and Nature s41598-020-79311-0.

question: Buried head-up in the sand, a bobbit worm strikes at passing fish in a blur. Yet its jaws sit at the front of a soft, boneless body, with no arm or claw to swing them forward. How does the worm launch its jaws at its prey?
answer: It turns its throat inside-out, hurling the jaws forward
choices: It turns its throat inside-out, hurling the jaws forward
It coils and snaps a muscular tail like a whip
It flicks them out on the tip of a long, sticky tongue
It rams its whole burrow upward against the fish
context: The strike is powered by pharynx eversion: the worm turns its muscular throat inside-out, flinging the jaw apparatus — interlocking mandibles plus serrated maxillae — forward like a spring-loaded gin trap, then retracts the whole thing to drag prey underground. Having no hard skeleton, the worm holds its long shape with a hydrostatic (fluid-pressure) skeleton — the same pressurized-fluid trick that powers the launch. The record wild specimen measured 299 cm (about 9.8 ft) yet was only ~25.5 mm wide, making it the longest known polychaete; despite the fearsome hunting it also scavenges algae and dead matter and lives only about 3–5 years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunice_aphroditois, with strike-eversion mechanics corroborated by ScienceInsights and BiologyInsights secondary summaries.

question: A female bolas spider hunts moths at night without building any web at all. She dangles from a branch on a single silk thread. When a moth flutters close, how does she catch it?
answer: She swings a sticky glue ball on a thread at it
choices: She swings a sticky glue ball on a thread at it
She leaps off her thread and grabs it in midair
She casts a small silk net over it
She spits sticky silk at it from a distance
context: The spider swings her single glue-tipped line like a bolas — a South American throwing weapon of weights on cords — to snag moths right out of the air, which is how the spider got its name. Source: https://spiderbytes.org/2015/03/17/bolas-spiders-masters-of-deception/

question: By day a bolas spider cannot hunt, so it curls up motionless on a small silk mat spun across the top of a leaf, holding a shape and color that no bird would choose to peck. What does the daytime bolas spider pretend to be?
answer: A fresh bird dropping
choices: A fresh bird dropping
A drop of morning dew
A curled dead leaf
A clump of pale fungus
context: Motionless on its silk mat, the bulbous, waxy-white spider looks exactly like a fresh bird dropping, so predators pass it by. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastophora_hutchinsoni

question: A North American bolas spider, Mastophora hutchinsoni, hunts moths all night, luring them in with a fake female-moth scent. The moths caught before 11 p.m. belong to one species, and those caught after 11 p.m. to an entirely different one. What does the spider itself change as the night goes on?
answer: It tones down one moth's scent, so its blend suits the later moth
choices: It tones down one moth's scent, so its blend suits the later moth
It swings its line faster to snag the bigger moths flying late
It creeps to a fresh leaf where the later moths gather
It brightens its lure so the later moths can see it
context: Mastophora hutchinsoni gives off a blend that mimics the sex scents of two moths: the bristly cutworm, which flies early in the evening, and the smoky tetanolita, which flies late at night. As the night goes on, the spider cuts back the cutworm scent, which would otherwise put off the later moth, so the species stuck to its glue ball changes through the night. Source: Haynes et al. 2002, Chemoecology 12:99-105, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00049-002-8332-2

question: Under a rotting log scurries a bombardier beetle, a dark beetle barely half an inch long. When an ant grabs it, the beetle aims the tip of its abdomen at the attacker and answers with a loud pop, like a tiny gun, and the ant lets go at once. What does it fire?

A cloud of sticky silk threads
A blinding flash of green light
A blast of foul-smelling gas only
context: When seized, the bombardier beetle fires a caustic spray from the rear of its abdomen with an audible pop. The spray is genuinely scalding, not just smelly: the jet shoots out at close to 100 C (212 F) -- the boiling point of water -- so it scalds the mouth or feet of an attacker. The beetle (subfamily Brachininae) is named for this artillery-like blast: it keeps two harmless chemicals stored apart inside its body and mixes them with enzymes in a hardened reaction chamber only when attacked, where the violently exothermic reaction flash-heats the fluid to near boiling. Source: Natural History Museum, London -- 'Bombardier beetles and their caustic chemical cannon' (nhm.ac.uk); Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle' citing Aneshansley & Eisner, 'Biochemistry at 100 C'; https://www.chemistrysteps.com/the-chemistry-behind-bombardier-beetles-spray/

question: A bombardier beetle carries the makings of a scalding chemical spray inside its own body, yet it never burns itself. The secret lies in how it keeps the two chemicals behind the spray. What setup keeps the beetle safe from its own weapon?

choices: The two chemicals are stored in separate sacs, apart
The two chemicals are frozen solid until needed
A thick layer of fat soaks up all the heat
The chemicals are diluted with water until harmless
context: The beetle stores hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinone in separate little reservoirs, safely apart, and only lets them meet at the instant of firing. Source: Natural History Museum, London; Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle'.

question: When cornered, a bombardier beetle sets off a reaction inside a reinforced chamber at the back of its abdomen. Powerful enzymes lining the chamber speed the reaction until, in an instant, it explodes outward at the attacker. Which enzymes trigger that explosion?

Pepsin and trypsin

context: The reaction chamber is lined with catalase and peroxidase; when the stored chemicals meet these enzymes the reaction is fast and hot enough to boil and blast outward. Source: Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle'; Chemistry Steps, 'The Chemistry Behind Bombardier Beetle's Spray'.

question: Thomas Eisner's team at Cornell aimed a high-speed camera at firing bombardier beetles for a 1990 study. Scientists had long assumed the scalding spray came out in one steady stream, but the film showed a rapid machine-gun burst of separate blasts, about 70 of them per firing. Roughly how fast is that pulsing?

About 5 pulses per second
About 50 pulses per second
About 5,000 pulses per second
context: The spray fires as a biological pulse jet -- roughly 70 pulses at about 500 per second -- as high-speed film by Thomas Eisner's team showed. The rapid pulsing also protects the beetle: each tiny explosion is released before the next, so the reinforced chamber never overloads. Source: Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle' citing Dean, Aneshansley, Edgerton & Eisner, 'Defensive spray of the bombardier beetle: a biological pulse jet,' Science (1990); https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.2349480

question: Toads in a lab experiment flicked out their sticky tongues and swallowed bombardier beetles whole. Deep in the toads' stomachs the trapped beetles fired their scalding spray, and faint pops sounded from inside. Then 43 percent of the toads did something that saved the beetles' lives. Passed it out whole in their droppings
Fell asleep for the rest of the day
Stopped digesting until its spray ran out

Beetles spent 12 to 107 minutes inside, scuttled off covered in slime, and nearly all survived; one lived at least 562 more days. Source: Sugiura & Sato, 'Successful escape of bombardier beetles from predator digestive systems,' Biology Letters (2018).

question: A male satin bowerbird gathers treasures for the small stage he has built on the floor of an eastern Australian forest. He will raid other males' stages to steal them, and he prizes objects of one color above all others. Which color does he collect?

Red
Yellow
White

Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird; Coffs Botanic Garden 'Bower Power'.

question: A female satin bowerbird spends days touring the decorated stages that rival males have built on the forest floor. She watches each male strut and quiver his blue-black wings, then picks the one that impresses her most. After they mate, who builds the nest and raises the chicks?

Female bowerbirds are the judges who inspect several rival bowers before choosing. Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird; Coffs Botanic Garden 'Bower Power'.

question: Scrappy trial bowers dot a forest floor in eastern Australia, built by a young male satin bowerbird still dressed in the dull olive-green of the females. His father is glossy blue-black with violet eyes. About how long does the young male take to molt into that adult plumage?

A single season
Two years
Twenty years

question: A sea creature moves through the warm shallows off northern Australia. Its clear, jelly-like bell is not the rounded dome of most jellyfish but a cube with four flat sides, and a bundle of tentacles trails from each corner. What is this square-shaped creature called?
answer: The box jellyfish
choices: The box jellyfish
The moon jellyfish
The sea gooseberry
The Portuguese man o' war
context: The box jellyfish is named for its body: a see-through, cube-shaped bell with four flat sides, unlike the round dome of an ordinary jellyfish. A cluster of tentacles trails from each of the four corners. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish

question: A box jellyfish in the warm water off northern Australia squeezes its cube-shaped bell like a fist and jets off at around 1.5 meters a second, while ordinary jellyfish drift wherever the current pushes them. How sharply can it turn?
answer: A full 180-degree turn in a few beats of its bell

Only in a slow, wide arc over several minutes

context: A box jellyfish does not just drift like most jellyfish; it actively swims, reaching about 1.5 metres per second and rapidly turning up to 180 degrees in just a few contractions of its bell. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish

question: Around the four flat sides of Chironex fleckeri, the Australian box jellyfish, hang four little grape-shaped sensory pods called rhopalia, and every pod carries its own set of eyes. Counting every eye on every pod, how many does this brainless jellyfish have?

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish; https://aussieanimals.com/profiles/box-jellyfish-chironex-fleckeri/

question: An Australian box jellyfish swims with no brain at all, just a simple ring of nerves around the rim of its cube-shaped bell. Even so, eyes stare out from its four little sensory pods, and not all of them work the same way. Some are simple pigmented patches that respond only to light; a few are far more advanced. What kind of eyes are those?

question: Hundreds of thousands of microscopic coiled harpoons called nematocysts line each tentacle of a box jellyfish, each ready to shoot a poisoned barb into prey. Yet when the jellyfish bumps into a piece of driftwood or a floating leaf, not one of them fires. What actually triggers a stinging cell to shoot its barb?

context: A box jellyfish tentacle is lined with hundreds of thousands of stinging capsules called nematocysts, microscopic coiled harpoons that fire not from touch alone but when they sense the chemicals on skin, so they don't waste on driftwood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4379534/

question: Swimmers on the beaches of northern Australia watch for the almost invisible tentacles of Chironex fleckeri, the Australian box jellyfish, far more carefully than they watch for sharks. It is among the most venomous animals alive. What can a serious sting do to a person if help does not come in time?

Cause hours of full-body paralysis while the victim stays conscious

Shut down the kidneys slowly over several days
context: Chironex fleckeri is among the most venomous animals alive; a serious sting can cause the heart to stop, and untreated victims have died within two to five minutes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chironex_fleckeri; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7285912/

question: An Australian box jellyfish's clear cube-shaped bell tumbles and tilts every which way as it swims through the water, so its eyes are constantly being rolled around. Inside each of the four sensory pods hanging off the sides of the bell, a heavy crystal weight called a statolith dangles at the end of a flexible stalk. context: In each rhopalium a heavy crystal weight called a statolith acts like a tiny plumb bob, hanging on a flexible stalk so the eyes stay pointed up-and-down no matter how the jellyfish's bell tumbles or tilts. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish

question: A fish hangs in a clear river, and beneath the hard bony flap on each side of its head, called the operculum, lie neat stacks of soft, feathery red tissue packed with tiny blood vessels. Underwater, what does the fish use this organ to do?

Sense water pressure
context: Those red feathery stacks are the gills - a fish's underwater lungs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_gill

question: Under the bony flap on each side of a fish's head, water streams over rows of soft, feathery filaments. They look nothing like ordinary flesh: they are a vivid, deep blood-red, not pink or gray, almost raw-looking. What makes them that startling color?
answer: Blood packed right at the surface
choices: Blood packed right at the surface
A red waxy coating that repels water
Red pigment cells for camouflage
Iron-rich slime the fish secretes
context: Each filament is crammed with tiny capillaries where blood picks up oxygen - the red you see IS the blood lying just under a wafer-thin surface. Source: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/fish-dissections/

question: A goldfish rests in the middle of a fishbowl, its fins still, swimming nowhere. Yet the bony covers over its gills keep fluttering open and shut, open and shut, without a pause. What is that endless flutter doing for the goldfish?
answer: Pumping a fresh flow of water across its gills
choices: Pumping a fresh flow of water across its gills
Cooling its blood in warm water
Shaking loose bits of trapped food
Signaling to other fish nearby
context: By opening its mouth and flaring the gill cover (buccal pumping), a resting fish drives water over its gills without swimming a stroke - which is why the covers visibly flutter. Source: https://poseidonsweb.com/how-fish-breathe-ram-ventilation-buccal-pumping/

question: A swimming fish takes water in at its mouth and lets it out under its gill covers, always one way, never washing back. A land animal, by contrast, pulls each breath in and pushes it back out through the same opening. What single advantage does the fish's one-way flow give its gills?
answer: They never bathe in water already drained of oxygen
choices: They never bathe in water already drained of oxygen
They pull oxygen across twice as fast per breath
They never touch water colder than the fish's blood
They filter out the salt before oxygen crosses
context: Lungs are a dead end - fresh and used air share one pipe, so some stale air always lingers. A fish's flow runs straight through, so its gills always face water it has not yet stripped of oxygen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_gill

question: Out in the open sea a tuna powers along at speed, while a fish of similar size spends its whole life resting on the seafloor. One of the two has unmistakably richer gills, with denser comb-like red filaments crowding each gill arch. Which fish has the richer gills, and why?
answer: The tuna's - a relentless swimmer needs far more surface to feed its muscles
choices: The tuna's - a relentless swimmer needs far more surface to feed its muscles
The bottom-dweller's - lying still, it must hoard every scrap of oxygen
The bottom-dweller's - the still water near the seafloor is poorer in oxygen
The tuna's - fast water flow scours its filaments larger over time
context: Bony fish carry four pairs of gill arches lined with comb-like filaments, and the more active the swimmer, the more developed those combs become - a hard-driving tuna packs far denser filaments than a fish that rests on the bottom. Source: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/fish-dissections/

question: A fish in a freshwater lake lives on thin pickings, because a liter of fresh water holds only a sliver of the oxygen in a liter of air. To grab enough oxygen from water that poor, what must its gills have above all?
answer: Enormous surface area
choices: Enormous surface area
A powerful pumping muscle
A way to warm the water first
Thick protective walls
context: With water holding only about a twenty-sixth of air's oxygen, gills solve it with sheer area - vast thin surfaces so more oxygen can cross into the blood at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_gill

question: Inside each thin gill plate, or lamella, a fish drives its blood the opposite way to the water flowing over the outside, so the two run against each other along the whole plate. This one design is why a fish can strip far more oxygen from water than it otherwise could. How does running them against each other manage that?
answer: The blood always meets water still richer in oxygen than itself
choices: The blood always meets water still richer in oxygen than itself
The two flows cancel out and let oxygen settle at a steady midpoint
The oxygen is squeezed across faster by the blood's higher pressure
The blood loads fastest right where it enters and then coasts
context: This is countercurrent exchange: because blood and water run opposite ways, the blood never catches up to water it has already emptied - it always faces water a little richer than itself, so oxygen keeps crossing along the whole lamella instead of stopping halfway. Source: https://fishbio.com/an-efficient-exchange/

question: A tuna races through the open sea too fast to pump water with its gill covers. Instead it swims with its mouth gaping to force water through its gills, and that locks it into a rule it can never break. What is that rule?
answer: It must keep swimming forever or it suffocates
choices: It must keep swimming forever or it suffocates
It can only breathe in warm surface water
It must return to shallow water each night
It can never swim faster than its own gill-pumping
context: This is ram ventilation - the tuna rams water through its gills by moving forward, so if it ever stops swimming, the flow stops and it drowns. Great white, mako and salmon sharks live under the same sentence. Source: https://poseidonsweb.com/how-fish-breathe-ram-ventilation-buccal-pumping/

question: A nurse shark lies motionless on the sandy floor of a warm Atlantic reef for hours at a stretch, its tail still and its long body flat against the bottom. It does not need to swim to stay alive. How does it keep breathing without moving?
answer: It pumps water over its gills with its cheek muscles
choices: It pumps water over its gills with its cheek muscles
It absorbs oxygen straight through its skin
It surfaces every few minutes to gulp air
It slows its heart until it barely needs oxygen
context: The nurse shark breathes by buccal pumping: its cheek muscles draw water into its mouth and force it out again over the gills, so the gills stay supplied with oxygen even while it rests on the bottom, where a ram-ventilating shark would suffocate. Source: Shark Trust, 'Creature Feature: Nurse Sharks' (https://www.sharktrust.org/blog/creature-feature-nurse-sharks)

question: The red feathery gill grabs oxygen - but tucked among that same tissue sit special cells busy with a second job that has nothing to do with breathing. A cod in the sea and a trout in a river both carry them, each tuned to its own water. What quiet task are these cells performing?
answer: Holding the blood at the right saltiness against the water outside
choices: Holding the blood at the right saltiness against the water outside
Sensing the water temperature so the fish knows when to spawn
Storing spare oxygen for moments the fish holds still and rests
Regrowing filaments worn thin by the endless rush of water
context: The fish gill is not just a lung-underwater - it is also the animal's kidney and its acid-base buffer. Beyond gas exchange, it is the dominant site where a fish dumps its nitrogen waste (as ammonia) and controls its blood salt and pH. The work is done by mitochondrion-packed cells wedged among the respiratory tissue, historically called 'chloride cells' and now 'ionocytes.' In seawater - saltier than the fish's blood - these cells actively pump excess salt OUT; a freshwater fish, flooded by dilute water, runs the very same cells in reverse to pull scarce ions IN. So the same organ that captures oxygen is quietly excreting waste and holding the fish's internal chemistry steady. Source: Wikipedia 'Fish gill' corroborated by Evans, Piermarini & Choe (2005), 'The Multifunctional Fish Gill,' Physiological Reviews 85:97-177.

question: A single sting from the giant black bullet ant of the South American rainforest brings waves of burning, throbbing agony that keep pounding through the victim's arm or leg long after the ant itself is gone. How long can the pain of one sting go on?
answer: Up to a full day
choices: Up to a full day
About ten minutes
About one hour
Up to a full week
context: The pain can continue unabated for up to a full day, which is why Venezuelans call it 'hormiga veinticuatro,' the 24-hour ant. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraponera_clavata

question: To pass into manhood, boys of the Satere-Mawe people of the Brazilian Amazon must slide a bare hand into a specially woven ceremonial glove and hold it there for about ten minutes. Enduring the pain in silence is what proves them ready to be men. They repeat this ordeal roughly twenty times over the course of their youth before the initiation is complete. What is packed inside that glove?
answer: Dozens of live bullet ants
choices: Dozens of live bullet ants
Glowing embers
Stinging nettles
Venomous spiders
context: The Satere-Mawe first sedate the ants in an herbal solution, then weave them into a glove of cashew-palm leaves with the stingers turned inward toward the wearer's hand. Source: https://whyevolutionistrue.com/2014/08/06/the-worst-pain-known-to-humans-the-bullet-ant-gloves-of-brazil/

question: A bullet ant stings, and one small protein in its venom, poneratoxin, gets into the victim's nerves and hijacks their electrical wiring. The agony comes not from acid burning the tissue or from swelling around the wound. What does poneratoxin do?
answer: Jams the sodium channels that carry nerve signals
choices: Jams the sodium channels that carry nerve signals
Dissolves the fatty sheath around each nerve
Floods the muscles with excess calcium
Starves the nerve endings of oxygen
context: Poneratoxin locks up the voltage-gated sodium channels nerves use to fire, scrambling the signals they send each other. There are no recorded human deaths from the sting, and the toxin fully clears the body within about a day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraponera_clavata

question: A long, ringed, slick-skinned animal squirms through wet tropical soil. It looks like a giant earthworm, yet it has a backbone, a skull and jaws, and no legs at all. What is it?
answer: A caecilian, a legless amphibian
choices: A caecilian, a legless amphibian
A slow-worm, a legless lizard
A worm snake, a burrowing snake
An amphisbaenian, a worm lizard
context: Caecilians (order Gymnophiona) are the least-known group of amphibians - true amphibians like frogs and salamanders, but with no legs and a long, segmented, worm-like body. They are not worms and not snakes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caecilian

question: A caecilian spends its life burrowing out of sight through warm, wet soil, and few people ever see one. More than 220 kinds live in the tropics of several continents. One big continent, with plenty of tropical forest, has none of its own. Which one?
answer: Australia
choices: Australia
Africa
South America
North America
context: There are over 220 caecilian species across 10 families, found in the tropics of South and Central America, Africa, southern Asia and the Seychelles - but never in Australia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caecilian

question: A caecilian hunts through pitch-dark soil almost blind, yet it still tracks down prey. Between each eye and nostril sits a small organ found in no other animal with a backbone, which it pushes out and pulls back as it burrows. What is this one-of-a-kind organ?
answer: A chemical-sensing tentacle
choices: A chemical-sensing tentacle
A warmth-sensing tentacle
An electric-sensing tentacle
A magnetism-sensing tentacle
context: The tentacle sits in a groove between eye and nostril, can be pushed out and pulled back, and connects to the animal's smell system - a sensory organ unique among all vertebrates that lets a nearly blind caecilian hunt underground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caecilian

question: A mother caecilian, Boulengerula taitanus, lies coiled in her nest in a wet mountain forest of Kenya, and her newly hatched young swarm over her body. They scrape at her with a special set of teeth found only in the young. What are those teeth for?
answer: Peeling and eating her skin
choices: Peeling and eating her skin
Gripping her as she carries them
Combing parasites from her sides
Tearing up worms she brings in
context: Alexander Kupfer and his team first documented this skin-feeding (dermatophagy) in Boulengerula taitanus. The babies scrape off the fatty skin about every three days - the time a new layer takes to regrow - and can grow up to 10 times their own weight in a single week. It is a form of maternal care, not cruelty. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04403

question: Brazilian researchers studying the ringed caecilian, Siphonops annulatus, a limbless burrowing amphibian, reported in 2020 that it may share a trait long famous in snakes. If the finding holds up, caecilians could be the oldest land animals with a backbone to have it, older even than snakes. Which trait?
answer: A venom system in its mouth
choices: A venom system in its mouth
Heat-sensing pits on its face
A forked, scent-tasting tongue
Jaws that stretch around prey
context: Researchers found tiny glands at the base of the teeth that release fluid when the caecilian bites, carrying phospholipase A2, an enzyme also found in bee, wasp and snake venom. This reported finding is still under study, but if confirmed it may make caecilians the oldest land vertebrate with an oral venom system, older even than venomous snakes. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7385905/

question: A one-humped camel plods calmly over loose desert dunes, hardly sinking, where a horse would punch its narrow hooves straight down into the sand and bog itself. What keeps the camel walking on top of the dunes?
answer: Broad two-toed feet
choices: Broad two-toed feet
Tiny hardened hooves
A single padded toe
Long curved climbing claws
context: Each broad, two-toed foot spreads and flattens under the camel's weight, then contracts when lifted, working like a natural snowshoe that keeps it from sinking into loose sand. Source: San Diego Zoo, Camel.

question: A camel plods on through a long, hot desert crossing, and day by day its hump shrinks and flops over to one side. What is really stored in the hump?
answer: Fat stored for the journey
choices: Fat stored for the journey
Water stored for the journey
A spongy sac of blood
Coiled muscle for climbing
context: The hump is a concentrated fat reserve the camel burns when food is scarce. Keeping the fat in one hump rather than spread under the skin also lets the rest of the body shed heat more easily. Source: WWF, What do camels store in their humps?

question: A desert camel wanders up to a fat green cactus bristling with long needles. It chomps the cactus down, spines and all, and swallows without a scratch. What inside its mouth handles the needles safely on the way down?
answer: Cone-shaped mouth spikes that steer each needle point-first down
choices: Cone-shaped mouth spikes that steer each needle point-first down
A thick saliva coating that dissolves the spines before swallowing
Molars that snap each needle off cleanly at its base
A second set of lips that strips the spines away first
context: Cone-shaped keratin papillae line the camel's mouth and rotate the spines so they slide straight down the throat point-first; a vet described them as feeling almost like plastic. Source: National Geographic, Arabian Camels Eat Cacti With Hardened Mouth Structures.

question: A badly dehydrated camel reaches a stone trough at an oasis after days on hot sand with no water. It plunges its muzzle in and drinks nonstop for about ten minutes, its belly swelling. How much water can it take on in that one long drink?
answer: Over 100 liters
choices: Over 100 liters
About 10 liters
About 60 liters
Around 30 liters
context: A dehydrated camel can gulp well over 100 liters in about ten minutes; the San Diego Zoo cites up to 145 liters (32 gallons) in a single drink, replacing about a third of its body weight almost at once. Source: San Diego Zoo, Camel.

question: A camel stands on blazing desert sand through the burning day. Sweating would shed the heat but spend water it cannot spare, so instead it does something with its own body that most mammals never risk. What does the camel do?
answer: Lets its body temperature climb by day and cool at night
choices: Lets its body temperature climb by day and cool at night
Slows its heartbeat to a near-standstill until dusk
Shunts blood away from its skin to trap heat inside
Shuts down its kidneys to hoard every last drop
context: Rather than sweating, a camel lets its core temperature swing widely, cooling to about 34-35 C overnight and coasting up to 41-42 C by day. Storing the heat in its own body instead of evaporating water to shed it saves enormous amounts of water. Source: Schmidt-Nielsen, 1956, Body Temperature of the Camel and Its Relation to Water Economy.

question: A barrel-shaped grazer plods along a South American riverbank, chomping grass. It stretches about four feet long, can weigh as much as a grown man, and is the biggest rodent alive. What is it?
answer: The capybara
choices: The capybara
The beaver
The porcupine
The muskrat
context: The capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) is the largest living rodent: adults grow to about 106 to 134 cm (3.5 to 4.4 ft) long and typically weigh 35 to 66 kg (77 to 146 lb). The heaviest wild one on record was a 91 kg (201 lb) female from Brazil. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara

question: A capybara spends its waking hours grinding tough, gritty grass with its big front teeth, wear that would file an ordinary tooth down to a useless stub. Yet an old capybara bites just as well as a young one. What trick of a rodent's front teeth beats the wear?
answer: The teeth never stop growing
choices: The teeth never stop growing
New adult teeth replace the worn ones each year
A hard enamel cap makes them wear-proof
Saliva slowly rebuilds the worn edges
context: Like all rodents, the capybara's front incisors grow continuously throughout its life, replacing exactly what constant grass-grinding wears away. That is the defining rodent trait — the word 'rodent' comes from Latin for 'to gnaw.' Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/things-you-might-not-know-about-capybaras.html

question: A jaguar prowls the riverbank, and a capybara slips into the water to hide, its big body vanishing below the surface. It keeps watching and listening for the cat, and it goes on breathing the whole time. What makes that possible?
answer: Its eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on its head
choices: Its eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on its head
A snorkel-like snout it lifts above the surface
It floats on its back with its face upturned
A long neck that holds its head above water
context: A capybara's eyes, ears, and nostrils are all set high on the top of its head, so it can float with almost its whole body submerged and still see, hear, and breathe — the same layout a hippopotamus uses. It can even sleep in the water with just its nose poking out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara

question: A capybara lives on grass, a food so tough that bacteria in its gut must break it down. Those bacteria make protein and B vitamins, but much of that would slip out of its body unabsorbed. Each morning the capybara does something that startles people who watch it. What does it do?
answer: It re-eats its own soft morning droppings
choices: It re-eats its own soft morning droppings
It licks mineral-rich mud from the riverbank
It swallows small stones to grind grass
It eats the droppings of the young in its group
context: The capybara is a hindgut fermenter: an enlarged cecum and colon full of bacteria break down grass cellulose its stomach cannot. Because the nutrients those bacteria make would otherwise be lost, it re-eats its soft morning droppings (coprophagy), passing the food through twice to absorb the protein and B vitamins — the same trick rabbits use. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00264639

question: Deep in the rainforests of Australia and New Guinea, a shiny black bird as tall as a grown man walks across the forest floor. Its neck is electric blue, and a tall helmet like a horn rises from its head. What bird is it?
answer: The cassowary
choices: The cassowary
The greater rhea
The secretary bird
The shoebill stork
context: The southern cassowary stands up to about 2 metres (6 feet) tall, with glossy black feathers, bright blue skin on the head and fore-neck, red on the rear neck, and a tall greyish 'casque' helmet. Source: Australian Museum, Southern Cassowary.

question: A cassowary cornered on a rainforest path does not run. It leaps and drives both powerful feet forward at the threat, like a kung fu kick. The weapon rides on the inner toe of each foot. What is it?
answer: A long, dagger-like claw
choices: A long, dagger-like claw
A ring of backward-facing barbs
A gripping talon like an eagle's
A blunt spur it uses to trip
context: The inner toe on each foot ends in a dagger-like claw up to about 12 cm (5 inches) long. A threatened cassowary leaps and kicks, and the claw can slash open internal organs. Source: Wikipedia, Cassowary / Southern cassowary.

question: A cassowary chick trots behind its father across the dark rainforest floor, looking nothing like the glossy black adult. For its first months a bold striped pattern hides it against the ground. What do field guides say the chick most resembles?
answer: A watermelon
choices: A watermelon
A newborn fawn
A ring-tailed lemur
A rolled-up pangolin
context: Cassowary chicks hatch striped like watermelons — brown-and-cream banded down the back and thighs for camouflage — and lose the stripes at about 3 to 6 months, turning plain brown. Source: Birdfact, 'Baby Cassowaries' / San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance factsheet.

question: Unseen in the gloom of the forest, a cassowary gives a booming call near 32 hertz, right at the bottom of what human ears can pick up. Researchers think the bird uses so deep a note to do one thing a higher call could not. What is it?
answer: Carry far through thick rainforest foliage
choices: Carry far through thick rainforest foliage
Startle predators into freezing
Echo off the ground to map the forest
Mimic the calls of other animals
context: Cassowaries produce some of the lowest-frequency sounds known in any bird — deep booming notes reaching about 32 Hz — thought to carry through dense foliage where higher-pitched calls fade. The casque may act as a receiver/amplifier for these calls, though its exact function is still debated. Source: Researchgate, 'Low-Frequency Vocalizations by Cassowaries' / Rainforest Trust, 'Seven Things'.

question: A chameleon sits perfectly still on a branch, spots an insect a good distance off, and strikes without moving its body. Its weapon shoots out, hits the bug and reels back in about the time a human takes to blink. What is the weapon?
answer: Its tongue, flung out past twice its body length
choices: Its tongue, flung out past twice its body length
A jet of sticky venom sprayed from its jaw
A whip of its coiled, grabbing tail
A puff of glue blown from its throat
context: A chameleon's tongue rockets out about 2.5 times its own body length and slams into an insect in roughly 20 milliseconds, a fraction of a blink. Source: Brown University, 2016 (Christopher Anderson study of Rhampholeon spinosus); Wikipedia, Chameleon.
