question: From its perch, a chameleon keeps watch on a hawk circling overhead and a beetle crawling on the branch behind it, both at once. Its eyes bulge like little turrets from the sides of its head. What can its two eyes do?
answer: Each eye swivels on its own, aiming in a different direction
choices: Each eye swivels on its own, aiming in a different direction
Both eyes glow to spot warm-blooded prey in the dark
The eyes see straight through leaves and thin bark
The eyes flatten to give a single wide panorama
context: A chameleon's two eyes swivel independently inside cone-shaped turrets, letting it watch two directions at once and scan almost a full 360-degree circle without turning its head; its brain analyzes two separate images. Source: Wikipedia, Chameleon; AskNature 'Eyes Give 360-degree Vision'.

question: A chameleon on the hunt scans the leaves, its two turret eyes roaming. The instant it spots a bug worth catching, the eyes do something sudden together. What happens just before the strike?
answer: Both eyes snap forward onto the same target to judge distance
choices: Both eyes snap forward onto the same target to judge distance
Both eyes squeeze shut to protect against the recoil
The eyes flash a bright color to freeze the prey
The eyes retract deep into the skull for safety
context: When a chameleon locks on, both eyes fix forward on the same target, and it judges the distance to within a few millimeters, because once the tongue fires there is no chance to correct its aim. Source: animalsaroundtheglobe.com; AskNature 'Eyes Give 360-degree Vision'.

question: A chameleon flushes from green to yellow to bright orange in seconds, even with nothing hunting it. Most people assume the color change is camouflage, but biologists who watch chameleons closely say that is mostly wrong. What is the change mainly for?
answer: Broadcasting its mood and controlling its temperature
choices: Broadcasting its mood and controlling its temperature
Poisoning any predator that bites its bright skin
Confusing prey so insects freeze in place
Marking a trail so it can find its way home
context: Chameleons change color mainly to signal mood and intentions and to warm up or cool down, not chiefly to camouflage; a calm chameleon and an angry, showing-off one are literally different colors. Source: Wikipedia, Chameleon; Nature Communications ncomms7368 (Teyssier et al. 2015).

question: Nearly a hundred kinds of chameleon creep through the trees of one place on Earth and are found wild nowhere else. That is about half of all the chameleon species known to science, which number roughly 200. Where do they all live?
answer: Madagascar
choices: Madagascar
The Galapagos Islands
New Zealand
Borneo
context: About half of all roughly 200 described chameleon species live only on Madagascar, found nowhere else on Earth. Source: Wikipedia, Chameleon ('200 species described as of June 2015'; about half restricted to Madagascar).

question: Two male Jackson's chameleons meet on the same branch in the mountains of East Africa. Each carries three forward-pointing horns on his face, one above each eye and one on the nose, like a tiny Triceratops. What do the rivals do with those horns?
answer: Lock them together and try to shove each other off the branch
choices: Lock them together and try to shove each other off the branch
Rub them to make a buzzing sound that scares off hawks
Dig them into bark to pry out hidden grubs
Flash them bright red to attract nearby females
context: Male Jackson's chameleons wear three forward-pointing horns reminiscent of a tiny Triceratops, and rival males lock horns and try to push each other off a branch. Source: Wikipedia, 'Jackson's chameleon'.

question: Scientists searching deep in a rainforest found the nano-chameleon, Brookesia nana. A grown male could perch on the tip of a finger: his body measures only 13.5 millimeters, or about 22 counting the tail. What size record might this lizard hold?
answer: It may be the smallest reptile on Earth
choices: It may be the smallest reptile on Earth
It is the smallest chameleon but not the smallest reptile
It is the smallest lizard, though a snake is smaller
It is the smallest land animal with a backbone
context: The nano-chameleon Brookesia nana from Madagascar has a body just over half an inch long (male body 13.5 mm, total ~22 mm) and may be the smallest reptile on Earth. Source: Mongabay 2021; Wikipedia 'Brookesia nana'; discovered by Frank Glaw's team.

question: Swiss researchers studying panther chameleons in 2015 watched a single patch of skin on one animal shift from blue to yellow and red with no waiting, the very same skin each time. What lets one patch of skin flip colors on demand?
answer: Structural color from a grid of tiny crystals
choices: Structural color from a grid of tiny crystals
Pigment released from color glands under the skin
Reflected heat glowing out through the scales
Dye absorbed from the leaves it eats
context: Chameleon skin holds a grid of guanine nanocrystals; tightening or loosening the grid changes which wavelengths reflect, blue when packed tight, yellows and reds when spread apart, a structural color, not pigment. Source: Teyssier et al., Nature Communications 2015 (ncomms7368); phys.org 2015.

question: A chameleon fires its tongue at an insect, and the club-shaped tip slams on and does all the holding. The faster the tongue yanks back, the harder the tip grips, so the chameleon can reel in prey heavier than seems possible. What does the tip hold on with?
answer: A super-sticky slime about 400 times thicker than human spit
choices: A super-sticky slime about 400 times thicker than human spit
Rows of tiny backward-curved hooks like a cat's tongue
A ring of muscle that clamps shut like a fist
A patch of static charge that pulls the bug in
context: The tongue tip is coated in mucus about 400 times more viscous than human saliva, and it grips harder the faster the tongue snaps back, letting the chameleon reel in surprisingly heavy prey. Source: Nature Physics, Fabian Brau/Pascal Damman (U. Mons), 2016; National Geographic 'Chameleons' Secret Hunting Weapon: Super-Sticky Mucus'.

question: A chameleon launches its tongue with about 14,000 watts of power for every kilogram of muscle. Scientists ranked that against every animal with a backbone, from fish to mammals, and only one kind of creature out-powered it. Which animals beat the chameleon?
answer: Salamanders
choices: Salamanders
Cheetahs
Hummingbirds
Rattlesnakes
context: A chameleon's tongue produces about 14,000 watts per kilogram of muscle, the highest per-kg power of any reptile, bird, or mammal, and second among all vertebrates only to salamanders. Source: Brown University, 2016, Christopher Anderson (14,040 W/kg).

question: A chameleon still snatches insects at a body temperature of just 3.5°C, a chill that leaves muscle slow. Tests found the cold barely dented its tongue launch, while the muscle-driven pull back lost much of its strength. What powers the launch?
answer: A slow muscle first loads coiled collagen sheaths that then recoil like a bow
choices: A slow muscle first loads coiled collagen sheaths that then recoil like a bow
A fast muscle contracts hard enough to fling the whole tongue like a whip
Blood pumped in under high pressure swells the tongue and shoots it out
A burst of air suction behind the tongue snaps it out at the target
context: The tongue is a spring, not a muscle flung by brute force. An 'accelerator' muscle contracts slowly and stretches a sleeve of at least ~10 collagen sheaths wrapped around a stiff tongue-bone spur (the entoglossal process); the loaded sheaths then slide off the bone's rounded tip and recoil all at once, releasing stored elastic energy for accelerations up to ~500 m/s squared. The giveaway that it is elastic and not direct muscle: in veiled chameleons tested from 15 to 35 C, projection power fell only ~10-19% per 10 C, while muscle-powered RETRACTION fell 42-63% per 10 C, letting the animal keep feeding down to a body temperature of 3.5 C. Source: de Groot & van Leeuwen 2004, Proc. R. Soc. B (https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspb.2003.2637); Anderson & Deban 2010, PNAS 107:5495 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2851764/).

question: A chameleon fixes a single turret eye on a bug and judges how far away it is, with no second view to compare. Humans and most predators judge distance by matching the slightly different pictures from two eyes. How does the chameleon's one eye measure the range?
answer: It focuses that eye and reads the focus setting as the distance
choices: It focuses that eye and reads the focus setting as the distance
It clocks how fast the bug drifts across the eye as the head sways
It judges how bright the bug looks against the leaves behind it
It matches the bug against a remembered size to estimate range
context: A chameleon judges depth by monocular corneal accommodation: it focuses one eye and reads the focal setting as a distance. Its eye pairs a negative (concave) lens behind a strongly positive (convex) cornea, enlarging the retinal image so tiny focus changes are readable, and it can shift focus about 60 diopters per second with an amplitude near 45 diopters, faster and more precise than any other reptile. Source: Harkness 1977, Nature 267:346 (https://www.nature.com/articles/267346a0); Ott, Schaeffel & Kirmse 1998, J. Comp. Physiol. A (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s003590050182).

question: A small brown bug in a garden springs 70 centimeters straight up, more than twice as high as a flea, the insect long crowned the champion high-jumper. Which insect really holds the high-jump record?
answer: The froghopper (spittlebug)
choices: The froghopper (spittlebug)
The click beetle
The desert locust
The mole cricket
context: The froghopper (Philaenus spumarius) leaps about 70 cm straight up -- roughly 100 to 140 times its own body length, more than twice as high as a flea, making it the true insect jump champion. It gets the name spittlebug because its young hide in blobs of froth on plant stems. Source: Nature (Burrows 2003, 'Froghopper insects leap to new heights', 424:509) via NPR 2003-08-01.

question: A froghopper, a garden bug about 6 millimeters long and smaller than a grain of rice, vanishes in a blur when it jumps. Measured in its own body lengths, roughly how high does one leap carry it?
answer: Over 100 times its body length
choices: Over 100 times its body length
About 5 times its body length
About 15 times its body length
About 40 times its body length
context: The froghopper leaps roughly 100 to 140 times its own body length. Scaled to a six-foot human, that would be like clearing a stack of tall buildings. Source: Nature (Burrows 2003, 424:509).

question: A froghopper, a tiny sap-sucking insect, launches itself over half a meter straight up. Its jumping legs are barely half its body length and only 2 percent of its mass, far too little muscle to fling it that high. Where does the launch power come from?
answer: Springs built into its body that muscle slowly loads and then releases
choices: Springs built into its body that muscle slowly loads and then releases
A rapid drumbeat of many small muscle twitches
Air forced out through breathing pores as a jet
A running start that builds momentum before liftoff
context: The legs are only about half the body length and just 2% of body mass, so the power cannot come from the leg muscles firing directly -- it is stored in springs first. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology 209:4607 (Burrows).

question: A froghopper crouches on a garden plant stem, its hind legs cocked and locked in place by microscopic grippy teeth, ready to fire. Then it trips that latch and is gone in a single leap. What sound does the launch make?
answer: An audible click
choices: An audible click
A faint buzz
A soft hiss of air
A high whine
context: The froghopper locks its cocked legs with microscopic teeth (microtrichia) and fires with an audible click as the latch releases. Source: BMC Biology 6:41 (Burrows, Shaw & Sutton 2008).

question: A biologist shines ultraviolet light on a froghopper. Inside the little sap-sucking insect sits its jump spring, a bow of stiff shell coated in resilin, a rubber-like protein, and the light picks out exactly where it lies. What does the ultraviolet light reveal?
answer: A bright blue glow along the spring
choices: A bright blue glow along the spring
A red heat shimmer around the legs
A green shadow under the wings
A crackling spark at the joints
context: The spring material is resilin, a rubber-like protein that fluoresces bright blue under UV light; the glow traces the bow-shaped cuticle arch whose snap-back recoil -- not muscle -- powers the leap. Source: BMC Biology 6:41 (Burrows, Shaw & Sutton 2008).

question: A froghopper leaps, and its launch is over in under a thousandth of a second. The acceleration slams through its tiny body. A trained fighter pilot begins to black out near 9 times the pull of gravity. Roughly what force does the froghopper take at takeoff?
answer: Around 400 to 550 times gravity
choices: Around 400 to 550 times gravity
Around 20 times gravity
Around 90 times gravity
Around 200 times gravity
context: The froghopper accelerates at about 5,400 m/s2, briefly experiencing roughly 400 to 550 g (versus 2 to 3 g for a human), reaching take-off speed in under a thousandth of a second. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology 209:4607 (Burrows).

question: A grasshopper squeezes its huge thigh muscle to build each jump, but the muscle supplies only about half the energy. The rest is stored by bending two crescent-shaped braces of hard shell and resilin, a rubbery protein. Where on the leg do those braces sit?
answer: At the knee
choices: At the knee
At the ankle
Along the foot
At the hip
context: The grasshopper/locust bends two curved braces at the knee called semi-lunar processes -- composites of hard cuticle and resilin -- banking about half the extensor muscle's energy before release. Source: J. Exp. Biol. 215:3501 (Burrows).

question: A flea and a froghopper, each only a few millimeters long, slowly load a spring and trip a latch to launch, a trick biologists name latch-mediated spring actuation. Their muscles alone could never throw them so high. What is it that muscle cannot do?
answer: Contract fast enough to deliver the power in a single instant
choices: Contract fast enough to deliver the power in a single instant
Stay contracted long enough to hold a pose
Work at all in a cold-blooded body
Push and pull in the same motion
context: Muscle contracts too slowly to deliver power fast enough for a tiny launch, so small animals slowly load a spring and trip a latch to release the energy in an instant -- called latch-mediated spring actuation (LaMSA). Source: J. Exp. Biol. 226:jeb246070 review.

question: A trap-jaw ant slides down the loose sand of an antlion's pit, and the hidden hunter below flicks grains up to bring it tumbling down. Larabee and Suarez staged such encounters, then glued some ants' jaws shut to test whether the jaws help them escape. What did gluing the jaws do?
answer: Far fewer of them escaped the pits
choices: Far fewer of them escaped the pits
About as many escaped as before
More of them escaped, running instead
They learned to steer clear of pits
context: The trap-jaw ant Odontomachus latches its mandibles open under spring tension, then releases them in one of the fastest movements in the animal kingdom, fast enough that slamming the jaws against the ground hurls the ant clear of danger. Larabee and Suarez staged encounters with pit-digging antlions, predators that ambush ants sliding into their sand pits. Ants with free jaws escaped the pits significantly more often than ants whose jaws were glued shut, which the study put at 4.7 times more likely to escape. The ants use two launch styles: a steep vertical 'escape jump' (take-off angle around 76 degrees) to flee the pit, and a low 'bouncer defense' jump (around 27 degrees) that knocks the ant backward off an attacker. Source: Larabee & Suarez 2015, 'Mandible-Powered Escape Jumps in Trap-Jaw Ants Increase Survival Rates during Predator-Prey Encounters', PLOS ONE 10(5):e0124871 -- https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0124871 ; Patek et al. 2006, PNAS on ballistic jaw propulsion -- https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0604290103

question: A slim spotted cat crouches in the grass of an African plain, eyeing a herd of gazelles. In a chase it can beat a sports car off the line, reaching 60 miles an hour from a standstill in under three seconds. Which animal is it?
answer: The cheetah
choices: The cheetah
The lion
The leopard
The African wild dog
context: The cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) is the fastest land animal, accelerating from a standstill to about 97 km/h (60 mph) in under three seconds and out-accelerating many sports cars; its highest reliably reported speed is about 104 km/h. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheetah

question: A researcher in a jeep photographs a cheetah on the savanna, then checks her files to be sure she has not counted that cat already. Every cheetah carries a sign of identity as unique as a fingerprint. What does she compare?
answer: Its spot pattern and tail rings
choices: Its spot pattern and tail rings
The exact shade of its golden coat
The number of whiskers on its face
The curl and length of its tail
context: A cheetah's spots cover nearly its whole body, and -- like a human fingerprint -- the spot pattern and the ring pattern of its tail are unique to each individual. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/news/why-do-cheetahs-have-spots-and-other-cheetah-facts

question: A cheetah mother needs to gather her cubs, scattered and hidden in the tall grass of the savanna. Unlike a lion, she cannot roar to summon them. What surprising sound does she make instead to call the cubs in?
answer: A birdlike chirp
choices: A birdlike chirp
A wolflike howl
A drawn-out yowl
A rumbling bellow
context: Unlike other big cats, the cheetah cannot roar; instead it chirps like a bird, purrs, growls, hisses and stutters, and a mother uses birdlike chirps to call her cubs. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/news/why-do-cheetahs-have-spots-and-other-cheetah-facts

question: A cheetah tears across the savanna with its claws poking out like a dog's, blunt and only partly pulled in, where other cats keep theirs sheathed and sharp until they strike. What job are those claws doing as it runs?
answer: Gripping the ground like a sprinter's track spikes
choices: Gripping the ground like a sprinter's track spikes
Cushioning each footfall like a shock absorber
Sharpening themselves against the dirt as it runs
Sensing vibrations in the ground from fleeing prey
context: The cheetah's claws are blunt and only semi-retractable, staying partly out like a dog's -- they bite into the ground like a sprinter's track spikes for traction, and ridges on the hard paw pads grip like tire tread. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo; SeaWorld, seaworld.org/animals/all-about/cheetah/characteristics/

question: A cheetah hunts by day across the open African plains. Two black stripes run from the inner corner of each eye down toward its mouth, the marks cheetah watchers call 'tear marks.' What are those dark stripes thought to do for the hunting cat?
answer: Cut the sun's glare off its face
choices: Cut the sun's glare off its face
Channel rain and sweat away from its eyes
Trap dust before it reaches its eyes
Cool the thin skin beneath its eyes
context: The black 'tear marks' are thought to work like the eye-black athletes wear, cutting sun glare off the cheeks so the cat can keep prey in focus across the bright plains. Their role is not fully understood; another idea is that they sharpen the cat's facial expressions at close range. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheetah ; Cheetah Conservation Fund.

question: Racing after a gazelle, a cheetah stretches out long, then bunches up tight, with every bound of its gallop. Each time, its hind feet swing so far forward that they land ahead of its front paws. Which part of its body makes that enormous reach possible?
answer: Its springy, flexible spine
choices: Its springy, flexible spine
Its double-jointed knees
Its wide, deep ribcage
Its stretchy hip ligaments
context: The cheetah's flexible spine flexes and extends like a spring with every stride, throwing the hind legs far forward; at full gallop it lifts all four feet off the ground twice per stride -- once stretched full-out and once with legs tucked under. Source: Cheetah Conservation Fund; SeaWorld, seaworld.org/animals/all-about/cheetah/adaptations/

question: A fleeing gazelle jinks sideways in an instant, a turn that would send most chasing animals tumbling head over heels. The cheetah close behind it stays with the turn without ever falling. What does it use to shift its balance?
answer: Its long tail, swung as a counterweight
choices: Its long tail, swung as a counterweight
Its forelegs, leaning hard into the bend
Its head, thrown sideways into the turn
Its hips, swung low through the bend
context: The cheetah's long tail works as a counterweight and rudder: it swings side to side to shift the cat's balance so it can make hairpin turns at speed that would send other animals tumbling; the flattened, ringed tuft at the tip acts like the rudder. Source: Cheetah Conservation Fund; SeaWorld, seaworld.org/animals/all-about/cheetah/adaptations/

question: A cheetah sprinting all-out after a gazelle burns oxygen at a furious rate, and its breathing jumps to around 150 breaths a minute, up from about 60. Which feature of its head and airway lets it gulp down air fast enough to feed the chase?
answer: Enlarged nostrils opening into air-filled sinuses
choices: Enlarged nostrils opening into air-filled sinuses
A long muzzle packed with extra scent receptors
A wide mouth it pants through to cool the blood
A flexible windpipe that coils to store spare air
context: To feed the sprint, the cheetah gulps air through enlarged nostrils and air-filled sinuses; its breathing leaps from about 60 breaths a minute at rest to around 150 during a chase, fed by an oversized heart, lungs, liver and large arteries. Source: SeaWorld, seaworld.org/animals/all-about/cheetah/adaptations/

question: Deep in a chase, a cheetah can hold its top speed for only seconds. If it has not caught its quarry in about 30 seconds, it must break off and let the animal go. What forces it to quit so soon?
answer: Lactic acid floods its muscles and it runs out of energy
choices: Lactic acid floods its muscles and it runs out of energy
Its heart cannot pump fast enough to stay conscious
Its blunt claws wear down and lose their grip
Its spine cramps and locks from the constant flexing
context: A cheetah can only hold its top speed for a matter of seconds, and prey must be caught within roughly 30 seconds, because the anaerobic sprint floods its muscles with lactic acid and it simply runs out of energy. Source: Cheetah Conservation Fund; National Geographic.

question: When researchers fitted five wild Botswana cheetahs with GPS-and-motion collars, the cats logged a blistering top speed of 93 km/h -- yet most of their hunts were run at only moderate speed. What did the collars show actually decided most successful hunts?
answer: Grip and sharp maneuvering, with muscle power for braking and turning
choices: Grip and sharp maneuvering, with muscle power for braking and turning
Sheer top-end speed reached in a dead-straight sprint line
Hunting in coordinated pairs to trap and corner the prey
Ambushing from cover instead of chasing at all in open ground
context: A GPS-and-motion-collar study of five wild cheetahs in Botswana recorded a top speed of 25.9 m/s (58 mph / 93 km/h), but found most hunts were run at only moderate speed -- success came from grip, sharp maneuvering and muscle power for braking and turning, not from raw top speed. Source: Wilson et al., 'Locomotion dynamics of hunting in wild cheetahs,' Nature 2013, nature.com/articles/nature12295

question: Miracinonyx, a lean, spotted sprinter, roamed ice-age North America looking so much like a cheetah that scientists long counted it as an 'American cheetah.' Then genetic and skeletal studies redrew its family tree. What did they reveal about this vanished cat?
answer: It was a close cousin of the cougar that only looks cheetah-like through convergent evolution
choices: It was a close cousin of the cougar that only looks cheetah-like through convergent evolution
It was the direct ancestor of the African cheetah before the cats crossed into Asia
It was a giant relative of the lion that had lost its mane over generations
It was a big cat unrelated to any feline alive today, a lineage all its own
context: Miracinonyx trumani, the 'American cheetah,' died out at the end of the last ice age. Genetic and skeletal analyses now place it as a close relative of the cougar (Puma), not the true cheetah -- the two lineages arrived at the same lean, fast-pursuit body independently, a textbook case of convergent evolution. Unlike the African cheetah, Miracinonyx kept retractable claws and could rotate its forelimbs to grapple prey, and recent elbow-joint studies suggest it hunted in a way with no living analogue. It also anchors the famous 'ghost predator' idea: the pronghorn, still the fastest runner in the Americas, is far faster than any predator alive today, and its speed was long explained as an escape from Miracinonyx -- yet a 2026 analysis argues pronghorns were already fast BEFORE Miracinonyx appeared, so the coevolution story is now contested. Source: Sci.News, 'Miracinonyx trumani' (cougar-relative, convergence) https://www.sci.news/paleontology/miracinonyx-trumani-11656.html ; Royal Society Biology Letters 2022 elbow morphology https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsbl.2022.0483 ; Kort and colleagues, Journal of Mammalogy (2026), on Miocene pronghorn-ancestor ankle bones, reported by Nautilus https://nautil.us/how-the-fastest-land-animal-in-north-america-got-its-need-for-speed-1267620/ ; Wikipedia, Miracinonyx https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miracinonyx

question: Stephen O'Brien and his team grafted skin from one unrelated cheetah onto another fourteen times in 1985. In most species, skin grafted from an unrelated animal is rejected as foreign, yet every cheetah graft healed in, as if it had passed between identical twins. What is it about cheetahs that explains this?
answer: A recent population bottleneck left every cheetah so genetically uniform its immune system reads any other as itself
choices: A recent population bottleneck left every cheetah so genetically uniform its immune system reads any other as itself
A cheetah heals wounds so fast that grafted skin bonds before the immune system can react
Cheetahs alone among cats never mount an immune attack on transplanted living tissue
The tested cats had all descended from a single famous zoo pair a few years earlier
context: In a landmark 1985 study, Stephen O'Brien and colleagues made 14 reciprocal skin grafts between unrelated cheetahs, and all 14 were accepted, an outcome normally seen only between identical twins. The cats are so uniform at their MHC genes (the 'self ID' the immune system checks) that one cheetah's tissue does not register as foreign. Surveying 200-plus genetic loci, the team traced this to a severe population bottleneck in the species' recent past. The uniformity persists in wild-born cats, ruling out mere captive inbreeding. Source: O'Brien et al. 1985, 'Genetic Basis for Species Vulnerability in the Cheetah,' Science 227:1428, https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.2983425 ; Cheetah Conservation Fund summary https://cheetah.org/resource-library/genetic-basis-for-species-vulnerability-in-the-cheetah/

question: A striped skunk ambling past a dog at dusk stops and turns to face it. It does not spray at once; first it gives the dog fair warning. What does that warning look like?
answer: It stamps its front feet, raises its tail and hisses
choices: It stamps its front feet, raises its tail and hisses
It rolls over and plays dead with its tongue out
It screeches and thumps its tail on the ground
It chatters its teeth and spits at the dog
context: A skunk (family Mephitidae) warns before it sprays, stamping its feet, raising its tail, and hissing to give a predator a chance to back off. Its musk is made of sulfur compounds called thiols, which sear a predator's eyes and nose. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/science/Why-Do-Skunks-Spray ; https://www.dvm360.com/view/skunk-spray-toxicosis-odiferous-tale

question: A bombardier beetle fires a scalding chemical spray from its tail when something bites it. The spray is brewed on the spot from two liquids that are each harmless on their own. Which two chemicals does the beetle mix?
answer: Hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide
choices: Hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide
Vinegar and baking soda
Formic acid and alcohol
Venom and saliva
context: Kept apart, hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide are harmless; only when the beetle mixes them with enzymes in its reaction chamber do they react. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_beetle

question: A cornered striped skunk turns and lands its reeking musk squarely on a dog's face from several feet away. People who watch skunks closely are surprised less by the smell than by the accuracy. How does the skunk aim its shot so precisely?
answer: Each musk gland ends in its own nozzle it can point
choices: Each musk gland ends in its own nozzle it can point
It sprays a wide cloud and hopes to hit
It waits until the threat is pressed against its tail
Wind currents steer the droplets to the target
context: The skunk fires musk from two glands under its tail, each with its own aimable nipple, accurate to about 3 meters (with the smell then carried on the wind up to 1.5 km). Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/skunk

question: A shark clamps its jaws on a hagfish, a jawless, eel-shaped creature that lives in the deep sea, and in a fraction of a second the water around the shark's mouth turns into nearly a liter of choking slime. The slime clogs the shark's gills, and it lets go. What did the hagfish release to make that slime?
answer: Packets of coiled threads and mucus
choices: Packets of coiled threads and mucus
A sticky oil leaked from its gills
A jelly coughed up from its gut
A gum squeezed from glands in its mouth
context: A grabbed hagfish releases tiny thread-and-mucus packets that explode on contact with seawater into about a liter of choking slime in a fraction of a second. One liter is 99.996% seawater; the rest is tens of thousands of silk-like protein threads plus mucin. Sources: https://www.nature.com/articles/srep00131 ; https://sites.chapman.edu/fudge/project/biophysics-of-hagfish-slime/

question: Every time a bombardier beetle defends itself, it brews a scalding chemical spray in a small reaction chamber inside its own abdomen and fires it out of its tail. That ought to cook the beetle from the inside, yet it survives shot after shot. As the pressure spikes in that chamber, what keeps its own organs safe?
answer: The pressure slams shut the valves to its storage tanks
choices: The pressure slams shut the valves to its storage tanks
A thick layer of fat insulates the chamber
It cools the fluid down just before firing
It only fires while facing away from itself
context: Inside the reaction chamber the vapor pressure spikes so hard it slams shut the valves from the storage chambers, protecting the beetle's own organs, then vents the blast outward. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3565695/

question: A boy pokes a ladybug crawling on his fingertip, and a bitter yellow droplet oozes out at the joints of its legs. The beetle's bright red shell dotted with black spots warns birds and lizards that it tastes terrible, and any bird would spit that droplet right out. What is the yellow fluid?
answer: Its own blood, bled on purpose when poked
choices: Its own blood, bled on purpose when poked
Venom squeezed from a gland in its leg
Saliva welling up from its mouth
An oil sweated out through its shell
context: A cornered ladybug reflex-bleeds, oozing bitter yellow fluid from the leg joint nearest the poke, laced with the alkaloid coccinelline. Its red-and-black colors advertise that it tastes foul. Source: https://www.colorado.edu/asmagazine/2020/07/21/ladybugs-bright-colors-advertise-toxic-chemical-defenses

question: Skeptics long argued the bombardier beetle's aimed, scalding spray was too intricate to have evolved by degrees. Biologists answered with Metrius contractus, the most primitive bombardier beetle alive: its two-chambered glands hold the same hot quinone chemistry, yet it cannot shoot a jet. What does it do with its chemicals instead?
answer: Oozes a bubbling froth that clings over its own body
choices: Oozes a bubbling froth that clings over its own body
Wipes the fluid onto an attacker with its hind legs
Leaks the fluid slowly from pores along its own back
Dribbles the mix as droplets out of its mouth
context: Metrius contractus (subfamily Paussinae) is the crucial living intermediate that answers the old 'irreducibly complex' objection to the bombardier beetle. Where advanced Brachininae fire a pulsed, steerable jet, Metrius has the same two-chamber gland and hot quinone chemistry but discharges its secretion as a froth that clings to its own body, the ancestral 'foam' stage that preceded the explosive spray. The full graded pathway (quinones already made to harden the shell, then stored as a deterrent, then catalase making it hotter and foamier, then aimed pulsed fire) shows the weapon could build up in useful steps. Source: Eisner et al. 2000, Journal of Experimental Biology 203:1265, 'Spray mechanism of the most primitive bombardier beetle (Metrius contractus)' (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10729276/); Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle' on the incremental-pathway rebuttal.

question: A hungry fish attacks a sea cucumber on the seafloor, and the sea cucumber fires sticky white threads, called Cuvierian tubules, out through its rear at the attacker. Milky and floppy inside the animal, the threads shoot into the seawater, stretch to about twenty times their length, then snare the predator in cords it cannot pull free. How do the soft threads turn tough and inescapable?
answer: Their collagen tissue stiffens for good
choices: Their collagen tissue stiffens for good
Backward barbs along them catch in the skin
Seawater sets their coat into a hard glaze
They twist together into a tight rope
context: These are Cuvierian tubules, distinct from the sea cucumber's better-known trick of ejecting its guts. Demeuldre, Flammang and colleagues found that the tubule wall is a mutable collagenous tissue, the kind of connective tissue that lets echinoderms switch between floppy and stiff. Tubules about 2 cm long at rest stretch to about 40 cm as they shoot out, turn sticky within seconds of touching a surface, and then stiffen irreversibly. Tensilin, a known stiffening protein of such tissue, sits in cells inside the tubules, though its exact role there is still being worked out. Source: Demeuldre et al. 2017, Journal of Experimental Biology 220(11):2108, https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/220/11/2108/17941

question: A snorkeler drifting over a tropical reef spots something like a matched pair of tiny spiral fir trees, bright red or blue, poking out of a living coral head. They are not plants. What are the twin spirals really?
answer: The two feathery crowns of one worm
choices: The two feathery crowns of one worm
A colony of tiny coral polyps stacked in a spiral
A pair of small sea anemones sharing one rock
Two baby starfish curled up to feed
context: The Christmas tree worm (Spirobranchus giganteus) lives head-down inside a tube bored into the living coral, with only its two spiral crowns showing. The 'trees' are not two animals but the twin crowns of one worm. Source: NOAA, oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/xmas-tree.html.

question: A Christmas tree worm pokes two bright spiral crowns out of a living coral head, out in the open where a hungry fish could snap them off. A shadow slides over it. What does the worm do?
answer: Yanks its crowns down into its tube in a blink
choices: Yanks its crowns down into its tube in a blink
Puffs the crown up bigger to look dangerous
Squirts a cloud of ink and drifts away
Flashes a warning color and holds its ground
context: The worm is so sensitive it retracts at the slightest touch or a passing shadow, then re-emerges very slowly about a minute later to test the water. Sources: MarineBio; NOAA.

question: A Christmas tree worm spreads the hair-fringed branches of its spiral crowns like a net, catching drifting plankton and sweeping it to its mouth. Those same branches, called radioles, do a second job at the same time. What is it?
answer: They pull oxygen out of the seawater, working like gills
choices: They pull oxygen out of the seawater, working like gills
They soak up sunlight to make sugars like a plant
They inject venom into anything that brushes past
They glow to lure prey closer in the dark
context: The radioles do double duty: catching food AND absorbing oxygen from the water like gills, so the worm eats and breathes with the very same feathery crown. Sources: NOAA; Wikipedia (Spirobranchus giganteus).

question: A Christmas tree worm hides inside its tube in the living coral of a tropical reef, and it does not leave the door open. It seals the entrance shut behind itself. What does the worm use to cork the tube?
answer: A trapdoor lid made from one of its own modified branches
choices: A trapdoor lid made from one of its own modified branches
A blob of sticky mucus it spits over the opening
A borrowed empty snail shell wedged in the gap
A flap of the coral it pinches closed like a mouth
context: After retracting, the worm plugs its tube with an operculum — a modified radiole (one of its crown branches) reshaped into a trapdoor lid that seals the hole while the worm hides. Sources: Wikipedia (Spirobranchus giganteus); MarineBio.

question: A fish glides toward a Christmas tree worm on a tropical reef, and the worm vanishes into its tube while the fish is still some way off. The early warning comes from its feathery spiral crown itself. What is built into the branches of that crown?
answer: Clusters of tiny compound eyes
choices: Clusters of tiny compound eyes
Heat-sensing pits like a viper's
Pores that sense electric fields
Tiny ears tuned to a fish's sounds
context: Serpulid worms like Spirobranchus evolved compound eyes built into the radioles, the feathery feeding branches, and in the S. giganteus complex each eye packs hundreds of tiny light-catching units. Their visual pigment peaks near 464 nm, the blue of downwelling reef light, so the eyes work as a silhouette-detecting 'burglar alarm': they catch the shadow of an approaching object and fire the withdrawal reflex before the worm is ever touched. Source: Bok, Porter, ten Hove, Smith & Nilsson, 'Radiolar Eyes of Serpulid Worms,' The Biological Bulletin 233(1), 2017.

question: A Christmas tree worm sits cemented into a living coral head, filtering food from the water, and can look like a freeloader. Marine biologists still argue about the arrangement, and reef studies point in opposite directions. What do some studies suggest the worm may do for its coral host in return?
answer: Shield it from crown-of-thorns starfish that would eat it
choices: Shield it from crown-of-thorns starfish that would eat it
Feed it sugars the way algae inside the coral do
Cement its loose rubble together after a storm breaks it
Ferry its spawning larvae out to colonize fresh reef
context: Whether these worms help or harm their host is a real, unsettled debate. A Great Barrier Reef study (DeVantier, Reichelt & Bradbury, Marine Ecology Progress Series 32:307-310, 1986) found the worms may protect Porites coral from crown-of-thorns starfish: in 5 of 7 colonies, living coral tissue was significantly associated with the worms near the feeding fronts, hinting at a coevolved partnership. But later work off Curacao (Hoeksema and colleagues, Marine Biology, 2019) found the worm's scraping operculum often injured the coral, worst when turf algae grew on the lid. The relationship appears to swing between help and harm depending on the reef.

question: A male club-winged manakin, a tiny chestnut-brown bird with a bright red cap, perches on a twig in a mossy cloud forest of Colombia. To impress a female he plays a pure, violin-like tone with his beak shut. What does he make the sound with?
answer: His wings
choices: His wings
His tail
His feet
His chest
context: The male club-winged manakin (Machaeropterus deliciosus) is the only bird known to sing with its wings rather than its voice. He rubs two specially thickened wing feathers together behind his back to produce a pure, violin-like tone. Source: All About Birds / Cornell Lab, 'Singing With His Wings'; Bostwick et al., PMC2842718 ('Resonating feathers produce courtship song').

question: A male club-winged manakin courts a female the way a cricket chirps, by rubbing one body part over another. Behind his back, one stiff wing feather scrapes over its neighbor like a bow across a string, more than a hundred times a second. What is special about the feather it scrapes?
answer: It is ridged like a tiny washboard
choices: It is ridged like a tiny washboard
It is coated in slippery oil
It is hollow like a flute tube
It is tipped with a hard claw
context: One of the manakin's wing feathers has a shaft bumpy with a row of ridges, like a tiny washboard; a stiff neighboring feather scrapes across those bumps the way a bow crosses a violin string, and each bump adds a click that blurs into a pure tone. This rub-to-sing method is called stridulation — the same trick a cricket uses — but only the manakin does it among birds. Source: All About Birds / Cornell Lab, 'Singing With His Wings'; AskNature, 'Resonating feathers produce courtship song'; Bostwick et al., PMC2842718.

question: A male club-winged manakin knocks his wing feathers together so hard to make his violin-like tone that his arm bone is unusually thick and solid, not hollow. The female never makes the sound. According to the ornithologist Richard Prum, what are her wing bones like?
answer: Thickened and shaped like his
choices: Thickened and shaped like his
Thin and ordinary, unlike his
Fused into a single stiff rod
Threaded with an extra air sac
context: The male's wing bone (the ulna) is filled in and mineralized to more than three times the volume of the ulna in birds of comparable size, so it survives being knocked together over and over (Bostwick, Riccio & Humphries 2012, a study of males). Richard Prum, who worked on the species with Kimberly Bostwick, reports that females carry the same thickened wing bones even though only males make the sound, a case where a mating display reshaped the whole species' skeleton. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3440988/ ; Prum on the club-winged manakin, https://bigthink.com/?p=45870 ; Wikipedia, 'Club-winged manakin'.

question: At dusk on a warm Pacific island, a coconut crab climbs the trunk of a palm. It is as heavy as a house cat and spans about 3 feet across its outstretched legs. What record does it hold among animals that live on land?
answer: The largest land arthropod on Earth
choices: The largest land arthropod on Earth
The fastest-running crab on Earth
The longest-legged crab on Earth
The most venomous crab on Earth
context: The coconut crab (Birgus latro) is the biggest land arthropod alive: its legs can span about 90 cm to 1 m (about 3 feet) from tip to tip, and it can weigh up to about 4.1 kg (9 pounds). Source: Wikipedia, Coconut crab (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_crab); Grokipedia, Coconut crab.

question: Islanders of the Indian and Pacific Oceans who share their land with the coconut crab, whose huge claws can crack a coconut, call it by another name: the robber crab. What earned it that nickname?
answer: It hauls off pots, silverware, and shiny objects
choices: It hauls off pots, silverware, and shiny objects
It steals eggs from other crabs' burrows
It raids island beehives for their honey
It digs up buried seeds people have planted
context: The nickname 'robber crab' comes from its habit of carrying off anything it can grab — pots, silverware, shiny objects. Its claws can lift objects up to about 29 kg (64 lb). Sources: Wikipedia, Coconut crab (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_crab); GreaterGood (greatergood.com/blogs/news/cs-robber-crabs-bio).

question: Shin-ichiro Oka and his team on Okinawa clamped a force gauge in the pincers of 29 wild coconut crabs, one after another, in 2016. They wanted to know how hard the giant land crabs that pry open coconuts can squeeze. What did the strongest pinch outdo?
answer: The canine bite of a lion
choices: The canine bite of a lion
The kick of an adult zebra
The hug of a grown python
The bite of a hippopotamus
context: The strongest of the 29 crabs gripped with about 1,765 newtons — stronger than a lion's canine bite (~1,315 N). By scaling the data the team estimated the biggest crabs could pinch with roughly 3,300 N, outmuscling nearly every land predator except the alligator. Sources: Oka et al. 2016, 'A Mighty Claw,' PLOS ONE (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5120803); Science News (sciencenews.org).

question: A grown coconut crab held underwater will drown, though it began life drifting in the open ocean as a tiny larva before it crawled ashore on a tropical island. What happened to its body as it grew up on land?
answer: Its gills shrank and it now breathes air
choices: Its gills shrank and it now breathes air
Its gills now work only in fresh water
Its gills clogged for good with sand
Its shell grew too heavy to swim up
context: As an adult the coconut crab has abandoned the sea: its gills shrank and it breathes air through a lung-like organ called a branchiostegal lung, so it will drown if held underwater too long — even though it began life in the ocean. Sources: Wikipedia, Coconut crab (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_crab); Stensmyr et al. 2005, Current Biology (cell.com).

question: A young coconut crab on a tropical island shelters its soft rear end inside a borrowed snail shell, as hermit crabs do. A grown one becomes far too big for any shell it could find. How does the adult protect its soft body instead?
answer: It hardens the plates of its own body into armor
choices: It hardens the plates of its own body into armor
It coats itself in a shell of dried mud
It shelters its rear under a flat stone
It grows a thick mat of stinging bristles
context: Unlike other hermit crabs, the adult coconut crab gives up wearing a borrowed shell entirely — it hardens the plates on its own abdomen (the terga) into built-in armor. Juveniles still wear snail shells, and adolescents sometimes wear broken coconut shells. Source: Wikipedia, Coconut crab (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_crab).

question: Ambling through an island forest, a coconut crab breathes through a spongy organ inside its shell, one that works only while it stays damp. If that organ dries out, the crab suffocates. What does the crab do to keep it moist?
answer: It strokes water over the tissue with its hind legs
choices: It strokes water over the tissue with its hind legs
It swallows seawater and holds it in its gut
It rolls in wet sand after every meal
It waits out dry spells buried and asleep
context: Its branchiostegal lung must stay damp, so the crab uses its smallest, hindmost pair of legs to stroke water over the spongy tissue — and seals its burrow with a claw to keep the moist air in. Source: Wikipedia, Coconut crab (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_crab).

question: A newly hatched coconut crab spends its first three or four weeks adrift far out at sea, a tiny shrimp-like larva among the plankton. Then the survivor crawls ashore, and from that moment one strange thing is true of it for the rest of its life. What is it?
answer: It can never swim again
choices: It can never swim again
It never eats meat again
It never sheds its shell again
It never leaves its burrow again
context: Its babies start life as tiny larvae drifting in the open ocean for 3–4 weeks; a survivor then finds a snail shell to wear and crawls ashore, and after that the coconut crab can no longer swim. Source: Wikipedia, Coconut crab (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_crab).

question: From far across a tropical island, a coconut crab tracks the smell of rotting fruit or meat. Biologists who studied its antennae and the part of its brain that reads scents expected the hardware of a sea crab. What did they find?
answer: They had come to resemble an insect's
choices: They had come to resemble an insect's
They were the largest of any crab known
They could detect scents only underwater
They had shrunk almost entirely away
context: The coconut crab evolved an air-sniffing nose so land-adapted that its smell organs and brain independently came to resemble an insect's rather than a sea crab's, letting it home in on rotting meat, fruit, and coconut from far off. Source: Stensmyr et al. 2005, 'Insect-Like Olfactory Adaptations in the Terrestrial Giant Robber Crab,' Current Biology (cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(04)01048-6).

question: On the Chagos Islands at night, Mark Laidre filmed a coconut crab, the giant land crab of tropical islands, climbing a tree toward a red-footed booby asleep in its branches. What did the crab do when it reached the bird?
answer: Broke its wing so it could not fly off
choices: Broke its wing so it could not fly off
Shook the branch until the bird fled
Snatched a fish from the bird's beak
Plucked feathers to line its burrow
context: The crab broke the sleeping booby's wing, and within about 20 minutes the smell of blood drew rival crabs that squabbled over the bird for hours. Laidre admitted, 'I had a lot of trouble sleeping that night.' Source: Audubon (audubon.org/news/in-surprising-scientific-find-enormous-crab-kills-booby-camera).

question: Mark Laidre compared three nearly identical islands in the Indian Ocean, alike in trees, climate and size. Two were crawling with coconut crabs; the third had none. On the crab-free island, what were the seabirds doing that they never dared on the other two?
answer: Nesting on the open ground
choices: Nesting on the open ground
Diving for fish at night
Flocking in enormous numbers
Raising two broods a year
context: Laidre found the crabs quietly rule the islands: of three near-identical islands he surveyed, the one without coconut crabs was the only place where seabirds dared nest on the ground. Source: Audubon (audubon.org/news/in-surprising-scientific-find-enormous-crab-kills-booby-camera).

question: Charles Darwin, on the Beagle's visit to the Keeling Islands in the 1830s, wrote down how a coconut crab opens a coconut, as a man living there had watched it done again and again. The crab strips the husk fibre by fibre, always starting at one particular spot on the nut. Which spot?
answer: The end with the three eye-holes
choices: The end with the three eye-holes
The pointed tip farthest from the stalk
The seam running down one side
The rough patch where it met the branch
context: Darwin recorded, on the word of Mr. Liesk, a resident who had repeatedly seen it, exactly how the crab works: it tears the coconut husk 'fibre by fibre,' always from the end with the three eye-holes, then hammers a claw on one eye-hole until it breaks through to the meat inside. He called it 'as curious a case of instinct as ever I heard of.' Source: Darwin, The Voyage of the Beagle, Ch. 20 (standardebooks.org/ebooks/charles-darwin/the-voyage-of-the-beagle/text/chapter-20).

question: Once a year or so, a coconut crab digs a burrow as deep as a meter, plugs the entrance and waits underground for weeks while its new armor forms. When the old shell finally slips off, what does the crab do with it?
answer: Eats it to reclaim the calcium for its new shell
choices: Eats it to reclaim the calcium for its new shell
Lines the burrow with it to block out predators
Carries it to the shore and buries it in wet sand
Leaves it as a decoy to fool hunting seabirds
context: Molting is the coconut crab's most vulnerable moment: it burrows up to a meter down, plugs the entrance, and stays underground for three to sixteen weeks while its new exoskeleton mineralizes (the shell itself hardens in one to three weeks). Rather than waste the calcium locked in its cast-off shell, the crab eats the old exoskeleton and reabsorbs the mineral to help harden the new one -- so almost nothing is lost. Source: Coconut crab, Wikipedia (molting/burrow durations) -- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_crab ; Ohashi & Kamezaki (2022), 'Peculiar Molting Behavior of Large Hermit Crabs', Pacific Science 76(2), citing Fletcher for shell-eating -- https://bioone.org/journals/pacific-science/volume-76/issue-2/76.2.7/

question: Jakob Krieger's team fitted Christmas Island coconut crabs with GPS tags, tracking an arthropod by satellite on a scale never tried before, then carried some far from home and let them go. Several made their way back to within a few hundred meters of where they were caught. One crab was moved twice. What did it do?
answer: Came home by the same route twice, S-bend and all
choices: Came home by the same route twice, S-bend and all
Waited out the heat in a stranger burrow
Doubled its speed after the first rainfall
Followed the coastline the entire distance
context: Jakob Krieger and colleagues tagged 55 male coconut crabs on Christmas Island (2008-2011), logging over 1,500 crab-days, with inland-to-coast treks averaging 1.8 km and reaching 4.2 km. Of eight crabs moved inland or seaward, five returned to within about 100-300 m of their capture spot or to the spot itself, and one crab, moved twice, came home both times along an identical path with a characteristic S-bend: evidence of route memory in a crustacean. Four crabs moved along the coast never returned. Source: Krieger J et al. (2012), 'Giant Robber Crabs Monitored from Space: GPS-Based Telemetric Studies on Christmas Island', PLOS ONE 7(11):e49809, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3498180/

question: Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, a museum curator, was sorting a South African catch in 1938 when a blue fish caught her eye. It had an extra tail and four fins like stubby limbs, and its kind was thought to have died with the dinosaurs. What was it?
answer: The coelacanth
choices: The coelacanth
The blue marlin
The oarfish
The sturgeon
context: The coelacanth (Latimeria) is the classic 'living fossil': its last fossils date to the same end-of-Cretaceous mass die-off that killed the dinosaurs, until a live one was caught in 1938. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coelacanth

question: A coelacanth paddles through deep water on four thick, fleshy fins tipped with muscle. Divers filming it found that the four fins move in a set rhythm of their own. Where else in nature does the same rhythm show up?
answer: In a four-legged reptile walking on land
choices: In a four-legged reptile walking on land
In a frog kicking through a pond
In a sea lion rowing with its flippers
In a ray flapping its wing-like fins
context: The coelacanth's lobed fins move in the same alternating pattern a four-legged animal uses to walk, hinting at the fish-to-land transition, though the coelacanth is not the direct ancestor of land animals. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00004739

question: Mark Erdmann, a marine biologist, was on his honeymoon in Indonesia in 1997 when he came across a second species of coelacanth, sixty years after the first was found off South Africa. Where did he first see it?
answer: Laid out for sale at a local fish market
choices: Laid out for sale at a local fish market
Tangled in a coral reef during a dive
Beached on the sand after a storm
Frozen in a hotel restaurant's kitchen
context: Erdmann and his wife Arnaz Mehta spotted it by pure luck at a fish market in Sulawesi in September 1997; it was later named Latimeria menadoensis. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesian_coelacanth

question: A coelacanth in the deep water off eastern Africa lunges at a smaller fish, and a special muscle goes to work on the real hinge that runs across the middle of its skull, a joint no other living animal has. What happens to its head?
answer: The front of its head tips up to open wider
choices: The front of its head tips up to open wider
Its jaws shoot forward like a moray eel's
Its lower jaw drops free like a snake's
Its skull locks rigid to brace the bite
context: A basicranial muscle swings the front of the head upward at the intracranial joint, opening the mouth wider and boosting bite force to swallow larger prey. Source: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/pdfExtended/S0960-9822(15)00329-2

question: A coelacanth mother gives birth to fully formed live pups, but for decades no one knew how long she carries them. Scientists counting growth rings on coelacanth scales in 2021 found it is longer than any other known animal's pregnancy. How long is it?
answer: About five years
choices: About two years
About three years
About five years
About eight years
context: Coelacanths gestate for roughly five years, then bear 5 to 25 fully formed live pups. The same scale-ring study found they can live nearly a century and don't mature until about age 55. Source: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(21)00752-1

question: A see-through comb jelly about the size of a plum drifts through the open sea while waves of pink, green and blue ripple down its sides. The animal is not making any light of its own. Where does the shimmering rainbow come from?
answer: Rows of tiny beating hairs scatter passing light like a moving prism
choices: Rows of tiny beating hairs scatter passing light like a moving prism
A glowing chemical it swallows from the algae it eats
Colored scales that flash as they catch the current
Ink it releases in shimmering swirling clouds
context: This is structural color: the eight rows of beating hair-combs (cilia) scatter passing light like a moving prism, completely different from bioluminescence (chemically making light). Source: Shape of Life (shapeoflife.org) & Smithsonian Ocean (ocean.si.edu/ocean-life/invertebrates/jellyfish-and-comb-jellies).

question: A clear comb jelly glides through the sea, driven by eight long rows of giant fused hairs running down its sides, the combs that give it its name. How do the eight rows of combs move it along?
answer: They row it along like rows of tiny oars
choices: They row it along like rows of tiny oars
They jet it backward like a squid's siphon
They undulate its whole body like an eel
They catch the current and let it drift helplessly
context: Each comb is a row of giant fused cilia (beating hairs) that act like tiny oars to row the animal through the water. Source: Smithsonian Ocean (ocean.si.edu/ocean-life/invertebrates/jellyfish-and-comb-jellies); Wikipedia Ctenophora.

question: A see-through ocean animal up to 1.5 meters long, about 5 feet, swims on beating hairs called cilia, the way many single-celled creatures do. No bigger animal on Earth gets around like this. Which is it?
answer: The comb jelly
choices: The comb jelly
The giant squid
The sea sponge
The manta ray
context: Comb jellies are the largest animals on Earth that swim using cilia (beating hairs) instead of muscle. Source: Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ctenophora); WHOI (whoi.edu/ctenophores).

question: A tiny shrimp brushes against the long trailing tentacle of a comb jelly, an animal that looks like a jellyfish but belongs to its own ancient line of life. How does the comb jelly seize and hold its meal?
answer: Sticky glue cells burst and cement the prey in place
choices: Sticky glue cells burst and cement the prey in place
Venom stingers fire tiny harpoons into the prey
It wraps the prey in a net of mucus and reels it in
It stuns the prey with a jolt of electricity
context: A comb jelly has no stinging cells; its tentacles carry sticky 'glue cells' called colloblasts, mushroom-shaped cells that burst and glue prey in place. True jellyfish use venom-loaded nematocysts instead. Source: WHOI (whoi.edu/ctenophores); ScienceDirect ctenophore evo-devo review.

question: Beroe, a glassy drifter of the open sea, has no tentacles at all, though most of its relatives trail long sticky ones to snag their food. Its body is little more than a huge gaping mouth. What does Beroe hunt, and how?
answer: Swallows other comb jellies whole
choices: Swallows other comb jellies whole
Drills into fish eggs and sucks out the yolk
Filters clouds of plankton through a fine mesh
Ambushes sleeping shrimp buried in the sand
context: Beroe hunts by swallowing other comb jellies whole, gripping them with stiff, tooth-like bundles of hairs called macrocilia that line its mouth. Comb jellies are voracious predators that eat each other. Source: WHOI (whoi.edu/ctenophores); Shape of Life.

question: A comb jelly, Bathocyroe fosteri, drifts through the dark twilight zone as clear as glass, except for one brightly colored organ, its stomach. That color hides the glow of the luminous prey it has swallowed, so no bigger hunter spots the meal. What color is the stomach?
answer: Bright red
choices: Bright red
Pale gold
Bright white
Deep violet
context: Bathocyroe fosteri has a bright red stomach; red hides the blue-green glow of luminous prey it has swallowed, so the meal doesn't shine out and attract bigger hunters. Source: WHOI (whoi.edu/ctenophores).

question: A jelly-like drifter called the sea walnut rode into the Black Sea in ships' ballast tanks in the 1980s. Free of enemies, it bred out of control and ate up the sea's zooplankton and young fish. Late in the 1990s something knocked it back down. What was it?
answer: Another comb jelly that hunts and eats comb jellies
choices: Another comb jelly that hunts and eats comb jellies
A cold winter that froze the surface waters
A new fishing fleet that netted them by the ton
A virus that spread through the swarm
context: Beroe ovata, a comb-jelly-eating predator, arrived by ship in the late 1990s and knocked the sea walnut's numbers back down. Source: IUCN GISD (iucngisd.org/gisd/species.php?sc=95); NASA Earthdata 'Invasion of the Ctenophores'.

question: Scientists comparing ancient gene patterns argue over which creature split off first from all other animals, making it our most distant animal cousin. Textbooks usually give that place to sponges, but some of these scientists point to another animal. Which one?
answer: The comb jelly
choices: The comb jelly
The flatworm
The sea anemone
The tiny water bear
context: Some studies argue the comb jelly, not the sponge, was the first branch to split off from all other animals. Whether comb jellies or sponges are the 'sister to all other animals' is still a live, unsettled scientific debate. Source: Nature 2023 (nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05936-6); Nature Ecology & Evolution 2017 (Whelan et al.).

question: Kei Jokura and his team at Woods Hole cut two sea walnuts, small comb jellies, in 2024 and placed the injured animals next to each other in a dish. About nine times out of ten, something happened that no shark or human could ever do. What became of the two animals?
answer: They fused into one animal, their nervous systems wiring together
choices: They fused into one animal, their nervous systems wiring together
They sealed their own wounds and drifted apart unharmed
They devoured each other until only the larger one was left
They cloned themselves, budding off dozens of tiny copies
context: When Kei Jokura's team cut partial lobes off two sea walnuts (Mnemiopsis leidyi) and set them together, the pair merged roughly 90% of the time. Within about two hours their two nerve nets had wired together so tightly that muscle contractions beat in near-perfect sync, and food swallowed by one mouth traveled through the shared, merged gut. This works because comb jellies lack allorecognition, the self-versus-nonself check that in most animals rejects foreign tissue. Source: sci.news coverage of Jokura et al., Current Biology, Oct 2024 (https://www.sci.news/biology/mnemiopsis-leidyi-rapid-physiological-integration-13322.html).

question: A tardigrade's patch of moss dries out in the sun, and the tiny eight-legged animal pulls in its head and legs, losing more than 95 percent of its body water. What shape does it shrivel into to wait out the drought?
answer: A shriveled barrel called a 'tun'
choices: A shriveled barrel called a 'tun'
A hard sealed ball called a 'pellet'
A flat papery disc called a 'scute'
A coiled spring called a 'spiral'
context: Losing over 95% of its water, the tardigrade curls into a barrel-shaped 'tun' — and hours later a single drop of water swells it back up and it walks away. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-022-04015-2

question: A hungry mite in a patch of damp moss happily eats a tardigrade, and a careless fingertip can squash one flat. Yet tardigrades are famous for surviving boiling heat, bitter cold and crushing pressure. In what state does a tardigrade shrug off those extremes?
answer: Only as a dried, shriveled, dormant tun
choices: Only as a dried, shriveled, dormant tun
Anytime, whether wet or dry
Only while it is actively feeding
Only when many are clustered together
context: The toughness belongs to the dried tun, not the living animal. An active, water-filled tardigrade is soft and delicate — easily crushed or eaten; only the shriveled, dormant state shrugs off boiling, freezing, and crushing. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/invertebrates/facts/tardigrades-water-bears

question: A dried tardigrade can lie in the moss for years without food or water, waiting for rain. To last that long, its metabolism falls so low that instruments can barely detect it. Roughly how low does it fall compared with normal?
answer: Below 0.01% of normal
choices: Below 0.01% of normal
About 10% of normal
About half of normal
About 2% of normal
context: In the tun state a tardigrade's metabolism falls below 0.01% of normal — so faint it's basically undetectable — letting it wait years, even up to about 30. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/invertebrates/facts/tardigrades-water-bears

question: European scientists running a test called Tardigrades in Space bolted dried tardigrades to the outside of a satellite in September 2007. The animals spent about ten days exposed to a place no animal had been shown to survive before. Where were they?
answer: The open vacuum beyond the atmosphere
choices: The open vacuum beyond the atmosphere
The mouth of an undersea volcano
The heart of a nuclear reactor
The core of an Antarctic glacier
context: On the Foton-M3 capsule, dried tardigrades survived raw space vacuum for about 10–12 days — the first animal shown to endure it. Many revived on Earth; some even withstood added solar UV and later reproduced. Source: https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Human_and_Robotic_Exploration/Research/Tiny_animals_survive_exposure_to_space

question: A kid tears open a packet of dry dust from an old comic-book ad for 'Sea-Monkeys' and pours it into a bowl of water. A few days later the bowl is full of tiny swimmers, hatched from eggs that can lie dried out for years. What is the animal really called?
answer: The brine shrimp
choices: The brine shrimp
The pond snail
The water flea
The mud minnow
context: Brine shrimp — marketed as 'Sea-Monkeys' — hatch from cysts, dormant eggs that survive years bone-dry until water revives them. Source: https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/211/18/2899/17660/

question: A midge larva, the young of a small mosquito-like fly, lies in a seasonal pool in central Africa as the pool dries up. It gives up about 97 percent of its body water and stiffens on the parched ground, yet water brings it back as if nothing had happened. What is the longest a dried larva has waited and still revived?
answer: About 17 years
choices: About 17 years
About 17 days
About 17 weeks
About 17 months
context: The sleeping chironomid larva can lose ~97% of its water, vitrify, and revive after roughly 17 years dried out — one of the toughest known cases of surviving without water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polypedilum_vanderplanki

question: Russian scientists in 2021 thawed a bdelloid rotifer out of Siberian permafrost soil. Once warmed, the microscopic animal, smaller than a grain of sand, woke and began to reproduce. When they radiocarbon-dated the mud it was frozen in, they learned how long it had been dormant. How long?
answer: About 24,000 years
choices: About 24,000 years
About 240 years
About 2,400 years
About 240,000 years
context: A bdelloid rotifer from ~24,000-year-old Arctic permafrost revived and began reproducing — one of the longest 'comebacks' ever recorded for a dormant animal. Source: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(21)00624-2

question: Ralph Hengherr heated nine species of dried tardigrade in 2009 to test their famous toughness. A dried tardigrade can take a quick scald, and headlines say it survives 150 degrees Celsius, but revival stayed high only up to about 80 degrees and then fell steeply. What happens to the dried animal at that point?
answer: Its protective inner glass softens and melts
choices: Its protective inner glass softens and melts
Its outer claws snap off one by one
Its stored trehalose caramelizes to syrup
Its curled body unrolls and floods with air
context: The 'survives 150 C' headline hides a ceiling written into the very glass that protects the animal. Using calorimetry, Hengherr et al. measured each species' glass-transition temperature — the point where the solid inner glass softens back toward a liquid — at roughly 35 to 87 C depending on species. Revival stayed high up to about 80 C and then dropped steeply, and that steep drop lined up with the glass transition: once the glass un-sets, the frozen-in protection is lost and the cell is exposed. So the tun can survive a brief scald, but sustained heat melts the very thing keeping it alive. Source: Hengherr et al. 2009, Physiological and Biochemical Zoology 82(6):749-755, 'High-Temperature Tolerance in Anhydrobiotic Tardigrades Is Limited by Glass Transition' (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/605954; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19732016/).

question: A dragonfly perches on a reed, its huge eyes wrapped around most of its head. A human eye has a single lens, but a dragonfly eye is a bundle of tiny units, each with its own lens. How many units can one eye hold?
answer: Up to about 30,000
choices: Up to about 30,000
Up to about 300
Up to about 3,000
Up to about 300,000
context: A dragonfly's eye is a bundle of up to ~30,000 ommatidia — each a lens over a light-catcher (rhabdom) that sees one dot of light. The brain stitches all those dots into a mosaic, not a smooth photo. Source: grrlscientist/ScienceBlogs '30,000 Facets Give Dragonflies a Different Perspective' (2009); Britannica 'Ommatidium'.

question: A cook's hand swoops down to swat a housefly on the kitchen counter, and the fly darts away before the hand connects. To the fly, the giant hand seems to come down in slow motion. Roughly how much faster does a housefly see than a human?
answer: About four times as fast
choices: About twice as fast
About four times as fast
About ten times as fast
About a hundred times as fast
context: A fly sees about 250 flashes per second where a human sees about 60, roughly four times faster, so a descending hand looks like slow motion, and the fly dodges. Compound eyes are poor at fine detail but brilliant at catching motion. Source: Big Think 'You're not fast enough to swat a fly'; ACSH 'Flicker Fusion is More Than Meets the Eye'.

question: A mantis shrimp peers out of its burrow on an Indo-Pacific reef, scanning for prey and rivals. Each of its eyes rides on a movable stalk. How do the two eyes move?
answer: Each on its own, in different directions
choices: Each on its own, in different directions
Always together, as a locked pair
Only up and down, never side to side
Only when the shrimp turns its body
context: Each mantis-shrimp eye sits on its own stalk and moves independently, left, right, up, down and even twisting, so the two eyes can point in totally different directions at once. Source: Daly, How, Partridge & Roberts, 'Complex gaze stabilization in mantis shrimp' (PMC5966611); Wikipedia 'Mantis shrimp'.

question: Biologists kept finding wounds like melon-baller scoops on whales, tuna and even great white sharks: something in the deep was carving round plugs of flesh out of the biggest animals in the sea. When the culprit was caught, one thing about it stunned them. What?
answer: It was barely half a meter long
choices: It was barely half a meter long
It hunted in coordinated packs
It had venomous spines
It could swallow prey whole
context: The cookiecutter shark (Isistius brasiliensis) reaches only about 56 cm in females and 42 cm in males, yet it bites chunks out of whales, dolphins, orcas, tuna, swordfish, seals, and even great white sharks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookiecutter_shark

question: A fisherman hauls a cookiecutter shark onto his boat deck at night, and the little shark soon goes still. Yet for up to three hours it keeps doing one eerie thing. What?
answer: Its belly keeps glowing green
choices: Its belly keeps glowing green
Its skin keeps changing color
Its eyes keep flashing silver
Its gills keep pulsing light
context: The cookiecutter shark's green belly light is the strongest bioluminescence known in any shark, and it can keep glowing for up to three hours after the shark is taken out of the water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookiecutter_shark

question: A predator prowls the black deep, looking upward for anything drifting overhead. A cookiecutter shark cruises above it, belly aglow with soft green light, yet the hunter cannot pick it out. Why does the glowing belly make the shark harder to see, not easier?
answer: Its glow matches the faint light from the surface, erasing its silhouette
choices: Its glow matches the faint light from the surface, erasing its silhouette
Its green glow matches the water color, blurring its outline
Its glow flickers fast enough to smear its shape into a haze
Its glow is too dim for deep-sea eyes to register at all
context: This is counter-illumination camouflage: lit from below, the shark's glowing belly cancels its own silhouette against the faint light above, making it nearly invisible to anything looking up from the deep. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookiecutter_shark

question: A cookiecutter shark hangs in the dark midwater of a warm ocean, its whole underside glowing pale green except for one dark band beneath its throat. Biologists think that dark collar is no accident. What do they think it does for the little shark?
answer: It looks like a small fish and lures big hunters in
choices: It looks like a small fish and lures big hunters in
It hides the shark's eyes from the prey below it
It warns rival cookiecutters off its patch
It marks the shark as a male to females
context: The dark collar looks like the silhouette of a small fish, drawing big predators in close so the little shark can bite THEM. Scientists believe it is the only known case where the ABSENCE of glow works as a lure. Source: https://sharkangels.org/cookiecutter-sharks-use-glow-in-the-dark-ability-to-attract-prey-10x-its-own-size/

question: A cookiecutter shark bites with one connected row of lower teeth, locked together like a saw blade, where most sharks lose their teeth one at a time. Once the row is worn out, all of it drops free together. What does the shark do with the old set?
answer: It swallows the set whole
choices: It swallows the set whole
It spits the set onto the seabed
It keeps the set embedded for life
It grinds the set down on rocks
context: The shark's lower teeth interlock into one connected saw-like blade, and it swallows the whole old set entire, recycling the calcium. One shark shed 15 full sets growing from 14 cm to 50 cm, some 435 to 465 teeth swallowed over its life. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookiecutter_shark

question: To core a plug from a whale, a cookiecutter shark must stay clamped to thrashing flesh while it saws and spins. Its lips form a seal, but a seal alone would peel off. What second move drops the pressure inside its mouth and locks the grip like a suction cup?
answer: It retracts its tongue to suck the pocket empty like a piston
choices: It retracts its tongue to suck the pocket empty like a piston
It pumps sticky mucus between its lips and the skin
It hooks rows of gill rakers into the wound edge
It inflates its throat to press the seal outward
context: The 'suction' is an active hydraulic trick, not just sticky lips. The shark closes its spiracles and pulls back its basihyal (the shark's tongue), dropping the pressure inside its mouth below the surrounding water while the thick suctorial lips form a gasket. Once it is vacuum-locked and anchored by the hook-like upper teeth, it drives in the lower saw and spins its whole body to core out the plug. It works like a syringe: pull the plunger back and the low pressure sucks everything tight. Source: Wikipedia, Cookiecutter shark (basihyal/spiracle-closure vacuum mechanism), corroborated by multiple secondary sources.

question: Carlisle and colleagues read the cookiecutter shark's menu from the chemistry of its own tissue in 2021: isotopes, fats and traces of DNA. The results did not fit the little shark's fame as a whale biter. What did the tracers reveal?
answer: Tiny midwater fish and squid, not big surface animals, are its staple
choices: Tiny midwater fish and squid, not big surface animals, are its staple
It fasts for months between rare feasts on large prey
It scavenges dead whales far more often than it bites live ones
Its bites on whales deliver most of its yearly calories
context: Chemical-tracer detective work overturned the shark's own reputation. Carlisle et al. (2021, Scientific Reports) used stable isotopes, fatty acids, and eDNA and found that big surface victims (whales, tuna, dolphins) make up only a minor part of the diet: roughly 55% small mesopelagic fish and squid, about 39% vertically migrating midwater prey, and only around 5% large epipelagic prey. The shark's nitrogen-isotope (delta-15N) signature sat above that of the large prey, the mark of a diet drawn from the deeper midwater food web. The shark famous for coring whales mostly eats tiny midwater prey. Source: Carlisle et al. 2021, Scientific Reports (nature.com/articles/s41598-021-89903-z; PMC8175345).

question: A cuttlefish hovers just above the sandy seabed, arms fanned out, watching a shrimp below. In a blink too quick to follow, it strikes and the shrimp is gone. What shoots out from between its arms to seize the prey?
answer: Two long, hidden feeding tentacles
choices: Two long, hidden feeding tentacles
A jet of scalding water from its funnel
A sticky net spun from its own slime
A ring of hooks flicked from under its arms
context: A cuttlefish is a mollusk and cephalopod, a cousin of the octopus and squid. It spreads its eight arms, then fires two long, coiled feeding tentacles so fast the strike is nearly impossible to follow with the naked eye.
