Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium, Common Cuttlefish (montereybayaquarium.org/animals/animals-a-to-z/common-cuttlefish).

question: Leonardo da Vinci and other Renaissance artists drew with a rich brown ink squeezed from the ink sac of one soft-bodied sea creature. The color still carries the animal's Latin genus name, 'sepia.' Which creature is 'sepia' named after?
answer: The cuttlefish
choices: The cuttlefish
The squid
The octopus
The sea hare
context: The cuttlefish's brown ink gave the color 'sepia' its name; it was used for writing in Greco-Roman times and for drawing by artists such as Leonardo da Vinci. The animal's genus name, Sepia, and the ink share the word. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sepia_(color); Monterey Bay Aquarium, Common Cuttlefish.

question: A pet shopkeeper clips a white oval inside a parakeet's cage, as shops have done for more than a hundred years, so the bird can rub its beak on it and take in calcium. What is the oval really?
answer: A cuttlefish's internal shell
choices: A cuttlefish's internal shell
A dried piece of coral reef
A hardened lump of sea salt
A whale's polished ear bone
context: The 'cuttlebone' found on beaches and clipped into bird cages is the cuttlefish's internal shell. For over a hundred years it has been sold to pet birds as a beak-sharpener and calcium supplement. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'Everything you wanted to know about cuttlefish'; americansingercanary.org cuttlebone article.

question: In the open water of a shallow sea, a cuttlefish hangs perfectly still and level. A snail's shell is armor, but the porous shell inside the cuttlefish, its cuttlebone, does a very different job. What is the cuttlebone doing as it hovers?
answer: Acting as a float it fills with gas or liquid
choices: Acting as a float it fills with gas or liquid
Storing calcium it draws on to grow
Charging the cells that change its color
Holding ink in reserve for its next cloud
context: Unlike a snail's shell, the cuttlebone is a hard buoyancy tank stacked into tiny chambers the cuttlefish fills with gas or liquid to sink or rise, hovering like a submarine adjusting ballast. Source: AskNature, 'Layered Bone Holds Gas to Control Buoyancy'; PNAS 2020, 'Mechanical design of the highly porous cuttlebone' (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2009531117).

question: On a coral reef, a cuttlefish flashes stripes, spots and rolling waves of color across its skin in a heartbeat, using color cells called chromatophores. When biologists counted the kinds of light-sensing cells in its eyes, how many did they find?
answer: Just one kind
choices: Just one kind
Three kinds
Four kinds
Twelve kinds
context: The great irony of the cuttlefish, master of color, is that its eye holds only ONE type of photoreceptor, so it likely cannot see the dazzling color displays it produces the way humans do. Source: Bailey-Matthews National Shell Museum, 'The Amazing Cuttlefish Eye' (shellmuseum.org); PNAS 2016 (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1524578113).

question: A broadclub cuttlefish creeps toward a crab on an Indo-Pacific reef, sending dark stripes rolling downward across its head and arms again and again, like a moving television screen. How does this 'passing cloud' help it close in on the crab?
answer: It swamps the crab's eyes with fake motion, hiding the approach
choices: It swamps the crab's eyes with fake motion, hiding the approach
It makes the hunter look like seaweed swaying in the current
It warns rival cuttlefish to keep away from its prey
It hides the cuttlefish's eyes from the crab
context: A 2025 Bristol study found the moving stripes of the 'passing-cloud' display flood the prey's vision with fake downward motion, masking the fact that the predator is looming closer. Source: Santon & How et al., Science Advances 2025 (science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adr3686); ScienceDaily 2025-03-26.

question: Giant Australian cuttlefish crowd into the shallow bays of South Australia each winter to breed, and the big males stand guard and fight off rivals for the females. A small male has no hope in a straight brawl, so he cheats, and his trick fools the guard more than half the time. What does he do?
answer: He poses as a female to slip past the guard
choices: He poses as a female to slip past the guard
He plays dead until the guard drifts away
He blasts ink to blind the guard and dashes in
He bluffs with the guard's own warning pattern
context: A small 'sneaker' male can't win a fight, so he pales his skin, tucks his arms to fake a female's outline, and hides his male display to slip right past the guarding male to the female. The disguise works over half the time. Source: Norman/Hanlon, reported in Nature News 2005, 'Cuttlefish win mates with transvestite antics' (nature.com/news/2005/050117); ScienceDaily 2005-01-24.

question: Alexander and Christopher Stubbs, a father and son, studied a cuttlefish's strange W-shaped pupil, set off-center, and in 2016 proposed a way it might let the animal see color. By the usual rules of vision, its eyes should not tell colors apart at all. How could such an eye still read color?
answer: The pupil smears each wavelength to a different focus depth, and the eye reads color from how far it must refocus for a sharp image
choices: The pupil smears each wavelength to a different focus depth, and the eye reads color from how far it must refocus for a sharp image
The pupil rotates through colored filters, sampling one wavelength at a time before the brain stitches them together
The lone cell secretly holds three pigments that fatigue at different rates, mimicking three separate color receptors
The skin sends color data straight to the optic nerve, letting the body sense hues the eye alone never could
context: The cuttlefish is a color-changing champion yet has only one type of photoreceptor. Alexander and Christopher Stubbs (PNAS, 2016) argued the non-circular, off-axis W-shaped pupil deliberately MAXIMIZES chromatic aberration: the lens bends short (blue) and long (red) wavelengths to focus at different depths behind it, so no single image is ever sharp for all colors at once. By accommodating, refocusing the lens until the image snaps sharp, a single-receptor eye can infer the wavelength from the focus depth that worked. It is a color sense built from blur rather than from multiple pigments. Still a hypothesis under study, but a clever candidate answer to the puzzle. Source: Stubbs & Stubbs 2016, PNAS (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27382180/); Berkeley News 2016-07-05; phys.org summary.

question: A cuttlefish, like its octopus and squid kin, rewrites the working copies of its genes far more than most animals do. In the squid brain more than 60 percent are altered; humans alter well under 1 percent. Joshua Rosenthal and Eli Eisenberg showed in 2017 that this flexibility has a steep price. What did these animals give up for it?
answer: The normal speed of DNA evolution, since the genome around each editing site had to freeze in place to protect it
choices: The normal speed of DNA evolution, since the genome around each editing site had to freeze in place to protect it
The ability to pass any brain traits to offspring, since the edited messages are wiped before eggs are ever formed
A working immune memory, because the busy editing machinery mistakes their own nerve proteins for foreign invaders
Half of all their protein diversity, because each new edit permanently silences the original gene it was copied from
context: Coleoid cephalopods — cuttlefish, octopus, and squid — bend biology's 'central dogma' by editing their RNA (the working copy of a gene) so heavily that one gene can yield many protein variants, especially in nerve-signaling proteins. The trade-off Joshua Rosenthal (Marine Biological Laboratory) and Eli Eisenberg (Tel Aviv) found: the editing enzymes need specific genomic structures around each editing site to do their job, so the DNA flanking those sites became evolutionarily frozen — its mutation rate is severely suppressed. In effect these animals traded the ordinary speed of DNA-based evolution for on-the-fly protein flexibility. Source: Rosenthal & Eisenberg, Cell 2017; ScienceDaily 2017-04 (sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/04/170406121601.htm); Nature news d41586-017-00612-y.

question: A hungry bird lands right beside a Darwin's frog on the forest floor, close enough to snatch it. The frog does not bolt or fight back — instead it pulls a trick that makes the bird lose all interest and move on. What is the frog doing to save itself?
answer: Flopping onto its back to play dead
choices: Flopping onto its back to play dead
Puffing up huge to look too big to swallow
Oozing a bitter poison from its back
Screaming loudly to startle the bird
context: When a predator threatens it, Darwin's frog plays dead: it flops onto its back and lies still, and it may leap into a stream and float belly-up, motionless, until the danger passes — a leaf-shaped frog pretending to be a lifeless leaf. Source: https://www.wildlifeexplained.com/darwins-frog/

question: A male Darwin's frog waits beside a clutch of eggs in a beech forest of southern Chile. In most frogs the mother's work ends once the eggs are laid, but when these eggs begin to twitch, he scoops them up and keeps them with him while the tadpoles grow. Where does he keep them?
answer: Inside his throat's vocal sac
choices: Inside his throat's vocal sac
Glued in a neat row along his back
Wrapped in strings around his hind legs
Tucked into folds of skin on his belly
context: In Darwin's frog it is the father who broods the young: when the eggs begin to twitch, the male scoops them into his mouth and holds them inside his vocal sac — the balloon-like throat pouch he normally uses to call — where the tadpoles grow. Source: https://www.edgeofexistence.org/blog/life-within-a-vocal-sac/

question: A southern elephant seal, biggest of all seals, slips beneath the waves off Antarctica to hunt squid far below the sunlit surface, sometimes as deep as 2,000 meters. On a single breath, how long can it stay under?
answer: Up to about two hours
choices: Up to about two hours
Up to about forty minutes
Around four minutes
Roughly fifteen minutes
context: Southern elephant seals can occasionally dive as deep as 2,000 meters and stay under for up to about two hours on a single breath. Source: Ocean Tracks; Discover Wildlife, 'Southern elephant seal'.

question: A sperm whale dives a mile down, where the water presses on it with about 160 times the pressure at the surface. Instead of snapping under that weight, its chest does something no human chest could survive. What happens to its ribs and lungs on the way down?
answer: Its ribs hinge backward and its lungs collapse on purpose
choices: Its ribs hinge backward and its lungs collapse on purpose
Its ribs lock rigid and its lungs swell with extra air
Its ribs fuse into solid bone plating
Its lungs fill with seawater to equalize
context: The sperm whale's flexible ribcage folds inward, ribs hinging toward the tail, and its lungs deflate as it dives. Source: Orca Ireland, 'Deep-diving Adaptations in the Sperm Whale'.

question: A Weddell seal gulps one last breath at a breathing hole in the Antarctic sea ice and slips under for a dive that can last more than an hour. The moment it goes down, its heartbeat slows far below a normal mammal's pace. How slow does it get at its slowest?
answer: As few as 16 beats a minute
choices: As few as 16 beats a minute
Around 40 beats a minute
About 90 beats a minute
Roughly 150 beats a minute
context: As a Weddell seal dives, its heart deliberately slows (a slowdown called bradycardia) to as few as 16 beats per minute, saving oxygen. Source: Kooyman et al., 'Heart rates in freely diving Weddell seals'.

question: Deep in a dive under the Antarctic ice, a Weddell seal cannot spend its oxygen everywhere, because one breath must last up to an hour. It cuts the blood flow to its skin and flippers and lets them go cold. Where does it send the oxygen-rich blood instead?
answer: The brain, heart, and lungs
choices: The brain, heart, and lungs
The stomach, gut, and liver
The eyes, ears, and whiskers
The muscles, joints, and blubber
context: During a dive, blood is shunted away from skin and limbs toward the brain, heart, and lungs so the organs that most need oxygen get it. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology, 'Adaptations to deep and prolonged diving in phocid seals' (2018).

question: A Weddell seal is halfway through a long dive under the Antarctic sea ice and the oxygen it stored before diving is running low. To keep going, it squeezes a special reserve organ deep inside its belly like a sponge, dumping a fresh load of oxygen-rich red blood cells straight into its bloodstream. Which organ is the seal's hidden blood reservoir?
answer: The spleen
choices: The spleen
The liver
The bladder
The pancreas
context: A diving seal squeezes its spleen to dump stored oxygen-rich red blood cells into the bloodstream mid-dive. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology, 'Adaptations to deep and prolonged diving in phocid seals' (2018).

question: Groups of beaked whales washed ashore during naval sonar exercises, and Jepson and colleagues examined their bodies in 2003. Deep-diving whales were long thought safe from the bends, yet the team found an injury many believed could never form in a whale. What did they find?
answer: Gas bubbles scattered loose through the soft tissues all over the body
choices: Gas bubbles scattered loose through the soft tissues all over the body
Gas-filled cavities walled off inside the liver alone, and nowhere else
Fat globules clogging the fine vessels of the lungs, with no free gas
Pitted dead patches in the leg and arm bones from a lifetime of diving
context: Whether beaked whales are truly immune to the bends is a real, unsettled debate. Jepson and colleagues (Nature, 2003) found gas-bubble lesions in the tissues of beaked whales that mass-stranded during naval sonar exercises -- evidence of in-vivo bubble formation, essentially decompression sickness, in animals long assumed protected from it. The leading hypothesis is that loud mid-frequency sonar triggers a panicked change in dive behavior, surfacing too fast or altering depth profiles, so dissolved nitrogen bubbles out of blood and fat. The finding overturned the flat 'whales can't get decompression sickness' dogma and remains debated and controversial. Source: Jepson et al. 2003, Nature, 'Gas-bubble lesions in stranded cetaceans' (https://www.nature.com/articles/425575a); follow-up 'Whales, sonar and decompression sickness' (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15085881/).

question: A mile beneath the ocean surface, in pitch darkness, a female anglerfish hangs motionless and slowly waves a glowing bulb on a fleshy rod, the only speck of light for miles. What is the glow for?
answer: Luring prey close enough to eat
choices: Luring prey close enough to eat
Lighting the water so she can see
Warning rivals off her patch
Guiding her young through the dark
context: The rod is a modified dorsal fin ray called the illicium, and the glowing tip is the esca; it works like a fishing pole. Each species has its own uniquely shaped lure, which she waves to draw curious prey right to her mouth. Source: MBARI, 'Deep-sea anglerfish' (https://www.mbari.org/animal/deep-sea-anglerfish/).

question: A female anglerfish may go weeks without a meal in the deep sea, so she cannot let a chance pass. Her jaw opens like a trapdoor, and her needle teeth curve inward. How big a meal can she swallow?
answer: Prey larger than her own body
choices: Prey larger than her own body
Prey up to half her length
Prey no wider than her head
Only shrimp and tiny plankton
context: The inward-curving teeth trap anything that enters, and the hinged jaw stretches to engulf prey bigger than herself — a crucial trick where a missed meal might be the last one for a long time. Source: MBARI, 'Deep-sea anglerfish'; Live Science.

question: A female anglerfish dangles a tiny glowing lure right over her mouth in the black deep sea. If prey could make out the big fish behind the bulb, it would flee. What is special about her skin?
answer: It is ultra-black and soaks up almost all light
choices: It is ultra-black and soaks up almost all light
It is clear as glass, so light passes through
It is mirror-silver, like a hatchetfish's
It glows faintly to match the light from above
context: This ultra-black skin absorbs nearly all light, so in the deep only the glowing esca gives her away while the rest of her body disappears into the dark. Source: MBARI, 'Deep-sea anglerfish'.

question: Deep in the dark ocean, far below the last of the sunlight, a female anglerfish waves a tiny glowing bulb on a fleshy rod over her open jaws, the only light for miles around. Where does the glow in her lure come from?
answer: Bacteria living packed inside the lure
choices: Bacteria living packed inside the lure
A glowing chemical her own cells make
Glowing plankton trapped inside the bulb
Crystals that gather faint light from above
context: The light comes from symbiotic bacteria living inside the esca. The bacteria have shed many of their genes and lean heavily on their host, yet each young female still picks them up from the seawater. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, 'Meet the Tiny Bacteria That Give Anglerfishes Their Spooky Glow'; Baker et al. 2019, eLife 8:e47606.

question: A male deep-sea anglerfish, sometimes no bigger than a fingernail, drifts alone through miles of black water searching for a female. For his size, he carries the largest of one body part of any animal. Which body part, and why?
answer: Nostrils, to smell her species' scent in the dark
choices: Nostrils, to smell her species' scent in the dark
Eyes, to spot her faint lure from far off
Fins, to swim great distances quickly
Ears, to hear her moving through the water
context: The tiny male has the largest nostrils in proportion to head size of any animal, and uses this super-sense of smell to track a female's species-specific scent across the pitch-black deep sea. Source: Natural History Museum & Live Science, 'Animal Sex: How Anglerfish Do It'.

question: A tiny male Ceratias anglerfish drifts through the black deep far below the sunlight, sniffing for a mate, until at last he finds a female many times his size. He bites onto her side and holds on. What happens to the two fish?
answer: His flesh permanently fuses to hers
choices: His flesh permanently fuses to hers
He drops off and swims away after mating
He rides along, holding on by his teeth
She swallows him whole as a meal
context: In Ceratias, as in other anglerfish whose males fuse for life, enzymes dissolve the tissue where the two touch, so the male's flesh fuses permanently into the female's body, the union biologists call sexual parasitism. In some other anglerfish the male clings on only for a while. Source: Yale News, 'Sea of love: Behind the unusual sexual parasitism of deep-water anglerfish' (2024); Swann et al. 2020, Science.

question: A male anglerfish, a fraction of the female's size, clamps onto her in the midnight zone and never lets go. Plumbed into her blood supply, he lives on what her blood brings him. What becomes of the little male over time?
answer: His eyes and organs waste away to a lump of tissue
choices: His eyes and organs waste away to a lump of tissue
He grows large and dominant on her nutrients
He detaches, having passed her his genes
He develops a second lure of his own
context: He draws all his food straight from her blood, so his eyes and internal organs waste away and he shrinks to little more than a lump of sperm-supplying tissue hanging off her body. Sources: Yale News (2024); University of Washington, 'Deep-sea anglerfishes have evolved a new type of immune system' (2020).

question: Ted Pietsch studied a preserved anglerfish of the species Photocorynus spiniceps, a female 46 millimeters long with her tiny mate fused to her back like a barnacle on a whale. The male measured just 6.2 millimeters, about the size of a grain of rice. What record does he hold?
answer: World's smallest known sexually mature vertebrate
choices: World's smallest known sexually mature vertebrate
First anglerfish male ever photographed alive
Only anglerfish male found without a host
Largest size gap ever measured in a fish
context: Pietsch's 6.2 mm male of Photocorynus spiniceps, fused to a 46 mm female, is the smallest known sexually mature vertebrate on record. Source: UW News, 'Small tale: Parasitic anglerfish takes size prize, prof says' (2006).

question: A female anglerfish carries a male fused into her bloodstream for life, and her body ought to attack his foreign tissue the way a person's body rejects a transplant. Instead the union holds. What has her species thrown away to let it work?
answer: Key parts of the adaptive immune system
choices: Key parts of the adaptive immune system
Her inborn, first-line immune defenses
The clotting system that seals wounds
The nerves that feel pain in her skin
context: Permanently-attaching anglerfish have discarded the MHC genes, killer T cells, and antibodies that protect humans from disease. Thomas Boehm, who led the study, noted that in a human, that combined loss 'would result in fatal immunodeficiency', yet the fish survive on a beefed-up innate immune system scientists are still working to understand. Source: Swann et al. 2020, 'The immunogenetics of sexual parasitism,' Science.

question: A young female anglerfish hatches in the dark deep ocean, far below the sunlight, with a dark, empty lure. Every new female must gain her own colony of light-makers before it can shine. How does each young anglerfish come to glow?
answer: She catches fresh light-makers from the seawater
choices: She catches fresh light-makers from the seawater
She inherits the bacteria from her mother
She grows the glowing cells from her own tissue
She absorbs them from the male when he fuses
context: The glowing symbionts (Candidatus Enterovibrio luxaltus and Ca. E. escacola) are picked up fresh from the environment each generation, not passed down through the egg. The tell is in the bacteria's own genes: they still carry a complete flagellar-motility and chemotaxis toolkit that is useless inside a sealed light organ and only makes sense for a free-living swimming stage. Their DNA also shows up in ordinary seawater samples, and host and symbiont family trees do not track each other, so a single symbiont species turns up across four separate ceratioid families rather than each fish lineage having its own inherited strain. Source: Baker et al. 2019, 'Diverse deep-sea anglerfishes share a genetically reduced luminous symbiont that is acquired from the environment,' eLife 8:e47606 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/47606); PubMed 31571583.

question: Swann and colleagues lined up anglerfish species by how the males mate: some never attach to the female, some cling on for a while, and some fuse to her for life. Then they compared the immune genes each species has lost. What pattern did they find?
answer: The more permanent the fusion, the more immunity is lost
choices: The more permanent the fusion, the more immunity is lost
Every species had discarded the same set of genes
Only the briefly-attaching species had lost any genes
The losses appeared at random, unlinked to mating
context: The immune losses are graded, a dose-response pattern rather than one freak deletion, and this is still active research. Swann et al. found that species whose males attach only temporarily had already lost a working aicda (AID) gene, which fine-tunes antibodies, while among the species that fuse permanently some had gone further and also lost working RAG genes (rag1 and rag2, the machinery that builds antibody and T-cell receptors), along with other immune genes. So the amount of adaptive immunity discarded scales with how committed the fusion is. Source: Swann et al. 2020, 'The immunogenetics of sexual parasitism,' Science (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaz9445); review 'Histocompatibility and Reproduction: Lessons from the Anglerfish,' Life 2022 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8780861/).

question: A farmer checking his pasture at midday finds a dairy cow standing still in the sun, eyes half shut. Her jaw grinds steadily from side to side, though she has not taken a fresh bite of grass in a long while. What is she doing?
answer: Chewing the cud, food she swallowed earlier
choices: Chewing the cud, food she swallowed earlier
Scraping grit from between her teeth
Grinding seeds too hard to swallow whole
Cooling herself by working her jaw
context: A resting cow that looks like it's doing nothing is 'chewing the cud': it swallowed grass quickly, its stomach fermented and softened it, then sent a wad back up the throat to be chewed again and re-swallowed. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Ruminant

question: A safari guide on the African savanna tells her group that one of the big plant-eaters around them belongs to the same club as cattle, deer and sheep: the ruminants. Which one?
answer: The giraffe
choices: The giraffe
The elephant
The rhinoceros
The zebra
context: A giraffe is a ruminant too — one of the tallest cud-chewers alive — and the club also includes deer, sheep, goats, antelope, and cattle, all mammals of the suborder Ruminantia that regurgitate and re-chew their food. Elephants, rhinos, and zebras are not ruminants. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/ruminant

question: Wildebeest and gazelles graze in huge herds on the open African savanna, cropping the grass as fast as they can. They gulp it down barely chewed and do the slow, careful chewing much later. Why eat first and chew afterward?
answer: To grab food in the open, then retreat somewhere safe to finish chewing
choices: To grab food in the open, then retreat somewhere safe to finish chewing
To let the grass warm to body temperature before their teeth touch it
To save their teeth, which wear down fast on gritty grass
To swallow the morning dew on the grass before it dries off
context: The whole point of eat-fast-then-chew-later: a grazer bolts down mouthfuls of grass in the open, then retreats to safety and does the careful chewing out of a predator's reach. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/ruminant

question: A herd of cattle grazes a green pasture, yet not one of the animals can digest the grass it eats: none of them produces cellulase, the enzyme needed to cut apart cellulose, the tough fiber grass is built from. How do they live on it?
answer: They rent trillions of gut microbes that make the enzyme and digest it for them
choices: They rent trillions of gut microbes that make the enzyme and digest it for them
Their four stomachs grind the grass so fine the fiber falls apart on its own
Their saliva contains a mineral that dissolves the tough fiber
They only absorb the sugary sap, and pass the fiber through undigested
context: A grazing mammal can't digest grass itself — it makes no cellulase. It hosts trillions of gut microbes that make the enzyme and do the digesting, then the animal lives off the products. The partnership is the real trick. Source: https://bio.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Microbiology/Microbiology_(Boundless)/16:_Microbial_Ecology/16.05:_Microbial_Symbioses/16.5B:_The_Rumen_and_Ruminant_Animals

question: A cow chewing in her pasture is running a huge fermenting tank in her gut, the rumen, and all that fermenting throws off gas: 150 to 500 liters of methane a day. By what route does more than 80 percent of it leave her body?
answer: Out the mouth, as a burp
choices: Out the mouth, as a burp
Out the back end, as flatulence
Through her skin, in her sweat
Dissolved into her milk and urine
context: A single cow burps out roughly 150 to 500 liters of methane a day, and over 80% of it leaves through the mouth by belching — not from the other end. Source: https://beef.unl.edu/understanding-and-mitigating-methane-emissions-cattle/

question: A grazing cow swallows a stray nail along with the grass she eats. In the reticulum, the honeycomb-lined second chamber of her stomach, a sharp piece of metal can pierce the wall and cause deadly 'hardware disease.' What do many farmers feed their cattle to guard against it?
answer: A magnet that pins the metal in place
choices: A magnet that pins the metal in place
A rubber ring that filters out anything hard
A dose of clay that coats swallowed metal
A second lining grafted over the honeycomb wall
context: Because the honeycomb-lined reticulum traps swallowed metal that can pierce its wall ('hardware disease'), farmers feed cattle a magnet that sits in the reticulum for life, pinning stray nails and wire safely in place. Source: https://vivo.colostate.edu/livestock/hardware.html

question: A horse and a rabbit live on tough grass, like a cow, yet neither has a cow's four-chambered stomach or brings its meal back up to chew again. Their grass still has to ferment somewhere along the gut. Where does that happen?
answer: In a big pouch called the cecum, well past the stomach
choices: In a big pouch called the cecum, well past the stomach
In the stomach itself, the very first stop
In a fifth chamber unique to grazing horses
In the mouth, mixed with fermenting saliva
context: Horses and rabbits are hindgut fermenters: they digest first and ferment later in a large cecum past the stomach, instead of fermenting up front like a cow. It's the other main solution to living on grass. Source: https://www.furrycritter.com/pages/articles/rabbits/hindgut_fermentation.htm

question: A rabbit digests its grass in an order that wastes some of the goodness: the vitamins and protein made deep in its gut would pass out of its body before it could absorb them. What does the rabbit do to get a second pass at them?
answer: Eats special soft droppings straight from its bottom, then digests them again
choices: Eats special soft droppings straight from its bottom, then digests them again
Licks the nutrients off the grass a second time before swallowing
Stores the droppings in its cheek pouches to reabsorb overnight
Grinds its droppings back into the fresh grass it eats
context: A rabbit produces soft, grape-cluster droppings called cecotropes — packed with vitamins and protein its microbes made — and eats them straight from its bottom to absorb the goodness on a second pass. This is cecotrophy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecotrope

question: A dire wolf chased huge plant-eaters across ice-age America, looking much like a gray wolf. A naturalist might guess the two were the same size. How did the biggest kind of dire wolf compare with a big male gray wolf?
answer: The dire wolf was heavier, its largest kind near 68 kg to a gray wolf's 43
choices: The dire wolf was heavier, its largest kind near 68 kg to a gray wolf's 43
The dire wolf was leaner at about 30 kg, a sprinter beside the 43 kg gray wolf
The two matched almost exactly, both close to 43 kg despite the coat difference
The dire wolf was the lighter of the two, near 35 kg to a gray wolf's 43
context: The largest dire wolves averaged about 68 kg (150 lb); a big male gray wolf runs about 43 kg (95 lb) — the dire wolf was the bulkier, more powerfully built animal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dire_wolf

question: With jaws built for crushing, the dire wolf brought down giant plant-eaters in ice-age America. Paleontologists studying its prey find one menu of big ice-age animals turning up again and again. Which animals did it mostly hunt?
answer: Ancient bison, horses, ground sloths, and camels
choices: Ancient bison, horses, ground sloths, and camels
Woolly mammoths, mastodons, and giant beavers
Musk oxen, caribou, and moose of the far north
Woolly rhinos, cave bears, and giant elk
context: The dire wolf hunted huge ice-age plant-eaters: ancient bison, western horses, ground sloths and camels, with pronghorn and peccaries also suggested. When those big animals died out at the end of the ice age, the dire wolf vanished with them, while smaller, more flexible true wolves survived. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dire_wolf

question: Scientists filed the dire wolf, the ice-age hunter dug from the La Brea tar pits by the thousand, as a bigger cousin of the gray wolf for over a century. Then in 2021 Angela Perri's team recovered DNA from the bones of dire wolves, and the results rewrote its family tree. What did the DNA show?
answer: It was no close cousin of wolves, distant enough to warrant its own genus, Aenocyon dirus
choices: It was no close cousin of wolves, distant enough to warrant its own genus, Aenocyon dirus
It was a hybrid, born when gray wolves crossed with coyotes deep in the ice age
It was the direct ancestor of every gray wolf and coyote alive today
It was a dog line domesticated by early Americans, then gone wild again
context: The 2021 ancient-DNA study found the dire wolf was not a close relative of the gray wolf, and it was reclassified into its own genus, Aenocyon dirus. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/dire-wolves-were-not-really-wolves-new-genetic-clues-reveal/

question: Paleontologists counting broken teeth among the dire wolves dug from La Brea's tar pits find them in 5 to 17 percent of the specimens. Among modern wolves and lions, only 0.5 to 2.7 percent have cracked or broken teeth. What does all that dental damage point to?
answer: They were crunching bone during hard, competitive feeding
choices: They were crunching bone during hard, competitive feeding
They ground down their teeth chewing tough plants and roots
They were losing fights with sabertooth cats over kills
They ate abrasive sand and grit while scavenging in dunes
context: 5 to 17 percent of La Brea dire wolf specimens show cracked teeth, versus 0.5 to 2.7 percent in modern predators — evidence of crunching bone during hard, competitive feeding on big carcasses. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dire_wolf

question: Paleontologists digging in Los Angeles's La Brea tar pits pulled up thousands of dire wolf skeletons, far more than an occasional unlucky misstep into the sticky asphalt could explain. What kept luring dire wolves into the pits, again and again?
answer: Trapped plant-eaters drew them in to feed, and they stuck too
choices: Trapped plant-eaters drew them in to feed, and they stuck too
Whole packs deliberately denned in the warm asphalt through winter
Floods swept dead wolves from miles around into one low pit
The wolves drank from the shiny asphalt, mistaking it for water
context: A big plant-eater got mired in the asphalt, its cries drew predators and scavengers, and the dire wolves that came to grab a meal got stuck too — repeating over millennia. Source: https://tarpits.org/research-collections/tar-pits-collections/mammal-collections

question: Björn Kurtén split the dire wolf into two kinds in 1984, divided by the Rocky Mountains. The eastern form had a modern wolf's long, chase-built legs. The western form, the one found in thousands at La Brea, was built differently. What set it apart as a hunter?
answer: Its hind legs ran shorter and stockier, making it the poorer sprinter of the two
choices: Its hind legs ran shorter and stockier, making it the poorer sprinter of the two
Its skull grew longer and narrower, trading crushing force for a faster snap
Its shoulders rode higher and leaner, letting it lope for miles without tiring
Its paws spread wider and flatter, keeping it atop soft ground the other sank in
context: Bjorn Kurten named the split in 1984: Aenocyon dirus guildayi (west of the Rockies, including La Brea) averaged about 60 kg with shorter, stockier legs, its rear limbs roughly 8% shorter than a Yukon wolf's, making it a weaker runner, while the larger eastern A. d. dirus averaged about 68 kg with limbs 10 to 14% longer than guildayi and comparable to a modern wolf's. A 2019 reanalysis (Ruiz-Ramoni & Montellano-Ballesteros) even questioned whether the two are truly distinct subspecies. Source: Kurten (1984); Wikipedia 'Dire wolf' (subspecies section); Dire Wolf Project size page; 2019 Ruiz-Ramoni & Montellano-Ballesteros reanalysis.

question: A hunting bird swoops onto a porch post in the southern United States and snatches a green anole by the tail. In a heartbeat the anole sprints off, leaving the bird holding only its tail, and it is not even bleeding. How can it part with its tail so fast and so cleanly?
answer: The tail is built to snap off at a weak seam
choices: The tail is built to snap off at a weak seam
The tail is soft and has no bone in it
The bird's grip crushed the tail loose
The lizard chewed through its own tail
context: This is autotomy: deliberately dropping a body part to escape a predator, then often regrowing it. The tail snaps at a built-in weak point so the lizard can run while the predator is left holding the piece. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autotomy

question: A fox pounces on a leopard gecko among dry rocks, and the gecko's tail snaps off in its jaws while the little spotted lizard scurries away. For as long as half an hour afterward, the tail left behind keeps the fox busy. What is the tail doing all that time?
answer: Thrashing and flipping on its own after it detaches
choices: Thrashing and flipping on its own after it detaches
Oozing a bitter poison that stings the predator's mouth
Screeching to warn other geckos of the danger
Clinging to the predator's teeth with tiny hooks
context: In leopard geckos the severed tail performs acrobatic flips up to 3 cm high and jumps and lunges for as long as 30 minutes, holding the predator's attention while the gecko escapes. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2817253/

question: A gull seizes a shore crab by one claw, and the crab breaks free by shedding the whole claw at a special weak joint, the basi-ischium. Its body is full of watery fluid instead of tidy blood vessels, so an open stump ought to bleed it dry. What stops the leak?
answer: A membrane at the break plane instantly seals the wound
choices: A membrane at the break plane instantly seals the wound
It plugs the stump with a fast-forming scab of dried mud
Its fluid is too thick to leak from the open joint
It grows a knot of new shell over the gap in seconds
context: Crabs and lobsters can shed a whole leg or claw on purpose at the pre-made break point, the basi-ischium. A membrane there seals the wound instantly so the animal doesn't lose its body fluid. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autotomy

question: A blue crab scuttles across the sea floor one claw short, weeks after shedding the claw to escape a gull. A soft, folded bud of new claw already waits at the stump, but it will not unfold just yet. When does it finally become a working claw?
answer: When the crab molts and sheds its shell
choices: When the crab molts and sheds its shell
When the crab finds and eats enough calcium
When the crab returns to the exact spot it lost it
On the first full moon after the loss
context: A soft, folded limb bud forms at the break and stays tucked away, then unfolds and hardens into a working claw the next time the crab sheds its shell. Source: https://aquariumbreeder.com/detailed-guide-to-regeneration-in-crustaceans/

question: A leopard gecko waits out a hot, dry season in its burrow. Like many skinks and geckos, it drops its tail only when it must, since the tail holds a store the lizard would badly miss. What does the tail store?
answer: Fat for lean times
choices: Fat for lean times
Water for droughts
Venom for its bite
Calcium for its eggs
context: In many skinks and geckos the tail is the main fat-storage organ, so losing it burns stored reserves. A tailless lizard is also slower and often drops in social rank, losing fights and territory to rivals with intact tails. Source: https://www.mdpi.com/1424-2818/17/11/780

question: A skink caught by the tail in a bird's beak lets the tail go and runs, the same let-go escape a crab makes with a claw. Lizards, crabs, sea cucumbers and worms sit on wildly different branches of the animal kingdom, yet all of them have the trick. How did they all come by it?
answer: Evolution arrived at it independently many times
choices: Evolution arrived at it independently many times
It came down from one ancient sea-worm ancestor
Viruses carried the genes for it between groups
It is a leftover from the very first animals
context: Autotomy is such a good survival trick that evolution arrived at it independently at least nine separate times across the animal kingdom, in groups as different as lizards, sea cucumbers, crabs, and worms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autotomy

question: One European spider almost never leaves the water. It lives, hunts, and raises young among the plants of a still pond. Underwater it shines a bright silver against the dark. What makes the diving bell spider gleam like that?
answer: A film of trapped air clinging to its body
choices: A film of trapped air clinging to its body
Rows of tiny mirror-like scales on its back
A slick of oil it secretes to shed water
Silver pigment in its shell that reflects sunlight
context: Underwater the diving bell spider looks silvery because a film of trapped air clings to the water-repelling (hydrophobic) hairs on its body. This glinting bubble is behind its name Argyroneta, from Greek 'argyros' (silver) — roughly 'silver spinner.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell_spider

question: Below the surface of a still pond, a diving bell spider rests inside a silk dome full of air. Every breath uses up a little of that air, and the silk has no way to make more. How does the spider keep its dome topped up?
answer: Swims all the way up to the surface and ferries a bubble back down
choices: Swims all the way up to the surface and ferries a bubble back down
Pumps the water out of the dome with strokes of its legs
Lets rising marsh gas from the mud collect under the dome
Cracks the bell open to let stale water flush the old air out
context: To restock the bell, the spider swims to the surface and carries air back down trapped against a dense layer of water-repelling (hydrophobic) hairs on its abdomen and legs, ferrying the bubble down like a delivery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell_spider

question: A male diving bell spider grows to about 15 millimeters, bigger than the 12-millimeter female sharing his pond. Among the world's fifty-thousand-plus spider species it is nearly always the other way round, with the female the bigger sex, sometimes many times over. What does the male do that the extra size likely helps with?
answer: Swims around actively hunting through the water
choices: Swims around actively hunting through the water
Carries the female's egg sac on his back
Spins the entire bell for the whole colony
Burrows into mud to survive the winter freeze
context: Unlike almost all other spiders, the male diving bell spider is the larger sex, likely because males swim around actively hunting and need extra strength against the water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell_spider

question: A diving bell spider resting in its silk dome under the water needs to swim up for fresh air only about once a day, far longer than the trapped air alone should last. Seymour and Hetz showed that the dome is no mere tank. How does it keep supplying the spider with oxygen?
answer: It works like a gill, pulling oxygen out of the surrounding water
choices: It works like a gill, pulling oxygen out of the surrounding water
It slowly releases oxygen frozen into the silk fibers
It captures rising oxygen from plants rooted below it
It converts the spider's own carbon dioxide back into oxygen
context: The silk bell works like a physical gill: as the spider uses up oxygen, dissolved oxygen from the surrounding water diffuses IN through the bell's surface while carbon dioxide diffuses OUT, so the bell keeps refilling itself. A resting spider only needs to surface about once every 24 hours. Source: https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/214/13/2175/10328/The-diving-bell-and-the-spider-the-physical-gill (Seymour & Hetz 2011)

question: Fresh oxygen keeps arriving in a diving bell spider's silk dome, so the spider might seem able to seal itself in for the whole winter. Seymour and Hetz concluded it probably cannot: the dome keeps shrinking all the while, and in their model a small one drops to half its size in about 37 hours. What makes the dome shrink?
answer: Nitrogen slowly diffusing out of the bubble into the water
choices: Nitrogen slowly diffusing out of the bubble into the water
Carbon dioxide building up faster than it can escape
Silk dissolving under the steady pressure of the water
Oxygen leaking back out as quickly as it enters
context: The gill is not a free lunch. As the spider burns oxygen, nitrogen's share of the bubble rises (Dalton's law) and that nitrogen slowly diffuses out into the water, so the bell keeps deflating even while oxygen flows in. Seymour and Hetz's model shows a 0.5 ml bell at 100 mm depth shrinking to half its volume in about 37 hours, which is why the spider must still renew its bell from time to time and why, they concluded, bells are unlikely to last all winter under the ice. Source: Seymour & Hetz 2011, 'The diving bell and the spider: the physical gill of Argyroneta aquatica', Journal of Experimental Biology 214(13):2175-2181, https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/214/13/2175/10328/The-diving-bell-and-the-spider-the-physical-gill

question: A dolphin rises from the sea, opens the blowhole atop its head and takes a long breath before diving again. Its sleek body looks like a fish's, but that breath gives it away. What kind of creature is it really?
answer: A warm-blooded mammal
choices: A warm-blooded mammal
A fish that gulps air
A reptile, like a turtle
A cold-blooded amphibian
context: The bottlenose dolphin (genus Tursiops) is not a fish but a small toothed whale: a warm-blooded mammal that breathes air through a blowhole on top of its head and must surface to breathe. Source: WDC / Whale and Dolphin Conservation, Tursiops biology overview.

question: A young bottlenose dolphin swimming with its mother off a tropical beach makes up a whistle all its own in its first months and keeps it for life. How do other dolphins use that whistle?
answer: To tell who is calling, like a name
choices: To tell who is calling, like a name
To tell where food is, like a map
To warn of danger, like an alarm
To show its mood, like a face
context: Every bottlenose dolphin invents its own 'signature whistle' within its first months, and it becomes a personal name for life; signature whistles make up about half of all the whistles a dolphin produces. Source: University of St Andrews (King & Janik); PNAS 2013.

question: A few bottlenose dolphins off Shark Bay, on Australia's west coast, hunt fish hiding in sharp, rocky rubble on the seafloor. A soft nose poked through that rubble would be scraped raw, so before each dig these dolphins tear something off the bottom and wear it as a protective cap. What do they wear?
answer: A cone-shaped sea sponge over the beak
choices: A cone-shaped sea sponge over the beak
A ring of seaweed around the neck
A shell cupped in the mouth
A crab claw held against the fin
context: Shark Bay 'spongers' tear a cone-shaped sea sponge off the seafloor and wear it over the beak like a glove, using it as a shield while poking through sharp rubble to flush out hidden fish (sandperch) other dolphins can't reach. Source: Whale & Dolphin Conservation USA, Meet the Shark Bay Spongers; PNAS 2005.

question: A bottlenose dolphin hunting in dark, muddy water cannot see the fish hiding there, so it fires clicks from its head and reads the returning echoes, a trick called echolocation. Each click passes through the fatty bulge in its forehead, called the melon, on its way out. What does the melon do to the click?
answer: Bends it into a tight, aimed beam
choices: Bends it into a tight, aimed beam
Muffles it so prey can't hear it
Stretches it into a long, low hum
Splits it into two, one per side
context: The melon is a fatty, dome-shaped lump in the dolphin's forehead that works like an acoustic lens, bending the clicks into a narrow beam so the dolphin can 'see' prey by echo in murky, dark water. Source: biologyinsights.com, Dolphin Sonar; DolphinsPlus echolocation explainer.

question: A dolphin spends its whole life at sea and never comes ashore to rest. A land mammal's breathing runs on automatic even in deep sleep, but a dolphin must decide to open its blowhole for every breath. How does a dolphin sleep without drowning?
answer: It sleeps with only half its brain at a time
choices: It sleeps with only half its brain at a time
It floats belly-up and holds its breath for hours
It stores enough oxygen to sleep for hours
It naps only during the safe daylight hours
context: A dolphin, like a whale, is a 'conscious breather': it actively contracts muscles to open its blowhole for every breath. Because breathing is not automatic, it can never sleep fully. Instead it uses 'unihemispheric sleep': only half its brain sleeps at a time while the other half stays awake so it never forgets to surface and breathe. It closes just one eye, the eye opposite the sleeping half. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, Dolphins Sleep With Only Half Their Brain; WDC; Scientific American 'How do whales and dolphins sleep without drowning?'; baleinesendirect.org (respiratory system).

question: A dolphin firing its hunting clicks is not using its mouth at all, even though the sound seems to pour out ahead of it. To make each click, it snaps pressurized air past a pair of tissue flaps nicknamed monkey lips. Where in the dolphin do those flaps sit?
answer: Just below the blowhole, atop the head
choices: Just below the blowhole, atop the head
Deep in the throat behind the tongue
Inside the fatty melon of its forehead
Down in the chest beside the lungs
context: A dolphin makes its clicks not with its mouth but with 'phonic lips' (nicknamed 'monkey lips') just below the blowhole on top of the head, snapping pressurized air past them to buzz out sound. Source: biologyinsights.com, Dolphin Sonar: How Dolphins Use Echolocation to See.

question: A dolphin has no ear flaps on its smooth head, only pinhole openings where ears would be. Yet a bottlenose hunting by echolocation catches faint returning echoes with great precision. The sound does not come in through those tiny holes; it travels through a different part of the dolphin's face. Through which part of its body do the echoes reach its inner ear?
answer: Its fat-filled lower jawbone
choices: Its fat-filled lower jawbone
The blowhole atop its head
The tip of its long snout
The bones around its eyes
context: A dolphin hears returning echoes not through ear-holes but through its lower jaw: a thin, fat-filled channel in the jawbone funnels the vibrations straight to its inner ear. Source: biologyinsights.com, Dolphin Sonar; Dolphin Communication Project FAQ.

question: Every wild bottlenose dolphin has a signature whistle all its own. Vincent Janik, a dolphin researcher, found that a dolphin will learn a close friend's whistle and repeat it back, usually after the two are apart. He called it the first known example, in mammals other than humans, of what?
answer: Calling another animal by name
choices: Calling another animal by name
Teaching a skill by sound alone
Holding a two-way conversation
Copying a call to fool a rival
context: Dolphins learn a friend's signature whistle and copy it to address that specific individual, most often when separated from a close friend, as if calling out the friend's name to reunite. Janik: 'Our results present the first case of naming in mammals.' Source: University of St Andrews (King & Janik); Science.org.

question: A few female bottlenose dolphins in Shark Bay, Western Australia, tear a cone-shaped sponge off the seafloor and wear it on the beak while they poke through rocks for hidden fish. Almost no other dolphins in the world do it. Scientists wanted to know whether a sponger is born knowing the trick or picks it up somehow. Where does a young sponger get the skill?
answer: It learns it from its own mother
choices: It learns it from its own mother
It is hardwired into its genes at birth
It figures it out alone by trial and error
It copies whichever adults hunt nearby
context: Sponging is a taught tradition, not an instinct: calves go to 'sponge school' with mom from birth and start wearing their own mini-sponge by age two or three. Nearly every sponger shares one mitochondrial DNA marker inherited only from the mother, tracing the whole tradition back through the mother line. Source: Science News, Sponge Moms; PNAS 2005.

question: A dolphin's sonar is tested by asking it to tell two metal cylinders apart from several meters away. The cylinders look identical; they differ only in how thick their walls are. How small a difference in wall thickness can a dolphin's clicks reliably detect?
answer: Thinner than a credit card
choices: Thinner than a credit card
About as thick as a coin
About as thick as a pencil
About as wide as a fingernail
context: Dolphin sonar can tell apart aluminum cylinders whose walls differ by just 0.23 millimeters, thinner than a credit card, from 8 meters away, and can detect targets more than 100 meters away. Source: biologyinsights.com, Dolphin Sonar: How Dolphins Use Echolocation to See.

question: A bottlenose dolphin plunges hundreds of meters down, far past where a human diver would be crushed or crippled by the bends. As it descends, its heart slows to a crawl, and the crushing pressure flattens the tiny air sacs in its lungs. Why is that collapse good for the dolphin?
answer: To keep deadly nitrogen from dissolving into its blood
choices: To keep deadly nitrogen from dissolving into its blood
To force stale air out through the blowhole faster
To squeeze extra oxygen into its blood for the dive
To hold in body heat against the cold deep water
context: On a deep dive a dolphin's body runs a 'dive reflex': the heart slows dramatically (bradycardia) to conserve oxygen, and blood is shunted away from non-essential tissue. The water pressure squeezes the lungs until many of their tiny air sacs collapse, so little gas is left in contact with the blood and very little nitrogen dissolves into the body, a defense against decompression sickness, the bends, which can kill human divers who surface too fast. A 2018 hypothesis adds that part of the lung may stay open for gas exchange while blood is steered away from the collapsed part. In Navy tests reported in 1969, a trained bottlenose named Tuffy dived to about 300 m (nearly 1,000 ft). Sources: Ridgway, Scronce & Kanwisher 1969, Science 166:1651; Garcia-Parraga, Moore & Fahlman 2018, Proceedings of the Royal Society B 285:20180482.

question: A Draco, the flying dragon of Southeast Asia's rainforests, clings to a tree trunk like any brown lizard. Then it leaps, and two wide wings snap open from its sides. Those wings are thin skin stretched over what part of its body?
answer: Hugely elongated ribs that fan outward
choices: Hugely elongated ribs that fan outward
Long webbed fingers on each hand
Flaps of loose belly skin between its legs
A frame of stiffened tail spines
context: Unlike a bat's or bird's wing (built from arm and hand bones), the Draco's wing is skin (the patagium) stretched over five to seven greatly elongated ribs that swing out from the body like the sticks of a folding fan; special muscles open them and fold them flat against the flanks. Source: PLOS ONE, 'How lizards fly: A novel type of wing in animals'.

question: Under his chin a male Draco lizard carries a bright yellow flap of skin. He flicks it out to warn rival males and to attract females. To make this flag blaze against his camouflaged body, what does he actually do with it?
answer: Angles it toward the sun so the flap glows
choices: Angles it toward the sun so the flap glows
Pumps it full of blood until it turns scarlet
Rattles it to make a buzzing sound
Coats it in sticky sap that catches the light
context: The throat flag is called the dewlap (or gular flag). Because it is translucent, the male holds it perpendicular to the sun so light shines through and it glows, standing out sharply against his otherwise camouflaged body. Sources: Wikipedia, Draco (lizard); A-Z Animals, Draco volans.

question: High in the rainforest canopy, Draco lizards glide from tree to tree eating ants and termites, and they almost never touch the forest floor. Yet some of them must climb all the way down to the ground. Which ones, and why?
answer: Females, to bury a clutch of eggs
choices: Females, to bury a clutch of eggs
Males, to gather nesting sap
The young, to drink from puddles
Old lizards, to escape rivals above
context: Only females descend to the ground: a female digs a hole, lays a clutch of about 2 to 5 eggs, fills it in, and returns to the canopy. Otherwise the lizards spend their entire lives aloft. Source: Wikipedia, Draco (lizard).

question: A Draco leaps from a rainforest trunk and spreads its skin wings. Halfway through the glide to the next tree, it reaches forward with both front hands, something no other gliding animal is known to do. What is it doing with them?
answer: Gripping the front edge of each wing to hold it taut
choices: Gripping the front edge of each wing to hold it taut
Paddling the air to gain a little more speed
Clutching a leaf it tore off as a rudder
Covering its eyes against the rushing wind
context: The Draco grabs the leading edge of each wing membrane with its hands, holding it taut. Scientists call this a 'composite wing' because two different body parts (the ribs plus the forelimbs) build one wing surface, which also frees the legs to instantly climb or run the moment it lands. Source: PLOS ONE, 'How lizards fly: A novel type of wing in animals'.

question: Over a summer pond a slender four-winged insect skims low, its wings held straight out from its body. It stops dead and hovers, then darts sideways, backward or straight up, and hangs still again. Huge eyes almost fill its head. Which insect is this?
answer: Dragonfly
choices: Dragonfly
Honeybee
Housefly
Grasshopper
context: The dragonfly's mastery of the air, including hovering and flying backward, sets it apart from most other insects. Source: Iowa DNR '6 cool things you should know about dragonflies'; Sciencenews.org 'The flap on dragonfly flight'.

question: A dragonfly perched on a reed has a head that is almost all eye: two huge glossy domes, each built from thousands of tiny lenses. How much of the world around it can the dragonfly see at once?
answer: Nearly a full circle around it
choices: Nearly a full circle around it
About half, the whole view in front
About a quarter, mostly ahead
Only a narrow cone straight ahead
context: A dragonfly's compound eyes wrap almost entirely around its head, giving it nearly 360-degree vision; it can see everywhere except directly behind its own head. Source: Natural History Museum 'Dragonflies: The ultimate hunters' (nhm.ac.uk); ScienceBlogs '30,000 Facets Give Dragonflies a Different Perspective'.

question: Locked onto a hovering midge, a dragonfly shoots forward to strike. Scientists filmed hunt after hunt in high-speed video and counted how often the strikes worked. About how often does a hunting dragonfly catch what it chases?
answer: Around 19 times out of 20
choices: Around 19 times out of 20
Around 3 times out of 4
Around 1 time out of 2
Around 1 time out of 4
context: A hunting dragonfly catches prey on about 90-95% of its attempts, one of the highest success rates of any predator on Earth. Source: Nature World News 'Master Hunter Dragonflies Kill Prey 95 Percent Of The Time'; Smithsonian Magazine '14 Fun Facts About Dragonflies'.

question: Halfway across a pond, a dragonfly stops dead, hangs in a perfect hover, then flies straight backward, tricks few other insects can manage. Most insects flap all their wings together, in unison. What is different about the dragonfly's four wings?
answer: Each wing has its own muscles and moves alone
choices: Each wing has its own muscles and moves alone
Its wings flex like a bat's skin wings
It rides rising warm air and cannot truly flap
It folds two wings away and flies on just two
context: Each of a dragonfly's four wings is worked by its own muscles and moves independently, letting it hover, fly straight backward, and turn on a dime. Source: Sciencenews.org 'The flap on dragonfly flight'; Iowa DNR '6 cool things you should know about dragonflies'.

question: A hunting dragonfly bears down on a fly, but it does not aim at the fly the way a chasing hawk or dog would. It heads for an empty patch of sky ahead of where the fly is now, and high-speed footage catches it doing so again and again. Why does it fly toward empty air?
answer: It is aiming where the prey will be
choices: It is aiming where the prey will be
It is dazzled and simply guesses a direction
It is trying to herd the prey toward the water
It flies upwind first to save energy
context: A dragonfly does not chase its prey; it predicts where the prey will BE and flies to that interception point, computing the course before the target even tries to escape. Source: UC Davis Biology, 'How Dragonflies Catch Prey in Midair' (biology.ucdavis.edu/news); Wiederman & Olberg interception research.

question: The dragonfly zipping over a summer pond has only a few weeks left to live as a winged adult, yet the insect may already be several years old. It spent nearly all of those earlier years in a completely different form and a different place, growing up unseen. Where did it spend them?
answer: Underwater as a hunting nymph
choices: Underwater as a hunting nymph
High in the treetops
Buried in dry sand
Drifting on the open ocean
context: A dragonfly spends most of its life underwater as a fierce nymph, often for months or years, while the winged adult stage lasts only a few weeks. Source: KQED Science 'A Baby Dragonfly's Mouth Will Give You Nightmares' (kqed.org); Schlitz Audubon 'Dragonflies: Nature's Aerial Hunters'.

question: A dragonfly nymph, a stocky brown creature with no wings yet, sits perfectly still on the floor of a pond as a tadpole drifts past. Faster than a human eye can follow, the nymph snatches the tadpole and drags it in. What does it strike with?
answer: A hinged lower jaw that shoots out
choices: A hinged lower jaw that shoots out
A sticky tongue it flicks out like a frog
A cloud of venom it puffs into the water
A net of silk it casts around the prey
context: The nymph hunts with a hinged lower jaw, the 'mask', shot out almost too fast to see to snatch mosquito larvae, tadpoles, and even small fish, then folded back under its head. Source: KQED Science 'A Baby Dragonfly's Mouth Will Give You Nightmares' (kqed.org); makeham.org 'Feeding and predation in dragonflies and damselflies'.

question: A naturalist walking the edge of a pond on a summer morning finds a hollow brown husk clinging to a reed just above the water. It is shaped exactly like a dragonfly nymph and split open down the back, but it is completely empty inside. What happened here?
answer: An adult dragonfly crawled out of it
choices: An adult dragonfly crawled out of it
A dragonfly laid its eggs inside it
A spider drained the nymph and left it
The nymph shed it to grow, then swam back down
context: When ready, the nymph climbs out onto a reed or rock, its skin splits down the back, and the adult pulls itself out, leaving behind the empty shell called an exuvia. Source: Field of Mar 'Dragonfly fact sheet' (fieldofmar-e.schools.nsw.gov.au); Schlitz Audubon.

question: A globe skimmer, a small dragonfly, rides the monsoon winds out over the open Indian Ocean between India and East Africa, with no land beneath it. No insect is known to migrate farther, and four or more generations in turn each fly a leg of the round trip. About how long is the whole round trip?
answer: About 11,000 miles
choices: About 11,000 miles
About 2,000 miles
About 4,000 miles
About 7,000 miles
context: The globe skimmer makes the longest migration of any insect: a multi-generation round trip of about 11,000 miles across the Indian Ocean, riding the monsoon winds. Source: Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 'Unraveling the World's Longest Non-stop Migration: The Indian Ocean Crossing of the Globe Skimmer Dragonfly' (frontiersin.org).

question: A hunting dragonfly tracks a darting fly wherever it moves, its aim off by only about a degree. Researchers traced the steering signal to a small control circuit running from its brain to its wing muscles. How many nerve cells carry the prey's direction?
answer: Just sixteen cells, eight paired neurons steering the wings
choices: Just sixteen cells, eight paired neurons steering the wings
A dense web of several thousand cells across the brain
One giant command cell wired to every flight muscle
About two hundred cells lining each of the huge eyes
context: These are the target-selective descending neurons (TSDNs): eight pairs whose combined firing forms a population vector tracking prey across the full 360 degrees with a mean directional error near 1.2 degrees, firing about 30 milliseconds after the prey moves, matching the reaction time seen in real hunting flights. Source: Gonzalez-Bellido, Peng, Yang, Georgopoulos & Olberg, PNAS 2013, https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1210489109 (PMC3545807, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3545807/).

question: Two miles down in the pitch-black Pacific, a pale dumbo octopus does not jet like its shallow-water cousins. It slowly beats a pair of broad, floppy paddles that stick out from the top of its body, one on each side. What are those paddles?
answer: Ear-like fins
choices: Ear-like fins
Jet siphons
Sucker arms
Feathery gills
context: The dumbo octopus (Grimpoteuthis) 'flies' by flapping two big ear-like fins on its head/body, named for Disney's flying elephant Dumbo. No shallow octopus swims this way. Source: National Geographic (MBARI Davidson Seamount footage), https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/dumbo-octopus-monterey-seamount-news

question: On the pitch-dark seafloor, a dumbo octopus meets a small worm. Most octopuses grab their prey and tear it apart with a hard beak, but this one spreads the web between its arms around the worm to trap it. What does it do next?
answer: Swallows it whole
choices: Swallows it whole
Bites it in half
Stings it first
Sucks it dry
context: The dumbo octopus swallows prey whole, trapping worms or tiny crustaceans in its webbed arms and gulping them down, instead of tearing them apart with a beak like most octopuses. Source: Smithsonian Ocean + DiscoverWildlife, https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/marine-animals/dumbo-octopus-guide

question: A female dumbo octopus drifts over the pitch-black ocean floor thousands of meters down. Most shallow-water octopus mothers lay one big clutch of eggs and then die guarding it, but she handles her eggs in a way that surprised the scientists who studied her. How does she manage them?
answer: She carries eggs at many stages of ripeness at once
choices: She carries eggs at many stages of ripeness at once
She lays every egg together in a single spring batch
She waits years and then dies after one huge clutch
She glues her whole clutch to a rock and guards it till it hatches
context: The female dumbo octopus is a 'continuous spawner': she carries eggs at many stages of ripeness at once and lays only one or two at a time, whenever conditions suit, because the deep sea has no seasons to time breeding to. She can also store a male's sperm and fertilize her ripest eggs when she chooses. Source: Wikipedia (Grimpoteuthis, reproduction) + Smithsonian Ocean, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grimpoteuthis

question: A dumbo octopus beats its two big fins with real muscular power, flying through the deep water, though like any octopus it has no bones. Muscles that strong need something firm to pull against, and inside its mantle it keeps one small hard part that almost every other octopus has lost. What do its fins anchor to?
answer: A tiny saddle-shaped internal shell
choices: A tiny saddle-shaped internal shell
A ring of stiffened stomach muscle
A rod of calcium in each fin
A knot of hardened skin at the neck
context: Almost all octopuses have no shell of any kind, but Grimpoteuthis kept a small U- or V-shaped cartilaginous shell vestige, tucked in a shell sac inside the mantle. The two big fins anchor to this saddle-shaped shell, which gives the muscular fin strokes a rigid base to pull against; its shape is a genus-defining feature of the whole group. So the whimsical ear-flapping is powered by the single bit of hard skeleton the animal chose to keep. Source: Grokipedia 'Cirrina' and 'Grimpoteuthis'; corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grimpoteuthis and marinebio.org/species/finned-deep-sea-octopuses/grimpoteuthis-spp/ (Villanueva et al. functional-morphology work on cirrate fin cartilage).

question: On the African savanna, a stout, glossy black beetle finds a fresh heap of animal droppings. It packs a wad of the dung into a neat round ball, then rolls the ball away to bury underground as food for its young. Which insect is this?
answer: The dung beetle
choices: The dung beetle
The stag beetle
The firefly
The praying mantis
context: The dung beetle finds a fresh pile of droppings, packs some into a ball, and rolls it off to bury as buried food it can eat later. Source: Sci-News, https://www.sci.news/biology/article00844.html

question: A female dung beetle sculpts one special ball into a pear shape, tucks a single egg into its narrow end, and buries it deep underground. In most insects the mother now abandons the eggs entirely. What does this beetle mother do instead, making her unusual among insects?
answer: She stays underground tending the buried ball until her young mature
choices: She stays underground tending the buried ball until her young mature
She flies off at once and never returns to the burrow
She lays hundreds more eggs in the same ball to raise the odds
She dies on top of the ball so her body feeds the grub
context: In many dung beetle species the mother sculpts a pear-shaped brood ball, lays one egg in the narrow end, and then remains in the burrow tending and guarding the developing young — parental care that is rare among insects. Source: NCBI PMC3815100 brood-ball study + San Diego Zoo.

question: A dung beetle on the sunlit African plains must roll its ball of fresh dung away fast, before a rival can steal it. Before setting off, it climbs on top of the ball and turns a slow full circle there, a strange little dance in place. Scientists who filmed the spin found it does one crucial job. What is the beetle doing up there?
answer: Storing a snapshot of the sky to hold a straight bearing
choices: Storing a snapshot of the sky to hold a straight bearing
Scanning below for rival beetles creeping up to raid it
Softening the ball's surface so it packs tighter
Warming its wings for a quick escape flight if attacked
context: Atop the ball the beetle does a spinning 'dance,' storing a single snapshot of the sky in its brain to lock in a straight bearing before rolling. Source: Lund University, https://www.lunduniversity.lu.se/article/when-dung-beetles-dance-they-photograph-firmament

question: To keep its ball moving dead straight, a dung beetle steers by the Sun by day and the Moon by night. But on a black, moonless night, with no Sun and no Moon to guide it, it still rolls arrow-straight. What faint light in the sky does it lock onto — a first, for any animal on Earth?
answer: The glowing band of the Milky Way
choices: The glowing band of the Milky Way
The faint red shine of the planet Mars
The greenish shimmer of the northern lights
The dim afterglow left along the horizon
context: On moonless nights dung beetles steer by the diffuse band of the Milky Way, the first animal shown to navigate by the galaxy. Marie Dacke's team confirmed it in a planetarium, where beetles rolled just as straight with only the Milky Way's band showing. Source: Science/AAAS on Dacke et al. 2013.

question: The male Onthophagus taurus dung beetle can pull over 1,100 times its own body weight — the strongest insect on Earth for its size, like a man dragging six double-decker buses. Researchers found this monstrous strength did not evolve to move dung at all. What is the beetle actually straining against with all that power?
answer: Rival males it wrestles in the breeding tunnel to win a mate
choices: Rival males it wrestles in the breeding tunnel to win a mate
The packed soil it must plow through to dig its burrow
The suction of wet mud gripping its buried ball
A predator's jaws it must break free from to escape
context: The male Onthophagus taurus can pull 1,141 times its own body weight, the world's strongest insect for its size. This power evolved for tunnel combat: horned males brace and shove head-to-head in the breeding burrow, and the strongest wins the female. Source: Queen Mary University of London; Knell & Simmons, Proc. Royal Society B 2010.

question: Dunkleosteus, a fish as long as a small car, ruled the Late Devonian seas about 380 million years ago, in the stretch of time known as the Age of Fishes. Its head and shoulders were sheathed in thick, joined plates fitted like tank armor. What were the plates made of?
answer: Bone
choices: Bone
Scales
Cartilage
Shell
context: Dunkleosteus belonged to the placoderms — 'plate-skinned' fish whose heads and front bodies were cased in thick, interlocking bony plates. Every placoderm vanished in the end-Devonian extinction ~359 million years ago. Source: fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/placoderm/dunkleosteus

question: With one of the strongest bites ever estimated for a fish, Dunkleosteus sheared through armored prey. Yet a look inside its huge open mouth shows that one thing every shark has today is missing entirely. What did Dunkleosteus lack?
answer: Teeth
choices: Teeth
Scales
A tongue
Gills
context: Dunkleosteus had no teeth at all. Instead of teeth, the front of its jaws grew into self-sharpening bony blades. Source: discovermagazine.com — 'A Prehistoric Sea Monster Wielded Bone Blades'

question: Hall and colleagues examined the fossil head plates of the armored fish Dunkleosteus, top predator of the Late Devonian seas, and found some marked with deep punctures and scrapes. Something had broken right through that thick armor. Which kind of attacker do those wounds fit?
answer: One of its own kind
choices: One of its own kind
A large early shark
A giant sea scorpion
A big lobe-finned fish
context: Hall and colleagues (2016) described scrape and puncture marks on Dunkleosteus head armor that match the bladed jaws of other Dunkleosteus, so it attacked its own kind. Their report offered the wounds as possible evidence of cannibalism, though fights between rivals could also explain them. Source: Hall et al. 2016, 'Possible evidence for cannibalism in the giant arthrodire Dunkleosteus' (conference abstract); Wikipedia 'Dunkleosteus' (puncture damage from the bony fangs of other Dunkleosteus); fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/placoderm/dunkleosteus

question: For years, artists drew Dunkleosteus as a suction feeder, flinging its jaws open in a fiftieth of a second to whip a vacuum in front of its mouth and inhale prey. Then Engelman and colleagues restudied the skull in 2025, found far more cartilage than that model assumed, and took a fresh look at its cleaver-like blades. What feeding style did they argue for?
answer: Biting with a wide gape and tearing prey into pieces
choices: Biting with a wide gape and tearing prey into pieces
Inhaling prey whole by suction through a fast-opening mouth
Filtering plankton through fine sieves inside the gill arches
Crushing hard shells slowly between broad flat tooth plates
context: The suction picture came from Anderson & Westneat's 2007 biomechanical model, which found the four-bar jaw could snap open in about 20 milliseconds and complete a full open-and-shut cycle in 50-60 milliseconds. Engelman and colleagues (2025) argued that model rests on anatomy that doesn't match the real skull, which held far more cartilage than assumed, and that the big slicing blades resemble predators that bite with a wide gape and actively tear prey apart (oral processing) rather than true suction feeders, which have small gapes and packed tooth patches. The feeding style of Dunkleosteus is now genuinely contested. Source: Engelman et al. (2025), 'Functional anatomy, jaw mechanisms, and feeding behavior of Dunkleosteus terrelli,' The Anatomical Record, https://anatomypubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ar.70075 ; Anderson & Westneat (2007), Biology Letters, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17443970/ ; summarized at Wikipedia 'Dunkleosteus' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkleosteus

question: Paleontologists digging out the giant armored fish Dunkleosteus keep finding compact clumps of fish bones and half-broken prey remains lying beside it. They read the clumps as something the fish produced, not something it swallowed. What do the clumps show Dunkleosteus did?
answer: It spat back up the bones it could not digest
choices: It spat back up the bones it could not digest
It stored crushed prey in a pouch for later meals
It ground shells into gravel to ballast its body
It brooded its young among piles of gathered debris
context: These compact masses are called boluses, and paleontologists interpret them as material Dunkleosteus regurgitated rather than passed through its gut, evidence that it apparently could not digest bone and other hard parts. Because some boluses contain the teeth of other fishes such as the shark-relative Orodus, they give a direct look at its menu, a rare glimpse of what an animal 360 million years dead actually ate. Source: Wikipedia 'Dunkleosteus' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkleosteus (bolus / regurgitation and Orodus stomach-content evidence)

question: A great gray owl, the owl with the largest facial disc of all, waits on a perch above the winter snow of a northern forest. Suddenly it plunges straight down, punching through as much as a foot and a half of snow onto prey it never sees. What is it catching?
answer: Voles it hears tunneling below the snow
choices: Voles it hears tunneling below the snow
Fish it hears splashing under thin ice
Insects it hears chewing at buried roots
Eggs it smells inside a hidden burrow
context: The great gray owl (Strix nebulosa) locates voles purely by the sound of them tunneling, then punches through roughly 18 inches of snow to grab prey it never sees. Its enormous facial disc gathers that muffled sound. Source: Cornell Lab, All About Birds / Living Bird; UC Riverside News.

question: Listening for prey beneath the snow, a great gray owl hears it in the wrong place: snow bends sound the way a lens bends light, so the prey can sound as if it is up to 5 degrees off its true position. Before diving, the owl does one thing that probably helps it beat this acoustic mirage. What is it?
answer: It hovers in place, beating its wings
choices: It hovers in place, beating its wings
It closes one ear against the snow
It calls out and waits for an echo
It presses its face flat to the snow
context: Researchers found the great gray owl hovers just before the dive, likely to lock onto the true position from the angle where the mirage error is smallest. Source: Whitchurch et al. 2022, Proc. R. Soc. B 289:20221164, 'Great Gray Owls hunting voles under snow hover to defeat an acoustic mirage.'
