question: A moth flutters through the night carrying one of the simplest ears in nature, just one to four nerve cells wired to a thin patch of skin. That tiny ear is tuned to a single deadly sound, and the instant the sound arrives the moth veers away or tumbles wildly out of the sky. What is the moth listening for?
answer: The ultrasonic sonar of a hunting bat
choices: The ultrasonic sonar of a hunting bat
The wingbeat of a diving owl
The buzz of a rival moth's wings
The crackle of a spreading wildfire
context: These bare-bones ears exist for one job: hearing a bat's ultrasonic hunting calls in time to dodge. Kenneth Roeder first recorded moth ears reacting to bat calls in the early 1960s. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ultrasound avoidance'; PMC2679932; Roeder's foundational recordings.

question: A bat hunting in the dark fires bursts of ultrasound and listens for the faint echo that bounces back off a moth's wings. Some moths answer with a fuzzy coat of microscopic wing scales, and the bat sweeps right past without ever hearing them. How do the scales beat the bat's sonar?
answer: They swallow the ultrasound so almost no echo returns
choices: They swallow the ultrasound so almost no echo returns
They scatter it into a confusing double echo
They retune the echo to sound like empty air
They bounce it straight back to deafen the bat
context: The wing scales act as a natural sound-absorbing 'metamaterial,' soaking up as much as 72% of the ultrasound that hits them, while fuzzy body fur absorbs about 69% -- so almost no echo returns and the moth is nearly invisible to sonar. One move in a moth-vs-bat arms race roughly 65 million years old. Source: Neil et al. 2020, PNAS 117, 'Moth wings are acoustic metamaterials' (University of Bristol).

question: Researchers in one study wired up the ear of the tiny greater wax moth to find the highest pitch it could still pick up. A hunting bat's shrillest call reaches about 212 kilohertz, already far above anything a human ear can catch. How high did the moth's ear still respond?
answer: Up to about 300 kHz
choices: Up to about 300 kHz
Up to about 250 kHz
Up to about 150 kHz
Up to about 90 kHz
context: In this single reported study, the greater wax moth (Galleria mellonella) responded to about 300 kHz -- far past the ~212 kHz peak of even a bat's call -- described as a defense over-evolved to stay one jump ahead of bat sonar. Reported as a study finding, not a settled superlative. Source: Moir, Jackson & Windmill 2013, Biology Letters (Univ. of Strathclyde); ScienceDaily.

question: The parasitic fly Ormia ochracea tracks down a chirping cricket to lay its eggs on it, yet its eardrums almost touch, about half a millimeter apart. A chirp hits the closer eardrum just about one or two microseconds before the other, a gap too small for its nerves to read. How does the fly still pin down where the chirp came from?
answer: A stiff bridge links the eardrums so they rock like a see-saw
choices: A stiff bridge links the eardrums so they rock like a see-saw
It swivels its whole head to sweep the chirp across both ears
It floods the gap with fluid that stretches the delay tenfold
It waits for the echo off the ground to double the signal
context: The fly's eardrums sit only about 520 micrometers apart, so a male cricket's 5 kHz song reaches one just 1-2 microseconds before the other -- far too small a gap for nerves to read directly. Miles, Robert & Hoy (1995) found the fix: a stiff cuticular bridge pivoted in the middle joins the two eardrums and works like a see-saw, mechanically amplifying that microscopic time-and-loudness difference into a large motion the nervous system can sense. The result is directional hearing accurate to about plus-or-minus 2 degrees -- as good as a human's -- from ears almost touching. Engineers now copy the trick to build tiny directional microphones and hearing aids. Source: Miles, R.N., Robert, D. & Hoy, R.R. (1995), 'Mechanically coupled ears for directional hearing in the parasitoid fly Ormia ochracea,' J. Acoust. Soc. Am. -- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8550933/ ; mechanics/520 um & MEMS mic: Nature Sci. Rep. -- https://www.nature.com/articles/srep02489

question: To prove a barn owl hunts by sound and nothing else, Roger Payne switched off every light and dragged a mouse-sized wad of dry paper across dead leaves. The owl struck it dead-on in the pitch dark. Why did that one crumpled wad settle the question for good?
answer: It gave off no body heat and could not be seen, only rustled
choices: It gave off no body heat and could not be seen, only rustled
It moved far too fast for any eye to track in the dim gloom
It carried the exact scent trail a real live mouse leaves
It warmed under the lamps to mimic a live mouse heat glow
context: Roger Payne's 1971 study (Journal of Experimental Biology) was the landmark that proved owls hunt by sound alone. In a totally dark room a trained barn owl struck not only live mice but a mouse-sized wad of paper dragged across dry leaves. Because a cold paper wad emits no body heat and cannot be seen, its successful strike ruled out both vision AND any infrared/heat-sensing, leaving only the rustling sound. Filmed under infrared, the owl's strikes landed with an error of less than 1 degree in both the horizontal and vertical planes -- and it needed sound frequencies above 5 kHz to do it. This later proved to be the smallest sound-localization error of any land animal ever tested, humans included. Source: Payne, R.S. (1971), 'Acoustic Location of Prey by Barn Owls (Tyto alba),' J. Exp. Biol. 54(3):535 -- https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/54/3/535/21635/ ; accuracy-vs-other-animals: Springer, J. Comp. Physiol. A -- https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00663105

question: A mother mammal lays an egg, just as a bird or a reptile would. Only five living kinds of mammal do this; nearly every other mammal bears live young. Which animal is one of the five?
answer: The echidna
choices: The echidna
The wombat
The pangolin
The koala
context: The echidna is one of only five living monotremes — the only mammals on Earth that lay eggs. It shares that rare club with the platypus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echidna

question: Sharp spines bristle all over an echidna's back as it shuffles through the leaf litter in search of food. They look like a porcupine's quills, and they are built the same way. What is each spine, deep down?
answer: A stiff, overgrown hair
choices: A stiff, overgrown hair
A sharpened bony scale
A spike of solid bone
A hardened flake of skin
context: An echidna's spines, like a porcupine's quills, are modified hairs made of keratin, the same protein as human hair and fingernails, and they grow up to about 5 cm (2 in) long. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-beaked_echidna

question: A tiny, pink hatchling shaped like a jellybean breaks out of a grape-sized leathery egg, about ten days after its mother rolled the egg into a fold on her belly. What do keepers call a baby echidna?
answer: A puggle
choices: A puggle
A joey
A kit
A pup
context: A baby echidna is called a 'puggle' — a pink, jellybean-shaped hatchling that breaks out of its egg after only about 10 days inside the pouch. Source: https://sandiegozoowildlifealliance.org/story-hub/2022/09/30/two-snuggly-puggles

question: An echidna rips into the wall of a nest with its claws, and hundreds of insects come pouring out to defend the colony. It must gather them up fast, yet it has no teeth at all. How does it snatch up its swarming meal?
answer: It shoots out a long, gluey tongue
choices: It shoots out a long, gluey tongue
It sucks them up through its snout
It scoops them with cupped forepaws
It scrapes them off with sharp lips
context: The echidna flicks out a long, sticky tongue that can shoot up to about 18 cm (7 inches), coated in gluey mucus, to snatch ants and termites from a nest it has torn open. Source: https://scienceinsights.org/what-does-an-echidna-eat-its-diet-and-feeding-habits/

question: A hungry dingo catches an echidna out in the open on soft ground. A slow shuffle is the echidna's top speed, so running is hopeless. Instead it stays in the very same spot and does something else to survive the next few seconds. What does it do?
answer: It digs straight down until only spines show
choices: It digs straight down until only spines show
It rears up and slashes with its claws
It sprays a foul musk from its tail
It freezes and plays dead until the threat leaves
context: On soft ground an echidna sinks its whole body straight down in place, until only a shield of sharp spines is left sticking out for a predator to face. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/echidna

question: An echidna shuffles through the bush, pushing its snout into the soil, and homes in on ants it cannot see or smell. About 400 sensors in its snout pick up a faint signal that sharks and rays hunt by too. What is that signal?
answer: Weak electric fields from their bodies
choices: Weak electric fields from their bodies
Faint warmth given off by their bodies
High-pitched squeaks from the nest
Traces of gas from their breathing
context: The echidna's snout carries roughly 400 electroreceptors that detect the faint electrical signals given off by the muscles of buried insect prey — a power almost unheard of in a land animal, otherwise found mainly in sharks and rays. Source: https://echidna.net.au/?p=58

question: A bat hunts over a meadow on a moonless night, in air so black that it cannot see the moth just ahead. A moment later it snatches the moth out of the air. How does a hunting bat find prey it cannot see?
answer: It screams sounds and reads the returning echoes
choices: It screams sounds and reads the returning echoes
It feels the moth's warmth from a distance
It follows the moth's scent trail on the wind
It feels the air the moth's wings stir up
context: The bat fires high-pitched clicks, most of them above what humans can hear, and maps flying moths by the shape of the sound bouncing back — hunting by echo, not by sight. Source: Wikipedia 'Animal echolocation'; AAAS 'Discovering sonar in bats'.

question: An oilbird flies through a pitch-black cave in northern South America, giving sharp clicks and listening for echoes, like a bat. But its clicks are far lower in pitch than a bat's ultrasound. How does the lower pitch change the oilbird's picture of the cave?
answer: It is blurrier than a bat's, missing fine detail
choices: It is blurrier than a bat's, missing fine detail
It is sharper, catching even tiny insects
It reaches only a few inches past its beak
It works only when the cave is completely silent
context: The oilbird clicks around 2,000 cycles per second — low enough for people to hear, and giving a blurrier picture than a bat's ultrasound, though it still carries well off big cave walls. Lower pitch means coarser detail. Source: Frontiers in Physiology 'Echolocation in Oilbirds and swiftlets' (2013).

question: A hunting bat has been sweeping through the night sky, giving out a slow, steady stream of clicks and listening for the faint echoes bouncing off a moth. In the very last split-second before its jaws close on the moth, that calm rhythm suddenly erupts into a machine-gun rattle — dozens of clicks in a single heartbeat. Why does the bat pour out clicks that fast right at the end?
answer: To fix the prey's exact position for the grab
choices: To fix the prey's exact position for the grab
To stun the moth with a wall of loud sound
To signal other bats to keep their distance
To drown out the moth's own warning clicks
context: This 'feeding buzz' fires up to 200 clicks a second, giving the bat rapid position updates to pin the prey in the final moment of the chase. Source: Maryland DNR 'Bat Echolocation'; PMC 'Adaptive Vocal Behavior Drives Perception by Echolocation in Bats'.

question: Bats took to the air and toothed whales to the sea, on far-apart branches of the mammal family tree, yet both evolved echolocation. Biologists comparing their Prestin, a protein that helps mammal ears pick up sound, found it had changed the same way in both. Then they zoomed in on one single position in it. What did they find there?
answer: The identical building-block swap in both
choices: The identical building-block swap in both
Two different swaps that both sharpen hearing
A swap in the bat but none in the whale
A missing letter deleted from both
context: Prestin, the protein that powers the inner ear's outer hair cells, shifted in the same direction in echolocating bats and in toothed whales. At one position an asparagine became a threonine in both: the identical swap, tied to sharper high-frequency hearing, the same molecular answer arriving twice, independently. Source: Liu et al. 2010 Current Biology; Science 'Bats and Dolphins Evolved Echolocation in Same Way'; Academic OUP MBE 'Parallel Sites Implicate Functional Convergence of the Hearing Gene Prestin among Echolocating Mammals' (2014).

question: A sperm whale hunts squid far below the surface by clicking, and the sound starts not in its throat but in its nose. It pushes air past a pair of lip-shaped flaps just below the blowhole, at the front of its huge head, nicknamed the monkey lips. What happens to that first pulse inside the whale's head before a full click shoots forward?
answer: It bounces between two air sacs in the head
choices: It bounces between two air sacs in the head
It is swallowed and re-fired through the throat
It splits evenly out of both sides at once
It fades out and a fresh pulse starts over
context: The pulse ricochets between two air sacs inside the head, and a slice of energy escapes forward as each click. Source: Wikipedia 'Sperm whale'; ScienceInsights 'How the Spermaceti Organ Works in a Sperm Whale'.

question: A horseshoe bat speeds toward its target, holding its call on one exact note, with its hearing tuned to that very note. Its own motion should raise the pitch of the returning echo, a Doppler rise that would throw those ears off. How does the bat cancel the shift mid-chase?
answer: It lowers the pitch of its own outgoing call
choices: It lowers the pitch of its own outgoing call
It briefly stops flapping to slow itself down
It closes its ears until the echo settles
It fires a second call at a matching pitch
context: By shifting its call frequency down to offset its own speed, the greater horseshoe bat keeps the returning echo at the fixed pitch its ear is tuned to. Source: Wikipedia 'Doppler shift compensation'; Springer 'Control of Doppler shift compensation in the greater horseshoe bat, Rhinolophus ferrumequinum'.

question: Among the leaves of a bush, a moth hides in silence, yet a horseshoe bat whose call stays locked on a single steady tone still finds it. Riding on top of the steady note of the returning echo is a quick, rhythmic flicker. What makes the flicker?
answer: The beating of the moth's wings
choices: The beating of the moth's wings
The moth's warm body cooling the air
The rustle of the leaves in the wind
The bat's own heartbeat in its ears
context: A fluttering moth's wingbeats show up as a 'glint' in the pitch-locked echo — telling the bat there's living prey ahead, even hidden in foliage. Source: Springer 'Auditory fovea and Doppler shift compensation: adaptations for flutter detection in echolocating bats using CF-FM signals'.

question: Bertholdia trigona, a tiger moth of the American deserts, does not flee when a hunting bat's calls lock onto it. It fights back, firing ultrasonic clicks of its own up to 4,500 times a second, the first proven case of one natural trick in the wild. What does the barrage do to the bat?
answer: It jams the bat's sonar and spoils the strike
choices: It jams the bat's sonar and spoils the strike
It lures the bat toward a decoy target
It signals the bat that the moth is poisonous
It deafens the bat for the rest of the night
context: Bertholdia trigona fires clicks up to 4,500 times a second, blanketing the air so the bat's returning echoes turn to static: the first proven case of sonar jamming in nature, and the most effective anti-bat defense documented, cutting the bat's capture success roughly tenfold. Attacking big brown bats often reversed or aborted their approach. Source: Corcoran, Barber & Conner 2009, Science 325:325, 'Tiger Moth Jams Bat Sonar'; Scientific American 'Moths Use Sonar-Jamming Defense'.

question: A big brown bat reads echoes so finely that Simmons, Ferragamo and Moss set out in 1998 to find the smallest gap it could detect between two surfaces, one behind the other. The answer was finer than one wavelength of its own call. How close can the two surfaces sit and still register as two?
answer: About 0.3 millimetres apart
choices: About 0.3 millimetres apart
About 3 millimetres apart
About 3 centimetres apart
About 30 centimetres apart
context: Simmons, Ferragamo and Moss (1998) found the big brown bat can separately perceive two echoes arriving as little as ~2 microseconds apart, letting it pin two reflecting points only about 0.3 mm apart in range. Earlier 'jitter' experiments from the same lab reported the bat detecting delay shifts on the order of tens of nanoseconds — far shorter than one cycle of its own call, a still-debated case of temporal hyperacuity. Source: Simmons, Ferragamo & Moss 1998, PNAS 95:12647 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC22885/); corroborated https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9770540/.

question: Nancy Simmons and her colleagues described Onychonycteris finneyi, the oldest well-preserved fossil bat. The animal, from 52 million years ago, already had fully formed wings, but the coiled hearing organ in its ear, the cochlea, was small like a fruit bat's rather than enlarged like an echolocator's. What did the team argue this mix showed?
answer: Bats flew before they evolved echolocation
choices: Bats flew before they evolved echolocation
Bats echolocated before they could fly
Bats flew and echolocated from the very start
Bats did neither, only gliding between branches
context: Nancy Simmons and colleagues (Nature, 2008) read Onychonycteris's small cochlea as a sign it flew but could not yet echolocate, evidence for the 'flight-first' hypothesis — while the contemporary Icaronycteris already had an enlarged, echolocation-type cochlea. The debate is not closed: a 2010 re-evaluation of the same skull argued certain features hint it may have echolocated after all. Source: Simmons et al. 2008, Nature 451:818 (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature06549); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onychonycteris ; https://www.amnh.org/research/science-news/2008/researchers-find-bats-evolved-ability-to-fly-before-echolocation.

question: A tiny hummingbird hovers at a garden flower, and an ostrich sprints across the savanna. From the smallest bird to the largest, every species brings its young into the world the same way, without a single exception. How does every bird do it?
answer: By laying eggs
choices: By laying eggs
By live birth
By splitting in two
By carrying young in a pouch
context: No bird gives live birth. The leading reason is flight: carrying developing babies inside the body for weeks would add too much weight for a flying animal to bear, so birds lay the egg and let it finish developing outside. Source: Live Science 'Why Do Birds Lay Eggs?'.

question: A soft, leathery egg the size of a marble, only 16 to 18 millimeters across, lies in a burrow with its mother curled around it to keep it warm. About ten days later a tiny baby hatches out. Which animal laid it?
answer: A platypus
choices: A platypus
A python
A garter snake
A boa constrictor
context: A platypus mother lays one to three marble-sized eggs with soft, parchment-like shells like a reptile's, then curls around them to keep them warm until a tiny 'puggle' hatches after about ten days. Source: Australian Platypus Conservancy 'Platypus reproduction'; Wikipedia 'Platypus'.

question: An echidna mother lays an egg the way a reptile does, yet scientists are certain she is a true mammal. Once her egg hatches, she does one very mammal thing that settles the matter. What does she do for her young?
answer: Feeds her young on milk
choices: Feeds her young on milk
Guards a nest of dozens of eggs
Swallows the eggshell for calcium
Carries the hatchling on her back
context: Making milk is the defining mammal trait. Monotremes have no nipples, so the milk oozes out through patches of skin and the hatchling laps it up. Source: Australian Museum 'What is a monotreme?'; Australian Platypus Conservancy.

question: When a male seahorse gives birth, it is no gentle release: his pouch contracts in strong waves for hours, and the tiny young shoot out in bursts. From a single father in one birth, roughly how many babies can emerge?
answer: Up to about 2,000
choices: Up to about 2,000
Up to about 200
Up to about 20
Up to about 20,000
context: A single male seahorse can release up to about 2,000 young at once, shooting them out of his brood pouch in bursts over hours of labour. Source: University of Sydney; Biology Insights 'How Many Babies Do Seahorses Give Birth To?'.

question: A female python lays a clutch of eggs and coils tightly around them until they hatch. A boa constrictor looks so much like her that people often mix the two snakes up, yet the boa brings her young into the world another way. When a female boa's young are ready, what does she do?
answer: Gives birth to live snakelets
choices: Gives birth to live snakelets
Guards a hidden clutch until it hatches
Carries her young inside her throat
Coils around a warmed nest for weeks
context: Boa constrictors are live-bearers. A female carries her young inside for about four to five months, then gives birth to a wriggling litter of ten to sixty-five live snakelets. Source: A-Z Animals 'Snakes That Give Birth to Live Young'; Study.com 'Boa Constrictor vs. Python'.

question: A European adder, Vipera berus, basks on a sunny patch of ground, the dark zigzag down her back soaking up the warmth. Unlike most snakes, she lays no eggs; she carries her young inside her and gives birth to them alive. That habit lets the adder hold a record no relative on Earth can match. What is it?
answer: It lives farther north than any other snake
choices: It lives farther north than any other snake
It is the largest snake in Europe
It survives longer without food than any snake
It gives birth to the most young at once
context: By bearing live young and basking to warm them, Vipera berus reaches all the way up to 69 degrees North, inside the Arctic Circle, farther north than any other snake alive. Source: Wiley/Evolution, Lynch 2009; NCBI PMC8415537.

question: A beachcomber finds a tough, leathery pouch washed up on the sand, dark and dried out, with four curly 'horns' curling from its corners. Sharks and skates leave these behind. People who find them gave them a name straight out of a fairy tale. What is a case like this called?
answer: A mermaid's purse
choices: A mermaid's purse
A dragon's tooth
A siren's shell
A kraken's egg
context: Some sharks and skates lay eggs instead of bearing live young, sealing each embryo in a tough leathery case with four curly horns. Beachcombers who find them washed ashore call them a 'mermaid's purse.' Source: UF/IFAS Extension 'Mermaid's Purse'; Wikipedia 'Egg case (Chondrichthyes)'.

question: Inside a pregnant sand tiger shark, up to 50 tiny embryos begin to grow at once, split between her two wombs, through a pregnancy of about a year. In each womb, the biggest embryo grows a set of real teeth first, months before birth. What does it do to the smaller embryos around it?
answer: Devours all its smaller siblings
choices: Devours all its smaller siblings
Pushes them out to be born early
Shares its food to keep them alive
Splits off to form a twin
context: In the sand tiger shark (Carcharias taurus), the largest embryo, first to grow teeth, turns cannibal and eats its smaller siblings, so only one pup survives in each of the mother's two wombs, born about 3 feet long. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History 'Sand Tiger Shark'.

question: A frog stays chained to its pond because its naked jelly eggs dry out in the open. Then some early four-legged animals evolved an egg sealed inside a shell with four inner membranes, carrying its own supply within. That one invention branched into three great groups of backboned animals alive today. Which three?
answer: Reptiles, birds, and mammals
choices: Reptiles, birds, and mammals
Reptiles, birds, and sharks
Reptiles, mammals, and lungfish
Birds, mammals, and salamanders
context: The amniotic egg, with its shell plus four membranes (amnion, chorion, yolk sac, and allantois), was one of the greatest inventions in the history of life. By carrying its own sealed supply, it gave rise to all reptiles, birds, and mammals, freeing backboned animals from the ponds that trap frogs. Source: Cleveland Museum of Natural History 'The Amniotic Egg'; Lumen Learning 'Amniotes'; Wikipedia 'Amniote'.

question: Biologists warmed clutches of American alligator eggs across a wide range of temperatures and mapped which became male and which female. The eggs carry no sex chromosomes, so the warmth of the nest alone decides. What did the temperatures produce?
answer: Cool and hot nests both gave females; males came only from the middle
choices: Cool and hot nests both gave females; males came only from the middle
Cool and hot nests both gave males; females came only from the middle
Cool nests gave males and hot nests gave females, in a clean split
Cool nests gave females and hot nests gave males, in a clean split
context: This is 'temperature-dependent sex determination,' and the alligator follows the counterintuitive Pattern II: females emerge at both the cool and the hot extremes, while males appear only in a narrow middle band, roughly 90.5 to 92.3 F (32.5 to 33.5 C); below about 88.7 F (31.5 C) or above about 94.1 F (34.5 C), all females. In the wild this maps onto habitat, so warmer nests built up on levees tend to produce males while cooler wet-marsh nests produce females. It is also why a warming climate can skew whole populations toward one sex. Sources: Wikipedia 'American alligator' and 'Temperature-dependent sex determination.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature-dependent_sex_determination

question: In a murky African river swims a blunt-headed catfish with no dorsal fin and three pairs of whiskery barbels. A grown man who grabs one can be knocked clean off his feet. What is this fish's built-in weapon?
answer: A powerful electric shock
choices: A powerful electric shock
A mouthful of venomous fangs
A cloud of blinding ink
A row of poisonous spines
context: The electric catfish (Malapterurus electricus) can deliver a jolt measured up to about 350 volts in a half-meter fish, and higher in big adults — enough to knock a grown person back. It grows up to about 1.2 meters (4 feet) and 20 kg (44 lb). Source: Wikipedia, Electric catfish; Animal Diversity Web, Malapterurus electricus.

question: An electric catfish hides in the mud of an African river all day, then comes out after sunset to hunt for about four or five hours. In the dark it stuns its prey with sudden bursts of electric shocks. How big a meal can it swallow?
answer: Prey up to half its own size
choices: Prey up to half its own size
Only tiny insects and worms
Prey no bigger than its barbels
Prey even larger than itself
context: The catfish hunts in the dark: it has tiny eyes and comes out for about 4 to 5 hours after sunset, firing bursts of shocks to paralyze fish, frogs, and other prey — and it can swallow prey up to half its own size. Source: Animal Diversity Web, Malapterurus electricus.

question: An electric eel in the Amazon carries its shock organ packed into its tail, like almost every electric fish. The electric catfish of the Nile and other African rivers breaks that rule. Where on its body is its electric organ?
answer: Spread as a jelly-like sheet under most of its skin
choices: Spread as a jelly-like sheet under most of its skin
Spread as a jelly-like sheet across its blunt head
Spread as a jelly-like sheet along its lower belly
Spread as a jelly-like sheet around its whiskery barbels
context: In most electric fish the electric organ sits in the tail, but the electric catfish's organ wraps almost its whole body, forming a jelly-like layer just under the skin over the trunk — so the shock radiates from all around the fish. Source: Animal Diversity Web, Malapterurus electricus; Wikipedia, Electric catfish.

question: The shock an electric catfish fires at its prey comes from an organ built of millions of stacked, flat cells, the electroplaques. Over millions of years that organ evolved out of an ordinary body part that every fish already has. Which part did it evolve from?
answer: Its muscle
choices: Its muscle
Its liver
Its gills
Its skin scales
context: Its electric organ evolved out of ordinary body muscle, turning millions of stacked flat cells called electroplaques into a shock-producing sheet (derived from anterior body musculature). Source: Wikipedia, Electric catfish; en-academic.com electric catfish entry.

question: When an electric catfish strikes, its prey takes one clean jolt, never a stagger, though the jolt comes from millions of separate shock-cells. All of them fire at the very same moment. What keeps that whole swarm of cells in step?
answer: A single giant nerve cell commands them all
choices: A single giant nerve cell commands them all
A tiny pacemaker crystal in its skull
A ring of muscle that squeezes them together
A chemical signal released into its blood
context: All those millions of shock-cells are wired to fire together by a single giant nerve cell — one neuron in the spinal cord commands the whole electric organ, which is why scientists prize this fish for studying nerves. Source: Animal Diversity Web, Malapterurus electricus; Springer, electromotor system of Malapterurus electricus.

question: A long, snake-shaped fish glides through a muddy South American river, carrying the jolt that made it famous, and its body looks much like a marine eel's. What kind of fish is the electric eel?
answer: A knifefish
choices: A knifefish
A true eel
A catfish
A lamprey
context: Despite its name, the electric eel is not a true eel at all. It belongs to the order Gymnotiformes, the knifefishes, and is more closely related to the banded knifefish than to the marine eels (order Anguilliformes) it superficially resembles. Source: Wikipedia, Electric eel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_eel).

question: An electric eel spends its life underwater. Yet if a keeper blocked one from reaching the top of its tank, it would die. Every few minutes the eel does something no goldfish ever needs to do. What must it do to stay alive?
answer: Surface to gulp air
choices: Surface to gulp air
Rest on the bottom
Shed its slime coat
Empty its stomach
context: The electric eel is an obligate air-breather: it must rise to the surface and gulp air through its mouth roughly every two minutes, and can drown if kept from reaching the top. Source: Wikipedia, Electric eel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_eel).

question: Squeezed into the front fifth of an electric eel's body are its heart, stomach and other vital organs, sealed away from whatever lies behind them. What fills the long tail-end, about 80 percent of the eel?
answer: Its electric organs
choices: Its electric organs
A long, coiled gut
Fat for buoyancy
Egg sacs
context: The electric organs make up about 80% of the electric eel's long body. Its vital organs are packed into just the front ~20% and sequestered from the electricity the animal generates in the rest of its length. Source: Wikipedia, Electric eel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_eel).

question: Down the length of an electric eel's body run about 6,000 tiny cells called electrocytes, and the eel fires them all at once. Their small voltages add up to one huge jolt. Which everyday power source builds its voltage the same way?
answer: Batteries stacked in a flashlight
choices: Batteries stacked in a flashlight
A single big capacitor
The coils in an electromagnet
A spinning generator
context: An electric eel's jolt comes from roughly 6,000 electrocytes wired end-to-end in series, exactly like the batteries stacked in a flashlight, so their individually tiny voltages add up into one enormous discharge. Source: Wikipedia, Electric eel; Science ABC (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_eel).

question: The electric eel hunts at night in water so dark and muddy that its eyes are almost useless, yet it still homes in on fish hidden in the murk. Besides the high-voltage blast it saves for the kill, it runs a second, gentler electric setting all the time. How does the eel find its way and its prey in the blackness?
answer: It reads faint electric fields it makes
choices: It reads faint electric fields it makes
It follows scent trails in the water
It listens for the prey's heartbeat
It feels for warmth given off by prey
context: The electric eel has two electrical modes from one organ system: a weak, constant low-voltage pulse from Sachs' organ that works like radar (electrolocation), letting it navigate murky water and detect hidden prey, plus a separate high-voltage blast to stun. Source: Catania, The Astonishing Behavior of Electric Eels (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6646469/).

question: Kenneth Catania at Vanderbilt was lifting electric eels with a metal-rimmed net when a cornered eel did something no textbook had described. Instead of shocking down into the water, it rose up and pressed its chin against the metal. What was the eel doing?
answer: Leaping out to shock the threat directly
choices: Leaping out to shock the threat directly
Trying to climb over the rim
Biting to test the net
Playing dead against the metal
context: Kenneth Catania discovered by accident that a cornered electric eel will leap out of the water and press its chin against a threat to deliver its shock through the air. Source: Vanderbilt News, Electric eels make leaping attacks (https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2016/06/06/electric-eels-make-leaping-attacks/).

question: When a cornered electric eel rises out of the water and presses its chin against an attacker, it is climbing higher and higher up the target as it goes. Kenneth Catania measured the jolt at each height. What happens to the shock the higher the eel climbs?
answer: It grows stronger
choices: It grows stronger
It stays the same
It briefly cuts out
It scatters harmlessly
context: Underwater the eel's current dissipates in every direction, but when it rises out of the water the circuit is forced through the target and back. The higher the electric eel climbs, the greater the voltage and current delivered. Source: Vanderbilt News; AIP Inside Science (https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2016/06/06/electric-eels-make-leaping-attacks/).

question: A fish lies frozen in the mud in front of an electric eel, where the eel cannot see it. The eel fires a rapid doublet of two high-voltage pulses, and the hidden prey instantly twitches and gives itself away. Kenneth Catania showed the pulses remotely trigger something inside the prey. What do they trigger?
answer: The prey's own muscles
choices: The prey's own muscles
The prey's sense of smell
A rush of prey blood
The prey's swim bladder
context: To find prey it cannot see, an electric eel fires two high-voltage pulses about 2 milliseconds apart. This remotely fires the hidden prey's own muscles, making it twitch and reveal its location. Catania described it as the eel asking 'are you alive?' and the prey being unable not to answer. Source: Catania (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6646469/).

question: Alexander von Humboldt told how, in 1800, electric eels leaped from a pool at about 30 horses driven into it, and two of the horses were stunned and drowned. For roughly 200 years scientists dismissed the tale. What finally became of Humboldt's story?
answer: Catania's study showed it could be true
choices: Catania's study showed it could be true
New records proved it exaggerated
It was traced to a mistranslation
No eel was ever found there again
context: Humboldt's account of eels battling horses was dismissed for two centuries, until Kenneth Catania's discovery that electric eels leap to shock threats above the water showed the story was plausible after all. Source: Catania 2016, PNAS, 'Leaping eels electrify threats, supporting Humboldt's account of a battle with horses' (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1604009113).

question: C. David de Santana's team split the electric eel, long counted as one species, into three in 2019. One of the newcomers, Electrophorus voltai, which lives in clear highland rivers, set a record against every other animal on Earth. What did it register?
answer: The highest voltage of any animal
choices: The highest voltage of any animal
The longest body of any fish
The oldest known lifespan
The deepest freshwater range
context: In 2019 de Santana's team split the electric eel into three species. One of them, Electrophorus voltai, discharged 860 volts, the highest voltage ever measured from any living animal. Its record jolt is thought to be an adaptation to the poorly conducting clear highland water it lives in. Source: Cornell Chronicle; Nature Communications 2019 (https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2019/09/scientists-shocked-discover-two-new-species-electric-eel).

question: A big catfish thrashes too hard for the electric eel to pin down with a single blast. So the eel bends its whole body into a tight horseshoe, folding head toward tail with the struggling fish trapped in the curve between them. Kenneth Catania measured what this pose does to the jolt. Why does curling up help?
answer: It brings the eel's two poles close, doubling the shock
choices: It brings the eel's two poles close, doubling the shock
It shields the eel's soft belly from the prey's spines
It lets the eel breathe air while its head stays down
It hides the eel's shape from other hunting eels
context: The positive pole of the eel's electric field sits in its head and the negative pole in its tail. By curling into a horseshoe, the eel sandwiches struggling prey between the two poles, and Catania's instrumented dead-fish 'chew toy' recorded that this more than DOUBLES the voltage driven into the victim. The doubled field fires the prey's muscles in repeated ~100 Hz volleys until they seize up in total fatigue and paralysis - Catania likened the effect to dosing the prey with the paralytic drug curare. This is a second body maneuver, distinct from the leap-and-chin-press. Source: news.vanderbilt.edu/2015/10/28 (Catania, Current Biology 2015); coverage in Scientific American and Christian Science Monitor.

question: A great white shark closes on a thrashing seal, a camera recording every frame of the strike. In the last instant before its jaws close, it does something that looks reckless, giving up one of its senses just when it seems to need it most. What does the shark do just before the bite?
answer: It shields its eyes and finishes the strike blind
choices: It shields its eyes and finishes the strike blind
It rolls completely upside down
It stops swimming and drifts in
It flares its gills wide open
context: In the final second before biting, a shark shields its eyes from a thrashing meal, a protective reflex caught on camera. With its vision shut off, it steers the last strike by the electric sense of its ampullae. Source: americanscientist.org, 'The Discovery of the Shark's Electric Sense'.

question: Two knifefish meet in a dark, muddy river, each wrapped in the weak electric field it makes for itself, and the two fields happen to pulse at nearly the same frequency. Neither fish can read its own signal cleanly any more, yet within milliseconds both are sensing sharply again. What did they do?
answer: Each nudged its own discharge frequency away from the other's
choices: Each nudged its own discharge frequency away from the other's
Each fired one strong pulse to swamp the other's signal
One fish went silent and coasted until the other swam off
Both matched to one shared frequency and pulsed in unison
context: When two knifefish overlap at nearly the same frequency, their fields interfere. Each fish then shifts its own discharge frequency away from the other — a reflex scientists named the 'jamming avoidance response' — so each keeps its private radar channel clear. Source: Neuroethology: Jamming Avoidance Response in Electric Fish, nelson.beckman.illinois.edu.

question: A bumblebee lands on a flower that carries a faint static charge, and the bee can tell. Clarke's team showed in 2013 that bumblebees sense that weak charge, and in 2016 the same Bristol group found out how. Through what part of its body does the bee detect it?
answer: Its body hairs, which bend in the presence of the charge
choices: Its body hairs, which bend in the presence of the charge
Its antennae, which taste the charge chemically
Its compound eyes, which see the charge as a glow
Its wings, which vibrate faster near a charge
context: Clarke, Whitney, Sutton and Robert reported in Science (2013) that bumblebees sense the weak static charge a flower carries. In 2016 Sutton, Clarke, Morley and Robert showed in PNAS that the bee's mechanosensory body hairs bend in the field and fire nerve signals; the antennae move less and send no signal. Source: Clarke et al., 'Detection and Learning of Floral Electric Fields by Bumblebees', Science (2013); Sutton et al., 'Mechanosensory hairs in bumblebees (Bombus terrestris) detect weak electric fields', PNAS 113:7261 (2016).

question: Josberger and colleagues tested the clear jelly that fills the ampullae of Lorenzini, the pores that carry a shark's electric sense inward. The jelly is about 97 percent water, yet their 2016 measurement of how well it moves electric charge gave a result nobody expected from ordinary animal goo. What did they find?
answer: It conducts protons better than any other biological material that scientists have yet tested
choices: It conducts protons better than any other biological material that scientists have yet tested
It conducts electrons swiftly yet blocks protons entirely, unlike any known biological tissue
It insulates so completely that the signal must instead creep along the walls of the pore
It shuttles charge only in one direction, acting like a living diode that bars any reverse flow
context: The jelly filling the ampullae of Lorenzini is about 97% water, yet Josberger et al. (2016) measured its proton conductivity at only ~40 times below Nafion, the best synthetic proton-conducting polymer humans have engineered for fuel cells - making it the most proton-conductive biological material ever found. The conduction comes from a polyglycan, keratan sulfate, donating protons into the watery gel. Source: Josberger, Hassanzadeh, Deng, Sohn, Rego, Amemiya & Rolandi (2016), 'Proton conductivity in ampullae of Lorenzini jelly', Science Advances 2:e1600112, https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.1600112 ; UW News https://www.washington.edu/news/2016/05/13/proton-conducting-material-found-in-jelly-that-fills-organs-of-sharks-skates-and-rays/

question: A shark and a skate, the flat, kite-shaped cousin of the rays, both feel the faint electric fields of living bodies, using the same kind of cell, whose signal begins at one shared calcium channel. Yet the shark tunes its sense to a hidden prey's twitch, while the skate's is tuned to the weak signals of a mate. What splits one shared cell into two senses?
answer: A different second channel in each: one drives sharp repeated spikes, the other soft graded ripples
choices: A different second channel in each: one drives sharp repeated spikes, the other soft graded ripples
A different body of water in each: one hunts in salt, the other only ever in fresh
A different number of pores in each: one carries thousands, the other barely a dozen
A different nerve in each: one wires straight to the jaw, the other to the swimming muscles
context: Bellono, Leitch & Julius (2018) found that shark and skate electrosensory cells both start a signal with the same low-threshold voltage-gated calcium channel, CaV1.3 - but they amplify it differently. Sharks add voltage-gated potassium channels that let the cell fire big, repetitive voltage spikes, dumping neurotransmitter at near-maximum: perfect for catching a prey twitch. Skates instead use a calcium-activated potassium channel that produces small, finely graded oscillations, better for reading the steady field of another skate. Same starter channel, a different second 'amplifier' channel - predator-tuning versus social-tuning. Source: Bellono, Leitch & Julius (2018), 'Molecular tuning of electroreception in sharks and skates', Nature 558:122-126, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0160-9 ; Harvard MCB summary https://www.mcb.harvard.edu/department/news/investigating-sharks-skates-sense-electric-fields/

question: A bull of this species, shot in Angola in 1955, measured about 13 feet tall at the shoulder, with an estimated weight of 10 tonnes or more. Nicknamed Henry, the mounted bull still stands in the Smithsonian. Which living land animal is the largest?
answer: The African elephant
choices: The African elephant
The white rhinoceros
The hippopotamus
The giraffe
context: A record African bush elephant bull from Angola stood roughly 13 feet at the shoulder and weighed an estimated 10 or more tonnes; the mounted specimen, nicknamed 'Henry,' still stands in the Smithsonian. It is the largest land animal alive today. Source: Guinness World Records, 'Largest land mammal'; IFLScience, 'Henry the Fenykovi Elephant.'

question: On a scorching afternoon, an elephant reaches its trunk down to the riverbank and plasters something over its hide and the backs of its ears. What does it use to beat the heat and block the sun?
answer: Sticky mud
choices: Sticky mud
Dry leaves
Loose feathers
Tree bark
context: When ear-flapping isn't enough, an elephant sprays water, flings wet river-sand, or plasters sticky mud onto its skin and the backs of its ears to cool down and shield itself from the sun. Source: AskNature, 'Large Ears Aid Cooling'; Shenton Safaris, 'Cooling down.'

question: An elephant wraps its trunk around a small tree and rips it out of the ground. Moments later the same trunk is at work on a task that needs a gentle, exact touch. What lets one limb manage both brute strength and such precision?
answer: It contains no bone at all, only muscle
choices: It contains no bone at all, only muscle
It is jointed like a finger
It is filled with air sacs
It has a flexible cartilage rod inside
context: An elephant's trunk is a 'muscular hydrostat' like a human tongue or an octopus arm, containing no bone at all, only muscle, long counted at around 40,000 muscle units. Source: Cleveland Zoological Society, 'Truth or Tail: 40,000 muscles.'

question: Under the midday sun of the African savanna, an elephant stands almost still while its huge ears fan slowly back and forth. Each ear is thin and laced with big blood vessels close to the surface. What is all that flapping accomplishing?
answer: Cooling the blood before it returns to the body
choices: Cooling the blood before it returns to the body
Sensing distant thunder
Storing water for later
Warning rivals with the flapping sound
context: The ears work as living radiators: blood vessels near the surface let flapping fan the blood cool. The returning blood can be 3 to 5 degrees C cooler, and an elephant can cool its whole blood supply this way in about 20 minutes. Source: Kariega Game Reserve; AskNature, 'Large Ears Aid Cooling.'

question: A safari guide on the Kenyan savanna points to a distant gray elephant and says she already knows it is African, not Asian, just from the very tip of its trunk. What difference at the trunk tip is she reading?
answer: The tip has two finger-like lips, not one
choices: The tip has two finger-like lips, not one
The tip is bright pink, not gray
The tip splits into three prongs
The tip has a small tuft of hair
context: An African elephant's trunk ends in TWO finger-like tips, or lips; an Asian elephant's ends in only ONE, a quick field way to tell the two species apart. Source: A-Z Animals, 'Exploring the Fascinating World of Elephant Trunks.'

question: An elephant's two tusks lengthen by some 6 to 7 inches every year of its life, and the longest pair ever recorded topped 11 feet. The elephant digs up roots, strips bark and fights rivals with them, and people often call them ivory horns. What kind of body part is a tusk?
answer: An overgrown incisor tooth
choices: An overgrown incisor tooth
A curved horn of keratin
An extended jawbone
A hardened nasal bone
context: Tusks are overgrown incisor teeth that never stop growing, adding roughly 6 to 7 inches a year; the longest on record exceeded 11 feet. Source: Britannica, 'Tusk (anatomy)'; Inverdoorn, 'Elephant Tusks: 10 Facts.'

question: An elephant in a zoo shoves over a small tree with its trunk, and the keepers watching are stunned by what that same trunk does next. Its tip carries hair-thin bundles of muscle. What delicate feat can that trunk manage?
answer: Picking up a single blade of grass
choices: Picking up a single blade of grass
Untying a knotted length of rope
Threading a strap through a buckle
Balancing a pebble on its very tip
context: With no bone or joints, the same trunk that uproots a tree can curl around a single blade of grass; the tip's hair-thin muscle bundles give it that fingertip precision. Source: Science/AAAS, 'Elephant trunk's stunning microscopic musculature may explain its dexterity.'

question: Drought has dried up the nearest water hole, and an elephant family on the African savanna now lives or starves on one thing: whether its leader remembers where water still flows, a memory perhaps carried from a drought decades before. Who leads the herd?
answer: The oldest female, the matriarch
choices: The oldest female, the matriarch
The largest tusked bull
A pair of scout males
The youngest breeding female
context: Herds are led by a matriarch, the oldest female, whose memory of distant water can save the family. In the severe 1993 drought in Tanzania's Tarangire National Park, the two groups whose matriarchs were old enough to remember an earlier drought, in 1958 to 1961, left the park and lost far fewer calves, while the group led by a matriarch of only about 33 stayed and suffered most of the calf deaths. Source: Foley, Pettorelli & Foley, Biology Letters 2008 (ScienceDaily 2008-08-11); Live Science, 'Elephants' Legendary Memories Help Herds Survive.'

question: At a water hole, an elephant draws several liters of water into its trunk, then curls the trunk to its mouth and pours. It does not sip through the trunk like a straw. A 2021 study estimated how hard it sucks. How fast does air rush in through its nostrils?
answer: About 330 miles per hour
choices: About 330 miles per hour
About 15 miles per hour
About 60 miles per hour
About 900 miles per hour
context: Georgia Tech researchers (Schulz et al., Journal of the Royal Society Interface, 2021) worked out from how hard elephants sucked up water that they can inhale at over 150 meters per second, some 330 miles per hour, nearly 30 times the speed of a human sneeze; in the tests an elephant drew 3.7 liters of water into its trunk in 1.5 seconds. The figure is the speed of the air, calculated rather than clocked directly. Source: Schulz et al. 2021, J. R. Soc. Interface 18:20210215; Georgia Tech / EurekAlert news release (2021).

question: Katy Payne stood in a zoo's elephant house in 1984 and felt a strange throbbing in the air, though she could hear nothing at all. She had stumbled onto the way elephants call to one another across miles. What was carrying their messages?
answer: Infrasound rumbles too low for human ears
choices: Infrasound rumbles too low for human ears
Ultrasonic squeaks too high to hear
Puffs of scent on the wind
Flashes of light from their eyes
context: Elephants communicate in infrasound, rumbles around 14 to 35 Hz, below the roughly 20 Hz floor of human hearing. Katy Payne discovered it in 1984 when she felt the throbbing in the air; the calls carry for miles. Source: academic.oup.com/BioScience, 'A throbbing in the air'; Psychology Today.

question: A herd of African elephants, mostly related females and their calves, comes upon the body of a dead elephant they once knew. Field researchers in Kenya, Namibia and Tanzania have watched this moment again and again over decades. What do the elephants do at the body?
answer: Gather quietly and touch it with their trunks
choices: Gather quietly and touch it with their trunks
Trumpet loudly and charge past it
Bury it under piles of branches
Ignore it and move on at once
context: Elephants behave as if they mourn: they gather quietly, touch the body with their trunks, and return to the bones for years. Field tests found they lingered far longer over elephant skulls and ivory than over other species' bones, even the bones of strangers. This is described as observed behavior, not proven human-style grief. Source: Londolozi Blog; Biology Letters field study, summarized at Forbes.

question: Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell noticed that elephants at the Mushara waterhole sometimes froze like statues even when the source of alarm was far off. When she played an alarm call through speakers buried in the ground, a herd closed ranks and froze. What were the elephants listening with?
answer: Their feet, sensing vibrations in the ground
choices: Their feet, sensing vibrations in the ground
Their trunk tip, feeling shifts in air pressure
Their broad ears, catching faint distant echoes
Their long tusks, picking up tremors in the earth
context: Elephant rumbles also travel through the ground as seismic waves, and elephants can 'listen' with their feet. O'Connell-Rodwell's buried-speaker experiments at Mushara showed an underground alarm call made a herd close ranks and freeze. Source: Science/AAAS, 'Talking Through the Ground'; KQED, 'How Elephants Listen With Their Feet.'

question: Vincent Lynch asked why elephants, whose huge bodies hold trillions of cells, each one a chance for cancer, so rarely get it. He found one reason: something in their cells forces a cell whose DNA is damaged to self-destruct before it turns into a tumor. What did he find?
answer: A reawakened "zombie" gene, LIF6
choices: A reawakened "zombie" gene, LIF6
An always-active repair enzyme
A newly evolved stress hormone
A gene borrowed from a virus
context: This puzzle is called Peto's Paradox: bigger, longer-lived bodies have more cells and more chances for cancer, yet elephants get it less than humans. LIF6 was a dead pseudogene, a broken copy of the leukemia inhibitory factor gene, that the elephant lineage switched back on. When DNA is damaged, the tumor-suppressor TP53 flips LIF6 on; the LIF6 protein travels to the cell's mitochondria and triggers apoptosis, killing the damaged cell before it can become a tumor. This TP53-to-LIF6 switch evolved around the time elephant ancestors grew to giant size, so the anti-cancer gene came online as they got big. (Elephants also carry about 20 copies of TP53, versus one in humans.) Source: Lynch et al., Cell Reports 2018, PubMed 30110634; 'Solving Peto's Paradox,' PMC6369797.

question: An elephant seems to stand on five toes, but John Hutchinson's CT scans found a sixth prop hidden in the fatty heel pad, so long overlooked that museum staff used to slice it off and throw it away. What is that hidden sixth structure?
answer: A giant sesamoid bone, a false sixth toe
choices: A giant sesamoid bone, a false sixth toe
A true toe built for bearing weight
A wedge of stiffened heel cartilage
A fused knot of foot tendons
context: It is a giant sesamoid bone, called a prepollex in the front foot and a prehallux in the hind, that projects downward like a stiletto heel, spearing the fat pad and propping the foot up so the elephant effectively walks on tiptoe. It was missed for centuries because it starts as cartilage and only turns to bone late in adult life, and preparators routinely cut it off. Hutchinson's team at the Royal Veterinary College confirmed it with CT scanning; the structure appears to have evolved as early elephants grew larger, roughly 40 million years ago. Source: Hutchinson et al., Science 2011, 'From Flat Foot to Fat Foot' (doi:10.1126/science.1211437); phys.org 2011-12.

question: An elephantnose fish hunts at night in African rivers too muddy for eyes to help, yet it finds buried prey. An organ near its tail puts out a weak field, and the fish feels how nearby objects bend it. What kind of field is it?
answer: An electric field
choices: An electric field
A magnetic field
A sound field
A heat field
context: This sense is called active electrolocation: an organ near the fish's tail puts out a weak electric field, and receptors all over the skin feel how objects distort it, letting the fish 'see' shape and distance in total darkness. The brain that runs it burns roughly 60% of the fish's oxygen, about three times the share of any other vertebrate measured. Source: ScienceDaily / University of Bonn, von der Emde group (2016), https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/06/160624100245.htm; Nilsson, 'Brain and body oxygen requirements of Gnathonemus petersii,' J. Experimental Biology 199:603 (1996), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9318319/

question: A long, bendy flap droops from the face of the elephantnose fish, so like an elephant's trunk that it gave the fish its name. But it is not a nose at all: the fish's true nostrils are a pair of tiny holes farther up. What is the 'trunk' really?
answer: A mobile chin that sweeps the riverbed
choices: A mobile chin that sweeps the riverbed
An extra-long upper lip
A fleshy antenna on its forehead
A breathing tube to the surface
context: The 'trunk' is a movable chin extension called the schnauzenorgan. The fish sweeps it over the mud like a metal detector, hunting for buried insect larvae by feel. Source: Nature News, 'Seeing through the chin' (2007), quoting Gerhard von der Emde, https://www.nature.com/news/2007/070820/full/news070820-10.html

question: A juicy insect larva lies buried in the mud, invisible, right beside a pebble of the very same size and shape. Without ever seeing either one, the elephantnose fish tells the living larva from the dead stone. What difference does it feel between them?
answer: The larva stores charge like a tiny capacitor
choices: The larva stores charge like a tiny capacitor
The larva sits a little warmer than the stone
The larva leaks a faint smell the stone lacks
The larva hums at a pitch the stone cannot
context: Living tissue — animals, plants, larvae — stores electric charge like a tiny capacitor, while stones and mud only resist current. The fish feels that difference, so it knows a buried larva is alive without seeing it. Source: von der Emde, 'Active electrolocation of objects in weakly electric fish,' J. Experimental Biology 202:1205 (1999), https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/202/10/1205/

question: When several elephantnose fish gather, each one can sense objects well beyond its own short range; a computer model puts the gain at up to three times as far. How does simply being in a group extend one fish's range this way?
answer: It reads its neighbors' pulses too
choices: It reads its neighbors' pulses too
It swims in tight, fast circles to scan more water
It stirs up mud to feel the current
Its own pulses grow stronger near other fish
context: Each fish can read the pulses its neighbors emit, so a group acts like a shared radar network; by Pedraja and Sawtell's computer model, that could extend how far each fish can sense up to threefold. Nathaniel Sawtell says these electric images are 'beamed to nearby fish at the speed of light.' Source: Phys.org / Columbia (2024), Sawtell & Pedraja on collective sensing, https://phys.org/news/2024-03-scientists-uncover-evidence-electric-elephantnose.amp ; ScienceDaily 2024-03-06.

question: Huddled against a blizzard on the frozen sea ice stands the biggest and tallest penguin alive, about four feet tall and up to about a hundred pounds. Which penguin is it?
answer: The emperor penguin
choices: The emperor penguin
The gentoo penguin
The Adelie penguin
The little blue penguin
context: The emperor penguin stands roughly 1.15 m (about 4 feet) and weighs up to about 45 kg (100 lb) — bigger than any other living penguin. Source: Britannica, https://www.britannica.com/animal/emperor-penguin

question: A mother emperor penguin lays a single egg on the sea ice in the black of the Antarctic winter, hands it to the father, and sets off on a weeks-long walk to the sea to feed. If the egg touches the ice, it can freeze in seconds. Where does the father hold it?
answer: Balanced on the tops of his feet
choices: Balanced on the tops of his feet
Cradled inside his folded wings
Buried in a scrape of packed snow
Carried in his long beak
context: The father balances the egg on the tops of his feet and covers it with a warm fold of belly skin called the brood pouch. Source: British Antarctic Survey, https://www.bas.ac.uk/about/antarctica/wildlife/penguins/emperor-penguin/

question: On the sea ice, a father emperor penguin stands hour after hour through the endless Antarctic winter, keeping his mate's single egg warm while she feeds far away at sea. In the 65 to 75 days before the egg hatches, how much does he eat?
answer: Nothing at all
choices: Nothing at all
A few small fish a week
Krill scooped from the snow
Whatever the mother brings back
context: The male incubates the egg on his feet for about 65 to 75 days without eating anything at all, surviving entirely on stored fat through the polar winter. Source: British Antarctic Survey, https://www.bas.ac.uk/about/antarctica/wildlife/penguins/emperor-penguin/

question: A father emperor penguin weighs around 38 kilograms when the breeding season begins. He then guards a single egg through the pitch-black Antarctic winter, standing still through months of freezing storms. By the time the mother finally comes back from the sea, what has happened to his body?
answer: He has lost about half his weight
choices: He has lost about half his weight
He has lost about a tenth of his weight
He has lost about a quarter of his weight
He weighs about the same as when he began
context: Across the whole breeding cycle the fasting father goes roughly 120 days without food and can lose about 20 kg, dropping from around 38 kg down to 18 kg. Source: Wikipedia, Emperor penguin, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_penguin

question: When the Antarctic air falls to minus 40 degrees Celsius in a howling wind, thousands of father emperor penguins press together into one enormous huddle. A bird stuck on the outer edge would freeze, while the birds packed in the middle stay warm. How does the huddle keep every father alive?
answer: It shuffles so each bird takes turns inside
choices: It shuffles so each bird takes turns inside
The biggest males stand guard on the edge
Birds on the edge flap to stay warm
The whole huddle lies down to cut the wind
context: The fathers pack into a huddle of over 4,000 males; the birds constantly shuffle in slow waves every 30 to 60 seconds so no one is stuck on the freezing edge for long. Source: Audubon (reporting Zitterbart et al., PLoS ONE), https://www.audubon.org/news/not-so-black-and-white-research-reveals-intricacies-penguin-huddles

question: Outside an emperor penguin huddle, the Antarctic air sits near minus 40 degrees Celsius, and a howling wind blows. Deep inside the packed mass of thousands of fathers, researchers recorded temperatures climbing higher. What top temperature did they measure inside the huddle?
answer: About 37.5 degrees C, near human body heat
choices: About 37.5 degrees C, near human body heat
Just above freezing, around 2 degrees C
About -10 degrees C, only a little warmer
Around 15 degrees C, like a cool room
context: Inside the packed huddle it gets so warm that recorded temperatures reach up to about 37.5 degrees C — near human body heat — even while the outside air is around -40 degrees C. Source: Audubon (Zitterbart huddle research), https://www.audubon.org/news/not-so-black-and-white-research-reveals-intricacies-penguin-huddles

question: Out on the Antarctic sea ice, an emperor penguin chick sometimes hatches before its mother is back from the sea with food. Its father can still feed it, though only for about three to seven days. How does he do it?
answer: With 'crop milk' produced in his throat
choices: With 'crop milk' produced in his throat
With regurgitated fish from his stomach
With fat scraped from his own belly
With melted snow warmed in his beak
context: If the chick hatches before the mother returns, the father feeds it 'crop milk' — a protein-rich, curd-like substance made in his throat — but he can only produce it for about 3 to 7 days. Source: Penguins International, https://www.penguinsinternational.org/how-do-penguins-feed-their-chicks/

question: An emperor penguin can dive deeper than any other bird, and the deepest of its dives ever reliably measured hit 564 meters. Researchers logged more than 137,000 emperor dives, and only 12 of them went past 500 meters. What was strange about those 12?
answer: Every one was made by the same single penguin
choices: Every one was made by the same single penguin
They all happened during the same storm
They were all made by chicks, not adults
None of them caught any prey
context: The deepest reliably measured dive was 564 m (1,850 ft), and out of 137,364 dives recorded in the study, all 12 that passed 500 m were made by the same single penguin. Source: Guinness World Records, https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/deepest-dive-by-a-bird

question: On a long dive, an emperor penguin must ration every scrap of oxygen, and it does so by throttling its own heart. At rest the heart runs at about 73 beats a minute. During one 18-minute dive, how low did it fall?
answer: Just 3 beats a minute, one every 20 seconds
choices: Just 3 beats a minute, one every 20 seconds
Just 1 beat a minute, one every 60 seconds
About 12 beats a minute, one every 5 seconds
About 30 beats a minute, one every 2 seconds
context: A resting emperor penguin's heart runs near 73 bpm and climbs to about 175 bpm just before a dive. But once a dive passes the roughly 5.6-minute aerobic limit, the heart drops into extreme bradycardia, averaging a minimum near 14 bpm. In one 18-minute dive it fell to just 3 bpm and held near 6 bpm for over 5 minutes; about 10% of long dives dropped to 5 bpm or lower. Slowing the heart to near-stopped meters out the bird's limited oxygen so it lasts the whole dive. Source: Meir, Stockard, Williams, Ponganis & Kooyman (2008), 'Heart rate regulation and extreme bradycardia in diving emperor penguins,' Journal of Experimental Biology 211(8):1169 -- https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/211/8/1169/18165/

question: Carolina Acosta Hospitaleche examined bones of Palaeeudyptes klekowskii, dug from 34-million-year-old rock on Seymour Island, off the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula. In 2014 she used those fossil bones to estimate how big the animal had been in life. What did she conclude?
answer: A penguin up to 2 m long and about 115 kg
choices: A penguin up to 2 m long and about 115 kg
A penguin about the size of a modern emperor
A penguin no bigger than a modern gentoo
A penguin up to 4 m long and about 500 kg
context: Palaeeudyptes klekowskii, the 'Mega Penguin', came from the Late Eocene La Meseta Formation on Seymour Island, Antarctica, dated to about 34-37 million years ago. A 2014 study by Carolina Acosta Hospitaleche, working from the most complete Eocene penguin skeleton yet found, estimated it reached up to 2 metres (6.6 ft) in length and weighed as much as 115 kg, nearly twice a modern emperor's mass and the largest penguin then known to science. Giant penguins once ruled the same Antarctic coasts where emperors breed today. Source: Acosta Hospitaleche (2014), Geobios 47(3), on Palaeeudyptes klekowskii; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palaeeudyptes_klekowskii

question: A young common swift leaves its nest under a rooftop and climbs into the sky over Europe. From then on it eats, drinks and mates on the wing. About how long can it stay airborne before it lands again?
answer: About 10 months
choices: About 10 months
About 10 weeks
About 10 days
About 10 hours
context: The common swift (Apus apus) can stay aloft for about 10 months straight — eating flying insects, mating, and sleeping on the wing — the longest continuous flight known for any bird. Source: https://www.sci.news/biology/common-swifts-stay-ten-months-air-04324.html

question: A bar-tailed godwit, a long-legged shorebird that probes tidal mud with its long, slightly upturned beak, was five months old when it left Alaska in 2022 carrying a satellite tag. It flew without stopping, with no food, no water and no rest, and set the record for the longest nonstop flight ever measured for any bird. Where did that flight end?
answer: Tasmania, off southern Australia
choices: Tasmania, off southern Australia
New Zealand's North Island
Hawaii, in the mid-Pacific
Japan, on the Asian coast
context: Juvenile bar-tailed godwit '234684' flew nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania, about 13,560 km, in 11 days and 1 hour (departed October 13, 2022) — the longest nonstop flight ever recorded for a bird. Source: https://www.usgs.gov/centers/alaska-science-center/news/juvenile-bar-tailed-godwit-b6-sets-world-record

question: A frigatebird, a lean black seabird with pointed wings and a deeply forked tail, can spend weeks over the open ocean without landing. It sleeps in flight with just half of its brain at a time, while the other half keeps it flying. Scientists tracking the birds found the waking half is usually linked to one particular eye. Which eye stays open?
answer: The one facing the direction it is turning, to watch its path
choices: The one facing the direction it is turning, to watch its path
The one facing the sun, to hold a steady heading
The one facing down, to spot fish on the water
The one facing the wind, to feel the gusts coming
context: When a frigatebird circles on a rising air current, the brain half linked to the eye facing the turn stays awake to watch its path while the other half sleeps. Source: https://www.mpg.de/10673637/frigatebirds-sleep

question: A bar-tailed godwit rebuilds its own body before its nonstop flight across the Pacific, shrinking some of its working organs and absorbing as much as a quarter of them. Why would it give up working organs just before the biggest trip of its life?
answer: To make room for fat and enlarge its heart and flight muscles
choices: To make room for fat and enlarge its heart and flight muscles
To become light enough to be lifted by tailwinds alone
To stop needing food or water for the whole journey
To pack extra water into the space they leave behind
context: The godwit shrinks its liver, kidneys, and gut to make room for fat and to grow its heart and breast muscles for the flight — because 'guts don't fly.' Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/ecology-and-evolution/articles/10.3389/fevo.2021.685764/full

question: Niels Rattenborg's team taped tiny brainwave recorders to nesting frigatebirds, which then flew off over the ocean for up to 10 days. The recordings caught the birds sleeping in mid-air, mostly around sunset, but the amount surprised the team. How much did a frigatebird sleep each day on the wing?
answer: About 42 minutes, a fraction of what they get on land
choices: About 42 minutes, a fraction of what they get on land
A full 8 hours, the same as on the nest
Almost none — under a single minute
Exactly half a day, one brain-half at a time
context: Rattenborg's recorders showed frigatebirds slept in flight as the sun set, but only about 42 minutes a day — far less than on land. Source: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/08/160803111738.htm

question: Gottfried Sachs and his team pieced together the flight loops of wild wandering albatrosses from GPS loggers in 2013. Each loop has four phases: a climb into the wind, a turn at the top, a dive downwind and a turn low over the waves. In which phase did the bird gain most of its energy from the wind?
answer: The turn at the top, wheeling from upwind to downwind
choices: The turn at the top, wheeling from upwind to downwind
The climb into the wind, rising off the waves
The dive downwind, speeding toward the sea
The turn low over the waves, skimming the troughs
context: Sachs and colleagues tracked 16 wandering albatrosses in the southern Indian Ocean with GPS loggers precise enough to resolve each dynamic-soaring cycle: a windward climb, an upper curve, a leeward descent and a lower curve. They found that the primary energy gain from the shear wind comes in the upper curve, where the bird turns from flying into the wind to flying with it. Source: Sachs et al., 'Experimental verification of dynamic soaring in albatrosses,' Journal of Experimental Biology 216:4222 (2013), doi 10.1242/jeb.085209.

question: Out over the open tropical ocean, a great frigatebird, black and fork-tailed on seven-foot wings, can keep flying for up to two months without landing. It cannot settle on the sea, since its feathers would soak right through. It climbs thousands of metres into the sky and then glides long distances back down. How does it get so high?
answer: It flies into cumulus clouds and rides their updrafts
choices: It flies into cumulus clouds and rides their updrafts
It flaps in a steep spiral until the thin air levels it off
It waits on a floating log until a sea breeze lifts it
It skims the waves and lets each crest bounce it higher
context: Unlike most seabirds, a frigatebird cannot float — its plumage soaks through — so the open ocean gives it nowhere to land. Henri Weimerskirch's team satellite-tagged frigatebirds near Madagascar (Science, 1 July 2016) and found they deliberately fly INTO cumulus clouds to ride the updrafts to nearly 4,000 m — into freezing air — then glide long distances back down without flapping. Individuals stayed aloft for up to about two months, covering more than 400 km a day; young birds can remain almost continuously airborne for over a year. Source: Weimerskirch et al., Science 353 (2016).

question: On a coral reef in a warm, shallow sea, an octopus settles down and folds its eight sucker-lined arms over a rock, hiding all but one watchful eye. Under its soft skin, its blood keeps moving through gills, arms and brain. What color is that blood?
answer: Blue
choices: Blue
Bright red
Green
Yellow
context: Octopus blood is blue because it carries oxygen with hemocyanin, a copper-based protein, instead of iron-based hemoglobin; the copper turns blue when it meets oxygen the way the iron in human blood turns red. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Ten Wild Facts About Octopuses'.

question: Three hearts pump the blood of an octopus. Two of them, the branchial hearts, sit right beside the gills and do just one job: they push blood through the gill tissue, where it loads up on fresh oxygen. The third sends it on to every other part of the body. Why does the gill job get a pair of hearts all its own?
answer: It takes a high pressure of its own
choices: It takes a high pressure of its own
The gills lie too far from the main heart
The gills hold their own separate blood
The gills need cold blood to hold oxygen
context: The octopus must hold different blood pressures at the same time: high pressure at the gills to load oxygen, and a separate push from the systemic heart to send that blood to the body — so the gill-loading job gets its own dedicated pair of hearts. Source: Smithsonian Magazine; This Amazing World comparative physiology summaries.

question: As an octopus slips across the reef, its blood carries oxygen out to every arm. Human blood carries oxygen on iron, packed into hemoglobin, and the iron turns it red. Octopus blood uses a different metal, held in a protein called hemocyanin, which gives it a color of its own. Which metal does an octopus use?
answer: Copper
choices: Copper
Vanadium
Zinc
Manganese
context: The octopus carries oxygen with hemocyanin, a copper-based protein; copper turns blue with oxygen the way iron-based hemoglobin turns human blood red. The horseshoe crab has blue blood for the exact same reason. Source: Smithsonian Magazine octopus article.

question: Squirting water out of its siphon, an octopus can shoot through open sea in a fast burst, yet it almost always crawls slowly across the sea floor instead. Its blood is a weaker oxygen carrier than human blood. What happens inside the octopus that makes a single burst of jetting so exhausting?
answer: Its main heart stops beating
choices: Its main heart stops beating
Blood pools uselessly in its arms
Its arms lock up from the strain
It burns through its stored fat
context: The systemic (main) heart actually stops beating when the octopus jets through open water, which exhausts it, so octopuses usually prefer to crawl. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Ten Wild Facts About Octopuses'.

question: A giraffe, standing up to 5.5 metres tall, browses leaves at the top of an African acacia tree. Its heart must drive blood straight up a neck about two metres long to reach the brain, fighting gravity the whole way. How does the giraffe's blood pressure compare with a human's?
answer: About double a human's
choices: About double a human's
About ten times a human's
About five times a human's
About a third higher than a human's
context: A giraffe's blood pressure reaches roughly 280/180 to 300/180 mmHg, about double a human's, to force blood up the long neck. Source: Novartis, 'Giraffes have high blood pressure. Why don't they drop dead?'; Giraffe Conservation Foundation.

question: At an African waterhole, a giraffe splays its long front legs and lowers its head far below its own heart to drink. All that blood should rush downhill into its skull and knock it out cold. Something stops the flood from ever reaching its brain. What does the job?
answer: One-way valves in its neck veins
choices: One-way valves in its neck veins
A muscular ring inside its aorta
A valve at the exit of its heart
A clamp of muscle at the base of the skull
context: Valves in the neck veins block blood from rushing back into the skull, so the giraffe does not pass out from the sudden pressure surge when it lowers its head to drink. Source: Novartis, 'Giraffes have high blood pressure...'; Hemodynamics and Drinking in the Giraffe, PMC12012874.

question: An earthworm slithers through wet garden soil with no chest, no ribs and no single chambered heart at all. Instead, a set of muscular tubes wraps around the front of its gut and squeezes rhythmically, one after another, to push its dark red blood along. How many of these pumping hearts does an earthworm have?
answer: Five pairs
choices: Five pairs
A single pair
Twelve pairs
Two pairs
context: The earthworm has no single heart; it uses five pairs of pulsing 'aortic arches' (often called pseudohearts) that squeeze rhythmically to push blood around its closed circulatory system. Source: Sciencing, 'How Many Hearts Does An Earthworm Have?'; CK-12, 'What is unique about an earthworm's heart?'.

question: An icefish swims through the cold Antarctic sea with blood as clear as water, carrying no hemoglobin at all.
