Biologists once assumed it had simply switched off making the protein in the cold. Reading its genome overturned that view, with an answer more final than a switched-off gene. What had happened to the hemoglobin gene?
answer: The gene itself is physically deleted
choices: The gene itself is physically deleted
The gene is silenced but still intact
The protein misfolds and is destroyed
A cold-triggered mutation stalls it
context: In 15 of the 16 crocodile-icefish species the beta-globin gene is entirely gone and the alpha-globin gene is partly deleted — the DNA is missing, not merely switched off. The loss of myoglobin, the oxygen-store protein in muscle, happened separately and independently at least four times, so 6 of the 16 species also lack myoglobin in the heart. To move oxygen dissolved straight in watery plasma, icefish evolved blood volumes up to four times a red-blooded fish's, unusually wide capillaries, and a cardiac output about five times greater — yet their blood still carries under 20% the oxygen of their hemoglobin-bearing relatives. Source: Sidell & O'Brien, 'When bad things happen to good fish: the loss of hemoglobin and myoglobin expression in Antarctic icefishes,' Journal of Experimental Biology 209:1791 (2006); Wikipedia 'Crocodile icefish' (gene-deletion, 4x blood volume, 5x cardiac output).

question: Two coins of greenish-gold light flare in a car's headlights at the edge of a dark country road, then vanish as a deer turns its head. The glow comes from a layer built into the deer's eye. What is that layer?
answer: A mirror behind the retina that bounces light back
choices: A mirror behind the retina that bounces light back
A clear, oily film across the front of the eye
A layer of cells that make their own glow
A second lens that magnifies the light
context: That mirror is the tapetum lucidum, Latin for 'bright tapestry.' It sits behind the retina and reflects light that the photoreceptors missed on the way in, sending it back through them so the eye gets a second chance to catch each scrap of light. Humans and most other primates have none, so human eyes don't shine. Source: Britannica, 'tapetum lucidum'; Wikipedia, 'Tapetum lucidum.'

question: A cat's eyes blaze back from a dark room, while a person's eyes in a flash photo glow plain red. The cat's eyes carry the layer that makes eyeshine; human eyes have none. Where does the red glow in a human flash photo come from?
answer: Blood in the retina at the back of the eye lighting up in the flash
choices: Blood in the retina at the back of the eye lighting up in the flash
The camera's own flash bulb reflected off the wet cornea
The colored iris reflecting the camera's light straight back
A film of tears scattering the flash across the front of the eye
context: Because humans and most primates lack a tapetum lucidum entirely, a flash reaches the back of the eye and lights up the blood-rich retina, and the camera catches that red. A cat's mirror, by contrast, retro-reflects the light straight back, so its eyes shine instead of going red. Source: Institute for Environmental Research and Education, 'What animals have a tapetum?'; Wikipedia, 'Tapetum lucidum.'

question: A house cat spots a mouse moving in near-total darkness, where a person would see nothing. Yet it cannot tell a red toy mouse from a green one as a person can. Its retina, the light-catching sheet at the back of the eye, traded color for night sight. What is it packed with?
answer: Rod cells, six to eight times as many as a human eye holds
choices: Rod cells, six to eight times as many as a human eye holds
Cone cells, packed far more densely than a human's
Extra lenses layered inside to magnify what little light there is
A second, deeper retina that switches on only after dark
context: A cat's retina packs six to eight times more rods than a human's and very few cones. Rods register dim light and movement superbly but not color or fine detail, so the cat trades a rich color world for the power to see shapes and motion in near-blackness, exactly what a small ambush predator needs. Source: ScienceInsights, 'Can Cats See in the Dark?'

question: Caught in a car's headlights, a cat's eyes flash green, a raccoon's yellow and many dogs' bright blue. The difference is not the color of the headlights. What decides the color each animal's eyes shine back?
answer: What the mirror layer is made of
choices: What the mirror layer is made of
How wide its pupil happens to be open
The color of the fur around its eyes
How far away the headlights are
context: The tapetum lucidum can be built from crystals of zinc, riboflavin, or collagen, and each material reflects a different band of wavelengths. So the mirror's own recipe sets the glow color, which is why a fox, a cat, and a raccoon flash different hues in the same headlights. Source: scienceabc.com, 'Why Do Cats' Eyes Glow?'

question: A reindeer forages through the long, dim twilight of an Arctic winter. Stokkan and colleagues found in 2013 that its eyeshine layer changes color with the seasons, something never seen before in a mammal. In summer it is gold. In winter it scatters more light sideways through the retina instead of throwing it straight back. What color is it by winter?
answer: Deep blue
choices: Deep blue
Bright red
Silvery white
Pale green
context: Stokkan and colleagues (2013, Proc. R. Soc. B) showed the reindeer tapetum shifts from gold in summer to deep blue by winter. Blue reflects less light straight back out and scatters more of it sideways through the retina, raising sensitivity in the long Arctic twilight. It was the first seasonal color change of an eye-mirror ever shown in a mammal. Source: Stokkan et al. 2013 via ScienceDaily; National Geographic.

question: In the near-black midwater of the deep ocean, a barreleye fish hangs motionless, watching through a see-through forehead for faint silhouettes. Its eyes are long tubes rather than balls. What does a tube-shaped eye do better than a round one?
answer: Gathers more light for its width
choices: Gathers more light for its width
Takes in a wider view all around
Resists the crushing deep-sea pressure
Sees colors more sharply in dim light
context: The deep-sea barreleye grows tubular, barrel-shaped eyes: a tube of the same width gathers more light than a round eye, pure light-harvesting for the dark. To beat the narrow field of view a fixed tube would give, it can swivel the eyes: it hangs with them pointed up, then rotates them forward and swims up to feed when it spots a jelly. Source: MBARI, 'Researchers solve mystery of deep-sea fish with tubular eyes and transparent head.'

question: A harmless scarlet kingsnake, banded red, yellow and black, slides through the pine woods and swamps of the southern United States. Its little jaws could never hurt a person, yet predators leave it alone, because it looks almost exactly like a deadly banded snake of the same region. Which venomous snake is it imitating?
answer: The coral snake
choices: The coral snake
The copperhead
The cottonmouth
The timber rattlesnake
context: The harmless scarlet kingsnake and milk snake copy the coral snake's banded pattern so predators leave them alone. People use rhymes to tell them apart: 'red touches yellow, kill a fellow; red touches black, venom lack.' Source: Wikipedia 'Scarlet kingsnake / Milk snake'.

question: In one part of the Carolinas, a harmless scarlet kingsnake wearing the red, yellow and black bands of a deadly snake is left alone. Elsewhere in the same region, predators attack it. What makes the borrowed warning work where it does?
answer: Real coral snakes live there and taught predators to fear the pattern
choices: Real coral snakes live there and taught predators to fear the pattern
Kingsnakes there interbreed enough to keep their colors bright
Kingsnakes there smell like coral snakes, not just look like them
The soil there matches the color of the kingsnake's bands
context: Batesian mimicry only works where the dangerous model lives. In a study published in 2001, Pfennig and colleagues set out kingsnake-patterned models across the Carolinas, and predators attacked them far less where coral snakes live, because predators there have learned to fear the pattern; the bluff failed where no coral snakes exist to teach the lesson. Source: Pfennig, Harcombe & Pfennig 2001, Nature, 'Frequency-dependent Batesian mimicry'; PBS NOVA 'How the Kingsnake Is Still Fooling Predators'; UNC Endeavors 'A Striking Resemblance'.

question: A wasp and a bee of two different stinging species wear almost the same yellow-and-black stripes. Dozens of other stinging species wear them too, and none of them is a harmless faker: every one can really sting. Why would so many truly dangerous species evolve to look alike?
answer: So a predator only has to learn the one warning look once
choices: So a predator only has to learn the one warning look once
So they can recognize and swarm each other in defense
So the strongest species can hide among the weaker ones
So the pattern blends them into yellow flowers
context: This is Mullerian mimicry — several genuinely dangerous species converge on ONE warning look, so predators learn the lesson faster and every species benefits. It's different from Batesian mimicry, where a single harmless faker cheats off a dangerous model. Source: Wikipedia 'Mullerian mimicry'.

question: On the muddy bottom of a river an alligator snapping turtle sits stone-still with its mouth wide open. Something small and pink wiggles gently deep inside that gaping mouth, and a fish darts in to grab it — then the jaws slam shut. What is that wriggling pink lure?
answer: A worm-shaped part of the turtle's own tongue
choices: A worm-shaped part of the turtle's own tongue
A leech clinging to its jaw
A live minnow it caught earlier
A dangling bit of algae
context: The alligator snapping turtle wiggles a worm-shaped appendage on its tongue — a hunting trick called lingual luring, a form of aggressive mimicry, where a fake friendly signal LURES prey close instead of scaring predators off. Source: Wikipedia 'Alligator snapping turtle / Lingual luring'; HowStuffWorks.

question: A mimic octopus crawls over a sandy Indo-Pacific seafloor, and it does more than hide: it imitates other animals at will. In one of its best-known disguises it poses as a venomous, spiny-finned fish. Which fish?
answer: A lionfish
choices: A lionfish
A pufferfish
A moray eel
A stonefish
context: The mimic octopus shapeshifts into several animals: arms held out radially to look like a spiny lionfish, six arms hidden and two held straight to mimic a banded sea snake, and all eight flattened behind it to glide like a flatfish. Source: Wikipedia 'Mimic octopus'.

question: Researchers have watched the mimic octopus, Thaumoctopus mimicus, turn itself into copies of several different sea animals, and they suspect it does not pick at random. There is evidence that its choice of disguise depends on one thing in particular. What seems to decide which animal it becomes?
answer: The specific predator it is currently facing
choices: The specific predator it is currently facing
The temperature of the surrounding water
The time of day it is hunting
How recently it last ate
context: The mimic octopus is the first cephalopod known to impersonate several different animals, and there is evidence it selects its disguise to suit the specific predator confronting it. Source: Grokipedia 'Mimic octopus'; Wikipedia 'Mimic octopus'; AMNH 'The Talented Mimic Octopus'.

question: Akcali and Pfennig measured museum scarlet kingsnakes from the North Carolina Sandhills, collected in the decades after the venomous snake they copy had died out there by about 1960. With no live model left for birds to fear, biologists expected the borrowed warning to blur and fade. What did the red and black bands do instead?
answer: Grew ever closer to the vanished coral snake’s exact proportions
choices: Grew ever closer to the vanished coral snake’s exact proportions
Faded toward the plain brown of unrelated local snakes
Split into a brand-new pattern no coral snake ever wore
Stayed frozen at the 1960 proportions with no further change
context: This is one of the strangest results in mimicry science. Akcali & Pfennig measured red-versus-black proportions on scarlet kingsnake (Lampropeltis elapsoides) museum specimens from the 1970s through the 2010s, after the venomous coral snake (Micrurus fulvius) had already vanished locally by about 1960. Rather than decaying once the real model was gone, the mimicry got statistically MORE precise over five decades (F1,26 = 6.997; p = 0.014). They call it 'evolutionary momentum': a predator that mistook a real coral snake for a harmless mimic died, while wrongly avoiding a harmless kingsnake cost almost nothing — so that lopsided selection keeps sharpening the disguise for the few predator generations after the model disappears. Source: Akcali & Pfennig 2014, 'Rapid evolution of mimicry following local model extinction,' Biology Letters — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4090552/ ; summary https://phys.org/news/2014-06-mimicry-scarlet-kingsnake-snake-coral.html

question: A Heliconius numata butterfly can wear any of up to seven warning patterns, each copying a different toxic species. Every form passes to the next generation clean, never as a muddled half-and-half wing. What locks each disguise together and passes it on as one unit?
answer: A supergene—one chromosome block, held intact by an inversion
choices: A supergene—one chromosome block, held intact by an inversion
A gut microbe passed from the mother to each new caterpillar
The temperature the chrysalis happens to develop at
The particular Melinaea species the caterpillar feeds beside
context: Heliconius numata carries an entire mimicry wardrobe on one chunk of chromosome 15, a locus called P. Joron and colleagues showed that a set of chromosomal inversions — a roughly 400-kilobase inverted block holding about 21 genes — suppresses recombination there, so the whole color-pattern gene cluster is inherited as one indivisible Mendelian unit. Without the inversion those separate pattern genes would recombine and shuffle into blurred, half-and-half wings that copy no protected model and get picked off; the inversion 'freezes' each working disguise as a single allele. That is why one species can carry seven complete, distinct disguises at once. Source: Joron et al. 2011, Nature 477:203, 'Chromosomal rearrangements maintain a polymorphic supergene controlling butterfly mimicry' — https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10341 ; corroboration https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223682/

question: A harbor seal hunts fish along a cold coast, in water often too murky to see through. For an experiment published in 2001, Georg Dehnhardt blindfolded one and sent a miniature submarine on a winding course through its pool. Moments later the seal set off along the sub's exact path, though the water looked perfectly still. What was it following?
answer: The invisible wake the sub stirred up
choices: The invisible wake the sub stirred up
The faint hum of the sub's motor
A trail of oil the sub left behind
The warmth left behind by its engine
context: A swimming fish leaves a swirling trail of disturbed water, its hydrodynamic wake, and a harbor seal can feel such a trail with its whiskers alone. In Georg Dehnhardt's 2001 study a miniature submarine laid down a repeatable wake, and blindfolded seals tracked it to the sub in about 80% of trials. With a stocking mask over its whiskers, a seal failed even to find the trail, showing it was hunting by touch. Source: Dehnhardt, Mauck, Hanke & Bleckmann 2001, Science 293:102-104; EurekAlert news release; Schulte-Pelkum et al. 2007, J. Exp. Biol. 210:781.

question: A star-nosed mole tunnels blind through wet North American soil, feeling its way with the ring of pink feelers around its snout. When one feeler brushes something, the mole must decide whether it is food, usually a worm, and swallow it before it can wriggle free. It holds the record as the fastest-eating mammal on Earth. From first touch to swallow, how long does a typical meal take?
answer: About a quarter of a second
choices: About a quarter of a second
About three seconds
About ten seconds
About half a minute
context: A typical meal takes about 227 milliseconds, roughly a quarter of a second, and the fastest recorded took just 120 milliseconds, about an eighth of a second. Guinness lists the star-nosed mole as the world's fastest forager. Packed into that tiny star are more than 25,000 microscopic touch sensors wired to over 100,000 nerve fibers, letting it identify a worm almost instantly in total darkness. Source: Grokipedia, Star-nosed mole (227 ms average, 120 ms minimum); Wikipedia, Star-nosed mole (Guinness); Carnegie Museum, 'The Nose that Sees.'

question: A manatee feeds in water so murky it can barely see, yet it feels out one water plant from another with the stiff whiskery bristles on its snout, telling them apart by touch alone. Biologists compare the fineness of that touch to one body part of another large animal. Which?
answer: An elephant feeling with its trunk tip
choices: An elephant feeling with its trunk tip
A giraffe curling its long tongue
A rhino probing with its horn
A hippo sweeping its wide lips
context: A manatee's face carries about 600 stiff bristles (and thousands more sensory hairs over its body) that it works like fingers, grasping and sorting plants it can barely see. Researchers judge this facial touch to be at least as fine as an elephant feeling with the tip of its trunk - precise enough to tell one plant from another by feel. Source: Reep et al. 2001 (~600 facial bristles); Scholarpedia, 'Tactile hair in Manatees'; asknature.org.

question: A wrinkled, pink, buck-toothed naked mole-rat scurries through its narrow, branching tunnels beneath the deserts of East Africa. It is almost completely bald, but stiff sensory hairs run in neat rows along its flanks and tail like trip-wires. Those hairs give it one strange ability most animals lack. What can a naked mole-rat do?
answer: Reverse through a tunnel as fast as it runs forward
choices: Reverse through a tunnel as fast as it runs forward
Regrow the hairs within a day if they break
Sense an intruder three tunnels away
Feel the temperature of soil to the degree
context: Those rows of body hairs act as feelers all along its sides and tail, so the naked mole-rat can move backward through its tunnels just as fast and accurately as it moves forward - handy when there is no room to turn around underground. Source: Scholarpedia, 'Tactile sensing in the naked mole rat'; ScienceDirect Topics, Naked Mole Rat.

question: Kenneth Catania filmed a hunting star-nosed mole with high-speed cameras and saw that its star never sweeps smoothly over the soil. It dabs 10 to 15 separate spots a second, hopping between them in quick darts. What did Catania say this darting was like?
answer: The quick flicks of an eye scanning a scene
choices: The quick flicks of an eye scanning a scene
A dog sniffing the ground in short bursts
A snake flicking its tongue to taste the air
A bat sending out pulses of sonar
context: Catania called the star a 'tactile eye': as the mole hunts, the star jumps from spot to spot the same way primate eyes make quick darting movements called saccades. It is feeling the world in rapid glances rather than one smooth sweep. Source: Wikipedia, Star-nosed mole; Kenneth Catania, Vanderbilt (tactile eye / saccades).

question: Suppose you ran your hand along the inside of a blue whale's mouth. You would find no teeth, only hundreds of stiff, fringed baleen plates hanging from the upper jaw to strain krill from each gulp. Which part of your own body is made of the same material?
answer: Your fingernails
choices: Your fingernails
Your kneecaps
Your eardrums
Your tooth enamel
context: Baleen is keratin -- the same protein that builds human fingernails and hair. Hundreds of these plates hang like a curtain and sieve krill and small fish out of the water. Source: Natural History Museum, 'Baleen whales: Filter feeding explained'; Whale & Dolphin Conservation, 'What is baleen?'

question: A flamingo stands on one leg in a shallow salt lake, sieving its food from the water with its curved beak. Its chicks hatch a dull gray and stay that way for months, yet the grown adults blaze bright pink. The bird is not born with that color. Where does a flamingo's pink come from?
answer: Pigments in the shrimp and algae it eats
choices: Pigments in the shrimp and algae it eats
A dye gland under the wing
Sunlight bleaching the feathers
Minerals in the mud it stands in
context: Carotenoids -- the same kind of pigment that makes carrots orange -- come from the brine shrimp and algae the flamingo filters, and get laid down in its feathers. Take the pigment out of the diet and new feathers grow pale. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, 'Why Are Flamingos Pink'; webexhibits.org, 'Flamingos | Causes of Color'.

question: Wading into a shallow, salty lake, a flamingo plunges its whole head upside down to feed on tiny brine shrimp. Its bent bill works as a strainer, and something drives the water in and out against that sieve, over and over. What does the pumping?
answer: Its thick tongue, moving like a piston
choices: Its thick tongue, moving like a piston
A muscular pouch under its chin
Rapid gulping at the back of its throat
Beats of its half-open wings
context: With its head inverted, the flamingo sweeps side to side while a piston-like tongue pumps water in and out; comb-like plates called lamellae inside the bent bill sieve out brine shrimp and algae as the water rushes back out. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, 'Why Are Flamingos Pink and Other Flamingo Facts'; SeaWorld, 'All About Flamingos - Diet'.

question: A blue whale lunges at a swarm of krill and takes one enormous gulp of seawater with the krill scattered through it. Stiff, hairy baleen plates hang from the roof of its mouth as a strainer, but they trap krill only when the water moves the right way past them. How does the whale shed the seawater and keep the food?
answer: It squeezes the water back out through the plates
choices: It squeezes the water back out through the plates
It pumps the water out through blowhole-like slits
It tilts head-down so water drains off the front
It filters as water rushes IN through the plates on the gulp
context: Baleen works as a one-way sieve: the whale pushes the water back out through the bristly plates, trapping krill as small as about half a millimeter on the inside, then swallows what is left. Source: AskNature, 'Hairlike Fringe Filters Food'; Natural History Museum baleen article.

question: Up to 30 metres long and the biggest animal that has ever lived, a blue whale drives sideways into a swirling swarm of thumb-sized krill. As it lunges, it unfolds the long pleats along its throat like a giant expanding bag, taking in one huge gulp of seawater to strain through its baleen. How much water does a single lunge engulf?
answer: More than the whale's entire body weight
choices: More than the whale's entire body weight
About a bathtub's worth
About a tenth of its own body weight
About as much as a small car weighs
context: One lunge engulfs around 70,000 liters -- a gulp heavier than the whale itself, holding roughly 10 kg of krill -- then the whale forces the water back out through the baleen and swallows what remains. Source: American Scientist, 'The Ultimate Mouthful: Lunge Feeding in Rorqual Whales'; Goldbogen et al., Journal of Experimental Biology 214(1):131.

question: A giant manta ray, its diamond-shaped wings spanning over five meters, glides through a swarm of drifting plankton off a tropical reef. Two paddle-shaped fins called cephalic lobes stick out on either side of its mouth. Rather than letting the plankton drift in on its own, the manta puts those fins to a particular job. What does it do with them?
answer: Curls them into an O to funnel water into its mouth
choices: Curls them into an O to funnel water into its mouth
Beats them like wings to swim faster
Digs them into the seabed for buried prey
Snaps them shut to trap fish like jaws
context: The manta curls its two cephalic lobes into a funnel that channels water and plankton into its wide-open mouth, then strains the food through feathery gill plates; in a thick swarm it does barrel-roll somersaults to keep cycling through. Source: NOAA Fisheries, 'Giant Manta Ray'; Manta Ray Advocates Hawaii, '8 Unique Techniques Manta Rays Use for Filter-Feeding'.

question: An Antarctic crabeater seal, despite its name, hunts almost nothing but krill, and its kind may be the most plentiful large wild mammal on Earth, numbering in the many millions. It strains the krill from the water with one body part shaped into a sieve, like a whale's baleen in miniature. Which body part?
answer: Its bizarre interlocking lobed teeth
choices: Its bizarre interlocking lobed teeth
A fringed pouch under its jaw
Long stiff whiskers around its mouth
Ridges lining the roof of its throat
context: The crabeater seal's teeth are intricately lobed and interlock into a strainer, letting it sieve krill from the water the way baleen does for a whale. Source: whalescientists.com, 'This seal has the craziest teeth in the carnivore world'; Wikipedia, 'Crabeater seal'; Oceanwide Expeditions.

question: A right whale, a slow, stocky baleen whale of the cold northern and southern seas, carries baleen beaten for length only by its cousin, the bowhead: single plates over two meters tall hang from its upper jaw like a vast curtain. That length suits the particular way it feeds, nothing like a lunging blue whale. How does a right whale gather its food?
answer: It cruises slowly with its mouth held open
choices: It cruises slowly with its mouth held open
It dives deep and ambushes prey in the dark
It herds fish into shallow bays
It filters mud from the seafloor
context: The right whale is a skim feeder: it swims steadily with mouth agape, straining tiny plankton continuously, and that non-stop skimming suits baleen plates over two meters long, second in length only to the bowhead's. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Baleen whale'; Wikipedia, 'Bowhead whale' (the longest baleen of any whale).

question: Not a single tooth ever grows in a blue whale's mouth; it strains its krill through baleen instead. Yet when biologists read its DNA, they found the instructions for building tooth enamel still sitting in its genome. What has become of those enamel-making genes?
answer: They have decayed into broken pseudogenes, silent leftovers of a toothed past
choices: They have decayed into broken pseudogenes, silent leftovers of a toothed past
They were copied and repurposed to grow the keratin plates of the baleen rack
They still work perfectly, but a blocker gene keeps them silenced for life
They now build the dense ear bones the whale uses to hear across the ocean
context: Baleen whales evolved from toothed ancestors, and the molecular ghost of those teeth is still written in their DNA. The genes for making tooth enamel -- including AMBN, ENAM, and the enamel-specific MMP20 -- have decayed into non-functional pseudogenes, broken by mutations once teeth were no longer used. So a blue whale still 'has' the instructions for teeth; they simply no longer work. This genome-level evidence matches the fossil record (forms like Aetiocetus weltoni had baleen-whale skulls but still bore teeth) and the fact that modern baleen-whale fetuses grow tooth buds in the womb that are reabsorbed before birth. Source: 'Baleen,' Wikipedia (enamel trait became a pseudogene in developing mysticetes); Meredith et al. work on cetacean enamel-gene loss (AMBN/ENAM/MMP20).

question: A glimmer of green-gold light drifts and blinks across a country yard on a warm summer night. Children call the little creature a lightning bug or a firefly, but it is not a fly, and not a true bug either. What kind of insect is it?
answer: A beetle
choices: A beetle
A moth
A wasp
A dragonfly
context: The firefly belongs to the beetle family Lampyridae, in the insect order Coleoptera -- about 2,000 species worldwide. 'Firefly' and 'lightning bug' are both misnomers: it is a beetle. Source: Britannica, 'Firefly | Insect'.

question: A firefly can glow on a person's palm, while an old incandescent bulb burns the fingers, because the bulb loses about nine-tenths of its energy as heat. What does the firefly's glow give off?
answer: Light, with very little heat
choices: Light, with very little heat
Heat, with only a faint light
Light, with a faint electric charge
Light, with heat to warm its wings
context: Firefly light is called 'cold light': it comes with very little heat, the reverse of an incandescent bulb, which loses roughly 90% of its energy as heat. Older sources say nearly all of the reaction's energy leaves as light; a 2008 measurement found that about 41% of the reacting luciferin molecules give off a photon, still far better than a bulb. Source: Grokipedia 'Firefly'; Britannica, 'Firefly | Insect'; Ando et al. 2008, Nature Photonics.

question: A firefly makes its light in its lower belly, through a chemical reaction rather than a battery or a spark. There a glowing molecule combines with oxygen and ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the body's energy molecule, sped along by a special enzyme. What is that enzyme called?
answer: Luciferase
choices: Luciferase
Catalase
Amylase
Lipase
context: The molecule luciferin, combined with oxygen and ATP energy and catalyzed by the enzyme luciferase, produces light with almost no heat. Source: sciencenewstoday.org, 'Why Fireflies Glow'; Bohrium sciencepedia.

question: Somewhere in a pitch-dark field, a male firefly searches for a female of his own species hidden in the black grass. The two find each other through a back-and-forth conversation. What are they using to talk?
answer: Their flash patterns
choices: Their flash patterns
Their wing-beats
Clicking sounds
Vibrations in the soil
context: Each species has its own signature flash code -- single, double, or multiple pulses at set intervals. A patrolling male flashes his species' code and a matching female flashes back, a light 'conversation' until they meet in the dark. Source: Firefly Atlas, 'Firefly Life History'.

question: A male Photinus firefly drifts over a summer meadow at night, blinking his code; when a female of his species flashes back the answer, he lands beside her. Some nights a female of another genus, Photuris, seizes and eats the male who lands. How does she draw him in?
answer: She fakes another firefly species' mating flash-code
choices: She fakes another firefly species' mating flash-code
She glows far brighter to blind approaching males
She releases a scent that paralyzes males mid-flight
She baits a leaf with a drop of sweet nectar
context: A Photuris female mimics the answering flash of a Photinus female to lure the male in, then catches and eats him. A single Photuris female can imitate the answering signals of several firefly species; Lloyd's 1975 study counted four. Source: Lloyd, 'Aggressive Mimicry in Photuris' (PubMed 17747574); Lloyd 1975, Science 187:452; phys.org 2018.

question: A female Photuris firefly catches and eats males of another firefly genus, Photinus. She gets more than a meal from them: Photinus males carry steroids called lucibufagins that her own body cannot make. What does eating them give her?
answer: Toxic chemicals that guard her from predators
choices: Toxic chemicals that guard her from predators
A brighter glow for the rest of the night
The ability to fly much farther
Hormones that make her grow larger
context: Photuris cannot make the defensive steroids called lucibufagins on its own; by eating Photinus males it acquires these toxins, which then protect it from predators like birds and spiders. Source: Eisner et al., PNAS 1997; Cornell Chronicle 1997.

question: Crowds hike into the Great Smoky Mountains on certain June nights and sit in the dark to watch one firefly, Photinus carolinus, do something few fireflies anywhere can do. Rangers even run a lottery for the parking spots. What do the crowds come to see?
answer: The males all flash in perfect unison
choices: The males all flash in perfect unison
Each firefly glows a different color
Thousands crowd onto one tree to glow
Their glow stays on all night unblinking
context: Photinus carolinus males synchronize, blinking together in bursts of about 5-8 flashes, then a shared pause of darkness of roughly 8 seconds or more -- whole sections of forest pulsing on and off at once. It was the first North American firefly found to synchronize; Photuris frontalis of the Southeast and Photinus knulli of Arizona also flash in sync. Source: Wikipedia 'Photinus carolinus'; NPS 'Synchronized Fireflies at Congaree'; firefly.org 'Synchronous Fireflies'.

question: A diver watches a cuttlefish on a sandy reef in the warm waters off northern Australia, its skin flashing bands of purple, yellow and white. Most cuttlefish jet and swim through open water, but this flamboyant one does not. How does it get around?
answer: It ambles along the bottom on two arms and two fin-flaps, like legs
choices: It ambles along the bottom on two arms and two fin-flaps, like legs
It burrows under the sand and pops up ahead of its prey
It rides the current, drifting wherever the water carries it
It anchors to a rock and waits for food to come to it
context: The flamboyant cuttlefish (Metasepia pfefferi) is one of the very few cuttlefish that WALKS rather than swims, ambling along the seabed on two of its arms plus two flaps of its lower fins that combine into leg-like appendages. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium (montereybayaquarium.org, animals-a-to-z/flamboyant-cuttlefish).

question: Divers off Indonesia are surprised the moment they meet a flamboyant cuttlefish in the wild, rolling bands of purple, yellow and white across its skin. A soft-bodied cousin of the octopus and squid, it has eight arms and two extra tentacles. How big does a full-grown adult get?
answer: About 2.5 to 3 inches long, roughly half a typical cuttlefish
choices: About 2.5 to 3 inches long, roughly half a typical cuttlefish
About a foot long, the same as most reef cuttlefish
About the length of a human arm, one of the largest cuttlefish
About the size of a dinner plate across its outstretched arms
context: It is tiny, only about 2.5 to 3 inches (6-8 cm) long, roughly half the size of a typical cuttlefish. Source: Ocean Conservancy (ode-flamboyant-cuttlefish); Monterey Bay Aquarium.

question: Purple, yellow and white flash across a flamboyant cuttlefish's skin on a tropical Indo-Pacific seabed, and it makes no attempt to hide. A report from Mark Norman of Museum Victoria described something in its muscle tissue that no other cuttlefish was known to have. What was it?
answer: A poison reportedly as lethal as a blue-ringed octopus's venom
choices: A poison reportedly as lethal as a blue-ringed octopus's venom
A store of ink far larger than any relative its size
A mesh of tiny chalky grains stiffening its muscles
A magnetic mineral it uses to navigate across the seabed
context: Mark Norman reported that its muscle tissue was poisonous, with a toxin said to match the blue-ringed octopus's, which would make it the only toxic cuttlefish known and one of only three cephalopods found to be poisonous. Its rolling color show was read as a warning (aposematism), the same 'don't eat me' billboard a poison dart frog uses, though later tests found far less toxin than the first report claimed. Source: MarineBio (marinebio.org, pfeffers-flamboyant-cuttlefishes); Wikipedia (Ascarosepion_pfefferi).

question: A flamboyant cuttlefish stays tied to the seabed while other cuttlefish hover weightless in open water, buoyed by a large internal shell called a cuttlebone that works like a float. The flamboyant one has a cuttlebone too, but it is built differently, and that difference keeps the animal on the bottom. What is different about it?
answer: It is shrunken and lacks the outer cone the others use, so it provides too little lift
choices: It is shrunken and lacks the outer cone the others use, so it provides too little lift
It has hardened into solid calcite, adding weight the animal cannot swim off
It draws in seawater on purpose, ballasting the body down onto the sand
It has shifted back into the arms, tipping the animal toward the bottom
context: Its cuttlebone is only two-thirds to three-quarters of the mantle length and, unlike most cuttlefish, lacks the outer cone the others rely on for buoyancy. With so little lift, it can't hover for long and is effectively tethered to the seafloor -- the walking is a consequence of a scaled-down buoyancy organ, not a lifestyle choice. Its sister species, the paintpot cuttlefish, shares the trait and is the only other cuttlefish known to walk. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ascarosepion pfefferi' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascarosepion_pfefferi), corroborated via science20.com and diving-indo.com.

question: Mark Norman reported that the flamboyant cuttlefish's muscle held tetrodotoxin, a deadly nerve poison, and it became known as the only toxic cuttlefish. Researchers from Georgia Southern and Utah State universities later went looking for that toxin in its tissue. What did they find?
answer: Only trace tetrodotoxin, far too little to harm a vertebrate, contradicting the original report
choices: Only trace tetrodotoxin, far too little to harm a vertebrate, contradicting the original report
A second, stronger toxin the first team had entirely missed in the muscle
The poison only in the ink sac, never in the muscle the first team had sampled
Tetrodotoxin at lethal levels, but produced by bacteria living in the tissue
context: Mark Norman (Museum Victoria) reported the muscle held tetrodotoxin -- the blue-ringed octopus's poison -- and called it 'highly toxic.' But teams at Georgia Southern University and Utah State University-Uintah Basin, testing directly for tetrodotoxin, found only trace amounts, too low to poison a vertebrate. Whether the 'only toxic cuttlefish' claim survives, and what the real poison even is, stays genuinely disputed -- the warning-color story rests on evidence scientists are still arguing over. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ascarosepion pfefferi' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascarosepion_pfefferi).

question: A flashlight fish glides through the black water where a coral reef slopes into the deep. It shines a bluish light so bright that divers can spot it from more than a hundred feet away, the brightest of any bony fish. Where does it carry that light?
answer: In a pouch under each eye
choices: In a pouch under each eye
Along its bony spine
On the tip of its tail
Deep inside its mouth
context: The flashlight fish (family Anomalopidae) carries a glowing pouch beneath each eye. It is the brightest light produced by any bony fish, a bluish glow visible from over 100 feet (30 m) away in the dark ocean. Source: Georgia Aquarium, 'Flashlight Fish'.

question: Two bluish lights blink on a dark reef at night, carried by a flashlight fish. Yet the fish does not make that light itself. Something living inside each light organ makes the glow, and the fish shelters and feeds it in return. What is it?
answer: Billions of glowing bacteria
choices: Billions of glowing bacteria
A colony of glowing algae
A cluster of tiny glowing shrimp
Threads of glowing fungus
context: The light comes from billions of light-making bacteria (Candidatus Photodesmus katoptron) living inside the fish's eye-pouch. It is a partnership: the fish houses and feeds the bacteria, and the bacteria give a light the fish could never make itself. Source: PLOS One / PMC5298212, 'The Flashlight Fish Anomalops katoptron Uses Bioluminescent Light to Detect Prey in the Dark'.

question: A predator closes in on a lone flashlight fish in the black water. The fish flashes, switches its light off, and in that instant the hunter loses it. Morin's team saw the fish make one move in the dark that leaves the hunter lunging at empty water. What does it do the moment its light goes out?
answer: It darts off at an angle in the dark
choices: It darts off at an angle in the dark
It sinks straight down and holds still
It doubles back the way it came
It hides motionless against the reef
context: Morin's team called it 'blink-and-run': the fish flashes, then darts off at an angle in the dark and goes dark, so the predator lunges at the spot where the light WAS. In a school they flash and zigzag so a predator cannot lock onto any single fish. Source: Morin et al. 1975, Science 190:74-76, 'Light for All Reasons: Versatility in the Behavioral Repertoire of the Flashlight Fish'.

question: All night long, a flashlight fish blinks its light on and off, flashing signals into the dark. Yet the glow inside its light organs never stops and can never be turned down. How does the fish go dark when its light cannot stop shining?
answer: It rotates the organ down into a black-lined pocket
choices: It rotates the organ down into a black-lined pocket
It clouds the pouch with a squirt of dark ink
It rolls its eyes back into their sockets
It buries its glowing head in the reef
context: Because the bacteria glow constantly, the fish cannot dim them. To 'blink,' Anomalops rotates the whole light organ downward into a black-lined pocket, hiding the glow behind the organ's heavily pigmented back, like flipping a lamp face-down. Source: Oxford Academic, Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society 94(1):65, 'Mechanisms of light organ occlusion in flashlight fishes'.

question: On the deep drop-offs of a Pacific coral reef at night, a flashlight fish shines a steady bluish light from each of its light organs. That beam is far brighter than the glowing contents alone could manage. The back wall of each organ boosts it. What lines that wall?
answer: Mirror-like crystals that reflect the light forward
choices: Mirror-like crystals that reflect the light forward
A layer of the fish's own glowing cells
A clear lens that magnifies the glow
A ring of muscle that squeezes it brighter
context: Behind the glowing bacteria, the pouch is lined with mirror-like guanine crystals that act as reflectors, bouncing the bacterial light forward and out to make the beam even brighter, a built-in reflector cup like a real flashlight. Source: Georgia Aquarium 'Flashlight Fish' / Techtimes summary of the PLOS One study on Anomalops katoptron.

question: Blinking its lights on and off about 90 times a minute, a flashlight fish patrols a Pacific coral reef at night. The moment it spots a cloud of tiny drifting plankton to eat, it changes what it does with the light. What does it do with its light to hunt the plankton down?
answer: Holds it steadily ON as a headlight
choices: Holds it steadily ON as a headlight
Blinks it faster to dazzle them
Snaps it fully off and strikes blind
Flickers it to herd them together
context: When it spots plankton, the fish stops blinking so much and holds the light ON, keeping the organ open nearly 90% of the time so it can use the beam as a headlight to spot and chase its tiny prey. At night an active fish otherwise blinks about 90 times a minute. Source: PLOS One / PMC5298212, 'The Flashlight Fish Anomalops katoptron Uses Bioluminescent Light to Detect Prey in the Dark'.

question: A colugo, a cat-sized furry mammal of Southeast Asian rainforests, leaps from a high branch and coasts a long way down on a wide flap of skin, gliding. Only one kind of mammal beats its wings to climb into the air and truly fly. Which mammals are the true fliers?
answer: Bats
choices: Bats
Sugar gliders
Flying lemurs
Gliding possums
context: Bats are the only mammals capable of true powered flight. Colugos ("flying lemurs"), sugar gliders, and gliding possums only glide on a stretched skin flap and cannot gain height. Source: Smithsonian 'Bat Facts'; Wikipedia 'Flying and gliding animals'.

question: A dragonfly hovers over the edge of a pond in the summer sunshine, then darts sideways and snatches a mosquito right out of the air. It flies on four thin, see-through, hard-veined wings. Where on a dragonfly's body do those four wings actually grow out from?
answer: From the body wall of its back
choices: From the body wall of its back
From a pair of its front legs
From a pair of its middle legs
From a stiffened pair of antennae
context: An insect's wings grow from the body wall of the thorax, not from any of its six walking legs, which is why an insect keeps all six legs and flies at the same time. Their deep origin is still studied: some evidence suggests they formed long ago from leg segments of a crustacean ancestor that merged into the body wall. No other animal built flight this way. Source: Wikipedia 'Insect wing'; University of Chicago News 'How insect wings evolved from the legs of an ancestral crustacean'.

question: Beating its wings, a bird lifts itself off the ground under its own power: true flapping flight. Gliding lizards, flying fish, colugos and flying squirrels cannot do that; they only glide, falling in style. Over the whole history of life on Earth, how many separate times did true powered flight evolve?
answer: Four times
choices: Four times
Two times
Nine times
Once, then it spread
context: Powered flight has been built independently only four times: insects, pterosaurs, birds, and bats. None inherited flight from a shared flying ancestor — each family solved the same problem alone. Everyone else (flying squirrels, flying fish, colugos, gliding frogs) only glides. Source: UCMP Berkeley 'Evolution of Flight'; Wikipedia 'Flying and gliding animals'.

question: Wings already hummed through the humid air over the giant ferns of the Carboniferous swamps, about 325 million years ago. Which group of animals was the first ever to fly under its own power?
answer: Insects
choices: Insects
Birds
Bats
Pterosaurs
context: Winged insects were already flying about 325 million years ago (the oldest known is Delitzschala bitterfeldensis), tens of millions of years before any backboned animal left the ground. Source: Wikipedia 'Insect wing'; Stanford Doerr School 'Insects took off when they evolved wings'.

question: A bat spreads its wings, and they look nothing like a bird's: no feathers laid over a stiff arm, only a thin sheet of skin stretched between long, spread fingers. Scientists named the order it belongs to Chiroptera, from two ancient Greek words that describe what that wing really is. What does Chiroptera mean?
answer: Hand-wing
choices: Hand-wing
Night-flyer
Skin-glider
Blood-drinker
context: A bat's wing is a webbed hand: skin (the patagium) stretched between four elongated finger bones. Chiroptera is Greek for 'hand-wing' (kheir 'hand' + pteron 'wing') — hold a bat's wing to the light and you see the thin finger bones running through it like the spokes of an umbrella. Source: Wikipedia 'Bat'; UCMP Berkeley bat flight page; Animal Diversity Web 'Chiroptera'.

question: A bird flaps with two big flight muscles, and oddly both of them sit down low on its chest, below the wing. One is the pectoralis; the other is the supracoracoideus. What job does the supracoracoideus do, and how can a muscle down on the chest manage it?
answer: Raises the wing for the recovery stroke, using a bony pulley over the shoulder
choices: Raises the wing for the recovery stroke, using a bony pulley over the shoulder
Stiffens the hollow wing bones so they don't crack in flight
Locks the wing folded flat against the body at rest
Twists the wingtip feathers to steer the bird in a turn
context: Both big flight muscles sit LOW on the chest, yet the supracoracoideus raises the wing: its tendon threads up through a tunnel of bone over the shoulder, like a rope over a pulley, so a chest muscle pulls the wing UP. The pectoralis pulls it DOWN for the power stroke — and with no keel to anchor them, flightless birds like ostriches barely have one. Source: Wikipedia 'Keel (bird anatomy)'; Britannica 'Bird — Skeleton'.

question: Pterosaurs built their wings from the same body part that birds and bats use for theirs, though the three lines are only distant relatives and the wings look nothing alike. Each line inherited that part from a shared four-legged ancestor and stretched a different piece of it. Which part did all three rebuild into a wing?
answer: The forelimb
choices: The forelimb
The rib cage
The shoulder blade
The tailbone
context: The three flying vertebrates all rebuilt the same forelimb into a wing — homologous, inherited from a common four-legged ancestor — but each stretched different bones: pterosaurs one finger, bats four, birds the whole arm. Same starting parts, three different wings. Source: Science World 'The Evolution of Flight'; Wikipedia 'Convergent evolution'.

question: Against the light, a bat's open wing shows thin bones fanning out through the skin like the ribs of an umbrella. Those ribs are the bat's own finger bones, stretched out enormously. How many of its finger bones does the wing skin spread between?
answer: Four finger bones
choices: Four finger bones
Three finger bones
Five finger bones
The whole hand's worth of eight
context: A bat's wing is a webbed hand: skin (the patagium) stretched between four hugely elongated finger bones, spread through the wing like umbrella spokes — the recognition mark that tells a bat wing from a pterosaur's one finger or a bird's feathered arm. Source: UCMP Berkeley 'The Three Solutions to Flight'; Wikipedia 'Bat'.

question: A housefly beats its wings about 200 times a second, and a mosquito faster still, quicker than any nerve can fire one signal per stroke. So the fly's brain cannot drive each wingbeat with its own nerve pulse, the way a person's brain moves a hand. Something else keeps the blur of its wings going. What powers each rapid wingbeat?
answer: Two muscle sheets stretch and re-fire each other, ringing the thorax like a bell
choices: Two muscle sheets stretch and re-fire each other, ringing the thorax like a bell
A single giant muscle contracts once and coasts through many strokes on momentum
One nerve fires a rapid burst that paces every downstroke in perfect lockstep
Air trapped in the chest recoils elastically to snap the wings up and down
context: These are asynchronous flight muscles. Instead of one nerve impulse per wingbeat, two antagonistic muscle sheets in the thorax pull against each other, and each one, when stretched, fires back after a tiny delay ('delayed stretch activation'), so the elastic thorax resonates like a rung bell in a self-sustaining oscillation. A single nerve pulse can drive dozens of beats -- frequencies no nerve could command one-for-one, since direct 'synchronous' muscle tops out near 100 Hz. Roughly three-quarters of flying insect species use this trick: flies, bees and wasps, and beetles are asynchronous, while dragonflies, butterflies and moths (~25 Hz), and locusts stay synchronous with one impulse per beat. Source: Nature 2023 'Bridging two insect flight modes' (PMC10599994); Science.org 'Molecular Trigger for High-Speed Wing Beats in a Bee'; JEB flight-muscle reviews.

question: A small green-and-black tree snake, Chrysopelea, travels from treetop to treetop in the rainforest canopy of Southeast Asia without climbing down one trunk and up the next. It crosses open air with no wings, no flaps and no limbs. How does it cross the gap?
answer: It flattens its whole body into a ribbon and glides
choices: It flattens its whole body into a ribbon and glides
It leaps and grabs the far branch with its tail
It spins a silk line and swings across
It inflates a pouch of air like a balloon
context: The flying snake has no flaps or appendages at all. It turns its own body into a wing: it flattens itself flat as a ribbon and glides tree to tree, moving through the air like a water snake crossing a pond. Source: National Wildlife Federation, 'Borneo's Wild Gliders,' via a-z-animals + NWF.

question: Biologists at Virginia Tech trained high-speed cameras on a flying snake, Chrysopelea, and filmed it launching itself from a branch into the air 239 times. In 177 of the 239, nearly three in four, it started the exact same way. What did the snake do just before it left the branch?
answer: Hung down and lifted its head into a 'J,' then sprang up and out
choices: Hung down and lifted its head into a 'J,' then sprang up and out
Coiled into a tight spiral and rolled off the edge
Dropped straight down and opened out once falling
Ran its body flat along the branch and slid off the tip
context: The snake hangs from a branch, lifts its head up into a 'J' shape, then springs upward and outward like releasing a coiled spring. This anchored J-loop takeoff was used in 74% of trials, 177 of 239. Source: Socha, 'Becoming airborne without legs,' Journal of Experimental Biology 209:3358 (2006).

question: A paradise tree snake, one of the flying snakes of Southeast Asia's rainforests, looks like an ordinary rope lying along a branch, round in cross-section. The instant it leaps from a high treetop and goes airborne, it changes that shape so its body can catch the air and make lift. What does it turn its cross-section into?
answer: A flattened, semicircular shape, slightly hollow underneath
choices: A flattened, semicircular shape, slightly hollow underneath
A hollow tube it pushes air through like a straw
A twisted spiral that screws forward through the air
A row of stiff spines that fan out sideways
context: In the air the snake sucks in its belly and splays its ribs, morphing its round cross-section into a flattened, semicircular shape that is slightly concave below. This 'morphing wing' catches air and makes lift as the snake falls. Source: Socha et al., J. Exp. Biol. 217:382 (2014); NWF 'Borneo's Wild Gliders.'

question: A flying snake launches from a high branch in a Southeast Asian rainforest and sails toward another tree. A gliding animal might be expected to hold itself rigid and still, but this snake bends into a wide S and keeps sweeping from side to side, like a swimmer, the whole way down. Why does it never stop moving in the air?
answer: The constant motion keeps it from tumbling and spinning out
choices: The constant motion keeps it from tumbling and spinning out
The swimming motion pushes it forward like paddling
It's searching the treetops for prey as it falls
It's shaking loose water to keep its skin dry
context: The snake keeps making side-to-side waves not to swim but for stability: high-speed study found this aerial undulation enhances rotational stability, preventing the body from tumbling during glides. Researchers even found two waves at once, a big horizontal one and a smaller vertical one rippling at twice the rate. Source: Virginia Tech / Socha 2020 study, bme.vt.edu.

question: A fish swims with eyes whose clear front dome, the cornea, does almost no focusing at all. On land the cornea does most of an eye's focusing, bending light hard as it crosses from air into the eye. Why does water switch the fish's cornea off?
answer: Water bends light almost as much as the cornea does, leaving it little to do
choices: Water bends light almost as much as the cornea does, leaving it little to do
Water pressure flattens the cornea so it can no longer curve light
Salt in seawater clouds the cornea and scatters the light
Cold water freezes the cornea fluid solid
context: A cornea works by bending light as it crosses from thin air into denser eye tissue. Underwater there is no jump: water (refractive index ~1.33) is so close to the cornea and the eye's own fluid that light barely bends passing through. So the cornea, which does most of the focusing on land, is nearly useless underwater, and the lens must do essentially all the work. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vision in fish' / 'Accommodation (vertebrate eye)'.

question: Underwater, a fish must bend incoming light with its lens alone, and bend it far more strongly than any land animal's lens has to. To do that, the fish's lens takes a shape never found in a land animal's eye. What does a fish's lens look like?
answer: A hard, near-perfect glass-clear ball
choices: A hard, near-perfect glass-clear ball
A thin flat disc, like a contact lens
A soft teardrop that flattens when squeezed
A curved crescent, like a sliver of moon
context: A fish eye lens is not the soft, flattened disc land animals carry. It is a hard, near-perfect sphere that bulges out through the pupil. A round ball of a lens is exactly what a fish needs to bend light strongly enough to focus it underwater, where the cornea gives no help. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vision in fish'; Land & Nilsson, 'Animal Eyes' (2012).

question: Shifting its gaze from a distant shape to a shrimp right in front of its nose, a fish must bring the shrimp into focus. A person would squeeze the soft lens in the eye fatter to focus up close, but a fish's lens is rigid and cannot change shape. How does the fish do it?
answer: It slides the whole lens back and forth, like a slide-projector lens
choices: It slides the whole lens back and forth, like a slide-projector lens
It swells the whole eyeball to make it longer front to back
It swivels the lens to a fresh angle inside the eye
It stacks a second lens in front of the first
context: Because its lens is a rigid ball it cannot reshape, a fish focuses by physically moving the whole lens back and forth, the way a projectionist slides a projector's lens to sharpen the picture, rather than squeezing the lens to change its shape as humans do. Source: Wikipedia, 'Accommodation (vertebrate eye)' / 'Vision in fish'.

question: A tiny muscle anchored to the iris focuses a fish's eye by pulling on its rigid lens. With that muscle relaxed, the fish's eye is already set to see things up close. To bring a far-off shape into sharp focus, which way must the muscle drag the lens?
answer: Backward, toward the retina at the rear of the eye
choices: Backward, toward the retina at the rear of the eye
Forward, toward the pupil at the front of the eye
Sideways, closer to the outer edge of the eye
Downward, toward the floor of the eye socket
context: The muscle that does the pulling is the retractor lentis, a smooth muscle anchored to the iris that grips the lens around its equator. It hauls the lens backward toward the retina to focus on far-away things; when it relaxes, the lens drifts forward and the eye is set for near objects. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vision in fish'; Grokipedia, 'Vision in fish'.

question: An octopus looks out on the world through a full picture-forming eye. Its clear round lens focuses much the way a fish's does, and the whole eye is almost a copy of a fish's, though an octopus is no fish and has no backbone at all. How did it end up with what looks like a fish's eye?
answer: The two lineages each invented the same camera eye entirely on their own
choices: The two lineages each invented the same camera eye entirely on their own
The octopus inherited its eye from the same ancestor the fishes did
The octopus borrowed fish genes by living alongside them
Fish and octopuses are far more closely related than they look
context: This is a textbook case of convergent evolution: two unrelated animals arriving at the same solution independently. The octopus's family tree split from the fishes more than 500 million years ago, back when each line had only crude patches of light-sensing skin and no eyes at all. It did NOT inherit its eye from a shared eyed ancestor; each line built the same spherical-lens, sliding-focus camera eye on its own. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cephalopod eye'; PMC, 'Comparative Analysis of Gene Expression for Convergent Evolution of Camera Eye'.

question: A fish's ball-shaped lens throws a razor-sharp image onto its retina, though a plain glass ball of the same shape makes a blurry mess: rays skimming the edge bend to a different point than rays through the middle. What lets the fish's lens do what the glass ball cannot?
answer: Its center is far denser than its rim, so every ray bends to a single point
choices: Its center is far denser than its rim, so every ray bends to a single point
Its surface carries a thin oily film that straightens the stray rays
Its back surface is flattened to catch the rays that skim the edge
A ring in the iris masks off the edge rays before they enter
context: The blur is called spherical aberration. The fish beats it with a graded lens: its refractive index climbs from about 1.33 at the outer surface (matching the watery fluid around it) to roughly 1.55-1.65 at the dense core. That inside-out gradient bends edge rays and center rays to the very same point, so a simple ball of a lens forms a sharp picture. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vision in fish' (gradient refractive index); Land, 'The evolution of lenses' (2012).

question: Ludwig Matthiessen studied fish eyes in the 1880s, from goldfish to tuna and sharks, expecting each species to have its own design. Instead the same tidy number turned up in every one, now called Matthiessen's ratio. By measuring only the size of a fish's lens, what can a biologist predict about its eye?
answer: How far behind the lens its retina must sit
choices: How far behind the lens its retina must sit
How sharp the fish's vision is at a glance
Which color of light the fish sees best
How wide the fish could open its pupil
context: This is Matthiessen's ratio: the distance from lens center to retina is about 2.5 times the lens radius (measured near 2.55 across most fish). Multiplying a lens's radius by that constant shows where the retina must lie, no dissection needed. It is named for Ludwig Matthiessen, the 19th-century German physiologist who also first showed the fish lens had a refractive-index gradient shaped like an inverted parabola. Source: Wikipedia, 'Matthiessen's ratio'.

question: Deep in the ocean, a barreleye called Rhynchohyalus grows a side pocket off each of its tube-shaped eyes, and the pocket casts a bright, sharp picture of the dark water below onto a second retina. Nearly every other eye focuses with a lens. What does the focusing in that pocket?
answer: A curved mirror of crystal, reflecting the image instead of bending it
choices: A curved mirror of crystal, reflecting the image instead of bending it
A lens of silvery crystal plates, bending the dim light to a focus
A ring of light-bending oil droplets massed at the pocket's mouth
A cluster of pinholes casting the image the way a pinhole camera does
context: Partridge and colleagues confirmed by ray-tracing that the barreleye's side pocket focuses light with a curved reflector of stacked guanine crystals, making Rhynchohyalus only the second backboned animal known to form images with a mirror rather than a lens; a relative, the brownsnout spookfish Dolichopteryx, was the first. Where nearly every other eye uses a lens to recover the focusing power water steals from the cornea, this fish built a working eye around a mirror. Source: Partridge et al., 'Reflecting optics in the diverticular eye of a deep-sea barreleye fish (Rhynchohyalus natalensis),' Proc R Soc B (2014).

question: A sleek, reddish-brown hunter with a long tail and a cat-like face leaps between branches high in a Madagascar rainforest, chasing lemurs. The island has no big cats at all, and this animal sits at the top of its food chain. Which animal is it?
answer: The fossa
choices: The fossa
The dingo
The jackal
The ocelot
context: The fossa (Cryptoprocta ferox) is Madagascar's largest carnivore and the island's apex predator. A 2016 assessment estimated roughly 2,600 to 8,600 adults in the wild, and it can roam up to 16 miles (26 km) in a day. Source: Grokipedia 'Fossa (animal)'; San Diego Zoo (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/fossa); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossa_(animal).

question: A lemur fleeing through the trees usually gains time whenever a predator chasing it loses ground coming down a trunk. A fossa on its trail gives it no such break. What can the fossa's body do that a house cat's cannot?
answer: Run straight down the trunk head-first
choices: Run straight down the trunk head-first
Match the lemur's leaps branch for branch
Grip with claws that never retract
Sprint on the ground faster than any lemur
context: The fossa has hyper-flexible ankles that rotate almost 180 degrees, letting it grip a trunk from any angle and sprint straight DOWN it head-first while most predators can only back down tail-first. A tail nearly as long as its body acts as a counterbalance for tree-to-tree leaps. Source: San Diego Zoo (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/fossa); discvr.blog/the-fossas-feline-disguise-hides-a-mongoose-lineage/.

question: A slender, cougar-shaped fossa hunts lemurs high in the trees of Madagascar, climbing like a cat and looking like a small mountain lion, yet it is not a cat at all. Its family traces back to one meat-eating ancestor that reached the island about 21 million years ago. Beyond Madagascar, which living animals are its family's closest relatives?
answer: Mongooses
choices: Mongooses
Genets
Weasels
Raccoons
context: The fossa belongs to the family Eupleridae, Madagascar's own family of carnivores, and the closest living relatives of that family are the mongooses. Its cat-like build is convergent evolution — it independently evolved a big-cat body to fill the niche of an agile tree-hunter. The whole family of Malagasy carnivores descended from one mongoose-like ancestor that reached Madagascar about 21 million years ago. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossa_(animal); San Diego Zoo (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/fossa).

question: Hundreds of metres down in the Atlantic and Pacific, a thin-bodied shark nearly two metres long cruises the dark. Frilly gill folds give it the name frilled shark, and it is also nicknamed the lizard shark. Which creature does its body most call to mind?
answer: A snake or eel
choices: A snake or eel
A stingray
A pufferfish
A sea turtle
context: The frilled shark looks less like a shark than a giant snake or eel, with a slender body and its mouth at the very front of its head — a look that earned it the nickname 'lizard shark.' Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/marine-animals/frilled-shark

question: Ruffled red gill slits line the neck of a frilled shark, the front pair circling its throat in a collar, and they give the shark its name. Most sharks have five pairs, but this one breaks the rule. How many pairs of gill slits does it carry?
answer: Six pairs
choices: Six pairs
Four pairs
Nine pairs
Twelve pairs
context: The frilled shark is named for its six pairs of frilly red gill slits — most sharks have only five — and the first pair wraps around the throat like a collar, a mark of its ancient body plan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frilled_shark

question: In the dark, a frilled shark grabs a squid with a mouth holding about 300 tiny teeth, set in some 25 rows, each shaped like a three-pronged trident. The squid is muscular and thrashes to twist free, yet it almost never escapes. What is it about these teeth that traps it?
answer: Each point curves backward, so struggling only drives the squid deeper
choices: Each point curves backward, so struggling only drives the squid deeper
A venom seeps from the teeth and stuns the squid limp
The teeth grind the squid to paste against a bony plate
The teeth glow, freezing the squid still in the dark
context: The frilled shark's ~300 needle-sharp teeth are each shaped like a tiny trident with three backward-curving points, in about 25 rows. Together they work like a net that snags slippery squid and lets nothing slide back out. Squid make up about 60% of its diet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frilled_shark

question: A frilled shark's long jaws sit right at the front of its head and hinge onto the skull behind the eyes, so its bite is weak. It cannot roll under its prey as other sharks do. Instead it anchors its tail, coils its body back and springs forward. How big a meal can it take this way?
answer: Prey more than half its own size, swallowed whole
choices: Prey more than half its own size, swallowed whole
Only prey smaller than its own eye
A dozen tiny shrimp at a single gulp
Only soft jellies, slurped without a bite
context: With its mouth at the front of its head, the frilled shark strikes like a snake — bending its body, bracing its tail, and lunging to swallow whole prey more than half its own size. One 1.6-meter specimen was found with a whole 590-gram Japanese catshark inside it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frilled_shark

question: Deep in the cold, food-poor sea, a frilled shark mother carries her pups alive inside her, each embryo adding about 10 to 17 mm of length a month. From that slow growth, scientists have estimated how long she stays pregnant, a figure still debated. Roughly how long?
answer: About 3.5 years
choices: About 3.5 years
About 2 months
About 11 months
About 7 years
context: Because its embryos grow only ~10–17 mm per month in the cold deep sea, the frilled shark may have one of the longest pregnancies of any vertebrate — an estimated 3.5 years. The figure is an estimate and disputed; some studies suggest it could be as short as 1–2 years. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7497067/

question: Lopez-Romero and colleagues followed the frilled shark's mouth as it formed in embryos in 2020, to test the old story that its front-set mouth is a relic of some ancient body plan. The jaws started out tucked underneath, as in ordinary sharks, and crept forward to the front only late in development. What did the authors conclude?
answer: The terminal mouth is a derived specialization, not an ancient ancestral trait
choices: The terminal mouth is a derived specialization, not an ancient ancestral trait
The terminal mouth confirms the original chondrichthyan jaw was front-set
The terminal mouth is convergent with the jaws of modern deep-sea eels
The terminal mouth's late shift is an artifact of slow deep-sea growth
context: A landmark embryo-staging study (Lopez-Romero, Klimpfinger, Tanaka & Kriwet, 2020) found the frilled shark's signature front-of-the-head (terminal, or antero-terminal) mouth is not a retained primitive trait. In the embryos the jaws begin in a subterminal position, as is typical for most sharks, and only reach the terminal position late in development through anterior elongation of the jaws (across late stages 31-36). The authors concluded the terminal mouth 'has to be considered a derived feature' — a genuine reappraisal of how 'unchanged' this shark really is. Source: Lopez-Romero, Klimpfinger, Tanaka & Kriwet (2020), 'Growth trajectories of prenatal embryos of the deep-sea shark Chlamydoselachus anguineus,' Journal of Fish Biology, PMC7497067: 'the jaws start to develop in a subterminal position as is typical for most sharks, but reach a terminal position late in development through anterior elongation of the jaws... the antero-terminal mouth opening of the frilled shark has to be considered a derived feature.'

question: A frogfish, a lumpy ambush hunter of the reef, sits on the seabed while other fish glide past through open water, rippling their bodies and beating their tails. The frogfish hardly swims at all. How does it get around the reef floor?
answer: Walking on its arm-like fins, one after another
choices: Walking on its arm-like fins, one after another
Rolling sideways along the sand like a barrel
Drifting wherever the tide happens to carry it
Burrowing under the sand and popping up ahead
context: The frogfish moves its stubby, limb-like fins one after the other, taking 'steps' much like a two-legged animal. Instead of swimming, it strolls across the seabed. (Source: Natural History Museum, 'Frogfish: The fish that walk'; frogfish.ch locomotion page)

question: A fist-sized frogfish sits pressed against a coral reef, painted in the reef's own colors. It never chases anything, yet small fish keep swimming right up to its huge mouth. What trick draws them into striking range?
answer: It waves a built-in fishing rod tipped with a wriggling, worm-like lure
choices: It waves a built-in fishing rod tipped with a wriggling, worm-like lure
It flashes bright colors along its side to hypnotize passing fish
It releases a cloud of sweet-smelling slime that attracts hungry fish
It mimics the call of a mother fish to lure in the young
context: The frogfish's first dorsal spine (the illicium) is tipped with a fleshy lure (the esca) shaped like a worm, shrimp, or tiny fish. It wiggles this bait to draw curious prey within striking range, like a mini anglerfish. (Source: frogfish.ch behavior page; Longlure frogfish, Wikipedia)

question: Squatting disguised on the coral reef floor, a frogfish fishes for prey with the fleshy bait it grows on its own head. Sometimes a prey fish is too quick and bites the bait clean off. Left without its lure, what happens to the frogfish over the months that follow?
answer: It slowly grows a brand-new lure in its place
choices: It slowly grows a brand-new lure in its place
It stays lure-less for the rest of its life
It switches to chasing prey in open water
It moves to deeper water to hunt in the dark
context: If the lure gets bitten off or damaged, the frogfish grows a replacement over roughly four to six months. (Source: frogfish.ch feeding page)

question: Suppose you blinked just as a frogfish struck at a passing fish. Your blink would last about three hundred milliseconds. The frogfish's mouth flies open and sucks in its prey in one of the fastest feeding strikes ever measured in a fish. How long does that strike take?
answer: About six milliseconds — fifty times quicker than a blink
choices: About six milliseconds — fifty times quicker than a blink
About ninety milliseconds — a third of a blink
About the same as a blink, three hundred milliseconds
About half a second, slower than a blink
context: The frogfish's 'gape and suck' strike engulfs prey in about six milliseconds — six-thousandths of a second, roughly fifty times quicker than a human blink. It ranks among the fastest feeding strikes known in any animal. (Source: frogfish.ch feeding page, Pietsch & Grobecker; Grokipedia, Frogfish)

question: A small fish drifts within reach of a frogfish. In a fraction of a second the floor of the frogfish's mouth drops and the whole cavity swells outward, and the sudden empty space sucks in the prey along with a torrent of water. To make suction that violent, how far must the cavity swell from its resting size?
answer: It balloons to about twelve times its resting size
choices: It balloons to about twelve times its resting size
It swells to a little under double its resting size
It puffs up by roughly a third, then snaps shut
It swells to about five times its resting size
context: The mouth cavity balloons to up to 12 times its resting volume, creating a powerful suction that pulls the prey in with a rush of water. (Source: frogfish.ch feeding page; Wikipedia, Frogfish)

question: Perfectly still on the reef, a frogfish waits for prey to swim right up to its mouth. None of its teeth can cut, so every meal goes down whole in a single gulp. That whole swallow lets it pull off a feat most predators cannot. What can a frogfish do when it catches a large victim?
answer: Swallow a fish as big as itself, or even bigger
choices: Swallow a fish as big as itself, or even bigger
Crush the prey against a rock before swallowing it
Spit out anything too large and wait for smaller prey
Store the extra food in a special pouch for later
context: The frogfish's small teeth cannot cut, so it swallows prey whole, and its stomach stretches enough to engulf a fish as large as or larger than the frogfish itself; Grokipedia puts the limit at prey up to about twice its size. (Source: frogfish.ch feeding page; Wikipedia, Frogfish; Grokipedia, Frogfish)

question: Divers off Indonesia found a frogfish in 2008 so strange that scientists named it a new species the next year: the psychedelic frogfish, swirled in wild colors. It walks on its fins like its relatives, but it has another way of getting around too. How does it move?
answer: It bounces along the bottom like an inflated rubber ball
choices: It bounces along the bottom like an inflated rubber ball
It hovers upright in the water column like a seahorse
It swims in fast tight circles near the surface
It clings to passing fish and hitches a ride
context: Described in 2009, the psychedelic frogfish walks on its fins but can also push off and jet water from its gills, bouncing along the bottom like an inflated rubber ball with its tail curled to one side; jetting like this is common among frogfishes, though rare in other fish. (Source: ScienceDaily 2009; Psychedelic frogfish, Wikipedia; Pietsch, Arnold & Hall, Copeia 2009)

question: A tawny frogmouth, a stocky, mottled night bird the size of a small owl, hides in plain sight in an Australian forest by day. It lies lengthwise along a limb, stiffens, points its short beak straight up and squeezes its eyes to thin slits. What does the frozen bird look like?
answer: A broken-off branch stub
choices: A broken-off branch stub
A clump of hanging moss
A curled brown snake
A knot of dry leaves
context: The tawny frogmouth's silvery-grey, black-and-brown streaked plumage matches tree bark, and holding perfectly still while pointing its beak skyward completes the illusion of a snapped-off branch stub. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawny_frogmouth

question: People constantly mistake the tawny frogmouth for an owl: it hunts at night in soft, streaky plumage much like an owl's, and its round eyes complete the look. Its true family lies elsewhere. Which group of birds does it belong with?
answer: Nightjars and their relatives
choices: Nightjars and their relatives
Kookaburras and other kingfishers
Hawks and falcons
Herons and bitterns
context: Despite the resemblance, the tawny frogmouth belongs with the nightjars, oilbirds and potoos, not with owls. The nighttime habits and coloring are a case of look-alike lifestyles, not a family bond. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawny_frogmouth

question: After dark in an Australian forest, a tawny frogmouth hunts insects and small prey. An owl seizes its prey with powerful gripping talons, but the frogmouth's weak little feet could never do that job, so its bill must do all the catching. What shape of bill does it use to snap up a big insect or a spider?
answer: A wide, forward-facing scooping gape
choices: A wide, forward-facing scooping gape
A narrow, hooked tearing bill
A long, spear-like stabbing bill
A slim, tweezer-fine probing bill
context: Instead of an owl's narrow tearing bill and gripping talons, the frogmouth has a huge, cavernous, forward-facing gape that it snaps shut on prey it pounces onto from a perch. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawny_frogmouth

question: By day a tawny frogmouth freezes stiff along a tree limb, its beak pointed at the sky, hiding in plain sight. Now the trick has failed: a hawk has spotted the bird, and the frogmouth is cornered with nowhere to go. It drops the still act and does the exact opposite. What is its last-ditch move?
answer: It throws its mouth wide open, hisses, and puffs up big
choices: It throws its mouth wide open, hisses, and puffs up big
It flattens down and plays completely dead
It sprays a foul musk from its tail
It flashes bright warning colors under its wings
context: Cornered, the frogmouth gapes to flash a big yellow-green cavernous mouth, hisses loudly, and puffs its feathers to look as large and threatening as possible — a bluff to startle the attacker. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/animals/tawny-frogmouth/
