question: A Gaboon viper lies on the leaf-littered floor of a central African rainforest. Its fangs are the longest of any snake, about 5 centimeters (2 inches), and if they stood upright they would pierce its own lower jaw. How does it pack them away between strikes?
answer: The fangs are hinged, folding flat against the roof of the mouth
choices: The fangs are hinged, folding flat against the roof of the mouth
The fangs retract into hollow sockets deep in the throat
The fangs shrink and regrow between meals
The lower jaw unhinges sideways to clear them
context: The Gaboon viper grows the longest fangs of any snake on Earth — up to about 5 cm (2 inches), the length of two U.S. quarters laid end to end. Being hinged, they fold back flat so the snake can close its jaws, then swing forward to strike. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaboon_viper; Smithsonian National Zoo (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/gaboon-viper).

question: Lying fully exposed on the African rainforest floor, a huge, heavy Gaboon viper can still be almost impossible to spot. Its broad, flat, triangular head is the key to the trick, and predators and prey walk past it every day without noticing. What does the head look like?
answer: A fallen leaf, right down to a central vein
choices: A fallen leaf, right down to a central vein
A knot of bare tree roots in the soil
A gray river stone slick with mud
A cluster of pale mushrooms on rotting wood
context: The head mimics a dead leaf right down to a central vein-like line, and the body wears pale rectangles, dark hourglass markings, and fawn diamonds — so precise that a snake lying fully exposed in the leaf litter nearly vanishes. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/gaboon-viper); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaboon_viper.

question: An inland taipan carries the most toxic venom of any snake, drop for drop, yet one bite delivers only about 44 to 110 mg of it. Scientists have also milked the Gaboon viper, a thick, heavy snake of central Africa. How did its record milking compare with a single taipan bite?
answer: As much as dozens of taipan bites
choices: As much as dozens of taipan bites
As much as hundreds of taipan bites
About as much as one taipan bite
Less than half of one taipan bite
context: One milking has yielded up to about 2,400 mg (2 grams) of dried venom, and a single bite can inject roughly 200 to 1,000 mg — among the largest venom loads of any snake, far outstripping the inland taipan (about 44 to 110 mg) or Russell's viper. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaboon_viper; Smithsonian National Zoo; Forbes/Scott Travers 2024-09-07.

question: Buried under the leaves of an African rainforest, a Gaboon viper has lain still as stone for hours when at last a rat steps over it and the viper strikes. In the seconds after its fangs go in, it does the very thing that sets it apart from most other vipers. What happens next?
answer: It clamps down and holds the rat fast until the venom finishes it
choices: It clamps down and holds the rat fast until the venom finishes it
It releases at once and tracks the fleeing rat by scent
It coils around the rat and constricts to speed the kill
It swallows the rat whole while it is still struggling
context: Unusually for a viper, the Gaboon does not strike-and-release: it holds the prey in its fangs until the venom does its work. It is a sit-and-wait ambush hunter, lying motionless for hours in the leaf litter and striking only when a rat, hare, or bird walks right over it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaboon_viper; Smithsonian National Zoo.

question: Thousands of feet down in the pitch-black sea near Antarctica drifts the colossal squid, an enormous many-armed hunter. Today only the giant squid's eye comes close to its own, which dwarfs any whale's or fish's. About how big is a colossal squid's eye?
answer: The size of a basketball
choices: The size of a basketball
The size of a golf ball
The size of a human fist
The size of a pinhead
context: A colossal squid eye measures around 27 cm (about 11 inches) across, as big as a basketball, among the largest eyes ever documented. Among living animals only its cousin the giant squid, whose eye reaches at least 27 cm, rivals it, and the extinct ichthyosaur Temnodontosaurus had eyes at least 25 cm across. Source: Britannica, 'colossal squid'; Wikipedia, 'Colossal squid', 'Giant squid' and 'Temnodontosaurus'.

question: Stretched out on a dock, a female giant squid measures about 13 metres (43 ft) from the tip of her tail fin to the tip of her longest tentacle, longer than a school bus. That headline length is a bit of a cheat. Where does most of it come from?
answer: Two long feeding tentacles, around 10 metres by themselves
choices: Two long feeding tentacles, around 10 metres by themselves
A single, immensely long tail spike
A body cavity that inflates with seawater
Rows of stacked, telescoping body segments
context: The giant squid's actual body, the mantle, is only about 2 metres long; most of the rest of its length is its two enormous feeding tentacles, which can reach roughly 10 metres on their own. Source: Britannica, 'giant squid'; Grokipedia, 'Giant squid' (mantle up to 2.25 m, tentacles up to 10 m).

question: Hunting in the deep with eight arms and two long tentacle clubs, a colossal squid carries a weapon that no other member of its squid family has. It lets the squid keep its grip on slippery deep-sea fish that would otherwise slide free. What is the weapon?
answer: Rows of sharp hooks, mixed among its suckers
choices: Rows of sharp hooks, mixed among its suckers
A ring of venom-tipped spines around the beak
Electrically charged suckers that stun on contact
Sticky glue glands that fire threads at prey
context: Its two feeding tentacles end in clubs studded with rotating hooks, and its arms mix swiveling hooks with suckers — hooks that can turn a full 360 degrees. It is the only member of its squid family with arm hooks, and the frozen specimen's hooks really were a hazard for the researchers handling it. Source: https://collections.tepapa.govt.nz/topic/588

question: A sperm whale comes up from a hunting dive more than a mile down in the dark, its head and flanks marked with pale, round scars. The oldest whales carry so many that they look like scarred old veterans. What made the scars?
answer: The sucker rings of giant squid gripping the whale
choices: The sucker rings of giant squid gripping the whale
Barnacles that bore into aging whale skin
Welts from swarms of stinging jellyfish
Scrapes from squeezing through Antarctic sea ice
context: Sperm whales dive to hunt these squid, and the squid's suckers leave round scars on the whale's skin. The suckers themselves are only about 2 to 5 cm across, though a scar can stretch as the whale grows, so old reports of plate-sized marks do not mean plate-sized suckers. The oldest bulls carry so many overlapping rings they look weathered by combat. Source: Wikipedia, 'Giant squid' (suckers 2 to 5 cm); Smithsonian Ocean, 'Giant Squid Sucker Marks.'

question: The crew of the San Aspiring, a New Zealand toothfish boat, was hauling a longline up from 1,500 metres down in the icy Ross Sea, off Antarctica, in February 2007 when they landed a 495 kg colossal squid, the heaviest ever measured. Yet the squid itself had never taken a hook. What let the crew bring the whole animal up to the surface?
answer: It had seized a hooked toothfish and would not let go
choices: It had seized a hooked toothfish and would not let go
It had wedged itself beneath the boat's steel hull
It had snarled its own tentacles in the winch cable
It had frozen stiff in the chilly near-surface water
context: The immature female weighed 495 kg (about 1,091 lb) — the heaviest colossal squid ever recorded. It had grabbed a toothfish on the longline about 1,500 metres down and refused to release it as the crew raised the gear. It is now on display at Te Papa museum in Wellington, New Zealand. Source: https://tepapa.govt.nz/discover-collections/read-watch-play/colossal-squid/colossal-squid-te-papa

question: A colossal squid stares into the black deep through one of the largest eyes ever measured, its lens alone as big as an orange. For spotting prey close by, an eye that big would seem like overkill. Dan-Eric Nilsson and Eric Warrant argued in 2012 that the eye is built to catch one faint signal in the dark. What is it?
answer: The glow of plankton stirred up by an approaching sperm whale
choices: The glow of plankton stirred up by an approaching sperm whale
The blue-green flashes of the bioluminescent prey it hunts
The lantern lures of anglerfish hanging in the dark below it
The glow of a passing shoal of lanternfish drifting overhead
context: When a sperm whale swims, it disturbs tiny bioluminescent plankton that glow in its wake. Nilsson's team (Current Biology, 2012) showed the squid's enormous eyes are built to detect that faint glow — spotting an oncoming whale from about 120 metres, a football-field away, in time to flee. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/120315-giant-squid-eyes-basketball-whales-nilsson-science

question: A giant squid has no bones and no gas-filled swim bladder like a fish, yet it hangs motionless in the deep instead of sinking. Something dissolved throughout its flesh and body fluid, lighter than seawater, keeps it neutrally buoyant. What is loaded into its tissues?
answer: Ammonium ions, so its own flesh floats like a raft
choices: Ammonium ions, so its own flesh floats like a raft
Pockets of oily wax that store lift like a float
Tiny gas bubbles trapped between the muscle bands
Chambers of fresh water sealed off from the sea
context: Giant and colossal squid replace the fish's swim bladder with an ammonium chloride solution soaked through their tissues and body fluid; it is less dense than seawater and gives near-neutral buoyancy so the animal drifts without effort. The trade-off is on the plate: that ammonium-rich flesh is bitter and faintly reeks of ammonia, which is why giant-squid meat is not eaten. The same chemistry that lets it hover is what makes it taste foul. Source: Cambridge Core, 'On the use of ammonium for buoyancy in squids,' J. Marine Biological Assoc. UK (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-marine-biological-association-of-the-united-kingdom/article/on-the-use-of-ammonium-for-buoyancy-in-squids/ABF61ADBB1FFC507CFDBB3DFD35F6F1E).

question: When a small coastal squid such as Loligo flees a hungry fish, it fires its whole mantle in one convulsive jet, so the escape signal must reach the muscles almost instantly. The nerve that carries it is so enlarged that the physiologists Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley threaded electrodes right inside one. How is that nerve pathway built?
answer: One giant unmyelinated axon up to a millimetre thick
choices: One giant unmyelinated axon up to a millimetre thick
A dense braid of thousands of thin insulated fibers
A hollow tube pumped full of charged seawater
A ring of short relay cells firing one to the next
context: In small squid such as Loligo, the giant axon runs up to about 1 mm across, hundreds of times thicker than a typical human nerve fiber. It has no myelin sheath, so the sheer width is what speeds the impulse: a fatter fiber means less internal resistance and a faster signal to the escape-jet muscles. That size was also a gift to science: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley could push electrodes inside a living nerve, and their 1952 model of how nerves fire won the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Source: Wikipedia 'Squid giant axon' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squid_giant_axon); Hodgkin-Huxley history, MBL archives (https://history.archives.mbl.edu).

question: Megatherium, a giant ground sloth, walked the plains of South America on all fours during the last ice age, a long-vanished relative of the little cat-sized sloths dangling upside down in the rainforest today. Set beside a living animal, how big was it?
answer: As big as a bull elephant
choices: As big as a bull elephant
As big as a brown bear
As big as a buffalo
As big as a rhino
context: Megatherium stretched about 6 metres (20 ft) long and weighed roughly 3,700-4,000 kg -- comparable to an Asian elephant -- yet it was a relative of today's tiny tree sloths. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megatherium

question: To feed on leaves high in the trees, far above the reach of an animal on four legs, Megatherium, the giant ground sloth, braced against a trunk and lifted its huge frame off the ground, turning its body into a tower. What did it stand on to reach the branches?
answer: Its hind legs and tail, like a tripod
choices: Its hind legs and tail, like a tripod
Its front legs, nose to the branch
A fallen log it dragged over
The lower limbs it climbed onto
context: Reared up, Megatherium towered about 3.5 metres (12 ft) and braced against the trunk with its tail as a third support, pulling down high branches with its forelimbs. Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-was-megatherium.html

question: On front claws that curved out about 30 cm, a full foot long, the giant ground sloth Megatherium lumbered across South America as recently as about 12,000 years ago. Claws that long kept it from setting its front feet flat on the ground. Like a modern anteater, how did it walk on them?
answer: It walked on the outer sides of its feet, claws curled in
choices: It walked on the outer sides of its feet, claws curled in
It walked on the tips of its claws, like stilts
It dragged itself forward on its belly
It hopped on its broad hind feet
context: With claws that long, Megatherium couldn't put its feet flat -- like a modern anteater, it walked on the outer edges of its feet and curled the claws inward as it moved. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megatherium

question: A full-grown Megatherium, the giant ground sloth, browsed leaves across the plains of ice-age South America. Sabre-toothed cats, the top predators of its world, probably rarely dared to attack an adult. What would have made this giant so risky to attack?
answer: A swipe of its foot-long claws could kill an attacker outright
choices: A swipe of its foot-long claws could kill an attacker outright
Its herd trampled anything that came too close
It could outrun a sabre-tooth over open ground
Its bellow could stun a predator at close range
context: Those foot-long curved claws probably doubled as the giant sloth's main weapon: a single swipe could likely have killed a smaller predator, so even the sabre-toothed Smilodon would have thought twice before attacking a full-grown adult. Source: animalsaroundtheglobe.com, 'The giant sloth that used its claws like swords'; Wikipedia, 'Megatherium'.

question: Under the shaggy fur of Mylodon, a giant ground sloth of ice-age Patagonia, lay a hard, pebbly layer of little bony bumps studding its skin, still visible in scraps of hide preserved in a Chilean cave. What did that hidden layer do for the sloth?
answer: It armored the skin against a predator's bite
choices: It armored the skin against a predator's bite
It stored calcium for the sloth's diet
It carried a network of scent glands
It held a layer of insulating fat
context: Some giant ground sloths, the mylodontids such as Mylodon, Glossotherium and Paramylodon, carried built-in armor: their skin was studded with thousands of tiny bones (dermal ossicles), from lentil-sized to about 2 cm, forming a chain-mail-like mesh under the fur to defend against predators. Such skin armor is known mainly from this one family of ground sloths. Source: slothconservation.org, 'The hidden armor found in the skin of a giant ground sloth'; Anza-Borrego Desert Paleontology Society, 'Sloth dermal ossicles'; Toledo et al. 2021, Journal of Morphology (mummified Mylodon skin, Cueva del Milodon).

question: On an ancient New Mexico mudflat at White Sands, fossil footprints froze a single tense moment between two animals crossing the same ground. One set belongs to a giant ground sloth. The other set reveals exactly what a person was doing behind it. What do the human tracks show?
answer: A person stepping inside the sloth's own tracks, stalking it
choices: A person stepping inside the sloth's own tracks, stalking it
A person fleeing away from the sloth at a run
A child walking calmly beside the sloth
A person carrying the sloth's young
context: At White Sands, fossil footprints capture a person and a giant ground sloth meeting: a human stepped inside the sloth's own tracks, which the researchers read as stalking it across the ancient mudflat. The trackway is at least 11,700 years old, evidence that giant sloths and people walked the same ground. Source: https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/news/nr100920.htm

question: A two-toed sloth and a three-toed sloth hang upside down from branches across the rainforests of Central and South America. For a hundred years, scientists who sorted sloths by their bones took the two for close cousins. Then ancient DNA and fossil proteins from old bones, read in 2019, tore that family tree apart. What did they reveal about the two living tree sloths?
answer: Each evolved its slow tree-hanging life on its own, from different giant ground-sloth ancestors
choices: Each evolved its slow tree-hanging life on its own, from different giant ground-sloth ancestors
They are twin offshoots of a single tree-dwelling lineage that never touched the ground
They descend directly from Megatherium, shrunk down over the last few thousand years
They are not true sloths at all, but a separate branch of armadillo relatives
context: In 2019, two landmark studies -- ancient DNA (Delsuc's group, Current Biology) and collagen-protein sequencing of 100-plus fossils (Presslee et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution) -- overturned the sloth family tree. The living three-toed sloth turned out to nest deep INSIDE the extinct giant ground sloths, near Megatherium and Nothrotheriops; the two-toed sloth instead groups with Mylodon. So today's two tree sloths aren't close cousins at all -- each descends from different giant ground-dwellers and evolved its slow, hanging life in the trees independently. That's convergent evolution: the same solution reached twice, from separate starting points, contradicting a century of skeleton-based classification. Source: Science.org 'Ancient molecules reveal surprising details on origins of bizarre sloths'; Sci.News 'DNA and Protein Studies Shake Up Sloth Family Tree'; Presslee et al. 2019 Nat Ecol Evol; Delsuc et al. 2019 Curr Biol.

question: Richard Fariña and Ernesto Blanco measured the elbow of Megatherium, the giant ground sloth long pictured as a peaceful leaf-eater, and found it built wrong for that job. The bony lever where the triceps attaches is short, trading pushing force for speed, as in meat-eaters. What role did they propose the giant might have played?
answer: A part-time predator or scavenger, driving its foot-long claws like daggers
choices: A part-time predator or scavenger, driving its foot-long claws like daggers
A tunnel-digger that carved the vast burrows found in South American hillsides
A swimmer that raked shellfish from riverbeds with its hooked forelimbs
A bark-stripper that fed by prying trees apart rather than reaching upward
context: Richard Farina and Ernesto Blanco ('Megatherium, the Stabber') measured the olecranon -- the elbow lever where the triceps attaches -- and found it short, tuned for speed over strength, unusual for a giant plant-eater and typical of carnivores. For an animal this size they calculated an optimal fast-stabbing lever of about 3-5 inches; the fossil's is roughly 4.75 inches, a close match. They proposed Megatherium drove its foot-long claws like daggers, perhaps even flipping armored glyptodonts to reach the soft underside. The idea stays contested: carbon and nitrogen isotopes from the same bones point to a herbivorous diet, so this is a debated interpretation, not the consensus. Source: Farina & Blanco, 'Megatherium, the Stabber' (Proc. R. Soc. B); Discover Magazine 'Killer Sloth'; National Geographic 'Revenge of the Meat-Eating Megatherium'; isotope rebuttal ScienceDirect S1342937X16304944.

question: A scavenger the size of a small dog walks the seafloor a kilometer down, its back armored in plates that overlap like tiles. The giant isopod is a deep-sea cousin of a bug found under garden rocks. Which bug is it?
answer: The roly-poly pillbug
choices: The roly-poly pillbug
The garden earthworm
The cabbage caterpillar
The house centipede
context: The giant isopod (Bathynomus giganteus) is a deep-sea relative of the little garden pillbug, or roly-poly, blown up to enormous size — the largest confirmed specimen was about 50 cm (20 inches) long, roughly the size of a small dog. Source: Wikipedia, Giant isopod (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_isopod).

question: A giant isopod, built like the little armored bugs under garden rocks but grown to a foot long, scavenges dead animals on the pitch-black ocean floor. Caught out on open mud as a hungry predator closes in on its softer underside, what does it do?
answer: Curls up into a tight ball
choices: Curls up into a tight ball
Squirts a cloud of ink
Buries itself in the mud
Sheds a leg and flees
context: Just like its tiny pillbug cousin, the giant isopod can curl up into a ball when threatened, tucking everything inside and exposing only its tough overlapping armored back plates. Source: Wikipedia, Giant isopod (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_isopod).

question: A giant isopod walks the ocean floor a kilometer or more down, where food almost never arrives. Then a dead whale or a big fish sinks out of the dark and thuds into the mud. How does the isopod handle a feast that may have to last it months, or even years?
answer: It gorges until it can barely move
choices: It gorges until it can barely move
It stores scraps in its burrow
It shares the kill with its brood
It nibbles a little and moves on
context: Meals are so rare in the deep that when a dead whale or big fish sinks down, the giant isopod gorges itself so completely that it can barely move afterward, loading up energy that may need to last months or years. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium, Giant isopod; A-Z Animals, Giant Isopod.

question: A giant isopod called No. 1 lived at Japan's Toba Aquarium. It ate a chunk of horse mackerel on January 2, 2009, and stayed plump and healthy until it died in 2014. What did No. 1 do in all that time?
answer: Refused all food for over five years
choices: Refused all food for over five years
Molted its entire shell in one night
Laid a pouch of hundreds of eggs
Doubled in length within a year
context: No. 1 ate its last meal — a 50-gram piece of horse mackerel — on January 2, 2009, then refused all food for 5 years and 43 days until it died in February 2014, still fat. Its slow, cold-water metabolism let it survive in a kind of semi-hibernation. Source: SoraNews24 obituary (soranews24.com, 2014-02-17); Practical Fishkeeping.

question: The giant isopod scours a seafloor so deep it gets only about a millionth of the sunlight that reaches the surface. In that near-total blackness it must still find carrion scattered across the mud. One feature of its head is scaled up to a startling degree. What is it?
answer: Huge compound eyes with nearly 4,000 facets
choices: Huge compound eyes with nearly 4,000 facets
A glowing lure dangling from its head
Heat-sensing pits along its jaw
Feathery gills fanned across its face
context: A giant isopod has huge compound eyes with nearly 4,000 separate facets to catch the faintest glimmers of light in the near-total darkness of the deep sea, where it lives between roughly 170 and 2,100 meters down — getting about one-millionth of the sunlight that reaches the surface. Source: Wikipedia, Giant isopod (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_isopod); Monterey Bay Aquarium, Giant isopod.

question: The giant isopod grows to the size of a small dog, and scientists still argue over why the cold deep breeds such giants. One much-studied explanation ties its huge body to a physical property of that frigid water. Which explanation is it?
answer: Frigid deep water holds far more dissolved oxygen, so a larger body can still take in enough to breathe
choices: Frigid deep water holds far more dissolved oxygen, so a larger body can still take in enough to breathe
Crushing pressure at depth compacts the shell, forcing the whole body to grow outward to compensate
Perpetual darkness removes the visual cues predators need, so prey can safely balloon in size
Slow deep currents let a heavier animal drift with less effort, rewarding ever-greater bulk
context: This is 'deep-sea gigantism,' and the giant isopod is its poster creature, but it is a genuine open debate rather than a settled fact. One much-studied OXYGEN hypothesis comes from a 1999 study of benthic amphipod crustaceans (Chapelle & Peck): the maximum body size an animal can reach rises directly with the dissolved oxygen in the cold deep, because more oxygen dissolves in frigid water and a bigger body can still take in enough to breathe. Rivals still compete, including Bergmann's rule (cold makes cells larger, so cold-water animals grow bigger) and scarce-food selection (a bigger body survives starvation longer), and scientists consider the causes unresolved. Source: Deep-sea gigantism, Wikipedia and Grokipedia (https://grokipedia.com/page/Deep-sea_gigantism); Chapelle & Peck 1999 oxygen study; Timofeev 2001 (Bergmann's principle).

question: A giant isopod on the cold, dark seafloor can go years between meals without wasting away. In 2022 scientists read the genome of a close relative, Bathynomus jamesi, and found part of the reason written in its genes. What did they find?
answer: Its fat-burning genes are cut back, so its stores last
choices: Its fat-burning genes are cut back, so its stores last
Extra genes let it digest its own cast-off shell
Its gut microbes make food straight from seawater
Its genes let it stop its heart for weeks at a time
context: A 2022 study (Yuan et al., BMC Biology) sequenced the genome of the giant isopod's relative Bathynomus jamesi: at 5.89 billion base pairs, the largest crustacean genome sequenced up to then. Gene families for breaking down fat (lipid degradation) are contracted, so it burns its reserves slowly. It also stores fat in a fat body spread through its body cavity, and a full stomach can fill about two-thirds of its body. A low metabolic rate, slow fat burning and bulk food storage together help explain fasts of more than five years. Source: Yuan et al. 2022, BMC Biology, PMC9107163 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9107163/).

question: A stocky bear sits back on its haunches hour after hour in the misty bamboo forests of central China, munching stalks of bamboo. Its coat is boldly patched in black and white, with dark eye-patches like a bandit's mask and small round black ears. Which famous animal is it?
answer: Giant panda
choices: Giant panda
Sloth bear
Spectacled bear
Sun bear
context: The giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca) is a true bear in the order Carnivora, unlike the red panda, which sits in a family of its own, the Ailuridae. Source: PMC4442137 (mBio, gut microbiota study); Wikipedia 'Red panda'.

question: The giant panda of China's bamboo forests holds a bamboo stalk in a neat pincer grip to strip and eat it, working almost like a person peeling a banana. But a bear's paw has no thumb — just five ordinary fingers all in a row. What does the panda press the stalk against its fingers with?
answer: An enlarged wrist bone acting as a sixth digit
choices: An enlarged wrist bone acting as a sixth digit
A hooked, retractable claw on its first toe
A bony spur growing from its elbow
A long fused knuckle on its middle finger
context: The 'false thumb' is the radial sesamoid, an enlarged wrist bone that works as a sixth, opposable digit, pinching bamboo against the true fingers. The red panda evolved the very same trick independently. Source: PMC9246853 (Scientific Reports 2022); biologyinsights.com 'The Panda Thumb.'

question: Stalk after stalk, a giant panda chews through bamboo, which makes up about 99 percent of everything it eats. Bamboo is tough, watery and poor in energy, yet the panda still has the short, simple gut of a meat-eating bear. How does it get enough energy from bamboo to survive?
answer: It keeps eating for most of the day, every day
choices: It keeps eating for most of the day, every day
It hibernates through winter to skip the shortfall
It stores fat reserves and eats only every few days
It eats its droppings to digest them twice
context: The panda kept a carnivore's short, straight gut and digests only about 17% of the bamboo it eats, so it must eat roughly 12-38 kg for up to 14 hours a day just to survive. Source: PMC4442137 (mBio); livescience.com 'Panda Poop Reveals They're Bad at Digesting Bamboo.'

question: Where its ancestors once ate meat, a giant panda crunches bamboo. Some 4.2 million years ago, just as its line turned almost entirely to bamboo, one of its genes broke and never worked again, a gene its meat-eating cousins still use at every meal. Which ability did the panda lose?
answer: The umami taste that senses the savoriness of meat
choices: The umami taste that senses the savoriness of meat
Its color vision for spotting ripe fruit
Its sense of smell for tracking prey
The night vision of a hunting predator
context: The panda's umami taste-receptor gene Tas1r1, which senses the savory glutamate taste of meat, is broken into a non-working pseudogene, disabled about 4.2 million years ago around the time it switched to bamboo. Source: PMC3108379 / Mol. Biol. Evol. 27(12):2669; PubMed 20573776.

question: A giant panda mother can weigh 90 kg, about as much as a grown man. Her newborn cub arrives pink, blind and completely helpless. About how big is the newborn?
answer: Around 100 grams, the size of a stick of butter
choices: Around 100 grams, the size of a stick of butter
Around 1 kilogram, the size of a kitten
Around 3 kilograms, like a human baby
Around 30 grams, the size of a mouse
context: A newborn panda weighs about 90-130 g, roughly 1/900th of its mother's weight, one of the biggest mother-baby size gaps of any mammal (most mammals, including humans, are born near 1/26th; even polar bear cubs are under 1/400th). Its skeleton looks like a 28-week human fetus. Source: Duke Today 'Why Are Giant Pandas Born So Tiny?' (2019).

question: A giant tube worm two meters long sways its red plume beside a hot crack in the black floor of the Pacific. The fully grown worm has no mouth, no gut and no anus. How does it get its food?
answer: Billions of bacteria living inside its body make food for it
choices: Billions of bacteria living inside its body make food for it
It filters tiny drifting plankton straight from the water
It absorbs dissolved nutrients through its outer skin
It slowly digests the tough tube it builds around itself
context: An adult Riftia pachyptila never eats. It gets ALL its food from billions of bacteria living inside a special organ in its body. Source: Wikipedia: Riftia pachyptila; Cavanaugh et al. 1981, Science.

question: Far below the sunlit sea, giant tube worms crowd into red-plumed gardens on the ocean floor, each standing in a long white tube. They pack around cracks in the crust where hot water full of minerals spurts up. What do these gardens cluster around?
answer: Hydrothermal vents
choices: Hydrothermal vents
Cold seeps
Brine pools
Undersea seamounts
context: Riftia lives around hydrothermal vents about 2,500 meters (over 8,000 feet) down, in total darkness where no sunlight ever reaches. Source: WHOI, The Discovery of Hydrothermal Vents (1977).

question: A giant tube worm pushes a bright red, feathery plume out of its white tube into the vent water, where the plume draws in chemicals the way a gill does. That red has the same cause as the red of human blood. What makes the plume red?
answer: It is packed with hemoglobin
choices: It is packed with hemoglobin
It is stained by the iron-rich vent water
It is coated in tiny red algae
It reflects the red glow of the hot vent
context: The plume is red because it is full of hemoglobin, the same oxygen-carrying molecule that makes human blood red. Source: Wikipedia: Riftia pachyptila; seasidesustainability.org.

question: A new vent splits open in the black sea floor, pouring out hot water, and young giant tube worms settle on the bare rock beside it. Each will grow a white tube with a red plume on top. Compared with most sea animals, how fast does such a worm grow?
answer: It is among the fastest-growing animals in the sea
choices: It is among the fastest-growing animals in the sea
It grows slower than nearly any other deep-sea animal
It stays a fixed size once it settles onto the rock
It shrinks and regrows with the seasons
context: Riftia is among the fastest-growing marine invertebrates: a baby can reach 1.5 meters and be fully grown in under two years, tubes lengthening up to 85 cm a year. Source: Wikipedia: Riftia pachyptila; Cleveland Metroparks.

question: On the sea floor, roughly 2,500 meters below the waves, where sunlight never reaches, the bacteria packed inside a giant tube worm build sugar. A green plant needs sunlight to do the same work. Where do these bacteria get the energy to build food?
answer: From energy stored in chemical bonds, no light needed
choices: From energy stored in chemical bonds, no light needed
From the faint warmth of the water around them
From the pressure of the crushing deep-sea depths
From the electric charge of the ocean currents
context: The bacteria make food by chemosynthesis, building sugars from chemicals in the vent water instead of from sunlight. Source: Wikipedia: Chemosynthesis; Cavanaugh et al. 1981.

question: The bacteria inside a giant tube worm feast on one particular chemical from the vents to make food. It is the very gas that gives rotten eggs their stink, and a poison strong enough to kill most animals. Which chemical do the worm's bacteria turn into nutrition?
answer: Hydrogen sulfide
choices: Hydrogen sulfide
Carbon dioxide
Ammonia
Methane
context: The bacteria live on hydrogen sulfide, the rotten-egg gas that is poisonous to most animals; the worm's bacteria turn this poison into food. Source: WHOI; microbewiki Kenyon.

question: The little submarine Alvin sank almost two miles down to the Galápagos Rift on February 17, 1977. Its crew found gardens of red-plumed giant tube worms thriving beside hot volcanic vents in the black deep, yet every scientist aboard was a geologist. Why had no biologists come along?
answer: No one expected any life down there at all
choices: No one expected any life down there at all
The dive was too dangerous for untrained scientists
The biologists' seats went to news reporters
A storm forced the biology team to stay ashore
context: Only geologists came, because nobody expected life in the dark deep; the discovery of the vent animals stunned everyone. Source: WHOI; EARTH magazine Benchmarks, Feb 17 1977.

question: A giant tube worm's blood ferries poisonous sulfide from the vent water to the bacteria that feed it, and oxygen too. Loose in the blood, the sulfide would wreck the worm's own cells on the way. How does its blood carry the poison safely?
answer: It clamps the sulfide onto a spot separate from where it carries oxygen
choices: It clamps the sulfide onto a spot separate from where it carries oxygen
It wraps each sulfide molecule in a coat of fatty oil
It freezes the sulfide into a harmless solid crystal
It splits the sulfide into two gentler, harmless gases
context: Riftia's hemoglobin grabs oxygen AND sulfide on two different spots at once, carrying both safely to the bacteria so the poison never reaches the worm's vulnerable cells. Source: PNAS 1998; ScienceDaily 2005.

question: A giant tube worm hatches as a minute larva, complete with a mouth and a working gut, and swims off through the dark water. Then its bacterial partners move into its body, and from then on they will feed it for life. What happens to the little worm's mouth and gut?
answer: Its whole digestive system seals up and vanishes forever
choices: Its whole digestive system seals up and vanishes forever
They grow larger to hold the new bacteria
They turn into the worm's bright red plume
They move to the outside to catch more bacteria
context: After the larva takes in its bacteria, its digestive tract degenerates and disappears; the adult has no mouth or gut. Source: Wikipedia: Riftia pachyptila; mBio.

question: A giant tube worm carries deadly sulfide in its blood and is never poisoned by it. The sulfide clips harmlessly onto atoms of a common metal built into the worm's blood protein, a metal people mostly know as a mineral in their diet. Which metal is it?
answer: Zinc
choices: Zinc
Copper
Silver
Calcium
context: Zinc atoms built into Riftia's hemoglobin bind the sulfide, keeping it from poisoning the worm's cells. Source: PNAS 2005, Sulfide binding mediated by zinc ions; RCSB PDB 1YHU.

question: Free-living bacteria from the vent water invade a young giant tube worm like a germ and work their way inward, while the worm sacrifices some of its own invaded cells to make room. A 2006 study traced how this partnership begins. How do the bacteria first get in?
answer: They bore in straight through the worm's outer skin
choices: They bore in straight through the worm's outer skin
They are drawn down the mouth and into the gut
They are filtered from the water by the red plume
They ride in through the pores of the white tube
context: Riftia larvae actually hatch symbiont-free. The free-living bacteria (Candidatus Endoriftia persephone) infect the worm transdermally, crossing the body wall and migrating inward, and the invasion triggers massive programmed cell death (apoptosis) of the host's own tissue; the trophosome organ is then built around the surviving colonized cells. So the partners aren't swallowed like a meal -- they burrow in like an infection the worm domesticates. Source: Nussbaumer, Fisher & Bright, 'Horizontal endosymbiont transmission in hydrothermal vent tubeworms', Nature 441:345-348 (2006), https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04793

question: A giant tube worm draws every meal from the bacteria crowded into one organ of its body, the trophosome. It does not simply soak up whatever its partners leak. Inside each lobe of that organ, what does the worm do to its bacteria?
answer: It fattens them on an inner assembly line, then digests them
choices: It fattens them on an inner assembly line, then digests them
It squeezes stored sugars out of them like juice from fruit
It ferries them out to the plume to trade with the seawater
It lets them die of old age and absorbs what drifts loose
context: Inside each trophosome lobule, small symbiont cells near the central blood vessel divide like stem cells; as they're pushed toward the outer edge they swell, turn round (coccoid), and hoard nutrients (large cells undergo endoreduplication, stockpiling up to ~10x more DNA). At the outermost zone the host digests these fattened bacteria -- it farms and eats its own crop. Radiolabel studies show fixed carbon appearing in symbiont-free host tissue within about 15 minutes. Source: eLife 2021, 'Bacterial symbiont subpopulations have different roles in a deep-sea symbiosis', https://elifesciences.org/articles/58371 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riftia_pachyptila

question: On a small forested island off New Zealand, a wingless giant weta, its body the length of an adult's finger, forages through the leaf litter after dark. A big egg-laden female can outweigh a common garden bird. Which bird does she outweigh?
answer: A house sparrow
choices: A house sparrow
A blackbird
A magpie
A wood pigeon
context: A big egg-filled female giant weta (genus Deinacrida) can top 70 grams - heavier than a house sparrow, making it one of the heaviest insects alive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_w%C4%93t%C4%81

question: Cornered on the forest floor, a giant weta, New Zealand's hulking, wingless cousin of the crickets, does not bite first. It rears up on its front legs and flings its huge, spiny hind legs straight up. What does it do next to warn the attacker off?
answer: Kicks the spiny legs outward at the attacker
choices: Kicks the spiny legs outward at the attacker
Squirts a jet of black ink
Inflates a bright red throat pouch
Sheds the legs and scuttles away
context: A frightened giant weta rears up, sticks its huge spiny hind legs into the air, and kicks them outward so the sharp spines threaten the attacker. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W%C4%93t%C4%81

question: Winter settles on a scree slope 1,200 meters up in the South Island mountains, and the air turns colder than about -5 C. There the scree weta, Deinacrida connectens, does something most animals could never survive, then undoes it when it warms. What happens to it?
answer: It freezes solid, then thaws back to life
choices: It freezes solid, then thaws back to life
It burrows below the frost line to stay warm
It shivers its flight muscles to make heat
It sleeps out the whole winter underground
context: The alpine scree weta, Deinacrida connectens, lives around 1,200 metres up and freezes solid below about -5 C, then thaws back to life - New Zealand's alpine weta are among the largest insects known to do this. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_w%C4%93t%C4%81

question: Among the acacias of the African savanna, one plant-eater calmly strips leaves from the treetops, far above where any other grazer can reach. Its long neck and legs lift its head some eighteen feet off the ground. What is it?
answer: The giraffe
choices: The giraffe
The African elephant
The ostrich
The black rhinoceros
context: The giraffe (Giraffa) is the tallest living animal on Earth — a big male stands over 5.5 metres (18 feet) tall, and most of that height comes from its enormous neck rather than especially long legs. Source: Britannica, How Tall Are Giraffes (https://www.britannica.com/science/How-Tall-Are-Giraffes).

question: A newborn giraffe tumbles nearly 2 meters to the grass at birth, because its mother delivers it standing up. Within an hour it is up on wobbly legs and running beside her. How big is the newborn?
answer: About as tall as a grown man
choices: About as tall as a grown man
About the size of a large dog
About the size of a house cat
About knee-high to its mother
context: A newborn giraffe is already about 1.8 metres (6 feet) tall — as tall as a grown man. It can stand within roughly 30 minutes and run within an hour of being born. Source: Giraffe Conservation Foundation, Starting Life (https://giraffeconservation.org/facts/starting-life/); National Geographic (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/giraffe-baby-film-standing-birth-news).

question: Stretching up into the acacia crowns, a giraffe browses leaves no other animal can reach on a neck about 2 meters long. Bone for bone, how does the count of vertebrae in that neck compare with a human neck's?
answer: The same number a human has
choices: The same number a human has
Ten times what a human has
Twice what a human has
Half what a human has
context: A giraffe has exactly SEVEN neck bones (cervical vertebrae), the very same number a human has. Each one is just gigantic, stretched up to about 25 cm (10 inches) long instead of the small bones in a human neck. Source: Cleveland Zoological Society, Truth or Tail (https://www.clevelandzoosociety.org/z/2021/03/02/truth-or-tail-giraffe-have-more-neck-bones-than-a-human); WorldAtlas (https://www.worldatlas.com/animals/the-long-neck-truth-about-giraffe-bones.html).

question: Reaching for the topmost leaves of an acacia, a giraffe does not just bite. It snakes out something long and muscular, nearly half a meter of it, wraps it around a twig and strips the leaves back into its mouth. What is it using?
answer: Its tongue
choices: Its tongue
Its trunk
Its lower lip alone
A curled front hoof
context: A giraffe's tongue can stretch 45–50 cm (about 18 inches) long — long enough that the giraffe uses it like a hand, wrapping it around leaves and pulling them off. Source: Giraffe Conservation Foundation, How long is a giraffe's tongue (https://giraffeconservation.org/facts-about-giraffe/how-long-is-a-giraffes-tongue-what-color-is-it/).

question: Under the blazing African sun, a giraffe browses for hours, and all that time its dark blue-black tongue, nothing like a human's pink one, keeps reaching out of its mouth into the glare. Scientists think the dark color does a real job. What is it for?
answer: Shield the tongue from sunburn
choices: Shield the tongue from sunburn
Warn rival males to keep away
Help it taste bitter leaves
Blend in against dark bark
context: Scientists think a giraffe's tongue is dark because it hangs out in the blazing sun all day while the animal feeds; the dark pigment (melanin) protects it from sunburn — a built-in sunscreen. Source: Giraffe Conservation Foundation, How long is a giraffe's tongue (https://giraffeconservation.org/facts-about-giraffe/how-long-is-a-giraffes-tongue-what-color-is-it/).

question: A browsing giraffe pulls at an acacia, its favorite food, whose branches bristle with thorns sharp enough to shred a soft mouth. It strips the leaves clean off and swallows them without a scratch. What lets it feed on the thorny branches unharmed?
answer: A tongue armoured with tough bumps and thick sticky saliva
choices: A tongue armoured with tough bumps and thick sticky saliva
Chewing the thorns off first with its flat back teeth
Waiting for the thorns to dry out and drop away
A horny beak that snaps the twigs off cleanly
context: The giraffe's tongue is coated with tough bumps (thickened papillae) and thick, sticky saliva, so it can strip nutritious leaves right off thorny acacia branches without getting hurt. Source: Giraffe Conservation Foundation (https://giraffeconservation.org/facts-about-giraffe/how-long-is-a-giraffes-tongue-what-color-is-it/).

question: Two male giraffes square off on the savanna to settle a rivalry. Each whips his long neck around like a sledgehammer and slams his head into the other, with blows estimated at over a ton of force. What is this kind of duel called?
answer: Necking
choices: Necking
Cresting
Bulling
Rutting
context: Male giraffes fight by 'necking' — swinging their long necks like sledgehammers and smashing their heads into each other. A full swing can land a blow estimated at over 2,000 pounds of force, like being hit by a small car. Source: A-Z Animals, This Is Why Giraffes Fight by Smashing Their Necks (https://a-z-animals.com/articles/this-is-why-giraffes-fight-by-smashing-their-necks-together/).

question: Researchers watching male giraffes club each other with their skulls found the fights oddly honorable. Each fighter favors one side, lefty or righty, and his rival respects it. When one of them stumbles and loses his balance mid-fight, what does the other do?
answer: Holds off and won't strike him
choices: Holds off and won't strike him
Presses in for a finishing blow
Chases him from the herd
Calls in a second bull to help
context: Researchers found giraffes fight fair: each giraffe is a 'lefty' or 'righty' when it swings, rivals respect each other's side, and they won't strike an opponent who has lost his balance. Source: CBC Radio, Giraffes fight fair when they spar, researchers find (https://www.cbc.ca/radio/asithappens/neck-to-neck-combat-giraffes-fight-fair-when-they-spar-researchers-find-1.6183914).

question: At a waterhole, a giraffe splays its front legs and lowers its head far below its heart to drink. The high-pressure blood that normally climbs its long neck should now surge into the brain and knock it out. A dense net of vessels at the base of the skull saves it. How?
answer: It soaks up the sudden surge before it reaches the brain
choices: It soaks up the sudden surge before it reaches the brain
It reverses the blood flow back down the neck
It chills the blood so the brain slows down
It stores spare oxygen for the long drink
context: When a giraffe bends its head down to drink, the high-pressure blood would otherwise rush to the brain and make it faint — so a sponge-like net of blood vessels at the base of the skull (the rete mirabile) soaks up the surge and protects the brain. Source: MDPI, Rostral Epidural Rete Mirabile in Giraffe (https://www.mdpi.com/2813-0545/2/2/13); Intrepid Odyssey (https://www.intrepidodyssey.com/the-giraffes-circulatory-system-a-marvel-of-evolutionary-adaptation/).

question: A giraffe finishes drinking and swings its head back up to eighteen feet in a few seconds. Blood should drain from the brain and pool in its legs, yet it never faints. Tight, inelastic skin wraps its lower legs and squeezes the veins. What everyday object does that skin work like?
answer: A tight compression stocking
choices: A tight compression stocking
A rigid splint or plaster cast
A hinged metal knee brace
A rubber tourniquet band
context: Tight, inelastic skin on the giraffe's lower legs works like a compression stocking so blood doesn't pool in its feet, while one-way valves in its neck veins stop blood pouring backward into the head — together they keep the animal from fainting when it stands back up. Source: Intrepid Odyssey Safaris (https://www.intrepidodyssey.com/the-giraffes-circulatory-system-a-marvel-of-evolutionary-adaptation/); Smithsonian Magazine (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/cardiovascular-secrets-giraffes-180977785/).

question: Every beat of a giraffe's heart must push blood 2 meters straight up the neck to the brain, so people expect a giant heart. A 2016 study found an ordinary one, just 0.5 percent of the animal's weight. What lets this normal-sized heart do the job?
answer: Its left chamber is walled with extra-thick, dense muscle
choices: Its left chamber is walled with extra-thick, dense muscle
Its chambers are unusually roomy and hold extra blood
It sits high in the chest, closer to the head it must feed
It empties in one slow, powerful squeeze each beat
context: The 'giant giraffe heart' is a myth. A 2016 study found the heart is only about 0.5% of body mass, the same relative size as in other mammals. What is extraordinary is the left-ventricle wall, thickened to roughly 2-3.5 cm around a strikingly small cavity. That thick wall generates the ~200-250 mmHg pressure needed to push blood up the long neck while keeping wall tension normal, but the small cavity means each beat pumps less blood, so the giraffe's cardiac output is low for its body size: power, not bulk. Source: Smerup et al., 'The thick left ventricular wall of the giraffe heart normalises wall tension, but limits stroke volume and cardiac output,' Journal of Experimental Biology 219:457 (2016).

question: A giraffe browses where no rival can reach, and since Darwin's day that has been the usual explanation for its long neck. In 2022, Discokeryx, a giraffe cousin from China some 17 million years old, revived an old rival idea. What idea did that fossil bring back?
answer: The neck was forged as a weapon in brutal mating duels
choices: The neck was forged as a weapon in brutal mating duels
The neck lengthened to cool the blood in fierce heat
The neck grew tall to spot lions across open plains
The neck stretched to reach water in flooded ground
context: Since Darwin's day the towering neck was read as a feeding advantage -- reaching foliage rivals cannot. In 2022 a fossil of the early giraffe relative Discokeryx xiezhi (~17 million years ago, China) revived a rival idea. It carried a thick helmet-like disc of bone on its head and some of the most heavily reinforced, shock-absorbing head-and-neck joints known in any mammal -- built to survive ferocious head-butting duels over mates. This is hard evidence for the 'necks for sex' hypothesis: that sexual combat, not only feeding, drove giraffe neck evolution. Both pressures may have acted together; the feeding story is no longer the only serious explanation. Source: Wang, Deng et al., 'Sexual selection promotes giraffoid head-neck evolution and ecological adaptation,' Science 376:eabl8316 (June 2022).

question: A tiny lime-green frog sits on a leaf over a rushing stream in a Central American cloud forest at night. A biologist turns it gently onto its back. What is strange about the skin of its belly?
answer: It is see-through, showing the organs inside
choices: It is see-through, showing the organs inside
It flushes bright red as a warning to predators
It puffs into a spiny ball twice its size
It oozes a milky poison that burns the skin
context: The glass frog (family Centrolenidae, about 160 species, 3.0-7.5 cm long) has transparent skin across its abdomen: turned over, it shows its organs right through the skin. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_frog

question: A biologist peers through the clear belly skin of a glass frog in a Central American rainforest and sees its organs at work, as if the frog were a tiny living aquarium. Most sit quietly in place, but one never holds still. Which organ is it?
answer: Its heart, beating and pumping blood
choices: Its heart, beating and pumping blood
Its lungs, drawing in air
Its kidney, filtering waste
Its stomach, churning food
context: Through a glass frog's see-through belly an onlooker can watch its actual heart beating and pumping blood -- the same beat a doctor listens for through a stethoscope -- along with its liver and looping intestines working inside its living body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_frog; https://allthatsinteresting.com/glass-frog

question: A clutch of glass frog eggs, tiny see-through blobs of jelly, clings to the underside of a leaf over a Central American stream, and egg-eating wasps are hunting for it. In almost a third of glass frog species, the eggs are guarded for days on end. Who keeps that long watch?
answer: The male
choices: The male
The female
Both parents, taking turns
Both parents, side by side
context: In almost a third of glass frog species the male stands guard over the clutch for long periods, and a single male may watch several clutches at once, each at a different stage; in many species the female broods the eggs only on the night they are laid. The eggs are laid above running water so that when the tadpoles hatch (after 10-20 days, often during heavy rain) they drop straight down into the stream. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_frog

question: A glass frog sleeping on a leaf by day turns two to three times more see-through than when it is awake. Filming resting frogs in 2022, scientists found how it hides the red tint that would give it away: it tucks away nearly 90 percent of the red cells in its blood. Where does it pack them?
answer: Crammed inside its liver
choices: Crammed inside its liver
Squeezed under its skin
Dissolved into its bladder
Drained down into its feet
context: A resting glass frog stashes almost 90% of its red blood cells (the cells that carry the red color) inside its liver, whose lining of reflective guanine crystals acts like a tiny mirror to hide them -- making the frog two to three times more transparent than when active. It releases the cells again at night to become active: a rare case of 'transparency on demand.' Cramming that much blood together should cause a deadly clot, yet the frog packs and unpacks it daily without clotting -- a puzzle scientists now hope to study to help prevent clots in humans. Source: Taboada, Delia et al. 2022, Science (doi:10.1126/science.abl6620); https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2022/12/221222162421.htm

question: Leaping from a high trunk at night, a flying squirrel spreads a furry sail of skin between its wrists and ankles and glides like a paper airplane. It has no wings to flap, yet it holds a steady course and slows itself just before it lands. What steadies its glide and brakes it?
answer: Its flattened, bushy tail
choices: Its flattened, bushy tail
Its long whiskers
Its clawed hind feet
Its round, tufted ears
context: The flying squirrel steers mainly by shifting its limbs and wrists, which changes the tension of its gliding membrane (the patagium); its flattened, bushy tail stabilizes the glide and works as an air brake before landing. Source: Wikipedia 'Flying squirrel'; National Geographic, 'Flying squirrels'.

question: A pencil-length lizard leaps from a tree trunk in a Southeast Asian rainforest and sails to the next tree on bright, fan-like wings that fold flat against its sides when it lands. People call it the flying dragon. What is its proper name?
answer: The Draco
choices: The Draco
The anole
The basilisk
The frilled dragon
context: The Draco lizard ('flying dragon') glides on membranes called patagia stretched over 4 to 7 greatly elongated ribs. A Draco usually glides about 10 meters between trees, but glides as long as 60 meters (200 feet) have been recorded. Source: Wikipedia 'Draco (lizard)'; Oxford Academic, 'Biology of Gliding in Flying Lizards'.

question: A biologist sets four gliders side by side: the flying squirrel of North American forests, the flying fish of the open ocean, a gliding lizard of Southeast Asia and the flying snake of Asian rainforests. Each turns a fall into a long glide. What does she find when she compares how each one builds its 'wing'?
answer: Each uses a completely different body part for the same result
choices: Each uses a completely different body part for the same result
They all reuse the same wrist-membrane design
Each stretches its wing on long, splayed ribs
They share one gliding organ inherited from a common ancestor
context: Because each glider evolved its 'wing' independently, they solved the same problem with completely different body parts — a skin flap (squirrel, colugo), giant fins (flying fish), elongated ribs (Draco), a flattened whole body (flying snake), and webbed feet (Wallace's frog) — five different anatomies, all producing the same falling-with-style result. This repeated independent solution is called convergent evolution. Gliding has evolved over and over among tree-dwelling animals (in mammals alone at least seven separate times), whereas true powered flight has evolved only four times: insects, pterosaurs, birds, and bats. Source: Wikipedia 'Convergent evolution'; Wikipedia 'Flying and gliding animals'.

question: A glider launches from a high trunk, spread on a sail of skin that runs from its neck to the tips of its fingers and toes and on down its tail. One was recorded gliding about 150 meters between trees. Which animal is it?
answer: The colugo
choices: The colugo
The flying squirrel
The sugar glider
Wallace's flying frog
context: The colugo's patagium is among the most extensive of any gliding mammal, running from the neck to the very tips of the fingers, webbing between every finger and toe, and continuing to the tip of the tail. Colugos often glide about 70 meters between trees, and one Malayan colugo was recorded covering about 150 meters (490 feet) in a single glide. Source: Wikipedia 'Colugo'; Natural History Museum, 'Colugos: expert gliders of the forest'.

question: A cat-sized furry glider sails from tree to tree in the dark of a Southeast Asian rainforest on a wide flap of skin. People call it the flying lemur, yet it cannot truly fly and is no lemur. When scientists read its DNA, which group proved to hold its closest living relatives?
answer: Primates, the group of monkeys and humans
choices: Primates, the group of monkeys and humans
Rodents, the group of rats and squirrels
Marsupials, the group of kangaroos
Insectivores, the group of shrews and moles
context: The colugo cannot fly and is not a lemur, so the name 'flying lemur' is wrong twice over. Its actual closest living relatives are primates (the group that includes monkeys and humans), which surprised scientists who once thought it was related to bats. The two living species are the Sunda flying lemur (Galeopterus variegatus) and the Philippine flying lemur (Cynocephalus volans). Source: Wikipedia 'Colugo'.

question: Small furred creatures leapt from tree to tree on wing-like skin in Jurassic forests near what is now Beijing. Their fossils, described in 2017 as Maiopatagium and Vilevolodon, preserve the gliding membranes. Their describers placed them just outside the true mammals, as forerunners on the branch leading to them. What do they prove about gliding?
answer: Mammal ancestors were gliding roughly 100 million years before modern gliders
choices: Mammal ancestors were gliding roughly 100 million years before modern gliders
Gliding first appeared only after the giant dinosaurs had died out
The earliest mammals could all fly under their own power
Skin-membrane gliding evolved just once and was inherited by every glider
context: Described in 2017 from the Tiaojishan Formation near Beijing, Maiopatagium furculiferum and Vilevolodon diplomylos are haramiyidans, which their describers placed among the mammaliaforms, the forerunners of crown mammals (other studies put haramiyidans inside the mammals). They preserve wing-like gliding membranes, long fingers, and tree-climbing limbs, showing the gliding, tree-dwelling way of life had already evolved about 100 million years before the first modern gliding mammals. The Jurassic lies deep in the age of dinosaurs. Source: Meng, Luo et al., Nature (2017), reported by University of Chicago News, 'First winged mammals from the Jurassic period discovered' -- https://news.uchicago.edu/story/first-winged-mammals-jurassic-period-discovered

question: A flying squirrel glides on a skin membrane that reaches past the end of its arm bones, held out by a rod of cartilage that swings out from its wrist. The tips of that membrane curl upward instead of lying flat. What did wind studies show those upturned tips do?
answer: They cut the drag of swirling wingtip air, like the winglets on an airliner
choices: They cut the drag of swirling wingtip air, like the winglets on an airliner
They catch rain and channel it away from the gliding membrane
They flash bright color to warn off rival squirrels in the canopy
They store fat that fuels the muscles powering each long glide
context: The flying squirrel is the only gliding mammal that extends its wingtip with a styliform cartilage -- a rod of cartilage at the wrist with no equivalent in colugos, sugar gliders, or Draco lizards. The thumb's abductor muscle swings it out to spread and tension the leading edge of the patagium beyond the length of the arm bones. Thorington & Darrow showed the resulting upturned wingtips form airfoils that reduce induced drag, functioning like the winglets on a modern airplane wing. Source: Thorington & Darrow, 'Wing Tip Anatomy and Aerodynamics in Flying Squirrels,' Journal of Mammalogy 79(1):245 (1998) -- https://academic.oup.com/jmammal/article-pdf/79/1/245/2504483/79-1-245.pdf

question: A beast the size of a small car lumbered across the grasslands of South America in the last ice age, its back sealed under a single great dome of bone. Estimates for the biggest run as high as 2 tonnes. What was this armored giant?
answer: the glyptodon
choices: the glyptodon
the giant ground sloth
the woolly rhino
the short-faced bear
context: Glyptodon was an ice-age relative of the armadillo that grew to about 3 metres long, its whole back hidden under a domed shell. Weight estimates vary widely, from several hundred kilograms up to about 2 tonnes for the largest. Source: Grokipedia 'Glyptodon'; Wikipedia, Glyptodon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyptodon).

question: Along a forest edge in ice-age South America, a glyptodon shuffled forward, its head capped in fused bone like a helmet and its back sealed under a huge bony dome. All that armor made it look like a killer. How did this giant actually feed?
answer: grazing low grass and plants
choices: grazing low grass and plants
cracking bones for marrow
tearing flesh from smaller mammals
trapping fish in shallow pools
context: Despite its armor and clubbed relatives, Glyptodon was a plant-eater with a wide muzzle built for bulk-feeding; it grazed and browsed low plants and grasses along the edges of forests and grasslands. Source: Wikipedia, Glyptodon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyptodon).

question: A modern armadillo rolls into a tight ball when a predator closes in, thanks to a shell of flexible bands. Its giant ice-age cousin, the glyptodon, wore a back dome that worked nothing like that. How was the glyptodon's shell built?
answer: the plates were fused solid and locked to its hips
choices: the plates were fused solid and locked to its hips
the plates overlapped like loose roof tiles
a row of soft hinges crossed its back
a thick keratin cap rode over free ribs
context: Glyptodon's shell was a single rigid dome of around 1,800 bony plates (osteoderms) fused solid and even locked onto its hip bones, so unlike a banded modern armadillo it could never roll into a ball. Source: Wikipedia, Glyptodon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyptodon).

question: On the grasslands of ice-age South America, Doedicurus, a cousin of the glyptodon, swung a tail tipped with a spiked club of bone. Some fossil glyptodont shells carry cracks and dents across the dome. What did scientists conclude those marks show?
answer: they clubbed each other in fights
choices: they clubbed each other in fights
big cats bit down and left the marks
rockfall crushed the shells after burial
disease pitted the bone from inside
context: Doedicurus carried a rigid, spiked tail club. A 1999 study by Alexander, Farina and Vizcaino estimated the energy of such tail blows and linked them to fractures found on glyptodont carapaces, and damage on some shells fits blows from another glyptodont's tail -- evidence these living tanks clubbed each other, likely in fights over mates or territory. Source: Alexander, Farina & Vizcaino 1999, 'Tail blow energy and carapace fractures in a large glyptodont,' Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society 126:41-49; Wikipedia, Glyptodon; TwilightBeasts, A home on the range (https://twilightbeasts.org/2014/09/11/a-home-on-the-range/).

question: A glyptodon carried a dome of about 1,800 bony plates on its back, each one some 2.5 centimeters thick. Fine X-ray scans show why one plate could take a heavy blow without cracking apart, and engineers designing light armor have studied it. How was each plate built?
answer: dense bone skins wrapped around a porous inner lattice
choices: dense bone skins wrapped around a porous inner lattice
a slick waxy coating that lets strikes slide off
interlocking hexagons that snap free one by one
a thick cushion of fat sealed beneath the bone
context: Each osteoderm was roughly 2.5 cm thick and built like an engineered sandwich panel: two dense outer layers of compact bone enclosing a porous inner lattice about 66% pore space, with struts only ~0.25 mm thick. That layout lets the plate soak up impact energy and stop a crack before it splits the whole plate (no catastrophic failure) -- the property engineers study for lightweight bio-inspired armor. Source: 'Analyzing nature's protective design: the glyptodont body armor,' J. Mech. Behav. Biomed. Mater. (2018), sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1751616118301656; corroborated via biomimetic-armor review literature and Glyptodon histology sources.

question: Delsuc, Poinar and their colleagues pulled mitochondrial DNA from Doedicurus, a giant club-tailed glyptodont, in 2016, and it put the glyptodonts deep within the armadillo family tree. Tracing that branch back to its small common ancestor with living armadillos gave a second jolt. By what factor had the line's body mass grown?
answer: More than 300-fold
choices: Roughly 10-fold
Roughly 50-fold
More than 300-fold
Nearly 1,000-fold
context: Delsuc, Poinar and colleagues sequenced the complete mitochondrial genome of Doedicurus, a giant club-tailed glyptodont. It nests deep inside the living armadillos, making glyptodonts the subfamily Glyptodontinae within family Chlamyphoridae, having split from other armadillos about 35 million years ago. The surprise: the last common ancestor of glyptodonts and modern armadillos weighed only about 6 kg, yet Pleistocene glyptodonts reached roughly 2,000 kg -- a more than 300-fold increase in body mass over that lineage. Source: Delsuc, Poinar et al., Current Biology 26(4):R155-R156 (2016), corroborated via Sci-News and ScienceDaily (2016/02/160222134051.htm).

question: A young goblin shark, the deep-sea fish named for a long-nosed goblin, looks ghostly white, and its color deepens as it grows older. The grown shark's pink is no trick of the light. What makes it pink?
answer: red blood vessels showing through its thin, pale skin
choices: red blood vessels showing through its thin, pale skin
a diet of pink shrimp staining its body
glowing pigment cells that ward off rivals
a coating of pink algae from the seafloor
context: The goblin shark's skin is so thin and pale that the red blood vessels underneath show right through it, giving a real pink hue that deepens with age. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History profile; Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'.

question: The goblin shark hunts in pitch-black water hundreds of meters down, where eyes are nearly useless. Its long, flat, blade-like snout is studded with jelly-filled sensors called ampullae of Lorenzini. What do those sensors let the shark find in the dark?
answer: the faint electric fields given off by hidden animals
choices: the faint electric fields given off by hidden animals
the warmth radiating from a prey animal's body
the chemical scent trail left by wounded fish
the pressure waves of a distant tail beat
context: Ampullae of Lorenzini are jelly-filled electroreceptors; the goblin shark's blade snout sweeps them through the dark deep sea to detect the weak electric fields of buried or hidden prey. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History profile; Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'.

question: A goblin shark hangs almost motionless in the black water, then drifts silently toward its prey. Its muscles are weak and its body flabby, yet it hovers there nearly weightless. One huge organ, up to about a quarter of the shark's whole weight, keeps it afloat. Which organ is it?
answer: its huge oil-filled liver
choices: its huge oil-filled liver
its air-filled swim bladder
its water-logged spongy skeleton
its air-gulping stomach
context: The goblin shark's oil-filled liver can reach about a quarter of its body weight; the light oil makes it nearly neutrally buoyant, so this slow ambush predator can hover in the dark and drift toward prey. Sharks have no swim bladder. Source: Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'; Smithsonian Ocean.

question: When a goblin shark strikes, its whole mouth catapults out of its face and then snaps back flush against its head. In 2016 Nakaya's team studied footage of two wild goblin sharks feeding, shot by Japan's national broadcaster, and measured each strike frame by frame. What record did the jaws turn out to hold?
answer: the fastest jaw of any shark
choices: the fastest jaw of any shark
the deepest recorded shark strike
the widest gape of any deep-sea fish
the longest teeth of any predatory shark
context: Nakaya's team measured the jaws shooting out at up to 3.1 m/s, to about 9% of the shark's length: by far the fastest and greatest jaw protrusion of any shark. Source: Nakaya et al. 2016, Scientific Reports 'Slingshot feeding of the goblin shark'; Hokkaido University press release.

question: A goblin shark's jaws fly out from under its snout to seize prey, reaching about 9 percent of its body length, far beyond an ordinary shark's reach. Its muscles are weak and flabby, yet the jaws move in a flash. What helps fling them forward?
answer: Stretched elastic ligaments at the jaw joint
choices: Stretched elastic ligaments at the jaw joint
A jet of water forced out through its gills
A gas-filled sac that swells behind the jaws
A rush of blood that stiffens the jaws
context: Two pairs of elastic ligaments at the jaw joint help drive the strike: when the shark bites, they release their tension and catapult the jaws forward. Nakaya's 2016 film study measured the jaws shooting out to 8.6-9.4% of the shark's length, 2.1 to 9.5 times farther than in other sharks. Source: Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'; Nakaya et al. 2016, Scientific Reports.

question: A goblin shark fires its whole mouth out of its face, so scientists expected it to feed like a vacuum gun, yanking its jaws open to suck prey in. Nakaya's 2016 study found otherwise: the shark keeps its gill slits open, gapes as wide as it can, and only then launches its jaws. What kind of feeder does that make it?
answer: a ram feeder that overtakes prey by rushing its mouth over it
choices: a ram feeder that overtakes prey by rushing its mouth over it
a suction feeder that draws prey in on an inward vacuum
a filter feeder that strains drifting plankton from the water
a bite-and-shake feeder that tears loose chunks of flesh
context: The giveaway is timing and plumbing. A suction feeder snaps its gape open first to build a vacuum and would clamp its gill slits shut to hold that low pressure. The goblin shark does neither: it fully opens its gape, keeps the gill slits open the whole time (so water flows out, not in), and only THEN catapults the jaws. From the open gill slits, Nakaya's team inferred that the pressure inside the mouth stayed positive, pushing water outward rather than sucking prey inward. So the fastest jaws of any shark are not a vacuum gun at all; they are a ram — the mouth lunges out and swallows the prey by overtaking it. Source: Nakaya et al. 2016, 'Slingshot feeding of the goblin shark Mitsukurina owstoni', Scientific Reports (PMC PMC4901258, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4901258/).

question: A goblin shark impales soft, slippery grenadiers and squid on its long, straight, lengthwise-grooved front fangs. But near the corners of its jaws sits a second, completely different set of teeth built for a different job. What are those rear teeth shaped to do?
answer: crush hard-shelled crustaceans
choices: crush hard-shelled crustaceans
slice chunks from large carcasses
filter tiny plankton from the water
grind up tough seafloor sponges
context: One shark, two toolkits. The front (anterior) teeth are long, narrow, nearly straight fangs, finely grooved lengthwise, made to punch through and hold soft, slick deep-sea prey like grenadiers (rattail fish) and squid. But the posterior teeth near the jaw corners are small and flattened for crushing hard, shelled prey such as crustaceans (decapods and isopods). A single goblin shark can carry roughly 35-53 upper and 31-62 lower tooth rows across those two jobs. Source: Wikipedia 'Goblin shark' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goblin_shark); diet corroborated by Yano et al.'s stomach-content survey of 121 specimens from Tokyo Submarine Canyon.

question: A Goliath birdeater, the heaviest spider on Earth, creeps across a rainforest floor in northern South America. Its hairy body is as large as a man's fist; its outspread legs reach across a dinner plate. A full-grown one weighs about as much as what?
answer: A large apple
choices: A large apple
A single grape
A garden snail
A bag of sugar
context: Theraphosa blondi tops out around 175 grams (6 oz), about as much as a large apple — the greatest mass of any spider. The giant huntsman spider has longer legs, but the Goliath wins on sheer bulk and body size. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goliath_birdeater

question: At night on the floor of a South American rainforest, a Goliath birdeater waits in silence, then pounces on whatever wanders past. Its name says it eats birds, but it seldom, if ever, catches one. What does it drag back to its burrow most often?
answer: Earthworms, insects and frogs
choices: Earthworms, insects and frogs
Fallen fruit and seeds
Nectar sipped from flowers
Roosting bats
context: On the forest floor it mostly takes large arthropods such as insects, along with earthworms and amphibians such as frogs and toads, and now and then lizards, small snakes and rodents; it only rarely preys on birds. The 'birdeater' name came from Maria Sibylla Merian's 1705 engraving of a tarantula attacking a hummingbird; one famous picture stuck the myth to the whole species. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goliath_birdeater ; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/invertebrates/facts/goliath-birdeater

question: A Goliath birdeater cornered on the floor of a South American rainforest seldom strikes with its fangs first, and their venom is only mildly harmful to people. Instead it turns around, rubs its back legs across its abdomen, and sends something flying at the attacker's eyes and skin. What does it launch?
answer: A cloud of tiny barbed itching hairs
choices: A cloud of tiny barbed itching hairs
A jet of stinging venom
A sticky net of silk
A spray of foul musk
context: The hairs are urticating setae — microscopic, harpoon-shaped barbs the spider flicks off its abdomen. They lodge in an attacker's eyes and skin and itch fiercely, a far better first defense than a bite whose venom is only mild to humans. Source: https://www.aaas.org/news/weird-wonderful-creatures-goliath-birdeater

question: Piotr Naskrecki, an insect scientist alone in the Guyana rainforest at night, heard a strange sound behind him and turned to find a Goliath birdeater right at his heels. The giant spider was making a noise almost no other spider makes. What was making that noise?
answer: Its hard-tipped feet clicking on the ground
choices: Its hard-tipped feet clicking on the ground
Its fangs snapping open and shut
Wind rattling through its leg hairs
Air hissing from its breathing holes
context: The Goliath birdeater is essentially the only spider that makes noise as it walks: its feet carry hardened tips and claws that tap the forest floor — Naskrecki described the clicking as 'not unlike a horse's hooves.' (It can also hiss loudly by rubbing leg bristles together — stridulation — but the walking-click is what gave it away that night.) Source: https://thesmallermajority.com/2014/10/08/the-sound-of-little-hooves-in-the-night/

question: A goliath frog squats on a boulder amid the white water of a rainforest river in Cameroon, one of the few places it lives. It is the largest frog alive. About how big does a full-grown one get?
answer: About the size of a house cat
choices: About the size of a house cat
About the size of a mouse
About the size of a large dog
About the size of a human hand
context: The goliath frog (Conraua goliath) can reach about 13 inches (34 cm) long and weigh up to 7.3 pounds (about 3.3 kg) -- roughly the size and weight of a house cat. It lives in southwestern Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. Source: Wikipedia, Goliath frog; Britannica.

question: A male goliath frog, the biggest frog on Earth, sits on a rock in a fast river in Cameroon, ready to court a mate. Most male frogs inflate a balloon of throat skin, a vocal sac, and boom out a croak, but he has no such sac and cannot croak. How does he attract a female?
answer: He opens his mouth and whistles
choices: He opens his mouth and whistles
He drums the water with his hind legs
He clicks his jaws together loudly
He waves a webbed hind foot in the air
context: Despite being the largest frog on Earth, the goliath frog has no vocal sac and cannot make a loud croak. To attract a mate, the male opens his mouth and makes a whistling sound. Source: Animal Diversity Web; Wikipedia.
