question: Goliath frogs, the biggest frogs on Earth, spend their lives along fast, rocky rivers in Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. In 2019 scientists watching them recorded behavior never before documented in any African frog or toad. On the riverbank, what were the frogs doing?
answer: Dragging rocks to wall off little ponds as nests for their eggs
choices: Dragging rocks to wall off little ponds as nests for their eggs
Carrying their tadpoles around on their backs
Spinning ropes of slime between the reeds
Digging deep burrows to sleep through the dry season
context: In 2019 scientists discovered the goliath frog builds nests: it clears little ponds along the riverbank and shoves rocks around the edge to wall them off, then a parent guards the eggs. It was the first nest-building ever documented in an African frog or toad. Source: Schaefer et al. 2019, Journal of Natural History; Mongabay.

question: In the fast, rocky rivers of Cameroon, a goliath frog grows far bigger than any other frog on Earth. Biologists have puzzled over what pushed this one species so far past all its relatives. Which explanation do the scientists who study it favor?
answer: Hauling the heavy stones it needs to build its nests
choices: Hauling the heavy stones it needs to build its nests
A diet of unusually large river crabs and fish
Being a leftover giant from a cooler ancient climate
Growing big armor to survive its riverbank predators
context: To build its nests the goliath frog drags rocks weighing more than half its own body weight -- up to about 2 kg (over 4 pounds). Scientists think this heavy lifting is so demanding it may have driven the species to become the biggest frog on Earth. Source: Schaefer et al. 2019, Journal of Natural History; Mongabay.

question: A wild gray wolf pack lopes across the winter snow of a northern forest, hunting as a team. Researchers who have watched packs for decades, in places like Yellowstone, see the same makeup almost every time. What is a wolf pack?
answer: A family: two parents and their pups from the last few years
choices: A family: two parents and their pups from the last few years
A crew of the strongest wolves drawn from many litters
A truce between two neighboring packs sharing a hunt
A group of females who drove off all the adult males
context: A wild pack is a breeding pair (the mother and father) plus their offspring from recent years, living and hunting together. Source: International Wolf Center, wolf.org/wolf-info/just-for-kids/wolf-families/.

question: A storm rolls into a snowy northern forest and scatters a gray wolf pack among the trees. One wolf throws back its head and howls, and the others answer from far away. Besides bringing the pack back together, what else does a wolf's howling do?
answer: Warns rival packs to keep off the pack's territory
choices: Warns rival packs to keep off the pack's territory
Frightens prey into freezing so it is easier to catch
Mimics an elk call to lure curious prey closer
Echoes off hills so the pack can map the terrain
context: Wolves howl to assemble the pack before and after a hunt, to relocate one another during a storm, and to warn neighboring packs to stay off their territory. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo; Wolf Conservation Center, 'Wolves and Howling'.

question: Seven or eight gray wolves slip out of the pines toward a hundred elk grazing in a Yellowstone meadow. The wolves are badly outnumbered, so the pack fans out along the herd, testing and waiting. What is the wolves' first aim?
answer: Split a single animal off from the rest of the herd
choices: Split a single animal off from the rest of the herd
Surround the whole herd so nothing can escape
Stampede the herd toward a cliff edge
Attack the largest and strongest bull head-on
context: Wolves try to cut one animal away from the group; if a prey animal stands its ground they often leave it and look for one that runs. Most hunts of large hoofed prey actually fail, so wolves test many animals to find a weak or slow one. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hunting behavior of gray wolves'.

question: L. David Mech spread the idea of the 'alpha wolf', the animal that fights its way to the top of the pack, in a 1970 book. In 1999 he corrected himself: the idea came from watching captive strangers thrown together. In a wild pack, who are the wolves everyone follows?
answer: Simply the parents — the breeding pair
choices: Simply the parents — the breeding pair
The oldest, most experienced wolf, kin or not
The single best hunter, who leads the chase
The mother alone, while the father ranges apart
context: The 'alpha' idea came from watching captive strangers thrown together, not wild families. Mech popularized it in 1970, then published a 1999 correction in the Canadian Journal of Zoology: in the wild the 'leaders' are just the parents. Source: Mech (1999); Scientific American, 'Is the Alpha Wolf Idea a Myth?'.

question: A gray wolf pack's babysitters have guarded the den all morning while its hunters were away chasing elk. When the hunters trot home from the kill, the pups, too young to chew raw meat, swarm them and lick at their mouths. How do the adults get meat to the pups?
answer: They regurgitate swallowed meat for the pups to eat
choices: They regurgitate swallowed meat for the pups to eat
They drag the whole carcass back to the den mouth
They lead the pups out to feed at the kill site
They store meat in cheek pouches and spit it out
context: Every wolf in the pack helps raise the pups: babysitters guard them while hunters are away, and returning hunters bring up swallowed meat, regurgitating it for the pups to eat. Source: International Wolf Center; Frontiers for Young Minds, 'It Takes A Pack To Raise A Pup'.

question: Gray wolves came back to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, after some 70 years' absence, and the elk changed where they dared to graze. They stopped lingering in the open valleys along the streams. What began to happen along those streams?
answer: Browsed-down aspen and willow started growing tall again
choices: Browsed-down aspen and willow started growing tall again
The rivers dried up as plants drank the water
Beavers abandoned the streams for good
Grass replaced every tree along the banks
context: With elk no longer lingering in open valleys, over-browsed willow and aspen recovered; taller willows let beavers return to build dams — a chain scientists call a trophic cascade. Researchers caution the effect is real but partly overstated, since drought, bears, and human hunting also thinned the elk. Source: Ripple & Beschta (2012), 'Trophic cascades in Yellowstone'; MeatEater Conservation.

question: A great white's jaws hold about 300 teeth stacked in up to seven rows, yet only a small share bite. When a front tooth breaks off in a seal, the gap fills within a day or two. Where does the new tooth come from?
answer: It rolls forward from a spare row waiting behind
choices: It rolls forward from a spare row waiting behind
It regrows slowly from the empty gum socket
It hardens from soft cartilage in the jaw
A neighboring tooth widens to close the gap
context: A great white's teeth are arranged in rows like a conveyor belt: of roughly 300 teeth in up to seven rows, most sit in reserve behind the working front row and are never used to bite until they roll forward. When a front tooth is lost, one from the row behind rolls forward into the working position, sometimes in as little as 24 to 48 hours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; smartscience.blog/sharks-teeth-rows-anatomy; nationalgeographic.com/animals/fish/facts/great-white-shark; americanoceans.org/facts/how-many-rows-of-teeth-do-sharks-have.

question: A great white shark closes on a struggling seal in the cold green water off the California coast. Its upper and lower teeth do very different jobs. The broad upper teeth, backed by huge jaw muscles, carry serrated, saw-toothed edges that shear through flesh and blubber like a row of steak knives. The narrower lower teeth are a different shape entirely. What are those lower teeth built to do?
answer: Grip and hold the catch in place
choices: Grip and hold the catch in place
Crush shell and bone to powder
Comb food particles from the water
Inject a paralyzing venom
context: The upper teeth are broad triangles with serrated edges built for shearing flesh, while the lower teeth are narrower and more pointed for gripping and holding the catch in place. Source: elasmo-research.org/education/white_shark/teeth.htm; americanoceans.org/facts/shark-teeth-facts.

question: Beachcombers on fossil coasts from South Carolina to Morocco pocket shark teeth by the handful, far more than the fossil bones of any other animal in the same rocks. Shark bodies rarely fossilize, yet the teeth are everywhere. What about a shark's life explains it?
answer: It sheds and replaces teeth endlessly, tens of thousands in a lifetime
choices: It sheds and replaces teeth endlessly, tens of thousands in a lifetime
Its teeth are made of near-indestructible diamond-hard enamel
It deliberately spits worn teeth onto known spawning grounds
It grows a fresh full set every single year like antlers
context: Because a shark never stops shedding and replacing teeth, it can go through tens of thousands of teeth across its lifetime, one reason fossil shark teeth are so common. Source: nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-can-shark-teeth-tell-us.html; americanoceans.org/facts/shark-teeth-facts.

question: A great white cruises the dark ocean, reading the weak electric fields thrown off by the muscle twitches of nearby prey. It senses them with tiny jelly-filled pores on its snout, the ampullae of Lorenzini, named for the 17th-century Italian anatomist who described them. How faint a field can they detect?
answer: Around five billionths of a volt per centimetre
choices: Around five billionths of a volt per centimetre
Around five thousandths of a volt per centimetre
Around five volts per centimetre
Around five hundred volts per centimetre
context: The ampullae of Lorenzini can detect electric fields as tiny as about five nanovolts per centimetre (five billionths of a volt), among the most sensitive electroreception known in any animal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampullae_of_Lorenzini; marinebiodiversity.ca/sharks-sixth-sense-how-electric-fields-guide-these-ocean-predators.

question: A great white patrols the murky green water off South Africa and picks out a wounded seal from a healthy one long before its eyes could see either animal. Even in cloudy water, the shark homes straight in on the hurt one. What gives the injured seal away?
answer: Its leaking electrolytes make an electric field up to three times stronger
choices: Its leaking electrolytes make an electric field up to three times stronger
Its blood turns the surrounding water faintly magnetic
Its panicked heartbeat sends out a low sound only sharks hear
Its torn skin glows under the shark's ultraviolet vision
context: A wounded animal leaks charged electrolytes into the water, creating an electric field up to three times stronger than an uninjured one, so to a great white's electric sense an injured seal or fish effectively lights up. Source: elasmo-research.org/education/white_shark/electroreception.htm.

question: A great white shark hunts seals in cold seas, and a net of blood vessels called the rete mirabile is laced through its body. Its swimming muscles make heat as they work. What does the net do with that heat?
answer: It traps the body's own heat instead of losing it at the gills
choices: It traps the body's own heat instead of losing it at the gills
It pumps the heat out fast to keep the brain from overheating
It converts the heat into a faint electric charge
It stores the heat in fatty deposits for the winter
context: Unlike most fish, the great white is partly warm-blooded (regional endothermy): a countercurrent network of blood vessels called the rete mirabile, Latin for 'wonderful net,' traps its own body heat instead of losing it at the gills. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; biologyinsights.com/are-great-white-sharks-warm-blooded.

question: A great white hunts hard in cold seas off California and South Africa, where most fish turn sluggish and its prey slows down. Biologists slipped temperature probes down the throats of great whites swimming in seas between 13 and 16°C. What did the probes read?
answer: Stomach temperatures near 25 to 27 degrees Celsius
choices: Stomach temperatures near 25 to 27 degrees Celsius
Stomach temperatures matching the water almost exactly
Stomach temperatures below freezing, kept liquid by salts
Temperatures that swung wildly with every burst of speed
context: The rete mirabile keeps a great white's swimming muscles, brain, and eyes several degrees warmer than the sea; one study measured stomach temperatures of 24.7 to 26.8 degrees Celsius in water of only about 12.9 to 16.1 degrees. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark.

question: A great white keeps its swimming muscles, brain and eyes warmer than the cold sea around it, so its muscles work faster and its senses stay sharp. Its fast relatives in the mackerel shark family share that trait. Which two sharks are among them?
answer: The shortfin mako and the salmon shark
choices: The shortfin mako and the salmon shark
The whale shark and the basking shark
The tiger shark and the bull shark
The hammerhead and the nurse shark
context: The warm-blooded trait is a family trait shared by all the mackerel sharks (family Lamnidae), including the great white's fast cousins the shortfin mako and the salmon shark. Source: sharks4kids.com/post/2019/01/31/endothermic-sharks; biologyinsights.com/are-great-white-sharks-warm-blooded.

question: A great white waits in the water far beneath a seal swimming off Seal Island, in False Bay, South Africa, then rockets straight up so hard its whole body can clear the surface. Researchers gave this vertical strike a nickname. What did they call it?
answer: The 'Polaris' breach
choices: The 'Polaris' breach
The 'Torpedo' roll
The 'Kraken' rise
The 'Thunder' lunge
context: At Seal Island, great whites hunt by lurking below and rocketing straight up at a seal, an ambush so violent the shark often launches its whole body clear of the surface. Researchers named this vertical strike the 'Polaris' breach, after the submarine-launched missile. Source: elasmo-research.org/education/white_shark/predation.htm; sharkdivingmosselbay.co.za/seal-island.

question: A great white rises from deep water toward an unsuspecting seal swimming at the surface. Like many ocean hunters, it is dark gray on its back and chalky white on its belly. Which part of that coloring hides it from the seal above, and how?
answer: Its dark back, blending into the dim water below
choices: Its dark back, blending into the dim water below
Its white belly, blending with the bright surface above
Its white belly, flashing sunlight to dazzle the seal
Its dark back, passing for a rock on the seafloor
context: This is countershading. Seen from above, the shark's dark gray back melts into the dim water beneath it, so a seal at the surface rarely spots the attacker rising from below at over 40 km/h; the white belly does the opposite job, hiding the shark against the bright surface from anything looking up from below. Source: Wikipedia, 'Countershading'; Wikipedia, 'Great white shark'.

question: Researchers at Seal Island spent years watching great whites hurl themselves at young Cape fur seals, counting how often a strike landed. Each strike is a breach, the shark rocketing up from far below. About how often does a breach attack succeed?
answer: Only about half the time, near 47 percent
choices: Only about half the time, near 47 percent
Almost always, near 95 percent
Rarely, near 5 percent
Every single time once launched
context: Long-term study at Seal Island found the success rate of a breach attack is only about 47 percent, so young Cape fur seals frequently escape. Source: sharkdivingmosselbay.co.za/seal-island; sharkresearch.earth.miami.edu.

question: California's Monterey Bay Aquarium once kept a young great white on show and then released it to the sea, a record run for a species that almost never survives in captivity. How long did that record run last?
answer: About 198 days
choices: About 198 days
About 5 years
About 20 years
About 3 days
context: No aquarium can keep a great white for long. The Monterey Bay Aquarium is the only one ever to display one successfully, and its record was 198 days in 2004 to 2005 before the young shark was released back into the wild. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monterey_Bay_Aquarium; pbs.org/wnet/nature/oceans-in-glass.

question: A great white penned in an aquarium tank keeps hurting itself against the walls and often refuses to eat; the species almost never survives in captivity. Part of the trouble is the way it breathes. What must a great white do every hour of its life to get oxygen?
answer: Keep swimming constantly to push water over its gills
choices: Keep swimming constantly to push water over its gills
Surface regularly to gulp air like a whale
Pump its cheeks to draw water while resting
Absorb oxygen through its skin when still
context: Great whites fail in tanks because they must swim constantly to push water over their gills to breathe, and they roam such distances that in a tank they injure themselves swimming into walls and often refuse to eat. Source: a-z-animals.com/animals/great-white-shark/facts; thejakartapost.com/life/2019/07/06.

question: California's great whites set off each year on a long journey out to a barren patch of the mid-Pacific between Baja and Hawaii, and satellite tags show them lingering there for months. Scientists gave that lonely spot a nickname. What did they call it?
answer: The 'White Shark Cafe'
choices: The 'White Shark Cafe'
The 'Blue Desert'
The 'Shark Graveyard'
The 'Midnight Reef'
context: California's great whites make an epic open-ocean migration to a barren patch of the mid-Pacific between Baja and Hawaii that scientists nicknamed the 'White Shark Cafe,' where they linger for months before returning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; sharkstewards.org/sharktober.

question: A Woods Hole team counted the growth bands in great white sharks' backbones in 2014, much as a forester counts the rings in a tree stump. Biologists had thought the sharks lived a few decades, maybe twenty or thirty years at most. How long can a great white live?
answer: Over 70 years
choices: Over 70 years
About 15 years
About 200 years
About 500 years
context: Great whites are among the longest-lived cartilaginous fish: a 2014 age study estimated they can reach over 70 years old, far older than scientists once believed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; fisheries.noaa.gov/species/white-shark.

question: Divers who swam beside Deep Blue, a female great white caught on film near Guadalupe Island, Mexico, in 2013, looked like small children next to her. Thought to be around 50 years old, she is one of the largest great whites ever filmed. Roughly how long is she?
answer: About 6 metres, some 20 feet
choices: About 6 metres, some 20 feet
About 3 metres, some 10 feet
About 12 metres, some 40 feet
About 1 metre, some 3 feet
context: 'Deep Blue,' filmed off Guadalupe Island and thought to be roughly 6 m (20 ft) long and about 50 years old, is one of the biggest great whites ever caught on camera. Source: surfertoday.com/environment/who-is-the-deep-blue-shark.

question: A great white's teeth look like shrunken copies of the giant megalodon's, so people long assumed it was that monster's dwindled descendant. Fossils of an in-between shark from Peru, its teeth caught partway through growing serrations, point to a different ancestor. What did the great white evolve from?
answer: A broad-toothed mako shark, not megalodon
choices: A broad-toothed mako shark, not megalodon
A shrunken, cold-water line of megalodon
An early hammerhead that lost its head-wings
A deep-sea goblin shark that moved to the surface
context: The great white (Carcharodon carcharias) descends not from megalodon but from a lineage of broad-toothed mako sharks (Cosmopolitodus/Carcharodon hastalis). The transitional Carcharodon hubbelli, described by Dana Ehret from Peru's Pisco Formation (about 6.5 million years old), preserves teeth mid-way through developing serrations. Megalodon sits in a separate family (Otodontidae, genus Otodus), and the tooth resemblance is now read as convergent evolution, not close kinship. One paleontologist quipped that fewer people believe the megatooth sharks are related to great whites than believe the Earth is flat. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, 'Shark Teeth Tell Great White Shark Evolution Story'; Florida Museum of Natural History (Ehret et al. 2012, Palaeontology); Wikipedia 'Great white shark' and 'Carcharodon hubbelli'.

question: A great white mother carries her pups for about a year, and several are born together, large and strong. Sand tiger shark embryos, by contrast, eat their unborn siblings until a single survivor is born. How do the great white pups feed in the womb without turning on each other?
answer: They eat unfertilised eggs, not their siblings
choices: They eat unfertilised eggs, not their siblings
They live off a huge yolk sac until birth
A cord ferries the mother's blood into each pup
They absorb nutrients straight through their skin
context: Great white embryos feed by oophagy, swallowing dozens of unfertilised nutrient eggs (one study counted 50 to 70 egg capsules per uterus) and drinking a lipid-rich 'uterine milk' the mother secretes, a process called lipid histotrophy documented at over 79 litres in one female. Because separate nutrient eggs are on offer, several embryos coexist and are born large and robust after roughly 12 months of gestation, rather than devouring their siblings the way sand tiger pups famously do. Source: Sato et al., 'How great white sharks nourish their embryos... lipid histotrophy in lamnoid shark reproduction' (PMC5051657, ncbi.nlm.nih.gov); Wikipedia 'Great white shark'.

question: A sluggish giant cruises the pitch-black, near-freezing water of the Arctic Ocean and the North Atlantic, hundreds of meters down. It can reach 21 feet, about 6.4 meters, and weigh over 1,000 kilograms. What is it?
answer: Greenland shark
choices: Greenland shark
Bull shark
Reef manta ray
Blue marlin
context: The Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) reaches about 6.4 m (21 ft) and over 1,000 kg (2,200+ lb), living in water from -1.1C to 7.4C at depths of 100 to 1,200 m. Source: Wikipedia 'Greenland shark' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_shark).

question: Almost every Greenland shark in the deep Arctic hosts a pinkish-white hitchhiker, a small copepod named Ommatokoita elongata. The copepod clamps onto one spot on the shark and feeds there, on the living shark, for years. Where on the shark does it make its home?
answer: on the cornea of each eye
choices: on the cornea of each eye
in the gill slits
inside the nostrils
on the tip of the snout
context: The ~30 mm copepod anchors to the cornea of each eye and, as it feeds, scars and clouds it, leaving the shark nearly blind. Source: Wikipedia 'Ommatokoita' and 'Greenland shark'; Ocean Action Hub (oceanactionhub.org/greenland-shark-eye-parasite/).

question: A Greenland shark, the sluggish giant of the Arctic deep, hunts half a mile below the surface, where almost no sunlight reaches. It is nearly blind, though eyes would be of little use there anyway. How does it find the prey it cannot see?
answer: a powerful sense of smell
choices: a powerful sense of smell
echolocation clicks
a lateral heat-sensing pit
bioluminescent lures
context: In the lightless deep the shark hunts by smell, aided by electroreceptive pores on its snout to detect prey it cannot see. Source: Wikipedia 'Greenland shark'; Institute for Environmental Research and Education (iere.org/why-do-greenland-sharks-have-parasites-in-their-eyes/).

question: A Greenland shark creeps along at roughly a foot each second, slower for its size than any other fish measured, and a healthy seal can easily outswim it. Yet fresh seal remains keep turning up in its stomach. How does so slow a shark catch a seal?
answer: it creeps up on seals asleep in the water
choices: it creeps up on seals asleep in the water
it herds them into shallow bays to trap them
it stuns them with a jolt of electricity
it waits at breathing holes to ambush them
context: Scientists think the shark sneaks up on seals dozing in the water, where they sleep to hide from polar bears, only to be caught by the silent, creeping shark. Source: Watanabe et al. 2012, J. Exp. Marine Biology and Ecology; NBC News (nbcnews.com/id/wbna47952603); Live Science.

question: A Greenland shark loads its tissues with urea to keep from freezing, but urea has a nasty side effect: on its own it creeps between proteins and pries them apart, unfolding them into useless tangles. The shark survives only because a second molecule, TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide), is always there. What does TMAO do?
answer: it holds the proteins folded and also braces them against the crushing deep-sea pressure
choices: it holds the proteins folded and also braces them against the crushing deep-sea pressure
it drives the leftover urea back out through the gills and into the surrounding seawater
it hardens into microscopic crystals that seal each protein away from the roaming urea
it seeps into the skin so that predators taste the bitter poison and spit the shark back out
context: The shark's flesh is a two-molecule pressure-armor system. Urea alone accumulates at a protein's surface and unfolds it, but TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide) counteracts both urea's damage and the protein-crushing effect of deep-sea hydrostatic pressure, so TMAO concentration rises with depth. PNAS 2024 work shows TMAO physically strips urea out of the water shell around proteins. The same chemistry that makes the raw meat toxic to eat is what keeps the shark's own proteins from unfolding in the freezing, high-pressure deep. Source: 'Trimethylamine-N-oxide depletes urea in a peptide solvation shell,' PNAS 2024 (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2317825121); Yancey et al., 'Unusual organic osmolytes in deep-sea animals.'

question: Nielsen's team set out in 2016 to learn how old Greenland sharks get, using the carbon-14 left in the sea by atomic bomb tests in the 1950s and 1960s. They read the cores of the sharks' eye lenses, and the bomb's mark turned up in some sharks but not in others. Which sharks carried it?
answer: only the smallest sharks, meaning the giant ones were already alive before the tests
choices: only the smallest sharks, meaning the giant ones were already alive before the tests
only the largest sharks, meaning they had been feeding most recently near the surface
every shark alike, since the carbon spread evenly through the whole ocean at once
only the female sharks, since a mother passes the carbon to her pups during pregnancy
context: The 2016 Nielsen study dated 28 female sharks (81-502 cm). Only the smallest sharks (about 220 cm or under) carried the bomb-pulse spike of carbon-14, proving those individuals were born after roughly 1960, while the big ones predated the atomic age entirely. This calibration pegged sexual maturity at about 156 plus or minus 22 years and the largest 5-meter shark at roughly 392 plus or minus 120 years old. Source: Nielsen et al. 2016, Science 353:702 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaf1703); ScienceDaily 2016-08-11.

question: A young crab's hard shell guards it like a suit of armor, but once the shell has set, it cannot stretch even a millimeter. How does a crab locked inside such stiff armor manage to grow?
answer: It sheds the whole shell and swells into a bigger new one
choices: It sheds the whole shell and swells into a bigger new one
It grows extra shell around the seams to widen the fit
It moves into a bigger empty shell that it finds
It adds new rings of shell along the outer edges
context: This shedding is called molting, or ecdysis. Because a hardened exoskeleton cannot be enlarged, the animal grows a new soft skeleton underneath, climbs out of the old one, and puffs up to a bigger size before the new shell sets. Source: Britannica, Ecdysis; EBSCO Exoskeletons ('Once formed and hardened, an exoskeleton cannot be enlarged').

question: After 13 or 17 years underground, a periodical cicada nymph climbs a tree at night, splits open along its back and hauls itself out one leg at a time. Its new shell has not yet set, and its adult colors have not come in. What does the fresh cicada look like in those first hours?
answer: Soft and ghostly pale - often white or light green
choices: Soft and ghostly pale - often white or light green
Deep brown, the same color as the shell it just left behind
Bright red as a warning to predators
Translucent like clear glass, showing its organs
context: A freshly emerged cicada is soft and pale - often white or light green - which earns it the nickname 'ghost cicada' until its body hardens, its wings expand, and its true colors come in within a few hours. Source: a-z-animals.com cicada crawl-out article; spiderzoon.com cicada-nymph.

question: A young garden spider spinning its web in a hedge loses one of its eight legs to a robin's beak. It will not stay seven-legged: spiders shed their whole outer skin to grow, and at its next molt a new leg appears. What is the new leg like at first?
answer: It is smaller and paler, catching up over later molts
choices: It is smaller and paler, catching up over later molts
It comes back full-sized and fully colored right away
It grows back longer than the leg it replaced
It grows back thicker and stronger than before
context: A spider can regenerate a lost leg at a molt. The new leg first emerges thinner, shorter, and paler than the original, then grows toward full size over the next two to four molts. Source: academicpath.org 'Can Spiders Regrow Legs'; pestwhisperer.com Spider Molting; NCBI PMC12211592.

question: A lobster that has just molted lies on the seabed beside its empty old armor, its new shell as thin as wet paper. Any hungry fish could make a meal of it. Before it hides, what does it often do with the shell it just crawled out of?
answer: Eats its own discarded shell
choices: Eats its own discarded shell
Buries the old shell to hide from predators
Carries the old shell on its back as armor
Leaves at once to find calcium-rich prey
context: After molting, a lobster often devours its own recently vacated shell. The old shell is rich in calcium, which the lobster reuses to harden its new, paper-thin shell faster. Source: lobsteranywhere.com Lobster Molt; parl.ns.ca American Lobster Life Cycle ('devouring their own recently vacated shells').

question: An axolotl, a Mexican salamander that biology labs prize, loses a whole leg and regrows it within 40 to 50 days, bone, muscle, nerves and blood vessels all rebuilt. What is remarkable about how the new leg turns out?
answer: It grows back perfectly, with no scar at all
choices: It grows back perfectly, with no scar at all
It grows back a slightly different color
It grows back smaller and thinner
It grows back covered in protective scales
context: The axolotl regrows an entire limb — bone, muscle, nerves and blood vessels — flawlessly and scar-free in roughly 40 to 50 days. Scar-free healing is exactly what makes it so precious to researchers. Source: Biology Insights (biologyinsights.com); MDI Biological Laboratory (mdibl.org).

question: A lizard grabbed by the tail lets it snap off and sprints away, and within weeks it grows a new one. Under X-rays the replacement turns out to be only a copy: the original ran on a string of small vertebrae of real bone. What forms the skeleton of the regrown tail?
answer: A single unsegmented tube of cartilage
choices: A single unsegmented tube of cartilage
A branching frame of cartilage rods
A chain of tiny cartilage beads
A fresh row of small new vertebrae
context: The replacement tail is not a true tail: instead of a jointed backbone of small vertebrae, its skeleton is one unsegmented tube of cartilage, with no bone at all. Dropping the tail to escape is called autotomy. Source: USC Stem Cell (stemcell.keck.usc.edu/perfect-lizard-tail/); ASU News.

question: Every year a male wapiti, the big deer also called elk, grows a whole new set of antlers, and no mammal grows bone faster. At peak summer growth, how much length can one of his antlers add in a single day?
answer: About 27 millimeters — roughly an inch
choices: About 27 millimeters — roughly an inch
About 3 millimeters — a pencil-tip's width
About 1 millimeter — barely visible
About 100 millimeters — a whole hand's width
context: Antler is the fastest-growing bone known in any mammal, elongating up to ~2 cm a day in big species, with wapiti hitting ~27 mm/day. A brand-new full set regrows annually. Source: NCBI PMC10733395; Alaska Dept. of Fish & Game.

question: A soft, sausage-shaped sea cucumber, cousin to the starfish, inches across the seabed grazing on scraps. When something attacks, it shoots a chunk of its own innards out through its rear, and the mess snares or startles the attacker while it creeps away. What happens to the emptied sea cucumber next?
answer: It regrows the lost organs over a few weeks
choices: It regrows the lost organs over a few weeks
It survives but can never feed again
It seals the wound and lives as an empty shell
It dies within hours from the loss
context: This defensive organ-dumping is called evisceration. Having startled or tangled a predator, the sea cucumber simply regrows the expelled organs over a few weeks. Source: Wikipedia: Evisceration (autotomy); PBS NOVA.

question: A lizard drops its tail to escape a predator and, within weeks, grows a replacement that looks fine from the outside. Inside, the new tail is built quite differently from the one it lost. Compared with the old tail, what is the new one like?
answer: Far less flexible along its whole length
choices: Far less flexible along its whole length
Far more flexible and whip-like
Exactly as bendy as before
Able to grip branches like a hand
context: One solid cartilage tube can't bend at joints the way a segmented backbone can, so the replacement is far less flexible. The lizard trades a perfect tail for a good-enough spare. Source: ASU News — 'Researchers discover regenerated lizard tails are different from originals'.

question: Each year a male deer grows a fresh set of branched, bony antlers wrapped in velvet, a fuzzy living skin rich in nerves and blood that nourishes the bone beneath. In late fall or winter the hardened antlers drop off on their own. What change in his body sets off that yearly fall?
answer: A drop in the deer's testosterone
choices: A drop in the deer's testosterone
A sudden rise in body temperature
The first heavy snowfall of winter
A shortage of calcium in the blood
context: Velvet is the nerve- and blood-vessel-rich skin that feeds fast-growing antler bone. The annual cycle restarts when a drop in testosterone makes the old antlers fall off. Source: Alaska Dept. of Fish & Game; onX Hunt.

question: In a lab dish, scientists slice a planarian, a tiny freshwater flatworm the size of a grain of rice, sideways or lengthwise into pieces, sometimes more than a hundred of them. Each piece then does something remarkable. What does each piece do?
answer: Regrows into a complete worm, whole new head and all
choices: Regrows into a complete worm, whole new head and all
Heals over into a lifeless lump of tissue
Grows back only the tail end, never a head
Fuses back together into the original worm
context: Cut a planarian into pieces and each piece regrows into a complete worm, including a brand-new head and brain. Source: Wikipedia: Planarian; Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (mpg.de).

question: Scientists study the axolotl, a Mexican salamander, in hope of one day healing human patients, because it can rebuild tissues that most animals lose forever. It can even rebuild a whole missing leg. Beyond limbs and tail, what other body parts can it regrow?
answer: Parts of its heart, jaws, brain, and spinal cord
choices: Parts of its heart, jaws, brain, and spinal cord
Its scales, whiskers, and swim bladder
Its skin, but never bone or inner organs
Its bones and muscles, but never nerves
context: The axolotl can regrow its tail, parts of its heart, its jaws, and even portions of its brain and spinal cord — which is why labs study it for possible human spinal-injury repair. Source: MDI Biological Laboratory (mdibl.org); Biology Insights.

question: Researchers blast a planarian with radiation that destroys its neoblasts, the adult stem cells that can turn into any body part and that number a fifth or more of all its cells. The worm can no longer regenerate, and it dies. What single step restores its power?
answer: Transplanting one neoblast back into the worm
choices: Transplanting one neoblast back into the worm
Feeding it a rich diet for several weeks
Placing it in warmer, cleaner water
Cutting it again to trigger a fresh response
context: Up to 20% or more of a planarian's cells are neoblasts. Radiation wipes them out and the worm dies; transplanting a single neoblast back restores regeneration. Source: Wikipedia: Planarian; Whitehead Institute (wi.mit.edu).

question: Crown-of-thorns starfish were eating their way across huge swaths of coral on Australia's Great Barrier Reef in the 1960s, so fishermen set out to destroy them. They chopped the starfish into pieces and tossed the pieces back into the sea. Most starfish can rebuild a whole body from a piece that keeps part of its central disc. What may the fishermen's effort really have done?
answer: It may have multiplied the starfish instead of killing them
choices: It may have multiplied the starfish instead of killing them
It poisoned the reef with rotting starfish
It drove the starfish into deeper water only
It had no effect on the starfish at all
context: Since some starfish regrow whole animals from pieces, chopping them up and returning them to the water may have accidentally multiplied the crown-of-thorns rather than killing them. Source: Wikipedia: Starfish regeneration.

question: Nineteenth-century scientists called the planarian, a little freshwater flatworm, 'immortal under the edge of a knife.' Later biologists put that to the test, slicing planarians into ever smaller scraps to find the tiniest piece that could still rebuild a whole worm. How small a fragment proved to be enough?
answer: About 1/279th of the worm
choices: About 1/279th of the worm
About one-tenth of the worm
About one-half of the worm
About one-thousandth of the worm
context: A fragment as small as 1/279th of a planarian can still rebuild a complete new animal — hence 'immortal under the edge of a knife.' Source: Wikipedia: Planarian.

question: A cut planarian regrows its lost parts under the direction of a chemical signal, the Wnt pathway, that decides for each cut end which part it becomes, head or tail. Scientists blocked that signal in a piece as it grew back. What grew where the tail should have formed?
answer: A second head — a two-headed worm
choices: A second head — a two-headed worm
No head at all, just a blunt stump
A body twice its normal length
A second, separate worm splitting off
context: Disrupting the Wnt/beta-catenin signal (or applying an electric field) makes a fragment grow a head where a tail should be — a two-headed planarian. Source: IFLScience; Whitehead Institute (wi.mit.edu).

question: Within a week of losing a leg, an axolotl grows a bud of new cells at the stump, and that bud goes on to rebuild cartilage, muscle and nerve. Adults of most other salamanders cannot do this. What odd fact about the axolotl's whole life do scientists tie to this power?
answer: It never fully grows up, keeping feathery gills and a larval body for life
choices: It never fully grows up, keeping feathery gills and a larval body for life
It swaps to breathing air and crawls onto land as it matures
It sheds and completely regrows its skin every few weeks
It slows its heartbeat to a near halt while a limb rebuilds
context: The axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) is neotenic, or paedomorphic: it never undergoes the metamorphosis that turns other salamanders into land animals, staying in a larval-like aquatic form with external feathery gills for life. That retained embryonic-like state is tied to its exceptional regenerative power. The blastema begins forming about 5–7 days after amputation, reaches an initial 1–2 mm, and peaks in cell proliferation around 14–21 days; its multipotent cells rebuild cartilage, muscle, and connective tissue while retaining positional memory. Source: Grokipedia 'Blastema' (timeline: 5–7 day onset, 1–2 mm, 14–21 day peak proliferation) and Grokipedia 'Axolotl' (neoteny).

question: A stag's velvet antler grows at a racing pace, driven so hard by growth-factor genes that its gene-expression fingerprint reads closer to a bone tumor than to normal bone. Zoo records put cancer in deer at around five times lower than in other mammals. Which built-in trio does most to keep the antler from turning malignant?
answer: Beefed-up tumor-suppressor genes, mass cell suicide, and the yearly casting of the whole antler
choices: Beefed-up tumor-suppressor genes, mass cell suicide, and the yearly casting of the whole antler
A chilled antler core, a hard blood cutoff at full size, and a mineral shell that seals the tip
An immune sheath that devours mutant cells, an acidic core, and a scab coat over the beam
A frozen store of stem cells, a walled-off growth zone, and a nightly pause in cell division
context: A fast-growing antler's gene-expression profile correlates more strongly with osteosarcoma, bone cancer (r = 0.67–0.78), than with normal bone (r = 0.33–0.47). Three proto-oncogenes (FOS, FAM83A, REL) are under positive selection in deer and cancer-promoting growth-factor genes (FGF19, FGF21, PDGFD) run hot. Deer restrain this with tumor-suppressor genes under positive selection — the p53-regulator PML shows the strongest selection signal of all — plus massive apoptosis (up to ~64% of cells in the inner antler layer are programmed to die) and the annual casting of the hardened antler, which physically discards any rogue cells. Zoo records show deer get cancer roughly 5x less often than other mammals. Source: PMC10733395 'Deer antlers: the fastest growing tissue with least cancer occurrence'; genetics corroborated by Science 2019 (doi:10.1126/science.aav6335).

question: Far below the sunlit surface of the open ocean, a slim deep-sea eel with only tiny teeth drifts in the dark as a shrimp swims by. It cannot chase quick prey through the blackness. How does it snatch a meal in an instant?
answer: Its mouth balloons open into a pouch bigger than its body
choices: Its mouth balloons open into a pouch bigger than its body
It fires a jet of venom that stuns the passing shrimp
It wraps its long tail around the prey and crushes it
It buries itself in the seafloor mud to ambush from below
context: The pelican eel (Eurypharynx pelecanoides) is famous for a mouth that balloons open into a huge pelican-like pouch, scooping up prey much larger than its own body in the empty deep. Source: Nautilus Live (nautiluslive.org/video/2018/09/20/gulper-eel-balloons-its-massive-jaws).

question: The pelican eel drifts through the deep ocean with a huge, gaping mouth that looks built to swallow big fish whole, the way a pelican gulps a herring. Inside it, though, are only tiny teeth and a thin, delicate jaw. What does the eel mostly eat?
answer: Small crustaceans it nets from the drifting water
choices: Small crustaceans it nets from the drifting water
Other eels nearly as long as itself
Jellyfish drifting through the dark
Chunks of whale carcass fallen to the seafloor
context: Despite its monstrous gape and tiny teeth, the pelican eel mostly eats small crustaceans, along with some squid and other small invertebrates -- the huge mouth is an all-purpose net for whatever rare meal drifts by, not a tool for swallowing big fish. Source: Wikipedia: Pelican eel (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelican_eel).

question: A pelican eel drifts far down in the pitch dark, its body tapering into a long, whip-thin tail that trails far behind it. At the very tip of that tail sits one special structure. What is it?
answer: A glowing organ that flashes pink and red
choices: A glowing organ that flashes pink and red
A cluster of taste buds that smells prey in the water
A whip-like flap it lashes to stir up drifting food
A dense knot of nerves that senses nearby movement
context: The eel's whip-thin tail is tipped with a bioluminescent organ that shines pink and gives off occasional bright red flashes -- a lure it may wave to draw prey toward its open mouth. Source: Wikipedia: Pelican eel (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelican_eel).

question: A pelican eel hangs in the dark water between 500 and 3,000 meters down, where food is scarce, and it does not sink. Yet it has no swim bladder, the gas-filled float most fish use. How is its body thought to stay afloat?
answer: Jelly-filled spaces around its backbone hold it up
choices: Jelly-filled spaces around its backbone hold it up
Large gulps of swallowed air trapped in its gut
Broad oily fins that spread its weight across the water
Constant slow swimming that keeps it from sinking
context: The pelican eel has no swim bladder. A gelatinous substance fills spaces around its backbone, and scientists think it does the swim bladder's job of keeping the eel afloat -- a cheap, low-energy body plan for a place where food is scarce. Source: Wikipedia: Pelican eel (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelican_eel).

question: The horror frog, as people nickname the hairy frog, sits plump and harmless-looking on a wet leaf in Cameroon. Then a predator grabs it, and it fights back in one of the strangest ways known in any animal. What does it do?
answer: It breaks its own toe bones and pushes them out as claws
choices: It breaks its own toe bones and pushes them out as claws
It inflates its body until the attacker cannot bite it
It squirts foul, sticky slime from glands on its spine
It sheds its tail, which keeps twitching as a decoy
context: This is why it earned the nicknames 'horror frog' and 'Wolverine frog.' At rest there are no claws to see at all; the frog literally wounds itself to arm itself when threatened. A 2008 study of museum specimens found such claws in 11 African frog species. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog; Blackburn, Hanken & Jenkins 2008, 'Concealed weapons: erectile claws in African frogs,' Biology Letters.

question: When a predator grabs a hairy frog in Cameroon, sharp claws burst from its back feet. A cat's claw and an eagle's talon are each a bone inside a hard sheath of keratin. What are the hairy frog's claws made of?
answer: Bare bone, its own toe-bones with no sheath
choices: Bare bone, its own toe-bones with no sheath
Stiffened hairs matted together with dried slime
Curved spurs of keratin like a rooster's
Hollow quills that snap off in the wound
context: Unlike a cat's or a bird's claw, the hairy frog's claws have no hard outer sheath. They are simply the frog's own toe-bones, sharpened and punched out raw through the skin of the foot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog; Blackburn et al. 2008, Biology Letters.

question: The male hairy frog grows what looks like a coat of 'hair' along his flanks and thighs in the breeding season, made of thin fringes of skin. But it is not hair at all. What are those fringes actually for?
answer: Soaking up extra oxygen from the water so he can stay under longer
choices: Soaking up extra oxygen from the water so he can stay under longer
Trapping a warm layer of air to survive cold mountain streams
Sensing ripples in the water to detect an approaching predator
Attracting females by shimmering in the light like a lure
context: The 'hair' is really fringes of thin skin flaps (dermal papillae) packed with tiny blood vessels, working like external gills. The male grows them so he can breathe underwater for long stretches while standing guard over the clutch of eggs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog; iere.org/what-is-the-hairy-frog-and-why-is-it-hairy.

question: Scientists studying museum specimens of the hairy frog, a plump frog of Cameroon's rainforest streams, have worked out how its claws are pushed out of its hind feet when it is threatened. One part of the trick still has them stumped. What is it?
answer: How the claw ever goes back in once the danger has passed
choices: How the claw ever goes back in once the danger has passed
Which of the toes fire their claws first when the frog is grabbed
How the frog avoids bleeding to death from the self-inflicted wound
Why only the males, and never the females, can grow the claws
context: The extension is well documented, but researchers can only hypothesize that the claw slides back passively as the torn skin heals. That 'retract-and-heal' half of the story is still unconfirmed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog, which states the retraction mechanism 'is not known' and is only hypothesized.

question: Scientists drew Hallucigenia, a fingernail-sized, worm-shaped creature from Canada's Burgess Shale, upside down for decades, mistaking its row of stiff spines for legs. Around 1991, researchers drilled into the rock that covered better fossils and found what that rock had hidden for over 500 million years. What was it?
answer: A row of soft clawed walking legs
choices: A row of soft clawed walking legs
A fringe of feeding tentacles
A set of gripping suckers
A line of breathing gills
context: Flipped right-side up, Hallucigenia walked on soft clawed legs while the roughly seven pairs of stiff spines stood up along its back as protection. Researchers found the second row of walking legs by drilling out rock that had hidden it. Source: PalaeontologyOnline.com; fossilguy.com (Ramskold and Hou).

question: Scientists long read a dark blob at one end of Hallucigenia, a tiny worm-shaped animal from the Cambrian seas preserved in Canada's Burgess Shale, as its head. In 2015 a study showed what the blob really was, and the true head turned out to be at the other end. What was the blob?
answer: Decay fluids squeezed out of the body
choices: Decay fluids squeezed out of the body
A cluster of unhatched eggs
A bundle of grasping tentacles
A hard shell it retreated into
context: The blob was decay fluid or gut contents that had oozed from the body during fossilization; the real head was at the opposite end. So scientists had the animal not only upside down but back-to-front. Under an electron microscope the true head showed a simple face with a pair of eyes and a ring of plates around a mouth lined with tiny needle-like teeth. Source: Smith and Caron 2015, Nature; PalaeontologyOnline.com; ROM.

question: Once scientists turned Hallucigenia right side up in the 1990s, its claws gave away its family tree. Each claw is three cones stacked one inside another, like paper cups nested together, and only one living group of animals has claws built that way. Which group?
answer: Velvet worms
choices: Velvet worms
Sea urchins
Horseshoe crabs
Tardigrades
context: The nested-cone claws match those of today's velvet worms (onychophorans), soft caterpillar-like animals. Hallucigenia sits near the base of the lineage that also led to insects, spiders, and crustaceans. It remains the classic textbook lesson in how hard the strangest Cambrian fossils are to read. Source: Smith & Ortega-Hernandez 2014, Nature 514:363, 'Hallucigenia's onychophoran-like claws and the case for Tactopoda'; ROM; Wikipedia.

question: On a warm coral reef, a shark cruises just above the sand, its head spread sideways into a flat crossbar with an eye set at either end. No diver who sees that shape mistakes it for any other shark. Which shark is it?
answer: Hammerhead shark
choices: Hammerhead shark
Tiger shark
Nurse shark
Lemon shark
context: That flattened head has a real name: the cephalofoil, or 'head-wing.' It is not a random shape but a sensory wing that spreads the shark's detectors far apart across its width. Source: Cape May Whale Watch & Research Center, 'The Hydrodynamic Head Of Hammerhead Sharks.'

question: Off a warm tropical coast, hammerheads cruise the water, most of them 5 to 10 feet long. One kind dwarfs the rest of the family: it averages about 15 feet, and the biggest come close to 20. Which hammerhead is the biggest?
answer: Great hammerhead
choices: Great hammerhead
Scalloped hammerhead
Bonnethead
Winghead shark
context: The great hammerhead (Sphyrna mokarran) tops the family at roughly 4.6 m on average, with the largest reaching around 6.1 m. Source: Wikipedia, 'Great hammerhead'; Florida Museum Discover Fishes.

question: A hammerhead cruises off a coral reef, sweeping its wide, flat head in slow curves low over bare sand. Suddenly it stops, drives its snout into the seafloor and digs out a stingray that lay buried and motionless where nothing showed at all. What was the shark's head picking up from the hidden ray?
answer: The faint electric fields of the buried ray
choices: The faint electric fields of the buried ray
The warmth rising off the buried ray
The ray's shadow cast on the sand
Vibrations from the ray's flicking tail
context: The underside of the hammer is studded with ampullae of Lorenzini, jelly-filled pores that sense the tiny electric fields of living animals. The wide head spreads them into a broad array, so the shark sweeps the seafloor like a wide-beam metal detector, feeling for prey it cannot see. Source: Reef Check, 'Why Do Hammerheads Have Hammer Heads'; Elasmo Research, 'Sandy Plains: Great Hammerhead Shark.'

question: Michelle McComb caught several kinds of hammerhead in the 2000s, sharks with an eye at each far tip of a wide, T-shaped head. She swept small flashing lights all around each one and recorded every eye's electrical response. What did her tests reveal?
answer: A nearly 360-degree field of view
choices: A nearly 360-degree field of view
A pair of long-range zoom eyes
Eyes that glow to light the seabed
A blind spot it herds prey into
context: An eye on each tip gives the shark a view almost all the way around itself, above and below, at once. McComb recorded the eyes' electrical response to light swept around the animal to prove the wraparound coverage. Source: Live Science, 'Hammerhead Sharks See 360 Degrees in Stereo'; McComb et al., Journal of Experimental Biology 2009.

question: A hammerhead follows a trail of scent with its two nostrils set far apart, out at the tips of its wide head. Stephen Kajiura's team argued that this spacing may give it an edge over a narrow-headed shark. What could the wide-set nose help it work out?
answer: Which direction a smell is coming from
choices: Which direction a smell is coming from
How far off the food still is
How big the hidden prey must be
Whether the prey is alive or dead
context: The idea is smelling in stereo: with nostrils far apart, a scent can reach one nostril sooner or more strongly than the other, telling the shark which way to turn. Kajiura's team found that the broad spacing could improve a hammerhead's ability to resolve the direction of a scent trail, though whether hammerheads truly smell better than other sharks is still debated. Source: Kajiura, Forni & Summers 2005, 'Olfactory morphology of carcharhinid and sphyrnid sharks: does the cephalofoil confer a sensory advantage?' (PubMed 15549717); BBC Earth, 'Why do hammerhead sharks look like that?' (2015).

question: A hammerhead hunting stingrays on the sandy seabed knocks one flat with a hard blow from above. Then, before it bites into the ray's wings, it makes a move no other shark makes. What is its next move?
answer: Pinning the ray flat with its own head
choices: Pinning the ray flat with its own head
Wrapping the ray up in its long tail
Spinning hard to tear the ray loose
Swallowing the ray whole in one gulp
context: The head is both sensor and sledgehammer: it knocks the ray down, pins it with the flat of the hammer, then pivots to feed. The great hammerhead even eats rays whole, venomous tail-spine and all; one caught off Florida had 96 stingray spines lodged in and around its mouth and was barely bothered. Source: Wikipedia, 'Great hammerhead,' citing Strong et al. Bahamas field observations.

question: Scalloped hammerheads, with a wavy front edge on their T-shaped heads, hunt alone through the open ocean at night. By day off Cocos Island, a volcanic island in the Pacific off Costa Rica, hundreds of these lone hunters mass in a slow-circling school. Where do the daytime crowds gather?
answer: Over an underwater mountain
choices: Over an underwater mountain
Inside a coral lagoon
Along a deep-sea trench
Around a sunken shipwreck
context: These underwater mountains are called seamounts. The most famous gathering is at the Alcyone seamount off Cocos Island, Costa Rica, where from June to September divers see schools of hundreds. Cocos, the Galapagos, and Malpelo form a route divers call the 'Hammerhead Triangle.' Source: PLOS One, Cocos Island scalloped hammerhead study; Diveplanit, 'The Hammerhead Triangle.'

question: A small tropical member of the hammerhead family wears a head so extreme that it stretches, wingtip to wingtip, nearly half the length of its whole body. No other hammerhead has a head so wide for its size. Which shark is it?
answer: The winghead shark
choices: The winghead shark
The bonnethead
The smalleye hammerhead
The scoophead
context: The winghead (Eusphyra blochii) has the most extreme cephalofoil of all, about 40-50% of its body length, versus roughly 23-27% for the great hammerhead. The wider the head, the farther apart its sensors and the wider its sensory sweep. Source: Aussie Animals, 'Winghead Shark'; Wikipedia, 'Great hammerhead.'

question: A scalloped hammerhead plunges below 800 meters into water close to freezing to hunt, yet its swimming muscles stay warm all the way down. Mark Royer tagged these sharks, filmed one at 1,044 meters, and found out how. What does the shark do on the way down?
answer: It clamps its gill slits shut the entire dive
choices: It clamps its gill slits shut the entire dive
It shunts warm blood inward away from the skin
It shivers its swimming muscles to make heat
It rides down inside a pocket of warmer water
context: The gills are where a fish's warm blood meets the sea across a thin membrane, so in 5C water at depth they would strip the shark's body heat away in minutes. By clamping the gill slits shut and holding its breath -- about 17 minutes per dive, with only ~4 minutes spent hunting on the bottom before it races back up to breathe -- the scalloped hammerhead seals off that heat leak, and tagged muscle temperature stays warm all the way down, cooling only as it nears the surface and opens its gills again. Source: Royer et al., 'Breath holding as a thermoregulation strategy in the deep-diving scalloped hammerhead shark,' Science (2023), DOI 10.1126/science.add4445, https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.add4445 ; ScienceDaily 2023-05-11 https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2023/05/230511164453.htm

question: A female bonnethead, a small shovel-headed hammerhead, had spent three years in a tank at an Omaha zoo with no male shark anywhere near her when, in 2001, she produced a healthy pup. Scientists ran DNA tests on the newborn. How was the pup made?
answer: Her egg grew into a pup with no sperm at all
choices: Her egg grew into a pup with no sperm at all
She had stored a male's sperm for those three years
A second female in the tank had fertilised her eggs
A shred of her own body tissue budded into a pup
context: Stored sperm was the obvious suspect -- some sharks bank it for months -- but the pup's DNA held only its mother's genetic material, ruling that out and marking the first genetically confirmed virgin birth (parthenogenesis) in any shark. The mechanism is automictic parthenogenesis: the unfertilised egg fuses with a sister cell (a polar body) from its own meiosis instead of a sperm, so the pup is homozygous, essentially a half-clone of the mother. Source: Chapman, Shivji et al., 'Virgin birth in a hammerhead shark,' Biology Letters 3(4):425-427 (2007), DOI 10.1098/rsbl.2007.0189, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2390672/

question: A tiny, brightly colored handfish makes its way across the cool seafloor of Tasmania's coast, though it is a hopeless swimmer. Lifted into open water, it barely gets anywhere. How does it get around the bottom?
answer: It walks step by step on hand-like fins
choices: It walks step by step on hand-like fins
It jets backward by squirting water
It undulates along the sand like an eel
It rides the current wherever it flows
context: The handfish is a poor swimmer that mostly crawls, a slow, sedentary bottom-dweller. It plants its splayed pectoral fins on the sand and pushes itself forward step by step. Those fins are so hand-shaped that the family name comes from the Latin 'bracchium', meaning 'arm'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handfish

question: A mother spotted handfish stands guard over her small cluster of eggs on the Tasmanian seabed. An invasive starfish, the Northern Pacific seastar, which arrived in Tasmania aboard foreign ships, creeps closer, and she plants her body between it and the eggs. How does she drive it off?
answer: She wipes it away with her tail
choices: She wipes it away with her tail
She stabs it with venomous fin spines
She squirts ink to blind it
She bites through its arm
context: A mother spotted handfish defends her eggs from the invasive Northern Pacific seastar by wedging herself between the predator and the eggs and wiping it with her tail to shove it off course. Source: https://handfish.org.au/spawning-behaviour-of-spotted-handfish/

question: Spotted handfish live on just a few patches of seafloor off Tasmania, and once a reef's handfish are gone, new ones almost never arrive, while an ordinary reef emptied of fish fills again in time. Biologists trace the difference to one quirk of how a handfish comes into the world. What is that quirk?
answer: Its young hatch as tiny walkers that never drift out
choices: Its young hatch as tiny walkers that never drift out
Its larvae drift far but survive only on their birth reef
Its females spawn just one clutch in an entire lifetime
Its eggs need a warm current no other reef can supply
context: Handfish have no free-swimming larval stage: the eggs hatch directly into fully-formed miniature adults that drop onto the sand and start walking. Because no larvae drift on the current, a wiped-out reef gets no settlers from anywhere else — the very trait that makes it wondrous also makes it fragile. Handfish also spawn every year, and their hatchlings settle wherever they drop. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handfish

question: Deep in the Amazon rainforest, a huge slate-gray eagle with a bright white belly perches high in the canopy, strong enough to pluck a monkey from the treetops. A double crest of feathers rises on its head. Which bird is it?
answer: The harpy eagle
choices: The harpy eagle
The bald eagle
The peregrine falcon
The snowy owl
context: The harpy eagle (Harpia harpyja) is a huge rainforest eagle of Central and South America -- slate-black above, white below, with a distinctive double crest it can raise on its head. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle.

question: A female harpy eagle grips a branch high in the South American rainforest with talons bigger than any other living eagle's. Her hind talon is nearly 5 inches long. Whose claw is it about as long as?
answer: A grizzly bear's front claw
choices: A grizzly bear's front claw
A house cat's front claw
A jaguar's front claw
A river otter's front claw
context: A female harpy eagle's rear (hind) talon reaches about 12.3 cm -- nearly 5 inches -- roughly the length of a grizzly bear's front claw, the largest talon of any living eagle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle; Audubon '10 Fun Facts About the Harpy Eagle'.

question: A howler monkey clings to a branch high in the canopy as a harpy eagle drops on it. Yet in one study at a nest in Brazil's Amazon, monkeys were not the harpy's main meal: a single kind of prey made up 79 percent of all it ate. What was it?
answer: Sloths
choices: Sloths
Snakes
Fish
Deer
context: At one nest studied at Parintins, in Brazil's Amazon, sloths made up 79% of the harpy eagles' prey. A harpy plucks sloths and monkeys straight off the branches and can carry off prey up to about half its own weight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle.

question: A harpy eagle hunts the Amazon canopy by daylight, snatching monkeys from the branches. Yet around its face it wears a ring of feathers it can raise into a shallow dish, a feature normally found on a night-hunting owl. What does raising that disc do for the eagle?
answer: Funnels faint sounds to its ears
choices: Funnels faint sounds to its ears
Shades its eyes from midday glare
Signals a warning to its mate
Sheds a rainforest downpour
context: Like an owl, the harpy eagle has a facial disc of feathers it can raise to funnel sound to its ears -- rare among diurnal (daytime) raptors -- helping it hear hidden prey before it sees them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle; Los Angeles Zoo.

question: When a pair of harpy eagles, the giant hunters of the Amazon canopy, vanishes from a patch of forest, that forest's harpy population can take many years to recover, even with plenty of sloths and monkeys left to hunt. How often does a harpy pair raise a chick?
answer: Just one chick every 2-3 years
choices: Just one chick every 2-3 years
One chick every single year
Two chicks raised every year
A clutch of four each spring
context: A harpy eagle pair raises just one chick every 2-3 years -- one of the slowest reproduction rates of any eagle -- which is why the species is so vulnerable to habitat loss. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle; Audubon.

question: A small silver hatchetfish hangs hundreds of meters down in the ocean's twilight zone, where no rock or seaweed offers cover. Hunters below it look up for dark shapes against the faint light from above. How does it hide its shadow?
answer: Shines rows of lights along its belly
choices: Shines rows of lights along its belly
Squirts a cloud of black ink
Folds its fins to shrink its outline
Turns its skin bright coral red
context: This is called counter-illumination. Rows of light organs (photophores) along the hatchetfish's belly glow pale blue and shine downward, matching the faint sunlight from above so a predator looking up sees only background light and no dark silhouette. In the open ocean the best way to vanish is not to be dark but to make light of its own. Sources: https://twilightzone.whoi.edu/explore-the-otz/creature-features/hatchetfish/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_hatchetfish

question: In the twilight zone of the deep ocean, where only faint blue light filters down, a marine hatchetfish almost vanishes when seen head-on. Yet when it turns sideways, it flashes a wide, silver flank. What about its body pulls off that vanishing act?
answer: Its body is a thin blade, flattened side-to-side
choices: Its body is a thin blade, flattened side-to-side
Its scales fold flat like closing shutters
Its skin turns clear as glass on cue
It hollows out a see-through gap down its middle
context: The body is a thin silver blade, so compressed side-to-side that seen edge-on it is nearly two-dimensional and almost vanishes, slipping through the water 'with barely a trace.' That hatchet-blade shape is what gives the fish its name. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_hatchetfish ; https://twilightzone.whoi.edu/explore-the-otz/creature-features/hatchetfish/

question: A hatchetfish of the genus Argyropelecus hunts in the dim twilight zone. Its eyes are nothing like the round domes most fish carry on the sides of their heads, and their odd form is a clue to how it finds food. What shape are they?
answer: Tube-shaped, pointing straight up
choices: Tube-shaped, pointing straight up
Flat, like a pair of coins
Ringed with glowing dots
Split into dozens of tiny lenses
context: Many hatchetfish, most strikingly those of the genus Argyropelecus, have huge tube-shaped eyes that point straight up. Such a fish stares at the dim glow above and spots prey by their dark silhouettes drifting overhead — hunting for shadows against the light, the very same weakness its own glowing belly hides from below. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_hatchetfish

question: Some deep-sea hatchetfish rise each night toward the ocean surface to feed, then sink back into the black twilight zone by dawn. The whole way, the pale-blue lights on a hatchetfish's underside keep glowing. What does it do with those lights on the journey?
answer: Turns them up and down like a dimmer switch
choices: Turns them up and down like a dimmer switch
Flashes them in a fast warning pattern
Swaps their color from blue to green
Pulses them in time with its heartbeat
context: Some hatchetfish species ride a daily vertical migration, rising at night to feed on copepods, ostracods, and fish larvae and sinking back down by dawn. A migrating hatchetfish turns its pale-blue belly lights up or down like a dimmer switch to track the changing brightness of the water, so it keeps erasing its own shadow the whole way. Being able to regulate that intensity gives it an edge over other twilight-zone fish using the same camouflage. Source: https://twilightzone.whoi.edu/explore-the-otz/creature-features/hatchetfish/

question: Down in the deep-sea twilight zone, a hunting fish sweeps a living searchlight through the black water toward a small silver hatchetfish. The hatchetfish's skin is packed with tiny crystals arranged in long parallel bundles. When the hunter's beam sweeps across those crystal bundles, what does the beam become?
answer: A soft, diffuse blur
choices: A soft, diffuse blur
A bright pinpoint glint
A mirror of the hunter's own beam
A ring of rainbow colors
context: The hatchetfish's skin doesn't just mirror light — it is packed with organized guanine crystals arranged in long parallel bundles that scatter light softly in every direction, so a predator's bioluminescent searchlight gets a diffuse blur instead of a bright flash. Penn physicist Alison Sweeney: 'nature is generally quite a bit more sophisticated in how it has evolved to manipulate light.' Source: https://www.futurity.org/hatchetfish-oceans-light-camouflage-1468942-2/

question: An emperor penguin stands barefoot on the Antarctic ice for hours, yet its feet never freeze to the surface. Warm skin would melt the ice into a puddle that would freeze back into a trap, and would bleed away precious heat. How warm does the penguin keep its feet?
answer: just above freezing, cold and cheap
choices: just above freezing, cold and cheap
as warm as its chest and belly
completely numb and bloodless
warmed by a layer of fat in the sole
context: Warm arteries running down into a penguin's legs are bundled right against the cold veins coming back up, so the outgoing blood hands its heat to the returning blood before it reaches the feet. Feet kept just above freezing lose almost no heat and don't melt into the ice. Source: Britannica Blog, 'Penguin Feet: Avoiding Frostbite in the Antarctic'; CoolAntarctica.

question: A penguin waddles across the Antarctic sea ice, and inside each leg, blood heading down to its feet, still hot from its body, passes right alongside chilled blood flowing back up. The two streams run side by side in opposite directions. How does that help the penguin?
answer: the warm blood hands its heat to the blood coming back
choices: the warm blood hands its heat to the blood coming back
the veins keep the arteries from freezing solid
it lets the leg pump blood without a heartbeat
it keeps the feet as warm as the chest
context: This is countercurrent heat exchange: warm blood flowing out runs against cold blood flowing in, and heat leaks across from one to the other, so it is recycled back into the body instead of being flushed out to the freezing feet. Herons and ducks stand for hours in near-freezing water using the same leg bundles. Source: Britannica Blog, 'Penguin Feet'; Biology Insights, 'How Do Penguins Stay Warm'.

question: A swordfish chases fast squid and fish through deep, cold water in the open ocean. A heater organ built from an altered eye muscle warms its brain and eyes by 10 to 15 degrees Celsius above the icy sea. What does a warm-eyed swordfish gain over a cold-eyed fish?
answer: it detects rapid motion far better and spots darting prey
choices: it detects rapid motion far better and spots darting prey
it can see colors invisible to warm-blooded animals
its eyes glow to lure prey in the dark
it never needs to blink while hunting
context: A heated retina responds faster, so the swordfish catches quick-flitting prey a cold-eyed fish would miss. Source: Fritsches, Brill & Warrant, 'Warm Eyes Provide Superior Vision in Swordfishes', Current Biology 2005; Science AAAS, 'Hot Eyes for Cold Fish'.

question: A reindeer wandering the Arctic tundra breathes air at 40 degrees below zero, yet the air reaching its lungs arrives warmed to body temperature. Scroll-like bones inside its nose, wrapped in warm blood vessels, take care of that on the way in. On the way back out, when the reindeer exhales into the cold, those same nose-bones do a second, energy-saving job. What is it?
answer: reclaim the heat and moisture from the outgoing air
choices: reclaim the heat and moisture from the outgoing air
filter frozen dust from the airway
pump extra oxygen into the blood
seal the nostrils shut against the wind
context: The nasal scroll-bones warm every incoming breath from -40 C up to about +38 C, then recover the heat and moisture back out of the exhaled air, so almost nothing is wasted. Source: Blix et al., 'Nasal heat exchange in the reindeer', PubMed 3992062; ScienceDaily, 'The magical reindeer nose'.

question: A whale swimming hard through cold ocean water builds up dangerous heat inside its huge working muscles. Only the flippers and tail flukes are thin and bare-skinned, with no blubber over them. When the whale starts to overheat, what does it do with its flukes?
answer: floods them with warm blood so heat pours into the water
choices: floods them with warm blood so heat pours into the water
clamps their blood vessels shut to hold warmth in
shivers them fast to burn off the extra energy
tucks them tight against the body to shed heat
context: The flippers and flukes are 'thermal windows.' Instead of routing blood through the vein bundles that normally recycle warmth, the overheating whale sends extra blood straight out to the bare skin, so the heat radiates into the sea. The very same countercurrent plumbing that saves heat can run in reverse to dump it. Source: Georgia Dolphin Ecology Program, 'Chill Out, Hot Stuff!'; SeaWorld, 'Baleen Whales - Adaptations'.

question: An opah, a round, silver fish of the deep sea, flaps its wing-like fins without stopping. Tuna and some sharks warm only certain parts of their bodies, such as the swimming muscles. In 2015 scientists measured the opah. What did they find it to be?
answer: warm right through, heart and all
choices: warm right through, heart and all
warm only along its spine
warm only in its eyes and brain
warm only after a fast burst of swimming
context: The opah (Lampris guttatus) is the first fish shown to be whole-body endothermic -- warm all over, heart included, not just in isolated muscle, eye or brain patches like tuna and sharks. It makes heat by constantly flapping its wing-like pectoral fins, then holds that heat in with counter-current vessel nets (retia) sitting right inside its gills -- the one place warm blood would normally dump all its heat straight into the sea. Those gill retia are wrapped in a fat layer with less than half the thermal conductivity of ordinary tissue, insulating the exchanger and letting the opah stay roughly 5 degrees C warmer than the cold water it hunts in. Source: Wegner, N.C., Snodgrass, O.E., Dewar, H. & Hyde, J.R. (2015) 'Whole-body endothermy in a mesopelagic fish, the opah, Lampris guttatus', Science 348(6236):786-790 (DOI 10.1126/science.aaa8902); National Geographic, 'Meet the Comical Opah, the Only Truly Warm-Blooded Fish'.

question: A deep-sea fish fills its swim bladder by forcing oxygen into it against the push of the gas already inside, at pressures of hundreds of atmospheres. Its vessel net manages this because oxygen carried off in the outgoing vein seeps back across into the incoming artery. Why does that let the oxygen keep building?
answer: each loop stacks onto the last, compounding the load
choices: each loop stacks onto the last, compounding the load
a molecular pump spends ATP to force gas across
the sluggish blood simply gives the gas more soak time
a vast folded surface lets more gas cross at once
context: The gill rete is a simple countercurrent EXCHANGER -- it just recovers heat or oxygen as two bloodstreams pass in opposite directions. The swim-bladder rete does something far stronger: it is a countercurrent MULTIPLIER. Oxygen unloaded on the outgoing venous side back-diffuses across onto the incoming artery, where it reloads onto hemoglobin; because that returned gas is added on top of what the artery already carries, each pass compounds the concentration, and the small single-step difference stacks up over and over along the long parallel capillaries. It is driven by the Root effect -- lactic acid from the gas gland acidifies the blood and forces its hemoglobin to dump oxygen -- and this compounding is what lets deep-sea fish secrete oxygen into the bladder against pressures of hundreds of atmospheres, starting from a partial pressure near 0.2 atmospheres in the water. No ATP pump, no extra surface, no slowed flow does this: it is pure recompounding geometry. Source: Wikipedia 'Rete mirabile' (rete pumps O2 from a partial pressure near 0.2 atm into a bladder at hundreds of atmospheres; Root effect drives back-diffusion so arterial O2 compounds until it exceeds bladder pressure); Pelster, PMC10209234 'The rete mirabile: a possible control site for swimbladder function'; PLOS One 2012, 'O2-Filled Swimbladder Employs Monocarboxylate Transporters ... Lactate-Induced Root Effect Hemoglobin'.

question: Fossil hunters keep pulling one strange thing out of Permian rock some 270 million years old: a tight spiral, wound like a clock spring, left by a sea predator called Helicoprion. For more than a hundred years it was almost the only part of the animal anyone found. What was the spiral made of?
answer: A whorl of saw-like teeth
choices: A whorl of saw-like teeth
A ring of armored bone plates
A coiled shell like a nautilus
A band of overlapping scales
context: Helicoprion means 'spiral saw' in Greek (helikos = spiral, prion = saw) -- a perfect name for a coil of teeth arranged like the blade of a circular saw. It swam the Permian seas roughly 290 to 270 million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicoprion

question: Paleontologists argued for a hundred years over where Helicoprion, a Permian sea predator, carried its strange spiral, since the spiral was nearly all of it ever found. In 2013 Leif Tapanila's team scanned a well-preserved specimen and settled the question. Where did the spiral sit?
answer: Coiled inside its lower jaw
choices: Coiled inside its lower jaw
