Curling off the tip of its snout
Standing up along its back fin
Trailing behind it on its tail
context: Scientists led by Leif Tapanila CT-scanned a fossil and found the whorl sat in the lower jaw. Tapanila said the teeth 'fit in the back of the mouth, right next to the back joint of the jaw.' Before that, guesses had stuck the spiral everywhere -- off the snout like an elephant's trunk, on the tail, on the back fin, even poking out of the throat. Source: https://phys.org/news/2013-02-helicoprion-scientists-mysteries-ancient-shark.html

question: Permian rock gives up almost nothing of Helicoprion but its coiled spiral: no ribs, no skull, no fin bones. For well over a century that kept the animal a puzzle. What made the rest of its body vanish before it could fossilize?
answer: Its skeleton was cartilage, which rots away
choices: Its skeleton was cartilage, which rots away
Deep-sea scavengers stripped every carcass
Its bones were too small to leave a trace
Acidic Permian mud dissolved the buried bone
context: Like sharks and their relatives, Helicoprion had a skeleton made of cartilage rather than bone. Cartilage rots away instead of fossilizing, so the hard tooth-whorl was almost the only piece that ever survived -- which is exactly why nobody could figure out where it went for so long. Source: https://phys.org/news/2013-02-helicoprion-scientists-mysteries-ancient-shark.html

question: Helicoprion, a Permian sea predator, never shed a single tooth in its whole life: its spiral held every tooth it ever grew. New teeth kept sprouting at the front as it aged. Where did the older, worn teeth end up?
answer: Curled inward into the center of the coil
choices: Curled inward into the center of the coil
Fused into one solid slicing ridge
Dissolved and reabsorbed into the jaw
Ground flat against the toothless upper jaw
context: Instead of falling out the way most teeth do, each old tooth stayed anchored and rolled inward toward the middle of the coil as fresh teeth grew at the working front. That is why the whorl coils tighter and tighter toward its center -- the innermost teeth are the ones the animal grew as a baby. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicoprion

question: Helicoprion, the Permian sea predator with the strange spiral, passed for a kind of shark for decades. Then in 2013 a scan of a well-preserved skull showed it was a closer cousin of a very different living group of fish. Which group?
answer: The ratfishes and chimaeras
choices: The ratfishes and chimaeras
The rays and skates
The lampreys and hagfish
The coelacanths
context: Only the teeth were shark-like; as Tapanila put it, 'everything else is Holocephalan' -- the group that includes today's ratfishes and chimaeras. When it closed its jaw, the whorl rolled backward in a slicing motion; Tapanila said 'the analogy to a circular saw is almost perfect,' and it likely sawed through soft prey like squid. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/buzzsaw-jaw-helicoprion-was-a-freaky-ratfish

question: Ramsay and colleagues worked out in 2015 how Helicoprion fed with its coiled spiral. As its jaw swung shut on prey, the spiral worked like a circular saw, and different stretches of it did different jobs. What job fell to the teeth at the front of the spiral?
answer: Hooking and dragging prey inward
choices: Hooking and dragging prey inward
Grinding shells into fragments
Filtering plankton from seawater
Anchoring the jaw to the skull
context: Ramsay and colleagues (Journal of Morphology, 2015) modeled the whorl as a multi-tool: as the lower jaw rotated shut the anterior teeth hooked and dragged prey inward, the middle teeth pierced and cut, and the rear teeth near the jaw joint sheared and shoved the food deeper toward the throat -- the tooth paths traced arcs like curved slashing swords. The animal likely fed by opening and closing the jaw in a repeating sawing cycle that caught, cut, and swallowed in one motion. Source: Ramsay et al. 2015, Journal of Morphology 276:47-64, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25181366/

question: Under a flat rock in a rushing Appalachian stream hides the largest salamander in North America, growing past two feet long, its baggy skin hanging in ruffled folds. Locals have called it the snot otter and the lasagna lizard. Which salamander is it?
answer: The hellbender
choices: The hellbender
The mudpuppy
The tiger salamander
The axolotl
context: The hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis) is the largest salamander in North America, about 30 to 74 cm long. Its ruffled, layered skin folds earned it folk names such as 'lasagna lizard', and its slimy skin 'snot otter', along with 'devil dog,' 'mud devil,' and 'Allegheny alligator.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellbender

question: A hellbender lies under its rock in a cold Appalachian stream, drawing nearly all the oxygen it needs out of the water through its skin and barely using its lungs. What about its skin helps it soak up so much?
answer: It hangs in loose, baggy wrinkles and side-folds
choices: It hangs in loose, baggy wrinkles and side-folds
It is coated in fine scales that trap a film of water
It secretes a thin mucus film that traps dissolved oxygen
It is riddled with microscopic pores like a sponge
context: Those loose folds hugely increase the skin's surface area, so more oxygen can soak in from the water. The ruffled look is exactly why one folk name is 'lasagna lizard.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellbender

question: On a still summer day the current in a cold Appalachian stream slows almost to nothing. A hellbender lying under its flat rock starts rocking its whole body back and forth and rippling its skin. Why does it bother with all that motion?
answer: To sweep fresh oxygen-rich water past its skin
choices: To sweep fresh oxygen-rich water past its skin
To warn rival hellbenders off its rock
To force stale water out of its lungs
To signal a mate hiding nearby
context: By swishing fresh water past its folds, the hellbender keeps the oxygen coming even when the water goes still - the skin can only soak up what actually flows past it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellbender

question: A male Hercules beetle, nearly seven inches long, carries two huge horns that close on a rival like a pincer when males wrestle in the rainforest. One horn is small; the other is much bigger. Where on his body does the bigger horn grow?
answer: His back, above the wing-covers
choices: His back, above the wing-covers
His head, between the eyes
His jaws, like a stag beetle's
The underside of his belly
context: Most of that seven-inch record length is horn, not body. A male grows a smaller horn jutting up from his head and a much larger one arching down from his back (the pronotum); the two meet like a giant pincer. Only males grow them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle

question: On a rainforest branch, two male Hercules beetles clamp horns and wrestle, with a female nearby. Each beetle tries to pin the other in the pincer his two horns make. Once one beetle has his rival caught, how does he win the fight?
answer: He pries the rival loose and hurls him off the branch
choices: He pries the rival loose and hurls him off the branch
He crushes the rival's shell until it cracks
He squeezes until the rival stops struggling
He drags the rival down into the leaf litter
context: Each beetle tries to catch the other between its upward head-horn and its downward back-horn, then pry and throw him off the branch. The horn works as a lever: muscles in the thorax rotate the head to drive the long horn upward and lift the enemy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle

question: In a Central American rainforest, a Hercules beetle, one of the largest beetles on Earth, wears hard wing covers that shine olive-green or pale yellow one hour and turn nearly black the next. Later they turn pale again. What flips its color back and forth like that?
answer: The humidity of the air around it
choices: The humidity of the air around it
The beetle growing older
A fresh meal of tree sap
A flash of a threat display
context: The elytra (wing-covers) shift with the weather: olive-green or yellow when the air is dry, darkening toward black as the humidity rises around the beetle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle

question: Long before it carries a horn, a Hercules beetle spends up to two years as a fat, C-shaped white grub, tunneling slowly through rotting logs on the forest floor and eating the soft, damp wood. How does that grub compare in size with the horned beetle it becomes?
answer: It grows heavier than the adult beetle
choices: It grows heavier than the adult beetle
It is far smaller than the adult
It has tiny working horns already
It is about the same size as the adult
context: A Hercules beetle larva can reach about 4.5 inches (11 cm) long and weigh over 100 grams, heavier than the horned adult it becomes. The giant adult is the short chapter: after years underground it lives only about three to six months, sipping sap and fruit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle

question: A grey giant weighing three tons or more wallows in an African river and hauls out at dusk to graze. Though it lives almost entirely on grass, it kills more people across Africa each year than lions or sharks do. Which animal is this?
answer: The hippopotamus
choices: The hippopotamus
The Cape buffalo
The white rhinoceros
The Nile crocodile
context: Hippos (Hippopotamus amphibius) kill an estimated 500 or more people a year in Africa — deadlier to humans than lions or sharks — yet they are grazers that live almost entirely on grass, though they have been filmed eating carrion. Their danger comes from aggression and sheer bulk, not from hunting. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/hippopotamus

question: A bull hippopotamus weighing three tons or more spends its days in African rivers and lakes. To reach the far bank of a deep pool, it heads straight in. How does it get across the deep water?
answer: It walks along the bottom, pushing off the riverbed
choices: It walks along the bottom, pushing off the riverbed
It floats high and dog-paddles across the top
It rolls sideways and lets the current carry it
It beats its stubby tail to scull forward
context: A hippo is too dense to float, so it can't truly swim. It walks and pushes off the riverbed in a slow-motion underwater gallop, toes barely touching the bottom. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/hippopotamus

question: A hippopotamus crops grass on an African riverbank at dusk, chewing with molars much like a pig's, and scientists once grouped it with the pigs for that reason. Blood-protein and DNA tests later traced its family tree. Which animals are the hippo's closest living relatives?
answer: Whales and dolphins
choices: Whales and dolphins
Pigs and warthogs
Rhinos and tapirs
Elephants and manatees
context: Until 1909 hippos were grouped with pigs based on their molars, but blood-protein and DNA evidence proved their closest living relatives are the cetaceans — whales, dolphins, and porpoises. The two lines are thought to have split from a shared water-loving ancestor around 55 million years ago. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippopotamus

question: A bull hippopotamus wading in a crowded, noisy African river throws its enormous head back and gapes its huge jaws wide open. It is not yawning; it is warning a rival bull. What weapons does that wide-open mouth show off?
answer: Tusk-like canines that never stop growing
choices: Tusk-like canines that never stop growing
Rows of razor-edged shearing molars
A pair of horns rooted in the jaw
Backward-curving fangs full of venom
context: Inside the gaping mouth are tusk-like canine teeth that keep growing throughout life, reaching about 50 cm (20 inches) long. They stay sharp by grinding against the lower incisors as the hippo chews. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippopotamus

question: A crow-sized bird with a spiky red crest, a bare blue face and red eyes perches over an Amazon swamp, eating leaves it ferments in an enormous crop, the way a cow does. Which South American bird is it?
answer: The hoatzin
choices: The hoatzin
The scarlet macaw
The great egret
The horned screamer
context: The hoatzin (Opisthocomus hoazin) is about 65 cm long but weighs only around 700 grams, with an unfeathered blue face, maroon eyes, and a spiky rufous crest. It lives in the swamps and riverside forests of the Amazon and Orinoco basins and eats mostly leaves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoatzin

question: A hoatzin chick clambers along a slim branch over an Amazon river, gripping the bark with something on each wing that it will lose as it grows up. What does the chick have on each wing?
answer: Two working claws on each wing
choices: Two working claws on each wing
A second, hidden set of eyelids
A hooked egg-tooth on each wing
A sticky pad under each wingtip
context: Hoatzin chicks are born with two functional claws on each wing and use them to clamber through branches over the water, a trait they lose as adults. Working wing claws are rare in living birds; turaco nestlings also climb with theirs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoatzin ; https://www.aip.org/inside-science/the-baby-birds-that-use-wing-claws-to-climb-through-the-amazon

question: A tree snake glides along a branch toward a hoatzin nest hanging out over an Amazon river. The chick inside cannot fly yet, and the snake blocks the way along the branch, with only open air and dark water behind. How does the chick escape?
answer: It flings itself off the branch and escapes underwater
choices: It flings itself off the branch and escapes underwater
It plays dead and lies limp in the nest
It shrieks without pause to summon both parents
It presses flat against the bark and holds still
context: When a predator threatens the nest, a hoatzin chick drops from the branch into the water below and swims to safety underwater — in tanks the chicks swim by moving both wings together in a breast-stroke-like motion — before later climbing back up to the nest. Source: https://www.aip.org/inside-science/the-baby-birds-that-use-wing-claws-to-climb-through-the-amazon

question: A hoatzin perches by an Amazon river, its huge crop full of leaves that bacteria are slowly breaking down; no other bird is known to digest its food that way. Anyone who walks close can smell the result. What does the hoatzin smell like?
answer: Like fresh cow manure
choices: Like fresh cow manure
Like sweet ripe fruit
Like crushed pine needles
Like a skunk's sharp musk
context: The hoatzin is the only bird known to digest its leafy diet by foregut fermentation, with bacteria in an enlarged crop breaking down the leaves much as in a cow. The fermenting leaves give it a disagreeable, manure-like smell, which is why local people call it the 'stinkbird.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoatzin

question: Cornered, an eastern hognose snake flops about as if hurt, then flips belly-up, gapes, lets its purple tongue loll out and lies limp, sometimes with a foul stink. What is this harmless snake pretending to be?
answer: Freshly dead and rotting
choices: Freshly dead and rotting
A venomous coral snake
A tangled clump of roots
A much larger snake
context: The hognose snake (genus Heterodon) is famous for this theatrical death-feign — belly-up, mouth agape, tongue lolling out. It is one of the animal kingdom's most committed fake-death acts. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_hognose_snake

question: A hognose snake lies belly-up and limp in the grass, its tongue lolling and its jaws agape. A naturalist gently turns it right side up onto its belly, just to check. What does the snake do the instant it is upright?
answer: Immediately rolls straight back onto its back
choices: Immediately rolls straight back onto its back
Bolts away at full speed
Bites the hand that touched it
Freezes stiff as a stick
context: The act is so committed that a hognose insists on being 'dead': turn it belly-down and it flops right back over, as if a corpse could only possibly be lying on its back. Source: https://animals.howstuffworks.com/snakes/hognose-snake.htm

question: A hognose snake menaced by a predator flips belly-up with its tongue lolling, but that is only the start of its act. It works to look and smell like a real corpse, not a stunned live snake. What does it add to sell the death?
answer: Smears foul musk and bleeds from its mouth
choices: Smears foul musk and bleeds from its mouth
Sheds its skin in one fast piece
Stiffens its whole body as if in rigor mortis
Rattles the dry tip of its tail
context: The hognose smears foul-smelling musk from its cloaca and can even rupture blood vessels to bleed from its mouth and cloaca — making the 'corpse' look and smell genuinely rotten to a predator. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_hognose_snake

question: An eastern hognose snake pushes its snout into loose sand. The scale at its tip is hardened and curled sharply upward, like the blade of a small shovel. What does the snake do with that upturned nose?
answer: Shovels toads out of the sand
choices: Shovels toads out of the sand
Cracks open bird eggs
Scrapes bark off logs
Combs seeds from grass
context: The upturned, keeled rostral scale at the tip of the snout works like a little shovel, letting the hognose dig burrowing toads out of sandy soil. Source: https://srelherp.uga.edu/snakes/eastern-hognose-snake/

question: An eastern hognose snake goes after a toad, the prey that makes up almost all its diet. The toad gulps air until it is a hard, round balloon too big for a snake's mouth, and its skin oozes a powerful poison that stops hearts. Its enlarged adrenal glands help the snake resist the poison. How does it beat the balloon?
answer: Enlarged rear teeth puncture and deflate the toad
choices: Enlarged rear teeth puncture and deflate the toad
It swallows the puffed toad whole anyway
It waits days for the toad to shrink
It squeezes the toad in tight coils
context: A puffed-up toad is meant to be un-swallowable, but the hognose has enlarged rear teeth that puncture and deflate it. Enlarged adrenal glands pump out hormones to counter the toad's skin toxins, and mild rear-fang venom helps subdue it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_hognose_snake

question: A stocky, low-slung animal about the size of a small dog, black with a pale back, stands its ground on the African savanna and drives off a lion. It holds the Guinness record for most fearless animal. What is it?
answer: The honey badger
choices: The honey badger
The wolverine
The Tasmanian devil
The African civet
context: The honey badger (Mellivora capensis) is the largest land mustelid in Africa yet weighs only about 5 to 16 kg. Its reputation for standing up to far larger predators earned the Guinness listing. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_badger ; https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/honey-badger-guide

question: Chased by a bigger predator across ground the dry-season sun has baked hard as brick, a honey badger digs a fresh burrow on the spot with its long front claws, which work like little picks. About how long does the digging take?
answer: About 10 minutes
choices: About 10 minutes
About half a day
About three days
About two weeks
context: Honey badgers are among the animal kingdom's best diggers and can tunnel a burrow into hard, sun-baked ground in about 10 minutes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_badger

question: A honey badger rips open a beehive on the African savanna and keeps eating while hundreds of angry bees sting it, barely reacting. That same tough hide shrugs off porcupine quills and the bites of other animals. What is the hide like?
answer: Very thick skin, as tough as rubber
choices: Very thick skin, as tough as rubber
A thin skin backed by a dense pad of fat
A hide sheathed in overlapping keratin plates
A hide coated in a thick protective mucus
context: The skin on a honey badger's neck is roughly 6 mm (a quarter inch) thick and tough and rubbery enough to shrug off bee stings, quills, and animal bites. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_badger

question: Colleen and Keith Begg tracked wild honey badgers for years across the Kalahari. One day a puff adder, a heavy snake whose venom can kill a person, struck a badger full in the face as it hunted. The badger convulsed, collapsed and lay as if dead for about two hours. What happened next?
answer: It woke up and went back to eating the snake
choices: It woke up and went back to eating the snake
It was carried off by a jackal before it could recover
It stayed down and did not survive the venom
Its mate dragged it into a burrow to sleep off the bite
context: Documented by Begg & Begg in National Geographic's 'Snake Killers: Honey Badgers of the Kalahari.' The badger passed out for about two hours, then recovered and finished its meal; full recovery came within about five hours. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=chtdRCrZKuw

question: A honey badger barely notices a dose of cobra venom, though the venom freezes most prey by locking onto a receptor on their muscle cells. Pigs and hedgehogs arrived at nearly the same defense separately. What protects the honey badger?
answer: A charged amino acid swapped into the receptor's toxin-binding site
choices: A charged amino acid swapped into the receptor's toxin-binding site
The muscle receptor is missing from its cells entirely
It grows extra receptors so the venom spreads too thin to work
Its receptors only change shape after the venom binds, shaking it loose
context: Drabeck et al. (2015), 'Why the honey badger don't care,' found a positively charged amino acid substituted into the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor's binding site, so the venom can't attach. Pigs and hedgehogs arrived at almost the same solution separately. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25796346/

question: Tens of thousands of honeybees crowd the comb inside a hollow tree. Nearly all are females that never lay eggs, and they gather nectar and pollen, build comb, feed the young and guard the door. What are these bees called?
answer: Workers
choices: Workers
Drones
Queens
Nymphs
context: A colony is overwhelmingly sterile female workers; a small hive holds about 20,000 bees, a large one can top 100,000, with one queen and a few hundred male drones. Source: https://www.mdbka.com/bee-information/ ; https://canr.udel.edu/maarec/honey-bee-biology/the-colony-and-its-organization/

question: A honeybee flies home from a rich patch of flowers. On the dark comb inside the hive she runs a tight figure-eight over and over, a straight dash with her body shuddering, then a loop back, as her sisters crowd close. What is this move called?
answer: The waggle dance
choices: The waggle dance
The swarm call
The scent trail
The nectar hum
context: The returning forager traces a figure-eight on the vertical comb, running a straight line while shaking her abdomen, then looping back to repeat it -- a symbolic message to her hivemates. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance

question: Through the glass wall of an observation hive in the 1940s, Karl von Frisch watched a forager home from the flowers. On the upright comb she ran a figure-eight, wagging her body along the straight middle run. The angle of that run, he found, was a code. What did it tell the other bees?
answer: Which direction to fly, measured from the sun
choices: Which direction to fly, measured from the sun
How many bees to send out
How sweet the nectar is
Which flower species to seek
context: The angle of the waggle run relative to straight-up equals the angle to the flowers relative to the sun: waggle straight up means fly toward the sun; a run 45 degrees left means fly 45 degrees left of the sun. Source: https://www.planetbee.org/post/the-waggle-dance-bees-high-tech-navigation-system ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance

question: A honeybee home from a clover patch runs her figure-eight on the dark comb while her sisters press close, shaking her belly from side to side along the straight stretch. Sometimes the shaking is brief and snappy, sometimes drawn out much longer. What does its length tell them?
answer: The distance to the flowers
choices: The distance to the flowers
The wind speed outside
The number of open blooms
The time of day to leave
context: The longer she waggles, the farther the food: a short waggle means the flowers are close, a long one means a longer flight. Direction lives in the angle, distance in the duration. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance

question: Deep in the dark hive, a honeybee home from the flowers runs her figure-eight on an upright comb. The angle of her run should match the angle between the flowers and the sun, yet she cannot see the sky at all. What does she use in place of the sun?
answer: Gravity, treating straight-up as 'toward the sun'
choices: Gravity, treating straight-up as 'toward the sun'
The Earth's magnetic field
The warmth radiating from the hive entrance
The scent drifting in from outside
context: In the dark she substitutes 'straight up' for 'toward the sun,' using gravity as her compass since she cannot see the sky -- an abstract translation from sun-angle to gravity-angle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance

question: Karl von Frisch claimed that the honeybee's figure-eight on the comb was a true coded language, and many scientists doubted him. To prove it, he read one bee's run himself, then watched where the bees who had seen it flew. What did those bees do?
answer: Flew straight to a spot none of them had ever visited
choices: Flew straight to a spot none of them had ever visited
Circled the hive at random until they stumbled on food
Simply followed the dancer back out to the same patch
Waited for a scent trail before leaving the comb
context: Von Frisch's tests showed the dance works as a symbolic code: recruits who only watched the dance flew directly to a food source they had never been to, guided solely by the coded angle and duration. He shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen. His claim of an insect 'language' met wide skepticism at first. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1973/frisch/facts/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_von_Frisch

question: Honeybees crowd over a row of wax cells, each holding a tiny larva no different from its sisters. One chosen larva will grow into a big egg-laying queen; the others will not. The difference lies in one special food the bees keep packing into her cell. What is it?
answer: Royal jelly
choices: Royal jelly
Extra pollen
Crushed drones
Fermented nectar
context: A queen is made, not born: the chosen larva is fed royal jelly throughout development, while workers are cut off from it after three days. The royal-jelly larva grows into a queen. Source: https://extension.psu.edu/an-introduction-to-queen-honey-bee-development ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_jelly

question: A honeybee queen in her prime lays one pale egg after another all day long, each about half the size of a grain of rice. In a single day her eggs outweigh her own body. About how many does she lay in a day?
answer: About 2,000
choices: About 2,000
About 50
About 200
About 40,000
context: In her prime a queen lays about 2,000 eggs a day -- more than her own body weight in eggs daily, each egg about half the size of a grain of rice. Source: https://www.mdbka.com/bee-information/

question: A honeybee building her comb never gathers wax; she makes it. Pale flakes ooze from eight glands under her abdomen, and she scrapes them off, chews them soft and presses them into comb. Her wax glands work only on one condition inside the hive. What must the hive be?
answer: Kept very warm
choices: Kept very warm
Humid and misty
Packed with fresh pollen
Freshly swept clean
context: Eight glands on the underside of a worker's abdomen secrete flakes of wax, which she chews and shapes -- but the hive must be warm (around 95 F / 35 C) for wax to form. Source: https://www.honeyflow.com/blogs/beekeeping-basics/how-do-bees-make-beeswax ; https://www.buddhabeeapiary.com/blog/honey-bee-wax-comb

question: A honeybee colony eats about eight pounds of honey to make a single pound of wax, so every flake is precious. Its builders shape the wax into storage cells of one particular shape, repeated across the whole comb. What shape is each cell?
answer: A hexagon
choices: A hexagon
A circle
A triangle
A square
context: Bees build hexagonal cells because the hexagon stores the most honey using the least wax and is one of the strongest shapes for the material -- and wax is costly, about 8 pounds of honey eaten per 1 pound of wax made. Source: https://www.sciencefriday.com/educational-resources/why-do-bees-build-hexagonal-honeycomb-cells/ ; https://www.vegasbees.com/post/honeybee-feats-of-strength-making-one-pound-of-beeswax

question: A honeybee stings a bear to defend her hive, and before long she is dead. A wasp can sting again and again and fly off unharmed. Something about the honeybee's stinger, unlike the wasp's, dooms her. Why does stinging kill her?
answer: The stinger tears free, ripping out part of her body
choices: The stinger tears free, ripping out part of her body
Her wings lock and she cannot fly
Her venom turns inward and poisons her
She goes permanently blind
context: The honeybee's stinger is barbed like a fishhook, so it lodges in the victim's flesh; when she pulls away it tears free along with part of her abdomen and venom sac -- fatal self-sacrifice for the colony. A wasp's smooth stinger slides out cleanly, so it can sting repeatedly and survive. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/Do-Bees-Die-After-Stinging ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee_sting

question: To a person, a meadow is a scatter of plain-colored flowers, but to a honeybee flying over it the blooms glow with bull's-eyes and stripes that lead her to the nectar. Her eyes catch light that human eyes cannot. Which light is it?
answer: Ultraviolet
choices: Ultraviolet
Infrared
X-rays
Radio waves
context: Bees see ultraviolet light invisible to humans; their receptors are tuned to ultraviolet, blue, and green. Flowers like buttercups, sunflowers, and pansies reveal UV 'nectar guides' -- landing strips and bull's-eyes -- only under UV light. Source: https://apiaryproject.com/blog/honey-bee-vision-uv-compound-eyes-how-bees-see ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nectar_guide

question: A honeybee queen mates in her first weeks of life, then lays her eggs one by one, deciding each egg's sex as she lays it. A fertilized egg becomes a female with 32 chromosomes, half from each parent. An egg she leaves unfertilized becomes a male drone carrying only his mother's 16. Which relative can a drone never have?
answer: A father
choices: A father
A brother
A daughter
A grandfather
context: This is haplodiploidy: in honeybees a fertilized egg becomes a female, an unfertilized egg becomes a male. So a drone develops from an egg with no sperm at all -- he is haploid, carrying only his mother's 16 chromosomes, and has literally no father. Yet he still has a maternal grandfather, because his mother hatched from a fertilized egg with two parents. He can also father daughters: every one of his roughly 10 million sperm is a genetic clone of his single genome. The 'no father, but a grandfather' family tree even traces out a Fibonacci sequence of ancestors -- 1, 1, 2, 3, 5. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(bee) -- drones haploid (16 chromosomes), arrhenotokous parthenogenesis, no father, maternal grandfather, Fibonacci ancestry, ~10M clonal sperm; haplodiploidy corroborated by multiple bee-genetics sources.

question: Adrian Wenner insisted in 1967 that honeybees track down food by smell, and that their figure-eights on the comb mean nothing. In 1989 Axel Michelsen's team sent a brass-and-beeswax robot bee onto the comb, its wing a razor blade buzzing near 280 times a second as it ran the figure-eight. What did it do that answered Wenner?
answer: Recruited real bees to a target spot only it had named
choices: Recruited real bees to a target spot only it had named
Released the exact floral scent the foragers were tracking
Out-danced the live bees until they abandoned their own runs
Proved the smell trail worked even with the dance removed
context: This was a real scientific fight, not a settled story. Von Frisch had claimed in the 1940s that the dance was a symbolic code; in 1967 Adrian Wenner mounted a serious challenge -- bees, he argued, find food by following floral and hive odors, and the dance carries no information. To test it, Axel Michelsen's team built a mechanical robot bee out of brass and beeswax, with a razor-blade wing that buzzed at about 280 cycles per second (Hz). Programmed to perform specific waggle dances, the robot successfully steered real recruits to a chosen spot in the field, strong evidence that the dance itself -- not smell -- carries the location. James Gould's manipulated-dance experiments pointed the same way. Source: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10739-005-0552-1 (The Bee Battles: von Frisch, Wenner and the dance-language controversy); Michelsen robot-bee corroborated via link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00166696 and the ACP Social Insects summary -- 280 Hz brass-and-beeswax robot recruited real bees to a target.

question: Deep under the Australian desert, honeypot ants feed a few chosen sisters nectar again and again, far past what any ordinary ant could eat. What happens to the body of one of these stuffed ants?
answer: Its abdomen swells into a see-through globe of honey
choices: Its abdomen swells into a see-through globe of honey
It grows a second pair of wings and flies off to start a new colony
It sprouts a hard armored shell to guard the nest entrance
It turns bright red to warn birds that it tastes bitter
context: These gorged workers are called repletes. Fed liquid nectar until its crop stretches, a replete becomes a living storage jar for the whole colony. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeypot_ant

question: A honeypot ant has been fed nectar until she can hold no more, and she has become a replete, one of the colony's living pantries, far too heavy to walk anywhere. Where does she spend the coming months in the underground desert nest?
answer: Hanging motionless upside down from the ceiling of the underground nest
choices: Hanging motionless upside down from the ceiling of the underground nest
Buried in a sealed mud cell at the very bottom of the nest
Floating in a shallow pool the workers dig near the entrance
Riding on the backs of ordinary workers who carry it from room to room
context: Too swollen to move, repletes hang from the nest roof — a wall of living honey jars overhead — sometimes for months. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrmecocystus_mexicanus

question: A hungry honeypot ant walks deep through her nest under the Australian desert, where drought has left the surface almost bare. She stops at one of the colony's repletes, a sister full of stored nectar, and taps her gently with her antennae. What does the replete do?
answer: Regurgitates a drop of stored liquid from its crop into the hungry ant's mouth
choices: Regurgitates a drop of stored liquid from its crop into the hungry ant's mouth
Splits open along its belly so the colony can scoop the honey out
Releases a scent that calls other workers to come and share
Drops from the ceiling and rolls toward the nest entrance
context: Nestmates 'milk' the repletes this way, and the whole colony drinks from these living jars through droughts and winter famines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeypot_ant

question: A slim pinkish-brown bird with black-and-white barred wings struts through an olive grove, probing for insects with its long curved bill. When it lands or takes fright, up flicks a black-tipped crest like a fan. Which bird is it?
answer: The hoopoe
choices: The hoopoe
The bee-eater
The nightjar
The waxwing
context: The hoopoe (Upupa epops) is unmistakable: cinnamon-fawn body, black-and-white barred wings, and a fan-like crest tipped with black that pops up in alarm, courtship, or on landing, then folds sleekly flat while the bird forages. In flight it bounds along like a giant butterfly, its broad wings half-closing at the end of each beat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_hoopoe

question: A mother hoopoe sits on her eggs in a cramped tree hole, with no way to flee a predator. Once nesting begins, the gland she normally uses to oil her feathers for waterproofing switches to a thick brown brew that she paints over her feathers and eggs. What is startling about it?
answer: It reeks of rotting meat
choices: It reeks of rotting meat
It glows faintly in the dark
It hardens into a shell
It tastes bitter to the tongue
context: During nesting, the female hoopoe's uropygial (preen) gland switches to a thick brown liquid that smells of rotting meat, and she paints it over her feathers and eggs to repel predators and parasites. Symbiotic Enterococcus bacteria living in her gland help produce the smelly secretion, and they also make antibacterial chemicals that shield the eggs from harmful microbes. Sources: https://www.audubon.org/news/the-hoopoe-emissary-kings-secreter-stink ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2842625/

question: A predator's head appears at the mouth of a hoopoe's nest hole. Inside, a chick about six days old hisses like a snake and stabs upward with its bill, and in the same moment it fires off a second, grosser weapon. What else does the chick do?
answer: Squirt streams of liquid feces
choices: Squirt streams of liquid feces
Flash a bright warning patch
Puff up to twice its size
Play dead until it leaves
context: From about six days old, hoopoe chicks add a second gross weapon to the mother's stink: they turn their tails toward an intruder and squirt streams of liquid feces at it while hissing snake-like and jabbing upward with the bill. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_hoopoe

question: A sea creature with a hard, domed shell and a long, spiky tail crawls out of the spring surf onto a beach in the eastern United States to bury its eggs. People call it the horseshoe crab. Which animals are its closest living relatives?
answer: spiders and scorpions
choices: spiders and scorpions
clams and oysters
true crabs and lobsters
jellyfish and corals
context: The horseshoe crab is a chelicerate, sharing a lineage with arachnids rather than crustaceans — which is why it is nicknamed the 'sea spider.' Source: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life (digitalatlasofancientlife.org); Defenders of Wildlife.

question: A horseshoe crab drags its domed shell across a sandy beach almost exactly as its kind did some 450 million years ago, which is why it is called a living fossil. About how much older is its lineage than the earliest dinosaurs?
answer: more than 200 million years
choices: more than 200 million years
about 20 thousand years
about 5 million years
more than 2 billion years
context: Horseshoe crabs are 'living fossils' — their form has barely changed in about 450 million years, meaning they walked the shallows more than 200 million years before the first dinosaurs and survived all five great mass extinctions. Source: Defenders of Wildlife.

question: A wave flips a horseshoe crab onto its back on a Delaware beach, its legs kicking at the sky; left there, it will dry out or fall to the gulls. Its long spiky tail, the telson, carries no sting or venom. How does the crab use the telson to get right side up?
answer: stabs it into the sand and levers itself over
choices: stabs it into the sand and levers itself over
grips a rock to haul itself upright
spins in circles to dig a righting pit
pushes off a neighboring crab's shell
context: Contrary to popular belief, the telson is neither a stinger nor poisonous; the crab jabs it into the ground and uses it as a lever to flip right-side-up when stranded on its back, and to steer while swimming. Source: South Carolina DNR; Maryland DNR.

question: In a lab near Delaware Bay, a worker draws a sample from a horseshoe crab, a helmet-shaped creature whose kind has crawled the sea floor for some 450 million years. The blood that flows out is not red but a startling milky blue. What does that blood use to carry oxygen?
answer: a copper-based protein
choices: a copper-based protein
iron-rich hemoglobin
dissolved chlorophyll
liquid silver droplets
context: Instead of iron-based red hemoglobin, horseshoe crab blood uses a copper-based protein called hemocyanin to carry oxygen; the copper turns the blood blue when it meets air. Source: The Horseshoe Crab (horseshoecrab.org); Britannica.

question: A lab worker tests a batch of vaccine for the poisons dead bacteria leave behind, which can cause a dangerous fever. She mixes in a blue-tinted fluid drawn from an ancient, helmet-shaped sea creature that crawls ashore each spring to lay eggs; if the poisons are there, it clots into a gel. Which animal's blood is it?
answer: horseshoe crab
choices: horseshoe crab
electric eel
sea cucumber
giant clam
context: Cells in horseshoe crab blood called amebocytes instantly clot into a gel when they touch bacterial toxins, trapping the germs. This 'LAL' test checks that injectable medicines and vaccines, including COVID-19 vaccines, are free of contamination. Source: The Horseshoe Crab (horseshoecrab.org); NCBI LAL technology review.

question: A horseshoe crab hauls itself up the sand with eyes almost everywhere on its body. Two big compound eyes ride on its shell, several smaller simple eyes sit on it too, another pair hides underneath by its mouth, and light-sensing spots run out along its spiky tail. How many eyes does it have in all?
answer: ten
choices: ten
eight
fourteen
twenty
context: A horseshoe crab has ten eyes scattered over its body — two large compound eyes (each with about 1,000 light-sensing units), several simple eyes, two on its underside near the mouth, and light sensors on its tail. Source: Florida FWC; Maryland DNR.

question: A red knot, a threatened shorebird on a 9,000-mile flight to the Arctic, stops at Delaware Bay in May, when the high tides of the full and new moons bring horseshoe crabs ashore to bury millions of green eggs. In two weeks of gorging on those eggs, what does the bird do to its own body?
answer: nearly doubles its body weight
choices: nearly doubles its body weight
grows longer flight feathers
adds a thick new layer of down
grows a heavier, sturdier bill
context: The fat-rich horseshoe crab eggs let the threatened red knot, mid-migration to its Arctic breeding grounds, nearly double its body weight in about two weeks — fuel it needs to finish the flight. Each female crab buries clusters of about 3,000–5,000 eggs. Source: Delaware DNREC; New Jersey DEP.

question: A ruby-throated hummingbird hangs still in front of a red trumpet-flower, dipping its needle beak in for nectar. Its wings are a smoky gray blur that hums in the air, the sound the bird is named for. About how many times a second do they beat?
answer: About 50 times every second
choices: About 50 times every second
About 15 times every second
About 200 times every second
About 500 times every second
context: In ordinary hovering a hummingbird beats its wings roughly 50 times a second — the blur that makes the humming sound it's named for. Source: BBC Science Focus; Science World, 'Flight of the Hummingbird.'

question: A hummingbird hangs perfectly still at a flower, a feat that takes enormous power from the breast muscle driving its wings. That muscle's share of a hummingbird's body is about twice its share in an ordinary bird. How much of the hummingbird's weight is breast muscle?
answer: Almost a third of its body weight
choices: Almost a third of its body weight
About a tenth of its body weight
Barely a twentieth of its body weight
Roughly two-thirds of its body weight
context: A hummingbird's breast (pectoral) flight muscles make up almost a third of its body weight — twice the muscle fraction of an ordinary bird. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'Super pecs and 1,200 heartbeats per minute.'

question: A hovering hummingbird, a tiny bird of the Americas, powers its upstroke with a big muscle, the supracoracoideus, so the upbeat pulls real weight, while most birds get almost no lift from theirs. About how much of the hummingbird's lift comes from that upstroke?
answer: About a quarter of its lift
choices: About a quarter of its lift
About a tenth of its lift
About half of its lift
Nearly all of its lift
context: Unlike other birds, a hummingbird's big upstroke muscle (the supracoracoideus) makes the lifting upbeat supply about a quarter of its total lift — the rest of the bird world barely uses the upstroke at all. Source: BBC Science Focus; Tough Little Birds, 'hummingbird flight.'

question: A hummingbird burns so much fuel hovering by day that it cannot store enough to last the night. So as darkness falls it lets its whole body go cold and its racing heart slow right down. How low does the beat fall before dawn?
answer: To about 50 beats a minute
choices: To about 50 beats a minute
To about 300 beats a minute
To about 450 beats a minute
To about 600 beats a minute
context: Hovering costs so much that a hummingbird cannot survive the night on its reserves, so it drops into torpor — heart falling from ~1,200 beats a minute to as few as ~50, body going cold until dawn. Source: forumscience.com; JEB, 'Flight Thermogenesis and Energy Conservation in Hovering Hummingbirds.'

question: On a summer afternoon a small creature hovers at a flowerbed, its wings a humming blur at about 85 beats a second, its long tongue dipping into one bloom after another. Passersby swear a tiny hummingbird has strayed into the garden, but it is no bird at all. What is it?
answer: A moth
choices: A moth
A bee
A hoverfly
A bat
context: The hummingbird hawkmoth (Sphingidae) hovers at flowers exactly like a hummingbird, beating its wings about 85 times a second — faster than a hummingbird's ~50 — so people mistake the insect for a tiny bird. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology jeb230920; A-Z Animals.

question: A hoverfly hangs dead still in the sunlight over a summer garden, its body striped black and yellow like a wasp's. A close look shows only two wings, not four: this is a true fly, armed with no sting, no venom and no bite. Why do those borrowed stripes keep it alive?
answer: Predators burned once by wasps avoid anything striped like one
choices: Predators burned once by wasps avoid anything striped like one
The stripes reflect sunlight and hide its outline in the glare
The pattern startles a bird into flinching just long enough
Wasps recognize the stripes and defend it as one of their own
context: The hoverfly wears the black-and-yellow stripes of a wasp or bee as pure bluff — Batesian mimicry — despite having no sting at all; predators that have learned to avoid stinging wasps leave the lookalike alone. Source: RHS, 'Hoverflies: Identification & Control'; Wikipedia, 'Hoverfly.'

question: A dragonfly hangs over a pond on four wings that it can steer one by one, then darts away with rare precision. It saves flapping power with one timing trick between its front and back pairs. What does it do with them to cut the cost of hovering?
answer: Beats the front and back wings out of phase
choices: Beats the front and back wings out of phase
Beats all four wings in perfect unison
Holds the back wings still and beats only the front
Folds the front wings and glides on the back
context: A dragonfly hovers with four independently controlled wings; when its front and back wings beat out of phase (crossing near mid-stroke) it saves flapping power, letting it hang and dart precisely. Source: Royal Society Interface, Usherwood & Lehmann; Royal Society Open Science rsos.202275.

question: A kestrel, a small falcon with a russet back, hangs pinned in one spot above an English hayfield, its head perfectly still as it scans the grass for the flicker of a vole. Unlike a hummingbird, it is not truly beating its wings in still air. How does it hold its place?
answer: It faces into a headwind and flaps just enough to cancel it
choices: It faces into a headwind and flaps just enough to cancel it
It hangs on a warm updraft rising off the sunlit field
It locks its wings and glides in a tight circle
It grips the air with specially slotted feathers
context: The kestrel 'wind-hovers' by facing into a headwind and flapping just fast enough to cancel it — not truly beating in still air — which is why its old English name is the 'windhover.' Source: Birdfact, 'Kestrel Hovering'; Opposite View Wildlife.

question: Alejandro Rico-Guevara's team filmed the tongues of 18 hummingbird species at high speed, catching the instant each tongue met nectar. Books had long said the grooved tongue wicks nectar up like a paper towel. What does the tongue do when its tips touch the nectar?
answer: Its flattened grooves spring open and suck up a column of nectar
choices: Its flattened grooves spring open and suck up a column of nectar
Its outer surface wicks a thin film upward by capillary action
Its muscular walls squeeze in a slow wave to push nectar back
Its hollow core draws nectar up like a straw under suction
context: A 2015 study (Alejandro Rico-Guevara, Tai-Hsi Fan, Margaret Rubega, Proc. R. Soc. B) high-speed-filmed 18 species and falsified 180 years of capillary-action textbook claims. The tongue is squeezed flat as it extends; the instant its grooved tips touch nectar, the collapsed grooves spring back open, and that elastic re-expansion actively sucks up a column of nectar an order of magnitude faster than capillarity could. It works as an elastic micropump, not a paper towel, which is what lets a hummingbird lick a flower up to ~20 times a second. Source: Rico-Guevara, Fan & Rubega, 'Hummingbird tongues are elastic micropumps,' Proc. R. Soc. B 2015 (royalsocietypublishing.org; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26290074).

question: Deep in a Cuban forest darts a hummingbird so small that Cubans call it the zunzuncito, the little buzzer. A male tips the scales at about 2 grams, lighter than an American penny, and no smaller bird lives anywhere on Earth. What is it?
answer: The bee hummingbird
choices: The bee hummingbird
The pygmy owl
The golden-crowned kinglet
The zebra finch
context: The bee hummingbird (Mellisuga helenae) is the smallest bird on Earth: a male averages about 5.5 cm (2 inches) long and about 2 grams, lighter than a penny, making it one of the smallest warm-blooded animals of any kind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee_hummingbird

question: A hummingbird hangs at a garden flower in still air, needing no headwind to hold its spot, its wings a humming blur. Then it does something almost no other bird can manage. What can it do?
answer: Fly backward
choices: Fly backward
Sleep in flight
Dive underwater
Glide for miles
context: Hummingbirds can hover in still air and fly backward, feats almost no other bird can manage. Other birds can hang briefly in a headwind, but the hummingbird can reverse in mid-air with no wind at all. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/birds/facts-about-hummingbirds

question: A hummingbird hovers at a flower, its wings pushing air down as they sweep forward and again as they sweep back, like a swimmer's hands sculling water. Most birds get lift only on the downstroke. What shape does each wingtip trace through the air?
answer: A figure-eight
choices: A figure-eight
A tight circle
A straight up-and-down line
A rising spiral
context: By sweeping its wings in a figure-eight, a hummingbird generates lift on both the forward stroke and the backstroke -- unlike other birds, which only get lift pushing down. This is what lets it hover and reverse. Source: https://news.oregonstate.edu/news/research-shows-hummingbird-flight-evolutionary-marvel

question: A hummingbird flits from blossom to blossom all day, sipping nectar every 10 to 15 minutes to keep from starving before dark. Its tiny body burns fuel almost as fast as it can take it in. About how much of its own weight in sugar does it eat in a day?
answer: About half
choices: About half
About a tenth
About a fiftieth
About a thousandth
context: A hummingbird eats roughly half its own body weight in sugar every day and must feed every 10 to 15 minutes -- it would starve overnight if it simply slept. Source: https://birdwatchingbuzz.com/hummingbird-heart-rate/

question: A hummingbird hovering at a red flower burns energy faster for its size than any other warm-blooded animal, and its heart races to feed its wing muscles. A resting person's heart beats about 80 times a minute, a fit person's tops out near 200. Roughly how many times can the hummingbird's beat in a minute?
answer: Over 1,200
choices: Over 1,200
Around 300
Around 70
Around 12
context: A hummingbird's heart can beat over 1,200 times a minute (rates up to about 1,260 bpm have been recorded), and it breathes roughly 250 times a minute even at rest. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/blog/10-incredible-hummingbird-facts/

question: In a Cuban forest, the female of the smallest bird on Earth, a hummingbird, weaves a tiny cup nest. She lays two eggs in it, among the tiniest eggs of any bird alive. What everyday object is each egg about the size of?
answer: A coffee bean
choices: A coffee bean
A sesame seed
A grape
A cherry
context: A bee hummingbird lays two eggs, each about the size of a coffee bean, in a cup nest only about 2.5 cm (1 inch) across. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee_hummingbird

question: A hummingbird stops feeding at dusk with too little fuel in its tiny body to last a cold night of ordinary sleep. Yet by dawn it is alive and ready to feed again. How does it get through the night?
answer: Its body cools and its heart slows to a crawl
choices: Its body cools and its heart slows to a crawl
It wakes every hour to sip nectar in the dark
It huddles in a pile with other hummingbirds
It sleeps one half of its brain at a time
context: In torpor a hummingbird's body temperature can fall from about 104 degrees F toward 50 degrees F and its heart rate from over 1,000 to as few as ~40-50 beats a minute, cutting energy use by about 95 percent -- letting it survive cold nights on its tiny fuel reserves.

question: A 3-gram ruby-throated hummingbird that nests in the eastern United States and winters in Central America crosses the Gulf of Mexico twice a year: up to 500 miles of open sea, flown alone and nonstop for 18 to 22 hours. How does its body prepare in the weeks before it leaves?
answer: Nearly doubles its body weight in fat
choices: Nearly doubles its body weight in fat
Grows a second set of flight feathers
Enlarges its heart permanently
Hollows out its bones for lightness
context: A ruby-throated hummingbird crosses the Gulf of Mexico in a single nonstop flight of up to 500 miles, flying alone for 18 to 22 hours -- nearly doubling its body weight in fat beforehand to fuel the trip. Source: https://www.reconnectwithnature.org/news-events/the-buzz/5-things-about-hummingbirds

question: For its backstroke to make lift, a hovering hummingbird must flip each wing upside down between strokes, leading edge one way and then the other. It does this by twisting one joint so far that the arm bone itself turns nearly 180 degrees. Which joint does the twisting?
answer: The shoulder
choices: The shoulder
The wrist
The elbow
The knuckle
context: To flip its wing over for the lift-generating backstroke, a hummingbird rotates its wing at the shoulder nearly 180 degrees -- the humerus itself twists. Source: https://www.threads.com/@museumofscience/post/DORoQMhiO9l/

question: A male Anna's hummingbird hurtles earthward in his courtship dive, wings folded tight against his sides. A diving peregrine falcon covers about 200 of its own body lengths a second. Measured against his own size, how does the hummingbird's dive compare?
answer: He covers nearly twice as many
choices: He covers nearly twice as many
He covers about half as many
He covers almost exactly as many
He covers about a tenth as many
context: During his courtship dive, a male Anna's hummingbird covers 385 times its own body length every second -- the highest length-relative speed known in any vertebrate, beating even the diving peregrine falcon (about 200 body lengths per second). Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/annas-hummingbird-outflies-falcons-and-fighter-pilots

question: At the bottom of his steep courtship dive, a male Anna's hummingbird spreads his wings and yanks out so hard that his tiny body takes a jolt of g-force. An untrained person can black out at 4 to 6 g, four to six times the pull of gravity. Roughly how many g does the bird pull?
answer: Nearly 9 g
choices: Nearly 9 g
About 3 g
About 30 g
About 100 g
context: Pulling out of its courtship dive, an Anna's hummingbird endures nearly nine times the force of gravity, the highest reported for any backboned animal in a voluntary aerial maneuver apart from jet fighter pilots. Source: Clark 2009, Proc. R. Soc. B, via https://www.scientificamerican.com/blog/news-blog/hummingbirds-outperform-pilots-pull-2009-06-10/

question: Osipova and colleagues traced the special way hummingbirds burn sugar back to a single change in the ancestor of every living hummingbird, made some 48 to 30 million years ago, just as hovering and nectar feeding evolved. What was that change?
answer: Their ancestor lost a muscle enzyme gene
choices: Their ancestor lost a muscle enzyme gene
Their ancestor gained a second sugar-storing organ
Their ancestor doubled its fat-making capacity
Their ancestor evolved a faster-emptying stomach
context: Osipova and colleagues found that FBP2 (fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 2), a gluconeogenic muscle enzyme, was inactivated in the common ancestor of all living hummingbirds about 48-30 million years ago -- exactly the window when hovering flight and nectar-feeding evolved. When they knocked FBP2 out of bird cells, glycolysis rose and the cells built more mitochondria and respired harder, running more efficiently. So a gene LOSS, not a gain, helped unlock hovering flight. Source: Osipova et al. 2023, Science 379:185, "Loss of a gluconeogenic muscle enzyme contributed to adaptive metabolic traits in hummingbirds."

question: Gerald Mayr took a fresh look at two small, long-billed skeletons that sat in a museum drawer, and in 2004 he named the bird they came from, a hummingbird some 30 million years old. What made his fossil bird a surprise?
answer: It lived in Europe, far from the Americas
choices: It lived in Europe, far from the Americas
It chased insects instead of sipping nectar
It could not hover despite a slender bill
It had teeth lining its slender bill
context: Mayr described Eurotrochilus in 2004 from Early Oligocene deposits (~28-34 million years ago) at the Wiesloch-Frauenweiler clay pit in southern Germany; more fossils later turned up in Germany, France, and Poland. It already had the diagnostic long nectar bill (~15.5-20 mm, about 2.5x its skull length) and hovering wing structure -- so the nectar-hovering lineage evolved in the Old World and only later vanished there, leaving today's hummingbirds solely in the Americas. Its full name, Eurotrochilus inexpectatus, means "unexpected European hummingbird."

question: A 40-ton whale surfaces beside a whale-watching boat off New England, its dark head covered in round bumps and its pale flippers almost 5 meters long, the longest limbs of any animal on Earth. Which whale is it?
answer: The humpback whale
choices: The humpback whale
The blue whale
The sperm whale
The narwhal
context: The humpback (Megaptera novaeangliae) has the longest flippers of any whale — up to about a third of its whole body, nearly 5 meters (16 feet), the longest limbs of any animal on Earth. Source: https://gentlegiants.is/news/2025/08/03/the-pectoral-fins-of-a-humpback-whale-nature-s-marvels-of-movement-and-communication/

question: A researcher in a small boat reaches down to a humpback whale surfacing alongside and runs her hand over its head. She feels rows of round bumps, each about the size of a golf ball. What grows from each bump?
answer: a single hair, thought to sense the water
choices: a single hair, thought to sense the water
a tiny suction cup for grip
a glowing spot to lure prey
a venomous spine for defense
context: Each knobbly bump on a humpback's head is a tubercle, about golf-ball sized, with one hair sprouting from it — thought to help the whale sense the water flowing around it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: On its breeding grounds near Hawaii, a 40-ton humpback whale beats the sea with its huge flippers and its tail, booming across the water. Then it does something no whale-watcher forgets. What does it do?
answer: hurls its whole body out of the water in a leap
choices: hurls its whole body out of the water in a leap
spins on its back for hours like an otter
sends up a spout of spray fifty meters high
dives and stays down for a full hour
context: Humpbacks slap their flippers and tails against the surface, and breach — hurling their whole bodies out of the water — which is why whale-watchers love them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: Scientists who described the humpback whale off New England in the 1780s gave it the name Megaptera novaeangliae. The second word means 'of New England'; the first comes from the Greek for 'great wing.' Which part of the whale does that first word celebrate?
answer: its enormous flippers
choices: its enormous flippers
its wide fluked tail
its arched, humped back
its fan-shaped blowhole spray
context: 'Mega-ptera' is Greek for 'giant wing' — the humpback was named for its enormous flippers, the longest limbs of any animal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: A humpback whale, as long as a bus at up to 17 meters and weighing 40 tons, spins around within its own length the way a dolphin does. Most big whales cannot match one other trick it has. What else can it do?
answer: swim backward
choices: swim backward
hold its breath for a whole day
sleep with its whole brain at once
drink seawater safely
context: The humpback's oversized flippers let a 40-ton, 17-meter animal turn inside its own body length like a dolphin, and even swim backward. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: Humpback whales gather each winter in warm seas off Hawaii and in the Caribbean to breed, and long, eerie songs fill the water around them, heard for miles. Not every humpback there joins in. Which humpbacks sing?
answer: only the males
choices: only the males
only the mothers with calves
only the oldest whales
the whole pod together
context: Only male humpbacks sing, mostly on the winter breeding grounds; the song is thought to be a mating display, not a message carrying a specific meaning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: Roger Payne and Scott McVay listened closely to humpback whale songs and found them built like music: small sounds, which they called units, join into phrases, phrases build into themes, and ordered themes form the complete song. What does a male do with his finished song?
answer: repeat it over and over for hours
choices: repeat it over and over for hours
sing it once, then never again
teach it only to his own calf
trade it for a different male's song
context: A single humpback song runs several minutes, and a male can sing it on repeat for hours — Hawaiian recordings caught sessions lasting up to seven hours. The musical structure was first described by Payne and McVay. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: A group of humpback whales dives beneath a school of fish and blows a rising spiral of bubbles, a curtain the fish will not cross, that packs the school into a dense ball. What does the whole group do next?
answer: lunges up through the middle with mouths open
choices: lunges up through the middle with mouths open
waits for the bubbles to stun the fish
drives the ball toward a second waiting pod
dives deep and lets the fish scatter
context: In bubble-net feeding, humpbacks blow a spiraling curtain of bubbles the fish won't cross, herding them into a ball, then all lunge up through the center with mouths open. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble-net_feeding

question: Off Alaska, a team of humpback whales herds herring with a net of rising bubbles, a skill the whales learn from one another rather than being born with, so only certain groups do it. In one team a single whale, the caller, adds something that makes the whole group strike as one. What does the caller add?
answer: a loud trumpeting call that cues the lunge
choices: a loud trumpeting call that cues the lunge
a burst of clicks that stuns the fish
a slap of its tail to start the dive
a wall of bubbles twice as tall as the others
context: Bubble-net feeding is learned and culturally transmitted, so only some populations do it; one 'caller' whale even trumpets a feeding call to signal the group to lunge at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble-net_feeding

question: Roger Payne's 1970 album of haunting humpback whale songs caused a stir far beyond science. Researchers kept listening to the singing males of each population, season after season, and found something stranger. What does each male in a population sing?
answer: the same song, and when it changes they all switch together
choices: the same song, and when it changes they all switch together
a new song every night, chosen at random
their mother's song, kept unchanged for life
a fixed song that never changes over generations
context: Every male in a population sings the same song, and when the tune changes the whole population adopts the new version together — a shared culture whales learn from one another. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9428538/

question: A new song catches on among humpback whales off eastern Australia and passes from whale to whale through New Caledonia, Tonga, the Cook Islands and French Polynesia, spreading like a fashion. A 2022 study followed such songs farther still. Where did they turn up next?
answer: Off Ecuador, on the far side of the Pacific
choices: Off Ecuador, on the far side of the Pacific
Off Hawaii, north across the equator
Off Madagascar, across the Indian Ocean
Back off eastern Australia, where they began
context: Humpback songs sweep eastward across the South Pacific, from eastern Australia to French Polynesia, and a 2022 study found songs from French Polynesia turning up off Ecuador, linking populations some 14,000 km apart: a cultural wave moving through a whole ocean. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9428538/

question: Engineers copying the humpback whale bolted a row of bumps onto the leading edge of a flipper-shaped wing, then raced it against a smooth one in a wind tunnel. The bumps split the oncoming flow and funnel it into the grooves between them — a trick designers now borrow for turbine blades and fans. What did the bumps buy?
answer: it kept its grip on the flow far past the angle where the smooth wing stalled out
choices: it kept its grip on the flow far past the angle where the smooth wing stalled out
it stalled out sooner, at a gentler tilt than the smooth wing could take
it gave more lift held level, but nothing extra once tilted up steeply
it cut the wing's drag in half but changed nothing about when it stalled
context: The humpback's leading-edge flipper bumps, called tubercles, are a stall-delaying wing device, not decoration. In a landmark 2004 Physics of Fluids study, Miklosovic, Murray, Howle and Fish tested two polycarbonate scale-model flippers — one smooth, one bumped — in a wind tunnel and found the tubercled model delayed the stall angle by about 40% while also increasing lift and cutting drag past stall. The rows of bumps split the incoming water and funnel it into the valleys between them, keeping flow attached at steep angles of attack so a 40-ton whale can bank into tight turns without its flipper stalling like a wing. This 'tubercle effect' has since been applied to wind-turbine blades, fans and airplane wings. Source: Miklosovic, Murray, Howle & Fish (2004), Physics of Fluids, 'Leading-edge tubercles delay stall on humpback whale flippers'; corroborated by Fish & Battle (1995), J. Morphology 225:51-60 (PubMed 7650744) and ScienceDaily 2004-05-12.

question: A humpback whale lunges into a bait ball and gulps a mouthful of water as big as its own body. Inside the flexible joint between the two halves of its lower jaw sits a grape-sized organ, discovered in 2012 and found only in this whale's family of giant gulpers. What does that organ do?
answer: it feels the jaw swing wide and the throat balloon out, timing the whole lunge
choices: it feels the jaw swing wide and the throat balloon out, timing the whole lunge
it stores a reserve of oxygen that feeds the brain through a long, deep dive
it strains the ocean salt back out of the seawater the whale gulps down
it shapes the deep booming notes the male threads all through his long song
context: Rorqual whales, including the humpback, carry a sensory organ that nothing else on Earth has, discovered only in 2012. Pyenson and colleagues, reporting in Nature, found a grape-sized organ embedded in the fibrous joint between the two unfused halves of the lower jaw. Packed with mechanoreceptors — nerve endings and papillae in a gel-like matrix derived from an ancestral tooth socket — it senses jaw rotation and throat-pouch expansion in real time and feeds that to the brain to choreograph the split-second timing of a lunge: when to open, how far the pouch has filled, and when to clamp shut. Source: Pyenson et al. (2012), Nature 485:498, 'Discovery of a sensory organ that coordinates lunge feeding in rorqual whales' (PubMed 22622577); Smithsonian Insider 2012.

question: An ichthyosaur cut through the sea in the age of dinosaurs, with a smooth body like a dolphin's or a tuna's, a triangular fin on its back, flippers and a crescent tail. One thing set it apart from every fish around it. What was it?
answer: It had to surface to breathe air
choices: It had to surface to breathe air
It beat its tail up and down
It never left the deep water
It laid its eggs on the seafloor
context: The ichthyosaur was a reptile, not a fish. It breathed air, so it rose to the surface the way a dolphin does today -- yet dolphins would not appear for another 200 million years. Source: Simple English Wikipedia, Ichthyosaur.

question: Eyes nearly as wide as dinner plates stared from the skull of a giant ichthyosaur, a dolphin-shaped reptile that swam the seas of the dinosaur age. Where did eyes that huge let it hunt?
answer: Hunting in the black depths of the deep ocean
choices: Hunting in the black depths of the deep ocean
Watching the shore for its egg-laying beach
Spotting prey across the bright open surface
Reading the color of coral in the reef
context: Enormous eyes gather as much light as possible, letting the ichthyosaur hunt where almost no light reaches -- the deep ocean, or the surface at night. Source: Kiddle, Temnodontosaurus facts for kids.

question: Scientists measured the eye socket of Temnodontosaurus platyodon, a giant ichthyosaur that hunted the seas of the dinosaur age, at about 25 centimeters across, about the width of a dinner plate. Which living animal has an eye that comes close to that size?
answer: The colossal squid
choices: The colossal squid
The blue whale
The great white shark
The saltwater crocodile
context: At more than 25 cm across, the ichthyosaur's eye rivals the colossal squid's, about 27 cm, among the very largest eyes ever measured. Source: Wikipedia, 'Temnodontosaurus' and 'Colossal squid'.

question: Turtles and lizards crawl ashore and bury leathery eggs in sand or soil. An ichthyosaur, a dolphin-shaped reptile that ruled the seas about 200 million years ago, swam on long flippers with a fluked tail and no true feet, and could never leave the water. Fossils show how it brought its young into the world. What did they reveal?
answer: It gave birth to live young in the open water
choices: It gave birth to live young in the open water
It carried its eggs in its mouth until they hatched
It glued its eggs to floating driftwood
It laid eggs that floated at the surface to hatch
context: Some ichthyosaur fossils preserve a mother caught mid-birth, a baby half-emerged from her body -- proof these sea reptiles bore live young rather than laying eggs on land. Source: Live Science, Oldest Fossil of Reptile Live Birth Found. (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: In China, paleontologists split open a fossil of a mother Chaohusaurus, an early ichthyosaur, and found three young preserved with her -- one already born, one still inside, and one caught halfway out. That halfway pup was emerging head-first, not the tail-first way of dolphins and whales. To scientists, that head-first exit was a clue about one thing. What did it tell them?
answer: Ichthyosaurs inherited live birth from land-living ancestors
choices: Ichthyosaurs inherited live birth from land-living ancestors
Ichthyosaurs had only recently returned to land
The mother was the last of an egg-laying line
The pup had turned the wrong way and drowned
context: Head-first birth points to land ancestors that already bore live young, rather than the trait being invented for sea life. Later ichthyosaurs are found giving birth tail-first, like dolphins. Source: NPR, Fossil Shows Triassic-Era Sea Creature Gave Birth.

question: Swimming the seas of the dinosaur age, an ichthyosaur, a reptile, was built much like a dolphin, a tuna and a fast lamnid shark are today, though the four come from unrelated branches of the animal kingdom. What one demand drove them all to the same body plan?
answer: The need to swim fast for long distances in open water
choices: The need to swim fast for long distances in open water
The need to hide their color against the seafloor
The need to survive freezing polar temperatures
The need to crush hard-shelled prey with strong jaws
context: The ichthyosaur (reptile), dolphin (mammal), tuna (bony fish), and lamnid shark (shark) are four separate lineages that all evolved the same streamlined 'thunniform' shape -- the optimal body for fast, sustained swimming in open water. Source: NCBI PMC, Skeletal convergence in thunniform sharks, ichthyosaurs, whales, and tunas.

question: A fossil of the ichthyosaur Stenopterygius from a German shale bed still shows traces of its real skin: dark along its back and pale underneath, a two-tone scheme known as countershading that dolphins and sharks also wear today. What job did that coloring do for the ichthyosaur?
answer: Camouflage from predators looking down or up
choices: Camouflage from predators looking down or up
Warned rivals off its hunting territory
Attracted mates during the breeding season
Soaked up sunlight to warm its blood
context: Dark-above, light-below coloring -- called countershading -- hides an animal against the dark depths from above and the bright surface from below. The same fossil also preserved a layer of blubber. Source: NC State News, Soft Tissue Shows Jurassic Ichthyosaur Was Warm-Blooded. (Legend-tier preservation.)

question: A poor family of fossil hunters pried the first complete ichthyosaur skeleton London's scientists ever saw, a 17-foot creature, from the crumbling Dorset cliffs at Lyme Regis in 1811. The one who dug out most of it was a surprise. Who was it?
answer: A twelve-year-old local girl
choices: A twelve-year-old local girl
A twelve-year-old apprentice boy
A young village schoolteacher
A young dockside fisherman
context: Mary Anning's brother Joseph spotted the skull in 1811 when Mary was just twelve; she dug out the rest of the 17-foot skeleton months later, on the Dorset cliffs. Source: Wikipedia, Mary Anning. (Legend of paleontology.)

question: Temnodontosaurus, a 9-meter ichthyosaur with knife-like teeth, ruled its sea as a top predator early in the dinosaur age. One fossil of it still preserves its last meal inside the stomach cavity, showing what it had been eating. What surprising meal was in there?
answer: Other, younger ichthyosaurs
choices: Other, younger ichthyosaurs
A large sea turtle
Its own shed teeth
Chunks of driftwood
context: One Temnodontosaurus skeleton preserves three juvenile Stenopterygius, smaller ichthyosaurs, and many cephalopod hooks in its gut: this top predator ate other ichthyosaurs. Source: Wikipedia, Temnodontosaurus (specimen SMNS 50000).

question: Workers draining a lagoon at Rutland Water, a reservoir in the English Midlands, spotted huge bones sticking out of the mud in 2021. They had found the biggest, most complete ichthyosaur skeleton ever unearthed in Britain, buried for some 180 million years, and they nicknamed it the Rutland Sea Dragon. How big was it?
answer: About 10 meters long, the length of a bus
choices: About 10 meters long, the length of a bus
About 6 meters long, the length of a rowboat
About 14 meters long, the length of two buses
About 8 meters long, the length of a large van
context: The Rutland Sea Dragon, probably a Temnodontosaurus, runs about 10 meters (33 feet); its 2-meter skull, still in its block of rock and plaster, weighs just under a tonne. It is the largest and most complete ichthyosaur skeleton ever found in Britain. Source: University of Leicester news, 'Britain's largest Sea Dragon discovered in Rutland' (January 2022).

question: Early fossil collectors kept finding ichthyosaur tails with a sharp downward bend near the tip. Certain it was damage from being crushed in the rock, they snapped the bones straight to tidy the specimens up. Then the flawless Holzmaden fossils, with body outlines intact, revealed the bend was no accident. What were the collectors destroying?
answer: The bony support for the tail fin's lower lobe
choices: The bony support for the tail fin's lower lobe
A store of insulating blubber under the skin
The last ribs protecting a swallowed meal
A row of spines that ran along the back
context: An advanced ichthyosaur's crescent tail is mostly soft tissue, but the backbone stiffens the lower lobe: the tail vertebrae bend sharply downward and run inside it. Before the exquisitely preserved Holzmaden (Germany) Stenopterygius specimens showed the true two-lobed tail with its body outline intact, collectors read that downward kink as post-mortem breakage and routinely straightened the tails to 'fix' them, wiping out the real anatomy. Source: Capeia 'The Evolutionary History of Ichthyosaurs' 2017 (https://beta.capeia.com/paleobiology/2017/09/25/the-evolutionary-history-of-ichthyosaurs); PeerJ Solnhofen ichthyosaur soft-tissue paper (https://peerj.com/articles/13173/).

question: An elephant on the African savanna catches a faint tremor in the ground, perhaps the rumble of a herd many miles away. She freezes, leans her huge head forward and lifts one front foot, toe aimed at the ground like a dancer's. As she presses it slowly down, what does the foot itself do?
answer: Spreads to widen its contact with the ground
choices: Spreads to widen its contact with the ground
Curls its edges up to form a hollow cup
Taps out a quick reply against the soil
Rolls onto its outer rim to muffle its weight
