context: When picking up a distant seismic signal, elephants freeze, lean forward, lift a foot and point the toe down, then press their feet into the ground — spreading the foot to expand its contact area by up to about 20% to feel the vibration better. The vibration is caught by Pacinian corpuscles, pressure-sensing receptors packed around the edges of the foot. Source: KQED, 'How Elephants Listen ... With Their Feet' (kqed.org/science/1926248).

question: A Namib Desert golden mole, a furry mammal no bigger than a mouse, sand-swims through the dunes of southwest Africa with no working eyes at all, only fur-covered skin where eyes used to be. It pauses to press its head to the sand, then heads straight for termites hidden beneath tufts of grass. What sense guides it?
answer: Reading vibrations in the ground
choices: Reading vibrations in the ground
Sniffing scent trails on the breeze
Sensing the warmth of the mounds
Tasting salts left in the sand
context: The Namib Desert golden mole is blind and 'sand-swims' through dunes, dipping its head to read seismic vibrations — finding termite prey clustered under grassy mounds largely by feeling ground vibrations, with no eyes to guide it. Source: Wikipedia 'Seismic communication'; Narins et al., 'Seismic sensitivity in the Desert Golden Mole' (researchgate.net/publication/11290943).

question: Researchers combed through 947 hours of recordings made after dark at zoos, listening to giraffes, animals long thought to be almost mute. They found the giraffes had been doing something in the dark that their keepers had never noticed. What were they doing?
answer: Humming to each other in low tones
choices: Humming to each other in low tones
Grinding their teeth in slow rhythm
Whistling sharply through their nostrils
Stamping a beat with their front hooves
context: 947 hours of zoo recordings turned up 65 low, sustained hums averaging about 92 Hz — a nocturnal sound the zookeepers themselves had never noticed. Source: Baotic, Stoeger et al., 'Nocturnal humming vocalizations,' BMC Research Notes (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4565008); PBS NOVA (pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/giraffes-hum-to-each-other).

question: Blue whales singing across the Northeast Pacific dropped one of their song types about 31 percent in pitch between 1963 and 2008, and seven song types out of ten worldwide are sliding lower as well. McDonald, Hildebrand and Mesnick have a still-debated explanation. What is it?
answer: As numbers rebound after whaling, mates live closer, so a loud high call is no longer needed
choices: As numbers rebound after whaling, mates live closer, so a loud high call is no longer needed
Ship-engine noise now masks the high notes, forcing whales to sing far lower to be heard
Warming, less salty water carries low pitches better, so the songs sank to match it
Older surviving males dominate the choruses, and their aging voices simply drop with age
context: The blue whale's song is among the deepest on the planet, and it is getting deeper: the best-documented Northeast Pacific song type dropped about 31% in tonal frequency between 1963 and 2008, and 7 of the world's 10 blue-whale song types are shifting downward. The leading (and still debated) idea from Mark McDonald, John Hildebrand and Sarah Mesnick is that as populations recover from whaling, potential mates are closer, so males no longer need to sing loud-and-high to be heard far away and can afford to drop the pitch. Crucially, the trend is worldwide and steady, which argues AGAINST human ocean noise as the cause. Source: McDonald, Hildebrand & Mesnick 2009, 'Worldwide decline in tonal frequencies of blue whale songs', Endangered Species Research; Scripps Institution of Oceanography news release, https://scripps.ucsd.edu/news/pitch-blue-whale-songs-declining-around-world-scientists-discover

question: The blind Namib golden mole carries a hugely swollen ear bone: its malleus weighs about 18 milligrams, nearer a human's than a mouse's, the most massive for body size of 117 mammals measured. How, by Matthew Mason's account, does all that mass sharpen its sense of low sounds?
answer: The heavy bone lags behind the moving skull, and that slip drives the inner ear
choices: The heavy bone lags behind the moving skull, and that slip drives the inner ear
The bone rings like a struck bell, amplifying each tremor into a lasting tone
The bone seals the ear canal, so only ground-borne shakes ever reach the nerve
The heavy bone stiffens the eardrum, tuning it to only the deepest tones
context: Golden moles have the greatest ossicular mass relative to body size of 117 mammal species measured: the Namib golden mole's malleus weighs around 18 mg, closer to a human's (28 mg) or a cat's than to a similarly sized mouse's (0.28 mg). Matthew Mason proposed the mechanism is 'inertial bone conduction' — when a seismic wave shakes the skull, the heavy malleus lags behind, and that relative motion drives the inner ear, a model predicting a 30–60 dB boost in low-frequency sensitivity. The blind mole uses it to home in on wind-shaken clumps of dune grass and the termites beneath. Source: Mason, 'Bone conduction and seismic sensitivity in golden moles (Chrysochloridae)' and 'Middle ear dynamics... Cape golden mole' (J. Exp. Biol. 2006); summarized via Wikipedia 'Golden mole' and the Afrotheria Specialist Group, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_mole

question: Inside a busy hive, about 50,000 honeybees go about their work, and nearly every one is a female who never lays an egg; all the eggs come from a single bee, the queen. The workers raise her young instead of their own. What are the workers to the queen?
answer: Her own daughters
choices: Her own daughters
Unrelated hired help
Her older sisters
Bees from other hives
context: Every worker in the hive is the queen's own daughter, hatched from her eggs, yet they forage, nurse, and build the comb instead of breeding. A colony is essentially one giant family serving one mother. Source: Animal Diversity Web, Apis mellifera account.

question: A honeybee queen lays a few thousand eggs each summer that she leaves unfertilized, and from them hatch the drones, big-eyed males with no sting. When autumn comes, the workers shove the drones out of the hive to die. What is the one job a drone exists for?
answer: To mate with a queen
choices: To mate with a queen
To guard the hive entrance
To fan the comb cool
To scout for flowers
context: Drones are the hive's only males — a seasonal few thousand whose sole role is to mate with a queen. They do no work inside the hive at all. Source: Animal Diversity Web, Apis mellifera account; 'Reproductive Senescence in Drones of the Honey Bee' (PMC6358831).

question: Leafcutter ants of the genus Atta march out of the leaf litter of Central and South American rainforests in long ribbons, each worker holding a snipped green leaf overhead like a flag. A single colony can grow to some five million workers, every one a daughter of the same queen. About how long can that queen live?
answer: Over a decade
choices: Over a decade
A single summer
About three years
Just a few months
context: One Atta queen — mother to up to five million sterile workers — can live over ten years, laying the eggs for the entire colony that whole time. Source: Britannica, 'Leafcutter ant'; San Diego Zoo Global Atta cephalotes fact sheet.

question: An Eciton army ant soldier marches beside its raiding column through a Central American rainforest, a big ant built as a living weapon, with huge curved jaws shaped like sabers for fighting off enemies. Those jaws are so specialized that the soldier cannot manage one basic need on its own. What can it not do for itself?
answer: Feed itself
choices: Feed itself
Groom its own body
Follow the scent trail
Right itself when flipped
context: An Eciton soldier's oversized sickle jaws are built purely for combat and can't handle food, so ordinary workers must feed the soldiers by mouth. Source: Britannica, 'Eciton army ant'; Bug of the Week, 'Rapacious raiders: Army ants, Eciton spp.'

question: A Macrotermes termite queen lies in a royal chamber deep inside a red-earth mound rising from the African savanna, her belly swollen to about 11 centimeters, far too big for her to move. Pale and helpless, she is tended by her workers, an egg-laying engine that runs for years. Roughly how many eggs can she lay in a day?
answer: About 30,000
choices: About 30,000
About 300
About 3,000
About 300,000
context: In Macrotermes the queen's swollen abdomen can reach about 11 cm (4.3 in) long, and she lays roughly 30,000 eggs a day for years. A near-legendary figure among social insects. Source: Britannica, 'Termite: Natural history'; ScienceDirect S0022191025000782.

question: W. D. Hamilton puzzled over why a worker bee or ant would give up breeding to spend her life raising her mother's young. His classic answer, a leading idea rather than settled fact, pointed to their odd genetics, in which males hatch from unfertilized eggs, so that two full sisters share an unusual fraction of their genes. On average, about what fraction?
answer: About three-quarters
choices: About three-quarters
About one-half
About one-quarter
About one-third
context: Under haplodiploidy, full sisters share on average about 75% of their genes — more than the 50% a mother shares with her own young. This is a leading idea (W.D. Hamilton's) for why workers raise sisters, not settled fact. Source: Wikipedia, 'Evolution of eusociality'.

question: Jacobus Boomsma saw a hole in the old genetic explanation for why worker bees and ants give up breeding: termites run the same kind of sterile-worker society, yet their genes pass down the ordinary way. His theory, meant to cover every case, traces each origin of such a society to a founding mother whose mating had one key feature. What was it?
answer: She mated with a single male for her whole life
choices: She mated with a single male for her whole life
She mated with many males and stored their sperm
She mated with several of her own brothers
She took a fresh mate every breeding season
context: Boomsma's 'monogamy hypothesis' (first set out in 2007 and developed in a 2009 review) argues that eusociality could only take its first step in lineages whose ancestral mother mated with just one male for life. Under strict lifetime monogamy, a female is exactly as related to her full siblings as to her own offspring, so staying home to raise siblings costs her nothing genetically. A 2008 study by William Hughes and colleagues found lifetime monogamy was the ancestral state in all eight independent origins of eusociality they examined among bees, ants and wasps, and this has largely displaced the older three-quarters haplodiploidy story as the explanation for the initial evolutionary step. Source: Boomsma, 'Lifetime monogamy and the evolution of eusociality,' Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 2009 (PMC2781870); Hughes, Oldroyd, Beekman & Ratnieks 2008, Science 320:1213. The haplodiploidy link itself was separately challenged by Nowak, Tarnita & Wilson, Nature 2010.

question: An Irish elk stag strode across Europe and northern Asia in the Ice Age, standing about 2 meters at the shoulder and weighing up to 700 kilograms, more than 1,500 pounds. The species died out only about 7,700 years ago. Which living animal was it about the size of?
answer: An Alaskan moose
choices: An Alaskan moose
A white-tailed deer
A wild boar
A red fox
context: The Irish elk (Megaloceros giganteus) was one of the largest deer that ever lived -- about 2 m at the shoulder and up to 700 kg, matching a modern Alaskan moose. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_elk ; smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/irish-elk-biggest-antlers-ever-180977706

question: A giant deer of the Ice Age ranged across Europe and Asia far beyond Ireland, yet its bones turn up so often in Irish peat bogs that people named it the Irish elk. It was not an elk at all. DNA from its bones has pinned down its closest living relative. Which deer is it?
answer: The fallow deer
choices: The fallow deer
The reindeer
The roe deer
The mule deer
context: Despite the name, the Irish elk was a giant deer, not an elk. DNA evidence settled that its nearest living relative is the fallow deer. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_elk ; sciencenews.org/article/dna-pegs-irish-elks-nearest-relatives

question: An Irish elk stag of Ice Age Europe carried antlers bigger than any other animal's ever found, great flat palms so wide that people who see the fossil skulls struggle to picture them on a living deer. About how wide did they span from tip to tip?
answer: As long as a family car
choices: As long as a family car
As wide as a doorway
As long as a school bus
As tall as a person
context: A male Irish elk carried the largest antlers of any animal ever known -- up to about 3.6 m (12 ft) tip to tip, and 4.26 m (14 ft) in the largest recorded specimen: as wide as a family car is long. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_elk ; iflscience.com/enormous-extinct-deer-had-even-more-enormous-antlers-but-we-dont-know-why-72818

question: An Irish elk stag of Ice Age Europe carried a rack of antlers weighing around 40 kilograms, some 90 pounds of solid bone, and wider than any other deer's. What happened to that rack over the course of a single year?
answer: Grew the whole rack anew and dropped it
choices: Grew the whole rack anew and dropped it
Kept the same rack for life
Only added a few new points each year
Grew it larger without ever shedding
context: Each spring the stag started from bare stubs and rebuilt the entire car-wide, ~40 kg (88 lb) rack, then shed it and did it all again the next year. Sources: smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/irish-elk-biggest-antlers-ever-180977706 ; nhm.ac.uk/discover/irish-elk-giant-deer.html

question: Two Irish elk stags met on the breeding grounds of Ice Age Europe, and rivals did sometimes clash, hooking the bases of their antlers to shove each other. Scientists who compare the fossil racks with red deer, which behave the same way, think the giant flat palms were built mostly for something else. What was their main purpose?
answer: Showing off to win mates
choices: Showing off to win mates
Digging for buried roots
Sweeping snow off grazing
Scaring away wolf packs
context: The giant antlers were mainly for display, an extreme case of sexual selection. Rivals interlocked the lower parts of their antlers to push and shove for the right to mate -- but the huge flat palms were chiefly a show. Sources: smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/irish-elk-biggest-antlers-ever-180977706 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_elk

question: An Irish elk stag of Ice Age Europe, growing his 40-kilogram rack of antlers in spring, needed a huge surge of calcium and phosphate within a single season. Where do biologists' models suggest he drew most of those minerals from?
answer: From the calcium in his own bones
choices: From the calcium in his own bones
From salt licks he swallowed
From mineral-rich spring grass
From bark stripped off trees
context: Models suggest up to 80% of the calcium a stag could draw came from its own skeleton -- about twice the mineral drain a moose faces. A stag that couldn't refill from good grazing risked osteoporosis, brittle bones. Source: markwitton-com.blogspot.com/2020/11/megaloceros-giganteus-behind-antlers.html

question: Stephen Jay Gould reopened the case of the Irish elk in a famous 1974 paper. People had long blamed its giant antlers for its end, saying the stags were crushed by the weight of their own racks. Gould compared its antlers with those of other deer. What did he find?
answer: They were just the size expected for so big a deer
choices: They were just the size expected for so big a deer
They were far too heavy for its neck to carry
They were smaller, for its size, than most deer's
They grew far larger than its bones could anchor
context: Gould's 1974 paper showed that across the deer family antler size climbs steeply with body size, and the Irish elk's antlers were just what that trend predicts for a deer so big; he argued they were a display advantage, not a fatal handicap. What did end the giant deer is still debated: Adrian Lister and Anthony Stuart concluded that environmental change over thousands of years left the herds vulnerable, and human hunting may have dealt the final blow. Sources: Gould 1974, Evolution 28:191; daily.jstor.org/the-cartoonishly-giant-antlers-of-the-irish-elk ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_elk

question: Moen, Pastor and Cohen ran a simulation in 1999 comparing the yearly antler growth of an Irish elk stag with that of a living moose, and found the giant deer paid a far steeper cost of one kind. What did growing that rack demand so much more of?
answer: Energy -- about three-quarters of what all his fat and muscle reserves took
choices: Energy -- about three-quarters of what all his fat and muscle reserves took
Sleep -- roughly double the daily rest a resting moose needed each night
Water -- nearly triple a moose's daily intake drawn straight from marsh pools
Salt -- far more than any mineral lick on the open steppe could ever supply
context: Antlers cost minerals AND raw energy. Moen, Pastor & Cohen's (1999) simulation estimated that growing the Irish elk's rack demanded roughly 75% as much energy as the stag needed to lay down all his summer fat and protein reserves combined -- versus only about 50% in a living moose. So the giant deer paid a proportionally far steeper springtime energy tax than any deer alive today, a hidden cost on top of the calcium and phosphorus it pulled from its own skeleton. Source: Moen, Pastor & Cohen (1999), 'Antler growth and extinction of Irish elk' (experts.umn.edu publication summary; WebSearch corroboration).

question: O'Driscoll Worman and Kimbrell modeled the Irish elk in 2008 and challenged the old story that its antlers doomed the stags: antlers can get smaller over generations without much trouble, and a herd hardly suffers when it loses its big-antlered males. As the late Ice Age's growing season shortened, which group did their model say took the real hit?
answer: The females, whose output of fast-growing young could fall by half
choices: The females, whose output of fast-growing young could fall by half
The calves, whose first-winter survival dropped as the cold set in
The eldest bulls, whose worn teeth failed on the coarser tundra grass
The wanderers, whose long migrations no longer reached green pasture
context: O'Driscoll Worman & Kimbrell (2008, Oikos 117:1397) modeled the extinction and argued the 'giant antlers doomed the stags' story is largely wrong -- antler size is evolutionarily flexible, and losing big-antlered males barely dents population growth. Their model instead squeezed the FEMALES: as the Pleistocene growing season shortened, the heavy cost of gestating and rearing fast-running precocial young could have cut female reproductive output by up to about 50%, so stressed mothers, not stressed big-antlered bulls, most plausibly drove the collapse. This remains a live scientific debate, not a settled verdict. Source: O'Driscoll Worman & Kimbrell (2008), 'Getting to the hart of the matter: did antlers truly cause the extinction of the Irish elk?', Oikos 117:1397-1405 (Wiley; ResearchGate abstract).

question: A squid in a hurry draws water into its muscular mantle, then blasts it out through a narrow, steerable tube and rockets off in the opposite direction. What is this way of swimming called?
answer: Jet propulsion
choices: Jet propulsion
Wave gliding
Fin paddling
Tail whipping
context: The squid works exactly like a rocket ship: fluid fired hard one way pushes the body the other way. The tube it fires through is called the funnel, or siphon. Source: https://www.sciencefriday.com/educational-resources/jet-setting-cephalopods/

question: On the sandy floor of a shallow bay, a shelled animal does what no clam should manage: it swims, clapping its two fan-shaped shells shut to squirt water out behind and hop away from a hungry starfish. Which animal is it?
answer: A scallop
choices: A scallop
A barnacle
A limpet
An oyster
context: Most clams and oysters are cemented down or buried, but a scallop can clap its shells to jet across the seafloor in awkward hops — one of very few swimming bivalves. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/scallop-bivalve

question: Swiveling one flexible tube on its underside, a squid steers through the sea by squirting water out of it. Aimed forward, the tube shoots the squid backward; swung to the side, it swings the squid around, so a single nozzle gives both thrust and steering. What is the tube called?
answer: The funnel
choices: The funnel
The mantle
The gill
The fin
context: The funnel (also called the siphon) is a bendy nozzle. By pointing it, a squid controls both direction and turns — steering and thrust from one organ. Source: https://www.sciencefriday.com/educational-resources/jet-setting-cephalopods/

question: A neon flying squid chased by dolphins or tuna in the Pacific jets water out so hard that it blasts clear of the sea. In the air it opens its fins and arms into little wings and sails above the waves before splashing down. About how far can one flight carry it?
answer: About 30 meters
choices: About 30 meters
About 30 centimeters
About 3 meters
About 300 meters
context: That's the length of a swimming pool, crossed entirely in the air. Spreading its fins and arms for lift, the squid truly 'flies' as an escape — though it risks being snatched by seabirds up there. Source: https://www.calacademy.org/explore-science/the-flying-squid

question: A jellyfish squeezes its bell to push out a ring of water, then coasts a long way before the next pulse, never swimming nonstop like a fish. Scientists measured the energy it burns for every meter it travels and compared it with fish, birds and mammals. Where does it rank among the swimmers they tested?
answer: The most efficient swimmer of any animal
choices: The most efficient swimmer of any animal
Roughly tied with a tuna
The least efficient large swimmer
Average for a soft-bodied animal
context: Measured by cost of transport — energy burned per distance — no swimming creature yet measured beats the jellyfish. The trick is coasting between pulses instead of paddling nonstop. Source: https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1306983110

question: A dragonfly nymph hunts along the bottom of a pond for months or years before it crawls out to grow wings. To lunge at prey or flee, it fires water out of its body and shoots forward like a tiny rocket. Where does the water go in and out?
answer: Its rectum, where it also breathes
choices: Its rectum, where it also breathes
Its mouth, then out through its gills
A pair of belly pores
Hollow tubes in its legs
context: The nymph breathes through gills lining its rectum. Firing that same water out the anus jets it forward to catch prey or flee, a rare way for an insect to swim. Source: https://www.iflscience.com/dragonfly-babies-breathe-through-their-butts-but-thats-not-all-76934

question: Each pulse of a jellyfish's bell ends with a recoil: as the bell springs back to its old shape, a spinning ring of water forms behind it and gives the animal a second push forward. What does the jellyfish gain from that extra push?
answer: It travels about 30% farther each cycle
choices: It travels about 30% farther each cycle
It roughly doubles the water it moves per squeeze
It cuts its muscle energy nearly in half
It adds a second full-power muscle stroke
context: The passive suction of the vortex ring is a second, free stroke — motion the jellyfish never paid muscle energy for. That recycled push is why it out-coasts every other swimmer measured. Source: https://phys.org/news/2013-10-reveals-jellyfish-efficient-swimmers-video.html

question: Long before fish ruled the oceans, one group of cephalopods was already jetting through the sea by squirting water through a tube, in the Late Cambrian and Ordovician seas, more than 450 million years ago. Several other cephalopod groups later swam the same way. Which group came first?
answer: The shelled nautiloids
choices: The shelled nautiloids
The coiled ammonites
The ten-armed belemnites
The hovering cuttlefish
context: All four are cephalopods that swim by jetting water through a funnel, but they did not arrive together. The shelled nautiloids came first: they were already jetting through a funnel-like 'hyponome' in the Late Cambrian and diversifying through the Ordovician, well over 450 million years ago — long before fish dominated the seas. The other three inherited the same water-jet design far later: the coiled ammonites appeared in the Early Devonian (~410 million years ago), and the bullet-shaped belemnites and the hovering cuttlefish are Mesozoic-and-later coleoids, closer cousins of modern squid. The squid's rocket has a half-billion-year backstory, and the nautiloids started it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautiloid (hyponome jet, Late Cambrian origin, Ordovician diversification); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonoidea (ammonoids first appear in the Early Devonian).

question: A shimmering green emerald jewel wasp, only about 22 millimeters long, hunts cockroaches far bigger than itself in the tropics of Africa and Asia. Instead of killing its giant prey, what does the wasp do to the roach?
answer: turns it into an obedient living zombie
choices: turns it into an obedient living zombie
spins it into a tight silk cocoon
paralyzes it as stiff as a statue
sticks it to a leaf as a food store
context: The emerald jewel wasp (Ampulex compressa) hunts cockroaches far bigger than itself. Rather than killing the roach, it turns it into a living, obedient zombie that later walks to its own grave under its own power. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_cockroach_wasp

question: For the delicate work ahead, an emerald jewel wasp needs its cockroach alive but perfectly still. Its first sting goes into the cluster of nerves that runs the roach's front legs and buys a couple of minutes of stillness. What does the wasp need those minutes for?
answer: to line up a second, precise sting
choices: to line up a second, precise sting
to lay all of its eggs at once
to drag it underground straight away
to drink from the roach's back
context: The wasp stings the cockroach twice. The first sting hits the front-leg nerve-cluster and paralyzes the front legs for a couple of minutes, just long enough to hold the roach still for the real strike that follows. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_cockroach_wasp

question: The second sting an emerald jewel wasp gives a cockroach far bigger than herself is the precise one. Afterward the roach still walks, rights itself and can even swim, yet its urge to flee danger is gone. Where does that sting go?
answer: straight into the roach's brain
choices: straight into the roach's brain
into the roach's wing muscles
into the roach's egg sac
into the roach's rear leg joint
context: The second sting goes directly into the cockroach's brain. The venom switches off the roach's escape reflex: it can still walk, right itself, and swim, but it has completely lost the urge to run away from danger. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_cockroach_wasp

question: An emerald jewel wasp, a shimmering green insect, has finished stinging a cockroach twice its size. Now the wasp must take the roach across the forest floor to its burrow, where it will lay an egg on the roach. How does the wasp get the roach there?
answer: it pulls the roach along by an antenna
choices: it pulls the roach along by an antenna
it rides on the roach's back and taps
it rolls the roach ahead like a ball
it flies while gripping the roach's wings
context: The wasp grabs what is left of an antenna and leads the docile roach on a walk to its burrow, pulling it along exactly like a dog on a leash. The roach walks under its own power to its own tomb. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_cockroach_wasp

question: In its burrow in a tropical forest of Africa or Asia, an emerald jewel wasp glues a single egg to a cockroach's side and seals the entrance. Three days or so later a larva hatches from the egg, and the roach never once fights back. What does the larva do to it?
answer: it chews inside and eats the roach alive
choices: it chews inside and eats the roach alive
it waits for the roach to die, then feeds
it spins a cocoon on the roach's back
it nibbles only the roach's wing tips
context: The egg hatches in about three days. The newborn larva chews a hole into the still-living roach and burrows inside, eating the roach's organs from within while the roach stays alive and never fights back. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_cockroach_wasp

question: An olive-green kakapo, a parrot the size of a small cat with an owl-like ring of feathers around its face, waddles across a mossy New Zealand forest floor at night. What can every other parrot on Earth do that the kakapo cannot?
answer: Fly
choices: Fly
See in the dark
Nest in trees
Make any sound
context: The kakapo (Strigops habroptilus) is the only flightless parrot on Earth. Its wings are too small and its feathers too soft to lift it, so it walks the forest floor and hauls itself up trees with beak and strong legs instead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81k%C4%81p%C5%8D

question: A kakapo forages on the forest floor of New Zealand, islands where for millions of years no ground-hunting mammal chased it. Living safe on the ground, its body changed as no other parrot's has. Which record does it hold among the world's parrots?
answer: The world's heaviest parrot
choices: The world's heaviest parrot
The world's fastest parrot
The world's longest parrot
The world's smallest parrot
context: A male kakapo averages about 2 kg (4.4 lb), some 400 g heavier than the flighted hyacinth macaw, the largest parrot that still takes to the air. Grounded life in a predator-free land let it grow bulky. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81k%C4%81p%C5%8D

question: A male kakapo climbs to a hilltop on a still New Zealand night, digs a shallow bowl and starts to boom: a deep pulse under 100 hertz that throbs out every second or two, felt in the chest more than heard. What part of his body does he puff up like a balloon to make the call?
answer: An air sac in his chest
choices: An air sac in his chest
His hollow leg bones
The pouch beneath his beak
The webbing of his feet
context: The male kakapo pumps up a stretchy air sac in his chest and releases a 'boom' below 100 Hz, so low it carries as a felt vibration. He repeats it every one to two seconds through the night. Source: https://www.doc.govt.nz/nature/native-animals/birds/birds-a-z/kakapo/behaviour/

question: High on a New Zealand ridge, a male kakapo, a rare ground-dwelling parrot the size of a house cat, scoops a shallow bowl in the dirt with his feet and settles into it. For hours after dark he booms out a deep call to attract a mate. What does lying in that bowl do for his booming?
answer: Amplifies it so it carries up to a kilometre
choices: Amplifies it so it carries up to a kilometre
Cools his body during the long hours of effort
Steadies its low pitch so females hear it clearly
Shields his soft feathers from the night rain
context: The dug bowl acts like a natural amplifier, bouncing the low boom out across the hills — up to a kilometre on a calm night, several kilometres in the wind. Legendary among New Zealand naturalists. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81k%C4%81p%C5%8D

question: On the New Zealand forest floor, where for millions of years no ground mammal hunted it, a heavy, moss-green kakapo relies on one instinct to stay safe from sharp-eyed birds of prey overhead. Against the cats and stoats that European settlers brought in the 1800s, that same instinct is deadly. What does a startled kakapo do?
answer: Freezes and trusts its camouflage
choices: Freezes and trusts its camouflage
Flees down a burrow
Screams to warn the flock
Plays dead and stops breathing
context: Freezing and relying on its mottled green feathers worked against sight-hunting hawks, but introduced cats and stoats hunt by smell — and a motionless bird is simply an easy meal. The kakapo's own strong, sweet, musty odour betrays exactly where the frozen bird hides. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81k%C4%81p%C5%8D

question: Kakapo can sit out two, three, even four years without laying a single egg, the whole population waiting together. Then one native New Zealand tree fruits heavily, and the birds breed all at once in a mass event conservationists know as a boom year. Which tree's rare bumper crop are they waiting for?
answer: The rimu tree
choices: The rimu tree
The rata tree
The kauri tree
The manuka tree
context: Kakapo breed only in 'mast' years, when the rimu fruits heavily — an event that comes just once every few years. The birds hold off until the forest can feast, so seasons can be years apart. Source: https://www.nzbirdsonline.org.nz/species/kakapo

question: At night in the Mojave Desert, a small, big-eyed rodent bounds across the sand on two long back legs. It can live its whole life without ever taking a drink of water. What is this desert rodent?
answer: The kangaroo rat
choices: The kangaroo rat
The jerboa
The antelope ground squirrel
The desert woodrat
context: The kangaroo rat (genus Dipodomys) of the American Southwest is famous for going its whole life without drinking. It survives on the water hidden inside dry seeds, wrung out by an extraordinary body. Source: trendingamerican.com; Open University OpenLearn (Schmidt-Nielsen desert-animal physiology).

question: A kangaroo rat hops through Death Valley, where months can pass without rain and there is no pool or stream to drink from. Yet it never dies of thirst. Where does nearly all the water in its body come from?
answer: Water its own body makes from dry seeds
choices: Water its own body makes from dry seeds
Dew it licks off cactus spines at dawn
Moisture stored in a special second stomach
Blood it drinks from insects it catches
context: When any animal burns food for energy through respiration, the chemistry releases water as a by-product — 'metabolic water.' The kangaroo rat lives almost entirely on this internal water made from the dry seeds it eats, drinking none from outside. Source: Open University OpenLearn; rockdoveblog.wordpress.com.

question: A kangaroo rat sprints across open desert sand at night, bounding on its two long back legs like a tiny kangaroo. Behind it trails a tail longer than its whole body. What does that tail serve as?
answer: A counterbalance for sharp mid-air turns
choices: A counterbalance for sharp mid-air turns
A whip to lash at pursuing snakes
A brush to sweep sand over its tracks
A store of fat to survive lean seasons
context: A kangaroo rat's tail is longer than its whole body, and it acts as a counterbalance — letting the animal make sharp, sudden turns in mid-leap without tumbling. Source: a-z-animals.com; desertmuseum.org.

question: A sidewinder rattlesnake lies buried in the moonlit sand of the Mojave, still as a stone. When a kangaroo rat bounds within inches, the snake strikes faster than the human eye can see, and the rat cannot leap fully clear in time. What does the rat do to the snake before the fangs land?
answer: Drop-kicks it away with both hind feet
choices: Drop-kicks it away with both hind feet
Sprays a cloud of scent to blind it
Bites down hard on the snake behind its head
Freezes flat so the strike passes over
context: Researchers filming these encounters found kangaroo rats that couldn't fully dodge would twist mid-air and drop-kick the snake 'ninja-style' with their powerful hind feet, flinging it away before venom could be injected — then land back on their feet. Source: news.mongabay.com; sciencedaily.com (Rulon Clark, SDSU, 2019).

question: A tall-eared animal bounds across a dry Australian plain on huge hind legs, its short front legs tucked up and its heavy tail held straight out for balance. A newborn no bigger than a jellybean rides in the mother's belly pouch. What is it?
answer: A kangaroo
choices: A kangaroo
A wombat
A capybara
An anteater
context: The red kangaroo is a marsupial that travels by hopping, using its thick tail as a counterweight to stay balanced through every bound. Source: Discover Wildlife, How and why kangaroos hop (discoverwildlife.com).

question: To outrun a dingo, a kangaroo speeds up across the open plain. Scientists filming kangaroos with high-speed cameras noticed that a slow one and a fast one hop at almost exactly the same rhythm. If it does not hop more often as it speeds up, how does it go faster?
answer: It takes longer leaps
choices: It takes longer leaps
It leans further forward to gain ground
It drops onto all fours to run
It pushes harder with its tail
context: Instead of hopping faster, a kangaroo lengthens each leap. Because the hopping rhythm barely changes, going faster costs it almost no extra energy. Source: trishansoz.com; Discover Wildlife.

question: Moving across a field too slowly to hop, a kangaroo walks on five legs instead: it plants its thick tail flat on the ground, leans on it and swings both hind feet forward. Researchers measured the forces as it walked over a force-measuring platform. How much forward push does the tail give?
answer: As much as all four limbs combined
choices: As much as all four limbs combined
Only a light steadying touch
About half what one hind leg gives
None -- it just balances
context: In this slow five-legged gait, which scientists call pentapedal walking, a kangaroo's tail provides as much forward push as its four limbs combined, doing about as much work as a human leg does in a stride. Source: O'Connor et al. 2014, Biology Letters; Science News.

question: Out in the Australian outback, a kangaroo hops to a stop and plants its long, thick tail on the ground behind it like a third leg. The tail can even push and take real weight, holding the animal up as it feeds or fights. What inside the tail lets it work like a limb?
answer: A long chain of jointed vertebrae
choices: A long chain of jointed vertebrae
A second set of hip muscles
A stiff internal rod of cartilage
A pad of springy fat
context: A kangaroo's tail contains over 20 jointed vertebrae, while each leg has only a few long bones, so the tail bends and pushes like a segmented limb. Source: O'Connor et al. 2014, Biology Letters, via Asian Scientist.

question: A red kangaroo gives birth after only about 33 days of pregnancy. Her joey is blind, hairless and no bigger than a jellybean, and it cannot survive in the open air. It must reach the pouch high on her belly within minutes. How does it get there?
answer: It crawls unaided up through her fur
choices: It crawls unaided up through her fur
She lifts it in her paws to the pouch
She carries it there in her mouth
It is born already inside the pouch
context: Weighing under 2 grams, the newborn joey drags itself up through its mother's fur to the pouch in three to five minutes, swimming with its forelimbs, with no help from her. Source: trishansoz.com; interestinganimals.net.

question: Terry Dawson and Richard Taylor ran red kangaroos on treadmills in 1973, measuring the oxygen each one used as it hopped faster and faster. In most running animals, more speed costs more oxygen. Once a kangaroo is hopping, what happens to its oxygen use as it speeds up?
answer: It stays almost flat as speed rises
choices: It stays almost flat as speed rises
It climbs steeply as speed rises
It spikes higher with every hop
It falls to almost nothing at all
context: Once it is hopping, extra speed costs a kangaroo almost no extra oxygen: the kangaroo's giant tendons store each landing's energy and snap back to launch the next hop, doing more of the work as speed rises. Source: Dawson & Taylor 1973, cited in eLife 96437.

question: A female red kangaroo can carry two young at once. While one joey nurses in her pouch, she can hold a second embryo, no more than a tiny cluster of cells, on pause in her womb for months, ready to start growing the moment the pouch opens up. What keeps that embryo on hold?
answer: The suckling of the pouch joey
choices: The suckling of the pouch joey
The mother's body temperature
A seasonal drop in daylight
The pouch joey's heartbeat
context: The suckling joey sends a hormonal signal that freezes the spare embryo; if the pouch joey dies, that signal stops and the paused embryo immediately starts growing. This pausing is called embryonic diapause. Source: PubMed 7014870; a-z-animals.com.

question: High in New Zealand's snowy Southern Alps, a crow-sized, olive-green bird nests at 1,600 metres and higher and hunts for food above the tree line. Very few birds of its kind ever live so high. What kind of bird is the kea?
answer: A parrot
choices: A parrot
A falcon
A pigeon
An owl
context: The kea (Nestor notabilis) is often called the world's only alpine parrot: it breeds at 1,600 m and higher in New Zealand's Southern Alps and is one of the few parrots that regularly spends time above the tree line. Ornithologist John Gould first described it in 1856; 'notabilis' means 'noteworthy,' and it earned the nickname 'the clown of the mountains.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kea

question: Tourists who park at New Zealand's ski fields come back to find the wiper blades and rubber trim pried off their cars, backpacks unzipped and shredded and boots dragged across the car park. Keas, the olive-green parrots of the Southern Alps, are the culprits. Why do they do it?
answer: Out of sheer curiosity and play
choices: Out of sheer curiosity and play
To build a nest from the scraps
To defend their territory from rivals
To find insects hidden in the rubber
context: Kea are notorious mountain vandals, dismantling skis and snowboards and flying off with unguarded clothing purely to investigate and play. One kea at Fiordland National Park famously made off with a tourist's passport, and keas have even been documented dragging traffic cones into roadways. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kea

question: At the Willowbank Wildlife Reserve near Christchurch lives Bruce, a kea whose upper beak broke off when he was a chick. He cannot preen his feathers the way other keas do, so his keepers watched him work out a fix of his own. What did Bruce teach himself to do?
answer: Preen himself with a pebble as a comb
choices: Preen himself with a pebble as a comb
Roll in dust to strip the dirt from his feathers
Rub his feathers clean on rough rocks
Dip his feathers in water to clean them
context: Bruce held a small pebble between his tongue and lower beak and used it to comb his feathers. Scientists judged it deliberate: more than 90 percent of the times he picked up a pebble he went on to preen with it, he chose pebbles of a particular size, and no other kea in his enclosure did it. Source: https://www.auckland.ac.nz/en/news/2021/09/10/disabled-kea-uses-tools-for-self-care.html

question: Six kea learned that a black token always won food and an orange one never did. Offered a pick from jars of mixed tokens, they chose the jar with more black, a feat once shown only in humans and great apes. The last ancestor shared by birds and humans lived some 312 million years ago. What does that say about the kea's feel for odds?
answer: It evolved on its own, inside a bird brain
choices: It evolved on its own, inside a bird brain
It was handed down from that shared ancestor
It was copied from watching its keepers
It shows parrots are close kin to apes
context: In a 2020 experiment, kea named Blofeld, Bruce, Loki, Neo, Plankton, and Taz bet on the jar with the higher proportion of winning tokens, making kea the first animals besides humans and great apes shown to grasp probability by statistical inference. Birds and humans last shared an ancestor about 312 million years ago, so this reasoning evolved independently in a parrot brain. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-14695-1

question: A king cobra, the longest venomous snake on Earth, slides through a rainforest in India. A big adult can stretch to nearly 18 feet from head to tail, more than three times a grown person's height. Laid out straight, that length is closest to which of these?
answer: A full-grown giraffe standing tall
choices: A full-grown giraffe standing tall
A stretch limousine parked at the curb
A city bus at a bus stop
A tennis court from end to end
context: The king cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) is the longest venomous snake in the world, reaching about 18 feet, roughly the height of a tall adult giraffe. A stretch limo, a city bus and a tennis court are all considerably longer. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/king-cobra

question: A cornered king cobra in an Indian rainforest rears up off the ground, spreads a wide hood behind its head and faces whoever threatens it. On a full-grown king cobra, how high can that reared-up front end reach?
answer: Enough to look a standing adult in the eye
choices: Enough to look a standing adult in the eye
Just a few inches, like a striking rattlesnake
Barely off the ground, coiled to spring
Onto its tail-tip, balanced fully upright
context: A threatened king cobra can raise up to a third of its body off the ground and still move forward, tall enough to meet a grown person eye to eye. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/king-cobra

question: A king cobra in a Southeast Asian jungle seldom troubles itself with rats or birds. Its prey is other snakes, even the deadliest, which it tracks down, bites and swallows whole. Which striped Asian snake, whose venom is a lethal neurotoxin, does it hunt and eat?
answer: The banded krait
choices: The banded krait
The Malabar pit viper
The green vine snake
The Russell's viper
context: Its genus name Ophiophagus means 'snake-eater.' The king cobra feeds mainly on other snakes and regularly hunts venomous species, including banded kraits, Indian cobras, and even other king cobras. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_cobra

question: A king cobra hunts other snakes, and its stretchy jaws let it swallow prey longer than itself. Some of its victims belong to one of the longest snake species in the world. Which of these big snakes is known to fall prey to it?
answer: A reticulated python
choices: A reticulated python
An Amazon anaconda
An African rock python
A boa constrictor
context: The king cobra hunts and swallows other snakes, including reticulated pythons, Indian cobras, banded kraits and rat snakes, and it will even eat other king cobras; only large pythons are more than its match. The anaconda, the African rock python and the boa constrictor live in the Americas and Africa, far from its Asian forests. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_cobra

question: A king cobra rises from the leaf litter of a forest in India and strikes at an intruder. One bite drives up to two-tenths of a fluid ounce of neurotoxin straight into the muscle. That single dose holds enough venom to kill roughly what?
answer: A full-grown elephant
choices: A full-grown elephant
A single large dog
A small flock of chickens
One grown man, barely
context: The neurotoxin in one bite is enough to kill 20 people, or even an elephant. It attacks the nervous system, and without treatment a person can die in as little as 30 minutes. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/king-cobra

question: A female king cobra in a forest in India lays her eggs and, unlike nearly every other snake, does not slither away. For nearly three months she guards her clutch, striking at anything that comes close. What does she build and guard until the young hatch?
answer: A mounded nest of dry leaves
choices: A mounded nest of dry leaves
A burrow dug into damp clay
A raft of woven floating reeds
A lined hollow up a tree
context: The king cobra is the only snake in the world that builds a nest. The female scrapes together a mound of dry leaf litter, lays her clutch of roughly 7 to 43 eggs inside, and guards it fiercely for the two-to-three-month incubation. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/king-cobra

question: Backed into a corner in a forest of Southeast Asia, a king cobra rears up and warns off the intruder in front of it. Most snakes give a thin, high hiss, but this one makes a sound nobody expects from a snake. What does its warning sound like?
answer: A low growl, like a dog
choices: A low growl, like a dog
A sharp rattling buzz
A shrill whistle
A wet clicking chatter
context: The king cobra's warning is unusually deep: it uses only frequencies below 2,500 Hz, with a dominant tone near 600 Hz, far lower than the hiss of other snakes, so it sounds almost like a growling dog. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_cobra

question: A king cobra follows the trail of another snake through the leaf litter of a South Asian forest. Its forked tongue flicks with every move, carrying scent to two tiny pits in the roof of its mouth called the Jacobson's organ. What does having two tips instead of one let the cobra do?
answer: Smell in stereo, telling which side a scent is stronger on
choices: Smell in stereo, telling which side a scent is stronger on
Taste whether the fleeing prey is venomous
Sense the warm body heat of the prey ahead
Feel ground vibrations from the prey scrambling away
context: Each tip of the forked tongue feeds its own sensor, so the king cobra smells in 'stereo' and can tell which side a scent is stronger on, letting it follow a trail like a bloodhound. Source: https://today.uconn.edu/2021/06/smelling-in-stereo-the-real-reason-snakes-have-flicking-forked-tongues/

question: A plump, chicken-sized bird snuffles across a New Zealand forest floor at night, probing the leaf litter with a long, slender beak. Its wings are too small to see, and its bristly feathers look like shaggy brown fur. It cannot fly, and it is New Zealand's national symbol. Which bird is it?
answer: The kiwi
choices: The kiwi
The kakapo
The emu
The takahe
context: The kiwi is a flightless bird of New Zealand whose wings are so tiny they are invisible, hidden under bristly, hair-like, two-branched feathers that look more like shaggy fur than plumage. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiwi_(bird)

question: A kiwi probes its long, slender beak deep into a New Zealand forest floor at night, hunting worms and grubs it cannot see, and snorts now and then to blow the dirt away. What lets it smell prey buried in the soil, a trick no other bird can manage?
answer: Its nostrils sit at the very tip of its beak
choices: Its nostrils sit at the very tip of its beak
It has feathered filters lining its throat
It tastes the soil with a forked tongue
It hears the worms with pits behind its eyes
context: The kiwi is the only bird in the world with its nostrils at the very tip of its long beak, letting it sniff out worms and grubs underground as it probes the soil. It makes loud snuffling and snorting noises to clear dirt from its nostrils. Source: https://savethekiwi.nz/about-kiwi/kiwi-facts/an-unusual-beak/

question: A female kiwi in a New Zealand forest, weighing about 1.7 kilograms, once laid a single egg weighing 406 grams, nearly a quarter of her own weight. Scaled up to a human mother, it would be like giving birth to what?
answer: A six-year-old child
choices: A six-year-old child
A newborn baby
A pair of twins
A full-grown teenager
context: A female kiwi lays an egg up to about a quarter of her own body weight, proportionally the largest egg of any bird, the equivalent of a woman giving birth to a six-year-old child. Framed as a memorable comparison. Source: https://www.audubon.org/news/why-kiwis-egg-so-big

question: A kiwi mother lays one of the largest eggs for her size of any bird, and about 65 percent of it is yolk, where the eggs of most birds are only 35 to 40 percent yolk. What does all that yolk let the newly hatched chick do?
answer: Hatch fully feathered and feed itself within days
choices: Hatch fully feathered and feed itself within days
Hatch blind and naked, then grow very fast
Live on its stored yolk until a year old
Grow to adult size within its first weeks
context: The kiwi egg is about 65% yolk, so the chick hatches fully feathered, opens its eyes, and can feed itself within days, with almost no help from its parents. Source: https://savethekiwi.nz/about-kiwi/kiwi-facts/enormous-egg/

question: Digging burrows the way a badger does, with cat-like whiskers around its long beak, the kiwi of New Zealand's forests has earned the nickname 'honorary mammal.' One trait of its body runs closer to a mammal's than nearly any other bird's does. What is it?
answer: A body that runs cooler than most birds'
choices: A body that runs cooler than most birds'
A four-chambered stomach that chews cud
Warm blood it pumps only while awake
A layer of blubber beneath tough leg skin
context: The kiwi has a low, mammal-like body temperature of about 38 C (100 F), among the lowest of any bird, while most birds run at a hot 39-42 C. It also digs burrows like a badger, has heavy marrow-filled leg bones, cat-like whiskers, and leg skin as tough as shoe leather. Source: https://savethekiwi.nz/about-kiwi/kiwi-facts/honorary-mammals/

question: Because it never flies, a kiwi's breastbone is flat, with none of the deep ridge, the keel, where a flying bird's wing muscles attach. Its leg bones hold a surprise for a bird as well. What is packed inside them?
answer: Solid marrow, like a mammal's bones
choices: Solid marrow, like a mammal's bones
Fat-filled channels for winter warmth
A honeycomb of calcium crystals
Twin canals that store extra water
context: Because the kiwi never flies, its breastbone has no keel, the deep ridge that anchors the powerful flight muscles in birds that fly. Unlike the hollow, air-filled bones of flying birds, the kiwi has heavy, marrow-filled bones, part of why it is nicknamed an 'honorary mammal.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiwi_(bird) ; https://savethekiwi.nz/about-kiwi/kiwi-facts/honorary-mammals/

question: The kiwi shared New Zealand with the giant moa, yet ancient DNA tested in 2014 showed that the moa was not its closest relative. That was a giant 3 metres tall that lived 11,500 kilometres across the ocean. Which vanished bird was it?
answer: The elephant bird of Madagascar
choices: The elephant bird of Madagascar
The dodo of Mauritius
The terror bird of South America
The great auk of the North Atlantic
context: Ancient DNA in 2014 revealed the kiwi's closest cousin is not the giant moa it lived beside, but the extinct elephant bird of Madagascar, a 3-metre-tall giant living 11,500 km away across the ocean. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1251981

question: High in an Australian gum tree, a little grey animal with fuzzy round ears clings to a branch, a baby riding in the pouch on its belly like a baby kangaroo. Visitors call it the koala bear. What group of animals does it belong to?
answer: A marsupial
choices: A marsupial
A bear
A monkey
A rodent
context: The koala (Phascolarctos cinereus) is not a bear at all. It is a marsupial that carries its baby in a pouch, and its closest living relative is the wombat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koala

question: Round-eared and black-nosed, a small grey koala spends its whole life up in the treetops of eastern Australia. Its stomach and liver let it safely eat one tough, oily kind of leaf that would poison most animals. What leaf makes up nearly its whole diet?
answer: Eucalyptus leaves
choices: Eucalyptus leaves
Bamboo shoots
Acacia seeds
Fig fruit
context: A koala eats almost nothing but eucalyptus (gum-tree) leaves, which carry bitter oils and cyanide-like compounds toxic to most animals. Source: https://koalainfo.com/koalas-diet-is-fully-poisonous-and-toxic

question: A koala clings to a eucalyptus branch in eastern Australia, chewing the tough, mildly poisonous leaves that are almost all it eats. They give back very little energy. To make its few calories last, what does a koala spend up to about 20 hours a day doing?
answer: Sleeping and resting
choices: Sleeping and resting
Grooming its fur
Foraging for leaves
Climbing between trees
context: A koala's food yields so little energy that resting almost all day, up to about 20 hours, is the only way to survive on eucalyptus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koala

question: A koala clings high in a tree in eastern Australia and can go a long time without climbing down to drink from a stream or a puddle. Where does it get almost all the water it needs?
answer: From the moisture in the leaves it eats
choices: From the moisture in the leaves it eats
From dew it licks off its own fur
From sap it laps from cuts in the bark
From water held in pouches in its cheeks
context: A koala gets almost all its water from the leaves it eats, so it rarely needs to drink, though big males sometimes drink water found on the ground or in tree hollows. Its name comes from the Dharug word gula, thought to mean 'no water'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koala ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Koala

question: A koala joey lives on milk until, around six months old, it must learn to eat toxic gum leaves. To survive them, it first eats a soft, oily dropping straight from its mother — food that seeds its gut with the live microbes needed to digest eucalyptus. What is this special dropping called?
answer: Pap
choices: Pap
Curd
Whey
Silage
context: Weaning koalas eat their mother's 'pap,' described by keepers as like droppings but softer and oilier. Unlike ordinary droppings it is packed with the live gut microbes the joey needs to digest eucalyptus. Source: https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/news/2022/07/pap-not-poop-the-gift-a-mother-koala-gives-her-joey/

question: A koala sits in the fork of a gum tree in eastern Australia. Under a microscope, the ridges on its fingertips loop and whorl so like a human's that fingerprint experts struggle to tell a lifted print from a person's. Its cousins the wombat and the kangaroo have none. Why did the koala evolve them?
answer: To grip branches and leaves
choices: To grip branches and leaves
To improve its sense of smell
To keep its paws from overheating
To leave scent marks on bark
context: Koala fingerprints match human ones so closely they are extremely hard to tell apart even under a microscope. Koalas are almost the only tree-climbing marsupial with them — wombats and kangaroos lack them — and they evolved the ridges to grip branches and leaves. This near-identical match to humans is a case of convergent evolution, the same trait arising independently in unrelated lineages. Source: https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/did-you-know/koalas-have-fingerprints-just-humans

question: A giant reptile hunts wild pigs and deer on a handful of Indonesian islands, among them Komodo, Rinca and Flores. Adult males stretch about ten feet long, and the heaviest ever weighed reached 366 pounds. Which reptile is it?
answer: The Komodo dragon
choices: The Komodo dragon
The Nile crocodile
The green iguana
The Gila monster
context: Males grow up to about 3 m (10 ft); the heaviest verified specimen reached 166 kg (366 lb). Wild Komodo dragons live only on Komodo, Rintja, Padar, and Flores in Indonesia. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/komodo-dragon).

question: A Komodo dragon, the biggest lizard alive, prowls the dry hills of a few Indonesian islands, flicking its long forked tongue. When it hunts a deer or a wild boar, how does this giant lizard catch it?
answer: It ambushes from cover and lunges at the legs, belly, or throat
choices: It ambushes from cover and lunges at the legs, belly, or throat
It runs its prey down over miles of open ground
It waits underwater and drags prey below the surface
It corners prey against cliffs in cooperative packs
context: An adult Komodo dragon is an apex predator that ambushes prey from beside game trails, striking deer, wild boar, and even young water buffalo. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo; ScienceInsights (scienceinsights.org).

question: On the dry islands of Indonesia, a Komodo dragon may go many weeks between meals. When it finally brings down a deer or a wild boar, it gorges in a way that would burst most animals. In one sitting, how much can it eat?
answer: Up to 80 percent of its own body weight
choices: Up to 80 percent of its own body weight
Up to 15 percent of its own body weight
About twice its own body weight
Roughly its body weight every day
context: A Komodo dragon can gulp down up to 80 percent of its own body weight in one meal. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/komodo-dragon).

question: Patrolling the dry hills of an Indonesian island, a Komodo dragon flicks its forked yellow tongue in and out. Each tip carries what it picks up from the air to its own side of the Jacobson's organ, a pair of pits at the top of its mouth. What does the forked tongue give it?
answer: A sense of which way a smell comes from
choices: A sense of which way a smell comes from
A way to cool its blood on hot days
A taste for salt that leads it to water
A way to sense the body heat of prey
context: The two forked tips deliver scent molecules separately to the Jacobson's organ, giving a directional, 3-D sense of smell; a dragon can detect a rotting carcass from up to 2.5 miles (4 km) away. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/komodo-dragon).

question: A University of Queensland team led by Bryan Fry dissected fresh Komodo dragon jaws in 2009 to learn why the lizard's bite is so deadly. For decades textbooks had blamed filthy, bacteria-choked saliva. What did the team find was the real killer in the bite?
answer: Venom glands in its lower jaw that stop blood clotting
choices: Venom glands in its lower jaw that stop blood clotting
A crushing bite force stronger than a crocodile's
A paralyzing nerve toxin coating the teeth
Jaws that inject digestive acid into the wound
context: Fry et al. showed the Komodo has real venom glands in its lower jaw; the toxins prevent blood from clotting and drop the victim's blood pressure. A later study found the mouth bacteria are no more dangerous than any other carnivore's. Source: Fry et al., PNAS 2009 (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0810883106); National Geographic.

question: Out of the brush on Komodo Island, a dragon lunges and sinks its teeth into a passing water buffalo, then lets the huge animal shake free and stagger away. The dragon does not sprint after it. What does it do instead?
answer: Trails it slowly for hours or days until it collapses
choices: Trails it slowly for hours or days until it collapses
Goes back to its burrow to wait for new prey
Calls other dragons to help bring the buffalo down
Climbs a tree to watch the herd from above
context: The venom keeps the wound bleeding and lowers blood pressure; the dragon trails the weakening prey at a leisurely pace, sometimes for hours or days, then moves in when it collapses. Source: Fry et al. PNAS 2009; ScienceInsights (scienceinsights.org).

question: Clamped in a Komodo dragon's jaws, a deer struggles to break free. About 60 curved teeth line those jaws, each edged like a tiny saw, much like a shark's, and worn ones are replaced all its life. What do those serrations do to keep the deer from getting away?
answer: They hook flesh so prey cannot pull away, opening deep wounds
choices: They hook flesh so prey cannot pull away, opening deep wounds
They grind bone into swallowable fragments
They inject venom directly through hollow grooves
They lock together to crush and hold a shell
context: The backward-curving serrations hook into flesh so prey cannot tear free, opening deep wounds the venom keeps bleeding. Like a shark, the dragon replaces its teeth throughout life. Source: Britannica; National Geographic; sciencedaily.com (2009 study).

question: Flora, a female Komodo dragon at England's Chester Zoo, had never shared an enclosure with a male of her kind. Yet in 2006 she laid a clutch of 11 eggs, and healthy babies hatched from them. With no father anywhere near, what made Flora's clutch possible?
answer: Parthenogenesis, a virgin birth from an unfertilized egg
choices: Parthenogenesis, a virgin birth from an unfertilized egg
Stored sperm saved from years earlier
A hormone shift that let her fertilize her own eggs
Eggs quietly swapped in by another female
context: Flora, kept with no mate, laid 11 eggs in 2006, and seven of them hatched into healthy young through parthenogenesis. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komodo_dragon ; Nature 444, 1021 (2006).

question: A female Komodo dragon on the Indonesian islands of Komodo and Rinca can sometimes lay eggs that hatch without her ever mating. When she does, every hatchling turns out to be the same sex. Which sex are they, and why?
answer: All male, because only the ZZ chromosome pairing survives
choices: All male, because only the ZZ chromosome pairing survives
All female, because eggs default to the mother's sex
All male, because heat during incubation sets sex
A random mix, just like normal fertilized clutches
context: The Komodo's sex system is the reverse of a mammal's: females are WZ, males ZZ. When an unfertilized egg doubles its chromosomes, only the ZZ (male) combination survives, so every parthenogenetic hatchling is male. Source: Scientific American (scientificamerican.com); Nature 444, 1021 (2006).

question: Suppose a storm sweeps a single female Komodo dragon across the sea and strands her alone on an empty island with no other dragons. Biologists say she could still start a new population all by herself. How could a lone female manage it?
answer: She births sons by parthenogenesis, then breeds with them
choices: She births sons by parthenogenesis, then breeds with them
She clones exact copies of herself indefinitely
She lures males across the sea with scent
She survives centuries until castaways arrive
context: Because a lone female can produce sons on her own and then mate with them, a single female washed onto an empty island could theoretically start a whole new population by herself. Source: Scientific American (scientificamerican.com/article/strange-but-true-komodo-d).

question: Jessica Maisano, a paleontologist at the University of Texas at Austin, ran a Komodo dragon through a CT scanner in 2019 to see what lay beneath its tough, scaly skin. She found thousands of tiny bones packed just under the surface, invisible to the naked eye. What role do they play?
answer: Osteoderms forming a chain-mail suit of bony armor
choices: Osteoderms forming a chain-mail suit of bony armor
Weights that anchor the dragon low against its prey
Reserves the dragon draws on to make eggshells
Buried plates that store heat soaked up while basking
context: The CT study found four osteoderm shapes (rosette, platy, dendritic, vermiform) forming a full-body 'chain mail' covering everything but the nostrils, eyes, and pineal 'third eye'. Babies hatch with no armor; it grows in with adulthood and mainly shields adults from other dragons' bites. Source: UT Austin News (news.utexas.edu/2019/09/12); The Anatomical Record, Sept 2019.

question: A Komodo dragon bares its teeth, and a deep orange stripe runs along each tip and saw-like edge while the rest of the enamel stays pale. Researchers studied the teeth at high resolution in 2024 to learn what the stripe is. What causes it?
answer: A coating of iron concentrated along the cutting edges
choices: A coating of iron concentrated along the cutting edges
Stains from years of feeding on bloody carrion
A film of pigment-producing mouth bacteria
Enamel worn thin to expose the reddish dentin beneath
context: Many reptiles carry a trace of iron in their enamel, but the Komodo dragon concentrates it along the cutting edges and tips, a coating seen only to a lesser degree in a few other monitor lizards. The iron hardens and protects the fine serrations so the teeth stay razor-sharp, staining them orange in the process. Fossilization hides whether meat-eating dinosaurs such as Tyrannosaurus rex had iron-coated teeth too, but the same study found that tyrannosaurs reshaped the enamel along their cutting edges. Source: LeBlanc et al., 'Iron-coated Komodo dragon teeth and the complex dental enamel of carnivorous reptiles,' Nature Ecology & Evolution, 24 July 2024; https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1052097 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komodo_dragon

question: Scott Hocknull described a set of fossil Komodo dragons in 2009 and rewrote the story of where the species came from. Textbooks had long said it grew huge on its isolated islands, evolving up from a small ancestor stranded there. Where did the Komodo dragon really evolve?
answer: On mainland Australia, before spreading west into Indonesia
choices: On mainland Australia, before spreading west into Indonesia
On the Indonesian islands, exactly as the old story held
In mainland Southeast Asia, then rafting south to the islands
On a since-sunken landmass between Asia and Australia
context: Komodo dragon bones dated from about 300,000 to 4 million years old, dug up in eastern Australia, are identical to living dragons. The lineage arose on the Australian mainland at least ~4 million years ago, then dispersed west across the Wallacean islands into Indonesia around a million years ago. It vanished from Australia about 50,000 years ago along with the continent's other giant beasts, so today's Indonesian dragons are the last survivors of an Australian dynasty that also produced the even larger extinct monitor Megalania. Source: Hocknull et al., 'Dragon's Paradise Lost: Palaeobiogeography, Evolution and Extinction of the Largest-Ever Terrestrial Lizards (Varanidae),' PLoS ONE, 2009.

question: A hiker in a Central American rainforest stops beside a path and sees a green ribbon flowing along the forest floor. Up close it is alive: thousands of small insects marching in line, each holding a snip of leaf overhead like a tiny sail, pouring into a hole in the ground. Which insects are they?
answer: Leafcutter ants
choices: Leafcutter ants
Army ants
Weaver ants
Fire ants
context: The column of green 'sails' streaming back to the nest is the classic sight of leafcutter ants -- each worker carries a leaf fragment far heavier than itself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafcutter_ant

question: Leafcutter ants carry fresh-cut pieces of leaf by the thousand down into their huge underground nests in the rainforests of Central and South America. Yet the leafcutters do not eat the leaves. What are they doing with them?
answer: Chew them into mulch to grow a fungus they eat
choices: Chew them into mulch to grow a fungus they eat
Line their tunnel walls to keep out rain
Feed them straight to the newborn larvae
Pile them at the entrance to block invaders
context: Leafcutters are farmers, not leaf-eaters: they compost the leaves to cultivate a fungus and eat the fungus. Source: https://asm.org/articles/2017/september/the-leaf-cutter-ant-s-50-million-years-of-farming

question: At dusk in a South American orange grove, a colony of Atta leafcutter ants, among the biggest leafcutters, pours out of its nest and swarms up a citrus tree. The workers cut leaves and haul them underground without a pause. When the grower walks out to his tree a day later, what does he find?
answer: Every leaf gone -- the whole tree bare
choices: Every leaf gone -- the whole tree bare
A few outer branches nibbled
Only the lowest leaves within reach
Just the soft new buds taken
context: Atta leafcutter ants can defoliate an entire citrus tree in less than 24 hours. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafcutter_ant

question: Huge armored majors stand guard at the entrance of a leafcutter nest in a South American rainforest, while middle-sized workers march out to snip leaves. Deep inside, the very smallest workers, with heads under a millimetre wide, have a job of their own. What do they do?
answer: Tend and weed the fungus garden
choices: Tend and weed the fungus garden
Dig every new tunnel by themselves
Chew wood pulp into nest walls
Carry the queen from room to room
context: The colony is a graded workforce: giant majors defend, mediae cut leaves, and the tiniest minims (heads under 1mm) care for the delicate fungus crop. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafcutter_ant

question: A column of leafcutter ants marches along a rainforest trail, each big worker carrying a slice of green leaf overhead like a flag. On top of many of the leaves rides a much tinier ant from the same colony. What is the little rider doing up there?
answer: Shooing off flies that try to lay eggs on the carrier
choices: Shooing off flies that try to lay eggs on the carrier
Resting because it is too small to walk far
Adding weight so the leaf will not blow away
Steering the carrier along the right trail home
context: The minims act as bodyguards, driving away parasitic phorid flies that try to lay eggs in the crevices of the busy carrier's head. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafcutter_ant

question: A mould called Escovopsis keeps attacking the gardens that leafcutter ants tend deep in their nests. To fight it, the ants carry a tiny living partner on their own bodies, tucked into little pits in their skin. What do they carry?
answer: Antibiotic-making bacteria
choices: Antibiotic-making bacteria
Poison-spraying mites
Acid-brewing yeasts
Mould-eating roundworms
context: The ants host living Pseudonocardia/Streptomyces bacteria as portable antimicrobials to kill the garden parasite Escovopsis; some colonies carry so much they look dusted with powdered sugar. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafcutter_ant

question: Deep underground in the American tropics, leafcutter ants tend a crop in their garden chambers, like farmers. Humans took up farming only some twelve thousand years ago, and the ants' ancestors had started long before them. How much earlier had those ancestors begun?
answer: Roughly fifty million years
choices: Roughly fifty million years
A few thousand years
About one million years
Around ten million years
context: The fungus-farming ancestors of leafcutter ants began roughly 50 million years before humans did, and fully domesticated their fungus about 15 million years ago. Source: https://asm.org/articles/2017/september/the-leaf-cutter-ant-s-50-million-years-of-farming

question: Drifting over a kelp reef off southern Australia, one 'leaf' of seaweed sways along with the current. It doesn't tumble loose like the rest. That is because it is really a fish, wearing long leaf-shaped skin flaps as a disguise. What is this master of seaweed camouflage?
answer: The leafy sea dragon
choices: The leafy sea dragon
The peacock flounder
The frogfish
The stonefish
context: The leafy sea dragon (Phycodurus eques) sprouts long leaf-shaped skin flaps that look exactly like drifting seaweed, and it keeps up the illusion even while moving, swaying through the water like a loose piece of floating kelp. Source: Australian Museum — australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/leafy-seadragon-phycodurus-eques/

question: A leafy sea dragon crosses a reef looking like a motionless scrap of weed, yet it is moving. Its big leafy lobes are no use for swimming; they are pure camouflage. What moves it along so secretly that it seems to float in place?
answer: Two tiny, nearly transparent fins fluttering almost invisibly
choices: Two tiny, nearly transparent fins fluttering almost invisibly
Slow undulating waves rippling down its whole body
A jet of water squirted from its gills
Sticky tube-feet gripping and pulling along the rocks
context: The leaf-shaped protrusions are NOT fins. The sea dragon moves with two tiny, nearly transparent fins — a pectoral fin on its 'neck' and a dorsal fin on its 'back' — that flutter so fast and faintly they are almost invisible, making it look like it is floating motionless like drifting weed. Source: Australian Museum — australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/leafy-seadragon-phycodurus-eques/

question: In a cool kelp forest of southern Australia hangs a leafy sea dragon, disguised as seaweed by the leafy flaps sprouting from its body. It has neither teeth nor a stomach, yet one can eat thousands of tiny mysid shrimp in a day. How does it eat?
answer: It sucks prey up its long, pipe-like snout like a straw
choices: It sucks prey up its long, pipe-like snout like a straw
It swallows prey whole into an expandable throat pouch
It stuns shrimp with a venomous spine, then engulfs them
It grinds prey against bony plates lining its cheeks
context: The leafy sea dragon has no teeth and no stomach. It feeds through a long, pipe-like snout that works like a drinking straw, and a single sea dragon may slurp up thousands of tiny mysid shrimp in a single day. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium — montereybayaquarium.org/animals-the-ocean/animals-a-to-z/leafy-sea-dragon

question: When a pair of leafy sea dragons breeds in the weed off southern Australia, up to about 250 bright pink eggs must be kept safe for weeks until they hatch. Who keeps them?
answer: The male, on the underside of his tail
choices: The male, on the underside of his tail
The female, tucked beneath her belly
Neither — the eggs are glued to a strand of kelp
Both parents take turns holding the clutch
context: Like its seahorse relatives, it is the MALE leafy sea dragon that carries the eggs. The female presses up to about 250 eggs onto a spongy brood patch on the underside of the male's tail, where they attach and he broods them until they hatch. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium — montereybayaquarium.org/animals-the-ocean/animals-a-to-z/leafy-sea-dragon

question: A leafy sea dragon hanging in the kelp wears no ordinary scales: under its thin skin runs a jointed suit of rigid bony rings, the same armor its seahorse and pipefish cousins wear. Its gills hold one more oddity that sets it apart from most fish. What do they open through?
answer: Small round holes
choices: Small round holes
Long crescent-shaped slits
A single flap behind the head
Feathery tufts on the outside of the neck
context: Under its thin skin the leafy sea dragon wears a suit of rigid bony ring-plates instead of ordinary scales — a hallmark of the syngnathid family it shares with seahorses and pipefish. It even has round, circular gill openings rather than the crescent-shaped slits of most fish. Source: A-Z Animals; Wikipedia — en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafy_seadragon

question: A toddler learns to talk by listening to the voices around him and copying them. Only a short list of animals must pick up their sounds that way, among them whales, elephants and humans; most are born with every call they will ever use. Which group also belongs on that list?
answer: Songbirds and parrots
choices: Songbirds and parrots
Frogs and crickets
Wolves and coyotes
Lions and hyenas
context: The 'vocal learners' are a surprisingly short list: songbirds, parrots, hummingbirds, whales and dolphins, seals, elephants, bats, and humans. Everything else is born knowing its calls and never changes them. Source: Wikipedia 'Vocal learning'; Royal Society Phil. Trans. B 2020.0234 'Vocal learning in animals and humans'.

question: A young white-crowned sparrow normally learns its song by listening to older males in the first weeks after it hatches. In a classic experiment, scientists raised one in total silence, with no adult of its kind ever singing within earshot. When the bird grew up and began to sing, what came out?
answer: A broken, simplified song
choices: A broken, simplified song
