The perfect song, note for note
No song at all, only silence
A different species' song entirely
context: A songbird learns its song during a short 'critical period' when it is too young to sing yet, by listening to an adult tutor. Raised in silence with no tune to copy, the sparrow grows up singing a broken, simplified version. Source: Springer 'Vocal learning in White-crowned Sparrows: sensitive phase and song dialects'; Nature Scitable 'The Development of Birdsong'.

question: When a young sparrow hatches, it cannot yet sing. It listens to an older tutor sparrow and memorizes the correct song note by note, storing it as a mental template in its brain. Then, before it has practiced a single note aloud, it is deafened. Months later it tries to sing, but the tune never comes out right. What did losing its hearing take away?
answer: Its ability to check its own voice against the memory
choices: Its ability to check its own voice against the memory
Its ability to sing that particular song at all
The memory of its tutor's song
The muscles that shape each note
context: A songbird needs to HEAR ITSELF, not just its tutor. Deafened after memorizing the song but before singing it, the bird still has the stored memory of the tutor's song, but it has lost the feedback loop that lets it match its own voice to the remembered tune. Source: Springer 'Critical Period for Song Learning'; Konishi white-crowned sparrow auditory-feedback studies (Caltech records).

question: A captive lyrebird at Adelaide Zoo lived beside a building site where the panda enclosure was going up, and he copied the sounds of the work. He also startled his keepers by greeting them in a clear human voice. What did the bird say?
answer: 'Hello, Chook!'
choices: 'Hello, Chook!'
'Time for lunch'
'Open the gate'
'Good morning, all'
context: The most famous lyrebird footage, a bird reproducing camera clicks, a car alarm, and a chainsaw for David Attenborough, came partly from captive birds. Chook had picked up drills and saws from construction next door and even greeted keepers with 'hello, Chook!' in a human voice. Source: The Conversation 'Lyrebirds mimicking chainsaws: fact or lie?'; Atlas Obscura 'The Strange Bird That Mimics Chainsaws'.

question: Each night, as Irene Pepperberg left her lab, Alex the African grey parrot called the same farewell after her. He had worked with her for 30 years, learning colors, shapes and numbers. On the morning of September 6, 2007, he was found dead, aged 31. What were the words he called each night?
answer: 'You be good. I love you. See you tomorrow.'
choices: 'You be good. I love you. See you tomorrow.'
'Goodnight now. Sleep well. See you soon.'
'Don't go yet. Please stay. I miss you.'
'Time for bed. Lights are off. Goodnight.'
context: Alex said this same phrase to Pepperberg each night as she left. He was found dead the next morning at age 31, ending a thirty-year study of a single parrot. Source: NPR 'Alex & Me: The Parrot Who Said I Love You'; Wikipedia 'Alex (parrot)'.

question: A diver in a tank in San Diego surfaced in 1984 and demanded to know, 'Who told me to get out?' The muffled, human-sounding words came not from a person but from a beluga whale named Noc, who had learned to lower his voice by several octaves to imitate human speech. How did Noc make those sounds?
answer: By changing the pressure in his nasal passages
choices: By changing the pressure in his nasal passages
By vibrating his tail against the tank
By forcing air out through his blowhole slowly
By humming from deep in his throat
context: NOC dropped his voice several octaves to sound like a human, producing the speech-like sounds by altering the pressure in his nasal passages, an unusual feat for a whale. Source: National Geographic 'NOC, the white whale that tried to sound like a human'; Scientific American podcast 'Whale Mimics Human Speech'.

question: A young zebra finch learns its song along a loop in its brain where one gene works hardest exactly while the bird is copying its tutor. When scientists turn that gene down during learning, the copy comes out sloppy and incomplete. The same gene helps shape human speech. Which gene is it?
answer: The FoxP2 gene
choices: The FoxP2 gene
The MC1R gene
The APOE gene
The BMP4 gene
context: The song system has two linked pathways: a motor pathway (nucleus HVC to RA to the vocal muscles) that produces the song, and an anterior forebrain pathway through Area X, a basal-ganglia nucleus, that is required to LEARN and fine-tune it. FoxP2 is active in Area X and spikes exactly during learning. When Sebastian Haesler's team knocked FoxP2 down in Area X of juvenile finches (about 70% reduction), their copies of the tutor's song fell from about 68% similarity in controls to about 40% -- tying one gene to the accuracy of imitation. Source: Haesler et al. 2007, 'Incomplete and Inaccurate Vocal Imitation after Knockdown of FoxP2 in Songbird Basal Ganglia Nucleus Area X,' PLOS Biology (journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0050321); song-system review, PMC5066577 and PMC2822067.

question: A young zebra finch has a few months to memorize and lock in its song; after that the tune 'crystallizes' and never changes again. Scientists think the window doesn't just fade -- it is bricked shut. Deep in the song-control circuit, something builds up around the neurons until no new connections can form. What do they think clamps the song in place?
answer: Perineuronal nets caging the neurons
choices: Perineuronal nets caging the neurons
Myelin sheaths wrapping the axons
Glial scars sealing the circuit
Calcium deposits hardening the synapses
context: Perineuronal nets (PNNs) are lattice-like sheaths of extracellular matrix that build up around inhibitory neurons in the song-control nucleus HVC. In male zebra finches their density starts rising around 50-60 days after hatching, as tutor-memorization ends, and plateaus near 90 days -- exactly when the song crystallizes and stops changing. Because the timing matches so closely, scientists think that by caging the neurons in a rigid net that blocks new synapses, PNNs lock the learned song in place, and males, who must crystallize a song, grow denser nets than females. This is the mechanism one layer beneath the 'sensitive period.' Source: Cornez et al. 2018, 'Timing of perineuronal net development in the zebra finch song control system correlates with developmental song learning,' Proc. Royal Society B, PMC6083260.

question: A leatherback, the biggest sea turtle alive, drags herself up a tropical beach to lay her eggs. Her dark, ridged shell is about 2 metres long, as long as a tall grown-up lying down. A big leatherback weighs about as much as which of these?
answer: A small car
choices: A small car
A large dog
A refrigerator
An elephant
context: An adult leatherback can reach roughly 500-700 kg (over 1,000 lb) - genuinely in the weight class of a small car, and the heaviest non-crocodilian reptile on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leatherback_sea_turtle

question: A diver who runs a hand down a green sea turtle's back feels hard bony plates locked into a shell. On the largest sea turtle in the world, the same hand would meet something no other sea turtle has. What covers that giant's back instead of a hard shell?
answer: Tough rubbery leathery skin
choices: Tough rubbery leathery skin
Overlapping snake-like scales
A thick coat of slippery slime
Rows of sharp, horny spikes
context: Alone among sea turtles, the leatherback has no hard bony shell at all. Its back is tough, rubbery, leathery skin - which is literally its name: Dermochelys coriacea means 'leathery skin-turtle.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leatherback_sea_turtle

question: A leatherback sea turtle lives almost entirely on jellyfish, sometimes hundreds of pounds of them in a day. Jellyfish are slick, slimy and mostly water, and a swallowed one should slide right back out of the turtle's mouth. What lines a leatherback's throat to stop it?
answer: Hundreds of backward-pointing spines
choices: Hundreds of backward-pointing spines
A patch of sticky glue-slime
Rows of grinding molar teeth
A ring of powerful suckers
context: A leatherback's throat is lined with hundreds of sharp, backward-pointing spines (esophageal papillae, the same keratin as fingernails). They grip slippery jellyfish so prey can't wriggle free, while letting the turtle spit out swallowed seawater without losing its meal. An adult can gulp close to its own body weight in jellyfish in a day.

question: Hauled from near-freezing Atlantic water, a leatherback sea turtle once had a thermometer pushed into its core. Reptiles usually run at whatever temperature the water or air around them happens to be. How far above the sea's temperature was this turtle running?
answer: About 18 degrees C warmer
choices: About 18 degrees C warmer
About 2 degrees C warmer
About 6 degrees C warmer
About 40 degrees C warmer
context: The turtle's core ran about 18 degrees C (32 degrees F) above the surrounding water, so it stays warm while swimming through near-freezing seas, extraordinary for a reptile. Activity alone would warm a reptile by only a degree or two. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.177.4051.791

question: Scientists strapped a satellite tag to a leatherback sea turtle off the Cape Verde islands in 2006 and let her go. Weeks later the tag radioed home a single plunge into the black cold, deeper than any reptile had ever been logged going and deeper than most whales go. About how deep did she dive?
answer: About 1,280 meters
choices: About 1,280 meters
About 120 meters
About 400 meters
About 3,500 meters
context: That 2006 dive reached 1,280 m (4,199 ft), the deepest then recorded for any reptile and deeper than most whales ever go. It stood as the record until 2024, when a leatherback tagged in the Solomon Islands was reported to have dived about 1,344 m. Source: Guinness World Records, 'Deepest dive by a turtle/chelonian'; https://www.livescience.com/animals/turtles/leatherback-turtle-dives-deeper-than-a-navy-sub-smashing-world-record-in-the-process

question: Winged mayflies rise from a river all at once, swarm in mating clouds above it and are dead by nightfall. But that flying adult is only the tail end of a mayfly's life. Where does it spend the long first part, often a full year and sometimes two or three?
answer: Underwater on the riverbed as a nymph
choices: Underwater on the riverbed as a nymph
Sealed in a cocoon buried in mud
Dormant inside a tree gall
Riding wind currents high in the sky
context: For most of its life a mayfly is an aquatic nymph, crawling on the river bottom and breathing through feathery gills. The winged adult everyone pictures is the tiny tail-end of the whole life cycle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfly

question: One warm afternoon a mayfly splits its old skin down the back and flies off as a winged adult, with only about a single day of life ahead of it. That rushed adult life hides an oddity few other animals share. What is it?
answer: Its mouthparts are shrunken and useless, so it cannot eat at all
choices: Its mouthparts are shrunken and useless, so it cannot eat at all
It must return to the water within hours or its wings dissolve
It can fly only at night and is blind in daylight
It is born already carrying a fatal parasite in its gut
context: The adult mayfly's mouthparts don't work. It emerges only to find a mate and reproduce, then dies -- eating was never part of the plan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfly

question: Fly fishermen tying trout flies know two mayfly stages by name. They tie one lure for the cloudy-winged mayfly they call a 'dun,' and another for the shinier, more elegant adult it soon becomes. To cross between those two winged stages, the mayfly does something no other winged insect does. What does it do?
answer: It molts again, shedding its skin, wings and all
choices: It molts again, shedding its skin, wings and all
It spins a silk cocoon and rests inside it
It drains the color from its wings by baking in the sun
It fuses its four wings into a single broad sail
context: The mayfly is the only insect that molts one more time AFTER it already has working wings. The cloudy-winged 'dun,' or subimago, sheds its skin -- wings included -- to become the shiny final adult. No other winged insect does this. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8463790/

question: The National Weather Service's radar station near La Crosse, Wisconsin, lit up late on June 23, 2012, with bright yellows and oranges rising off the Mississippi River, and the strange echo tracked steadily from about 9 p.m. until past 10:30. There were no thunderstorms anywhere near and no rain forecast. What was the radar picking up?
answer: A gigantic swarm of hatching mayflies
choices: A gigantic swarm of hatching mayflies
A wall of hail forming over the river
A flock of migrating starlings
Smoke from a riverside grass fire
context: Mayfly hatches can be so enormous they show up on weather radar like rainfall, and forecasters tracked this one just as they would a storm. The bugs pile up so thick under bridge lights that crews have to plow them off like snow. Source: https://www.weather.gov/arx/mayfly_tracking

question: A male antechinus, a mouse-sized Australian marsupial, throws himself into a breeding frenzy that lasts two or three weeks. He stops eating and sleeping, and he mates in sessions of up to 14 hours. What does that season do to every male?
answer: His own stress hormones flood his body and trigger fatal organ failure
choices: His own stress hormones flood his body and trigger fatal organ failure
He is driven off by rivals to live and starve alone in exile
He sheds his fur and burrows deep underground to slowly recover
He guards the newborn young while the females leave to go feed
context: During the frenzy a flood of the male antechinus's own stress hormone, cortisol, triggers organ failure -- so every single male drops dead at the end of the breeding season, his whole existence spent fathering the next generation. Source: https://theconversation.com/these-fierce-tiny-marsupials-drop-dead-after-lengthy-sex-fests-and-sometimes-become-cannibals-221009

question: A winged mayfly dances over a river at dusk with only a few hours left to find a mate. Inside its slender body, the gut that once digested the nymph's food no longer holds a single meal. What fills it instead?
answer: Air, instead of any food at all
choices: Air, instead of any food at all
Water, stored against drying out
Fat, burned to power its flight
Eggs, crowded in from its ovaries
context: In the winged adult the gut no longer digests anything; it is filled with air instead, which may help lighten the weak-flying body so it can stay aloft long enough to mate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfly

question: A female Dolania americana mayfly takes to the air over Florida's Blackwater River after up to two years buried in its sand as a nymph. No insect ever timed has a shorter adult life: she has just long enough to be found by a male, mate and drop her eggs. How long does her winged life last?
answer: Under five minutes, start to finish
choices: Under five minutes, start to finish
A single night, from dusk to dawn
About one full day and its following night
Roughly three days of steady flying
context: The American sand-burrowing mayfly Dolania americana holds the shortest adult lifespan of any known insect. After up to two years as a sand-burrowing nymph, the adult female lives less than five minutes -- she emerges, is mated, lays her eggs, and dies, all within about five minutes, and the whole population dies within roughly 30 minutes of emergence. Peters & Peters (1977) timed the pre-dawn emergence on the Blackwater River in NW Florida, where males appear about 1.5 hours before sunrise and patrol a 15-20 m stretch of river. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dolania' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolania), citing Peters & Peters 1977; corroborated by Live Science, 'Which animal has the shortest life span?'

question: The North American desert bakes under the sun, and the dry air steals moisture from any small creature caught in the open. The kangaroo rat, a tiny hopping rodent named for its long back legs, dodges the worst of it before the sun has risen. What does it do all day, from dawn until dusk?
answer: Stays underground in a cool, humid burrow
choices: Stays underground in a cool, humid burrow
Buries itself in wet riverbed mud
Floats in shaded rock pools
Shelters inside cactus flesh
context: The kangaroo rat stays in a cool, humid burrow through the heat of the day and only emerges at night, a behaviour that works alongside its body's water-saving tricks. Source: Schmidt-Nielsen & Schmidt-Nielsen 1951 (PubMed 14897858); OpenLearn 'Animals at the extremes' behavioural strategies.

question: A coyote corners a desert tortoise on the open flats of the Mojave, where rain can skip a whole year. The frightened tortoise has one panic reflex it cannot undo, and out in the dry country it can prove deadlier than the coyote. What does the tortoise do?
answer: It voids the huge water store in its oversized bladder
choices: It voids the huge water store in its oversized bladder
It bolts into the open sun and overheats
It freezes in place and stops eating for weeks
It holds its breath inside its shell until it faints
context: The desert tortoise stores water in an oversized bladder that can hold up to about two-fifths of its body weight in fluid; if a predator frightens it into emptying that bladder, it can lose a dangerous amount of its reserve. Source: WorldAtlas 'Which Animals Can Live Without Water For Years?'; desert tortoise physiology accounts.

question: When a long drought dries the Australian outback hard, the water-holding frog, Ranoidea platycephala, vanishes underground, sealed away from the hot, dry air above. It can stay down there as long as five years. How does the frog seal itself in?
answer: It wraps itself in a cocoon of its own shed skin
choices: It wraps itself in a cocoon of its own shed skin
It buries itself inside a ball of mud
It coats its body in tree sap
It fills a burrow with swallowed water
context: The water-holding frog soaks up half its body weight in water, wraps itself in a cocoon made of its own shed skin, and sleeps underground through drought for up to five years. Source: Australian Geographic 'Fact File: Water-holding frog (Cyclorana)'; Wikipedia 'Ranoidea platycephala'.

question: An Arabian camel goes days without water in the desert, and its blood grows thick and sludgy as it loses fluid. Blood that syrupy would jam the narrowest vessels, the capillaries, of almost any other animal. Something about the camel's red blood cells keeps the flow moving. What is unusual about them?
answer: They are oval rather than round
choices: They are oval rather than round
They carry no oxygen at all
They are ten times larger than ours
They dissolve and reform each day
context: A camel's red blood cells are oval, not round, a shape that lets its blood keep flowing even when dehydration thickens it, so a camel can safely lose up to about 25% of its body water, where most mammals die after losing about 12%. Source: ScienceInsights 'Where Does a Camel Store Water?'; Britannica 'Camel'.

question: Every breath a kangaroo rat lets out carries warm, moist air away from its body, a steady water leak it can hardly afford in a desert with no pools or streams. Its narrow, tightly coiled nose cools each outgoing breath and pulls the moisture back in. How much of each breath's water can it recover?
answer: Up to about 83%
choices: Up to about 83%
Up to about 50%
Up to about 20%
Up to about 5%
context: The kangaroo rat's cold, narrow, convoluted nose acts as a heat exchanger, condensing moisture from exhaled air and recovering as much as 83% of the water that would otherwise be lost with each breath. Source: Jackson & Schmidt-Nielsen 1964, 'Countercurrent Heat Exchange in the Respiratory Passages' (PNAS, JSTOR 72138); AskNature 'Nasal Turbinates Reduce Water Loss'.

question: A water-holding frog waits out years of Australian drought buried underground. Thirsty travellers have dug one up, squeezed it gently and drunk clean-tasting water straight from its body, a trick Aboriginal peoples have known for a very long time. What is that water?
answer: Dilute urine stored in a huge bladder
choices: Dilute urine stored in a huge bladder
Sap it absorbs from buried tree roots
Rainwater swallowed and held in its stomach
Fluid wrung from the fat in its thighs
context: The frog's bladder holds very dilute urine averaging about 57% of its body mass, a reserve calculated to offset water loss for two to three years underground. It also drops its oxygen use by roughly 70% during aestivation. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Ranoidea platycephala'; Cartledge et al., 'Water balance and arginine vasotocin in the cocooning frog Cyclorana platycephala,' 2007 (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18040971/).

question: A giant flightless insect once crawled through the forests of Lord Howe Island, off eastern Australia. Glossy black, armored and up to 8 inches long, it weighed nearly an ounce, and islanders called it the tree lobster. What kind of insect is it?
answer: A stick insect
choices: A stick insect
A beetle
A cockroach
A cricket
context: Dryococelus australis is a giant stick insect that grows up to about 8 inches (20 cm) long and weighs nearly an ounce (25 g); its heavy, armored bulk earned it the local name 'tree lobster.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dryococelus_australis

question: Black rats from a shipwreck ate every last stick insect on Lord Howe Island, and by the 1920s scientists had written the giant species off as gone forever. Then, in 2001, a survey team found a tiny colony still alive. Where were the last survivors clinging on?
answer: A bare sea stack out in the ocean
choices: A bare sea stack out in the ocean
A grassy islet inside the lagoon
A tiny coral cay far offshore
A wrecked ship's hull on the reef
context: In 2001 climbers found a small colony of Dryococelus australis alive on Ball's Pyramid — a sheer 20-km-distant ocean rock — decades after the species was declared extinct, the rediscovery of what's been called 'the rarest insect in the world.' Source: Australian Museum blog 'VIP: Very Important Phasmid'; ecoservantsproject.org.

question: A survey team found the giant stick insect of Lord Howe still alive in 2001, decades after rats had wiped it off the main island and biologists had given it up for extinct. Only about two dozen were left, the entire species. Where were they all living?
answer: On one single spindly bush
choices: On one single spindly bush
In one hollow tree trunk
Scattered across several islets
Under loose stones by the sea
context: Roughly 24 individuals survived, all clinging to and feeding on ONE spindly tea-tree bush (Melaleuca howeana) high on a narrow ledge of the sea stack — the whole species surviving on a single plant. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants; ecoservantsproject.org.

question: Two giant black stick insects of Lord Howe Island, glossy and heavily armored, sleep through the day coiled together, one pressed close beside the other. What does the male do as the pair rests?
answer: Drapes three legs over the female beside him
choices: Drapes three legs over the female beside him
Tucks her beneath his abdomen
Interlocks his antennae with hers
Rests his head on her back
context: Dryococelus australis pairs sleep coiled together, the male draping three of his legs protectively over the female — a kind of pair-bonding almost never seen in insects. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org).

question: A hamster-sized mammal noses through the leaf litter of a Madagascar rainforest, hunting earthworms. Quills cover it like a tiny hedgehog's, but they are black banded with yellow, and a yellow stripe runs down its nose. What is it?
answer: The lowland streaked tenrec
choices: The lowland streaked tenrec
The lesser hedgehog tenrec
The African pygmy hedgehog
The golden spiny mouse
context: The lowland streaked tenrec (Hemicentetes semispinosus) weighs only about 125 to 280 grams, wears black-and-yellow spines with a yellow stripe down its snout, and feeds mostly on earthworms in Madagascar's rainforests. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowland_streaked_tenrec

question: A streaked tenrec keeps in touch with its family in the undergrowth of a Madagascar forest with a buzzing, clicking chatter that does not come from its voice. It is the only mammal known to make sound this way. How does it make the buzz?
answer: It rubs special quills on its back together
choices: It rubs special quills on its back together
It hums air through hollow nasal chambers
It cracks the joints in its long hind legs
It flutters loose flaps of skin along its ribs
context: This is called stridulation, the same trick crickets and grasshoppers use with their wings. The tenrec grinds together a patch of 7 to 16 specialized quills arranged in three rows on the middle of its back, producing high-frequency clicks and buzzes. A foraging mother stays in touch with her young this way, and the babies buzz back once their own quill organ develops. It is the only mammal known to communicate by stridulation. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowland_streaked_tenrec ; https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Hemicentetes_semispinosus/

question: A tenrec swims a Madagascar stream like a tiny otter, while its island cousins look like shrews, hedgehogs and moles. All 31 or so kinds descend from one ancestor that reached Madagascar some 30 million years ago. How do scientists think it got there?
answer: It rafted across the sea on floating vegetation
choices: It rafted across the sea on floating vegetation
It walked over a land bridge from India
It was carried in the gut of a migrating seabird
It swam the channel from the African mainland
context: This is a textbook adaptive radiation: one ancestor, thought to have rafted from Africa on floating vegetation roughly 29 to 37 million years ago, diversified into shrew-like, hedgehog-like, mole-like and otter-like forms to fill Madagascar's empty niches. Despite the resemblances, tenrecs are not related to hedgehogs, shrews or moles; that likeness is convergent evolution, and their real cousins are elephants, aardvarks and sea cows in the African group Afrotheria. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenrec

question: A female bolas spider in an American forest spins no web. At night she hangs from a silk thread, dangling a single sticky ball of glue at the end of a short line, like a fisherman with a baited hook. A male moth of just the right species flies straight to her out of the dark, and she swings the ball and knocks him down. What draws the moth in?
answer: A scent that copies a female moth's mating perfume
choices: A scent that copies a female moth's mating perfume
A soft glow from the tip of her sticky glue-ball
A high buzz that mimics a female moth's wingbeat
A flower-like shape that draws him in to feed
context: The bolas spider releases a scent that mimics a female moth's mating pheromone; when a male flies in, she swings the glue-tipped thread like a cowboy's bolas to catch him. Source: Science 1977 (Aggressive Chemical Mimicry by a Bolas Spider); Wikipedia (Mastophora hutchinsoni).

question: A deep-sea anglerfish carries a tiny glowing bait at the end of a long, fleshy fishing rod rising from between its eyes. Over many millions of years, one part of an ancestral fish crept forward over its head, stretched into a stalk and grew the glowing lure at its tip. Which part became the rod?
answer: The front spine of its back fin
choices: The front spine of its back fin
A stiffened whisker beside its mouth
The first ray of its tail fin
A hardened tooth from its jaw
context: The rod is a modified first dorsal fin spine: over evolution the front fin ray migrated forward over the head to become the illicium (the rod), tipped by the esca (the glowing lure). Source: Wikipedia (Ceratioidei); Smithsonian Ocean.

question: A spider-tailed viper hides among the rocks of Iran's western mountains, wiggling a tail tip shaped like a spider to lure birds. Its close cousins look nearly identical but eat mammals. Researchers dripped each snake's venom into chicken blood plasma. What did the bird-hunter's venom do that its cousins' venoms did not?
answer: Made the blood clot much faster
choices: Made the blood clot much faster
Kept the blood from clotting at all
Made the blood clot more slowly
Left the blood completely unchanged
context: The spider-tailed viper (Pseudocerastes urarachnoides) is the only Pseudocerastes that specializes in birds. In thromboelastography tests its venom sped up the start of clotting in chicken plasma by about 96 percent, and it was strongly procoagulant in human and toad plasma too. The venoms of its mammal-eating relatives P. persicus and P. fieldi had no significant effect on bird plasma (about a 20 percent delay in clotting) but were strongly anticoagulant in human and amphibian plasma. Source: op den Brouw et al., 2021, Toxins 13(2):112 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7913145/).

question: In the damp forests of southeastern Australia lives a big, brown, ground-dwelling songbird the size of a pheasant. The courting male fans a spectacular tail forward over his own head like a shimmering silvery umbrella. What is the shape of that famous tail?
answer: A small ancient harp, a lyre
choices: A small ancient harp, a lyre
A folded paper fan
A peacock's eyed wheel
A drooping willow branch
context: The superb lyrebird's ornate courtship tail spreads into the shape of a lyre, a small ancient harp. Two outer feathers curve into an 'S' shape (called 'lyrates') and frame twelve fine silvery filament feathers between them. Source: Australian Museum, 'Superb Lyrebird'; Wikipedia, 'Superb lyrebird'.

question: A kookaburra on a branch in an Australian eucalyptus forest hears its own laughing call answer back from the bushes below, and it calls again in reply. No second kookaburra is there. The mimic in the bushes can copy some twenty other birds in a row. Which bird is it?
answer: The superb lyrebird
choices: The superb lyrebird
The common starling
The northern mockingbird
The Australian magpie
context: Australia's superb lyrebird is the animal kingdom's champion mimic. It can imitate a kookaburra's laugh so perfectly that a nearby wild kookaburra is fooled into thinking it hears one of its own and calls back. Roughly 70-80% of a male lyrebird's song is imitation, and it can copy more than 20 other bird species accurately enough that the real birds answer.

question: At Adelaide Zoo, a male lyrebird named Chook lived for months next to a building site that would later become the panda house. When keepers listened close to Chook's song, they heard sounds that had nothing to do with a forest. What had he woven into his song?
answer: Hammers, power drills and saws
choices: Hammers, power drills and saws
Thunderclaps and heavy rain
Church bells across the city
Lions roaring in the next paddock
context: Captive lyrebirds copy man-made machine sounds with uncanny accuracy. Chook reproduced the hammers, power drills and saws he heard during the panda-enclosure construction beside his cage. Source: The Conversation, 'Lyrebirds mimicking chainsaws: fact or lie?'; snootypaws.com.au blog on Chook.

question: Hollis Taylor spent years walking deep Australian forests in search of the lyrebird's most famous trick and came up empty-handed. She now says no known clean recording of it comes from a truly wild bird; the celebrated clips come mostly from captive lyrebirds. Which crowd-pleasing feat is almost never caught from a wild lyrebird?
answer: Imitating man-made machine sounds
choices: Imitating man-made machine sounds
Copying other birds' calls
Singing loudly before dawn
Fanning its tail while it sings
context: Hollis Taylor notes 'there is no known recording of a lyrebird in the wild mimicking man-made mechanical sounds.' The chainsaw and camera-shutter clips come mainly from captive birds (two of the three lyrebirds in Attenborough's Life of Birds were sanctuary and zoo birds); wild lyrebirds mostly copy forest sounds and other birds. Source: The Conversation, 'Lyrebirds mimicking chainsaws: fact or lie?' (Hollis Taylor).

question: A male lyrebird sings from a log in an Australian forest, his voice coming from the syrinx, the voice box where the windpipe splits toward the lungs. Recordings of his flute-like song hold a surprise. What can a single lyrebird do with that voice box?
answer: Sing two different melodies at once
choices: Sing two different melodies at once
Sing louder than any other bird
Hold one note for several minutes
Sing notes too high for people to hear
context: A lyrebird can carry two tunes at the same time: the two sides of a songbird's syrinx (voice box) can work independently, and researchers studying a lyrebird's flute-like song had to separate one melody from the other. Some other songbirds can also make two sounds at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyrebird ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrinx_(bird_anatomy)

question: A farmer kept a captive lyrebird in the 1930s in the New England district of New South Wales, and the bird learned to copy the tunes he played on his flute. Later it was set free in the forest, where it lived among wild lyrebirds and bred with them. What did its wild descendants do with the borrowed melody?
answer: Refined it and passed it down for generations
choices: Refined it and passed it down for generations
Abandoned it within a single season
Mixed it with a kookaburra's laugh
Split it into two rival songs
context: The captive bird copied the farmer's flute tunes ('The Keel Row' and 'Mosquito's Dance'); once released, its descendants refined and handed the melody down for generations, a documented case of cultural transmission, though the exact origin story remains debated. Source: Duke University Press, 'A Little Flute Music' (Environmental Humanities); NPR Krulwich, 'Nature's Living Tape Recorders'.  (Legend.)

question: A girl stands still in the tall grass of an American meadow as a summer dusk deepens. A tiny insect lights up its own body from inside with a soft yellow-green glow, blinks a few times and goes dark; then another lights up, and dozens more, across the meadow. Which insect makes this living light?
answer: The firefly
choices: The firefly
The dragonfly
The cicada
The praying mantis
context: A firefly's glow is a chemical reaction in its abdomen, not a hot bulb. Almost no heat is produced, so it is called 'cold light' - one of the most efficient light-makers known. Source: photobiology.info (Branchini, Chemistry of Firefly Bioluminescence).

question: On a warm night on certain beaches, a breaking wave flashes into a curtain of cold blue light, and every kick of a wading swimmer leaves a glowing swirl behind. Millions of tiny single-celled drifters are flashing blue each time the water around them is stirred. Which drifting sea creatures make the glow?
answer: Dinoflagellate plankton
choices: Dinoflagellate plankton
Baby glowing shrimp
Floating fish eggs
Drifting moon jellyfish
context: Dinoflagellates flash blue when the water around them is disturbed by a wave, a paddle, or a swimmer. The flash lasts about a tenth of a second and is thought to be a 'burglar alarm' - startling an attacker and drawing a bigger predator to eat it. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium, 'The magic of bioluminescence'.

question: A female hunter hangs almost still a mile down in the black, cold ocean. She is mostly one huge, tooth-lined mouth, and over it a tiny living lantern dangles on a thin stalk. Which animal is she?
answer: The deep-sea anglerfish
choices: The deep-sea anglerfish
The great white shark
The electric eel
The giant squid
context: The glowing lure is called the esca, dangled on a fishing-rod stalk right in front of the anglerfish's mouth to draw in both prey and mates in the dark. In the lightless deep, prey drawn to the little light swim into her jaws.

question: A Hawaiian bobtail squid, no bigger than a thumb, glides just under the moonlit surface off Hawaii at night. Predators in the darker water below stare up toward the bright surface, watching for the dark shape it should cast, yet they see nothing. Glowing bacteria inside the squid make a soft light. How does that light erase its shadow?
answer: It aims the glow downward to match the moonlight above
choices: It aims the glow downward to match the moonlight above
It flashes a burst bright enough to dazzle them
It coats itself in mirror-silver to reflect the depths
It puffs out a glowing cloud to hide behind
context: The Hawaiian bobtail squid (Euprymna scolopes) houses glowing Vibrio fischeri bacteria in a light organ and beams the light downward, dimming or brightening it to exactly match the moonlight above so predators see no silhouette. Source: UC Santa Cruz News (2021), 'A little squid and its glowing bacteria'.

question: DeLeo and colleagues rebuilt the family tree of one group of glowing animals in 2024 and traced their light far back into the fossil record, past the old record held by tiny ostracod crustaceans of the Permian. Which living animals now hold the record for the earliest glow?
answer: Octocorals, the soft corals, glowing back roughly 540 million years
choices: Octocorals, the soft corals, glowing back roughly 540 million years
Fireflies, whose glowing beetle lineage runs deepest in time
Anglerfish, whose lure-light reaches furthest into the fossil past
Vampire squid, whose glow predates every other animal lineage
context: A 2024 Smithsonian-led study (DeLeo et al., Proceedings of the Royal Society B) traced bioluminescence in octocorals -- the soft corals and sea pens -- back at least ~540 million years, pushing the oldest dated animal glow back nearly 300 million years from the previous record of ~267 Mya in ostracod crustaceans. The team mapped luminous species onto a genetic tree of 185 octocoral species (built in 2022) and combined it with fossil ages to infer the trait in ancient ancestors. Bioluminescence is also a textbook case of convergent evolution: a 2021 review (Lau & Oakley, Biological Reviews) counted that living light arose independently at least ~94 separate times across life, and in the ray-finned fishes alone at least ~27 times (Davis, Sparks & Smith 2016, PLOS ONE). Sources: Smithsonian 2024, octocorals ~540 Mya (https://www.si.edu/newsdesk/releases/bioluminescence-first-evolved-animals-least-540-million-years-ago); Lau & Oakley 2021, Biological Reviews (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/brv.12672); Davis et al. 2016, PLOS ONE (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0155154).

question: A red-gold animal on long, deer-like black legs peers over the tall grass of a Brazilian savanna, its face like a fox's. Standing up to 110 centimetres at the shoulder, it is the tallest wild dog on Earth. What is it?
answer: The maned wolf
choices: The maned wolf
The bat-eared fox
The dhole
The golden jackal
context: The maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus) stands up to 110 cm (43 inches) at the shoulder on its stilt-like legs — the tallest of all wild canids, nicknamed the 'fox on stilts.' Its long legs let it peer over the tall grasses of the Cerrado savanna to spot prey and danger. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maned_wolf; worldanimalprotection.us/latest/blogs/maned-wolf-facts/; oneearth.org/species-of-the-week-maned-wolf/

question: Police were once called to Rotterdam Zoo to track down someone smoking cannabis, so strong was the reek. They found no smoker: the skunk-and-weed smell was pouring off one animal's territorial scent marks. Which animal's urine was it?
answer: The maned wolf's
choices: The maned wolf's
The striped skunk's
The red fox's
The wolverine's
context: The maned wolf's urine smells strongly of skunk and cannabis, earning it the nickname 'skunk wolf.' The pungent compound is a pyrazine, a long-lasting chemical it uses to mark and hold its territory across the grassland. The Rotterdam Zoo incident was reported in the press in 2006. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maned_wolf; gizmodo.com/this-stretched-out-wolfs-pee-smells-like-marijuana-1707801636

question: A maned wolf on a Brazilian savanna gulps down a wolf apple, a tomato-like fruit that makes up much of its diet, and later leaves the seeds in its dung. Researchers compared those seeds with ones pulled fresh from the fruit. How do the seeds from the dung fare?
answer: More of them sprout
choices: More of them sprout
Fewer of them sprout
None of them sprout
Just as many sprout
context: Unlike a meat-craving wolf, the maned wolf loves fruit: Solanum lycocarpum (the 'wolf apple') can make up 40 to 90 percent of its diet. Studies in Brazil find that seeds passed through the wolf's gut germinate better than seeds taken straight from the fruit, though the figures differ from study to study. It often defecates on leafcutter-ant nests, and the ants haul the seeds to their refuse piles, a process that raises germination further. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maned_wolf; Veloso, Universidade Federal de Uberlandia dissertation (repositorio.ufu.br/handle/123456789/27043)

question: On a bright coral reef, a finger-length animal sits in a burrow it dug in the sand, looking harmless. Folded under its head are two heavy, club-shaped arms, and it uses them to crack snail and crab shells open. What is this reef hunter?
answer: The mantis shrimp
choices: The mantis shrimp
The hermit crab
The spiny lobster
The cleaner shrimp
context: The peacock mantis shrimp (Odontodactylus scyllarus) is a stomatopod, not a true shrimp. Its 'smasher' clubs pound open hard-shelled prey. Source: reefs.com 'Introduction to the Mantis Shrimps'; en.wikipedia.org 'Mantis shrimp'.

question: A peacock mantis shrimp swings a blunt, club-shaped arm to crush a snail's shell, while a cousin hides in a sandy burrow on the same reef and flicks out a long, spiny arm to stab a passing fish. What are these two body plans called?
answer: Smashers and spearers
choices: Smashers and spearers
Grinders and netters
Crushers and stingers
Diggers and lurkers
context: Smashers (like the peacock) bludgeon hard-shelled prey; spearers (like L. maculata) impale soft, fast prey such as fish and shrimp with barbed appendages. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Mantis shrimp'; nationalgeographic.com.

question: Kept in a home aquarium, a peacock mantis shrimp can shatter the glass of an ordinary tank with one strike of its club. Keepers are told to house it behind glass of a certain minimum thickness. What must the glass be?
answer: At least 8-10 millimeters thick
choices: At least 8-10 millimeters thick
At least 2-3 millimeters thick
Bulletproof polycarbonate only
Double-paned and vacuum-sealed
context: The peacock mantis shrimp can crack aquarium glass with one blow, so keepers use tanks with glass at least 8-10 mm thick to survive it. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Odontodactylus scyllarus'; gensou.sg mantis shrimp tank setup.

question: With one lash of its club, a peacock mantis shrimp cracks a crab's shell. Scientists measured the blow at about 1,500 newtons, an enormous force for so small an animal. How does that force compare with the shrimp's own body weight?
answer: Over 2,500 times its body weight
choices: Over 2,500 times its body weight
About 10 times its body weight
Roughly equal to its body weight
Around 100 times its body weight
context: About 1,500 newtons of peak force -- over 2,500 times the animal's own weight -- enough to crack snail shells, crab carapaces, and aquarium glass. Source: Patek & Caldwell, J. Exp. Biol. (2005), PubMed 16169943; en.wikipedia.org 'Odontodactylus scyllarus'.

question: To throw its club fast enough, a peacock mantis shrimp needs more than muscle. It slowly loads a saddle-shaped spring in its arm, holds it with a latch, then trips the latch to release all the stored energy at once. Which weapon works on the same principle?
answer: A crossbow
choices: A crossbow
A whip
A slingstone
A blowgun
context: This is a latch-mediated spring: the shrimp compresses a saddle-shaped spring, holds it with a latch, and releases it in a fraction of a millisecond -- exactly how a crossbow stores and releases energy. Source: pateklab.biology.duke.edu (4-bar linkage + saddle/meral-V spring-latch).

question: Scientists filmed a peacock mantis shrimp with high-speed cameras as it unfolded its club-shaped arm and punched at prey, to clock how quickly the club speeds up in one of the fastest moves measured in any animal. How hard does it accelerate, compared with gravity?
answer: Thousands of times the force of gravity
choices: Thousands of times the force of gravity
About twice the force of gravity
Roughly ten times the force of gravity
A few hundred times the force of gravity
context: The smasher's club accelerates at 6,300 to 8,000 times gravity, reaching 14-23 m/s (about 50-75 mph) -- among the fastest strikes measured in any animal. Source: Patek, Korff & Caldwell, Nature 428, 819-820 (2004); pateklab.biology.duke.edu.

question: When a peacock mantis shrimp punches a shell with its club, the water can barely react. High-speed films of one strike show two spikes of force about 400 microseconds apart, the whole event over in under a thousandth of a second. The first comes from the club striking the shell. What causes the second?
answer: The cavitation bubble collapsing
choices: The cavitation bubble collapsing
The club rebounding for a second hit
The prey's shell cracking apart
A muscle firing a follow-up blow
context: Two force peaks 390-480 microseconds apart: first the club's impact, then the collapse of the cavitation bubble -- both over in under 800 microseconds. Source: Patek & Caldwell, J. Exp. Biol. (2005), PubMed 16169943.

question: A peacock mantis shrimp's club moves so fast that the water in front of it boils into a tiny bubble of vapor. As that bubble collapses, its core flashes with light and briefly heats to tens of thousands of degrees, hotter than the surface of the sun. What is this light from a collapsing bubble called?
answer: Sonoluminescence
choices: Sonoluminescence
Bioluminescence
Phosphorescence
Incandescence
context: The collapsing bubble flashes light and spikes to roughly 20,000 K -- hotter than the sun's surface -- a phenomenon called sonoluminescence. LEGEND-tier; the exact temperature is a measured-but-debated inference. Source: academic.oup.com/icb 'Power of Mantis Shrimp Strikes' (2019); sonoluminescence literature.

question: Peering from its burrow on a coral reef, a mantis shrimp looks out through eyes far richer in color receptors than a human's, which has just three kinds, for red, green and blue. It even senses ultraviolet light that people cannot see. How many kinds of color receptor does a mantis shrimp eye have?
answer: Twelve to sixteen
choices: Twelve to sixteen
Four to five
Twenty-five to thirty
Six to eight
context: 12-16 color photoreceptor types (humans have 3), plus ultraviolet and polarized-light sensitivity. LEGEND-tier wonder. Source: Cronin & Marshall 1989; en.wikipedia.org 'Mantis shrimp'; nationalgeographic.com.

question: Hanne Thoen trained mantis shrimp in 2014 to pick between very similar shades of color. Their eyes carry far more kinds of color receptor than a human's three, yet they did worse than people at telling the shades apart. Why did all those extra receptors not give them finer color vision?
answer: Its receptors work alone instead of comparing signals
choices: Its receptors work alone instead of comparing signals
Its brain is too small to hold so many colors
Its color cells wear out within a few weeks
It can see color only in bright, direct sunlight
context: Despite 12 or more receptor types, mantis shrimp failed color tasks that people find easy, because their receptors do not compare signals against one another the way the three kinds in a human eye do. More receptors did not mean finer color vision. Source: Thoen et al., Science (2014).

question: Hunting on a coral reef, a mantis shrimp recognizes each color almost instantly, with very little work for its brain, though its eye is packed with far more kinds of color receptor than a human's. Researchers think the eye reads color the way a certain machine does. Which machine does it work like?
answer: A satellite or barcode scanner
choices: A satellite or barcode scanner
A telescope tracking a star
A camera capturing a full still image
A magnifying glass
context: Instead of comparing colors, the eye scans -- sweeping across the scene reading color line-by-line like a satellite or barcode scanner, recognizing a color instantly without heavy brain processing. LEGEND-tier. Source: Thoen et al. Science (2014); nationalgeographic.com 'The Mantis Shrimp Sees Like A Satellite'.

question: With just one eye, a mantis shrimp on a reef can judge how far away a target is, though most animals get depth perception by comparing what their left and right eyes see. What lets a single mantis shrimp eye judge depth by itself?
answer: Each eye has three zones aimed at one spot
choices: Each eye has three zones aimed at one spot
Each eye has two separate lenses inside
The eye rapidly refocuses back and forth
Two pupils sit side by side in each eye
context: Each eye is divided into three regions that see the same point at once -- 'trinocular' vision -- giving one eye depth perception, while the two eyes swivel independently. Source: nationalgeographic.com; zmescience.com; PMC5399772.

question: Inside a mantis shrimp's eye, cell membranes roll up into tiny tubes that twist light like the quarter-wave plate in a compact disc player or a camera filter. A plate made by people works for one color only; the shrimp's handles everything from near-ultraviolet to infrared. What were mantis shrimp the first animals shown to do?
answer: Detect circularly polarized light
choices: Detect circularly polarized light
See individual photons in total darkness
Hear ultrasonic pulses through the water
Sense electric fields from buried prey
context: In 2008 Tsyr-Huei Chiou and colleagues showed that mantis shrimp detect circularly polarized light, the first animals proven to do so; a 2010 study later reported a jewel scarab beetle responding to it too. Photoreceptor cell membranes are rolled into microtubes that act as a natural quarter-wave plate (retarder), converting linear polarization into circular and back. Human-made quarter-wave plates in CD/DVD players and camera filters work well for only one color, but the shrimp's version performs almost perfectly across the whole visible range, near-UV to infrared, outdoing any synthetic design. Source: Chiou et al., Current Biology 18:429 (2008); Brady & Cummings, American Naturalist 175:614 (2010); Roberts, Chiou, Marshall & Cronin, Nature Photonics 2009, https://www.bristol.ac.uk/news/2009/6591.html

question: One mantis shrimp swings a crushing club at a snail while a cousin waits in its burrow nearby to spear passing prey on long, barbed arms. The two body plans look like a matched pair that must have split apart together. What does the evidence of fossils and DNA show about where each came from?
answer: Spearing came first; smashing arose far later
choices: Spearing came first; smashing arose far later
Smashing came first; spearing arose far later
Both arose together from a single crushing ancestor
Each evolved separately on opposite sides of the globe
context: Spearing raptorial appendages evolved long before smashing ones. A total-evidence phylogeny (dated molecular plus fossil analysis) places the origin of the crushing club at roughly 126 million years ago, in the Early Cretaceous, while crown-group mantis shrimp (Unipeltata) themselves diverged around 340 million years ago. Primitive stomatopod suborders, Palaeostomatopodea (Devonian-Carboniferous) and Archaeostomatopodea (Carboniferous), show raptorial limbs far less differentiated than modern ones, with the front appendages not yet dramatically enlarged over the pairs behind. Source: total-evidence phylogeny, Mol. Phylogenet. Evol. 2025, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1055790325000636 ; evolutionary history of Stomatopoda, https://peerj.com/articles/3844/ ; Mesozoic fossils, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2955030/

question: Seen from behind, a huge African bird looks like a hunched figure wrapped in a black cloak, on skinny white legs, with a bald head and a great dagger of a bill. People nickname it the undertaker bird. Which bird is it?
answer: The marabou stork
choices: The marabou stork
The lappet-faced vulture
The southern ground hornbill
The shoebill
context: The marabou stork's cloak-like dark wings and back, spindly white legs, and occasional tuft of white 'hair' give it a Grim-Reaper silhouette from behind — earning it the nickname 'undertaker bird.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marabou_stork ; https://africafreak.com/marabou-stork

question: A marabou stork of sub-Saharan Africa, a heavy scavenger with a bald pink head, spreads dark wings that average about 2.6 metres across, among the widest of any land bird. It can travel huge distances day after day without tiring. How does it fly so far without wearing itself out?
answer: it soars on rising columns of warm air without flapping
choices: it soars on rising columns of warm air without flapping
it flies in V-shaped flocks, drafting off the bird ahead
it skims low over water, riding a cushion of air
it rides steady ocean winds the way an albatross does
context: With one of the largest wingspans of any land bird (about 2.6 m / 8.5 ft on average, and recorded up to ~3.2 m / 10 ft), the marabou soars on thermals — rising columns of warm air — like a vulture rather than powering along by flapping. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marabou_stork

question: A marabou stork stalks across an African plain, its head and long neck bare pink skin all the way down to the shoulders. That bald head is a clue to how it feeds. How does a marabou feed?
answer: it shoves its whole head deep inside carcasses to reach the meat
choices: it shoves its whole head deep inside carcasses to reach the meat
it filters tiny shrimp from muddy water, straining them through its bill
it plunges feet-first from the sky onto fish, like an osprey
it strips leaves and fruit from trees, feeding almost like a browser
context: Like a vulture, the marabou plunges its head deep into carcasses to reach the meat; a feathered head would get, in the birders' phrase, 'rapidly clotted with blood and other substances,' so its naked head and neck stay cleaner. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marabou_stork

question: Beneath a marabou stork's throat dangles a long, floppy pink pouch — up to 18 inches (46 cm) long. From a distance it looks exactly like the crop a bird uses to store swallowed food, and early observers assumed that is what it must be. But scientists later realized this dangling sac is not a food pouch at all. What is that hanging pink sac really for?
answer: it inflates with air to croak in courtship displays
choices: it inflates with air to croak in courtship displays
it stores water to drink during the long dry season
it holds gravel that grinds up the bones it swallows
it stores fat to draw on when carrion runs short
context: Despite looking like a food-storage crop, the pink throat pouch is an inflatable air sac connected to the bird's left nostril. Inflated, it acts as a resonator for guttural croaking during courtship and dominance displays, and it may help shed heat. It hangs about 25–35 cm (up to ~18 inches) when inflated. Source: https://www.torontozoo.com/animals/Marabou%20stork ; https://africafreak.com/marabou-stork

question: On the black lava shores of the Galapagos, a stocky, dark lizard the size of a house cat slips into the Pacific surf and grazes on algae on the rocks underwater. No other lizard on Earth feeds in the sea. What is this lizard called?
answer: The marine iguana
choices: The marine iguana
The Komodo dragon
The frilled lizard
The Gila monster
context: The marine iguana (Amblyrhynchus cristatus) of the Galapagos is the world's only lizard that forages in the ocean, grazing red and green algae off submerged rocks. No other lizard feeds at sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_iguana

question: Marine iguanas bask in a pile on black Galapagos lava, and the lizards come in two clear sizes. The big, bright ones fight for the highest, warmest rocks, while the plainer, smaller ones keep to the edges. What sets the big, showy lizards apart?
answer: They are the adult males of the colony
choices: They are the adult males of the colony
They are the oldest iguanas, swollen with age
They are females heavy with eggs
They are a separate, larger island subspecies
context: Adult male marine iguanas are much bigger than females, weighing about twice as much, and grow brighter breeding colors. The whole species spends only a small fraction of its time actually in the sea, basking on shore most of the day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_iguana

question: A marine iguana climbs out of the Galapagos surf after grazing on algae, a crusty white layer caked across its snout and forehead like frost. The crust is salt, swallowed by the mouthful along with seawater, and too much of it would poison the lizard. How does it get rid of the extra salt?
answer: It sneezes it out through glands in its head
choices: It sneezes it out through glands in its head
It sweats it out through its skin
It cries it out in salty tears
It coughs it up as a paste
context: Special nasal salt glands connected to the nostrils concentrate the salt swallowed with seawater and expel it in a forceful spray; the crystallized salt lands as a crusty white patch on the snout and forehead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_iguana

question: The chilly Galapagos sea drains the heat from a marine iguana as it grazes on algae underwater, until the lizard is too chilled to digest its food or move quickly. The moment it hauls out onto the shore, what does it do to warm back up?
answer: Basks on hot black lava rock in the sun
choices: Basks on hot black lava rock in the sun
Shivers its muscles to make heat
Burrows into warm volcanic sand
Soaks in a shallow, sun-warmed tide pool
context: A dive can drop a marine iguana's body temperature by roughly 10C, so it must haul out and bask on sun-heated black lava rock to reheat before it can digest or move well; its preferred body temperature is 35 to 39C. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_iguana

question: Diving in cold Galapagos water, a marine iguana clings to rocks 30 meters down and can hold its breath for up to an hour, while the chilly sea drains the heat from its body. What does its heart do underwater?
answer: Slows to about a third of its land rate
choices: Slows to about a third of its land rate
Speeds up to pump warm blood faster
Keeps the same steady beat as on land
Beats only when the iguana moves
context: While diving in cold water a marine iguana slows its heart rate to about 30 beats per minute, roughly a third of its on-land rate of about 100 bpm, conserving body heat and oxygen during the dive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_iguana

question: Martin Wikelski tracked about 6,000 marine iguanas through four El Nino years, when the algae they eat can vanish and the lizards starve. He found that a starving iguana does not stop at losing fat; it does something no backboned animal was known to do. What else does its body do?
answer: Shrinks its own skeleton, becoming physically shorter
choices: Shrinks its own skeleton, becoming physically shorter
Sheds its tail to save energy
Stops its heart between meals to conserve fuel
Turns its skin white to reflect the sun
context: Martin Wikelski documented that during El Nino food shortages a marine iguana can shorten its body length by up to 20 percent by resorbing bone, not just losing fat, then regrow to its former length when algae returns. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/47396 (Wikelski & Thom, Nature 2000)

question: A huge, shaggy, tusked beast lumbered across Ice Age North America, and from far off it looked a lot like a woolly mammoth. Up close it was a different animal, with stockier, shorter legs and a low, flat brow instead of the mammoth's tall, domed head. What was this mammoth look-alike?
answer: The mastodon
choices: The mastodon
The giant ground sloth
The woolly rhinoceros
The saber-toothed cat
context: The mastodon was an Ice Age elephant relative of the Americas. It resembled a mammoth but was a separate animal: stockier, shorter-legged, and lower-browed, without the mammoth's tall domed skull. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastodon

question: A paleontologist picks up a single molar from Ice Age North America and can tell in a second that it came from a mastodon, not a woolly mammoth, though the two giants look alike in a museum. What on the tooth gives the mastodon away?
answer: Rows of big blunt cones across the crown
choices: Rows of big blunt cones across the crown
Flat washboard ridges for grinding
A hollow root packed with marrow
Twin curving fangs along the edge
context: One tooth alone tells them apart. Mastodon molars are covered in big blunt cones (cusps); mammoth molars are flat with washboard ridges for grinding grass. Source: https://www.amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/mammoth-mastodon-differences

question: Mastodons and woolly mammoths, both huge and tusked, shared Ice Age North America, but a mastodon's big molars were built very differently from the mammoth's, and paleontologists can read the animal's whole way of life in those teeth. What was the mastodon eating?
answer: Woody twigs, leaves, and branches
choices: Woody twigs, leaves, and branches
Grass cropped short on the plains
Roots grubbed from river mud
Bark stripped only in deep winter
context: The cone teeth reveal the diet: the mastodon was a forest browser, crushing woody plants like twigs, leaves, and branches. The mammoth's ridged teeth made it a grazer, grinding open-grassland grass. Source: https://www.amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/mammoth-mastodon-differences

question: A woolly mammoth wandered the open, windswept grass steppe of Ice Age North America, and the mastodon, a tusked, elephant-sized giant, lived on the same continent at the very same time. What kind of landscape did the mastodon call home?
answer: Spruce and pine woodlands and boggy swamps
choices: Spruce and pine woodlands and boggy swamps
Open steppe grassland, same as the mammoth
Coastal beaches and salt marshes
Bare, rocky high-mountain slopes
context: The mastodon lived in woodlands, spruce and pine forests, and boggy swamps, not the open mammoth steppe. Because the two giants ate different plants in different places, they could share the same land without competing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastodon

question: A bull mastodon wandered Indiana during the Ice Age, his tusk laying down one layer a year like the rings of a tree. In 2022 scientists read the oxygen and strontium locked in each band as a lifelong travel diary. As an adolescent, the bull showed no seasonal pattern at all. What did the tusk reveal about his travels once he grew up?
answer: A repeated spring journey to one fixed mating ground
choices: A repeated spring journey to one fixed mating ground
A slow one-way drift toward the retreating ice sheets
A shrinking range as he was pushed off richer land
A restless wandering that never settled into a pattern
context: The 'Buesching' bull mastodon from Indiana had his whole life written in his tusk. Because a tusk lays down a new growth layer every year and never resorbs the old ones, isotopes sealed in each band record where the animal drank and stood that season. As a youngster his movements showed no seasonal structure, but the year he matured the pattern locked in: a repeated spring/early-summer journey of about 157 km to a specific northeast-Indiana mating ground, then back to his central-Indiana core range. The tusk isotopes let researchers reconstruct an annual migration in a long-extinct animal, the first such seasonally structured movement documented this way. Source: PNAS 2022, 'Male mastodon landscape use changed with maturation' (Miller, Fisher et al.), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9231495/ ; U-Michigan release, https://news.umich.edu/mastodon-tusk-chemical-analysis-reveals-first-evidence-of-one-extinct-animals-annual-migration/

question: A mata mata turtle lies motionless on a muddy Amazon riverbed, with bumpy skin and dangling flaps along its head and neck. Small fish drift right up to it without fear. What do they mistake it for?
answer: A dead leaf or a chunk of rotting bark
choices: A dead leaf or a chunk of rotting bark
A clump of freshwater sponge
A patch of drifting green algae
A tangle of sunken fishing net
context: Its shell is ridged and knobbly like tree bark, and its flat triangular head trails ragged skin fringes that mimic fallen leaves, so prey fish never spot the predator among the leaf litter. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mata_mata

question: A small fish swims right up to a mata mata turtle lying still on an Amazon riverbed. The turtle is slow and clumsy, yet in a heartbeat the fish is gone, swallowed whole before it can dart away. How does the turtle catch it?
answer: It sucks the fish in like a vacuum
choices: It sucks the fish in like a vacuum
It grabs the fish in powerful hooked jaws
It stuns the fish with an electric jolt
It snares the fish on a sticky tongue
context: Called gape-and-suck feeding: the mata mata throws its head forward and opens its mouth so fast that it creates a low-pressure vacuum, pulling the fish in on a surge of water. It then spits the water back out and gulps the fish down whole, because its mouth is built for sucking, not chewing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mata_mata

question: Pressed flat against the muddy bed of an Amazon river, a mata mata turtle lies hidden from the fish drifting above. Like any turtle, it must breathe air. How does it get a breath without lifting its head and giving itself away?
answer: Its long snout pokes the surface as a snorkel
choices: Its long snout pokes the surface as a snorkel
It absorbs oxygen straight through its skin
It gulps air bubbles trapped under the mud
It rises fully to the surface only at night
context: The mata mata's thin, tube-like snout works as a built-in snorkel: it can stay flat and concealed on the riverbed and just poke the tip up to the surface to breathe air, never lifting its head or revealing itself to nearby fish. Source: https://everywherewild.com/mata-mata-turtle/

question: In Amazon water so murky that it can barely see more than an inch past its snout, a mata mata turtle waits for fish. Ragged flaps of skin fringe its neck. Scientists first took them for camouflage, but now they suspect a second job. What else might the flaps be doing?
answer: Sensing the water ripples a swimming fish makes
choices: Sensing the water ripples a swimming fish makes
Releasing a scent that lures fish closer
Storing extra oxygen for long dives
Producing a faint glow to attract prey
context: Researchers think the neck fringes act as sensors, feeling the tiny water movements a passing fish creates, so the mata mata can time its suction strike even when the muddy water hides its prey from sight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mata_mata

question: Megalodon, the biggest shark that ever lived, cruised Earth's oceans about 15 million years ago. A single megalodon tooth was as big as a grown man's hand. About how long did this giant shark grow?
answer: As long as a school bus, around 50 to 60 feet
choices: As long as a school bus, around 50 to 60 feet
About the length of a canoe, around 15 feet
Roughly the size of a dolphin, around 8 feet
About as long as a bathtub, around 5 feet
context: Estimates put megalodon at roughly 15 to 18 meters, about 50 to 60 feet, longer than a school bus. A great white, by comparison, tops out near 20 feet. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History, 'Five Facts: Megalodon'; San Diego Natural History Museum.

question: In the movies, a huge megalodon, the biggest shark that ever lived, hides in the deep sea and waits to rise up and hunt again. What does real science say about megalodon today?
answer: It is completely extinct and lives nowhere on Earth
choices: It is completely extinct and lives nowhere on Earth
It survives in the deepest ocean trenches
A small population hides near Antarctica
It only comes up from the deep once a century
context: Despite the popular myth, megalodon is entirely extinct, not hiding in any deep-sea trench. The last of them died out millions of years ago. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History, 'Five Facts: Megalodon'; San Diego Natural History Museum.

question: Museum drawers around the world hold thousands of fossils of megalodon, a giant shark that swam the oceans for millions of years. Almost every one is the same body part; the rest of the shark almost never turned to stone. Which part is it?
answer: Its teeth
choices: Its teeth
Its jawbone
Its skull
Its backbone plates
context: Like all sharks, megalodon's skeleton was made of cartilage, which decomposes fast and almost never fossilizes. Only its teeth and a few calcified vertebrae survive, so its exact body shape is reconstructed and still debated. Source: San Diego Natural History Museum; Florida Museum of Natural History.

question: The biggest megalodon tooth anyone has dug up, a triangle nearly 7 inches long, would almost cover a man's open hand. About how big is a great white's tooth beside it?
answer: Around 2 inches, less than a third the size
choices: Around 2 inches, less than a third the size
Nearly the same, around 6 inches
A little bigger, around 8 inches
About half a foot, around 5 inches
context: A megalodon tooth can be as big as a human hand, close to 18 cm (about 7 inches), while a great white's teeth are only about 5 cm (roughly 2 inches). Those serrated megalodon teeth were built to slice and crush. Source: Natural History Museum London; Britannica.

question: Fossil hunters sometimes pull ancient whale bones out of the ground — bones that lay buried in mud for millions of years, back when megalodon still hunted the seas. Many of them are covered in huge, saw-edged bite marks. Every so often, a fossil whale bone turns up with a piece of the attacker itself still stuck fast in it. What has megalodon left behind, jammed into its meal's skeleton?
answer: A snapped-off tooth
choices: A snapped-off tooth
A shard of jawbone
A broken vertebra
A pointed fin spine
context: Whale vertebrae and flipper bones bearing large serrated bite marks show megalodon hunted big sea mammals, and some fossils preserve a broken-off megalodon tooth still embedded in the bone. Because a shark grows and sheds thousands of teeth in its life, a tooth was what it left behind, not a piece of its cartilage skeleton. Source: San Diego Natural History Museum; fossilguy.com megalodon diet article.

question: A whale rib from a North Carolina strip mine, 3 to 4 million years old, carries three megalodon tooth marks. Careful study of the bone around those marks told paleontologists something surprising about the moment after the attack. What did it reveal?
answer: The whale survived the bite and lived on for weeks
choices: The whale survived the bite and lived on for weeks
Megalodon dragged the whale to the deep
The whale died the instant the jaws closed
Two megalodons fought over the carcass
context: The whale grew new 'woven bone' over its wounds, proof it survived the bite before finally dying of infection weeks later. Paleontologist Stephen Godfrey said, 'The shark may have gone away with a mouthful, but it didn't kill the whale.' Source: Smithsonian Insider, 'Details of ancient shark attack preserved in fossil whale bone' (2011).

question: Unlike most sharks today, which simply take on the temperature of the water, megalodon kept part of its body about 13°F (7°C) warmer than the surrounding sea. A 2023 study read that warmth in the chemistry locked inside its fossil tooth enamel. What did the warmth do for the giant shark?
answer: It powered a huge, active hunting body
choices: It powered a huge, active hunting body
It let the shark glow to lure prey
It kept its eggs warm inside the mother
It helped it dive into freezing trenches
context: Being partly warm-bodied (regionally endothermic) helped fuel megalodon's enormous active body, but may have doomed it when the oceans later cooled. Source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, June 2023, 'Endothermic physiology of extinct megatooth sharks'.

question: Megalodon ruled the oceans for nearly 20 million years, then vanished about 3.6 million years ago in a perfect storm. Cooling seas shrank its warm coastal waters, and the whales it hunted moved to colder seas. One rising rival, smaller and more efficient, competed for the same prey and still hunts today. Which was it?
answer: The great white shark
choices: The great white shark
The killer whale
The tiger shark
The bull shark
context: As oceans cooled and whales migrated to colder water, the newly spreading great white, smaller and more efficient, competed for the same prey, part of the perfect storm that ended megalodon. Source: Natural History Museum London; San Diego Natural History Museum; extinctatlas.org.

question: Megalodon spent a century filed as a giant great white, since the two sharks share so many outward features. Then researchers looked closely at the fine serrations along megalodon's teeth and other traits, renamed it Otodus megalodon, and broke that old family tie. What did they conclude about the two sharks?
answer: They belong to separate lineages and only look alike from shared prey
choices: They belong to separate lineages and only look alike from shared prey
They are the same species caught at two different ages of growth
The great white is a shrunken, surviving population of megalodon
They interbred where their ranges met, blurring the line between them
context: The resemblance is convergent evolution: megalodon sits in the extinct genus Otodus (family Otodontidae), while the great white belongs to the mako-derived Carcharodon line, and both simply evolved for the same whale-hunting job. A key clue is in the teeth, megalodon bore much FINER serrations than the great white's coarse, steak-knife edge. This is why scientists dropped the old 'giant great white' idea and renamed it Otodus megalodon, though a minority of researchers still argue the differences are minor. Source: Wikipedia 'Megalodon,' classification section (genus reassignment to Otodus; Otodontidae-vs-Lamnidae convergent-evolution discussion), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalodon

question: Meganeura cruised above the coal swamps of the Carboniferous some 300 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs, on wings like a giant dragonfly's. Few insects have ever matched its size. How wide did its wings spread from tip to tip?
answer: About 70 centimeters, like a pigeon
choices: About 70 centimeters, like a pigeon
About 35 centimeters, like a robin
About 25 centimeters, like a large moth
About 15 centimeters, like a big dragonfly
context: Meganeura's wingspan reached roughly 65-75 cm (over 2 feet), about as wide as a pigeon's wings, making it among the largest insects that ever lived, flying over the Carboniferous coal swamps about 300 million years ago. Its name means 'large-veined,' after the dense network of veins in those huge wings. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meganeura

question: Over the steamy swamp forests of the Carboniferous, about 300 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs, flew Meganeura, a dragonfly-like insect and one of the biggest that ever lived. How did this giant make its living?
answer: Snatching other insects out of the air in flight
choices: Snatching other insects out of the air in flight
Filtering tiny plankton from swamp water
Grazing on fern fronds along the shore
Scavenging carcasses on the forest floor
context: Meganeura was a fast aerial predator, using large compound eyes and spiny, grasping legs to catch other insects in mid-flight - and it may even have hunted small early amphibians over the swamps. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/animals/meganeura/

question: David Grimaldi and Michael Engel coined a new name in 2005 for Meganeura and its giant look-alikes, which were not true dragonflies but extinct cousins of them. They wanted to end the confusion. What did they call such an insect?
answer: A griffinfly
choices: A griffinfly
A titanhawker
A paleodragon
A veinwing
context: Meganeura was NOT a true dragonfly; it belonged to an extinct cousin group. In 2005, David Grimaldi and Michael Engel coined 'griffinflies' for these giant look-alikes to stop people confusing them with modern dragonflies. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meganisoptera

question: Insect giants such as Meganeura grew in the coal-swamp forests of about 300 million years ago, among the largest insects of all time. Scientists think part of the reason lies in the air of that age, which differed from the air today. What was different about it?
answer: It held far more oxygen than today
choices: It held far more oxygen than today
It was far thinner and easier to fly through
It was dense with volcanic ash and warmth
It was thick with methane from the swamps
context: Geochemical models put Late Carboniferous oxygen around 30-35%, versus about 21% today. That oxygen-rich air let a much bigger insect body still get enough oxygen to survive; when the oxygen later fell, the giant insects vanished (though newer research argues the oxygen link is not the whole story). Source: https://spacedaily.com/t-the-largest-insects-that-ever-lived-were-dragonflies-with-wingspans-of-more-than-two-feet-grown-in-an-ancient-atmosphere-so-much-richer-in-oxygen-that-nothing-that-size-could-survive-in-the-air-we-b/

question: Alexander Kaiser's team X-rayed beetles of different sizes in 2007 to see how much room their breathing tubes take up. A beetle, like Meganeura, has no lungs, only a web of fine air tubes running through its body. As a beetle gets bigger, what do those tubes do?
answer: Take up a bigger and bigger share of its body
choices: Take up a bigger and bigger share of its body
Stay the same tiny fraction at every size
Shrink to a smaller share as the body grows
Stay a fixed number but each grows wider
context: Insects breathe through tiny air tubes called tracheae. A 2007 study by Kaiser and colleagues found that in beetles the tracheae take up a disproportionately larger share of the body as the insect grows - exactly what would be expected if oxygen supply were the ceiling on insect size. Because oxygen only diffuses over short distances, this caps how big an insect can get, so the oxygen-rich Carboniferous air let a bigger body still get enough oxygen. Source: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0611544104

question: A caterpillar munches leaves for weeks and does almost nothing else but grow. Then it stops eating, glues itself to a twig and seals itself inside a hard case, where the body comes apart and remakes itself into something entirely new. What winged adult crawls out?
answer: A butterfly
choices: A butterfly
A honeybee
A ladybird beetle
A housefly
