context: Caterpillar to butterfly is the classic first metamorphosis a kid learns. The caterpillar is the larva, whose only job is to eat and grow before the transformation begins. Source: Britannica, Metamorphosis (https://www.britannica.com/science/metamorphosis).

question: A small black tadpole wriggles among the weeds of a spring pond, with a wide finned tail and gills like a fish's. Over the next weeks it sprouts four legs and absorbs its own tail until the tail is gone. What has it turned into?
answer: A frog
choices: A frog
A newt
A salamander
A lizard
context: Tadpole to frog is the amphibian version everyone recognizes: a gilled, plant-eating water swimmer becomes a lunged, leaping adult. Source: Frontiers in Endocrinology, thyroid hormone in frog metamorphosis (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2019.00287/full).

question: When a butterfly caterpillar is ready to change, its own last skin hardens into a smooth, tough case that hangs from a twig by a silk pad. Many of these cases are dotted with shiny metallic flecks of gold or silver, and that glint gave the case its name, borrowed from an Ancient Greek word for gold. What is the case called?
answer: A chrysalis
choices: A chrysalis
A cocoon
A carapace
A husk
context: 'Chrysalis' comes from the Greek 'chrysos', meaning GOLD, for the gold-flecked sheen on many butterfly pupae. Source: Wikipedia, Pupa (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pupa); Florida Museum, Cocoon vs. Chrysalis (https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/exhibits/blog/butterfly-moment-cocoon-vs-chrysalis/).

question: A butterfly caterpillar sheds its skin one last time and hardens straight into a bare, smooth pupa. Most moth caterpillars go about it a little differently and take one extra step first. What extra step do they take?
answer: Spin a silk cocoon around themselves
choices: Spin a silk cocoon around themselves
Hang head-down from a silk pad
Pupate while still able to crawl
Overwinter as an egg instead of a pupa
context: Cocoon = moth, chrysalis = butterfly, as a rule. Most moths wrap themselves in a spun-silk cocoon; a typical butterfly forms a hard, bare chrysalis that hangs from just a small silk pad. Source: Florida Museum, Cocoon vs. Chrysalis (https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/exhibits/blog/butterfly-moment-cocoon-vs-chrysalis/).

question: Inside its hard case, a caterpillar floods itself with digestive enzymes that break down most of its own body from the inside out. It does not simply grow wings and stretch out its legs, and a case sliced open at just the right moment holds no tiny half-butterfly with folded wings. What oozes out instead?
answer: A thick yellowish soup
choices: A thick yellowish soup
A dry powder of scales
A ball of tangled silk
A pool of clear water
context: Inside the chrysalis the caterpillar dissolves most of its own body into a thick yellowish soup. Source: Scientific American, How Does a Caterpillar Turn into a Butterfly? (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/caterpillar-butterfly-metamorphosis-explainer/).

question: A caterpillar digests most of its own body inside its case, yet a whole winged adult is built back from what is left. A few clusters of cells survive the dissolving, one pre-grown for every adult part while the animal was still an egg. What are these survivor clusters called?
answer: Imaginal discs
choices: Imaginal discs
Stem nodes
Larval buds
Germ plates
context: Imaginal discs are tiny pre-formed cell clusters, a separate disc for wings, legs, eyes, and antennae, all grown back in the egg. They survive the soup and use it as raw material to build the adult. Source: Scientific American (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/caterpillar-butterfly-metamorphosis-explainer/).

question: Inside a fruit fly's pupal case, one small cluster of cells builds a single wing. When the maggot-like larva seals itself in, the cluster holds roughly 50 cells; by the time the adult fly emerges days later, it has multiplied enormously. About how many cells does the wing cluster hold by then?
answer: About 50,000
choices: About 50,000
About 5,000
About 500
About 200
context: A fruit fly's wing imaginal disc can start with about 50 cells and grow past 50,000 by the end of metamorphosis, feeding on the dissolved larva. Source: Scientific American (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/caterpillar-butterfly-metamorphosis-explainer/).

question: A young grasshopper hatches from its egg already looking like a tiny, wingless copy of its parents, nothing like the soft caterpillar a butterfly starts as. It feeds and grows for weeks. How does it reach its winged adult form?
answer: It molts into bigger bodies, growing wings bit by bit
choices: It molts into bigger bodies, growing wings bit by bit
It seals itself in a case and is rebuilt inside
It digs into the soil and grows wings while it sleeps
It molts just once and steps out full-grown
context: Incomplete metamorphosis (egg, nymph, adult) skips the pupa: the nymph molts bigger until it molts into a winged adult. Complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult) has the dramatic pupa in the middle. Source: Britannica, Holometabolous vs Hemimetabolous metamorphosis (https://www.britannica.com/science/holometabolous-metamorphosis).

question: A tadpole's tail is over twice as long as its trunk, yet within just a few days it vanishes. The tadpole is not cutting it off: a hormone triggers programmed cell death that dismantles the tail and recycles it. Which hormone drives the whole change from tadpole to adult?
answer: Thyroid hormone
choices: Thyroid hormone
Adrenaline
Growth hormone
Insulin
context: Thyroid hormone (thyroxine) runs the whole change: it resorbs the tail via programmed cell death, grows the hind legs first, builds lungs, and rebuilds the plant-eating gut into a meat-eater's. Source: Frontiers in Endocrinology (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2019.00287/full); PMC, Tail Resorption in Xenopus (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6426756/).

question: Martha Weiss and Doug Blackiston taught tobacco hornworm caterpillars to fear a certain smell by pairing it with a mild shock. The caterpillars then broke down inside their cases and rebuilt themselves as adult moths. When the two tested the moths with that smell, what happened?
answer: The moths still avoided the smell
choices: The moths still avoided the smell
The moths were drawn straight to it
The moths showed no reaction at all
The moths avoided every smell equally
context: Memory survived the soup: moths reared from trained caterpillars still avoided ethyl acetate, showing the rebuild preserves some of the larva's learning. Source: Weiss & Blackiston, PLOS ONE 2008 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2248710/); NPR (https://www.npr.org/2008/03/10/88031220/study-moths-can-remember-caterpillar-days).

question: A butterfly crawls out of its pupal case, but it cannot fly yet: its wings are small, damp and floppy, crumpled against its back like wet paper. For an hour or two it clings still to a twig while the wings swell to full size and stiffen into flight shape. How does it puff them up?
answer: It pumps its blood into the wing veins
choices: It pumps its blood into the wing veins
It bakes the wings dry in the sun
It coats them with fresh silk
It flaps them hard until they crack open
context: The butterfly pumps hemolymph (its blood) into the wing veins to inflate and harden them, then squirts out red meconium waste that looks alarmingly like blood but isn't. Source: Environmental Literacy Council (https://enviroliteracy.org/animals/what-is-the-red-liquid-when-a-butterfly-hatches/); Monarch Butterfly Garden (https://monarchbutterflygarden.net/monarch-butterflies-hatching-from-chrysalis/).

question: A caterpillar molts again and again, and each molt builds nothing but a bigger caterpillar. At every molt one chemical in its blood blocks the change; the switch to a pupa fires only once that chemical drops away in the last caterpillar stage. Which chemical is the brake?
answer: Juvenile hormone
choices: Juvenile hormone
Ecdysone
Eclosion hormone
Bursicon
context: Carroll Williams nicknamed juvenile hormone (JH) the 'status quo' hormone: as long as it is in the blood at a molt, the same trigger (ecdysone) that fires molting just builds another, bigger larva. Only when JH drains away can that trigger build a pupa instead. Williams found the abdomen of a male Cecropia silkmoth was so packed with JH that its yellow extract, the 'golden oil,' could force a pupa to make a SECOND pupa instead of an adult. So caterpillar-to-butterfly is really the switching-OFF of one hormone. Source: Grokipedia 'Juvenile hormone'; Frontiers/PMC7426621 'Rhodnius, Golden Oil, and Met: A History of Juvenile Hormone Research'; NCBI Bookshelf 'Metamorphosis: The Hormonal Reactivation of Development' (NBK9986).

question: A striped black, yellow and white monarch caterpillar hatches on a flowering plant in a meadow. It would starve before it would chew any other leaf nearby. Which plant is the only one it eats?
answer: Milkweed
choices: Milkweed
Clover
Nettle
Fennel
context: A female monarch lays her eggs directly on milkweed leaves, and the striped caterpillar eats nothing else. Source: Monarch Joint Venture, "Why Milkweed?" (monarchjointventure.org/monarch-biology/why-milkweed).

question: A monarch butterfly flaps across a meadow on bright orange wings veined in black. As a caterpillar it ate poisonous leaves, and their bitter chemicals live on in its body. What do its loud colors tell a bird?
answer: Do not eat me
choices: Do not eat me
Come find a mate
This is my territory
I am too fast to catch
context: Bright orange-and-black is a warning color (aposematism): it advertises that the monarch is loaded with milkweed heart-poison and foul to eat, training predators to leave it alone. Source: Monarch Watch Blog, "Monarch coloration, milkweed toxins, and predation by birds" (2020-11-05).

question: Monarch butterflies stream north each spring from central Mexico toward Canada, a trip of thousands of miles. An adult monarch usually lives only about a month, much too short a life to fly the whole way. How does the species make the journey?
answer: A relay across three or four short-lived generations
choices: A relay across three or four short-lived generations
One tireless butterfly flying nonstop for months
Each one rests for weeks between short hops
They drift the whole way on the wind while asleep
context: No single monarch flies the whole way north. Each butterfly lives about four weeks, so the spring journey is run as a relay: a butterfly flies partway, breeds, and its offspring carry on, taking three to four generations to reach Canada. Source: Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, "Multiple Monarch Generations Make 3000-Mile Migration Every Year."

question: The last monarchs to hatch each summer face the long flight south to central Mexico. Earlier monarchs live about a month, just long enough to mate, lay eggs and die. What is different about this final brood?
answer: It lives about eight months instead of one
choices: It lives about eight months instead of one
It grows twice as large as the others
It cannot eat and starves after mating
It flies only at night to save energy
context: This final brood is called the 'super generation' or 'Methuselah generation.' Instead of dying in a month, it lives roughly eight months and makes the long flight south. Source: Green Bay Botanical Garden, "The Magnificent Migration of Monarch Butterflies / super generation" (gbbg.org/monarch-migration-super-generation).

question: The super generation of monarchs flies up to 3,000 miles south each autumn into central Mexico, from Canada and the United States. None of them has been there before; last year's monarchs died months ago. Yet the newcomers do not settle just anywhere. Where does each one end up?
answer: The very same groves its great-great-grandparents left
choices: The very same groves its great-great-grandparents left
A warm coastal jungle far from any mountains
Wherever the wind happens to blow it that autumn
A brand-new forest each year, never the same twice
context: The super generation returns to the same oyamel fir groves in central Mexico that its great-great-grandparents departed the spring before, a place it has never itself been. Source: Interesting Facts, "Some monarch butterflies migrate 3,000 miles"; NC State Extension Forestry, "From Mexico's Oyamel Fir Forests."

question: A monarch caterpillar munches for weeks on the leaves of its food plant, which are laced with cardenolide, a heart poison that makes almost every animal sick or worse. The caterpillar never gets hurt. What does it do with the poison it swallows?
answer: Stores it in its body to stay poisonous for life
choices: Stores it in its body to stay poisonous for life
Breaks it down into harmless sugar for energy
Spits it back onto the leaf to warn other insects
Sweats it out through its skin within a day
context: The caterpillar keeps the milkweed toxins (cardiac glycosides, called cardenolides) inside its own body and holds them right through metamorphosis, so both the caterpillar and the adult butterfly are poisonous and foul-tasting. Source: Earth.com, "Monarch caterpillars turn milkweed toxin into a survival tool"; Monarch Watch Blog (2020-11-05).

question: A young blue jay in a North American forest swallows a monarch butterfly whole, though nothing has taught it that monarchs are dangerous. Minutes later it throws the meal back up, sickened by the poison. What does the jay do whenever it sees that orange-and-black pattern again?
answer: Refuses to touch a monarch ever again
choices: Refuses to touch a monarch ever again
Eats only the wings and leaves the body
Attacks every orange butterfly on sight
Learns to strip the poison out first
context: One bad experience is enough: the jay associates the orange-and-black pattern with the sickening heart-poison and avoids monarchs from then on. That learned avoidance is exactly what the warning color exists to teach. Source: Monarch Watch Blog, "Monarch coloration, milkweed toxins, and predation by birds" (2020-11-05).

question: A migrating monarch steers south by the sun, but the sun slides across the sky all day, so the butterfly needs a body clock to keep correcting its course. That clock is not in its brain. Without which body part does the monarch lose its bearings entirely?
answer: Its antennae
choices: Its antennae
Its front legs
Its wing scales
Its tail tip
context: The monarch uses a time-compensated sun compass, and the circadian clock that corrects for the sun's movement sits in the antennae, not the brain. Remove the antennae and the butterfly can no longer orient. Source: Merlin et al., Science 325:1700 (2009), "Antennal Circadian Clocks Coordinate Sun Compass Orientation in Migratory Monarch Butterflies."

question: The viceroy butterfly wears the monarch's orange-and-black uniform. For years scientists called it a harmless faker cashing in on the monarch's reputation. In 1991 David Ritland and Lincoln Brower tested it and overturned that story. What did they find?
answer: The viceroy tastes just as bad as the monarch
choices: The viceroy tastes just as bad as the monarch
The viceroy is even more poisonous than the monarch
Birds can tell the two apart with ease
The viceroy only copies females, never males
context: The viceroy was long taught as a Batesian mimic, a harmless copy borrowing the monarch's protection. Ritland and Brower showed the viceroy is itself distasteful, so the two are really Mullerian mimics: two bad-tasting insects sharing one warning uniform. The viceroy caterpillar feeds on willow and poplar, whose bitter salicylic acid (the aspirin family) helps make it taste bad too. Source: Ritland & Brower, Nature 350:497 (1991), "The viceroy butterfly is not a batesian mimic."

question: Ken Brugger, a volunteer, phoned Fred and Norah Urquhart from Mexico on the night of January 9, 1975. For years the two researchers had chased one mystery: where North America's monarchs vanish to each winter. What had Brugger found?
answer: Millions of monarchs clustered on mountain evergreens
choices: Millions of monarchs clustered on mountain evergreens
A single tagged butterfly from their own garden
That the monarchs had flown on to South America
Empty groves where the monarchs had all died
context: Answering a newspaper appeal from the Urquharts, engineer Ken Brugger located the long-hidden overwintering colony: 'We have located the colony! We have found them, millions of Monarchs, in evergreens beside a mountain clearing.' Source: Great Parks blog, "Monarch Tagging: How Did We Get Here"; Beauty on the Wing, "DISCOVERED: The Monarchs' Mexican Haven"; National Geographic, August 1976.

question: At the Mexican colonies, two birds crack the monarch's heart-poison armor and gorge on the clustered butterflies, each solving the poison problem its own way. The black-backed oriole slits each monarch open and eats only the least-toxic parts. Its neighbor the black-headed grosbeak needs no such trick. What lets the grosbeak feast so freely?
answer: Its body is genetically resistant to the poison
choices: Its body is genetically resistant to the poison
Its stomach acid destroys the poison as it eats
It eats only monarchs too young to be toxic
It drinks from a mineral spring to purge the poison
context: Black-backed orioles and black-headed grosbeaks together kill an average of about 15,000 monarchs a day, over two million across one winter, roughly 9% of the colony. The grosbeak is genetically resistant to the cardenolides, so it can swallow monarchs whole; the oriole, lacking that resistance, instead learned to gut the butterfly and eat only the least-toxic parts. Source: Fink & Brower, Nature 291:67 (1981), "Birds can overcome the cardenolide defence of monarch butterflies in Mexico"; Brower & Calvert, Evolution 39(4):852 (1985).

question: A migrating monarch holds its southward course even on a solid overcast day, when the sun it normally steers by is hidden for hours. Scientists put butterflies in a flight simulator and reversed an invisible force around them, watching the monarchs turn to match. What backup were the monarchs relying on?
answer: A second compass that reads Earth’s magnetic field
choices: A second compass that reads Earth’s magnetic field
A memory of the wind direction from the day before
A scent trail laid down by monarchs ahead of them
A count of the days ticking on their inner clock
context: The monarch carries two navigation systems. Beyond the antennal sun-compass, a 2014 study by Patrick Guerra, Robert Gegear, and Steven Reppert put migrating monarchs in a flight simulator with an artificial magnetic field and showed they read Earth's field to steer south, specifically its inclination, the tilt of the field lines, not just its direction. Reverse the field's inclination and the butterflies flip to flying north. The light-sensing magnetosensors sit in the antennae and only work in ultraviolet-A and blue light (roughly 380 to 420 nanometers). This lets a monarch hold its heading even when clouds hide the sun. Source: Guerra, Gegear & Reppert, 'A magnetic compass aids monarch butterfly migration,' Nature Communications (2014), https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms5164 ; PubMed https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24960099/

question: Geneticists went hunting for what lets a monarch caterpillar eat a heart poison that kills by jamming the sodium-potassium pump, a tiny protein every animal cell must run to stay alive. The monarch's own pump keeps working, and the answer turned out to be very small. What was it?
answer: Three tiny changes to one protein’s shape
choices: Three tiny changes to one protein’s shape
A whole extra copy of the gene for the pump
A thick gut lining that blocks the poison
A stomach microbe that digests the poison first
context: Milkweed cardenolides normally kill by jamming the sodium-potassium pump (Na+/K+-ATPase) that keeps cells alive. In monarchs, substitutions at just three sites in the pump's alpha subunit (positions 111, 119, and 122) block the toxin from binding. In a 2019 Nature study, Karageorgi et al. in Noah Whiteman's lab at UC Berkeley used CRISPR base-editing to install these same three mutations into ordinary fruit flies, and the edited flies became about a thousand times more resistant to the toxin, as insensitive as a monarch. It is one of the clearest demonstrations that a complex adaptation can rest on a tiny handful of specific mutations. (The other choices are all real anti-toxin strategies other animals use, gene duplication, physical gut barriers, and detox by gut microbes, but they are not how the monarch does it.) Source: Karageorgi et al., 'Genome editing retraces the evolution of toxin resistance in the monarch butterfly,' Nature (Oct 2019), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1610-8 ; full text https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7039281/

question: The mosasaur ruled the oceans at the very end of the age of dinosaurs, more than 66 million years ago. The sharp-toothed giant grew to about forty feet long and hunted fish and squid in shallow inland seas, yet despite the -saur in its name it was no dinosaur. What kind of animal was it?
answer: A lizard that had gone to sea
choices: A lizard that had gone to sea
A whale-like early mammal
A giant crocodile
A long-necked plesiosaur
context: A mosasaur belonged to Squamata, the group that today holds monitor lizards (like the Komodo dragon) and snakes. Its closest living relatives are monitors and snakes -- a true lizard, not a dinosaur, not a marine mammal. Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-is-a-mosasaur.html ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosasaurus

question: A mosasaur swam the seas of the Late Cretaceous about 80 million years ago, built for life in the open ocean. Its ancestors walked the land on four clawed feet. What did each of its four limbs become?
answer: Paddles for swimming
choices: Paddles for swimming
Stubby legs for crawling ashore
Tiny stubs it no longer used
Grasping hands for seizing prey
context: A mosasaur's four limbs were shaped into paddles, and a powerful tail drove it forward -- it was fully built for life in open water rather than crawling on land. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosasaurus ; https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-is-a-mosasaur.html

question: When a mosasaur seized a slick fish or a slippery squid, the prey thrashed to break free of its jaws. A second row of teeth stopped it cold. Where in the mosasaur's mouth did that second row sit?
answer: On the roof of its mouth
choices: On the roof of its mouth
Ringed around its lips
Set deep in its throat
Hidden under its tongue
context: These pterygoid teeth sat on the palate; the mosasaur used them to grip slippery prey and ratchet it back down the throat so it could not wriggle free. This double-row palate is one of the traits linking mosasaurs to snakes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosasaurus ; https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-is-a-mosasaur.html

question: A Prognathodon mosasaur from Harrana in Jordan, described in 2013, was fossilized with the soft outline of its tail still in the rock. Mosasaurs had long been pictured as sluggish, eel-like swimmers whose tails tapered to a point. What shape did this tail end in?
answer: A crescent fin like a shark's
choices: A crescent fin like a shark's
A flat paddle like a beaver's
A broad rudder-like ridge
A fan of stiff spines
context: The Jordanian fossil showed the tail ended in a crescent-shaped fluke, like a shark's tail turned upside down (the big lobe pointing down). It meant mosasaurs were fast pelagic swimmers, not sluggish eel-like ones. Source: https://phys.org/news/2013-09-mosasaur-fossil-early-lizards-tails.html ; https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms3423

question: Fossil hunters have dug up newborn Clidastes mosasaurs whose jawbones are barely 2 centimeters long, about the size of a paperclip. The kind of rock they lie in tells where a young mosasaur spent the most dangerous first days of its life. Where did a mosasaur begin life?
answer: Born live out in the open sea
choices: Born live out in the open sea
Born live in sheltered coastal shallows
Hatched from eggs laid ashore like a turtle
Hatched from eggs in a nest on the seafloor
context: Fossil newborns turn up alongside deep-water squid and fish, in rock laid down far out over open water -- showing mosasaurs gave live birth out in the open ocean and never came ashore (Daniel Field and colleagues, 2015). Source: https://insider.si.edu/2015/05/fossil-proves-prehistoric-reptile-gave-birth-in-open-ocean/ ; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/baby-mosasaurs-were-born-out-at-sea

question: A Tylosaurus lay fossilized in the seabed rock of South Dakota, laid down by an ancient sea that once split North America in two. Inside its ribs were its last meals: a diving seabird, a bony fish and one more animal that startled the scientists who found it. What was the third?
answer: Another, smaller mosasaur
choices: Another, smaller mosasaur
A spiny sea urchin
A giant swimming clam
A leathery sea turtle
context: The Tylosaurus proriger from the Pierre Shale had swallowed a Hesperornis (a flightless diving bird), a Bananogmius fish, AND a mosasaur about 2 m long -- proof it was an apex generalist that ate seabirds and even its own kind, not just fish. Another Tylosaurus was fossilized with a 2.5 m plesiosaur (Dolichorhynchops) half-digested inside it, a snapshot of one giant marine reptile swallowing another whole. Source: Everhart / Oceans of Kansas, Tylosaurus stomach contents (oceansofkansas.com/Tylo-prey.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tylosaurus).

question: The deep-diving mosasaurs Platecarpus and Tylosaurus left a strange record in their vertebrae: patches of dead bone, absent from the shallow-water Clidastes. The pattern tracks diving depth so exactly that it exposes the animals as imperfect divers. What had scarred their bones?
answer: Decompression sickness, the bends
choices: Decompression sickness, the bends
A slow-spreading bone cancer
Old healed bite wounds
A crippling vitamin shortage
context: Rothschild & Martin (1987) found avascular necrosis -- bone killed by nitrogen bubbles forming during fast ascents -- in 5 to 66 percent of the vertebrae of deep-diving Platecarpus and Tylosaurus, but none in the shallow-water Clidastes. That split, tracking presumed diving depth, is hard skeletal proof that some mosasaurs dived deep and often enough to injure their own bones -- and, ironically, that they were NOT perfectly adapted deep divers. Source: Rothschild & Martin 1987, Science 236:75-77 (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17759208/).

question: A snake on smooth glass throws its usual side-to-side S-curves and goes almost nowhere, sliding in place. On rough ground with bumps, pebbles and edges, the same S-waves send it gliding fast. What are the S-waves doing against the ground?
answer: Pushing sideways against bumps and edges to shove itself forward
choices: Pushing sideways against bumps and edges to shove itself forward
Gripping the ground with tiny hooked claws along its belly
Rippling the belly skin forward in slow straight-line waves
Bouncing off the surface to fling its body ahead
context: This is lateral undulation (serpentine motion), the S-wave every snake makes. The back edges of the belly scales catch on rocks, twigs, and bumps and push sideways to drive the body forward — which is why a frictionless surface leaves the snake stranded, sliding in place with nothing to push against. Source: The Mechanics of Slithering Locomotion, PNAS (Hu, Nirody, Scott, Shelley) — https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0812533106

question: A big python, which can reach 20 feet, creeps across open ground toward a resting deer. It makes none of the sideways S-curves most snakes use, sliding forward in one dead-straight line, smooth and quiet as a moving log. How does it move so straight?
answer: It pulls its belly skin forward, anchors it and glides over it
choices: It pulls its belly skin forward, anchors it and glides over it
It throws its body into sideways loops that only touch at two points
It bunches into tight folds, then unfolds them like a squeezebox
It flattens into a wide ribbon and rides its own momentum
context: This is rectilinear locomotion. The snake pulls its loose belly skin forward in slow waves, anchors the belly scales against the ground, and lets the ribcage and body glide over the anchored skin — no telltale wriggle. That silent straight-line creep is how a large constrictor stalks prey almost invisibly. Source: ScienceDaily / University of Cincinnati (Jayne & Newman, 2018) — https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/01/180112132922.htm

question: Across the scorching dunes of the American Southwest, a sidewinder rattlesnake travels in strange sideways loops, its head pointed where it is going while its body seems to roll over the loose, hot sand. What is unusual about how its body meets the sand?
answer: Only two short stretches touch the sand; the rest is lifted
choices: Only two short stretches touch the sand; the rest is lifted
Its whole belly stays pressed flat against the sand
It pushes off the sand with its tail tip alone
It rolls along on its side like a log
context: The sidewinder rattlesnake (Crotalus cerastes) throws loops of its body sideways so that at any instant only two short segments press on the ground — the rest is held in the air, minimizing contact with the burning loose sand. Sources: Britannica, Sidewinder — https://www.britannica.com/animal/sidewinder ; Jayne, What Defines Different Modes of Snake Locomotion (ICB 2020) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7391877/

question: A tracker on a Mojave dune finds a row of separate curved prints, each shaped like the letter J, left by a sidewinder rattlesnake looping sideways. Without ever seeing the snake, the tracker can read which way it was heading. What about each J gives the direction away?
answer: Each J-shaped mark hooks toward the way the snake was traveling
choices: Each J-shaped mark hooks toward the way the snake was traveling
The open mouth of each J faces the way the snake was traveling
The deeper end of each print shows where the heavier head pressed down
A faint drag-line links the prints and trails off behind the snake
context: A sidewinder's trail is a row of separate, disconnected J-shaped marks, and each hook points the way the snake was traveling — so even the empty tracks reveal its heading. (The prints stay disconnected because only two parts of the body touch down at a time, but it's the hook of the J that gives away the direction.) Sources: Wikipedia, Crotalus cerastes — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crotalus_cerastes ; Britannica — https://www.britannica.com/animal/sidewinder

question: A smooth vertical pole stands in a laboratory, with no bumps for a climbing snake to catch. If the snake tries its ordinary side-to-side slither, it slides straight back down, yet it hauls itself to the top by a slow squeeze-and-shove called concertina motion. What does its body do?
answer: Wedges in tight bends, pushes its front up, then drags the rest after
choices: Wedges in tight bends, pushes its front up, then drags the rest after
Rips its belly skin forward in waves and suctions itself flat to the metal
Whips into fast S-curves and rides the ripples straight upward
Splays its ribs into a wide ribbon and shimmies up on the flat
context: This is concertina locomotion, used to climb smooth poles or thread narrow tunnels: the snake bunches into tight bends to anchor itself, extends the front, re-anchors, and drags the back up — folding and unfolding like a squeezebox. There's nothing to push sideways against on a smooth pole, so this wedge-and-haul grip is the usual way up — which is why it's slow and tiring, the snake keeping a firm anchor with part of its body the entire climb. Sources: Jayne, What Defines Different Modes of Snake Locomotion (ICB 2020) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7391877/ ; Wikipedia, Concertina movement — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concertina_movement

question: A sidewinder lies half-buried in the loose sand of the American Southwest, waiting motionless for prey to wander past. Above each eye juts a pointed scale like a tiny horn, and these earn it its other name, the horned rattlesnake. What are the two horns thought to do for it?
answer: Shade its eyes and keep drifting sand off them
choices: Shade its eyes and keep drifting sand off them
Detect the body heat of approaching prey in the dark
Rattle together to add to its warning sound
Help it dig down into the loose sand to hide
context: The sidewinder is also called the 'horned rattlesnake' for its raised supraocular scales -- little horns above each eye. They may shade the eyes or keep sand from drifting over them while the snake lies almost buried; another idea is that they shield the eyes when the snake pushes into rodent burrows. Source: Wikipedia, Crotalus cerastes -- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crotalus_cerastes

question: A legless animal slides through the grass, pauses, and blinks its eyes. A small ear opening shows on the side of its head, just behind the eye. A true snake can do neither of those things. What is this animal?
answer: A legless lizard, such as a glass lizard
choices: A legless lizard, such as a glass lizard
A worm lizard, a burrowing amphisbaenian
A caecilian, a limbless burrowing amphibian
An eel that has crawled up out of the water
context: A 'snake' that can blink or has a visible ear-hole is really a legless lizard, like a glass lizard (Ophisaurus). Snakes have no eyelids — their eyes are sealed under a clear scale, the brille — and no external ears, so neither trait belongs to a true snake. Legless lizards also carry most of their length in the tail, and many can drop that tail to escape a predator, which no snake can do. Source: Mental Floss, 5 Slithering Differences Between Snakes and Legless Lizards — https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/85553/5-slithering-differences-between-snakes-and-legless-lizards

question: Belly scales called scutes line the underside of a gliding snake, overlapping like roof tiles, and turn each push of its muscles into forward travel instead of a wasted wiggle. Which way do the scutes slide most freely against the ground?
answer: Forward — they slip ahead but catch when dragged back or sideways
choices: Forward — they slip ahead but catch when dragged back or sideways
Backward — they slip behind but catch when pushed ahead
Sideways — they slip across but catch along the body's length
Every way equally — the scutes have no preferred direction at all
context: A snake's belly scales grip better in one direction than the other — like the treads on a tire. Friction is low sliding forward but high sliding backward or sideways: the trailing edges catch on tiny bumps to push while the leading edges slip forward almost freely. That one-way grip is what turns a wriggle into forward travel. Sources: Snakes move their scales to increase friction (Marvi & Hu); The Mechanics of Slithering Locomotion, PNAS — https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0812533106

question: An invasive brown tree snake on Guam climbed a smooth, snake-proof baffle in 2021 while researchers filmed it. For nearly a century biologists had counted just four ways for a snake to move; this was a fifth. How did it climb?
answer: Looping once around the pole and shifting bends to inch up
choices: Looping once around the pole and shifting bends to inch up
Gripping with a sticky pad newly found on the tip of its tail
Leaping upward in short hops off its coiled lower body
Rippling its belly skin to suction itself to the metal
context: This is 'lasso locomotion,' the surprising fifth mode discovered in 2021. The brown tree snake (Boiga irregularis) wraps its body into a single loop — a lasso — around a pole, then shifts tiny bends inside that loop upward to inch up a cylinder it otherwise couldn't climb. It was caught on camera because invasive brown tree snakes, accidentally brought to Guam around 1950, had wiped out most of the island's forest birds, and researchers filming snake-proof baffles on nest-box poles saw the snakes lasso straight up them. Bruce Jayne said the snake advances 'by shifting the location of each bend.' Source: Colorado State University / Warner College (Savidge, Jayne, Seibert; Current Biology 2021) — https://warnercnr.source.colostate.edu/scientists-discover-bizarre-new-mode-of-snake-locomotion/

question: Marvi, Hu and their colleagues filmed corn snakes and found that a snake's belly grip is not fixed: a snake that is awake and gripping hard has roughly double the friction of a limp, unconscious one. What are its belly muscles doing to earn that extra bite?
answer: Tilting each belly scale up on edge to dig its rear rim into the ground
choices: Tilting each belly scale up on edge to dig its rear rim into the ground
Sweating a sticky film from glands between the scales to glue itself down
Inflating the whole underside with air to press more scale area onto the ground
Curling the scale tips into tiny hooks that latch onto grit and roots
context: Marvi, Hu and colleagues showed corn snakes contract their belly muscles to lift and tilt the ventral scales, raising each scale's angle of attack against the ground — a conscious, actively-scaling snake roughly doubles its friction coefficient over an unconscious one whose scales lie flat. This is the deeper mechanism under the one-way grip of the belly scutes: the grip is not fixed hardware but muscle-tuned moment to moment, letting one section anchor while another slides. Engineers copied it into 'Scalybot,' whose individually-servoed belly scales climbed foam inclines up to 45 degrees, matching a real corn snake. Source: Marvi, Hu et al. 2016, 'Snakes move their scales to increase friction' (Biotribology) — https://hu.gatech.edu/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/Hu16SnakeTribo.pdf ; corroborated by newatlas.com Scalybot coverage and researchgate.net/publication/267491606.

question: A python embryo starts building tiny hindlimbs, buds and even a scrap of leg skeleton, then quits partway, leaving only the little spurs near its hips that an adult python keeps. Its limb gene, Sonic Hedgehog, still exists; only the switch that should turn it on in the limb bud is broken. What did Leal and Cohn argue happened to snake legs over deep time?
answer: Legs were lost, partly came back in some snakes, then were lost again
choices: Legs were lost, partly came back in some snakes, then were lost again
Legs shrank once, steadily and for good, as early snakes took to burrowing
A single ancestor lost all four at once, and no snake lineage ever varied again
Only the hindlimbs were ever reduced; snake forelimbs were lost far earlier
context: The Sonic hedgehog gene (SHH) drives limb growth in vertebrates, switched on in the limb bud by a regulatory enhancer called the ZRS. In snakes the ZRS is degraded — studies point to a snake-specific deletion (~17 base pairs) that knocks out essential transcription-factor binding sites — so python embryos still START a hindlimb, even a transient partial leg skeleton, before SHH fizzles and the limb aborts, leaving only vestigial pelvic spurs. Because the developmental program is only switched off, never erased, Leal and Cohn argued legs were lost and RE-ACQUIRED at least once across snake evolution. Fossils like four-limbed Tetrapodophis and hindlimb-only Najash (roughly 95–120 million years old) trace the reduction. This 're-emergence' reading is a genuine and still-debated claim, not settled textbook fact. Source: Leal & Cohn 2016, Current Biology, 'Loss and Re-emergence of Legs in Snakes by Modular Evolution of Sonic hedgehog and HOXD Enhancers' — pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27773569 ; corroborated via nature.com/articles/nrg.2016.149 and pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5484524.

question: The tide drains out of a tropical mangrove swamp, and a finger-length fish stays behind on the glistening mud. It mostly does not swim; it crawls and hops across the open flat. What is this animal?
answer: A mudskipper
choices: A mudskipper
A jellyfish
A sea urchin
A giant clam
context: The mudskipper is a fish, but it spends most of its life out of water, hauling itself across tidal mudflats and mangrove swamps instead of swimming. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudskipper

question: A mudskipper left behind on the wet mud of a tropical tide flat does not flop about helplessly. It moves steadily across the open flat, chasing bugs and guarding its patch. How does the little fish get around out of the water?
answer: It plants its two pectoral fins like little arms and hauls itself forward
choices: It plants its two pectoral fins like little arms and hauls itself forward
It wriggles from side to side like a snake
It inches along by bunching up like a caterpillar
It rolls its whole body sideways down the slope
context: A mudskipper 'walks' by planting its two muscular pectoral fins like little arms or crutches and hauling its body forward across the mud. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/articles/this-fish-walks-on-land-and-breathes-through-its-skin/

question: When a finger-length mudskipper needs to cover ground fast on its mudflat, it flexes and shoves hard with its tail, flinging its whole body up and forward in one hopping leap. Roughly how far can a single leap carry it?
answer: About 61 centimeters, some two feet
choices: About 61 centimeters, some two feet
About one centimeter, a fingertip
About 5 meters, most of a bus
About 20 meters, a swimming pool
context: By suddenly flexing and pushing with its tail, the mudskipper flings itself into a leap that can cover up to about 61 centimeters (2 feet) across the mud. This tail-flick skip is what gives the fish its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudskipper

question: Out on an open tropical mudflat, a mudskipper sits for hours in the sun, out of the water. Its fish gills work poorly in the air, so, like a frog on land, it takes in air another way. Through which parts of its body does it breathe out of the water?
answer: Through its moist skin and the wet lining of its mouth
choices: Through its moist skin and the wet lining of its mouth
Through two blowholes on its back
Through hollow spines along its spine
Through a snorkel-tube on its head
context: A mudskipper breathes air through its moist skin and through the wet lining of its mouth and throat, the way a frog does, rather than only through gills. This is called cutaneous and buccal respiration. Source: https://science.psu.edu/news/blinking-fish-reveals-clues-how-our-ancestors-evolved-water-land

question: Before a long crawl across open mud, a mudskipper takes a big mouthful and packs its enlarged gill chambers until its cheeks bulge out on both sides of its head. Like a scuba diver with a tank, it carries its own supply. What is stored in those puffed-out cheeks?
answer: A supply of water and air
choices: A supply of water and air
A clutch of its own eggs
A wad of sticky mud for building
A store of crushed shellfish
context: The mudskipper carries a mouthful of water and air in its enlarged gill chambers on land, like a built-in scuba tank. If those gills ever dry out, it can no longer take in oxygen. Source: https://oceanconservancy.org/blog/2022/05/12/5-facts-mudskippers/

question: A male mudskipper on the open mud rears up and drops down again and again, flares his back fin, drums his tail and hurls himself high into the air. The wild show warns a rival male away. Who else is it aimed at?
answer: A female he is trying to impress
choices: A female he is trying to impress
A flock of seabirds he is scaring off
A cloud of biting insects overhead
A change in the weather he is answering
context: Male mudskippers defend their mud territory with dramatic push-up displays, flaring the dorsal fin, beating the tail, and leaping high into the air to warn off rivals AND impress females. The same show does double duty as courtship. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Mudskipper

question: On a tidal mudflat in tropical Asia, a male mudskipper digs a burrow whose domed roof traps a pocket of air, then rises to the surface again and again to gulp air for the chamber where his eggs will develop. Karen Martin counted his trips to fill that first bubble. Roughly how many mouthfuls did it take?
answer: About 100 mouthfuls
choices: About 100 mouthfuls
About 3 mouthfuls
About 10,000 mouthfuls
About one big gulp
context: A male digs a burrow with a domed, air-trapping ceiling and gulps mouthful after mouthful of air at the surface to stock the chamber with oxygen for his eggs; Karen Martin found a male may take roughly 100 mouthfuls to build that first air bubble. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/mudskipper-builds-ideal-nest-for-his-offspring

question: A mudskipper father has spent days keeping his underground burrow stocked with air for his eggs, gulping mouthful after mouthful to keep the pocket full. Then he watches the rising tide, and at just the right moment he does one thing that lets the eggs hatch and the young swim out to sea. What does he do?
answer: Gulps the air back out and lets water flood the burrow
choices: Gulps the air back out and lets water flood the burrow
Carries each egg to the sea in his mouth
Seals the burrow shut and abandons it
Fans fresh air across the eggs until they dry
context: After stocking the burrow with air, the father tracks the tide, then deliberately gulps the air OUT of the burrow and lets water flood in at just the right moment so the eggs hatch and the larvae can swim away. Scientist Karen Martin called the male 'really a very good papa.' Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/mudskipper-builds-ideal-nest-for-his-offspring

question: A wolf pack closes in on a herd of shaggy musk oxen on the open Arctic tundra. The musk oxen overheat quickly in a long chase, so running is no escape. What do the grown musk oxen do instead?
answer: Wheel into a tight ring, horns facing outward, calves hidden inside
choices: Wheel into a tight ring, horns facing outward, calves hidden inside
Split up and sprint in every direction to confuse the pack
Climb the nearest rocky slope to a ledge out of reach
Dive into a river and swim to the far bank together
context: Musk oxen (Ovibos moschatus) form a defensive ring: adults face outward in a phalanx of heads and horns while the calves are pressed against their mothers in the center. Against a single wolf they form a line instead of a ring. Standing their ground works because they can neither outrun nor out-endure their predators. Source: NPS, Gates of the Arctic — Circle Defense (nps.gov/gaar/learn/nature/muskox-circle-defense.htm).

question: A musk ox grazes the open tundra through winters colder than forty below. Under its long outer coat grows a soft undercoat called qiviut, shed in one great moult each spring, and qiviut is what keeps it warm. How does qiviut compare with sheep's wool?
answer: About eight times warmer, and it won't shrink in water at any temperature
choices: About eight times warmer, and it won't shrink in water at any temperature
About the same warmth, but far more waterproof against snow
Slightly cooler, but it dries almost instantly after a soaking
Half as warm, but four times as strong and stiff
context: Qiviut (an Inuit word) is about eight times warmer than sheep's wool and finer than cashmere — roughly 18 micrometres versus cashmere's ~19 — and unlike wool it does not shrink in water at any temperature. The musk ox sheds it in one synchronized spring moult. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiviut; Textile School qiviut article.

question: Two musk ox bulls fight for a herd of cows in the autumn rut, ramming heads on the Arctic tundra. Each backs off up to fifty yards, charges at close to thirty-five miles an hour and slams his forehead into the other's, again and again. What takes the blow, right above each bull's brain?
answer: About 4 inches of solid horn boss over 3 inches of skull bone
choices: About 4 inches of solid horn boss over 3 inches of skull bone
A thick pad of muscle that flexes to absorb the shock
A hollow air-filled sinus that collapses and springs back
A ridge of cartilage running between the two horns
context: A bull's forehead is armored for the collisions: about 4 inches of solid horn boss lies over 3 inches of skull bone, directly above the brain at the point of impact. Bulls repeat the head-on smash up to 20 times — the crack can be heard a mile away on a calm day — until one bull flees. Source: Alaska Dept. of Fish and Game, Muskox Species Profile (adfg.alaska.gov/index.cfm?adfg=muskox.main).

question: Herds of musk oxen once ranged across Europe, Asia and North America in the ice ages, alongside woolly mammoths and sabre-toothed cats. Then, at the end of the last ice age, great die-offs took the mammoth and the sabre-tooth. What became of the musk ox?
answer: It endured, hanging on today as scattered herds in Greenland and Arctic Canada
choices: It endured, hanging on today as scattered herds in Greenland and Arctic Canada
It vanished from the wild and survives only in zoos and parks
It shrank to a dwarf form found only on remote Arctic islands
It moved south and now lives in the forests below the tundra
context: The musk ox lived alongside mammoths and sabre-toothed cats and endured the ice-age extinctions that killed the mammoth. Its wild herds survived only in Greenland and the Canadian Arctic, and people have since moved herds to Alaska, Norway and Siberia. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muskox ; pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0907189107

question: A naked mole-rat, wrinkled, nearly hairless and sausage-sized, spends its whole life digging tunnels through the packed earth of East Africa. Its family life is the most extreme of any mammal known. How does it live?
answer: like an ant or termite colony, ruled by one breeding queen
choices: like an ant or termite colony, ruled by one breeding queen
in mated pairs that share a burrow for life
alone, meeting others only to mate
in loose herds that graze the surface at night
context: The naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber) is eusocial: a single breeding queen rules while the rest are sterile workers who dig, gather food, and raise her pups for life. It is the most extreme case of eusociality known in any mammal. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, Naked mole-rat (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/naked-mole-rat).

question: Naked mole-rats deep under East Africa attack any stranger with the wrong smell. To carry the family scent, each one heads for the dirtiest room in the burrow and does one thing there on purpose. What does it do?
answer: it rolls around in the communal toilet chamber
choices: it rolls around in the communal toilet chamber
it licks the queen's fur clean each morning
it rubs noses with every rat it passes
it eats a pinch of soil from every tunnel
context: Naked mole-rats roll and wallow in their colony's communal latrine so every member picks up the same shared scent; a rat carrying the wrong colony smell is treated as an intruder and attacked. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo; O'Riain & Jarvis, colony odour studies.

question: A female naked mole-rat is not born a queen; she wins her throne in vicious fights with her sisters. Once she starts having pups, her body changes so that she can carry more and more young at once. What happens to her body?
answer: her backbone stretches, so her body grows longer
choices: her backbone stretches, so her body grows longer
she grows a thick protective layer of fur
her legs shorten so she can wedge into the nursery
her teeth fuse into a single digging blade
context: The queen's lumbar vertebrae stretch and lengthen with each pregnancy, so her whole body grows longer over time. A large queen can carry as many as 30 pups in a single litter. Source: 'Growing out of a caste', Journal of Experimental Biology (journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/210/2/261); San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance.

question: Through soil packed hard enough to break a shovel, a naked mole-rat bites its tunnels with its big front teeth, yet it never gets a mouthful of dirt. Where do its front teeth sit?
answer: outside its lips, which close behind the teeth
choices: outside its lips, which close behind the teeth
hidden deep inside a bony beak
folded flat against the roof of its mouth
set far back near its throat
context: Naked mole-rats dig with their incisors sticking out in front of their lips, which close behind the teeth so the animal can tunnel without swallowing dirt. Each front tooth can even move on its own, like a pair of chopsticks. Source: Britannica, naked mole-rat; Smithsonian National Zoo '10 Things You Didn't Know'.

question: All its life a naked mole-rat tunnels through dry earth as hard as baked concrete, and its body is built for the job: roughly a quarter of its total muscle is packed into one part of its body. Where is that muscle?
answer: the muscles that clamp its jaws shut
choices: the muscles that clamp its jaws shut
its shoulders and forelimbs
its neck and spine
its hind legs and tail
context: About a quarter of a naked mole-rat's entire muscle mass powers its jaw-closing muscles, which is how a hairless rodent chisels through hard-baked earth using its teeth. Source: Wikipedia, Naked mole-rat; Smithsonian National Zoo.

question: In the lab, a naked mole-rat carries on as if nothing had happened when scientists dab hot chili-pepper juice on its skin, where any other mammal would flinch. What one thing are its pain nerves missing?
answer: a pain-signaling chemical called Substance P
choices: a pain-signaling chemical called Substance P
a fast-firing pain receptor called TRPV1
a nerve wrapping called the myelin sheath
a touch-sensing organ called the Merkel cell
context: Naked mole-rat nerves lack Substance P, a chemical that carries certain pain signals, so acid or capsaicin that would sting other animals does nothing to them. Source: Park et al., 'Selective Inflammatory Pain Insensitivity in the African Naked Mole-Rat', PLOS Biology (PMC2214810); Max Delbrück Center.

question: A naked mole-rat feels no burn from chili pepper, and scientists suspected a missing pain-signal gene. Using a modified cold-sore virus to carry it, they slipped the gene back into just one hind foot and left the rest of the body alone. What happened to that foot?
answer: it alone could suddenly feel the chili-pepper burn
choices: it alone could suddenly feel the chili-pepper burn
it went completely numb to every sensation
it swelled and had to be treated
it stopped growing hair around the toes
context: After the Substance P gene was delivered to one hind foot, that foot could feel capsaicin burn while the rest of the animal still could not, proving the missing chemical was the cause. Source: Park et al., PLOS Biology 2008 (PMC2214810); National Geographic.

question: Scientists gave a naked mole-rat back the pain gene it was missing, expecting it to feel what any other rodent feels. Yet one thing still did not hurt it at all, a trait since seen in a couple of other African rodents. What was it?
answer: acid
choices: acid
cold
pressure
sound
context: Even after getting the pain gene back, naked mole-rats felt nothing from acid; their nerves are wired differently at a deeper level. In 2019 Eigenbrod and colleagues tested African rodents related to the naked mole-rat and found two more, the Cape mole-rat and the East African root rat, that also ignore acid. Source: Park et al., PLOS Biology 2008 (PMC2214810); Eigenbrod et al., Science 364:852 (2019), https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/african-mole-rat-pain-tolerance

question: When the oxygen runs out, a naked mole-rat keeps its brain alive in a way no other mammal can. Its cells stop burning their usual glucose and switch to a backup fuel that a human brain cannot use. Which fuel is it?
answer: fructose
choices: fructose
lactate
ketones
glutamate
context: When oxygen runs out, the naked mole-rat switches its cells to burn fructose, a plant-and-fruit sugar, instead of glucose, powering its body the way a plant does so its brain keeps running when a human would die. Source: Park et al., 'Fructose-driven glycolysis supports anoxia resistance in the naked mole-rat', Science 2017 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aab3896); UIC Today.

question: At oxygen levels low enough to kill a person in minutes, a naked mole-rat can survive at least five hours. Shut in air that has no oxygen at all, it holds out for a stretch, then gets up unharmed, as if nothing had happened. How long can it last with no oxygen?
answer: about 18 minutes
choices: about 18 minutes
about 10 seconds
about 3 days
about a full week
context: With no oxygen at all, a naked mole-rat can last about 18 minutes and then recover unharmed. Source: UIC Today / phys.org coverage of Park et al., Science 2017; ScienceDaily.

question: Starved of oxygen, a naked mole-rat carries a backup fuel into its brain through special molecular pumps. Every other mammal, people included, has those pumps in only one organ, and the mole-rat borrowed them from it and put them to work in the brain. Which organ?
answer: the gut
choices: the gut
the liver
the kidneys
the lungs
context: The naked mole-rat's fructose pumps normally exist only in the gut in other mammals; it borrowed the intestinal tool and put it to work in the brain. Source: UIC Today; Park et al., Science 2017 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aab3896).

question: A two-year-old naked mole-rat digging in its East African colony is barely middle-aged, though a house mouse of the same size is old at two and rarely sees four. How long can a naked mole-rat live?
answer: past 30 years
choices: past 30 years
about 6 years
about 12 years
about 20 years
context: Naked mole-rats can live past 30 years, the longest lifespan of any rodent and roughly ten times longer than a same-sized mouse. Source: AnAge / genomics.senescence.info (Heterocephalus glaber); University of Rochester news.

question: The cells of a naked mole-rat pump out a super-sized sugar molecule, more than five times the size of the human kind, and it makes them stop crowding together. Thanks to that signal, the rodent is almost never struck by one deadly process. Which process does the molecule block?
answer: tumors forming
choices: tumors forming
blood clotting shut
wounds going septic
organs scarring stiff
context: Naked mole-rat cells pump out high-molecular-weight hyaluronan, over five times larger than the human version, which tells cells to stop crowding and forming tumors. Source: Tian et al., 'High-molecular-mass hyaluronan mediates the cancer resistance of the naked mole rat', Nature 2013 (nature.com/articles/nature12234).

question: Deep in its tunnels, a naked mole-rat's body temperature drifts up and down with the warmth around it, while nearly every other warm-blooded mammal holds a steady inner temperature whatever the weather. In this one way, which animal does it behave like?
answer: a lizard
choices: a lizard
a sparrow
a dolphin
a rabbit
context: The naked mole-rat is almost the only mammal whose body temperature drifts to match its tunnel, so in this one way it behaves more like a lizard than a rodent. Source: Wikipedia, Naked mole-rat (thermoconformer), citing Buffenstein & Yahav.

question: Each naked mole-rat in a colony can barely warm its own body, so the colony has no inner furnace to rely on. When the burrow turns chilly, what do the mole-rats do to warm back up?
answer: they pile together into a tight warm huddle
choices: they pile together into a tight warm huddle
each one burrows off to trap its own heat
they eat extra food to burn for warmth
they seal the tunnels against the cold air
context: Because it cannot warm itself well, a cold naked mole-rat colony piles into a huddle and climbs to shallow, sun-warmed parts of the burrow, using teamwork instead of a furnace to stay warm. Source: 'Huddling Behavior Facilitates Homeothermy in the Naked Mole Rat', Physiological Zoology; Wikipedia.

question: A colony of naked mole-rats can carve a tunnel network up to 2.5 miles long under the dry grasslands of East Africa. The network is no random maze: like a house, it has separate rooms set aside for different jobs. What is one of those rooms?
answer: a designated toilet chamber
choices: a designated toilet chamber
a lookout tower to the surface
a graveyard for the dead
a hall for the queen to parade
context: A naked mole-rat colony can dig up to about 2.5 miles of tunnels, with separate chambers for the nursery, the food store, and even a designated toilet room. Newborn pups weigh less than a penny. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, '10 Things You Didn't Know About Naked Mole-rats'.

question: Naked mole-rats, wrinkled and nearly hairless, dig their tunnel colonies under East Africa, and for decades biologists called them the one mammal that cannot get cancer. Then, in 2016, that absolute claim finally cracked. What overturned it?
answer: two aging captive males were confirmed with tumors
choices: two aging captive males were confirmed with tumors
a wild colony was wiped out by a viral outbreak
their famous super-sugar was found in mouse cells too
a queen was shown to reabsorb her own unborn pups
context: The two cases were a 22-year-old male at Chicago's Brookfield Zoo, with an adenocarcinoma in his armpit, and a 20-year-old male at the National Zoo in Washington, D.C., with a stomach tumor. Cancer in these rodents is still astonishingly rare, only two confirmed cases out of hundreds of animals examined, so 'almost never' still holds. But 'never' does not: the naked mole-rat can get cancer, just far less often than most mammals. Source: Delaney, Ward, Walsh, Treuting et al., 'Initial Case Reports of Cancer in Naked Mole-rats (Heterocephalus glaber),' Veterinary Pathology 53(3):691-696 (2016); PubMed 26846576; Smithsonian Insider summary (2016).

question: Naked mole-rats live in the pitch-dark tunnels under East Africa and constantly trade soft greeting chirps in the blackness with the other rodents in their colony. Researchers recorded thousands of these chirps and then compared the calls from many separate colonies against each other. What did the recordings reveal about these chirps?
answer: each colony speaks its own learned, queen-enforced dialect
choices: each colony speaks its own learned, queen-enforced dialect
the chirp doubles as a warning that a predator is near
a chirp's pitch reliably reveals the caller's exact age
only the reigning queen's body can produce the chirp
context: Researchers recorded thousands of the soft 'chirp' greeting calls and found every colony has its own distinct dialect. Cross-fostering proved it is learned, not inherited: pups adopted into another colony grew up chirping in their adoptive colony's accent, not their birth colony's. And the queen enforces it, when a colony loses its queen the shared accent breaks down, and a coherent dialect only re-forms once a new queen takes power. It is one of the clearest cases of a learned vocal culture in any rodent. Source: Barker, Veitl, Brecht et al., 'Cultural transmission of vocal dialect in the naked mole-rat,' Science 371(6528):503-507 (2021); DOI 10.1126/science.abc6588; PubMed 33510012.

question: One Arctic whale swims under the sea ice with a long, straight, twisted tusk that pokes out from its head. That tusk gave it a nickname taken from a horse with a horn in old stories. Which whale is this?
answer: The narwhal, the 'unicorn of the sea'
choices: The narwhal, the 'unicorn of the sea'
The beluga, the 'canary of the sea'
The orca, the 'wolf of the sea'
The manatee, the 'cow of the sea'
context: The narwhal (Monodon monoceros) is a mid-sized Arctic whale famous for the long spiraling shaft that projects forward from its head, giving it the nickname 'unicorn of the sea.' Source: NOAA Ocean Exploration — 'What is a narwhal?' https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/narwhal/

question: A male narwhal swims through the icy waters off Greenland with a long, spiraling ivory shaft up to three meters long jutting from his head. It looks like a horn, yet it is no horn at all. What is that shaft really?
answer: A single overgrown tooth that juts through the lip
choices: A single overgrown tooth that juts through the lip
A rod of solid keratin, like a rhino's horn
A fused extension of the skull's frontal bone
A stiffened cartilage spike rooted in the blowhole
context: The narwhal's 'horn' is really a tooth: a single overgrown left canine that grows straight out through the whale's upper lip, reaching up to about 10 feet (3 m) long. Source: Narwhal.org — Dr. Nweeia research page https://www.narwhal.org/about-dr-nweeia

question: A narwhal catches a fish beneath the Arctic sea ice, but apart from its famous tusk it has almost nothing in its mouth, no rows of teeth at all. What does it do with the fish?
answer: It swallows the fish whole
choices: It swallows the fish whole
It shreds the fish against ridged plates in its throat
It grinds the fish with bony gum pads
It saws the fish apart with its tusk
context: Unlike most toothed whales, the narwhal has essentially no teeth in its mouth, just two teeth in the upper jaw (in males, the left one usually becomes the tusk). With nothing to chew with, it swallows its prey whole. Source: Polar Science Center, Univ. of Washington, Narwhal FAQ https://psc.apl.uw.edu/rp/laidre/narwhal-faq/

question: Under the Arctic sea ice, a male narwhal carries a tusk that is no smooth spike: it twists in a spiral along its whole length. Across every narwhal ever measured, even the rare two-tusked male, the spiral runs the same way. Which way does the tusk always twist?
answer: Counterclockwise, to the left
choices: Counterclockwise, to the left
Clockwise, to the right
Alternating left and right by age
Randomly, differing whale to whale
context: The narwhal tusk always spirals counterclockwise (to the left). Even in the rare narwhal that grows two tusks, both spiral left — and one is always longer than the other. Source: Natural History Museum — 'Narwhals: mysterious unicorns of the sea' https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/narwhals-mysterious-unicorns-of-the-sea.html

question: Over Tremblay Sound in Nunavut, drones filmed a narwhal in 2017 swimming up to a fish and landing quick, precise taps on it with the tip of its tusk. No one had caught the tusk at work on film before. What is the tap for?
answer: It stuns the fish, so the narwhal can suck up the dazed prey
choices: It stuns the fish, so the narwhal can suck up the dazed prey
It cracks the ice above to open a breathing hole
It signals rank to rival males nearby
It scrapes food loose from the seabed
context: In 2017, drone footage over Tremblay Sound, Nunavut, captured narwhals whacking Arctic cod with quick, precise taps of the tusk to stun the fish, then sucking up the dazed prey — the first time the behavior was ever filmed. Source: National Geographic — 'Video Solves Mystery of How Narwhals Use Their Tusks' https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/drone-footage-narwhal-tusk-mystery

question: Martin Nweeia, a dental researcher at Harvard, said a narwhal's tusk defies every rule he learned in dental school: it has no protective enamel, and about 10 million microscopic channels run through it, open to the sea. What do researchers think those channels let the whale sense in the water around it?
answer: Changes in its temperature and saltiness
choices: Changes in its temperature and saltiness
The direction of the nearest ice crack
The heartbeat of prey hiding in the dark
The pull of the Earth's magnetic field
context: Dr. Martin Nweeia found the tusk has no enamel, is permeable to seawater, and is packed with up to about 10 million nerve tubules running to its surface — leading researchers to propose it works as a sensory organ that can detect changes in the water's temperature and saltiness. The exact function is still active research, not settled fact. Source: PBS NOVA — 'Narwhal Tusks Might Be Nerve-Rich Ocean Sensors' https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/narwhal-tusks-are-actually-nerve-rich-teeth/

question: A narwhal dives more than a mile beneath the Arctic sea ice after Greenland halibut, holding its breath for 25 minutes or more. Down there the water pressure is crushing enough to squash a submarine. What does the narwhal's body do to survive it?
answer: Its rib cage folds and compresses
choices: Its rib cage folds and compresses
Its blood is rerouted to warm the fins
Its blowhole seals with a bony plug
Its eyes retract into protective sockets
context: Narwhals are among the deepest-diving whales, reaching about 1,800 meters (over a mile). To survive that pressure the rib cage folds and compresses, while muscles loaded with myoglobin let the whale hold its breath 25 minutes or more. Source: NOAA Climate.gov — 'The Narwhal's Tale'; UT Marine Science Institute — 'Deep-Diving Unicorns of the Sea'

question: A hunting crab closes in on a chambered nautilus, which fills a strong tube in its body with seawater and blasts it out all at once. When the jet fires, which way does the nautilus shoot off?
answer: backward
choices: backward
straight up
in tight circles
sideways
context: The nautilus swims by jet propulsion, squeezing water out through a forward-pointing funnel -- so the recoil shoots it backward through the sea, the same mechanism its squid and octopus relatives use. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautilus

question: About ninety thin tentacles, the cirri, fan out from a chambered nautilus to snag a passing crab. Its cousin the octopus grips prey with suckers, but not one of these tentacles has a single sucker. What lets them hold on?
answer: they are extremely sticky
choices: they are extremely sticky
tiny hooked claws
a coating of venom
rings of sharp teeth
context: A nautilus has about 90 tentacles (cirri) -- far more than an octopus's eight -- and none have suckers; they grip prey simply by being extremely sticky. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chambered_nautilus

question: Inside its spiral shell, a chambered nautilus lives in the biggest room, with over thirty sealed rooms behind it. It rises or sinks by pumping gas and water in and out of them, changing how heavy it is. Which human machine is it a living version of?
answer: a submarine
choices: a submarine
a hot-air balloon
a periscope
a diving bell
context: By pumping gas and liquid in and out of its sealed shell chambers to change its density, the nautilus rises and sinks at will instead of swimming constantly -- exactly the buoyancy trick a submarine uses. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chambered_nautilus

question: The octopus looks out through a sealed ball of an eye with a lens and cornea, like a human's, but its cousin the chambered nautilus has eyes with no lens at all. What sits right up against the nautilus's retina, bathing the surface that senses light?
answer: raw ocean seawater
choices: raw ocean seawater
a drop of oil
a layer of gel
trapped air
context: Because the nautilus eye has no lens sealing it shut, the inside is open to the sea -- raw seawater flows right up against the retina, unlike every other cephalopod whose eye is a sealed fluid ball. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/nautilus-eyes-inside-the-pinhole-vision-marvel/

question: To rise, a chambered nautilus drains liquid from the sealed rooms of its shell. A living tube that threads through the chambers, the siphuncle, pumps just one dissolved substance out of the trapped liquid and into the animal's blood, and the water seeps after it by osmosis. What does the siphuncle pump out?
answer: salt
choices: salt
oxygen
calcium
ink
context: The siphuncle's columnar epithelial cells actively pump salt (NaCl) out of the trapped cameral liquid into the nautilus's blood; water then follows the salt osmotically and drains the chamber, and nitrogen gas (at slightly below atmospheric pressure) simply diffuses in to fill the empty space — no mechanical suction at all. This osmotic pump has a hard ceiling: below roughly 240 m the outside seawater pressure driving water back INTO the shell exceeds what the siphuncle's salt gradient can overcome, a genuine puzzle since living nautiluses routinely forage far deeper than 240 m. Source: Greenwald & Ward, 'Cameral liquid transport and buoyancy control in chambered nautilus,' Nature 286:55 (1980), nature.com/articles/286055a0; Grokipedia 'Siphuncle' (grokipedia.com/page/Siphuncle); corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautilus.

question: Kahn and Pompea counted close to thirty fine parallel lines between one chamber wall of a nautilus shell and the next, like tree rings squeezed into a single room. They read the shell as a clock: each line marks the growth the animal added in exactly one span of time. What span does one line record?
answer: one day
choices: one day
one hour
one meal
one dive
context: Modern Nautilus pompilius lays down about 30 fine daily growth lines per chamber — one line per solar day — so a full chamber records roughly 30 days, close to the 29.53-day lunar month, and the animal appears to seal off and start a new chamber about once a lunar month. Kahn and Pompea used this daily-line count as a fossil clock: the earliest nautiloids, 420 million years ago, show only about 9 lines between septa, implying a 'month' of only ~9 days back then, when the Moon orbited far closer and Earth's day was only ~21 hours. Tidal friction has since slowed Earth's spin and pushed the Moon outward, lengthening both. Source: Kahn & Pompea, 'Nautiloid growth rhythms and dynamical evolution of the Earth-Moon system,' Nature 275:606 (1978), nature.com/articles/275606a0; summarized at the University of Alaska Geophysical Institute, 'When the Days were Shorter' (gi.alaska.edu).

question: European robins often migrate on cloudy, moonless nights with no sun or stars to steer by, yet they fly the right way. When the Wiltschkos changed the invisible force around robins in cages, the birds shifted to match. What sense do the robins steer by?
answer: An internal magnetic compass
choices: An internal magnetic compass
A memorized map of landmarks
A pull they feel from the tides
Faint sounds carried on the wind
context: On starless nights there is nothing overhead to steer by, so the robins must carry the reference inside them. When the Wiltschkos changed the field around caged robins, the birds shifted their heading to match — the classic demonstration of an internal magnetic compass. Source: Wiltschko & Wiltschko, 'Magnetic Compass of European Robins', JSTOR https://www.jstor.org/stable/1733331 ; NWF https://www.nwf.org/Magazines/National-Wildlife/1999/Navigating-With-A-Built-In-Compass

question: A caged European robin can tell 'toward the equator' from 'toward the pole' without ever knowing which pole is which. Its compass does not point north the way a hiker's needle does. Which feature of Earth's magnetic field is the robin reading?
answer: The angle the field lines dip into the ground
choices: The angle the field lines dip into the ground
Which way along the ground the field points
The strength of the field's steady pull
How fast the field shifts as the bird moves
context: The robin reads inclination — how steeply the field lines tilt down. That dip is shallow near the equator and steep near the poles, so 'equatorward' and 'poleward' feel different even in the dark, which is why the bird never needs to identify north or south. Source: Wikipedia Magnetoreception https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoreception ; Wiltschko & Wiltschko https://www.internationalornithology.org/PROCEEDINGS_Durban/Symposium/S17/S17.4.htm

question: Loggerhead hatchlings crawl off the beach with no parent and no map, yet each follows a route curving thousands of miles across the Atlantic. Every stretch of coast has its own magnetic feel. In copies of the fields from three far-apart spots on the route, hatchlings swam three different ways. What was each one reading from the field?
answer: Its own position on the globe
choices: Its own position on the globe
The single compass direction toward home
How far it has already swum from shore
Which way the ocean current is flowing
context: Each stretch of coast has a unique magnetic signature — a pairing of the field's angle and its strength — and the hatchling treats those like the latitude and longitude lines of a grid. Reproduce the field of a distant point on the route and the turtle swims the heading that would be correct there, proof it is reading its position, not merely a direction. Source: Lohmann Lab, 'Geomagnetic Imprinting in Sea Turtles and Salmon' https://lohmannlab.web.unc.edu/geomagnetic-imprinting/ ; Brothers & Lohmann, Current Biology 2015

question: A robin may steer by a compass built on quantum physics, though no one has proven how its compass works. The leading idea is that a protein called cryptochrome forms a pair of molecules whose electron spins are quantum-linked, and that Earth's weak field nudges those spins. If so, what might the robin experience?
answer: It may see the field as a pattern over its vision
choices: It may see the field as a pattern over its vision
It may taste the field on the back of its tongue
It may feel the field as heat along its wings
It may hear the field as a low tone in its ears
context: The reaction starts with light hitting cryptochrome (likely Cry4) in the retina, so the 'radical-pair hypothesis' suggests the bird sees the field as shading laid over what it looks at. In 2021 researchers found robin Cry4 more magnetically sensitive in a test tube than chicken or pigeon Cry4 — a good fit, but still a hypothesis, not proof the bird navigates by it. Source: Xu et al., Nature 2021 https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03618-9

question: Kenneth Lohmann's team fed young loggerhead turtles for two months only inside one artificial magnetic 'location' and never inside another. Later they set each turtle into the fed spot's field with no food anywhere in the tank. The turtles instantly gave themselves away, proving they had memorized that magnetic address. What did a turtle do?
answer: Tilted upright and dogpaddled with its mouth open
choices: Tilted upright and dogpaddled with its mouth open
Buried itself in the sand at the bottom of the tank
Swam a tight circle and then floated completely still
Snapped repeatedly at its own reflection in the glass
context: Researchers nicknamed it the 'turtle dance': the loggerhead tilts vertical, pokes its head above the surface, opens its mouth, and paddles with its front flippers — the excited feeding display, performed at a spot it had learned by magnetic field alone with no food present. The same 2025 study went further and showed the turtle carries TWO separate magnetic senses: this learned MAP (which location am I at?) kept working under a radio-frequency field, while its directional COMPASS (which way is which?) was scrambled by it — so the map appears to run on iron/magnetite and the compass on quantum radical-pair chemistry, two different mechanisms in one animal. Source: Goforth, Lohmann et al. 2025, Nature, 'Learned magnetic map cues and two mechanisms of magnetoreception in turtles' (nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08554-y); dance behavior and two-month conditioning from the UNC College of Arts & Sciences release and Scientific American coverage.

question: Thorsten Ritz and the Wiltschkos bathed caged robins in a radio field far too weak to move a needle, under a thousandth of Earth's own field.
