It wrecked the birds' sense of direction, but only when tuned to one narrow frequency near 1.3 megahertz. What is the compass sensor most likely to be, for so faint a signal to disrupt it?
answer: A single unpaired electron whose spin flips in step with that frequency
choices: A single unpaired electron whose spin flips in step with that frequency
A grain of iron pulled into a shudder that matches that same frequency
A beak nerve firing rhythmic bursts that lock onto that same frequency
A cluster of pressure cells that hum and ring at that same frequency
context: The magic pitch was about 1.3 MHz (measured at 1.315 MHz in Frankfurt) — and a field only ~15 nanotesla strong, weaker than a city's electrical hum, was enough to wreck the compass when tuned there. That exact frequency is the 'Larmor' rate at which a single unpaired electron spin precesses in Earth's ~50-microtesla field, so a radio field matching it disturbs the singlet/triplet spin flips at the heart of the proposed radical pair. Iron magnets don't respond to a signal that faint and precise; a lone electron spin does — which is why this remains the single strongest evidence for the radical-pair compass. Frame honestly: it SUPPORTS the leading hypothesis, which is still not proven inside a living bird. Source: Ritz et al. 2004, Nature, 'Resonance effects indicate a radical-pair mechanism for avian magnetic compass' (PubMed 15141211); 15 nT figure, Larmor formula, and 1.315 MHz value from review PMC5627152.

question: A glossy black crow winkles fat grubs out of rotting holes in dead wood on New Caledonia, a group of Pacific islands with no woodpeckers to do the job. It has no drilling beak like a woodpecker's. What does it use to pull the grubs out?
answer: Tools it makes and wields
choices: Tools it makes and wields
Its extra-long barbed tongue
A drumming beak that splits bark
Sticky saliva on its feathers
context: The New Caledonian crow (Corvus moneduloides) fills the ecological niche of a woodpecker on islands that have none, and it is one of the only animals besides apes known to make its own tools. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Caledonian crow' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Caledonian_crow).

question: A New Caledonian crow snips a twig from a fork in a branch, then trims the wood away until one particular shape is left at the tip. No animal but humans is known to make this kind of tool in the wild. What has the crow shaped?
answer: A hook
choices: A hook
A flattened spade
A hollow straw
A forked splinter
context: The crow trims a fork down to a hook at the tip, then hooks grubs out of crevices — the only non-human animal known to manufacture hooked tools in the wild. Source: Nature, Hunt 1996, 'Manufacture and use of hook-tools by New Caledonian crows' (nature.com/articles/379249a0).

question: Across New Caledonia, crows cut precise, stepped strips from the barbed edges of pandanus leaves, so the rows of tiny barbs become lines of snags. Researchers compared the strip designs of different crow populations, old shapes against new. How had the designs changed?
answer: Newer strips were more refined than older ones
choices: Newer strips were more refined than older ones
Newer strips were cruder than older ones
Populations copied one identical strip
Only lone crows ever tweaked a strip
context: Different crow populations make slightly different pandanus tool designs that grew more refined generation after generation — a bird version of cumulative culture, and the only non-primate case known where each generation builds on the last. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Caledonian crow'; Hunt & Gray pandanus tool diversification research.

question: Betty, a captive crow at Oxford, had to get a food bucket out of a deep tube in 2002. She had a straight wire and a hooked wire, but her mate Abel snatched the hooked one and flew off. Left with only the straight wire, what did Betty do?
answer: Bent it into a hook herself
choices: Bent it into a hook herself
Called Abel back with the food
Dropped it and gave up
Threaded it through the tube wall
context: Betty bent the straight wire into a hook and lifted the food bucket out — a landmark moment in animal-cognition research. Source: Weir & Kacelnik 2002/2006, Oxford; Science, 'Was Betty the crow a genius—or a robot?' (science.org). (legend)

question: Scientists at Oxford watched a captive New Caledonian crow named Betty turn a straight piece of wire into a tool and fish a food bucket out of a tall tube in 2002; she did it again in nine of ten later trials. Her feat was hailed as a flash of pure invention. Years later, new evidence revised that story. What did it show?
answer: Bending tools is a natural crow move
choices: Bending tools is a natural crow move
Crows can bend wire but never twigs
Only Betty ever managed the trick
Her wire had been pre-bent by staff
context: Wild crows were found to bend their tools the same way, so Betty's trick may be part of the species' natural repertoire rather than pure on-the-spot invention. Source: Science, AAAS; Royal Society Open Science, Rutz et al. 2016. (legend)

question: A wild New Caledonian crow is given a short stick and a scrap of meat it cannot reach with that stick alone. A longer stick lies locked in a box nearby. Six of seven crows given this puzzle solved it on their very first try. How?
answer: Used the short stick to fish out the long one, then reached the meat
choices: Used the short stick to fish out the long one, then reached the meat
Flung the short stick at the meat to knock it closer to the bars
Wedged the short stick into the box to pry the whole lid open
Tapped the short stick until a keeper handed over the long one
context: Six of seven crows solved this 'tool to get a tool' metatool problem on the first attempt — using the short stick to retrieve the long stick, then the long stick on the meat, a hallmark of planning. Source: Wikipedia citing metatool experiments; PubMed, 'New Caledonian Crows Use Mental Representations to Solve Metatool Problems'.

question: New Caledonian crows pass the challenge from Aesop's fable 'The Crow and the Pitcher': a treat floats out of reach in a water tube, and the crow must raise the water to reach it. Offered a mix of objects, the crows picked heavy sinking stones over floaters and solid over hollow. That grasp of cause and effect roughly matched what?
answer: A five-to-seven-year-old child
choices: A five-to-seven-year-old child
A trained laboratory rat
A newly hatched chick
An adult chimpanzee's ceiling
context: By dropping sinking stones to raise the water level, the crows displayed causal understanding roughly on par with a 5-to-7-year-old child. Source: Jelbert et al. 2014, PLOS ONE; ScienceDaily. (legend)

question: Hundreds of glowworms hang from the ceiling of a New Zealand cave, glowing blue-green and dangling sticky silk lines to snag flying insects. Despite its name, a glowworm is no worm. What kind of animal is it?
answer: the larva of a fly
choices: the larva of a fly
a young spider
a kind of caterpillar
a small cave slug
context: The New Zealand glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) is really a maggot -- the larva of a fungus gnat, a fly in the order Diptera, family Keroplatidae. It glows blue-green at the tail end of its body to lure flying insects into its sticky lines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arachnocampa_luminosa

question: Visitors drift by boat along a pitch-black underground river in New Zealand's Waitomo Caves, with no lamps at all. Overhead, thousands of tiny blue-green glowworm lights shine from the ceiling. What does the ceiling look like?
answer: a starry night sky
choices: a starry night sky
a field of glowing mushrooms
rows of hanging lanterns
streaks of lightning
context: In the famous Waitomo Glowworm Caves, thousands of Arachnocampa luminosa larvae cover the ceiling, and their blue-green lights look exactly like a starry night sky or a galaxy overhead -- a world-famous natural spectacle visitors float beneath in the dark. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave

question: A New Zealand glowworm hangs from a cave ceiling, dangling a sticky silk fishing line below it. A soft blue-green light at the tip of its body lures flying insects into the trap. When the glowworm is hungry for more prey, what does it do with the light?
answer: turns it brighter
choices: turns it brighter
switches it off
flashes it on and off
changes it to red
context: A hungrier Arachnocampa luminosa larva turns UP the intensity of its blue-green glow to lure more prey, then dims once it is well-fed. Its light is true bioluminescence -- a chemical light made at the end of its abdomen. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/glow-worm-new-zealand-caves

question: In a dark limestone cave in New Zealand, a glowworm spends 6 to 12 months hanging from the ceiling, fishing for insects with sticky silk threads. Then it changes into an adult that survives only a few days before it dies. Why can the adult not live any longer?
answer: it has no mouth and cannot eat
choices: it has no mouth and cannot eat
its wings are too weak to fly
the cave cold quickly freezes it
it burns out its last light
context: The adult fly that hatches from Arachnocampa luminosa has no functional mouth -- it cannot eat at all. It lives only days (females up to about 76 hours, males up to about 96 hours) with the sole purpose of mating and laying eggs before it dies. The long larval stage exists to fund that brief adult life. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arachnocampa_luminosa

question: Off the coast of Italy lives a jellyfish smaller than a pinky nail. It carries a nickname no other animal can claim: the 'immortal jellyfish.' Why are scientists watching Turritopsis dohrnii so closely?
answer: When stressed, an adult can rewind into its own younger stage and start over
choices: When stressed, an adult can rewind into its own younger stage and start over
It grows to the size of a dinner plate within a single week
It glows bright enough to read a book by on the sea floor
Its sting is the most powerful of any creature in the ocean
context: Turritopsis dohrnii's bell reaches only about 4.5 millimetres across, roughly the size of a pinky fingernail - yet a stressed adult can run its life cycle backwards, earning it the 'immortal jellyfish' name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii

question: A Turritopsis dohrnii medusa, the free-swimming adult of the Mediterranean's tiny immortal jellyfish, is badly starved or injured. Instead of dying, it sinks to the sea floor and balls up into a featureless blob. What does that blob then become?
answer: A young polyp, the stalked seabed stage
choices: A young polyp, the stalked seabed stage
A clutch of fertilized eggs anchored to the rock
A drifting swarm of newly hatched larvae
A cloud of a hundred identical adult jellyfish
context: A polyp is the stalk-like seabed stage that jellyfish grow from before budding off as free-swimming medusae. When stressed by starvation, injury, or a sudden change in temperature or saltiness, the adult Turritopsis reverts all the way back to this young polyp - running its life cycle backwards. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii

question: A starving immortal jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, rewinds its body to a younger form, and it does more than shrink. Its adult cells were each built for one job, yet now they do something that the cells of most animals never can. What do they do?
answer: Change into other kinds of cell
choices: Change into other kinds of cell
Fuse into one single giant cell
Split apart into a swarm of eggs
Harden into a tough outer shell
context: Transdifferentiation is a fully specialized cell switching straight into a different cell type, and it is how the jellyfish recycles its own adult body into a younger form. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii ; Piraino, Boero, Aeschbach & Schmid, Biological Bulletin (1996)

question: The immortal jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, makes headlines by rewinding its life when it is starved or badly injured. Yet in the wild most of these jellyfish never live long enough to rewind at all. Why does the immortal jellyfish still keep dying?
answer: Predators eat it or disease kills it while it's still an adult
choices: Predators eat it or disease kills it while it's still an adult
Its rewind only works three times before it stops
It freezes solid the first cold night of winter
It forgets how to revert once it becomes an adult
context: Myth-correction: 'immortal' only means Turritopsis dohrnii can rewind to a younger stage - it is NOT unkillable. In the wild most still die, eaten by predators or killed by disease in the medusa stage, before ever reverting. The trick is transformation, not invincibility. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii

question: A freshwater Hydra, a tiny green tube with waving tentacles, lives in a still pond. Most animals grow likelier to die with every passing year, and scientists tracked thousands of Hydras for years to test that rule. As a Hydra ages, what does its yearly chance of dying do?
answer: Stays flat - it doesn't rise as the animal ages
choices: Stays flat - it doesn't rise as the animal ages
Doubles every single month it survives
Drops to exactly zero after its first year
Climbs steeply, the way it does in most animals
context: This is called 'negligible senescence': the Hydra doesn't grow measurably more likely to die as it ages, because stem cells constantly rebuild its whole body. Source: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1521002112

question: In a pond, a freshwater Hydra about the length of a fingernail clings to the weeds, and an old one is no more likely to die in a given year than a young one. One team ran the numbers for a whole Hydra population, assuming nothing ever ate them. How long did they find a few percent would still be alive?
answer: More than 1,400 years
choices: More than 1,400 years
About 40 years
Around 200 years
Roughly 60,000 years
context: With a death rate that stays flat with age, the study calculated that even after 1,400 years, a few percent of a Hydra population would still be alive - if nothing ate them first. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4697432/

question: A lobster walks the ocean floor on clacking claws and does not slow down with age; the oldest, biggest females lay even more eggs than young ones. Part of the reason is that it keeps making telomerase, an enzyme that repairs part of every chromosome, the packed bundles of DNA in each cell. Which part does it rebuild?
answer: The tips, which normally fray shorter each time a cell divides
choices: The tips, which normally fray shorter each time a cell divides
The centromere, the pinched waist that guides the split
The histone spools the strand winds around for storage
The replication fork where the two strands unzip
context: Lobsters keep making telomerase, an enzyme that protects the ends (tips) of their chromosomes - which is partly why they keep growing and stay fertile their whole lives. Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/are-lobsters-immortal.html

question: Lobsters never stop growing, which is why some people call them immortal; the biggest, oldest ones can end up as heavy as a small dog. Yet the very act of getting bigger is what finally kills many of them. What ordeal must old giants face again and again?
answer: Molting, which exhausts them and leaves them defenseless
choices: Molting, which exhausts them and leaves them defenseless
Starving because their claws grow too heavy to lift food
Sinking too deep to ever return to warm water
Freezing when their blood can no longer flow
context: Lobsters are NOT truly immortal: the older and bigger they get, the harder it is to molt their shell, and many die of exhaustion or predation during that dangerous molt. Source: https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/student-contributors-did-you-know/lobsters-are-not-immortal-myth-they-are-seems-be

question: Maria Pascual-Torner and her colleagues compared the whole DNA of the immortal jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, with that of its cousin Turritopsis rubra in 2022. The cousin looks nearly the same but lives a plain mortal life and never rewinds. What did the immortal one carry that its cousin lacked?
answer: Extra copies of genes that repair and protect its DNA
choices: Extra copies of genes that repair and protect its DNA
A second nervous system that overrides its first
Venom strong enough to paralyze its own predators
A shell it can retreat into whenever it is injured
context: In 2022, Maria Pascual-Torner, Carlos Lopez-Otin, and colleagues sequenced Turritopsis dohrnii alongside its close cousin Turritopsis rubra, which cannot rewind. The immortal one carried duplicated copies of DNA-repair genes and DNA polymerases, plus protective variants for telomere upkeep, stem-cell maintenance, and clearing damaged proteins - roughly twice as many gene-protection/repair genes as its mortal cousin. So the trick isn't magic: it's an expanded genetic toolkit for keeping its DNA clean. Source: Pascual-Torner, Lopez-Otin et al., 'Comparative genomics of mortal and immortal cnidarians unveils novel keys behind rejuvenation,' PNAS 2022, 119(36) (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2118763119); corroborated by The Scientist.

question: A naked mole-rat's cells stop dividing while their neighbors are still far apart, long before a mouse's cells would quit. When researchers digested away the giant sugar molecule packed around them, the cells could form tumors. What had that molecule been doing?
answer: Tripping the p16 brake that halts growth early
choices: Tripping the p16 brake that halts growth early
Feeding the cell so it never needed to spread
Cloaking the cell from the animal's immune patrols
Cooling the tissue below the temperature tumors need
context: In 2013, Xiao Tian, Vera Gorbunova, Andrei Seluanov, and colleagues found naked mole-rats make a giant form of hyaluronan (HMW-HA) about five times larger than a mouse's or human's (roughly 6-12 million daltons vs 0.5-3 million). It makes cells arrest at much lower densities - 'early contact inhibition' - by triggering the p16 (p16INK4a) tumor-suppressor switch, slamming the brakes before a tumor can form. When researchers digested the molecule away or knocked out the HAS2 gene that builds it, the cells could then form tumors - proving the molecule is what protects them. Source: Tian et al., 'High-molecular-mass hyaluronan mediates the cancer resistance of the naked mole rat,' Nature 2013, 499:346-349 (nature.com/articles/nature12234).

question: A striped, squirrel-sized numbat noses into shallow termite tunnels in Western Australia and slurps up about 20,000 of them a day. What body part lets it pull so many out of those tight, narrow tunnels?
answer: A long tongue coated in sticky saliva
choices: A long tongue coated in sticky saliva
A set of powerful crushing jaws
A hollow snout it sucks air through
A mouthful of sharp shearing teeth
context: The numbat's tongue flicks out about 10 cm — nearly a third of its whole body length — and the sticky coating traps termites deep in their tunnels. It needs the reach because a small numbat can only work galleries close to the surface. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat

question: A little striped numbat of Western Australia is out and busy in broad daylight, though nearly every other marsupial, from kangaroos to wombats, sleeps through the day and moves at night. What forces the numbat onto a daytime schedule?
answer: Termites climb near the surface only in daylight
choices: Termites climb near the surface only in daylight
Its eyes are useless in total darkness
Daytime warmth keeps its small body from chilling
Night predators would easily catch it
context: Unlike nearly every other marsupial, the numbat is active by day; the musky rat-kangaroo of Queensland is one of the few others. A small numbat can only reach termites when they rise close to the top of their galleries, and that happens by day, so its whole schedule is set by its prey's, not by avoiding the dark. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musky_rat-kangaroo

question: A female numbat in a Western Australian eucalyptus woodland gives birth to four bean-sized young, and they spend their first months clinging to her four teats. For a marsupial, the way she carries them is very strange. Where do the young ride?
answer: Dangling in the open from exposed teats, with no pouch
choices: Dangling in the open from exposed teats, with no pouch
Sealed inside a deep fur-lined belly pouch
Tucked into stretchy pouches in her cheeks
Gripped in the curl of her bushy tail
context: Unusually for a marsupial, the female numbat has no pouch at all. Her four teats sit on a bare patch of belly protected only by crimped golden hair, and the clinging newborns dangle in the open air for months. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat

question: When a fox or a hawk comes hunting, a numbat shelters in a hollow log or a shallow burrow it can just fit inside, backing in as far as it can go. The entrance is still open. How does the little numbat stop the attacker from squeezing in after it?
answer: It jams the opening shut with its thick, tough-hided rump
choices: It jams the opening shut with its thick, tough-hided rump
It sprays a foul-smelling fluid at the entrance
It curls into a tight ball of sharp spines
It rakes the attacker back with its front claws
context: The skin over a numbat's rump is thick and tough, and it uses that hindquarter like a living door — backing in and plugging the entrance so nothing can get past it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat

question: Sailors swore for centuries that they had seen sea serpents, long silver monsters writhing at the surface. Marine scientists now think most sightings were a ribbon-shaped deep-sea fish, rolling in the waves as it died. Which animal was it?
answer: The oarfish
choices: The oarfish
The giant squid
The basking shark
The leatherback turtle
context: The giant oarfish is a scaleless ribbon of silver with a flaming red crest and fin running its whole length. A sick or dying one drifts up and rolls at the surface — a near-perfect match for the classic 'sea serpent' report. A 2016 River Monsters investigation concluded it is the most likely real-world origin of the myth. LEGEND (science-of-legend). Source: Florida Museum — Discover Fishes; Wikipedia 'Giant oarfish'.

question: On a lonely beach, a crowd gathers around a silvery ribbon of a fish washed up on the sand, its gleaming body stretched out roughly 8 meters, or 26 feet. No other bony fish alive grows so long. What is it?
answer: The oarfish
choices: The oarfish
The moray eel
The barracuda
The sturgeon
context: The giant oarfish (Regalecus glesne) is the longest bony fish alive, reliably reaching about 8 metres, with some reports up to 11. Sharks and rays grow longer, but their skeletons are cartilage, not bone. Old claims of 17-metre oarfish are considered exaggerations. Source: Florida Museum; Wikipedia 'Giant oarfish'.

question: Fishermen who now and then hauled an oarfish up in their herring nets called it the king of herrings, perhaps for what rose from its head like a crown above the long silver ribbon of its body. What was that crown?
answer: A tall crest of long red fin rays
choices: A tall crest of long red fin rays
A pair of curved, horn-like spines
A ring of glowing blue light spots
A frilled hood of loose silver skin
context: The front rays of the oarfish's dorsal fin are lengthened into a tall red crest above its head. The folk name 'king of herrings' may come from that crownlike crest, and from the fish being seen near herring shoals, which fishermen believed it led. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_oarfish ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Giant_oarfish

question: An oarfish cruises the deep ocean with its jaws hanging open, straining tiny krill and plankton straight from the seawater. Gentle for its size, it has no real teeth at all. What in its mouth filters out that swarm of tiny prey?
answer: Fine gill rakers in its mouth
choices: Fine gill rakers in its mouth
A sticky mucus net it casts out
Rows of grinding throat plates
A sucking, tube-shaped snout
context: The oarfish filters tiny krill and plankton through fine gill rakers — comblike structures in the mouth. One specimen was found with about 10,000 krill inside it. Despite its terrifying size, it is harmless. Source: Florida Museum — Discover Fishes.

question: A stranded oarfish flashes silver in the sun as if it were forged from polished metal, yet unlike most fish it wears no scales at all; its long body is bare skin. What coats that skin to give it a mirror shine?
answer: A soft layer of guanine crystals
choices: A soft layer of guanine crystals
A film of swallowed sea salt
A sheath of overlapping bony plates
A slick of reflective body oil
context: The oarfish has no scales; its body is coated in a soft, silvery layer of guanine — the same shimmering crystal that makes ordinary fish scales and mirrors flash. That is why a stranded one looks made of polished metal. Source: Florida Museum — Discover Fishes; Wikipedia 'Giant oarfish'.

question: Mark Benfield's team, diving in a submersible deep in the Gulf of Mexico, filmed a living oarfish, a fish known until then only from dead or dying ones. Its posture in the water startled them. How does an oarfish hold itself?
answer: Vertically, head-up and tail-down
choices: Vertically, head-up and tail-down
Coiled in a slow rolling spiral
Belly-up, drifting with the current
Flat on the seabed like a flounder
context: Benfield et al. (2013) filmed live oarfish in the Gulf of Mexico and discovered its true posture: it hangs vertically, head-up and tail-down, rippling its long red dorsal fin to hover in the water column. Scientists think this may be a hunting trick — hanging straight up, it uses faint surface light to silhouette prey drifting above it. Source: Benfield et al. 2013, Journal of Fish Biology (doi:10.1111/jfb.12144).

question: Sailors off a warm coast spot a fish like a giant swimming head, squashed flat from the side, with tall fins jutting up and down. Then it just stops, blunt at the back, with nothing behind. Which ocean giant is it?
answer: The ocean sunfish (mola)
choices: The ocean sunfish (mola)
The great white shark
The bluefin tuna
The manta ray
context: The ocean sunfish (Mola mola) really does look like a swimming head that ends abruptly with no real tail. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium — Ocean sunfish.

question: Where a shark or a tuna sweeps a tail, an ocean sunfish has only a stiff, blunt rudder, a scalloped fringe wrapped around the back edge of its body. That rudder is no shrunken tail. What forms it?
answer: The wrapped-around ends of its top and bottom fins
choices: The wrapped-around ends of its top and bottom fins
A stub of spine sheathed in tough skin
A fan of enlarged rear scales
A flap of cartilage grown back from the gills
context: The mola's rudder, the clavus, forms where its dorsal and anal fins wrap around and meet at the blunt rear — not a tail fin at all. Source: Wikipedia — Ocean sunfish; Monterey Bay Aquarium.

question: An ocean sunfish lies flat on its side at the surface, one flank turned up to the sky, and seabirds land on it. Scientists think the sunbathing pose is not only about warmth: it invites the birds to do something useful. What are the birds doing?
answer: Picking parasites off its exposed skin
choices: Picking parasites off its exposed skin
Guiding it away from shallow water
Warning it of approaching sharks
Cracking open its skin for food
context: Seabirds land on the basking mola and pick parasites off its skin while cleaner fish work its underside — the fish is loaded with parasites, so cleaning matters. Source: Wikipedia — Ocean sunfish; U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service.

question: Tagged ocean sunfish plunge as many as 40 times a day into the crushing dark near 1,000 meters, where they hunt jellyfish in cold water. After every dive, each fish labors its huge body all the way back up to the warm surface. Why does it keep coming back up?
answer: To reheat its body chilled by the cold deep
choices: To reheat its body chilled by the cold deep
To gulp air for buoyancy control
To digest food only in bright light
To shed the pressure of the deep
context: The mola dives deep to feed in cold water, then reheats its chilled body at the warm surface like a big solar panel — earning it the nickname 'solar-powered fish.' Source: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service — 'The Solar-Powered Fish with Jellies in Their Bellies: Molas'; Wikipedia — Ocean sunfish.

question: An octopus has eight rubbery arms and no bones anywhere in its soft, squeezable body. Just one small part of it is truly hard, the only firm piece in the whole animal. Which part is it?
answer: Its beak
choices: Its beak
Its inner shell
A plate in its gut
Its innermost sucker
context: The beak is the octopus's only hard part — everything else is pure muscle and skin. Source: Oregon Coast Aquarium DYK; sharksandco.com/the-octopus-that-can-squeeze-through-any-gap-1-7369/

question: A hungry fish corners an octopus on the reef. The octopus gulps seawater into its baggy body and blasts it out in one sharp push, rocketing backward like a jet. Through which body part does the water shoot?
answer: Its siphon, a muscular tube
choices: Its siphon, a muscular tube
Its gills, packed with feathers
Its beak, snapped wide open
Its arms, gripping the seabed
context: The octopus fills its mantle with water and blasts it out through a muscular tube called the siphon, rocketing itself backward. Source: cimi.org/blog/octopus-jet-propulsion/; ocean.si.edu invertebrates

question: An octopus is fleeing a hungry shark. In a single instant it shoots away with a jet of water pushed out of its body. Behind it, the octopus squirts a thick dark cloud into the sea. What does that dark cloud actually do for the octopus?
answer: It hides the octopus behind a smoke screen
choices: It hides the octopus behind a smoke screen
It stuns the predator with an electric jolt
It poisons the water for a mile around
It glows to blind the predator
context: The ink is squirted into the same water jet the octopus uses to escape, making a dark screen. The ink also contains tyrosinase, which irritates a predator's eyes and garbles its smell and taste. Source: cimi.org/blog/octopus-jet-propulsion/; smithsonianmag.com ten-wild-facts-about-octopuses

question: A giant Pacific octopus may weigh 50 pounds, but it has no bones anywhere in its body. It can pour its whole rubbery bulk through a hole no bigger than what?
answer: A two-inch coin
choices: A two-inch coin
A wedding ring
A keyhole
A walnut shell
context: With no skeleton, an octopus can squeeze through any gap its beak fits through — so a 50-pound animal can flow through a two-inch hole. Source: facebook.com/OregonCoastAquarium DYK post; sharksandco.com/the-octopus-that-can-squeeze-through-any-gap-1-7369/

question: With a beak tucked in the middle of its ring of eight arms, an octopus crushes the shells of crabs and clams. The beak looks and works like bone, but it is made of a tough material called chitin. Where else in nature is chitin found?
answer: In crab claws and insect shells
choices: In crab claws and insect shells
In fish scales and shark skin
In coral reefs and clam pearls
In turtle shells and cow horns
context: Chitin is the same tough material that builds crab claws and the exoskeletons of insects. Source: theenvironmentalblog.org/2025/07/do-octopuses-have-beaks/

question: Inside an octopus, a surprising number of hearts keep its blood moving, each pushing it through a different part of the animal, where most animals make do with one. How many hearts does an octopus have?
answer: Three
choices: Three
One
Two
Five
context: Two hearts pump blood only through the gills to load it with oxygen; a third pumps that blood to the rest of the body. Source: smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/ten-wild-facts-about-octopuses

question: In the blink of an eye an octopus flashes a whole new pattern across its body, while a chameleon takes many seconds to shift color by moving pigment inside its skin cells. Thousands of chromatophores, tiny bags of pigment, lie beneath the octopus's skin. What makes it so much faster?
answer: Muscles yank its color sacs open
choices: Muscles yank its color sacs open
Sunlight warms its skin
Its blood flushes into the skin
Hormones ripple across its body
context: Under the chromatophores sit even more skin cells: iridophores that flash shimmery colors and leucophores that mirror surrounding light. Source: livescience.com/how-do-octopuses-change-color; scienceabc.com colorblind-octopuses

question: One by one, an octopus presses the suckers of an arm against a rock, a crab and a scrap of food, exploring each in turn. Its suckers do something human fingers cannot. What does each sucker let the octopus do?
answer: Taste whatever it touches
choices: Taste whatever it touches
See in total darkness
Hear distant sounds
Smell across the whole ocean
context: Every sucker is studded with chemoreceptors, so the octopus tastes the world with its arms. A giant Pacific octopus has about 2,000 suckers — roughly 280 per arm. Source: gizmodo.com/researchers-finally-figured-out-how-octopuses-taste; americanoceans.org giant-pacific-octopus suckers

question: With around 500 million nerve cells, about the same number as a dog has, an octopus solves puzzles and opens jars. Most of those nerve cells are not packed into its head at all. Where do about two-thirds of them live?
answer: In its arms
choices: In its arms
In its three hearts
In its skin
In its eyes
context: Each arm has its own cluster of nerve cells acting like a mini-brain, so an arm can grab food or explore a hole without waiting for orders from the central brain. Source: maketecheasier.com octopus-neurons; biologyinsights.com octopus-brain-anatomy

question: Settling on a rock, a patch of coral or sand, an octopus vanishes, changing its skin to match the background so perfectly that its eyes seem to miss nothing. Yet when scientists tested those eyes in the lab, they found one surprising limit. What can an octopus eye not do?
answer: Tell one color from another
choices: Tell one color from another
Focus a crisp, sharp image
Swivel around on its own
Close behind a proper lid
context: An octopus's eyes carry just one visual pigment, making it colorblind — yet it still matches the colors around it, and exactly how it does that remains an open puzzle. Source: scienceabc.com colorblind-octopuses; pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1524578113

question: Bruce Robison and his team, from the Monterey Bay Aquarium, sent a submersible robot down to the same rocky ledge in the cold, deep Pacific, dive after dive, for years. Each visit, the same female octopus, a Graneledone boreopacifica, was curled over her eggs, never leaving them, never eating. How long did she guard them?
answer: About four and a half years
choices: About four and a half years
About three weeks
About six months
About ten years
context: For 53 months she guarded her clutch of about 160 eggs and never ate once, slowly starving, and died soon after they hatched. Source: journals.plos.org PLoS ONE 10.1371/journal.pone.0103437; nationalgeographic.com octopus-cares-for-her-eggs-for-53-months

question: A mother octopus guards her eggs in a rocky den, cleaning them and fanning them with water, and she stops eating. She slowly starves and dies soon after they hatch, a death her own body switches on. In the laboratory, scientists made one change to a mother that switched the dying off and kept her alive and feeding. What did they change?
answer: They cut out two glands behind her eyes
choices: They cut out two glands behind her eyes
They fed her a steady supply of crabs
They took every egg out of her den
They chilled the water in her tank
context: After a female lays her eggs, her optic glands release self-destructive chemicals that make her stop eating; in experiments, octopuses whose optic glands were removed stopped starving and kept living. Source: smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/ten-wild-facts-about-octopuses

question: Syllipsimopodi bideni swam the seas 100 million years before the first dinosaurs and left its fossil in what is now Montana; it is the oldest known fossil relative of the octopus. Its descendants later reduced its body plan to the eight arms of every octopus alive today. How many arms did it have?
answer: Ten, each with a double row of suckers
choices: Ten, each with a double row of suckers
Eight, exactly like octopuses today
Six, with the front pair fused into a hood
Twelve, ringing the mouth in a single crown
context: The ~12 cm Syllipsimopodi bideni fossil comes from the Bear Gulch limestone of Montana, dated to the Mississippian (Serpukhovian), roughly 330 to 323 million years ago. That is about 100 million years before the earliest dinosaurs, and its discovery pushed the octopus lineage's fossil record back some 82 million years past the previous oldest specimen. Crucially it had ten arms, each carrying a double (biserial) row of suckers, so the familiar eight-armed body plan came LATER, by reducing one arm pair. Source: Whalen & Landman, Nature Communications 13:1107 (2022), 'Fossil coleoid cephalopod from the Mississippian Bear Gulch Lagerstatte' (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8904582/).

question: An ogre-faced spider hangs head-down over a forest trail at night, a small stretchy web held between its four front legs. A beetle wanders through the leaf litter below. What does the spider do with the web?
answer: Throws it down over the beetle like a fisherman casting a net
choices: Throws it down over the beetle like a fisherman casting a net
Drops a sticky line to reel the beetle upward
Wraps the beetle after it blunders into a hanging trap
Spits a glue thread to pin the beetle in place
context: The ogre-faced spider (genus Deinopis) is a net-caster: it holds a small stretchy net between its four front legs and plunges it down over passing prey, then snaps it shut. The net is not sticky but is made of woolly cribellate silk whose coiled threads tangle up anything that touches them, and it can stretch to two or three times its relaxed size the instant it is flung, so a small net can wrap a much bigger insect. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinopis ; https://australian.museum/learn/animals/spiders/net-casting-spiders/

question: Right out in the open, in plain sight of birds and lizards, an ogre-faced spider spends the daylight hours with no hidden shelter or burrow. How does the slim, long-legged spider survive the day?
answer: Stretching its thin body and legs out straight to look like a stick
choices: Stretching its thin body and legs out straight to look like a stick
Curling into a tight ball resembling a dead bud
Wrapping itself in a papery cocoon of silk
Coating its body in bits of bark and lichen
context: By day the ogre-faced spider stretches its long thin body and legs out straight along a twig, looking exactly like a stick so predators pass it by. It only unfurls to hunt after dark. Source: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/spiders/net-casting-spiders/

question: Two huge round eyes, the largest simple eyes of any spider, stare from the face of the ogre-faced spider as it hunts at night, and they give it its name. What do those eyes let it do that few hunters can?
answer: Aim its throwing net in near-total darkness
choices: Aim its throwing net in near-total darkness
Spot a warm-blooded animal by its body heat
See the ultraviolet patterns painted on flowers
Snap into sharp focus on prey a meter away
context: The genus name Deinopis is Greek for 'fearful appearance' (deinos = fearful, opis = appearance), and the 'ogre face' is those two huge central eyes. They are the largest simple eyes of any spider and gather light about 2,000 times more efficiently than human eyes, giving superb night vision. Uniquely, the spider has no reflective tapetum like a cat's; instead it grows a fresh sheet of light-sensitive membrane inside each eye every night and destroys it at dawn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinopis

question: At Cornell, Jay Stafstrom and Ronald Hoy covered the eyes of some ogre-faced spiders. The blinded spiders missed bugs crawling below them, yet they still netted flying insects right out of midair. How, the pair showed in a 2020 paper, does a spider make that catch?
answer: Hearing the insect's wingbeats through sensors in its legs
choices: Hearing the insect's wingbeats through sensors in its legs
Feeling the wind gusts from the wingbeats on fine body hairs
Smelling the insect through chemical pits on its feet
Tasting vibrations carried up its own silk draglines
context: In 2020 Jay Stafstrom and Ronald Hoy at Cornell discovered the ogre-faced spider can hear despite having no ears, sensing sound through metatarsal organs near the tips of its legs. When they played low tones (about 150-750 Hz, the wingbeat frequencies of moths, flies and mosquitoes), more than half the spiders lurched into a backward flip-strike, netting the imagined flying insect out of the air. The finding confirmed a hunch Cornell's Charles Walcott had proposed roughly 60 years earlier and that other scientists had dismissed. Sources: https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2020/10/buzz-kill-spiders-hear-airborne-prey-their-legs ; https://www.sciencenews.org/article/ogre-faced-spider-hearing-catch-insects-prey-air-sound-sight

question: A big reddish-brown bird flies through a pitch-black cave in the mountains of South America, firing off fast clicks and listening for their echoes off the rock, the same trick bats use. Which bird is it?
answer: The oilbird
choices: The oilbird
The barn owl
The kiwi
The nightjar
context: The oilbird (Steatornis caripensis) of northern South America is one of the very few birds on Earth that echolocates. Its clicks are pitched low enough (about 2 kHz) that a person standing in the cave can hear them, unlike a bat's ultrasonic clicks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird

question: An oilbird leaves its cave every night and flies through the dark to oily palm and laurel fruits ripening high in the canopy. No other night-flying bird in the world lives on fruit alone. When it reaches a ripe one, how does it pick it?
answer: Hovers and twists in mid-air to pluck each fruit off the branch
choices: Hovers and twists in mid-air to pluck each fruit off the branch
Perches on the branch and works the fruit loose with its hooked beak
Shakes the whole branch until ripe fruits rain down to gather below
Snips through the fruit's stalk and lets it drop into the leaf litter
context: The oilbird is the only nocturnal flying fruit-eating bird known. It takes each palm and laurel fruit on the wing, hovering and contorting in the dark to snatch them one by one, then flies on -- making it a champion seed-scatterer, since it swallows fruit whole and drops the seeds far across the forest. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird

question: In a cave in Trinidad, oilbird parents fly home night after night with oily palm and laurel fruit and feed it to their chick on a ledge nest. By the time the chick is ready to fly, how does its weight compare with theirs?
answer: About a third heavier than they are
choices: About a third heavier than they are
About a third lighter than they are
About half as heavy as they are
About twice as heavy as they are
context: Fed on oil-rich fruit, oilbird chicks grow fat in the nest, and before they fly they weigh around a third more than the adults, up to about 600 grams. People once boiled the fat chicks down for lamp and cooking oil, which is why the bird's scientific name, Steatornis, means 'fat bird'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird

question: Fifteen thousand oilbirds can crowd a single cave, all clicking at once in the dark, a deafening racket of echoes. Yet each bird still picks out the echo of its own clicks in the storm of sound. How does an oilbird tell its echo from its neighbors'?
answer: Each bird clicks at a slightly different pitch from those around it
choices: Each bird clicks at a slightly different pitch from those around it
Each bird clicks only when the others fall briefly silent
Each bird fires its clicks in a rhythm it alone can recognize
Each bird aims a tight beam of clicks and ignores echoes off to the side
context: The oilbird's clicks come in astonishingly fast bursts, and neighbors pitch theirs slightly differently, so a bird can pick its own echo out of the noise of thousands clicking together. Its clicks only switch on when a cave grows too dark even for its super-sensitive eyes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird

question: A shy animal walks alone through the shadows of the Congo rainforest, nibbling leaves. It has a chocolate-brown coat, big round ears, and legs and rump striped black and white like a zebra's. What is it?
answer: The okapi
choices: The okapi
The bongo
The tapir
The forest buffalo
context: The okapi (Okapia johnstoni) lives only in the dense rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. So shy and solitary that it stayed hidden from Western science until 1901, it was one of the last large land mammals on the planet to be described. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: An okapi slips through the Congo rainforest on legs striped in bold black and white, and the first Europeans to hear of it guessed it was some kind of forest zebra. Its genes tell another story: it has just one living relative, an animal that looks very different. Which one?
answer: The giraffe
choices: The giraffe
The wild horse
The greater kudu
The bush pig
context: The okapi and the giraffe are the only two living members of the family Giraffidae, sharing a common ancestor about 11.5 million years ago. The okapi is essentially a giraffe that stayed short and hid in the forest — a short-necked forest cousin, the two the last survivors of their family. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: With no paws to wipe its face and no pond to splash in, an okapi of the Congo rainforest grooms itself with a blue-black tongue some 30 centimeters long, flexible enough to grasp like a finger. It reaches two body parts almost no other mammal can. Which two?
answer: Its own eyes and ears
choices: Its own eyes and ears
The soles of its feet
The middle of its back
The tip of its tail
context: The okapi's tongue runs around 30 cm and has been reported up to 46 cm (18 inches) — long enough to lick clean its own eyes and even its own ears, making it one of the very few mammals on Earth able to lick its own ears. The same tongue wraps around branches to strip off leaves, just as its giraffe cousin strips an acacia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: Chasing rumors of a striped 'African unicorn,' Sir Harry Johnston expected to find some kind of forest-dwelling horse. Then he examined the tracks the animal left, and one detail told him it was no horse or zebra at all. What did the tracks show?
answer: They were cloven — split into two toes
choices: They were cloven — split into two toes
They came in a slow spiral
They were webbed like a duck's
They were clawed like a big cat's
context: Legend: locals had long known the creature, and explorer Henry Morton Stanley heard of an 'atti' in 1887. Johnston expected a forest horse, but the tracks were CLOVEN-hoofed — two toes, not the single hoof of a horse or zebra. A striped skin and a skull sent to London let zoologist Ray Lankester declare it an unknown giraffe relative, naming it Okapia johnstoni in 1901. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: Heavy rains flood the caves under Postojna in Slovenia, and pale, slender animals wash out of the ground into the daylight. For centuries villagers took them for the young of a great dragon sleeping deep below the earth. What are they really?
answer: The olm, a blind cave salamander
choices: The olm, a blind cave salamander
The European eel, a river fish
The slow worm, a legless lizard
The axolotl, a lake salamander
context: For centuries people around Slovenia's caves believed the olm (Proteus anguinus), a blind salamander up to about a foot long, was the young of a dragon living deep beneath the earth, flushed to the surface by floods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olm  (Legend.)

question: An olm a century old still swims its cave river in a baby's body. Most amphibians start life as water-breathing larvae and remake themselves as they grow up, but the olm never does. What does the adult olm still wear that a grown frog has lost?
answer: Feathery external gills
choices: Feathery external gills
A slippery jelly coat
A sucker-tipped tail
Rows of armored scales
context: The olm keeps its larval external gills for life, a trait called neoteny that it shares with the axolotl. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olm

question: An adult olm hunts in pitch-black underground rivers where eyes are useless, and its own eyes are tiny and buried under skin. Yet it still finds the tiny animals it eats. Beyond smell and hearing, what faint signal does the olm sense to pinpoint hidden prey?
answer: The electric fields their bodies give off
choices: The electric fields their bodies give off
The warmth of their blood
The bubbles they release
The vibrations of their shells
context: The olm detects the weak electric fields of prey using special ampullary organs, letting it hunt in total darkness. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olm

question: Scientists tagged wild olms and went back to their cave rivers again and again to find them. Most of the animals had shifted less than 10 meters. One olm sat in the very same spot after a long, unbroken stretch. Roughly how long had that one olm stayed put?
answer: Over seven years
choices: Over seven years
About three months
Nearly forty years
A single winter
context: Most tracked olms moved less than 10 meters over years; one sat in the same spot for 2,569 days, over seven years. Lead researcher Gergely Balazs said 'they are hanging around, doing almost nothing' -- an energy-saving life for an animal that eats rarely and can live a century. Source: https://www.sciencealert.com/scientists-don-t-think-this-olm-bothered-to-move-much-in-7-years

question: A finger-sized swimmer called Opabinia nosed through the seas over 500 million years ago. Almost every animal alive keeps its eyes in a tidy matched set, but Opabinia's head carried a cluster of small eyes on short stalks, plus one big eye in the middle. How many eyes did it have?
answer: Five
choices: Five
Two
Four
Six
context: A cluster of four eyes on short stalks plus one large eye set in the center gave Opabinia five eyes on top of its head, an odd number no living animal has. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale.

question: Through the shallow Cambrian sea swam Opabinia, a soft-bodied creature just a few centimeters long. A long, bendy tube jutted from the very front of its head like the hose of a vacuum cleaner, some four times the head's own length. What did the far tip of that tube end in?
answer: A grasping claw studded with spines
choices: A grasping claw studded with spines
A fan of feathery breathing gills
A ring of tiny grinding teeth
A soft glowing lure for luring prey
context: At the front of its head Opabinia carried a long, flexible nozzle or hose, roughly four times longer than its head, ending in a grasping claw studded with small spines that it used to gather food. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale.

question: Opabinia plucked morsels off the seafloor with the long hose on its head, then had to pass each scrap to its mouth. Most animals keep the mouth up front, close to where food is caught, but Opabinia's sat in an odd spot that forced an extra maneuver. Where was its mouth?
answer: On the underside, opening backward
choices: On the underside, opening backward
At the very tip of the long hose
On the top of its head between the eyes
At the rear, flanking the tail fins
context: Opabinia's mouth sat on the underside of its body and pointed backward, so it used the claw on its hose to pluck food and pass it back and under to that rear-facing mouth. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale.

question: A sleek black-and-white orca hunts with its tight family group, taking big prey like seals and even sharks. Its famous nickname, the killer whale, gets its family wrong. What kind of animal is an orca really?
answer: The largest dolphin
choices: The largest dolphin
A kind of baleen whale
A cold-water shark
An overgrown porpoise
context: Orcinus orca is the biggest member of the dolphin family, Delphinidae — despite the "whale" in its common name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orca ; https://us.whales.org/whales-dolphins/facts-about-orcas/

question: A pod of wild orcas travels the open sea together. The world's seas are counted as five great oceans: the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Arctic and the Southern, the icy ring around Antarctica. In how many of those five do wild orcas swim?
answer: All five
choices: All five
Just the Pacific
The three coldest
Only two
context: Orcas live in all five of the world's oceans — they are the most widely distributed of all whales and dolphins, and one of the most widely distributed mammals on Earth. Source: https://us.whales.org/whales-dolphins/facts-about-orcas/

question: A big male orca can stretch 8 meters long and weigh more than 6 tonnes, as much as a truck. Inside its jaws sit more than 40 curved, interlocking teeth, built for gripping fish, seals and even other whales. About how long is each of those teeth?
answer: About 10 cm — the length of a finger
choices: About 10 cm — the length of a finger
About 1 cm — like a house cat's
About 30 cm — like a steak knife
About 3 mm — like a sesame seed
context: An orca's teeth are about 10 cm (4 inches) long and curve inward, interlocking to grip slippery prey. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orca ; https://www.britannica.com/animal/killer-whale

question: Far offshore, a rare, shy group of orcas eats only sharks. Every orca group locks onto its own kind of prey and passes down its own calls and hunting tricks, and this group's choice shows in its mouth. Shark skin feels rough as sandpaper. What does it do to the orcas' teeth?
answer: Wears their teeth down to the gum line
choices: Wears their teeth down to the gum line
Leaves them completely toothless at birth
Turns their teeth bright orange
Makes their teeth grow back doubled
context: The elusive "offshore" ecotype eats sharks, whose rough, sandpaper-like skin grinds the orcas' teeth right down to the gum line. Source: https://www.seadocsociety.org/offshore-killer-whale-facts ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12315212/

question: A Weddell seal lounges on a floating slab of Antarctic ice, well out of reach of the water below. Four orcas line up shoulder to shoulder just under the surface and charge the floe together at full speed. What are they making with that rush?
answer: A wave that sweeps the seal off the ice
choices: A wave that sweeps the seal off the ice
A loud noise to scare it into the sea
A ring of bubbles to trap it
A tunnel dug under the floe
context: Antarctic orcas hunt by "wave-washing" — charging four-abreast to push a wave over an ice floe and sweep the resting seal into the water. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/animals-up-close-wave-washing-killer-whales

question: A young Antarctic orca travels with one of the few pods that know how to get a resting seal off its ice floe: only about 100 orcas in the whole region have the skill. How does the young one come to learn it?
answer: The pod's older females teach it
choices: The pod's older females teach it
It is born knowing it by instinct
It copies the trick from seals
It works it out fresh each season
context: Wave-washing is a learned tradition held by roughly 100 Antarctic orcas, taught down the generations from the pod's matriarch. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/marine-animals/orcas-wave-washing-seals

question: Sea lion pups splash in the shallows off the beach at Península Valdés, Argentina, close against the sand. An orca hunting them there uses a move so risky that almost no other sea animal tries it. What does the orca do?
answer: Hurls itself right up onto the beach
choices: Hurls itself right up onto the beach
Dives to the seafloor and waits
Blows a net of bubbles around them
Lifts its head to peek above the surface
context: At Península Valdés, orcas deliberately beach themselves to grab sea lion pups, then squirm back to sea — and adults teach this risky technique to their young. Source: https://peninsulavaldes.com/wildlife/orcas

question: A grandmother orca swims with her pod decades after her last calf. Orca females stop having calves in their 30s and 40s yet live to 80 or more; few animals besides humans go through menopause like this. Lauren Brent's study found these old females change what they do in lean salmon years. What do they do?
answer: Lead the pod to food from the front
choices: Lead the pod to food from the front
Leave the pod and live on their own
Stop eating so the calves can feed
Drift at the back to save energy
context: After menopause, grandmother orcas become pod leaders; Brent's study found the oldest females lead from the front to salmon, especially when food is scarce and their memory matters most. Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/killer-whale-behaviour-shows-granny-knows-best.html ; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/after-menopause-killer-whale-moms-become-pod-leaders-180954480/

question: An orca of Puget Sound's K-pod started a fad in 1987 that spread to all three resident pods in a matter of months, died out, then came back in 2024. Each pod's own dialect of calls, by contrast, had stayed almost unchanged for decades. What was the fad?
answer: Balancing a dead salmon on its head like a hat
choices: Balancing a dead salmon on its head like a hat
Whistling in a brand-new tune
Slapping tails in a synchronized line
Chasing boats in circles
context: The 1987 "salmon hat" fad spread across the resident pods, disappeared, then reappeared in 2024 — still unexplained. Pod dialects, by contrast, pass down almost unchanged across decades. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_hat ; https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/for-orcas-dead-salmon-hats-are-back-in-fashion/

question: Off Norway, a pod of orcas circles a school of herring, blowing curtains of bubbles and flashing their white bellies to pack the fish into a tight glittering ball near the surface. Then one whale does the thing that actually kills the fish. What is it?
answer: Whips its tail into the ball, and the shockwave stuns the herring
choices: Whips its tail into the ball, and the shockwave stuns the herring
Lunges in with open jaws and swallows the whole ball at once
Bites the packed school clean in half with a snap of its teeth
Rams the ball at speed to crush the fish against the surface
context: This is carousel feeding. Norwegian orcas herd a herring school into a tight bait ball at the surface, working in shifts so it never scatters, then a whale swings its powerful flukes into the ball. The tail-slap sends out a shockwave and pressure change that stun or kill up to about 15 herring at once, and the whale picks off the stunned fish one by one. Herding and striking are traded around the pod so the ball stays packed. Source: Simon et al., acoustic behaviour of Norwegian killer whales during carousel foraging (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/240765692); National Geographic, "How Orcas Work Together to Whip Up a Meal" (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/orcas-feeding-cooperative-hunting-killer-whales); Wikipedia, "Carousel feeding" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carousel_feeding).

question: The orcas that hunt mammals in the North Pacific never mix with the ones that eat fish there. They keep separate calls and diets, and their lines split hundreds of thousands of years ago. In 2024 a taxonomy committee for marine mammals voted on how to classify them. How did the committee rank them?
answer: As two subspecies of one killer-whale species
choices: As two subspecies of one killer-whale species
As two full and separate killer-whale species
As one single species with no subdivisions at all
As two distinct genera, split above species level
context: In 2024 Morin and colleagues proposed splitting these into two full species: the mammal-hunting Bigg's (transient) orca as Orcinus rectipinnus ("erect wing," for its tall pointed dorsal fin) and the fish-eating resident orca as Orcinus ater. The Society for Marine Mammalogy's Taxonomy Committee narrowly fell short of the two-thirds vote needed for full species, so it recognized them instead as subspecies -- Orcinus orca rectipinnus and Orcinus orca ater. Whether these lifelong-separate lineages are one species or several is still a live, unsettled debate. Source: Morin et al. 2024, "Revised taxonomy of eastern North Pacific killer whales," Royal Society Open Science (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10966402/); NOAA Fisheries feature (https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/feature-story/new-research-reveals-full-diversity-killer-whales-two-species-come-view-pacific-coast); Society for Marine Mammalogy 2024 annual review (https://marinemammalscience.org/smm-news/taxonomy-committee-2024-annual-review/).

question: Deep in a Southeast Asian rainforest, a small pink-and-white insect perches on a bare green leaf. Its legs flare into rounded shapes like flower petals, and bees head straight in to land, taking it for a real blossom. What is this master of floral disguise?
answer: The orchid mantis
choices: The orchid mantis
A pink crab spider
A flower-mimic katydid
A blossom-shaped treehopper
context: The orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) has upper leg segments flattened into heart- and petal-shapes, so its whole body reads as a pink-and-white blossom; insects fly straight toward it thinking it is a flower. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymenopus_coronatus

question: A newly hatched orchid mantis looks nothing like the pink-and-white flower mimic it will become. Its first body is bright red-orange and black, and at this earliest stage it passes for a different kind of insect altogether. Which insect does the hatchling copy?
answer: A hard-biting, foul-tasting assassin bug
choices: A hard-biting, foul-tasting assassin bug
A stinging paper wasp on patrol
A blister beetle oozing toxic oil
A soldier ant marching in column
context: First-instar orchid mantis nymphs are red-orange and black and mimic a foul-tasting, hard-biting assassin bug (family Reduviidae), so predators leave them alone until they molt into the pink flower form. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymenopus_coronatus

question: James O'Hanlon set orchid mantises alone on plain green leaves, with no blossoms anywhere on them, beside beds of wild blooms in the field. Each pink-and-white mantis waited perfectly still, ready to ambush any bee, wasp or butterfly looking for nectar. Then he watched where the pollinators went. What happened?
answer: More pollinators flew to the fake mantis than to the real flowers
choices: More pollinators flew to the fake mantis than to the real flowers
The bees split about evenly between the mantis and the flowers
The bees ignored the mantis until it grew larger petal lobes
The mantis had to copy one orchid's scent to draw any bees
context: O'Hanlon's 2014 field experiments showed isolated mantises on plain leaves lured wild pollinators at a higher rate than real flowers growing nearby - the first confirmed case of an animal using floral mimicry as a lure, not just camouflage. Source: O'Hanlon, Holwell & Herberstein 2014, 'Pollinator Deception in the Orchid Mantis', The American Naturalist 183(1); https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/673858

question: An orchid mantis sat on its perch with the petal-shaped lobes trimmed from its legs, and insects still flew in and got caught. James O'Hanlon had cut the lobes away to test the old idea that they lure bees and flies in close. What does he now suspect the petal legs are really for?
answer: Hiding the mantis from its own predators
choices: Hiding the mantis from its own predators
Signalling health to rival mantises
Sweeping pollen loose to eat off the leg
Cushioning the mantis when it drops off a branch
context: When O'Hanlon removed or rearranged the petal-shaped leg lobes, pollinators still approached - suggesting the famous 'petals' may not lure prey at all, but instead help hide the mantis from its own predators. Source: https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/unraveling-the-orchid-mantis-mystery/

question: Up to nine feet tall and around 300 pounds, an ostrich strides across the African plains. Two big feathery wings fold on its back, yet it never once leaves the ground. What keeps this giant grounded?
answer: A breastbone too flat to anchor flight muscles
choices: A breastbone too flat to anchor flight muscles
Wing joints fused stiff so they cannot flap
Bones so hollow they snap under strain
A heart too weak to fuel flapping flight
context: The ostrich is the largest and heaviest living bird: males stand up to 9 feet tall and weigh 220-287 pounds, with some sources reporting 300+ lb. It is flightless because its flattened sternum (breastbone) has no keel to anchor flight muscles. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).

question: A lion chases an ostrich across the open savanna, and the biggest bird alive, unable to fly, leaves it behind on huge striding legs. In a full sprint, about how fast can an ostrich run?
answer: Around 43 mph
choices: Around 43 mph
Around 15 mph
Around 25 mph
Around 60 mph
context: The ostrich is the fastest running bird in the world. It can sprint up to 43 mph (70 km/h) in short bursts and hold a steady cruising speed around 31 mph (50 km/h) over distance. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).

question: On the dry African grassland, an ostrich hen settles a single pale egg into her shallow nest: the largest egg of any living bird. How many ordinary chicken eggs would it take to match that one egg?
answer: About two dozen
choices: About two dozen
About three
About eight
About fifty
context: The ostrich lays the largest egg of any living bird: about 3 pounds (1,500 g) and 6 inches long, roughly the weight of 24 chicken eggs in one shell. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).

question: An ostrich lays an egg about the size of a small pineapple, yet its shell is only about 3.5 millimeters thick, thinner than a short stack of coins. Its curved dome still holds a startling load before it cracks. About how much weight can the shell bear pressing straight down?
answer: Enough for a grown adult to stand on it
choices: Enough for a grown adult to stand on it
Barely the weight of a sparrow
No more than a stack of paper
Only the chick's own body weight
context: An ostrich eggshell is only about 3.5 mm thick but strong enough that a grown adult can stand on it without breaking it. It can bear roughly 220 kg pressing straight down. Source: Birdfact (birdfact.com/articles/largest-bird-eggs).

question: Danger nears an ostrich on the open African plain. The old tale says the frightened bird buries its head in the sand, but it never does. What does an ostrich really do to hide?
answer: Flattens to the ground so it looks like a low mound
choices: Flattens to the ground so it looks like a low mound
Crouches low and sprints in a zigzag for cover
Sidles behind the nearest bush and holds still
Presses flat against a termite mound and freezes
context: The head-in-sand story is a myth; an ostrich cannot breathe underground. What it really does is flop flat and press its long neck and head to the ground so its body blends into the dirt and looks like a low mound from a distance. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).

question: Fleeing lions and hyenas, an ostrich sprints on long, powerful legs, its feet pared right down for speed. Nearly every other bird alive grips the ground with three or four toes on each foot; the ostrich is the one exception. How many toes does each ostrich foot carry?
answer: Just two
choices: Just two
Only one
Four spread wide
Three, like most birds
context: The ostrich is the ONLY bird on Earth with just two toes per foot; every other bird has three or more. One toe is huge and the smaller second toe acts as an 'outrigger' to keep balance. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants; scienceinschool.org/article/2011/ostrich.

question: Two glossy dark eyes, each almost two inches across and rimmed with long lashes, look out from an ostrich's small feathered head: the largest eyes of any land animal. Each eye is so big it outsizes one particular thing inside the ostrich itself. What is it?
answer: Its own brain
choices: Its own brain
Its entire foot
A grown man's fist
One of its own eggs
context: The ostrich has the largest eye of any land animal, almost 2 inches (5 cm) across. Each eyeball is actually bigger than its own brain. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).

question: Cornered in the open by a hyena or a lion, an ostrich does not turn and flee. It swings around and strikes forward with one foot, tipped with a dagger-like claw. Its kick has a fearsome reputation, often repeated though hard to verify. What is one kick said to be able to do to a lion?
answer: Kill it outright
choices: Kill it outright
Merely bruise it
Trip it long enough to escape
Frighten it with the noise
context: When cornered, an ostrich defends itself with a forward kick from its clawed foot said to be powerful enough to kill a lion. The claw can act like a knife; the kick is its main weapon against big predators. This lion-killing reputation is often repeated but is difficult to verify, so it is framed here as reputation rather than established fact. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).  (Legend.)

question: The ancestors of every person alive today walked the cold world of the last ice age, and they were not the only humans in it. Other kinds of human, close cousins of their line, roamed beside them. Which of these was a real, separate kind of human that shared the planet with them?
answer: The Neanderthals of Europe and western Asia
choices: The Neanderthals of Europe and western Asia
The last surviving Australopithecus troops
The Homo habilis toolmakers of East Africa
The robust Paranthropus of southern Africa
context: During the last ice age at least two close cousins shared the planet with the ancestors of living humans: the Neanderthals of Europe and western Asia, and the mysterious Denisovans of Asia. Australopithecus, Homo habilis and Paranthropus had all died out long before. Source: Smithsonian Human Origins Program, humanorigins.si.edu; Max Planck Institute, mpg.de/5018269/denisovan-genome.

question: Stocky and strong, Neanderthals lived across Europe and western Asia in the deep cold of the last ice age, their bodies shaped for the frozen world. One feature of a Neanderthal face was strikingly broad and wide compared with a modern human's. Which feature was it?
answer: The nose
choices: The nose
The ears
The chin
The forehead
context: Neanderthals' big wide noses are thought to have warmed and moistened the frigid ice-age air they breathed, part of a body built for the cold. Source: Natural History Museum, 'Who were the Neanderthals?', nhm.ac.uk/discover/who-were-the-neanderthals.html.

question: Old-time cartoonists drew the Neanderthals, the ice-age cousins of modern humans who lived across Europe and western Asia, as dim, slouching 'ape-men' with tiny minds, barely thinking at all. Then scientists measured a Neanderthal braincase against a modern human's. What did they find?
answer: It was as large as a modern human's, often larger
choices: It was as large as a modern human's, often larger
It was roughly half a modern human's size
It had no room for a frontal lobe at all
It was identical to a chimpanzee's in size
context: A Neanderthal's brain was just as large as a modern human's, and often a bit larger, held in a long, low skull with a heavy brow ridge above the eyes. Source: Smithsonian Human Origins Program, humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/human-fossils/species/homo-neanderthalensis.

question: Neanderthal hunters brought down woolly mammoths, giant bison and cave bears by driving long spears into them up close, again and again. Their fossil skeletons carry a telling mark of that dangerous close-in work. What do the bones of grown Neanderthal hunters show?
answer: Broken bones like the injuries of modern rodeo riders
choices: Broken bones like the injuries of modern rodeo riders
Teeth worn perfectly smooth from eating only grass
Fingers fused together into flipper-like paddles
Skulls thickened into a solid bony helmet
context: Neanderthals were skilled toolmakers and big-game hunters who thrust spears into large animals at close range, so often that their skeletons show broken bones like the injuries of modern rodeo riders. Source: Smithsonian Human Origins Program, humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/human-fossils/species/homo-neanderthalensis.

question: In Denisova Cave, deep in the mountains of Siberia, scientists made one small find in 2008. When Svante Paabo's team decoded the DNA inside it in 2010, it revealed a whole new kind of human, a lost sister group to the Neanderthals. What had they found?
answer: A single tiny finger bone
choices: A single tiny finger bone
A complete lower jaw
A footprint pressed in mud
A painted handprint on the wall
context: The Denisovans were discovered not from a skeleton but from a single tiny finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia in 2008, whose genome was read in 2010 by Svante Paabo's team at the Max Planck Institute. Source: Max Planck Institute, mpg.de/5018269/denisovan-genome; Nobel Prize 2022 press release.

question: Modern humans did more than live near the Neanderthals: they met them and interbred. A geneticist read the DNA of a living man whose family roots lie outside Africa and searched it for the mark of that ancient mixing. What did she find?
answer: Roughly 1 to 4 percent Neanderthal DNA
choices: Roughly 1 to 4 percent Neanderthal DNA
Roughly 20 to 25 percent Neanderthal DNA
DNA from Homo erectus, but none from Neanderthals
No archaic trace at all, only in ancient fossils
context: The ancestors of modern humans met and interbred with both cousins, so most people alive today outside Africa carry a small slice of Neanderthal DNA, roughly 1 to 4 percent of their genome. Source: Max Planck Institute, mpg.de/5018269/denisovan-genome; Science, science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aad9416.

question: High on the Tibetan Plateau, the thin air holds far less oxygen than lowlands, yet Tibetans thrive there. Scientists traced part of their edge to a version of the EPAS1 gene inherited long ago from an extinct cousin. From which cousin did that high-altitude gene come?
answer: The Denisovans
choices: The Denisovans
The Neanderthals
Homo erectus
The Australopithecines
context: A version of the EPAS1 gene inherited from Denisovans helps Tibetans thrive in the thin high-altitude air. It is common in Tibetans but turns up only at very low frequency in their Han Chinese neighbours. Source: Huerta-Sanchez et al., Nature 2014, nature.com/articles/nature13408; PNAS, pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2020803118.

question: A teenage girl died about 90,000 years ago, and a small piece of her bone lay in Siberia's Denisova Cave until scientists dug it up. When Svante Paabo's team read her DNA, the part she got only from her mother was Neanderthal, and her main genome was almost exactly half Neanderthal and half Denisovan. What did that make her?
answer: A first-generation child of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father
choices: A first-generation child of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father
A late Neanderthal whose people had drifted north into Denisovan land
An early Denisovan carrying leftover Neanderthal genes from long ago
A modern human ancestor caught midway between the two older cousins
context: Nicknamed 'Denny,' this ~13-year-old girl was identified in 2018 from a single ~2 cm bone fragment (Denisova 11). Her mitochondrial DNA (inherited only from the mother) was Neanderthal, while her nuclear genome was almost exactly half Neanderthal and half Denisovan, meaning one parent was a Neanderthal and the other a Denisovan. She remains the only confirmed first-generation hybrid of two distinct human groups ever found, showing that when these cousins met, they could interbreed directly, not just with modern humans. Source: Slon, Mafessoni, Paabo et al., 'The genome of the offspring of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father,' Nature 561:113-116 (2018), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0455-x ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denny_(hybrid_hominin)

question: Scientists who mapped Denisovan DNA in people alive today found it spread very unevenly across the world. Most people carry little or none of it, yet in one region it piles up far above the rest. In whose genomes does it pile up?
answer: Papuans, Aboriginal Australians and other Melanesians
choices: Papuans, Aboriginal Australians and other Melanesians
Northern Europeans descended from the first cave painters
Peoples of the Siberian plains around Denisova Cave itself
East African groups near humanity's first homeland
context: Melanesians, Papuans/New Guineans and Aboriginal Australians carry roughly 4-6% Denisovan ancestry, by far the most of any human population, and a 2021 study found the Aeta Magbukon of the Philippines carry the highest known proportion of all. Most other populations carry little or none. This is a sharp contrast to the ~1-4% Neanderthal DNA shared by most non-Africans, and it maps onto where Denisovans and modern humans actually met in Ice Age Asia, far from the Siberian cave where the first Denisovan bones were found. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denisovan ; Larena et al. 2021 (Aeta Magbukon highest Denisovan ancestry), Current Biology; https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2405889121

question: On a moonless night in a farmer's field, a mouse rustles through fallen leaves after seeds. A round-faced night hunter with huge forward-facing eyes swoops down out of the black sky and snatches it in its talons. What bird is this famous night raptor?
answer: An owl
choices: An owl
A hummingbird
A pelican
A flamingo
context: Owls are the classic round-faced, forward-eyed nocturnal raptors, built to hunt in darkness. Source: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds.

question: A mouse in a dark field has sharp ears, and the swoosh of a hunting bird's wings usually warns it to bolt. When an owl attacks at night, the mouse hears no sound before the talons close. What is uncanny about how an owl flies?
answer: It flies almost completely silently
choices: It flies almost completely silently
It flies faster than any other bird
It glows faintly in the dark
It flies backward toward prey
context: An owl's wingbeats make so little noise that a mouse never hears it coming. Source: Audubon Magazine, 'The Silent Flight of Owls, Explained.'
