question: A duck's wings whistle as it flies overhead, yet a hunting owl crosses the dark with hardly a sound. Along the very front edge of each owl wing feather sits something that a duck's feathers lack. What is it?
answer: Tiny comb-like serrations
choices: Tiny comb-like serrations
A stiff bony ridge
A coat of waterproof oil
A row of hooked claws
context: Comb-like serrations on the leading edge break up the turbulent air that would otherwise make a swooshing sound. Source: Audubon Magazine, 'The Silent Flight of Owls, Explained.'

question: A hunting owl glides through the night on wings that barely make a sound. Krista Le Piane, comparing 70 species of owl, found that this silence does more than let the owl sneak up on a mouse. What else does quiet flight buy the hunting owl?
answer: Its ears stay free to track the prey's rustling
choices: Its ears stay free to track the prey's rustling
Its wings never tire on long flights
It stays invisible to other owls
It can fly through heavy rain unbothered
context: With almost no wing noise of its own, the owl's ears keep tracking the prey's faint rustling in the dark. Krista Le Piane's analysis of 70 owl species. Source: Audubon Magazine.

question: A white-faced barn owl hunts in almost total darkness, mostly by sound. It can tell whether a mouse's tiny rustle came from higher up or lower down, not just from the left or the right. One strange feature makes that possible. What is odd about a barn owl's head?
answer: Its two ear openings are offset, one higher than the other
choices: Its two ear openings are offset, one higher than the other
Its ears are hidden inside its beak
Its ears can be folded shut in the cold
Its ears glow to attract prey
context: The left ear opening sits higher and points down, the right sits lower and points up. This lopsided arrangement helps it place a sound in three dimensions. Source: Cornell Lab, All About Birds; Wikipedia, 'Sound localization in owls.'

question: In pitch dark, a barn owl knows a rustle came from the left or the right because the sound reaches one ear a hair before the other. Judging whether the sound came from above or below is a much harder puzzle. What cue does the owl use to place a sound high or low?
answer: How much louder the sound is in one ear than the other
choices: How much louder the sound is in one ear than the other
The pitch of the sound
The delay of its echo
The gap in arrival timing
context: Left-vs-right comes from which ear a sound reaches first, by millionths of a second; up-vs-down comes from which ear it's louder in. Sounds from below are louder in the lower-pointing left ear, from above louder in the right. Two different cues, timing and loudness, working together. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sound localization in owls.'

question: Hunting in near-total darkness, an owl leans on its ears as much as its eyes to find a mouse under the leaves. The owl's flat, round face is no wise-looking mask but a stiff dish of feathers set in a shallow bowl. What job does that facial disc do?
answer: It funnels sound waves toward the ear openings
choices: It funnels sound waves toward the ear openings
It dampens the noise of the owl's own wingbeats
It shields the eyes from bright sun
It keeps rain off the beak
context: The concave facial disc collects sound waves and funnels them to the ear openings, like a satellite dish. Source: Wikipedia, 'Facial disc'; 'Sound localization in owls.'

question: A field mouse tunnels beneath a foot of fresh snow, completely out of sight. A barn owl glides overhead on wide white wings, then folds them and drops, punching through the crust at the exact spot where the hidden mouse is running. How does the owl pin down a target it never sees?
answer: By hearing alone
choices: By hearing alone
By its keen sense of smell
By sensing the mouse's body heat
By feeling ground vibrations
context: A barn owl can pinpoint the exact 3-D spot of a mouse under a foot of snow guided by hearing alone, with no view of its target. Legendary but documented. Source: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds.

question: Enormous tubular eyes take up most of an owl's skull, gathering every scrap of moonlight in a dark forest. Yet the owl cannot glance sideways the way a person can: to look off to one side, it swings its whole head around. Why can't an owl simply roll its eyes?
answer: A ring of bone locks its huge eyes in place
choices: A ring of bone locks its huge eyes in place
Its eyes are too small to aim
It sees only straight ahead by instinct
Bright light freezes its eyes open
context: An owl's eyes are so huge and tube-shaped that they're locked by a ring of bone (the sclerotic ring) and can't roll in their sockets at all, so it must turn its whole head to look around. Source: California Academy of Sciences, 'The (Bird) Eyes Have It.'

question: Unlike a cat, an owl cannot roll or swivel its huge, forward-facing eyes, so to look around it swings its whole head instead. About how far can an owl turn its head?
answer: About 270 degrees, three-quarters of a full circle
choices: About 270 degrees, three-quarters of a full circle
A full 360 degrees, all the way around
About 90 degrees, a quarter turn
About 45 degrees, barely to the shoulder
context: An owl rotates its head up to about 270 degrees to either side. Legendary but true; the 'full circle' myth is false. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Solving the Mystery of Owls' Head-Turning Abilities' (Johns Hopkins study).

question: To watch a mouse behind it, an owl swivels its head around, a turn that would pinch shut the neck arteries and starve the brain of almost any other animal. Yet the owl's arteries come through unharmed, thanks to a piece of bony engineering wrapped around each one. What lets the vessels survive the turn?
answer: The bone channels around them are about ten times wider than the arteries
choices: The bone channels around them are about ten times wider than the arteries
The arteries pump blood in short bursts
A second heart sits in the neck
The blood carries built-in antifreeze
context: An owl has 14 neck vertebrae (humans have 7), and the bony holes around its neck arteries are about ten times wider than the arteries themselves, giving the vessels room to twist. Source: Smithsonian Magazine (Johns Hopkins CT/angiography study, 2013).

question: An owl cranks its neck nearly all the way around, and its brain must stay fed with oxygen the whole time. A team at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore ran dye into owls' arteries, then scanned the birds in a computed tomography scanner as they turned their heads. Where did the blood go?
answer: Into reservoirs at the base of the skull
choices: Into reservoirs at the base of the skull
Straight back down into the heart
Out to the wingtips for storage
Into the hollow bones of the legs
context: Scientists injected dye into owls' arteries and CT-scanned them as the necks turned, finding blood pools in reservoirs at the skull base that keep the brain supplied during the twist. Source: Smithsonian Magazine; phys.org (2013).

question: An owl drops out of the night sky and seizes a struggling rat in its four sharp talons. Its foot muscles could get tired holding on for the flight home — but they don't need to. Something inside the owl's foot clamps the talons closed and keeps them locked, almost without any effort from the bird. What clicks the talons closed and holds them there?
answer: A locking tendon that ratchets the grip shut
choices: A locking tendon that ratchets the grip shut
A sticky pad on each talon
A set of tiny hooks along the toes
A suction cup in the sole
context: When an owl grabs prey, its outer toe swings back so two talons point forward and two back, then a locking tendon ratchets the grip shut, clamping without any muscle effort. Source: The Owl Pages, 'Owl Feet & Talons.'

question: Christopher Clark studied exactly where the velvet on an owl's feathers grows densest. Scientists still argue over what that velvety surface is for: Kroeger and Lilley's long-dominant camp says it smooths the airflow over the wing. What does Clark, reviving an idea from 1934, say it mainly does?
answer: It muffles the noise of feathers scraping against each other
choices: It muffles the noise of feathers scraping against each other
It smooths the airflow rushing over the wing surface
It traps warm air to keep the flight muscles from stiffening
It scatters the moonlight so the owl casts no moving shadow
context: How an owl's feathers actually kill the sound is still a live scientific debate. The long-dominant view (Kroeger, Lilley) holds that the leading-edge comb and downy velvet reduce AERODYNAMIC noise by smoothing airflow and keeping the boundary layer attached over the wing. A competing hypothesis (Christopher Clark, reviving Graham's 1934 idea) points out that the velvety 'pennulae' and vane fringes are best developed exactly where one feather rubs against the next, arguing they mainly muffle STRUCTURAL, frictional noise from feather-on-feather contact during flapping rather than airflow noise. The two camps disagree over what the velvet is even for. Source: PMC 'Evolution and Ecology of Silent Flight in Owls' (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7671161/) - Clark vs. Kroeger/Lilley; Graham (1934).

question: A shy insect-eater shuffles through the forests of Africa and Asia, armored head to tail in hard, overlapping plates like a walking pine cone. The plates are keratin, the same stuff as a person's fingernails, though almost every other mammal wears fur or bare skin. Which animal is it?
answer: The pangolin
choices: The pangolin
The armadillo
The porcupine
The hedgehog
context: The pangolin is the only mammal covered in scales. Armadillos wear bony plates under their skin; porcupines and hedgehogs bristle with modified hairs. Only the pangolin's coat is true keratin scales. Source: https://www.savepangolins.org/what-is-a-pangolin/

question: A hungry leopard closes in on a pangolin in the forest. The shy, scale-armored ant-eater does not run, and it does not fight back; instead it does the one thing its Malay name describes. What does the pangolin do?
answer: Curls into a tight armored ball, tucking its soft belly inside
choices: Curls into a tight armored ball, tucking its soft belly inside
Freezes flat and plays dead until the danger passes
Sprays a jet of stinging venom from its snout
Puffs itself up huge with swallowed air
context: 'Penggulung' means 'one who rolls up.' The scaled back and tail wrap around the vulnerable belly and face, leaving nothing soft exposed. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/facts-about-pangolins

question: A whole pride of African lions surrounds a pangolin, a shy, scale-covered mammal about the size of a house cat. The lions paw at it, bat it back and forth in the dust, and try again and again to sink their teeth through its overlapping scales. How does the standoff end?
answer: The lions give up and walk away, leaving the pangolin unharmed
choices: The lions give up and walk away, leaving the pangolin unharmed
One lion finally cracks the shell and the pride feeds
The pangolin bolts free the moment the lions tire
The pangolin is crushed under the pride's combined weight
context: A rolled pangolin's overlapping keratin scales are tough enough that even a full pride cannot bite through. Frustrated, the lions simply move on. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/facts-about-pangolins

question: A pangolin rips open termite mounds with front claws so long and curved that they are wonderful for digging but clumsy on the ground. Walking flat-footed would drag those precious claws through the dirt and wear them down. To keep them safe, how does the pangolin often get around?
answer: It walks upright on its two hind legs, holding its arms and tail up for balance
choices: It walks upright on its two hind legs, holding its arms and tail up for balance
It drags itself forward on its belly like a seal
It knuckle-walks on the backs of its curled front paws
It hops with both hind feet together like a kangaroo
context: The three big digging claws on each front paw are useless for walking, so a pangolin often rears up and strides on its hind legs, tail and forelimbs raised as a counterweight. Source: https://africageographic.com/stories/fascinating-pangolin-facts/

question: Ants and termites are a pangolin's whole diet, yet it has no teeth at all and cannot chew a single insect. To reach the bugs deep inside a nest's tunnels, it uncoils an extraordinarily long tongue coated in thick, sticky saliva. In a big pangolin, how far can that tongue stretch?
answer: Up to about 40 cm (16 in), longer than its own head and body
choices: Up to about 40 cm (16 in), longer than its own head and body
Up to about 10 cm (4 in), like a house cat's
Up to about 1 m (3 ft), trailing on the ground
Just past its own lips, a few centimeters
context: A big pangolin's tongue can reach 40 cm, sometimes longer than its head and body combined, gluing ants and termites to it inside their tunnels. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangolin

question: Thousands of biting, stinging insects swarm at a pangolin's face each time it tears a termite nest apart with its long claws. Before it strikes, it protects itself in a way most other mammals cannot. What does the pangolin do?
answer: It clamps its ears and nostrils shut with strong muscles
choices: It clamps its ears and nostrils shut with strong muscles
It coats its face in a thick layer of mud first
It attacks only at night when the insects are asleep
It smears itself with the nest's own scent to hide
context: Muscles let a pangolin seal its ears and nostrils closed, keeping swarming ants out while it laps up as many as 20,000 in a single day. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/facts-about-pangolins

question: A pangolin walking the forests and savannas of Africa and Asia swallows its ants whole, for it has no teeth at all, yet somehow it grinds up their crunchy shells inside its body. It manages this with a trick a chicken would recognize. How does a pangolin's stomach break down its food?
answer: Swallowed stones churn in a muscular gizzard-like stomach lined with keratin spines
choices: Swallowed stones churn in a muscular gizzard-like stomach lined with keratin spines
Powerful acid dissolves the shells completely within minutes
A second set of throat teeth crushes the ants on the way down
It regurgitates and re-swallows each meal to soften it
context: With no teeth, a pangolin swallows small stones (gastroliths) that collect in a muscular, keratin-spined stomach and grind the insects up, exactly the way a bird's gizzard works. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangolin

question: A male peacock spider, a tiny Australian jumping spider, faces a female and lifts his back end straight up into the air. He opens something he normally keeps tucked against his body and waves it slowly at her like a flag, the show that gave his kind its name. What does he unfurl?
answer: A fan of brilliantly colored flaps
choices: A fan of brilliantly colored flaps
A sticky net of silk threads
A pair of transparent gliding wings
A cluster of glowing light organs
context: The male raises his abdomen and spreads a fan of vividly colored flaps, waving it like a peacock fanning its tail — which is exactly how the peacock spider got its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans

question: Dazzling blues, reds and oranges flash in the courtship display of the male peacock spider of Australia, one of the most brilliant in the animal world. Yet finding one in the wild is famously hard. How big is a peacock spider?
answer: About the size of a grain of rice
choices: About the size of a grain of rice
About the size of a jellybean
About the size of a housefly
About the size of a ladybug
context: Both males and females are only about 5 mm long — roughly a grain of rice — yet the male packs a dazzling courtship display onto that tiny frame. Their size hid them from science for years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans

question: A tiny male peacock spider dances before a watching female, every step of his courtship show done with great care, because the stakes for him are high. If his performance fails to impress her, what may the female spider do to him?
answer: Attack, kill, and eat him
choices: Attack, kill, and eat him
Trap him in her web for days
Sting him with venom to paralyze him
Chase him off her patch of ground
context: An unimpressed female may attack, kill, and eat the male — and she may even do it after mating. That deadly stakes-raising is why the dance has to be so spectacular. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans

question: In the Australian bush, a male peacock spider throws his whole body into courting a female, dancing and flashing his bright colors. Beyond that show, he opens a second, private channel to her. What is the other signal he sends?
answer: Vibrations she feels through her legs
choices: Vibrations she feels through her legs
Puffs of scent drifting on the breeze
High-pitched chirps only she can hear
Quick flashes of light bounced off the soil
context: As he dances, the male drums the ground with his abdomen, sending vibrations through the surface that the female picks up through her legs. Scientists named the three vibration types rumble-rumps, crunch-rolls, and grind-revs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans

question: On a sunlit leaf in Australia, a male peacock spider fans out the colorful flap on his back and dances for a female. Part of the fan is an ultra-black patch that reflects less than half a percent of light, darker than most black paint, yet no dark pigment makes it. What swallows the light?
answer: Tiny lens-like bumps on the cuticle that trap it
choices: Tiny lens-like bumps on the cuticle that trap it
A thin layer of black oil that soaks it up
Charcoal-like grains built into the scales
A living film of dark bacteria on the surface
context: The ultra-black comes from microscopic dome-shaped bumps on the cuticle, about 6 micrometers tall, that act like tiny lenses and trap incoming light — reflecting as little as 0.35% in Maratus karrie. No black pigment is involved. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6532503/

question: A courting male peacock spider raises the brilliant fan on his back, and its blues flash and shift as he moves, the way a soap bubble shimmers or a peacock feather changes color when tilted. There is no blue paint or blue dye on him at all. How does the spider make that blue?
answer: Nanostructures on its scales that bend light
choices: Nanostructures on its scales that bend light
A dye it absorbs from the insects it eats
Blue pigment cells packed under its skin
Trapped air bubbles beneath its shell
context: The blue is structural color: microscopic nanostructures on the scales bend and reflect just the right wavelength of light — the same physics behind a soap bubble's shimmer — rather than any pigment. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6532503/

question: A crow-sized bird cruises at between 25 and 34 miles an hour, no faster than a car in a school zone, then tucks its wings and drops like a stone at over 200 miles an hour, faster than any animal alive. Which bird is it?
answer: The peregrine falcon
choices: The peregrine falcon
The golden eagle
The great horned owl
The common raven
context: In its diving plunge the peregrine falcon is the fastest animal alive, far faster than any sprinting cheetah. Source: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds; Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'.

question: On city skyscrapers, rocky sea cliffs, windy tundra and hot desert canyons, peregrine falcons raise their young on almost every continent. Only one land has no peregrines at all. Which continent does the peregrine skip?
answer: Antarctica
choices: Antarctica
Australia
South America
Africa
context: Found on every continent except Antarctica, the peregrine is the world's most widespread bird of prey. Source: Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'.

question: Spotting a pigeon, a duck or a gull, a hunting peregrine falcon climbs high above it and then dives at hundreds of miles an hour. Those birds and songbirds are its usual prey. Where does the peregrine's strike happen?
answer: In mid-air, out of the sky
choices: In mid-air, out of the sky
In shallow water
In tree branches
On open ground
context: The peregrine hunts other birds on the wing, striking them out of the sky rather than catching prey on the ground. Source: Science.org; All About Birds.

question: Peregrine falcons once nested only on remote sea cliffs and mountain crags. Over the last fifty years they have spread into the hearts of cities like New York and Chicago, raising chicks on cathedrals, tall bridges and skyscraper ledges. What drew these wild cliff-hunters downtown?
answer: Flocks of city pigeons to hunt
choices: Flocks of city pigeons to hunt
Warmth rising off the pavement
Fewer eagles competing there
Bright lights that lure insects
context: Peregrines nest on skyscraper ledges and bridges where flocks of city pigeons give them an endless food supply. Source: Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'; All About Birds.

question: A peregrine falcon ready to lay her eggs gathers no twigs, weaves no grass and carries nothing home at all, the way so many birds do. What does a peregrine use for a nest?
answer: A shallow scrape in the gravel
choices: A shallow scrape in the gravel
A hollow in a tall cactus
A burrow dug in a sandbank
A bare fork in a treetop
context: A peregrine scrapes a shallow depression in gravel or soil on a high ledge and lays its eggs right there — the whole 'nest' is just a scratched-out dip. Source: All About Birds Life History; Wikipedia.

question: Farmers across North America sprayed the pesticide DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) on their fields after World War II to kill mosquitoes and crop bugs. The chemical climbed the food chain into peregrine falcons that ate poisoned birds and mice, and by the 1960s not one peregrine was breeding anywhere in the eastern United States. What had DDT done to their eggs?
answer: Thinned the shells so they cracked
choices: Thinned the shells so they cracked
Turned the yolks toxic to the chicks
Made the parents abandon them cold
Kept them from ever being fertilized
context: DDT thinned peregrine eggshells until eggs cracked under the parents' weight; by the 1960s the peregrine had vanished from the whole eastern U.S. Source: Wikipedia; Audubon 'Remembering Tom Cade'.

question: A peregrine falcon dives at over 200 miles an hour, and the wall of air slamming into its face should be enough to burst its lungs. Yet it breathes easily the whole way down, thanks to a small cone of bone inside each nostril. What does that cone do to the rushing air?
answer: Spins it into a slowed spiral
choices: Spins it into a slowed spiral
Warms it before the lungs
Filters the dust from it
Splits it into two streams
context: The bony tubercle (a baffle) in each nostril spins the rushing air into a spiral and slows it down, so the falcon can breathe at dive speed. Some jet-engine designers study it. Source: ResearchGate; Curious Sengi summaries.

question: High over a valley, a peregrine falcon spots a pigeon far below and folds its wings into a hunting dive called a 'stoop.' Hurtling downward at more than 200 miles per hour with the target locked in its sight, the falcon still needs to keep its eyes wet, clean, and in sharp focus at that killing speed. What sweeps across each eye during the plunge to protect it?
answer: A see-through third eyelid
choices: A see-through third eyelid
A clear sheet of skin from below
A slick of clear tear-fluid
A clear inner lens that slides up
context: The nictitating membrane, a transparent third eyelid, sweeps across each eye during the dive, wiping it clear while the falcon keeps its target in focus. Source: Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'.

question: Chasing prey flat-out in level flight, a peregrine falcon reaches only about 69 mph. But in 1999 a trained falcon named Frightful was dropped from a Cessna at 17,000 feet to chase her skydiving falconer as a lure, a chip on her back clocking the fastest bird dive ever measured. How fast did that plunge go?
answer: 242 mph
choices: 242 mph
210 mph
186 mph
273 mph
context: Frightful's 242 mph (389 km/h) dive is the fastest ever measured for a bird — more than triple her flat-out level-flight chase. Source: Guinness World Records; Smithsonian Magazine 'Falling with the Falcon'.

question: Tom Cade of Cornell set out in 1970 to bring the peregrine falcon back from near-extinction. His team raised captive-bred chicks in towers until they could fly and hunt free, and the people who fed them always stayed out of sight. Why did the feeders hide?
answer: So the chicks would not grow tame around people
choices: So the chicks would not grow tame around people
So the chicks would not catch diseases from people
So the chicks would not be frightened off the towers
So the chicks would not beg for food all day long
context: Cade's team used 'hacking': the young falcons were fed with as little human contact as possible, so they would not grow tame or come to rely on people, and they fledged and learned to hunt on their own. Released peregrines were breeding in the wild by 1980, and in 1999 the bird came off the U.S. endangered list. Source: Audubon 'Remembering Tom Cade'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacking_(falconry)

question: Scientists set a model of a diving peregrine falcon in a wind tunnel and turned the fans up to diving speed. Its shape turned out to be one of the sleekest in nature. Yet on a real falcon's back there are spots where fast air would normally tear away from the surface and drag the bird back. What keeps the flow smooth there?
answer: Tiny back feathers pop up to keep the air clinging on
choices: Tiny back feathers pop up to keep the air clinging on
It seals every feather flat into a single glassy skin
It sheds a thin film of oil that lets the air slide by
It vents warm air through its nostrils to fill the gap
context: A wind-tunnel and computer-flow study of a life-sized diving-falcon model measured a drag coefficient as low as CD around 0.094 in the full stoop — among the most streamlined shapes in nature. But the low drag is not just the teardrop body: right where the airflow would separate, small body feathers pop up during the dive and act as passive flow-control devices — the same trick as the vortex generators (turbulators) on an aircraft wing — keeping the airflow attached and drag low at extreme speed. Source: Ponitz, Schmitz, Fischer, Bleckmann & Brucker, "Diving-Flight Aerodynamics of a Peregrine Falcon (Falco peregrinus)," PLOS ONE 9(2):e86506, 2014.

question: A stooping peregrine falcon does not aim at the spot where a dodging starling is. It curves, and the faster the line between hunter and prey swings, the harder it turns. Physics simulations at Oxford found this is the same steering rule engineers built into one famous machine. What guides the falcon the way it guides that machine?
answer: The homing law that steers a heat-seeking missile
choices: The homing law that steers a heat-seeking missile
The autopilot loop that holds an airliner on course
The spinning gyroscope inside a ship’s compass
The braking rhythm of a train easing into a curve
context: Physics-based flight simulations (Oxford; Mills, Hildenbrandt, Taylor & Hemelrijk, PLOS Computational Biology 2018) found the peregrine steers by proportional navigation — the same guidance law used by heat-seeking, homing missiles — turning at a rate proportional to how fast the line of sight to the target rotates. The simulated navigation constant N of about 2.6 to 3.0 matched the median N of 2.6 measured in real peregrines. The study also showed why the ultra-fast stoop matters: only at high speed can the falcon out-turn an erratically dodging bird like a starling; against straight-flying prey a slow, low attack actually worked better. Source: Mills, Hildenbrandt, Taylor & Hemelrijk, PLOS Comp. Biol. 2018.

question: Sensing a predator on the dry sand of central Argentina, a pink fairy armadillo, the smallest of all armadillos, drives its huge front claws into the ground. How long does it take to vanish completely beneath the sand?
answer: A matter of seconds
choices: A matter of seconds
About two minutes
About fifteen minutes
Almost a full hour
context: The pink fairy armadillo (Chlamyphorus truncatus) can bury itself completely in a matter of seconds, and it is said to burrow through loose ground as fast as a fish swims through water, which earned it the nickname 'sand-swimmer'. The smallest armadillo in the world, about 9 to 11.5 cm (3.5-4.5 in) long, it spends almost its whole life underground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_fairy_armadillo

question: Under the dry sandy plains of central Argentina, a palm-sized pink fairy armadillo burrows along. Its thin shell flushes a deeper rose-pink, then fades paler again, because a dense web of blood vessels lies just beneath the surface. What does the shell mainly do?
answer: dump or hold body heat like a radiator
choices: dump or hold body heat like a radiator
shield the animal from predators' teeth
store water for the dry desert
warn rivals away with a bright signal
context: By pushing more blood into the shell the armadillo flushes pink and sheds heat; by draining blood out, the shell pales and it keeps its warmth. The shell is a thermoregulating organ, not armor. Source: https://factanimal.com/pink-fairy-armadillo/

question: A pink fairy armadillo digs forward through the dry sands of Argentina, and its backside ends in a flat plate of armor facing straight backward, like a shield glued to its bottom. Most armadillos wear a shell wrapped around the whole body, but this one is different. What does the back plate let it do as it digs?
answer: press and pack the soil behind it, corking its tunnel
choices: press and pack the soil behind it, corking its tunnel
flip upside down to roll away downhill
scoop food up toward its mouth
reflect sunlight to stay cool underground
context: The flattened rear 'butt plate' tamps and compacts the loose soil behind the digging armadillo, shoring the tunnel against collapse and sealing (corking) the burrow behind it. Its close cousin, the greater fairy armadillo, may also block its burrow with its hindmost plates. Source: https://www.sciencenews.org/article/pink-armadillos-aint-your-texas-critters ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_fairy_armadillo

question: A pistol shrimp on a warm reef hunts without chasing anything. Its oversized claw, almost half its body length, slams shut with a violent snap, and a passing fish is stunned before the shrimp moves an inch. What crossed the water and hit the fish?
answer: A jet of water fired by the snap
choices: A jet of water fired by the snap
A sticky thread it lassoed the fish with
A cloud of ink squirted to blind it
A venom spine flicked from its tail
context: The claw itself never touches the prey — the snap shoots out a jet of water that stuns the victim from a distance. Source: Versluis et al., 'How Snapping Shrimp Snap: Through Cavitating Bubbles', Science 2000; https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2000/09/000922072104.htm

question: A pistol shrimp snaps its one huge claw shut with a blast loud enough to stun a passing fish. A weapon like that sounds as if it belongs to a giant. How long is a pistol shrimp, tip to tail?
answer: 3 to 5 cm (an adult's thumb)
choices: 3 to 5 cm (an adult's thumb)
30 to 40 cm (a forearm)
1 to 2 mm (a grain of rice)
70 to 90 cm (an arm's length)
context: Only about 3 to 5 cm (1.2 to 2 inches) long, yet it produces one of the most powerful sounds, by body size, of any animal. Source: Wikipedia 'Alpheidae'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpheidae

question: American submarine crews in World War II listened at their sonar sets for enemy ships and kept hearing a popping crackle across the seafloor, like a giant pan of frying bacon. Clever captains learned to hide their boats inside the loudest patches, where the racket covered their own engines. What was making all that noise?
answer: Colonies of snapping shrimp
choices: Colonies of snapping shrimp
Beds of grinding sea urchins
Schools of drumming croaker fish
Currents rattling loose gravel
context: Colonies snap in such a constant din that in WWII they jammed sonar and confused submarine-detection operators — and subs hid inside shrimp beds to avoid being heard. Source: ScienceDaily, 'Snapping Shrimp Drown Out Sonar' (Science 2000); https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2000/09/000922072104.htm

question: A nearly blind pistol shrimp digs and cleans a burrow in the sandy seafloor and shares it with a small, sharp-eyed goby that hovers at the entrance on guard. Out on the open sand, the shrimp cannot see the goby's face. How does it know the instant the goby spots danger and bolts inside?
answer: It keeps one long antenna touching the goby
choices: It keeps one long antenna touching the goby
It watches the goby's shadow on the sand
It listens for the goby's alarm clicks
It tastes stress chemicals the goby releases
context: The shrimp keeps an antenna on the goby's body; if the goby flicks its tail and darts in, the shrimp instantly feels the signal and dives too. Source: Divers Alert Network, 'Symbiosis on the Sand'; https://dan.org/alert-diver/article/symbiosis-on-the-sand/

question: The pistol shrimp's water jet alone does not quite explain its killing blow, scientists found. The jet moves so fast that it drops the water pressure behind it and creates something there, and that is the real weapon. What forms and then destroys the prey?
answer: A collapsing bubble that unleashes a shockwave
choices: A collapsing bubble that unleashes a shockwave
A whirlpool that drags prey into the claw
A spark that electrocutes the water
A spray of jagged ice crystals
context: The low pressure forms a vapor-filled cavitation bubble; when it collapses it slams out a shockwave that stuns or kills. Source: Versluis et al., Science 2000; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7525291/

question: A pistol shrimp has one giant snapping claw and one small ordinary claw, and its snap shoots a jet of water hard enough to stun a small fish. In a fight, an attacker tears off the big claw. Rather than simply regrowing the same weapon on the same side, what does its body do over the next molts?
answer: Its small claw becomes the new weapon; the stump regrows small
choices: Its small claw becomes the new weapon; the stump regrows small
It regrows the snapper twice as large as before
It grows a matching snapper on the other side, giving it two
It stays disarmed and switches to scavenging for life
context: The claws swap roles: the lost limb grows back as a small claw while the original small claw enlarges into a new snapping weapon. Source: Wikipedia 'Alpheidae'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpheidae

question: A pistol shrimp's claw snaps shut, and the jet of water it shoots is so fast that a tiny bubble forms and collapses inside it, which scientists call cavitation. The collapse makes a shockwave that stuns fish, and for a sliver of a second it also gives off a flash of light too faint for the naked eye. Researchers gave the glow a playful name. What is it?
answer: Shrimpoluminescence
choices: Shrimpoluminescence
Bioflash cavitation
Crustaceoglow
Snapfire radiance
context: Named because it resembles sonoluminescence — light from a collapsing bubble. Source: Lohse, Schmitz & Versluis, 'Snapping shrimp make flashing bubbles', Nature 2001; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11586346/

question: A pistol shrimp's snap creates a tiny cavitation bubble, a void in the water that collapses almost at once. In that instant the heat inside spikes to at least about 5,000 kelvin. What does that pinprick of heat very nearly match?
answer: The surface of the Sun
choices: The surface of the Sun
The core of a lightning bolt
Molten lava from a volcano
A blacksmith's forge fire
context: About 5,000 K (roughly 4,700 °C) — nearly the Sun's surface at about 5,772 K. Source: Wikipedia 'Alpheidae' (citing Lohse et al. 2001); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpheidae

question: Scientists in London opened a crate from Australia in 1799 and suspected a hoax. The stuffed animal inside had fur, a beaver's flat tail, a soft, rubbery bill like a duck's and webbed feet, and its males were said to carry venom. What was it?
answer: Platypus
choices: Platypus
Muskrat
Otter
Capybara
context: The platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) of eastern Australia is one of the strangest animals alive: fur and milk like a mammal, a bill and eggs like a bird, and venom to boot. Source: Australian Museum, australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/

question: Along a river in eastern Australia, a mother platypus does something that only five living kinds of mammal do. Mice, cats and humans never do it. What sets the five apart?
answer: Lay eggs
choices: Lay eggs
Change sex
Breathe through skin
Live entirely underwater
context: These five are the monotremes. The platypus curls around one or two leathery eggs and incubates them for about ten days before they hatch. Source: Australian Museum, australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/

question: A newly hatched platypus, no bigger than a jellybean, needs its mother's milk like any baby mammal. Yet its mother has no nipples at all, nothing for the tiny baby to latch onto. How does the baby get its milk?
answer: Milk seeps through skin pores onto furry belly patches
choices: Milk seeps through skin pores onto furry belly patches
The mother regurgitates food into its mouth
It drinks river water rich in nutrients
It suckles milk from a slit in the mother's belly
context: The platypus's mammary glands are modified sweat glands, so milk seeps out through skin pores onto two furry patches where the young lap it up. Source: BBC Science Focus, sciencefocus.com/nature/do-platypuses-really-sweat-milk; Australian Museum

question: A platypus noses along a muddy riverbed and goes straight for a shrimp, though the shrimp gives off no smell it could follow. In 1986 Henning Scheich fooled one with a lifeless plastic shrimp full of wires, which it struck as if alive. What does a platypus bill pick up from its prey?
answer: The faint electric currents from the prey's twitching muscles
choices: The faint electric currents from the prey's twitching muscles
The warmth of the prey's body
The vibration of the prey's heartbeat
The color of the prey against the mud
context: About 40,000 electroreceptors pack the platypus's bill, sensing the tiny electric fields thrown off by a hidden animal's moving muscles. Hunting underwater with its eyes, ears and nose sealed, it relies on that electric sense plus touch-sensitive 'push rods' in the bill. Henning Scheich's platypus struck at a lure carrying only a faint electric signal, proving electroreception; the receptors respond to signals as weak as ~20 microvolts per square centimeter. Source: American Museum of Natural History, amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/platypus-electroreception-hunting; Australian Platypus Conservancy, platypus.asn.au/the-platypus-bill-push-rods-and-electroreception/

question: A shrimp flicks its tail on a dark riverbed, and two signals race to a platypus's bill: a fast one, and a slower pressure wave felt by touch-sensitive push rods. Jack Pettigrew, in 1998, argued that the platypus times the gap between them. What does the gap tell it?
answer: How far away the prey is
choices: How far away the prey is
How large the prey is
Which direction the current flows
How fast the water moves
context: Electricity races through water faster than a pressure wave travels, so a shrimp's tail-flick reaches the platypus's electric sensors a split-second before its touch-sensitive push rods. The delay between the two senses encodes distance, letting the platypus range its target like a stopwatch in total darkness. Source: Pettigrew et al. 1998; Pettigrew 1999, Journal of Experimental Biology; Australian Platypus Conservancy.

question: Two male platypuses wrestle in a river in the mating season, when their venom is at its strongest. Only the males carry this weapon; a female platypus is quite harmless. Where on a male's body is the venom weapon mounted?
answer: A hollow venom spur on each hind ankle
choices: A hollow venom spur on each hind ankle
A stinger at the tip of the tail
Fangs hidden inside the bill
Barbed claws on the front webbed feet
context: Each male carries a sharp hollow spur (about 12-18 mm) on each hind ankle, fed by a venom gland whose output spikes in the mating season. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platypus_venom; Australian Museum

question: Now and then an Australian bushwalker handles a male platypus the wrong way and gets a dose of its venom. It is not deadly to people, but the venom has earned a grim name among doctors, worse in one way than most snakebites. What makes it so notorious?
answer: The pain shrugs off morphine and can last weeks or months
choices: The pain shrugs off morphine and can last weeks or months
It causes the wounded limb to swell to twice its size
It leaves the victim unable to grip for months
It triggers violent, days-long fever
context: The venom is not lethal to humans but causes excruciating pain that morphine cannot relieve, persisting for weeks or months and able to incapacitate a grown adult. Source: Slate, 2015; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platypus_venom

question: Anich and colleagues carried old museum platypus pelts into a dark room in 2020 and shone ultraviolet light on them, expecting only brown fur under a purple lamp. Instead they saw something nobody had noticed on a platypus before. What did the fur do under the lamp?
answer: Glows an eerie blue-green
choices: Glows an eerie blue-green
Glows a deep blood-red
Glows bright orange
Shows no reaction at all
context: Anich and colleagues reported this biofluorescence in the journal Mammalia in 2020, the first ever found in a monotreme. Source: Live Science, livescience.com/platypuses-glow-uv-light.html; ScienceDaily (Anich et al., 2020)

question: Down on the bottom of an Australian river, a platypus scoops crayfish, worms and freshwater shellfish into stretchy cheek pouches, along with little pieces of gravel. It has no teeth, yet it cracks the hard shells once it paddles back up to the surface to chew. Why does it gather grit with its food?
answer: It grinds food against horny pads, using the swallowed grit like millstones
choices: It grinds food against horny pads, using the swallowed grit like millstones
It uses the stones as ballast to sink while diving
It spits the grit to stun approaching prey
It stores the stones to build its riverbank burrow
context: With no teeth, the platypus mashes prey between horny keratin pads, the swallowed grit acting as millstones to crack hard shells. Source: AskNature, asknature.org/strategy/mouth-sorts-and-grinds-food/; Australian Museum

question: Biologists reading the platypus genome in 2008 found a surprise in its sex chromosomes. Most mammals settle sex with a single pair, but the platypus has a whole chain of them, some resembling a chicken's. How many sex chromosomes does a platypus carry?
answer: Ten
choices: Ten
Two
Four
Twenty-three
context: The 2008 genome revealed 5 X and 5 Y chromosomes, and DNA blending mammal, bird, and reptile genes, with bird-like sex chromosomes echoing a chicken's. Source: WashU, source.washu.edu/2008/05/; ScienceAlert

question: An ancient gene that the platypus's egg-laying ancestors all carried still works in the platypus today, though placental and marsupial mammals threw their copies away long ago. The 2008 platypus genome showed it kept a working one. What does that surviving gene let the platypus do?
answer: Make egg yolk, even as it also makes milk
choices: Make egg yolk, even as it also makes milk
Grow a second, spare set of milk glands
Digest the shells of the eggs it lays
Regrow a lost venom spur within one season
context: The ancestral vertebrate had a cluster of three vitellogenin (egg-yolk protein) genes — chickens still carry all three. Placental and marsupial mammals lost every one when they swapped yolk for the placenta and milk. The platypus kept one working copy, an ortholog of the chicken's VtgI, sitting right beside its milk-casein genes. Low nonsynonymous-to-synonymous substitution ratios and almost no pseudogene decay confirm the gene is still functional, not a fossil — so the platypus is genetically half-reptile, half-mammal, making egg yolk and milk at once. Source: Warren et al. 2008 genome analysis (Nature nature06936); Wagner et al. 2008, 'Conservation of a vitellogenin gene cluster in oviparous vertebrates and identification of its traces in the platypus genome' (PubMed 18343608).

question: A fox corners a slow, cat-sized animal in a North American backyard, a creature with a bare pink tail, a long pointed snout and beady eyes. It flops onto its side, mouth open and tongue lolling, eyes glazed, looking totally dead. Which animal is famous for this trick?
answer: The Virginia opossum
choices: The Virginia opossum
The nine-banded armadillo
The striped skunk
The North American porcupine
context: The Virginia opossum (Didelphis virginiana) is the classic death-feigner, and its cornered collapse -- eyes glazed open, tongue out -- is literally where the phrase 'playing possum' comes from. Source: https://scienceinsights.org/do-possums-actually-play-dead-the-science-explained/

question: A dog grabs a possum, and the possum flops limp with its tongue lolling out; the dog often loses interest and drops it. Biologists call this kind of death-faking thanatosis, and it turns up in some unexpected corners of the animal world. Which of these groups has known death-fakers?
answer: Beetles, ducks, frogs, and sharks
choices: Beetles, ducks, frogs, and sharks
Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish
Bats, dolphins, and shrews
Corals, jellyfish, and sea anemones
context: Death-feigning shows up across an enormous range of animals -- beetles, spiders, crickets, ants, ducks, frogs, lizards, snakes, opossums, and even sharks and seahorses. It is one of nature's most widespread defenses. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5769822/

question: A fainting opossum lies limp on the dirt with its pink tongue hanging out, but its act does not rely on looks alone. As it faints, its anal glands leak a stinking greenish fluid, and at the same moment it drools, urinates and empties its bowels, staining the ground around it. What impression does all this create for a sniffing predator?
answer: It smells like a corpse dead for days
choices: It smells like a corpse dead for days
It masks its own scent so predators lose the trail
It gives off a musk that mimics the predator's own kind
It seems to be a healthy, easy catch
context: The musky fluid reeks of rotting flesh, so the opossum doesn't just look dead -- it smells and looks DAYS-dead. Many predators avoid spoiled meat, which can be poisonous, and drop it in disgust. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/many-animals-play-dead-not-just-to-avoid-predators

question: Scientists wired up Virginia opossums in the lab and watched their pulses through one of these faints. A fainted opossum does not merely look dead to a sniffing predator; real, measurable changes go on inside its body. About how far does its heart rate drop during the faint?
answer: By nearly half (about 46%)
choices: By nearly half (about 46%)
By about a tenth (roughly 10%)
It actually races faster than normal
It stops completely for minutes
context: Researchers measured the opossum's heart rate falling roughly 46%, its breathing dropping about 31%, and its body cooling slightly -- genuine physiology, not pretend, which is why the illusion is so convincing. Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/19169341_Physiological_responses_associated_with_feigned_death_in_the_American_opossum

question: A shark flipped upside down falls into a limp, helpless trance. Off the coast of Mexico, the orcas of Moctezuma's pod have learned to turn that trance against young great white sharks by flipping them over. Once a shark lies paralyzed, what do the orcas do?
answer: Rip out and eat its calorie-rich liver
choices: Rip out and eat its calorie-rich liver
Carry it to shore to eat later
Teach the trick to rival pods
Release it once it stops struggling
context: The orcas push young great whites to the surface and flip them upside down, locking them in tonic immobility, then tear out and devour the shark's huge, oil-rich liver -- a learned hunting move passed within the pod. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/orcas-in-mexico-have-learned-to-attack-young-great-white-sharks-by-flipping-them-upside-down-and-eating-their-livers-180987620/

question: On the misty shores of Loch Ness, tourists still swap stories of a long-necked, small-headed creature slipping through the water. The silhouette comes from a real sea reptile of the dinosaur age: a very long neck ending in a tiny head, and a broad body with a paddle at each corner. What was this animal?
answer: A plesiosaur
choices: A plesiosaur
A pterosaur
An ichthyosaur
A mosasaur
context: The plesiosaur was a genuine marine reptile of the Mesozoic seas, not a dinosaur and not a living lake monster; its four-flipper, long-necked shape is where the 'Loch Ness Monster' picture comes from. Ichthyosaurs were dolphin-shaped, mosasaurs were giant sea lizards, and pterosaurs flew. Source: Natural History Museum London, 'What is a plesiosaur?' (nhm.ac.uk).

question: A plesiosaur set out across the open sea in the age of the dinosaurs, a small head on a long neck, a stout barrel body and four wide flippers, a shape like almost nothing alive in the water today. How did it drive itself forward?
answer: It flapped all four flippers like underwater wings
choices: It flapped all four flippers like underwater wings
It sculled with a broad paddle-shaped tail
It swallowed water and jetted backward
It walked along the seafloor on its flippers
context: Almost no living animal does this. Computer simulations and a swimming robot showed the plesiosaur 'flew' through the water like a penguin, driving mostly with its two front flippers and adding a timed extra push with the back pair. Source: Muscutt et al. 2017, Royal Society Proceedings B; PBS NewsHour 'odd swimming style decoded by a robot'.

question: Built like a snake threaded through the body of a turtle, a plesiosaur spent its whole life in the open sea. Yet like a whale today, it kept rising to the surface again and again, however good the hunting was down deep. What forced it back up?
answer: It breathed air with lungs
choices: It breathed air with lungs
It needed sunlight to warm its blood
It hunted seabirds resting on the waves
It came up to shed its old skin
context: Plesiosaurs were air-breathing reptiles, so despite living their whole lives at sea they had to surface to breathe like whales do. Because they also gave live birth in the water, they never needed to come ashore at all. Source: Natural History Museum London, 'What is a plesiosaur?'.

question: A giraffe holds up a neck over six feet long on just seven bones, the same count as a person's, and nearly every mammal keeps to seven. The ancient sea reptile Elasmosaurus threw that rule out entirely. About how many bones stacked up in an elasmosaur's neck?
answer: About 72, more than almost any animal ever
choices: About 72, more than almost any animal ever
About 14, just double a giraffe's seven
About 25, like a very long-necked bird
The same 7, only each bone far longer
context: A giraffe stretches seven neck bones to enormous length; elasmosaurs instead stacked up 70-plus short vertebrae, and their cousin Albertonectes had at least 75. Source: Sachs et al. 2013, PLOS ONE, 'Revised Vertebral Count in the Longest-Necked Vertebrate Elasmosaurus platyurus'; National Geographic on Albertonectes.

question: Elasmosaurus cruised a shallow inland sea over what is now Kansas, a plesiosaur about 34 feet long, nearly as long as a school bus. Its head was a tiny triangle at the far end, big enough only to gulp small fish and squid whole. How much of that 34-foot body was neck?
answer: Around 23 feet, about two-thirds of the animal
choices: Around 23 feet, about two-thirds of the animal
A few feet, roughly the length of the head
Around half, evenly split with the tail
Almost the whole body, leaving a stub tail
context: About 23 of Elasmosaurus's 34 feet was pure neck, nearly two-thirds of its length, tipped with that small triangular head. Source: Wikipedia 'Elasmosaurus', citing Sachs 2005 and Everhart (~10.3 m long, neck ~7.1 m, about 69%).

question: An elasmosaur closed in on a passing school of fish, its tiny head far out ahead of it on an enormously long neck. One leading idea, not yet proven, says that strange shape solved a problem the reptile faced every time it neared a school. What was the problem?
answer: Its bulky body would scare the whole school off before it could strike
choices: Its bulky body would scare the whole school off before it could strike
Its own long shadow fell across the water and spooked the fish
It swam too slowly to chase a darting school down
Its tiny mouth could not open wide enough to engulf them
context: This is a leading hypothesis, not proven fact: the long reach may have let the plesiosaur ease its tiny head into a fish school and snatch one before its huge body spooked them. Source: Earth Archives, 'Plesiosaurs and their absurdly long necks' (eartharchives.org), flagged as a feeding hypothesis.

question: Pliosaurus funkei, the giant nicknamed Predator X, grew 40 to 50 feet long, with an enormous head on a short neck and foot-long teeth. Researchers estimated its bite force, though the skull is incomplete. How did it compare with a T. rex's bite?
answer: Even more powerful than a T. rex's bite
choices: Even more powerful than a T. rex's bite
Roughly a tenth of a T. rex's bite
About equal, but only when biting soft prey
Weaker, since its teeth were built for gripping not crushing
context: Pliosaurs were apex predators of their seas. Researchers estimated Predator X's bite as even stronger than T. rex's, though the exact figure is debated because the skull is incomplete. Source: National Geographic, 'Paleontologists Reveal the Identity of Predator X'; Britannica; Discover Wildlife on pliosaurs (~30 cm teeth).

question: A Polycotylus mother lay in rock for 78 million years with one large baby still inside her body. For 200 years scientists had argued over how plesiosaurs bred, since they never came ashore. What did this fossil reveal about how plesiosaurs had their young?
answer: They gave live birth at sea rather than laying eggs on land
choices: They gave live birth at sea rather than laying eggs on land
They laid a single leathery egg that hatched inside the mother
They released clouds of tiny eggs like most fish
They carried eggs in the mouth until the young hatched
context: The one large baby, rather than a litter, hints that plesiosaurs may have cared for their young like whales or dolphins do. Source: O'Keefe & Chiappe 2011, Science 333:870-873, 'Viviparity and K-selected life history in a Mesozoic marine reptile'; Natural History Museum of LA County.

question: Bernard and colleagues in France tested the oxygen chemistry locked in plesiosaur tooth enamel in 2010, and later studies read the growth of plesiosaur bones. A reptile might be expected to match the sea around it, the way a modern crocodile does: cool water, cool body. Both lines of evidence told the same story. What could plesiosaurs do?
answer: Generate their own body heat, at a bird's metabolic rate, instead of borrowing it from the water
choices: Generate their own body heat, at a bird's metabolic rate, instead of borrowing it from the water
Simply match the cold ocean around them, exactly like a modern crocodile does
Warm up only after basking flipper-first at the sunlit surface between dives
Stay sluggish and slow-burning, coasting on sheer bulk to hold warmth in
context: Two separate lines of evidence converge on active, self-generated heat in plesiosaurs. Bernard et al. (2010, Science 328:1379-1382) measured oxygen isotopes in fossil tooth enamel and estimated elevated, regulated body temperatures well above the cold seas the animals swam in. Independently, Fleischle, Wintrich & Sander (2018, PeerJ 6:e4955; PMC5994164) modeled plesiosaur bone microstructure and recovered resting metabolic rates (~12-13 mL O2/h/g^0.67) and bone growth rates (~93-100 um/day) squarely in the BIRD range, far above any cold-blooded reptile, concluding plesiosaurs were 'truly endothermic' -- generating heat actively rather than coasting on body size. A 2024 reassessment (Reassessment of body temperature and thermoregulation strategies in Mesozoic marine reptiles, Paleobiology, biorxiv 2024.07.26.605303) refines the picture: plesiosaurs read as poikilothermic endotherms, body temperature ~27-34 C that still ran an advantage over the sea rather than holding a fixed value, while ichthyosaurs were the homeothermic ones. Across all three studies the shared, robust finding is self-produced, bird-level metabolic heat, not passive matching of the water. Sources: Bernard et al. 2010, Science (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1187443); Fleischle, Wintrich & Sander 2018, PeerJ (peerj.com/articles/4955/; PMC5994164); 2024 Paleobiology reassessment (biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.07.26.605303v1).

question: Plesiosaurs swallowed smooth stones by the hundred, and one Styxosaurus held 253 in its gut. The tidy old explanation was ballast, weight to help the reptile sink and trim. Yet such stones come to at most about 0.2 percent of a plesiosaur's weight, far too little to sink it. What job do most researchers now give the stones?
answer: The stones ground up tough, shelled prey in the gut like a bird's gizzard
choices: The stones ground up tough, shelled prey in the gut like a bird's gizzard
The stones anchored the reptile to the seabed while it rested
The stones were swallowed by accident while snapping at fish
The stones stored minerals the reptile drew on to grow its bones
context: These swallowed stones are gastroliths; one Styxosaurus held 253, and some elasmosaurs preserve over 100. The old 'ballast for buoyancy control' idea runs into a hard quantitative wall: recovered gastrolith mass never exceeds about 0.2 percent of the animal's body mass in any plesiosaur, far too little to sink or trim a multi-ton reptile. That shortfall has shifted the leading view toward a digestive role, grinding tough prey such as shelled cephalopods in the gut the way birds use gizzard stones, though the debate is not fully closed. Sources: Everhart, 'Gastroliths Associated with Plesiosaur Remains ... Pierre Shale'; Wings & Sander on gastrolith function; corroborated by Open University 'Solving the Riddle of the Gastroliths' and PeerJ 2024 (PMC11373562), which report gastrolith mass consistently under ~0.2 percent of body mass, insufficient as ballast.

question: Frogs no bigger than a fingernail crawl over wet leaves on the rainforest floor of Central and South America, in fire red, sky blue, banana yellow and neon green. There are about 200 kinds of them. What are these jewel-bright frogs called?
answer: Poison dart frogs
choices: Poison dart frogs
Marsh peepers
Cave newts
River toads
context: The poison dart frog family holds roughly 200 species across 16 genera, many in dazzling electric colors, on the rainforest floor of Central and South America. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'.

question: A thumbnail-sized poison dart frog has a problem: its eggs have hatched on the forest floor, and the tadpoles need water. One parent lets them stick to the mucus on its back and carries them off. Where does it take each tadpole?
answer: A rain pool inside a bromeliad plant
choices: A rain pool inside a bromeliad plant
A hollow log floating in a stream
A wet burrow dug at the roots
A foam nest whipped up on a leaf
context: The newly hatched tadpoles cling to the mucus on a parent's back, and the adult climbs into the canopy to deposit each one, one at a time, in a tiny pool of rainwater trapped in a bromeliad plant. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'; World Frog Day, 'Strawberry Poison Dart Frogs And Their Parental Care'.

question: A tiny poison dart frog hops along the leaf litter of a rainforest in Central or South America in broad daylight, making no effort to hide. It wears blazing red, gold or electric blue, easy for any hungry bird to spot. What message is it sending to every predator that sees it?
answer: 'I am deadly -- don't eat me'
choices: 'I am deadly -- don't eat me'
'This patch of forest is mine'
'I am ready to find a mate'
'Look how big and strong I am'
context: Aposematic color is an honest warning signal -- a billboard telling predators the frog is toxic. Studies show the more toxic the frog, the more conspicuous its coloring, especially to bird predators that see color well. Source: The American Naturalist, 'Poison Frog Colors Are Honest Signals of Toxicity, Particularly for Bird Predators'.

question: In Colombia's misty Choco rainforest lives a bright yellow frog the size of a paper clip, the golden poison frog, one of the most poisonous animals on Earth. Its skin holds only about a milligram of toxin. Roughly how much damage could that one tiny frog do?
answer: Kill 10 to 20 people
choices: Kill 10 to 20 people
Kill a single small bird
Sting like a bee
Cause a mild rash
context: One wild golden poison frog carries about a milligram of batrachotoxin on its skin -- enough to kill 10 to 20 people, or roughly 20,000 mice. Source: Wikipedia, 'Golden poison frog'; National Geographic, 'Golden Poison Frog'.

question: Out in the rainforest, a poison dart frog eats toxic ants, mites and tiny beetles and concentrates their poisons in its skin glands; it is not born with any. A dart frog raised in a terrarium on ordinary fruit flies never gets that diet. What happens to the captive frog?
answer: It never becomes poisonous at all
choices: It never becomes poisonous at all
It grows a weaker but still deadly poison
It makes poison faster than in the wild
It loses its bright colors within weeks
context: Because the poison comes entirely from the diet, captive-bred dart frogs fed harmless insects never accumulate the alkaloids -- no captive-bred dendrobatid frog carries them, so they are completely safe to handle. Source: Understory Enterprises, 'Toxicity of Dart Frogs'; Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'.

question: In the rainforests of Central and South America, indigenous hunters used to wipe their blowgun darts along the back of a living frog, letting the frog's skin toxin coat the tip -- and that is where the name 'poison dart frog' came from. The frogs most people picture, the brilliant jewel-colored Dendrobates, were never the ones the hunters actually used. Which frogs actually armed the darts?
answer: A few species of the genus Phyllobates
choices: A few species of the genus Phyllobates
The tree frogs of the genus Hyla
Toads of the genus Rhinella
The glass frogs of family Centrolenidae
context: Only about four species, all in the genus Phyllobates, were actually used to poison darts -- not the more famous brilliant Dendrobates most people imagine. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'; AMNH, 'Dart Poison'.

question: A mother strawberry poison frog, a thumb-tip-sized frog splashed berry red, carries each of her tadpoles on her back to its own private pool of water in a Central American rainforest and leaves it there alone. Then she comes back, week after week, until it grows up. What does she bring each tadpole to eat?
answer: Her own unfertilized eggs
choices: Her own unfertilized eggs
Insects she has chewed soft
Algae she scrapes from the leaves
Ants she has drowned in the pool
context: The strawberry poison frog mother returns to each lonely tadpole in its private pool and feeds it unfertilized eggs; the tadpoles accept no other food and would starve without her. Source: World Frog Day, 'Strawberry Poison Dart Frogs And Their Parental Care'; NCBI PMC5702076, 'Induced parental care in a poison frog'.

question: The golden poison frog of Colombia carries a poison called batrachotoxin. It slips into nerve and muscle cells and jams their tiny sodium gates wide open, gates that normally flick shut to let a signal reset, so the cells fire without stopping. What happens to the victim as the poison spreads?
answer: The muscles freeze and the heart stops
choices: The muscles freeze and the heart stops
The blood slowly thins and clots fail
The nerves go numb and pain fades
The lungs fill with fluid over days
context: Batrachotoxin jams open the sodium channels in nerve and muscle so they can never close, freezing the muscles and stopping the heart. It is among the most potent natural poisons known: in mice, about 2 to 3 micrograms per kilogram of body weight is lethal. Source: McGill Office for Science and Society, 'Toxin on the Backs of Some Frogs Is Lethal to Humans'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batrachotoxin

question: A dyeing poison frog sits in plain view, its bold pattern warning off any predator close by. Researchers found that from farther off, those same markings do something that seems to contradict the warning. What do they do at a distance?
answer: They blur together and blend into the background
choices: They blur together and blend into the background
They flash brighter to mimic a bigger animal
They shift color to match the leaf litter
They vanish as the frog stops moving
context: From up close the bold pattern warns predators, but from a distance the same colors blur together and merge with the background -- giving the frog warning coloration and camouflage at once. Source: PNAS, 'Distance-dependent defensive coloration in the poison frog Dendrobates tinctorius'.

question: Across the frozen Arctic sea ice prowls the heaviest meat-eater that walks on land. A big male tips the scales at up to 1,760 pounds, more than a horse, and stands nearly ten feet tall when he rears up. Which land carnivore holds that title?
answer: The polar bear
choices: The polar bear
The Siberian tiger
The saltwater crocodile
The gray wolf
context: The polar bear (Ursus maritimus, Latin for 'sea bear') is the largest extant bear and the largest land carnivore by body mass, with adult males weighing 300-800 kg (660-1,760 lb) and standing nearly 10 feet tall on their hind legs. Source: Wikipedia, Polar bear; SeaWorld, All About Polar Bears - Characteristics.

question: A polar bear crouches on the Arctic sea ice beside a small round hole and holds perfectly still for long minutes, sometimes an hour or more, wind ruffling its white fur. It stalks nothing and chases nothing. What is it waiting for?
answer: A seal to surface for a breath, so it can strike the moment one does
choices: A seal to surface for a breath, so it can strike the moment one does
A crack of open water where it can warm its cold paws
The wind to shift so its own scent will not carry ahead of it
Its cubs to finish nursing in a den somewhere below the ice
context: This patient technique is called 'still-hunting': the bear finds a seal's breathing hole in the ice and simply waits, frozen and patient, for a seal to surface for air, then strikes. Source: Wikipedia, Polar bear; Britannica, polar bear.

question: Weighing over a thousand pounds, a polar bear pads across deep, soft Arctic snow, the kind that would swallow a caribou to its belly, and barely sinks. Something in its build spreads that enormous weight. What keeps so heavy a bear from breaking through?
answer: Front paws up to a foot across that spread its weight like snowshoes
choices: Front paws up to a foot across that spread its weight like snowshoes
Extra-long claws that hook the crust and pull it forward
Lightweight hollow leg bones that reduce how hard it presses down
A low belly that slides it along the snow like a sled
context: A polar bear's front paws reach up to 12 inches (30 cm) across, spreading its weight so it won't sink through snow, and doubling as paddles for swimming. Source: SeaWorld characteristics; ThePrimalX polar bear paws article.

question: Looking snowy white from nose to tail, a polar bear blends into the ice so well that seals sometimes miss it coming until too late. Yet the bare skin under its thick outer coat and fluffy undercoat holds a surprise. What color is a polar bear's skin?
answer: Jet black
choices: Jet black
Pale pink
Bluish gray
Snowy white, like the fur
context: A polar bear's skin is black, visible only on the nose and footpads; the dark skin soaks up the sun's warmth like a solar panel. Source: SeaWorld, All About Polar Bears - Characteristics ('A polar bear's skin, visible only on the nose and footpads, is black.').

question: On the open Arctic ice, a polar bear lifts its nose into the wind and freezes. Then it pads straight toward a seal's breathing hole far across the ice, one a person walking right past would never spot or smell. Roughly how far away can a polar bear smell such a hole?
answer: About a mile away
choices: About a mile away
About a hundred yards away
About ten miles away
Only when nearly on top of it
context: A polar bear's nose can detect a seal's breathing hole from about a mile away, and sniff out a seal hidden under three feet of packed snow. Source: Biology Insights, 'How Far Away Can a Polar Bear Smell?'; Polar Bears International seal-detection facts.

question: A polar bear stalks a seal across the Arctic sea ice — and against that endless white, her thick coat is perfect camouflage. But when a biologist plucks a single hair and puts it under the microscope, the hair looks nothing like white paint. What is each polar bear hair actually like up close?
answer: Clear and hollow, scattering light so it only looks white
choices: Clear and hollow, scattering light so it only looks white
Coated in a fine layer of reflective white pigment
Bright white all the way through the shaft
Silver-tipped over a darker brown base
context: Each hair is translucent with an air-filled core; the fur only LOOKS white because the rough hollow hairs scatter sunlight, the same way snow looks white. Source: Britannica, Why Are Polar Bears White; SeaWorld characteristics.

question: At forty below on the Arctic snow, a polar bear stays as warm inside as any mammal, around 99 degrees Fahrenheit. Yet on an infrared heat camera the huge animal almost disappears, reading nearly as cold as the ice around it. Why does so little of its warmth show up on the screen?
answer: Its insulation is so complete that almost no body heat escapes its surface
choices: Its insulation is so complete that almost no body heat escapes its surface
Its fur reflects the camera's infrared beam straight back
It lowers its body temperature to match the surrounding snow
The white fur blends into the white background on any camera
context: Hollow fur, dense underfur, and blubber insulate the bear so well that almost no body heat reaches its surface, which reads as cold as the surrounding snow. Source: AskNature, 'See-Through Fur Traps Light and Heat'; Harvard SITN, polar-bear-inspired invisibility cloak (2018).

question: Scientists in Alaska fitted a female polar bear with a GPS collar and tracked her as she left the ice edge in the Beaufort Sea while the summer ice thinned. She paddled across the freezing water without once hauling out to rest, until she reached solid ice on the far side. How long did that nonstop swim last?
answer: Nine days
choices: Nine days
Three days
Five days
Fourteen days
context: The tracked female swam about 426 miles (687 km) nonstop over nine days across the Beaufort Sea, losing 22% of her body weight before reaching ice. Reported from a USGS polar bear tracking study (2011). Source: USGS tracking study via Wikipedia, Polar bear, and PBS Nature Polar Bear Fact Sheet.

question: A Portuguese man o' war drifts on a warm sea like a pale blue jellyfish, a gas-filled balloon on top and stinging tentacles trailing below, sometimes thirty feet down. Biologists call it 'they,' not 'it.' Why do biologists say 'they' about a man o' war?
answer: It is a colony of many bodies
choices: It is a colony of many bodies
It changes sex through its life
It always swims in mated pairs
It splits in two when threatened
context: A Portuguese man o' war (Physalia physalis) is not a jellyfish and not even a single animal. It is a siphonophore: a floating colony of many specialized bodies called zooids, all genetically identical clones, so tightly fused that no one zooid could survive alone. That is why scientists say it is a 'they,' not an 'it.' Source: NOAA Ocean Service, oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/portuguese-man-o-war.html.

question: A Portuguese man o' war rides the warm ocean, its soft blue-purple bag of gas standing up from the water like a balloon. It has no fins, no tail and no way to swim, yet it travels for miles. How does it move?
answer: The wind blows its bag like a sail
choices: The wind blows its bag like a sail
It jets water to shoot forward
It hitches rides on passing fish
It slowly rolls with the tide alone
context: The blue-violet-to-pink gas bag on top (the pneumatophore, or float) rises up to about six inches above the water and acts as a sail to catch the wind. The man o' war has no way to swim or steer itself; it drifts wherever wind and current carry it. Source: NOAA Ocean Service; Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war.

question: At the surface, a Portuguese man o' war shows only a gas-filled purple float about a foot long. Out of sight below the waves hang its stinging tentacles, thin threads packed with venom. Stretched to their full limit, how far down can those threads reach?
answer: Longer than a blue whale
choices: Longer than a blue whale
Farther than a football field
About the height of a house
Roughly the length of a car
context: The stinging tentacles trail an average of about 10 meters (30 feet) below the float and can stretch as far as 30 meters (roughly 100 feet), longer than a blue whale, all hanging invisibly beneath a float only inches wide. Source: NOAA Ocean Service; Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war.

question: Inside a floating Portuguese man o' war, every body has its own job: one zooid forms the float, some sting, and others digest food or make young. The zooids are fused so tightly that the whole thing lives as one. What would become of a single zooid on its own?
answer: On its own it would die
choices: On its own it would die
It can regrow the whole colony
It swims off to hunt alone
It hardens into a protective shell
context: The colony is divided into jobs: one zooid type forms the gas float, dactylozooids form the stinging tentacles, gastrozooids digest, and gonozooids handle reproduction. Each body can do only its one job, and they are so dependent on one another that no single zooid could survive on its own. Source: Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war (zooid types); NOAA Ocean Service.

question: A Portuguese man o' war fills the sail-like float above its stinging tentacles not with gulped air but with gas made in special cells of its own. That homemade gas can be rich in the same poison that pours from a car's exhaust pipe. What poison is it?
answer: Carbon monoxide
choices: Carbon monoxide
Chlorine
Ammonia
Methane
context: The float doesn't just hold ordinary air; the animal actively makes its own gas inside the bag, and it can be as much as 13% carbon monoxide, the same poisonous gas that comes out of a car exhaust. Source: Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war (pneumatophore gas composition).

question: A blue dragon, a sea slug smaller than a grape, drifts upside down on the open ocean and eats the Portuguese man o' war, a jellyfish-like colony bristling with stinging cells, without coming to harm. Stranger still is what the little slug does with the most powerful stingers it swallows. What does it do with them?
answer: It stores them to fire as its own weapon
choices: It stores them to fire as its own weapon
It grinds them into harmless paste
It spits them back at the colony
It uses them to build a shell
context: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) sorts out the strongest stingers, does not fire them, and stores them in the tips of its own feathery arms to reuse as a stolen weapon, a trick called kleptocnidy. Source: Wikipedia, Glaucus atlanticus; HowStuffWorks, The Blue Dragon Sea Slug Eats Venomous Prey and Saves the Stingers for Later.

question: Portuguese men o' war sail with the wind, but their sails come in two mirror-image builds, so some veer off to the left and some to the right instead of all running straight downwind. Biologists think this split helps them in one specific way. How does it help them?
answer: A whole fleet never all strands on one beach
choices: A whole fleet never all strands on one beach
The colonies can steer toward richer feeding grounds
Left and right builds can mate only with each other
Rivals are pushed apart to reduce competition
context: The sail comes in two mirror-image forms: some men o' war are 'left-handed' and some 'right-handed,' so they tack off at about 45 degrees to either side of the wind. This split means a whole fleet never all blows onto the same beach at once, sparing part of the population from stranding and dying together. Source: Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war (dimorphism and drift); ScienceDirect, Relationship between dimorphism and drift in the Portuguese man-of-war.

question: By day, a big-eyed potoo in a forest of Central or South America sits bolt upright on the stump of a broken branch, bill pointed straight up at the sky, and freezes for hours without a twitch. What does the motionless bird look like?
answer: A broken-off, dead stub of the branch itself
choices: A broken-off, dead stub of the branch itself
A coiled snake draped over the wood
A clump of bright red berries
A patch of green moss on the bark
context: The potoo's daytime disguise is total: it aligns its body with a broken snag, points its bill upward, and stays motionless for hours, so it reads as a dead stub of the very tree it sits on. Its own nestlings can even resemble clumps of fungus on the wood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potoo

question: Its eyes shut tight, a potoo spends the day frozen upright on a broken branch. Yet when a hunting hawk creeps closer, the 'sleeping' bird shifts position before the hawk can strike. Something built into its eyelids lets it see the movement without opening its eyes. What is it?
answer: Notched slits set into its own eyelids
choices: Notched slits set into its own eyelids
A transparent inner eyelid it peers through
Oversized eyes that shine through thin skin
A reflective backing that glows when shut
context: The potoo has two or three notches, or slits, in its eyelids that stay open even when the eyes are shut, letting it sense light and movement — so it can detect an approaching predator while sitting frozen with its eyes 'closed.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potoo

question: A female potoo, a night bird of the forests of Central and South America, lays a single egg each season and builds no nest of twigs at all. When the moment comes, where does that lone egg go?
answer: Straight onto a bare dip on a branch or rotten stump
choices: Straight onto a bare dip on a branch or rotten stump
Inside a hole she chisels in a tree trunk
In a floating raft of reeds on the water
