In a deep scrape she digs in the forest floor
context: The potoo builds nothing at all — the female lays her single egg directly into a shallow depression on a bare branch or the top of a rotten stump, and a parent hides it by perching over it like part of the wood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potoo ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo

question: After dark, a common potoo sits in the forest and sends out a haunting phrase of up to eight whistled notes, one after another, into the night air. From the first whistle to the last, what do the notes do?
answer: Steadily drop in pitch and fade to silence
choices: Steadily drop in pitch and fade to silence
Rise steadily to a piercing shriek
Hold one long flat unbroken tone
Speed up into a rattling drum-roll
context: The common potoo's song is a series of up to eight whistled notes that steadily drop in pitch and fade in volume — a sound like a distant, sorrowful human cry drifting through the dark. That eerie, sinking wail earned folk names like 'ghost bird' and 'poor-me-one,' and a Peruvian tale calls it a lost child crying for its mother. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo ; https://www.iflscience.com/meet-the-great-potoo-south-americas-loud-but-elusive-ghost-bird-76689

question: In the Australian outback, a red kangaroo carries her baby inside her for only about 33 days, barely a month. The newborn comes out blind and hairless, not yet fully formed. About how big is a just-born red kangaroo?
answer: The size of a jellybean, under a gram
choices: The size of a jellybean, under a gram
The size of a house cat
The size of a rabbit
The size of a human baby
context: A newborn red kangaroo is roughly 2 cm long and weighs under a gram — about the size of a jellybean or grape — and is born blind and hairless after just ~33 days. It finishes developing outside the womb. Source: a-z-animals.com/articles/a-newborn-kangaroo-is-no-bigger-than-a-jellybean/

question: A newborn red kangaroo, blind and barely formed, climbs up through its mother's belly fur to her pouch the instant it is born. The whole climb is done in about three minutes, with no working eyes to steer by. What guides it to the pouch?
answer: An excellent sense of smell and direction
choices: An excellent sense of smell and direction
The mother's heartbeat
Faint warmth from the pouch
The sound of the mother's voice
context: The whole climb takes about three minutes, guided by a strong sense of smell and direction — remarkable for an animal whose body is almost entirely unformed except its grasping front limbs. Source: scienceinsights.org/how-do-kangaroos-give-birth-from-embryo-to-pouch/

question: Inside its mother's warm pouch, a newborn kangaroo joey, blind and hairless, finds a teat and latches on. In that moment something locks the pair together so tightly that the joey cannot be shaken loose, even when she bounds across the outback at top speed. What happens where the joey meets the teat?
answer: The tip of the teat swells into a bulb inside its mouth
choices: The tip of the teat swells into a bulb inside its mouth
The joey's jaws fuse shut around the teat
The pouch fills with a sticky fluid
The joey grips the teat with its claws
context: The teat tip swells into a bulb inside the joey's mouth, fusing the two together for months — it cannot be dislodged even at full speed. Newborn marsupials also have 'oral shields' narrowing the mouth to a round hole just wide enough for the teat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marsupial

question: Bounding across the dry red grasslands of Australia, a red kangaroo mother sometimes covers thirty feet in a single hop, with a tiny joey riding in her forward-facing pouch. Every jump should fling the joey out, yet it never does: she can close the pouch's mouth like the neck of a drawstring bag. What lets her do that?
answer: A strong sphincter muscle that tightens the pouch opening
choices: A strong sphincter muscle that tightens the pouch opening
A flap of skin she folds over by hand
Sticky glands lining the pouch rim
The joey hooking its claws over the edge
context: A ring of sphincter muscle at the pouch opening lets the mother cinch it shut like a drawstring, so a joey in a forward-opening pouch can't fall out mid-leap. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pouch_(marsupial)

question: A mother wombat, a stocky, badger-like marsupial, digs a deep burrow in an Australian eucalyptus forest, throwing dirt straight back under her belly with powerful claws. All the while a baby rides in her pouch, yet it never gets buried and stays perfectly clean. How does the baby stay clean?
answer: Her pouch opens backward, toward her hind legs
choices: Her pouch opens backward, toward her hind legs
She seals the pouch shut while digging
She digs only with her front paws held high
She carries the baby in her mouth while digging
context: A wombat's pouch opens backward, toward the hind legs, so a digging mother doesn't shovel dirt onto the baby inside — the opposite orientation to a forward-opening kangaroo pouch. Source: environment.sa.gov.au/goodliving/posts/2018/10/wombat-facts

question: A Virginia opossum, the only marsupial found wild north of Mexico, can deliver twenty or more babies in a single birth, far more than she can raise. The tiny newborns scramble blindly through her fur toward the pouch. What decides which of them survive?
answer: Only those that reach one of her ~13 teats live
choices: Only those that reach one of her ~13 teats live
The mother eats the weakest herself
The first-born pushes the rest out of the pouch
She raises whichever ones are largest at birth
context: A Virginia opossum mother has about 13 teats, so when she bears more young than that, as many as 20 or more in one litter, only those that reach and latch onto a teat survive. Her pregnancy lasts just 12-13 days, one of the shortest of any mammal. Sources: sdzwildlifeexplorers.org/animals/virginia-opossum ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Virginia_opossum

question: A red kangaroo mother often has two young at once: a big joey hopping along at her side and a tiny newborn latched to a teat in her pouch. Both drink from her, sometimes at the same moment, yet each gets milk suited to its age. How does she manage it?
answer: She makes two different milks from two teats at once
choices: She makes two different milks from two teats at once
She alternates one milk between the two by the hour
She feeds the newborn milk and the older one solid food
Both drink the same milk but at different times
context: From two teats simultaneously she produces fat-rich milk for the older joey 'at foot' and low-fat, immune-rich milk for the tiny newborn in the pouch — different recipes at the same time. Source: a-z-animals.com/articles/kangaroos-have-one-of-the-strangest-reproductive-systems-in-the-animal-world/

question: A female kangaroo carries two uteruses, with a birth canal between them that in many kangaroos opens only at her first birth. This double plumbing was set by an accident of how the marsupial embryo grows: a pair of tubes runs right between the two developing reproductive tracts, blocking them from ever joining into the one system placental mammals have. Which tubes are they?
answer: The ureters, draining the kidneys down to the bladder
choices: The ureters, draining the kidneys down to the bladder
The Wolffian ducts, the embryonic precursors of male plumbing
The lymphatic vessels, draining fluid back toward the heart
The urethra, draining the bladder to the outside
context: In the marsupial embryo the ureters run between the two developing reproductive tracts, so the tracts can never fuse the way they do in placental mammals — which is why marsupials keep three vaginal canals and two uteruses. The two side (lateral) canals carry sperm up to the two uteruses; a separate central 'median' canal is the road the tiny joey travels down at birth. Males match the paired lateral tracts with a two-pronged, bifurcated penis. Sources: 'Why do kangaroos have 3 vaginas?' Live Science — https://www.livescience.com/animals/land-mammals/why-do-kangaroos-have-3-vaginas ; 'Kangaroos Have Three Vaginas,' National Geographic — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/kangaroos-have-three-vaginas ; Australian Geographic — https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/nature-wildlife/2022/12/did-you-know-kangaroos-have-three-vaginas/

question: On a summer garden stem, a slender green insect waits perfectly still, its two spiky forelegs folded and held out in front as though about to grasp something. A fly or a grasshopper only has to wander close. What is this ambush hunter?
answer: A praying mantis
choices: A praying mantis
A walking stick
A leaf katydid
A green lacewing
context: The praying mantis gets its name from that folded-leg posture, which looks like praying but is really a cocked spring ready to snap. Source: Live Science, high-speed video of mantis strike; My Pet Mantis hunting overview.

question: When a fly finally drifts within reach of a praying mantis, the insect explodes into motion. Its two folded, spike-lined front legs snap forward and slam shut around the prey, pinning it in place. From the very moment the mantis launches those forelegs, how long does the whole grab take?
answer: About 50 to 70 milliseconds, faster than a blink
choices: About 50 to 70 milliseconds, faster than a blink
About half a second, quicker than a hand
Two to three seconds, a slow squeeze
A tenth of a minute, deliberate and steady
context: Those raptorial forelegs snap shut like a spring-loaded trap in as little as 50 to 70 milliseconds — faster than a human can blink. Source: Live Science, high-speed video of mantis strike.

question: A praying mantis strikes only when prey lands within reach of its spiked forelegs, in a narrow window right in front of its face. To judge that distance it uses a kind of sight no insect was known to have until mantises were tested. What is it?
answer: True 3D depth perception
choices: True 3D depth perception
Heat-sensing infrared sight
A 360-degree panoramic scan
Ultraviolet color vision
context: The praying mantis judges striking range with true 3D depth perception (stereo vision), comparing the views from its two eyes. Samuel Rossel showed it in 1983, the first time stereo vision was proven in an insect, and in 2018 Vivek Nityananda's team at Newcastle University found that the mantis version works differently from ours. Source: Grokipedia 'Mantis' (stereopsis rare among invertebrates); Rossel 1983, Nature; Newcastle University Press Office (2018).

question: Researchers gathering reports of praying mantis kills from around the world found the biggest mantises eating frogs, lizards, tiny fish, mice and small birds alive. One entry stood out as the strangest catch of all, seen just once. What was it?
answer: A small bat
choices: A small bat
A small snake
A newt
A hummingbird
context: Mantises have been recorded killing and eating small frogs, lizards, salamanders, snakes, mice — and, on one remarkable occasion, a small bat. Source: phys.org, 'Praying mantises hunt down birds worldwide' (2017); Nyffeler, Maxwell & Van Remsen study.

question: A female praying mantis, the old story goes, always bites the head off her mate. In fact the male usually survives the mating. Laboratory experiments show she does sometimes eat him, but mainly under one particular condition. What is it?
answer: When the female is hungry
choices: When the female is hungry
When the male is older than the female
When the pair mate in daylight
When the female has already mated once
context: Most matings end with the male alive; the head-biting legend is overstated. In experiments, females on poor diets were far likelier to eat their mates, and well-fed females rarely did. Source: Grokipedia 'Mantis'; Wikipedia 'Mantis'; Snopes, 'Does a Female Praying Mantis Always Eat Her Mate's Head?' (A real but overstated legend.)

question: Vivek Nityananda and his team at Newcastle University fitted praying mantises with tiny blue-and-green glasses, like the ones people once wore for 3D films, and played the insects a 3D movie of prey drifting on a screen. How did the mantises react?
answer: They lunged to grab prey that was not really there
choices: They lunged to grab prey that was not really there
They ignored the screen entirely
They fled from the flickering images
They froze until the movie ended
context: Nityananda glued tiny 3D glasses onto the mantises with a drop of beeswax; when shown a 3D illusion of prey, they tried to grab it right out of the air — proving they see in 3D. Source: Live Science, 'Praying Mantises Wear Tiny 3D Glasses, for Science'; Newcastle University. (Sounds like a tall tale, but it really happened.)

question: Like many of its kind, a praying mantis flying through the night listens with a single ear tucked into the middle of its chest, tuned to ultrasound too high for human ears. When that ear picks up the hunting cries of a bat closing in from behind, the mantis reacts in an instant. What does it do in midair?
answer: Throws itself into a spiraling power dive
choices: Throws itself into a spiraling power dive
Freezes in midair and drops straight down
Flashes bright wing spots to startle the bat
Emits its own ultrasonic clicks to jam the bat
context: On detecting a bat's ultrasonic calls, a flying mantis spirals into a steep power dive toward the ground, escaping about 80 percent of the time. Source: National Geographic, 'Praying Mantis Uses Ultrasonic Hearing to Dodge Bats'; Yager, 'The Cyclopean Ear,' Science (1986).

question: A house cat fixes both eyes on its prey, both pointing the same way, as a wolf's, an owl's and a person's do. Overlapping views let each hunter judge exactly how far off its prey is. Where do a hunter's eyes sit?
answer: on the front of the head
choices: on the front of the head
on the sides of the head
on top of the head
one on each end of a long stalk
context: Forward-facing eyes give overlapping fields of view, and that overlap is what lets a predator measure the distance to its target before it leaps. The old rhyme sums it up: 'Eyes in front, the animal hunts.' Sources: University of California / Berkeley News 'Hunter or prey? The eyes are the key' (2015-08-07); veterinaryvision.co.uk 'How animals see the World.'

question: A deer grazes with its head down, yet it can still spot a lion or a wolf sneaking up from almost any direction. So can a rabbit or a horse. Where on the skull are a grazer's eyes set to give it that wide watch?
answer: on the sides of the head
choices: on the sides of the head
on the front of the head
tucked under the ears
behind a bony hood
context: Side-set eyes give up the overlap that measures distance and trade it for a nearly all-around field of view, so a hunted animal can spot danger coming from behind or the flank. The rhyme is 'Eyes on the side, the animal hides.' Sources: New Hampshire State Parks 'Reading a Skull: Predator and Prey Differences' (nhstateparks.org); Nearby Nature 'Predators and Prey Background.'

question: A horse's eyes sweep almost the whole circle around it, close to 340 degrees of watch. Still, two spots stay hidden from it: the one directly behind its body, and a triangle a few feet long in one other place. Where is that second blind spot?
answer: right in front of its own nose
choices: right in front of its own nose
straight up above its mane
along its left flank only
under its own belly
context: The horse's panoramic side vision leaves two gaps: one directly behind the tail, and one triangle of blindness reaching a few feet straight out from the nose. A horse briefly raising or turning its head fills the front gap, which is why a grazing horse keeps bobbing its head up. Sources: Utah State University Extension 'Equine Vision and Its Effect on Behavior' (digitalcommons.usu.edu); equinehelper.com 'How Horses See.'

question: A grazing goat drops its head to the grass, and inside each eye the long, horizontal slit pupil rolls as much as 50 degrees, the two eyes turning in opposite directions as the head tilts down. What does each pupil roll to do?
answer: keep the pupil level with the ground
choices: keep the pupil level with the ground
seal shut against flying grit
let in far more light
point both pupils at the same blade of grass
context: This eye-roll is called cyclovergence: as the goat or sheep lowers its head to eat, each eye rotates so the wide horizontal pupil stays parallel to the horizon, keeping the whole sweep of ground in sharp focus for spotting a predator even while the animal is head-down grazing. Sources: Banks et al. 2015 'Why do animal eyes have pupils of different shapes?' (Science Advances); Berkeley News 2015-08-07; The Conversation 'Revealed: why animals' pupils come in different shapes.' (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: Martin Banks's team measured 214 land animals and found the vertical slit pupil isn't a mark of big cats at all — lions and tigers have round pupils. The slit shows up almost only in predators shorter than about knee height, like house cats and geckos. What hunting style does that low, close-to-the-ground slit belong to?
answer: an ambusher lying in wait for the pounce
choices: an ambusher lying in wait for the pounce
a runner chasing prey across open ground
a night-flying glider
a filter-feeder sifting the water
context: Banks's team found the vertical slit almost always in predators under about 42 cm at the shoulder. Down near the ground, the slit sharpens the blur and disparity cues a lying-in-wait hunter uses to time the exact moment of the strike — while tall chasers like lions keep round pupils. Sources: Banks et al. 2015 (Science Advances); Berkeley News 2015-08-07; sci.news 'New Study Reveals Why Some Animals Have Vertical Pupils.'

question: A shaggy orange monkey troops through the swampy forests of Borneo in a noisy family band. The adult male carries a feature on his face so unusual that scientists named the whole species after it. What is that feature?
answer: A drooping nose over four inches long
choices: A drooping nose over four inches long
A fan of bright blue cheek ridges
A bony crest like a rooster's comb
A mane of stiff white whiskers
context: The male proboscis monkey (Nasalis larvatus) grows the largest nose of any primate — a pendulous flap that can pass four inches (about 10 cm). Females and juveniles keep small, neat, upturned noses. Source: https://www.oneearth.org/species-of-the-week-proboscis-monkey/

question: A male proboscis monkey honks from deep in the Borneo jungle to monkeys he cannot see through the leaves. His oversized nose does something to the sound that helps it carry. What does the big nose do to the honk?
answer: It acts as a resonating chamber that deepens and amplifies the honk
choices: It acts as a resonating chamber that deepens and amplifies the honk
It squeezes shut to force the honk out in sharp bursts
It funnels the honk straight up above the canopy
It filters out low tones so only the sharp notes carry
context: The nasal cavity works like a built-in loudspeaker: it resonates, deepening and amplifying the honk so it reaches monkeys the male cannot see. A bigger nose makes a deeper, louder call — so a female choosing a big-nosed male is reading his fitness off the sound, part visual banner and part megaphone. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aaq0250

question: A skinny proboscis monkey of Borneo carries a huge round potbelly that can weigh a quarter of its whole body, a paunch that looks almost cartoonish. That belly lets it live on a diet of tough, bitter jungle leaves. What inside it does the work?
answer: A chambered stomach packed with bacteria that ferment tough leaves
choices: A chambered stomach packed with bacteria that ferment tough leaves
A crop of grit and gravel that grinds the leaves to paste
A pouch of stored fat that carries it through the dry season
A tangle of extra-long coiled intestine to soak up water
context: Like a cow, the proboscis monkey has a multi-chambered stomach full of cellulose-busting bacteria that ferment tough leaves — even detoxifying poisons in near-inedible mangrove leaves. It also regurgitates and re-chews its food, the first documented rumination-like remastication in a primate. Sweet ripe fruit is dangerous: its sugars ferment inside and can bloat the monkey badly, so it eats mostly young leaves and unripe fruit. Sources: https://hakaimagazine.com/features/the-wonderful-transcendent-life-of-an-odd-nosed-monkey/ ; https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/full/10.1098/rsbl.2011.0197

question: A troop of proboscis monkeys needs to cross a muddy Borneo river full of crocodiles to reach a good feeding tree. They belly-flop straight from the branches into the water and paddle across at the narrowest point. What body feature lets them out-swim other monkeys?
answer: Webbed hands and feet for paddling underwater
choices: Webbed hands and feet for paddling underwater
A hollow-boned tail that floats them like a cork
Oily fur that keeps water from soaking them down
Air-filled cheek pouches they gulp to stay buoyant
context: Proboscis monkeys are among the best swimmers of any monkey. Their webbed hands and feet let them dog-paddle and even swim underwater up to 20 meters (about 66 feet) to cross rivers. They slip in as silently as they can so the crocodiles don't notice them. Sources: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/proboscis-monkey ; https://www.discoverwildlife.com/tv/proboscis-monkeys-leap-into-crocodile-infested-river-bbc

question: Pterosaurs ruled the skies for over 150 million years while dinosaurs walked the Earth below. Cartoons call them flying dinosaurs, but they were not dinosaurs at all. What kind of animal was a pterosaur really?
answer: A flying reptile, its own separate branch
choices: A flying reptile, its own separate branch
A kind of early bird
A small feathered dinosaur
A giant flying insect
context: A pterosaur is NOT a dinosaur and NOT a bird -- it is its own kind of flying reptile, though a close cousin of the dinosaurs. Calling it a 'flying dinosaur' is a common mistake. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterosaur

question: The first pterosaurs, bird-sized reptiles of the Late Triassic some 230 million years ago, did something no animal with a backbone had ever done in the whole history of Earth. What was their history-making first?
answer: The first to fly under their own power
choices: The first to fly under their own power
The first to lay eggs on land
The first to grow a bony shell
The first to breathe air on land
context: Pterosaurs were the first vertebrates ever to achieve true flapping flight, taking to the air in the Late Triassic long before birds existed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterosaur

question: A pterosaur soared on a broad sheet of thin skin stretched taut like a kite. Almost the whole of that wing was held out by just one part of its body. Which part?
answer: One enormously long fourth finger
choices: One enormously long fourth finger
A fan of stiff tail feathers
A row of long back ribs
A double-hinged shoulder blade
context: The wing was a sheet of skin stretched from the body all the way to the tip of one hugely elongated fourth finger -- the entire wing rode on a single giant finger. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterosaur

question: Over what is now Texas, about 68 million years ago, Quetzalcoatlus soared on wings about 10 to 11 meters from tip to tip. It was one of the largest animals ever to fly. What everyday flying machine was it as wide as?
answer: A small airplane
choices: A small airplane
A hang glider
A kite
A ceiling fan
context: Quetzalcoatlus northropi spanned about 10-11 metres (33-36 feet) wingtip to wingtip -- as wide as a small airplane. It is named after Quetzalcoatl, the Aztec feathered-serpent sky god. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quetzalcoatlus

question: Wings about 11 meters across carried the giant pterosaur Quetzalcoatlus over Late Cretaceous Texas. An animal that big still had to lift its whole body off the ground and into the air. What kept such a giant light enough to fly?
answer: Hollow, air-filled bones
choices: Hollow, air-filled bones
A belly full of trapped gas
Wings lighter than paper
A body mostly made of fat
context: Pterosaur bones were hollow and air-filled, just like a bird's, which is how such huge animals stayed light enough to leave the ground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterosaur

question: After a flight, a Quetzalcoatlus came down to land and folded its huge leathery wings away, its head longer than a grown man is tall. It still had to get around on the ground. How did this giant move about on land?
answer: On all fours, limbs straight under its body
choices: On all fours, limbs straight under its body
Hopping upright on two legs
Dragging itself flat on its belly
Gliding between low branches
context: On the ground it folded up its wings and walked on all fours, with its limbs held straight underneath its body like a walking animal, not sprawled out. Standing, its head reached about as high as a modern giraffe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quetzalcoatlus

question: A Quetzalcoatlus weighed about as much as a full-grown giraffe, on wings some 33 feet across. It was far too heavy to sprint along on two legs and flap into the air the way a bird does. How did Michael Habib propose it got off the ground?
answer: Vaulting straight up off its front limbs
choices: Vaulting straight up off its front limbs
Diving off a cliff to catch the wind
Flapping in place until it slowly rose
Waiting to be lifted by rising hot air
context: In this 'quad-launch,' the giant planted all four limbs and exploded upward off its powerful front limbs like a pole-vaulter. Michael Habib proposed it in 2008 from the bones themselves -- a very strong arm bone (humerus) but a comparatively weak thigh bone, the reverse of a running animal, so the arms did the launching. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quetzalcoatlus

question: A giant Quetzalcoatlus flying over Late Cretaceous North America 68 million years ago had to eat, and paleontologists argued for decades over how it did. Ideas ranged from skimming fish on the wing to scavenging carcasses from above. What does the best fossil evidence support today?
answer: Striding the ground and snatching up small animals
choices: Striding the ground and snatching up small animals
Skimming low over water to snatch fish on the wing
Gliding down to feed on carcasses from above
Cropping tough plants with its long jaws
context: Rather than fishing from the air, giant Quetzalcoatlus probably stalked prey on foot, snapping up small animals on the ground much like a modern stork or ground hornbill. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quetzalcoatlus

question: A pterosaur flew at full speed on wings of thin, bare skin, and a membrane like that should have flapped and rippled uselessly, the way a loose sail flaps in a gust. Yet its wings held their shape and pushed firmly against the air. What kept the skin taut?
answer: Thousands of stiff internal fibers running across the membrane
choices: Thousands of stiff internal fibers running across the membrane
A hard outer shell of overlapping scales along the wing
A cushion of trapped air sealed between two layers of skin
Rows of small interlocking feathers anchored to the arm
context: The wing was not just skin. Packed inside it were thousands of thin stiffening rods called actinofibrils, each about 0.1 mm thick and crowded four to seven per millimetre, layered in criss-crossing sheets that fanned toward the long wing-finger. They worked like built-in battens or springs, spreading and tensioning the membrane so it held its shape against the air, yet still let the whole wing fold up compactly when the animal landed. Their exact material is still uncertain, most likely collagen, possibly keratin. Source: Wikipedia, 'Anatomy of pterosaurs' / 'Pterosaur', corroborating S. Christopher Bennett 2000, 'Pterosaur flight: the role of actinofibrils in wing function', Historical Biology 14:255-284.

question: Scientists examining a finely preserved little anurognathid pterosaur in 2019 looked closely at the fuzz on its body, long taken for simple hair-like insulation. Some of the filaments split into branches, a pattern thought to belong only to feathered dinosaurs. What did the find make them rethink?
answer: When feathers first arose, maybe in an ancestor long before birds
choices: When feathers first arose, maybe in an ancestor long before birds
Whether the animals ran warm-blooded or stayed cold-blooded
Whether the fuzz was colored for camouflage or for display
How big pterosaur eggs were and where the parents buried them
context: The body fuzz, called pycnofibers, turned out to be more than hair. Some filaments were grouped and bilaterally branched, a feather-like structure, and preserved melanosomes even hinted at their color. Because branched filaments were thought to belong only to feathered dinosaurs, this raised a striking possibility: that true feathers, or the genetic recipe for them, first appeared in a shared archosaur ancestor tens of millions of years before birds, rather than pterosaur fuzz and dinosaur feathers being two separate inventions. The idea remains debated, but it reframes the whole origin of feathers. Source: Zixiao Yang et al. 2019, 'Pterosaur integumentary structures with complex feather-like branching', Nature Ecology & Evolution 3:24-30 (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30568282); University of Bristol research-information page.

question: Deep in India's Western Ghats lives a bloated, dark-purple frog that spends almost its entire life buried underground. It hauls itself up to the surface only when the monsoon rains arrive. How much of the year does an adult purple frog actually spend above ground?
answer: About two weeks
choices: About two weeks
About four months
Roughly half the year
Almost all summer
context: The purple frog (Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis) surfaces for only about two weeks a year, emerging with the monsoon to breed in temporary streams before vanishing back underground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_frog

question: A glossy, dark-purple frog swollen like a small balloon spends almost its whole life underground in the Western Ghats mountains of southern India, coming up only to breed. People call it the pignose frog because of one odd feature of its face. What is that feature?
answer: A tiny, pointed pig-like snout
choices: A tiny, pointed pig-like snout
A pair of curved tusks
Bright pink cheek pouches
A flat, shovel-shaped bill
context: National Geographic describes shiny purple skin, a light-blue ring around each small eye, and a distinctive pig-like snout on the tiny pointed head. Its scientific name is Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/purple-frog-new-species-discovery-india-monsoon

question: A squat, blimp-shaped purple frog with a head that looks glued on wrong never comes to the surface to hunt. Buried in the wet soil of India's Western Ghats, it feeds entirely underground with a fluted tongue and a special groove in its mouth. What does it eat down there?
answer: Termites and ants
choices: Termites and ants
Earthworms and slugs
Beetle grubs
Small burrowing lizards
context: The purple frog uses a long fluted tongue and a special buccal groove to eat termites and ants entirely underground, never coming to the surface to feed. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/purple-frog-new-species-discovery-india-monsoon

question: A purple frog lies hidden in the damp soil of India's Western Ghats, the last of a family that has been evolving all on its own for a huge stretch of time. Its closest living cousins are the little Sooglossid frogs stranded on the Seychelles islands out in the Indian Ocean. When did the two lineages split apart?
answer: Around 100 million years ago, as Gondwana broke up
choices: Around 100 million years ago, as Gondwana broke up
Around 10 million years ago
Around 2 million years ago, in the last ice ages
Only a few hundred thousand years ago
context: The purple frog is a 'living fossil' relict. Its lineage split from the Seychelles Sooglossid frogs roughly 100 million years ago when the Gondwana supercontinent broke apart, leaving India drifting as its own island continent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_frog

question: On Rottnest Island, off Western Australia, a cat-sized furry marsupial called the quokka seems to grin right at the tourists lining up for selfies with it. What actually gives the quokka that grin?
answer: the fixed shape of its short muzzle and round cheeks
choices: the fixed shape of its short muzzle and round cheeks
a mineral stain that darkens the fur around its lips
the way it keeps leaves tucked in the sides of its mouth
loose folds of skin that curl upward as it grows older
context: The upturned mouth corners, round cheeks, short muzzle, and big dark eyes just happen to line up in the pattern humans read as a grin. It is a coincidence of anatomy, not a mood — the quokka is not actually 'happy,' and reading human emotion into an animal's face is a classic mistake. Source: Australian Geographic Fact File: Quokka; Wikipedia 'Quokka.'

question: A fox closes in on a mother quokka with a joey in her belly pouch. A viral internet story claims she flings the baby at the predator to save herself, but that is a myth. What does she really do to buy time to escape?
answer: loosens her pouch so the joey drops out and hisses on the ground
choices: loosens her pouch so the joey drops out and hisses on the ground
rears up and lashes at the fox with her clawed hind feet
freezes flat against the ground so the two of them go unnoticed
leads the fox on a long winding chase away from the joey
context: She relaxes her pouch muscles and the startled joey falls out and writhes and hisses on the ground, distracting the predator long enough for the mother to get away. It is a release, not a toss — the 'quokkas throw their babies' story is a myth, but the drop itself is a real anti-predator behavior. Source: Africa Check, 'No, quokkas don't throw babies at predators'; Biology Insights, 'Do Quokkas Toss Babies at Predators?'

question: A quokka on Rottnest Island, off Western Australia, lives through months of dry summer while the island's fresh puddles and streams all but vanish. Yet it can go about a month without a real drink of water. How does it keep from drying out?
answer: it pulls most of the water it needs straight from the plants it eats
choices: it pulls most of the water it needs straight from the plants it eats
it stores a water reserve in the fat of its thick tail
it soaks water through the skin of its belly from damp sand
it drinks seawater and filters the salt out through its kidneys
context: A quokka gets nearly all its water from its food, including water-storing succulents, letting it survive about a month without a drink on an island where fresh water is scarce. (Its tail does store fat, but that fuels it through lean food seasons — not thirst.) Source: The Nature Conservancy Australia, 'Meet the Quokka'; San Diego Zoo, 'Quokka.'

question: Seen from above, a drifting jellyfish is round as a pie: any line through its center divides it into matching wedges. The same goes for a sea anemone or a sea star. What do all three of these animals lack?
answer: A front end
choices: A front end
A stinging cell
An outer skin
A gut cavity
context: They are RADIALLY symmetric: built like a wheel around a center, with a top and a bottom but no front and no back. Cut one into wedges any way through the center and the pieces match. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_in_biology

question: A rooted sea anemone can never turn to face anything, and a jellyfish drifts wherever the current takes it. Their wheel-shaped bodies, the same all the way around, meet danger from any side equally well, but the plan costs them something a fish takes for granted. What can these radial animals never do?
answer: Chase or flee in one chosen direction
choices: Chase or flee in one chosen direction
Grow larger than a dinner plate
Survive in cold, deep water
Feel a touch anywhere on the body
context: A wheel-shaped body meets food or danger from any side equally well, but it has no leading point to drive toward, so it can never chase prey or flee in one committed direction. That directed speed is exactly what a bilateral, front-and-back body buys. Source: https://bio.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Introductory_and_General_Biology/General_Biology_(Boundless)/27:_Introduction_to_Animal_Diversity/27.02:_Features_Used_to_Classify_Animals/27.2A:_Animal_Characterization_Based_on_Body_Symmetry

question: A biologist sorting animals by body plan finds that about 99 percent of species, over a million kinds, have a mirror-image left and right and a definite front and back. Three of these four animals belong to that huge club. Which one is the rare exception, built like a wheel around its center?
answer: A jellyfish
choices: A jellyfish
A tuna
A honeybee
An earthworm
context: You, a fish, an insect, and a worm are all bilateral — a left and a right that mirror each other, a head and a tail — and about 99% of animals are built this way. The radial jellyfish is the rare exception. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_in_biology

question: A tuna and a shark each have a clear head end that leads the way and a tail that follows. A jellyfish, built like a wheel, just goes where the current carries it and has never needed that shape. What does a front-to-back body give a swimmer like a tuna or a shark?
answer: Less drag cutting through the water
choices: Less drag cutting through the water
More powerful tail muscles
A lighter, hollow skeleton
Far larger gills for oxygen
context: A bilateral body can taper to a leading point and cut through water or air with far less drag, which is why nearly every fast pursuer or escaper is bilateral, not radial. A radial drifter never needed to be streamlined. Source: https://bio.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Introductory_and_General_Biology/General_Biology_(Boundless)/27:_Introduction_to_Animal_Diversity/27.02:_Features_Used_to_Classify_Animals/27.2A:_Animal_Characterization_Based_on_Body_Symmetry

question: Creeping over the ocean floor, a sea star has barely a head at all: its nerves spread out in a ring instead of clustering up front, and a jellyfish's spread in a net. At the other extreme, one group of ocean hunters crams camera-like eyes, a sharp beak and a large brain together at its leading end. Which sea animals are they?
answer: Octopuses and squid
choices: Octopuses and squid
Clams and oysters
Barnacles and limpets
Sea cucumbers and sand dollars
context: Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish are highly cephalized — camera-like eyes and big brains packed at the front — while clams, barnacles, and sea cucumbers show little to no cephalization at all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cephalization

question: A grown sea star spreads five arms around its center, with no front and no back: it looks like the perfect radial animal. Yet its larva is a tiny swimmer with mirrored left and right halves, like a person's. When that larva transforms into a five-armed adult, how does the change happen?
answer: The left side takes over and rebuilds the body in five
choices: The left side takes over and rebuilds the body in five
It sprouts a new arm from the center each year
Its skin hardens into five plates that split apart
Both halves fuse into a single ring
context: The starfish larva is bilateral, but during metamorphosis its LEFT side grows at the expense of the right, which is absorbed and lost; the left side then rebuilds the whole body in five parts around a center. That is why echinoderms are counted as bilaterians that went radial second. Source: https://iere.org/are-starfish-larvae-bilateral/

question: A robin flings itself again and again at a window in spring, pecking and beating its wings at what looks like another robin on the other side of the pane. It attacks the same spot for days, and the rival never flies away. What is the robin really attacking?
answer: Its own reflection
choices: Its own reflection
A rival male robin
A hawk hunting nearby
A mate it is courting
context: Most animals treat a mirror image as another animal. A robin will batter its reflection in a window for days, and a betta fish flares its fins at the glass, because neither realizes the 'intruder' is itself. Source: PMC/Royal Society, 'On the mirror test and the evolutionary origin of self-awareness'; aeon.co mirror-test essay.

question: A chimpanzee woke from anesthesia with a red dye mark on one eyebrow, painted there by Gordon Gallup Jr. while it slept. It had no way of knowing the mark was there until Gallup showed it a mirror. What did a chimp that knew the reflection was itself do?
answer: Reached up and touched the mark on its own eyebrow
choices: Reached up and touched the mark on its own eyebrow
Touched the mirror where the mark appeared
Pressed its face flat against the glass
Groomed a clean, unmarked patch of fur
context: The mirror mark test hides a dye mark where the animal can only spot it in a reflection. Gallup's chimps woke, saw the mirror, and reached to touch the red marks on their own eyebrow and ear — proof they understood the reflection was themselves, not a stranger. Source: PubMed 4982211, Gallup 1970; Wikipedia, Mirror test.

question: Gordon Gallup Jr. left chimpanzees alone with a mirror for days in 1970. At first they bristled and threatened the 'stranger' in the glass. Then their behavior flipped to something no one had recorded in an animal before. What did the chimps start doing with the mirror?
answer: Grooming parts of themselves they couldn't otherwise see
choices: Grooming parts of themselves they couldn't otherwise see
Hoarding the mirror from other chimps
Smashing it to reach the intruder
Ignoring it completely and turning away
context: Gallup's 1970 study invented the mirror mark test. Once the chimps stopped treating the reflection as a rival, they used it as a tool — inspecting the insides of their mouths and other spots they could never see directly. Source: PubMed 4982211, Gallup 1970, 'Chimpanzees: self-recognition.'

question: Two bottlenose dolphins named Presley and Tab swam up to a mirror at the New York Aquarium, each with a mark on its body. They became the first animals outside the primates shown to recognize themselves, yet a dolphin has no hands to touch a mark. How did they inspect the spot?
answer: They twisted and circled to bring it in front of the mirror
choices: They twisted and circled to bring it in front of the mirror
They rubbed it against the tank floor
They called to a partner to check it
They spat a jet of water at the mark
context: With no hands, Presley and Tab contorted their bodies to maneuver the marked spot into view in the mirror and examine it — clear self-directed behavior. Source: Reiss & Marino 2001, PNAS, 'Mirror self-recognition in the bottlenose dolphin.'

question: At the Bronx Zoo, an Asian elephant named Happy stood before an eight-foot mirror. Painted above one eye was a white 'X' she could only see in the reflection; a matching but invisible mark sat on the other side of her head. Happy ignored the invisible one — but what did she do about the 'X' she could see?
answer: Reached her trunk up to touch it
choices: Reached her trunk up to touch it
Splashed water over that eye
Backed away from the mirror
Trumpeted at the reflection
context: Happy repeatedly brought her trunk to the visible white mark and ignored the invisible sham mark on the other side — evidence she recognized the elephant in the glass as herself. Source: Plotnik, de Waal & Reiss 2006, PNAS; Smithsonian Magazine.

question: A Eurasian magpie hopped up to a mirror in 2008 wearing a small colored sticker, placed where it could spot the mark only in the reflection. Magpies became the first non-mammals shown to pass the test, though birds lack the neocortex once thought necessary for self-recognition. Where on its body was the sticker?
answer: On its throat
choices: On its throat
On its tail
Under one wing
On its lower back
context: The magpies wore the sticker on the throat; those able to see it in the mirror scratched at their own throats to remove it, while birds given a sticker invisible against their dark feathers did not react. Source: Prior, Schwarz & Gunturkun 2008, PLOS Biology.

question: A wild gorilla sits before a mirror with a dot painted on its face, and like most wild gorillas it never notices the mark. Koko, the signing gorilla raised by people, passed the same test easily. Researchers say the failure is not about brains but about one habit of gorilla social life. What habit blocks a wild gorilla?
answer: Avoiding a long stare, which among gorillas is a threat
choices: Avoiding a long stare, which among gorillas is a threat
Grooming each other constantly instead of alone
Deferring every action to the dominant silverback
Treating any new object as food to sample
context: Among gorillas, a hard stare is a challenge, so most avoid gazing into a mirror long enough to notice a mark — a social block, not a mental one. Koko and other human-raised gorillas, less bound by that rule, passed. Source: Wikipedia, Mirror test, gorilla section.

question: Spotting a colored mark on its own throat in a mirror in 2019, a cleaner wrasse, a small reef fish, tried to scrape it off, a pass no one thought a fish could manage. Instead of settling the question, the result touched off a scientific fight, led by the primatologist Frans de Waal. What did the skeptics argue?
answer: An itch worth scraping falls short of true self-recognition
choices: An itch worth scraping falls short of true self-recognition
The wrasse simply mimicked a nearby fish's movements
Only warm-blooded animals can form a self-image
The mark's color must match the fish's own for a pass
context: Primatologist Frans de Waal argued the itchy mark and ambiguous behavior fall short of true self-recognition, calling it an in-between level closer to a monkey's than an ape's. The debate over what 'passing' even means remains unsettled. Source: Kohda et al. 2019, PLOS Biology; de Waal 2019, PMC6366752.

question: A cleaner wrasse that had already recognized itself in a mirror stared at two photographs of strange rival fish, one enlarged to a tenth bigger than itself, the other shrunk a tenth smaller. A wrasse that had never seen a mirror attacked both. This fish treated the two photos differently. What did it do?
answer: Backed away from the larger rival but attacked the smaller one
choices: Backed away from the larger rival but attacked the smaller one
Charged the larger rival but ignored the smaller one
Fled from both rivals into the nearest crevice
Circled both rivals without striking either photo
context: In a 2024 experiment (Kobayashi, Kohda et al., Scientific Reports 14:20202), wrasse that had passed the mirror test refrained from attacking a rival photo scaled 10% LARGER than themselves while still attacking one scaled 10% smaller — as if each opponent were being measured against a stored sense of the fish’s own body size. Mirror-naive fish attacked both. The researchers argue the fish carries a mental image of how big it is. Source: Kobayashi, Kohda, Awata, Bshary, Sogawa (2024), Scientific Reports, ‘Cleaner fish...precisely realize their body size based on their mental image’ — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11390716/

question: A crab-eating macaque spent roughly 2,400 hours in front of a mirror. Gordon Gallup, who invented the mirror test, says only chimpanzees and, more weakly, orangutans truly pass it, and this monkey is his hardest evidence. After all those hours, what had it still never done?
answer: Turned the glass to inspect a mark it could not otherwise see
choices: Turned the glass to inspect a mark it could not otherwise see
Stopped threatening the reflection as a rival monkey
Learned to reach food shown only in the reflection
Groomed a companion sitting beside it at the mirror
context: For Gallup and Anderson (2020 reviews), that failure despite endless practice marks a real cognitive divide, not a matter of time at the glass: they hold no animal reliably recognizes itself in a mirror except chimpanzees and, to a lesser degree, orangutans. The macaque was given roughly 2,400 hours of mirror exposure and never developed self-directed behavior or passed the mark test. This is the strict counterweight to Frans de Waal’s gradualist view that self-awareness comes in degrees across many species. Source: Anderson & Gallup, self-recognition review — https://courses.washington.edu/ccab/Gallup%20on%20mirror%20test.pdf ; Gallup & Anderson (2020) summarized in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_test

question: A cat-sized animal with rich reddish-brown fur sleeps away the day in a misty bamboo grove of the eastern Himalayas. Cream-white patches mark its face, and red and buff rings band its long, bushy tail. When it wakes, it munches bamboo shoots. Which animal is it?
answer: The red panda
choices: The red panda
The ring-tailed lemur
The pine marten
The raccoon dog
context: The red panda (Ailurus fulgens) is a small russet, cat-sized bamboo-eater of the eastern Himalayan forests, head-and-body about 20-25 in (51-63.5 cm), with a bushy ringed tail (red-and-buff bands, dark tip) and a white-marked face. Source: Wikipedia, Red panda.

question: A red panda perches on a branch in a misty forest of Nepal, pinches a single bamboo stalk in one paw and strips the leaves off with its teeth. A house cat's paw, all soft pads and claws, could never pinch a stalk like that. What extra part lets the red panda grip like a small hand?
answer: An enlarged wrist bone that juts out like an extra thumb
choices: An enlarged wrist bone that juts out like an extra thumb
A sixth true finger grown beside the other five
A sticky pad that glues the stalk to its palm
A hooked claw that curls all the way around
context: The 'false thumb' is not a real finger but an enlarged wrist bone, the radial sesamoid, that sticks out like an extra thumb, letting the paw pinch a stalk against the other digits. Source: Wikipedia, Red panda; Biology Insights, 'Red Panda False Thumb'.

question: Night falls freezing and windy in a high Himalayan bamboo forest, and a red panda curls into a tight ball on a branch, tucking its face and paws away from the wind. Its ringed tail is nearly as long as its body. What does it do with that bushy tail as it sleeps?
answer: Wraps it around its body like a blanket to trap heat
choices: Wraps it around its body like a blanket to trap heat
Props it upright as a windbreak against the gusts
Dips it in a stream to wash off the day's dust
Beats it against a branch to warn off rivals
context: In the Himalayan cold the red panda wraps its long bushy tail around its curled-up body like a blanket, tucking its face and paws under it to trap heat while it sleeps. It lives high up, at forest elevations of about 2,000-4,300 m (6,600-14,100 ft). Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, 'Is a Red Panda a Bear?'; Red Panda Network.

question: In an eastern Himalayan forest, a red panda lives almost entirely on bamboo, though it carries the short, simple gut of a meat-eater, handed down from ancestors that hunted. The tough leaves rush through it in only two to four hours, barely digested. How does the red panda survive on such poor, watery fuel?
answer: It eats enormous amounts and moves slowly to save energy
choices: It eats enormous amounts and moves slowly to save energy
It hunts mice at dawn to make up the missing calories
It hibernates through the leanest months of the year
It stores fat in its tail to burn during the winter
context: Having the gastrointestinal tract of a carnivore, the red panda cannot properly digest bamboo, so it eats about 1.5 kg (over 3 lb) of fresh leaves, or up to 4 kg (9 lb) of shoots, in a day (roughly 95% of its diet) and moves slowly on the low-energy fuel. Curiously, it still extracts nutrients from nearly a third of the dry matter it eats, versus about 17% for the giant panda. Source: Wikipedia, Red panda; Smithsonian National Zoo.

question: A giant panda in central China and a red panda high in the eastern Himalayas both strip bamboo stalks, and both grip them with the very same odd thumb on the paw. Family trees show that their lines split apart tens of millions of years ago. What does sharing that thumb most likely say about how it came to be?
answer: Each lineage grew it separately, landing on the same trick
choices: Each lineage grew it separately, landing on the same trick
The two pandas are close cousins sharing one ancestor
The red panda copied the giant panda by watching it feed
The thumb passed between them by an ancient hybrid mating
context: This is convergent evolution: two unrelated bamboo-eaters independently grew the same false-thumb wrist bone, on distant branches of the tree of life. A ~9-million-year-old red-panda relative, Simocyon batalleri from Spain, already had the thumb but was a meat-eater with no bamboo teeth, so the thumb first evolved for gripping branches in the trees, not for eating bamboo. The red panda is also its own family, Ailuridae, neither a bear nor a raccoon. Source: PNAS, 'Comparative genomics... convergent evolution between the bamboo-eating giant and red pandas'; PMC, 'Evidence of a false thumb in a fossil carnivore.'

question: A toothless giant anteater flicks a sticky, worm-shaped tongue nearly two feet long in and out of a termite nest on a South American grassland, almost too fast for the eye to follow. About how many times a minute can it flick that tongue?
answer: Up to 150 times
choices: Up to 150 times
Up to 15 times
Up to 5 times
Up to 30 times
context: The giant anteater is toothless — its 60 cm tongue is anchored all the way down at the breastbone, and it flicks in and out up to 150 times a minute to lap up ants and termites whole. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, 'Giant Anteater' (nationalzoo.si.edu).

question: A frog sits still on a lily pad as a fly buzzes past. In an instant the fly is gone, snatched by the sticky tongue and hauled back into the frog's mouth before a person could see it happen. How does that strike compare with a human blink?
answer: About five times faster than a blink
choices: About five times faster than a blink
About the same speed as a blink
About half the speed of a blink
About ten times slower than a blink
context: A frog's tongue strikes and captures an insect in under 0.07 seconds — about five times faster than you can blink — flinging the bug back toward its mouth at up to 12 times the acceleration of gravity. Source: Georgia Tech / Alexis Noel, reported in The Conversation & Physics World.

question: A chameleon clings to a twig high in an African forest and spots a fly a full body-length away. In a flash the fly is stuck to the tip of its tongue and hauled back to its jaws. The very tip seizes the prey the moment it touches. What is that tongue tip?
answer: A muscular pad that forms a suction cup
choices: A muscular pad that forms a suction cup
A ring of tiny gripping teeth
A hook of curved bone
A spray of fast-drying glue
context: The chameleon's tongue tip is a sticky, muscular pad that forms a suction cup on contact — it slaps onto prey and grips with both glue and suction, hauling the insect back before the eye can follow the strike. Source: AskNature, 'Chameleons Launch Ballistic Tongues' (asknature.org).

question: A woodpecker hammers a hole into a dead tree, then slides its tongue deep down the wormy tunnels inside to lick out ants and grubs. To reach that far, the tongue must be far longer than an ordinary bird's. Measured against the bird's whole body, beak to tail, how far can it stretch?
answer: About a third of its body length
choices: About a third of its body length
About a tenth of its body length
About a twentieth of its body length
About a fiftieth of its body length
context: A woodpecker's tongue can reach up to a third of the bird's total body length; the Northern Flicker holds the North American record, sticking its tongue two inches past the tip of its bill to reach ants. Source: American Bird Conservancy, 'The Amazing Secrets of Woodpecker Tongues' (abcbirds.org).

question: Like a sticky mop, a frog's tongue slaps onto a passing bug. Part of its secret is spit that changes on the job: watery when it hits, so it floods every crevice of the bug, then suddenly thick to grip on the way back. How soft is the tongue itself?
answer: As soft as brain tissue
choices: As soft as brain tissue
As firm as a fingertip
As stiff as cartilage
As hard as a fingernail
context: A frog's tongue is as soft as brain tissue — ten times softer than a human tongue — paired with 'reversible' saliva that is watery when it hits the bug and thickens to grip harder than honey as the tongue snaps back. Source: Georgia Tech, 'Reversible Saliva Allows Frogs to Hang on to Next Meal' (news.gatech.edu, 2017).

question: A tube-lipped nectar bat flits through a cloud forest in Ecuador. Its whole body is only 2.5 inches long, yet its tongue runs a full 3.5 inches, longer than the bat itself, with nowhere near enough room in the mouth to store it. Where is the base of that tongue rooted?
answer: Down in the rib cage, near the heart
choices: Down in the rib cage, near the heart
In a sac behind the jaw
Coiled at the base of the throat
In a pouch inside the cheek
context: The tube-lipped nectar bat (Anoura fistulata) has the longest tongue relative to body size of any mammal. There's no room for it in the mouth, so the base is stowed down in the rib cage, between the heart and the breastbone. Source: National Geographic, 'Super-tongue Bat Caught on Camera'; Tube-lipped nectar bat, Wikipedia.

question: With an acceleration no muscle contraction alone could produce, a chameleon's tongue shoots out at a bug. At the peak of the launch, the tongue puts out more power than the muscle driving it could ever deliver directly. By roughly how much does it beat that muscle's own maximum?
answer: Five to ten times more power
choices: Five to ten times more power
About double the power
Around a quarter more power
Roughly the same power
context: The chameleon's tongue launches at accelerations up to 500 m/s², storing energy in stretched collagen springs and releasing it in a burst — unleashing about 3,000 watts of power per kilogram, roughly 5 to 10 times more than the muscle could ever produce directly. Source: de Groot & van Leeuwen, Proc. Royal Society B (PMC1691657).

question: A tuna slams into a churning school of silvery sardines off South Africa. Hundreds of fish twist and dart at the same instant, their flanks flashing every which way. What does all that twisting and flashing do to the hunting tuna?
answer: It swamps its eyes, so it can't single out one fish
choices: It swamps its eyes, so it can't single out one fish
It wears the tuna out before it can strike
It hides the school in a cloud of churned sand
It scares the tuna off with a rush of noise
context: A schooling mass overloads a predator's eyes: with so much moving prey in view, it struggles to track and target any single fish. Biologists call this the confusion effect. Source: Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 2019, doi 10.3389/fevo.2019.00141 (the confusion effect).

question: A superpod of common dolphins closes on a shoal of sardines off South Africa. In open water one dolphin could never catch enough of the darting fish, and sardines crowd closer together whenever danger comes. How do the dolphins turn that crowding against them?
answer: They herd the shoal up into a tight ball against the surface
choices: They herd the shoal up into a tight ball against the surface
They split the shoal into lone fish they can pick off
They drive the shoal into the shallows over a reef
They chase the shoal down into the cold, dark deep
context: A single dolphin can't eat a whole shoal, so a superpod herds sardines into a bait ball against the surface — turning the sardines' own safety-in-numbers instinct against them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardine_run; discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/fish/what-is-sardine-run.

question: A meerkat sentinel stands on a lookout mound in the Kalahari while its family digs for beetles. For a hawk overhead it gives one alarm, and the family ducks for cover. For a cobra on the ground it gives a different call. What does the family do when it hears that one?
answer: Gathers together and mobs the snake
choices: Gathers together and mobs the snake
Falls silent and slips quietly away
Freezes flat until the snake slides away
Scatters in every direction at once
context: Meerkats give different calls for different dangers. An aerial alarm sends the family crouching or running for cover, while a call for a snake recruits the others, who gather with tails raised and mob it together. The calls even encode how urgent the danger is. Source: Wikipedia 'Meerkat'; Manser 2001, Proc. R. Soc. B; Rauber & Manser 2017, Scientific Reports, doi 10.1038/srep44436.

question: A peregrine falcon dives at a swirling cloud of thousands of starlings over Rome on a winter evening, and the whole flock folds away from it like a single body. Andrea Cavagna's team filmed such flocks with paired cameras and rebuilt them in 3D. What did they find each bird keeps track of?
answer: about seven nearby birds
choices: about seven nearby birds
every bird within ten feet
only the two birds at its side
the whole flock at once
context: In 2008 scientists in Rome filmed flocks of up to 4,000 starlings from multiple angles and rebuilt them in 3D, proving each bird follows a fixed NUMBER of neighbors (about seven) rather than everything within a set distance — which is what keeps the flock from tearing apart. Source: Ballerini et al. 2008 PNAS; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4436282.

question: Inside a churning bait ball off South Africa, the sardines press tighter and tighter while a tuna circles the edge. W. D. Hamilton offered a blunt explanation in 1971 for why a crowd like this one forms. What was it?
answer: Each fish edges inward to hide behind the others
choices: Each fish edges inward to hide behind the others
Each fish follows a single leader at the front
Each fish takes turns guarding the outer edge
Each fish is drawn in by a scent the school shares
context: The 'selfish herd': isolated individuals move inward to become less vulnerable, so the crowd forms simply because every fish tries to hide behind its neighbors — the safest spot is the middle. Source: Hamilton 1971, 'Geometry for the Selfish Herd', J. Theoretical Biology 31(2):295-311; sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0003347213002601.

question: A goat-sized grazer runs with a huge herd across the dry steppe of Kazakhstan. An oversized, floppy nose droops over its mouth like a short trunk, and only the males carry ridged, amber-colored horns. Which antelope is it?
answer: Saiga antelope
choices: Saiga antelope
Pronghorn
Gazelle
Springbok
context: The saiga's bulbous proboscis-like nose droops over the mouth and is often compared to a whale's nasal cavity. Only males grow horns: thick, slightly translucent, amber/wax-colored and heavily ridged. Source: San Diego Zoo (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/saiga) + Wikipedia 'Saiga antelope'.

question: When saiga herds thunder across the steppe on migration, thousands of hooves throw up choking clouds of grit and fine soil for hours on end. Their oversized drooping nose is quietly keeping the running herd alive. How does that strange nose save them?
answer: Its inner chambers trap the grit in mucus before it reaches the lungs
choices: Its inner chambers trap the grit in mucus before it reaches the lungs
It cools overheated blood as the herd sprints
It amplifies alarm calls so the herd stays together
It sniffs out buried steppe water along the route
context: The floppy nose is an air filter: its convoluted internal chambers, lined with mucus glands, trap dust and particles kicked up by the migrating herd before they reach the lungs. Source: Fauna & Flora International (fauna-flora.org/species/saiga) + San Diego Zoo.

question: A saiga breathes in on a Central Asian winter morning, when the steppe air has dropped far below freezing. If that razor-cold air reached its lungs raw, the animal would be in serious trouble. As the breath passes through its long, chambered nasal passages, what do they do to the incoming air?
answer: Warm and humidify it before it hits the lungs
choices: Warm and humidify it before it hits the lungs
Strip the oxygen from it and store it for later
Slow it so the saiga breathes only a few times a minute
Draw scent from it to track the herd ahead
context: The same nose that filters summer dust also warms and humidifies frigid, sub-zero air in winter, so the saiga isn't breathing freezing air straight into its chest. Source: San Diego Zoo + Kee Science (keescience.com/saiga-antelope).

question: Saiga dropped dead across the Kazakh steppe in May 2015, roughly 200,000 of them in about three weeks, more than two-thirds of the whole species; in some calving herds every animal died. Investigators traced the deaths to a heat-and-humidity spike in the days just before. What actually killed the animals?
answer: A bacterium in the saiga's own airways that turned deadly
choices: A bacterium in the saiga's own airways that turned deadly
A new virus carried in by migrating birds
A toxin in the spring steppe grasses
Poisoned water at the calving grounds
context: The killer was Pasteurella multocida serotype B, which normally lives harmlessly in the saiga's respiratory tract. An unusual heat-and-humidity spike in the ~10 days before let it multiply and invade the bloodstream, causing hemorrhagic septicemia and systemic organ failure across whole herds. Source: CDC/PMC 'Mass Die-Off of Saiga Antelopes, Kazakhstan, 2015' (PMC6537709) + National Geographic + Science Advances (science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aao2314).

question: On a muddy riverbank in northern Australia lies a scaly, armor-plated reptile with a long broad snout full of teeth. It is the largest living reptile on Earth. Big males stretch about 20 feet from nose to tail and can weigh close to a ton -- as heavy as a small car. Which animal is this?
answer: The saltwater crocodile
choices: The saltwater crocodile
The Galapagos tortoise
The green anaconda
The Komodo dragon
context: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile; big males reach about 20 feet long and can weigh up to roughly a ton (1,000 kg or more). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltwater_crocodile

question: Fishermen and sailors have spotted a giant crocodile swimming hundreds of miles from any river, crossing between islands. Almost every other kind of crocodile keeps to the fresh water of rivers, lakes and swamps. Where does the saltwater crocodile actually live?
answer: The open ocean and coastal river mouths
choices: The open ocean and coastal river mouths
High mountain streams
Underground cave pools
Cold northern lakes
context: Unlike almost every other crocodile, the saltwater croc thrives in the open sea and in the salty water where rivers meet the ocean -- earning it the nickname 'saltie.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltwater_crocodile

question: A saltwater crocodile floats still as a log at the water's edge, only its eyes above the surface. When a wading buffalo steps too close, the croc explodes upward, seizes it, and hauls it into deep water. How does it finish off prey too big to overpower on land?
answer: It drags the prey underwater and drowns it
choices: It drags the prey underwater and drowns it
It squeezes the prey to death in its coils
It injects venom through its fangs
It waits for the prey to bleed out on shore
context: The saltwater croc is an ambush hunter: it lies hidden, lunges up in an explosive burst, then drags large prey like water buffalo into deep water and drowns it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltwater_crocodile

question: Clamping its jaws on the leg of a carcass far too big to swallow whole, a saltwater crocodile has a problem: its teeth are made for gripping, not chewing. To tear off a chunk, it does something violent with its entire body. What is the move called?
answer: The death roll
choices: The death roll
The tail slap
The gape strike
The bank charge
context: Because its teeth grip but cannot chew, the saltwater croc performs the 'death roll' -- it clamps on a limb or chunk of flesh and spins its whole body along its long axis until the piece twists off. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/blog/crocodile-death-roll-everything-you-wanted-to-know/

question: Saltwater crocodiles in northern Australia snapped down on a padded force meter that Gregory Erickson's team held between their jaws. The biggest set the record for any living animal, a bite that crushes bone and shatters a sea turtle's shell in one snap. Roughly how hard does a big saltwater crocodile bite down?
answer: About 3,700 pounds of force
choices: About 3,700 pounds of force
About 400 pounds of force
About 90 pounds of force
About 12,000 pounds of force
context: The saltwater croc has the strongest bite ever measured in a living animal, about 3,700 pounds of force (some 16,400 newtons), enough to crush bone and a turtle's shell in one snap. It beat even the American alligator, which Erickson's lab had measured at about 2,980 pounds. The figure is often reported as 3,700 pounds per square inch, but it is a force, not a pressure. Source: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/03/120316093427.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltwater_crocodile

question: In the pitch-black water of a mangrove swamp in northern Australia, a saltwater crocodile cannot see a thing, yet it snaps up a fish the instant the fish moves. Its jaws, face and skin are freckled with thousands of tiny black dome-shaped sense organs. What faint signal in the water do they pick up?
answer: The ripple from a single drop of water
choices: The ripple from a single drop of water
The body heat of warm animals
The faint electric fields of muscles
The scent trail dissolved in the water
context: Tiny dome-shaped pressure sensors dot the crocodile's jaws and skin (thousands over its body); they feel the ripple of a single drop of water, letting it strike unseen prey in the dark. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/121108-nile-crocodile-duncan-leitch-science-human-sensitive-touch

question: Far out in the open ocean, a saltwater crocodile floats with no fresh water anywhere to drink, yet it never dies of thirst from the salt. A special organ pumps the extra salt back out, working nearly three times harder in seawater than in fresh. Where on its body is this salt-purging organ?
answer: On its tongue
choices: On its tongue
Behind its eyes
In its stomach lining
Under its scaly back
context: Special salt glands on its TONGUE pump out excess salt, letting it survive in the sea with no fresh water -- and those glands work almost three times harder in seawater than in fresh. Source: https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/211/9/1482/18227/Functional-and-morphological-plasticity-of

question: A tagged male saltwater crocodile slipped out of Queensland's Kennedy River and covered 590 kilometers, about 370 miles, in just 25 days. Satellite tags on many crocodiles tracked long journeys like his across open water. What was the one thing the crocodiles almost never did?
answer: They almost never swam against the current
choices: They almost never swam against the current
They almost never traveled after dark
They almost never left their home estuary
They almost never strayed from the coastline
context: Across the study, in 96% of long journeys the crocodiles moved WITH the current and almost never fought against it; one tagged male covered 590 km (about 370 miles) in 25 days. Source: https://www.discovermagazine.com/planet-earth/steve-irwins-last-gift-to-croc-science-a-study-of-their-surfing-habits

question: Jamie Oaks used DNA to build a family tree of the true crocodiles, the genus Crocodylus that the saltwater crocodile belongs to. Crocodiles are called living fossils, their body plan barely changed in 200 million years, but the design and the species are two different clocks. When and where did the genus first appear?
answer: About 13 to 8 million years ago, in the tropical Indo-Pacific
choices: About 13 to 8 million years ago, in the tropical Indo-Pacific
About 55 million years ago, alongside the first primates
About 30 million years ago, in the rivers of Africa
About 2 million years ago, during the Ice Age of the north
context: The basic crocodilian design is roughly 200+ million years old, but the true crocodiles are one of the most RECENT reptile radiations. Oaks's 2011 molecular phylogeny dates the origin and rapid diversification of the whole modern genus Crocodylus to only about 13.6-8.3 million years ago (mid-to-late Miocene), from an ancestor in the tropical Indo-Pacific -- not Africa, the Eocene, or the Ice Age. The genus spread worldwide during a period of mass crocodilian extinction, its genera dropping from about 26 to 8 by the Pliocene. So the saltwater crocodile is a young species wearing an ancient design: the shape is old, but the species is new. Source: Oaks 2011, 'A time-calibrated species tree of Crocodylia reveals a recent radiation of the true crocodiles,' Evolution 65:3285-3297; Wikipedia 'Crocodylus.'

question: A few-inch fish with a huge, frog-like mouth backs into an empty snail shell on the seafloor off California until only its head sticks out; a soda can would do as well. It lunges at any fish that swims too close. Which oddly named fish is it?
answer: The sarcastic fringehead
choices: The sarcastic fringehead
The garden eel
The tompot blenny
The sand goby
context: The sarcastic fringehead (Neoclinus blanchardi) lives on the Pacific seafloor from northern California to Baja California, usually about 3 to 8 inches long. It has no burrow of its own, so it moves into any empty shell, crevice, or piece of human junk it can defend. Source: Wikipedia, Sarcastic fringehead; Ocean Conservancy (oceanconservancy.org/blog/2019/10/10/sarcastic-fringehead/).

question: Two sarcastic fringeheads meet at the border of their turf on the seafloor off California, each guarding its own empty shell. Each flares its huge mouth wide open, and both lunge forward together. Divers find the collision strange. How do the two fish clash?
answer: Mouths pressed together, like a monstrous kiss
choices: Mouths pressed together, like a monstrous kiss
Tails whipped together, slapping hard
Bellies shoved flat against each other
Fins locked in a gripping tug-of-war
context: Divers describe the territorial display as two fringeheads pressing their flared-open mouths together, mouth-to-mouth, like a monstrous kiss. Source: Live Science, 'The angry little fish that engages in mouth-to-mouth combat' (livescience.com); AAAS, Weird & Wonderful Creatures.

question: A male sarcastic fringehead guards a bottle-sized hole in the rocky seabed off California. When a rival comes near, he unfolds the front of his head into a giant frilled mouth like a colorful umbrella. Compared with his mouth when shut, how large does that gape flare open?
answer: About four times the size
choices: About four times the size
About the same size
Roughly one and a half times
Around ten times the size
context: When a male fringehead gapes, the whole front of his head unfolds so the open mouth is about four times the size of the closed one. Source: Wikipedia, Sarcastic fringehead; Oceana (oceana.org/marine-life/sarcastic-fringehead/).

question: Mouths flared wide, two sarcastic fringeheads square off over a piece of turf, but the clash rarely turns into a real fight. What usually decides which fish keeps the territory?
answer: Whoever has the bigger gaping mouth
choices: Whoever has the bigger gaping mouth
Whoever bites first
Whoever is a darker color
Whoever is the older fish
context: The mouth-pressing contest is mostly a bluff. The fringehead with the smaller gape usually backs down, so the one with the bigger mouth wins the turf without an actual fight. Source: AAAS, Weird & Wonderful Creatures; Oceana.

question: Floppy fronds of skin called cirri dangle from one spot on the head of a sarcastic fringehead peering out of its shell off California, giving it a shaggy, ragged look and the 'fringe' in its name. Where on the fish do those fronds droop?
answer: Over its eyes
choices: Over its eyes
Along its belly
Off its tail fin
Around its gills
context: The 'fringehead' name comes from cirri — floppy fronds of tissue that hang over the fish's eyes like a shaggy fringe. Source: BBC Science Focus; Wikipedia, Sarcastic fringehead.

question: A sawfish glides over a shallow sea floor, a long blade of teeth leading its shark-like body. Yet its gill slits open on its underside, the mark of one flattened, bottom-dwelling group. What is a sawfish really?
answer: ray
choices: ray
shark
eel
catfish
context: Despite the shark-like look, sawfish are rays (superorder Batoidea) — one of five living species of a flattened, bottom-dwelling group. The giveaway is the gill slits on the underside, like a ray's. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sawfish'.

question: A largetooth sawfish, the biggest of all sawfish, swims up a warm coastal river. From its snout to its tail it can stretch about 7 meters, roughly 23 feet. What is a fish that long about as long as?
answer: school bus
choices: school bus
surfboard
canoe
dining table
context: The largetooth sawfish grows to about 7 m (23 ft) — roughly a school bus — making it one of the biggest fish in any shallow water it enters. Source: National Geographic, 'Largetooth sawfish'; Wikipedia, 'Sawfish'.

question: A hungry sawfish charges into a swirling school of mullet in shallow tropical water, and the mullet scatter in panic. Out ahead of its face juts a long, flat blade of a snout, the rostrum, lined on both edges with sharp tooth-like points. What does the sawfish do with that blade to catch them?
answer: swipes it sideways to slash through the school
choices: swipes it sideways to slash through the school
clamps it shut like scissors on one fish
spins it like a drill to bore forward
spits out a jet of stunning ink
context: The rostrum carries 14 to 37 tooth-like points per side depending on species. The sawfish swipes it sideways to slash through fish schools; mullet have been filmed fleeing a hunting sawfish. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sawfish'.

question: In a muddy river mouth where the water is too dark to see a hidden fish, a sawfish still strikes at prey it never sees. Barbara Wueringer showed in 2012 that its toothed snout-blade is more than a weapon. Its surface is freckled with thousands of tiny pores. What do those pores do?
answer: detect the faint electric fields of living animals
choices: detect the faint electric fields of living animals
taste chemicals dissolved in the water
glow to lure curious fish closer
feel pressure waves from a fish's tail
context: Wueringer et al. 2012 (Current Biology) proved the saw both SENSES and STRIKES: pores studding the rostrum pick up the faint electric fields all living animals give off, so the sawfish finds prey it cannot see, then slashes exactly where the fish is. Source: Wueringer et al. 2012; National Geographic.
