question: Barbara Wueringer filmed captive sawfish hunting. Sometimes one blow of a saw cuts a small fish clean in half; other times it only wounds the fish. Before turning its underslung mouth around to eat, what does the sawfish do with its saw?
answer: pins the wounded fish down against the seabed
choices: pins the wounded fish down against the seabed
tosses the fish up to swallow it whole
carries the fish to a burrow to store it
rubs the fish against rocks to scrape it clean
context: After a swipe wounds prey, the sawfish presses the injured fish down against the seabed with its saw, holding it in place so it can turn and eat. Source: National Geographic, 'How the sawfish wields its saw... like a swordsman'.

question: Andrew Fields DNA-tested 190 wild smalltooth sawfish off Florida and found seven pups that carried genes from their mother alone: virgin births, the first ever confirmed in the wild in any shark or ray. About 3 percent of the pups in that estuary had no father. Under what condition do scientists suspect this happens?
answer: when mates grow too scarce to find
choices: when mates grow too scarce to find
when the water turns colder than usual
when a predator threatens the estuary
when food becomes suddenly plentiful
context: Fields et al. 2015 (Current Biology) confirmed facultative parthenogenesis in wild smalltooth sawfish — the first documented wild virgin birth in sharks or rays. About 3% of pups in one Florida estuary were fatherless, a hint it may happen when mates grow scarce, exactly the situation of a species crashing toward extinction. Source: Fields et al. 2015; Stony Brook University; National Geographic.

question: A dried sawfish saw lies in a museum drawer, its teeth grown over a whole lifetime and never shed or replaced. The balance of strontium and barium laid down in each growing tooth changes with the water the fish swam in. Reading that one saw from base to tip, what can scientists reconstruct?
answer: every migration between rivers and sea the fish ever made
choices: every migration between rivers and sea the fish ever made
the exact species of every fish that individual ate
how many pups the female carried in each pregnancy
the depth of the seabed where it usually rested
context: Because the saw-teeth grow continuously and are never replaced, they lock in a lifelong chemical diary. Barium runs high in freshwater and strontium high in seawater, so the strontium-to-barium ratio deposited in the growing tooth tracks the salinity of the water the fish was in at the time. Reading a single museum saw from its base (birth) to its tip (death) lets researchers replay every trip an individual made between rivers and the sea across its whole life -- all without ever having studied the living animal. Source: Scharer et al., 'Sawfish, Read in Tooth and Saw: rostral teeth as endogenous chemical records of movement and life-history,' Aquatic Conservation (2021) 31, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/aqc.3635 (preprint biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/753293v2.full).

question: Onchopristis, a giant saw-snout of the Cretaceous, grew a 4-meter body and a saw lined with barbed teeth, long before today's sawfish. It was no true sawfish: its separate line invented the saw on its own. What fate do its fossils reveal for this ancient saw-bearer?
answer: its remains turn up inside Spinosaurus as prey
choices: its remains turn up inside Spinosaurus as prey
it beached itself in huge stranding events
it survived the asteroid to become todays sawfish
it used the saw to dig burrows in the seabed
context: Onchopristis lived roughly 125-94 million years ago and reached about 3-4+ meters, with barbed rostral denticles up to ~7 cm. Its remains have been found in the jaw and gut region of the huge predatory dinosaur Spinosaurus -- so this sawfish-like giant was dinosaur food. Crucially, Onchopristis was NOT a true sawfish: it was a sclerorhynchid 'sawskate' that grew its saw on an entirely separate lineage. That different fish independently evolved the same toothed saw is a classic case of convergent evolution, which biologists studying these animals nickname 'pristification.' Source: Wikipedia 'Onchopristis' (Barremian-Cenomanian ~125-94 mya; 2.94-4.25 m; 7 cm denticles; Spinosaurus prey; sclerorhynchoid convergence), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onchopristis (corroborated by ScienceDirect S1464343X11002172).

question: A scout ant finds a crumb and hurries home, dabbing a chemical scent the whole way, and soon a highway of ants streams along that exact line. No ant is in charge and none gives orders. What makes the colony agree on the one best path to the food?
answer: Ants on the shortest route finish the round trip fastest, so their scent piles up first
choices: Ants on the shortest route finish the round trip fastest, so their scent piles up first
The scout ant returns to lead each new group of foragers out by the antenna
The queen smells all the routes from the nest and points the workers down the best one
Older ants remember last season's paths and march the young ones along them
context: The shortest path gets walked more times in the same span, so its scent trail is reinforced fastest and grows strongest; ants prefer the strongest smell, and the colony converges on the best route with no leader at all. Source: Scholarpedia, 'Ant colony optimization' (Dorigo & Stutzle); Deneubourg double-bridge experiment.

question: Long after the scout that discovered the food has gone, a forager sets out from the nest; the two never meet or trade a signal. Marco Dorigo later copied their trick for a computer routing method. How does one ant get its find across to ants it never meets?
answer: It leaves a mark on the ground itself, and later ants react to that mark
choices: It leaves a mark on the ground itself, and later ants react to that mark
It waggles a dance into the nest wall that hatching foragers copy for weeks
It seeds the air near the nest with a lasting cloud the next wave flies into
It grooms a scent onto the eggs so the young hatch already knowing the way
context: Ants coordinate by changing the shared ground -- a dab of scent -- rather than by talking; each ant simply reacts to the altered trail the previous ant left. This indirect, mark-the-world kind of communication is called stigmergy, and Dorigo turned the whole trick into a real routing algorithm, Ant Colony Optimization. Source: Scholarpedia, 'Ant colony optimization'; Dorigo & Stutzle, MIT Press ACO book.

question: A male silk moth sits in the dark and never lays eyes on the female he is about to find. Yet he launches into the wind and flies straight toward her, sometimes from far off. With his eyes no help in the dark, what is he actually following all the way to her?
answer: A scent she releases that drifts to him on the wind
choices: A scent she releases that drifts to him on the wind
A faint call she beats out by drumming her wings
The warmth of her body glowing against the cold night
A patch of the leaves she has chewed and marked
context: The female silk moth releases a scent called bombykol into the breeze, and the male flies upwind toward the smell alone. Bombykol was the first pheromone ever chemically identified, by Adolf Butenandt in 1959. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bombykol'; RSC Education, 'In pursuit of bombykol'.

question: Huge, feathery antennae spread from the head of a male silk moth, studded with more than 20 million tiny pores tuned to one chemical the female gives off. Scientists tested how faint a trace of it his smell-detecting nerve cells can catch. How little of it will set one of them firing?
answer: A single molecule of it
choices: A single molecule of it
About a thousand molecules
Roughly one part in a million of the air
A puff of it he must swim through directly
context: A single molecule of bombykol can fire one of the male's smell-detecting nerve cells, and only a few molecules landing per second get him flapping to hunt down the female. Source: RSC Education, 'In pursuit of bombykol'; PMC3978319 on the silkmoth Bombyx mori.

question: A worker ant returns to a busy nest packed with thousands of others, and the guards let her walk right in. Moments later a lone ant from a rival colony tries the same door and is swarmed and attacked. How do the guards tell friend from foe?
answer: Each colony carries its own blend of waxy scent on the body, like an ID badge
choices: Each colony carries its own blend of waxy scent on the body, like an ID badge
Nestmates share a special call the intruder could not answer
The guards knew every one of their thousands of sisters by sight
Home ants march in step while a stranger's gait gives her away
context: Every colony has its own chemical ID: a blend of waxy cuticular hydrocarbons on the body. An ant that smells right gets in; one with the wrong smell is attacked as an intruder. Source: AntWiki, 'Cuticular Hydrocarbons'; Frontiers in Ecology & Evolution (2015).

question: An Alcon blue caterpillar lies on the ground, and passing Myrmica ants, instead of eating it, gently pick it up and carry it into their nest. There they feed it ahead of their own grubs. Ants normally attack any outsider. How does this one win such treatment?
answer: It coats itself in chemicals matching the colony's own scent
choices: It coats itself in chemicals matching the colony's own scent
It plays dead so convincingly the ants mistake it for a corpse
It bites a nurse ant and mimics her alarm scent to seize control
It hatches from an egg the ants themselves carried in by mistake
context: The caterpillar counterfeits the colony's smell so exactly that the ants raise it as one of their own, even feeding it ahead of their own grubs; the better it copies the smell, the more it fools them. Source: National Geographic, 'Evolutionary arms race turns ants into babysitters for Alcon blue butterflies'; ResearchGate, 'Chemical mimicry of Myrmica ants by Alcon blue caterpillars'.

question: A sea angel, a tiny snail with no shell, flaps slowly through the icy Arctic sea on two thin wings. They grew from a part of the body that a garden snail uses for something very different. What does a garden snail use that part to do?
answer: Crawl along the ground
choices: Crawl along the ground
Grip a leaf to feed
Seal its shell shut
Sense the air ahead
context: The sea angel (Clione) is a shell-less sea snail whose two wing-like flaps, called parapodia, evolved from the muscular foot a land snail crawls on. It swims where a snail's foot should be. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium, 'Sea angel'; Smithsonian Ocean, 'Angels of the Sea'.

question: Out in the dim open ocean, a sea angel drifts on a pair of little flapping wings. It has no armor, no venom and nowhere to hide in that vast middle water, yet fish and shrimp swim right past without noticing it. What trick of its body lets it vanish in plain sight?
answer: Its body is transparent, like glass
choices: Its body is transparent, like glass
Its skin flashes a silvery mirror
It puffs out a cloud of dark ink
It turns jet-black to match the deep
context: The sea angel's body is transparent and gelatinous, with red-orange guts glowing faintly through the clear tissue. In dim deep water the see-through body works as camouflage, hiding it from predators. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium, 'Sea angel'; Smithsonian Ocean, 'Angels of the Sea'.

question: Flapping through Arctic waters on two little wing-like flaps, a sea angel is a fussy hunter that ignores almost every kind of prey and chases just one food its whole life. What does it hunt?
answer: The sea butterfly, a shelled swimming snail
choices: The sea butterfly, a shelled swimming snail
The copepod, a drifting flea of the sea
The krill, a swarming shrimp of cold seas
The arrow worm, a see-through drifting hunter
context: Clione limacina feeds almost exclusively on the 'sea butterfly' (genus Limacina, a swimming snail), especially Limacina helicina and Limacina retroversa. The other choices name other real cold-water zooplankton (copepods, krill, arrow worms) the sea angel does not specialize on. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clione limacina'; Sea Slug Forum, 'Clione limacina'.

question: When a sea angel seizes its prey, the meal is still locked inside a hard coiled shell. In one second the graceful 'angel' turns monster, shooting six grabbing cones from its head to clamp the shell tight. How does it then get the soft animal out of the shell to swallow it?
answer: It drags the body out with rows of hooks
choices: It drags the body out with rows of hooks
It dissolves the shell in a splash of acid
It crushes the whole shell in strong jaws
It waits for the trapped snail to crawl out
context: After its buccal cones clamp the prey's shell, the sea angel uses rows of chitinous hooks (and a radula) to grip the soft body of the sea butterfly and drag it out of the shell, then swallows it whole. It does not crush or dissolve the shell. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clione limacina'; Sea Slug Forum, 'Clione limacina'.

question: In the Antarctic, a tiny shrimp-like amphipod grabs a passing sea angel and clamps it onto its own back, then swims around carrying the little angel everywhere like living cargo. A fish that eats bare amphipods all day will not touch one wearing this rider. What is it about the sea angel that turns the amphipod into off-limits food?
answer: It oozes a foul chemical that fish find revolting
choices: It oozes a foul chemical that fish find revolting
It stings any fish that swims too close to the pair
It glows brightly and startles a hunting fish away
It blends the amphipod into the dark open water
context: The Antarctic sea angel (Clione antarctica) makes a defensive molecule scientists named pteroenone that tastes so bad fish spit it out. The amphipod Hyperiella dilatata exploits this: it captures a sea angel and carries it clamped on its back as a living chemical shield. Fish readily eat amphipods without a rider but reject any that carries one. It was documented as one of the first known cases of an animal 'abducting' another purely for chemical protection. Source: Baker & McClintock, Nature (1993); Wikipedia, 'Clione antarctica'; Springer, 'A survival pack for escaping predation in the open ocean' (2018).

question: A sea cucumber slumps across the seafloor like a fat, dark worm, but it is no worm: it is a cousin of the sea star. Hidden inside that drooping body is the very same geometry a starfish shows on the outside. What body plan does the sea cucumber keep?
answer: a five-fold, wheel-like symmetry
choices: a five-fold, wheel-like symmetry
a left-right mirror symmetry
a coiled spiral like a snail
no symmetry, just a shapeless blob
context: Despite its wormy look, the sea cucumber is an echinoderm — a soft-bodied relative of sea stars and urchins. It keeps the family's hidden five-fold symmetry, most visible in the ring of five tentacles around its mouth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_cucumber

question: With its mouth to the sand, a sea cucumber crawls slowly across the muddy ocean bottom all day. It has no teeth to grab prey and no legs to chase it, yet its steady work earns it the nickname 'the seafloor's vacuum cleaner.' What does it actually eat?
answer: mud and sand, digesting the dead scraps inside
choices: mud and sand, digesting the dead scraps inside
small fish it stuns with a shock
seaweed it scrapes off rocks
plankton it filters from open water
context: A sea cucumber swallows sediment, digests the tiny scraps of dead matter inside, and passes the cleaned sand out the other end — recycling nutrients as it goes. A single one can clean more than 45 kilograms (about 99 pounds) of seafloor sediment in a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_cucumber

question: A hungry crab clamps its claws onto a sea cucumber, and the soft, tube-shaped animal seems doomed. Then, in one sudden act, it startles the crab or tangles it in sticky white threads, and creeps slowly away. What does the sea cucumber do to escape?
answer: shoots its own internal organs out its rear
choices: shoots its own internal organs out its rear
inflates into a spiny ball
squirts a cloud of black ink
snaps off its tail and swims away
context: Scientists call this 'evisceration.' The sea cucumber ejects its own guts out the rear to shock or entangle a predator, then slowly regrows the lost organs over the following weeks. Source: https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/nature/sea-cucumbers.html

question: On the seafloor, a sea cucumber pulls oxygen from the water though it has no gills at all. Inside it, a branching organ called the respiratory tree takes up the oxygen, fed by water the animal pumps in and out of one surprising opening. Which opening does it breathe through?
answer: its anus
choices: its anus
its mouth
a blowhole atop its back
a slit along its side
context: A sea cucumber draws seawater in through its anus into a branching 'respiratory tree' just inside, pulls out the oxygen, then pushes the water back out. This respiratory tree is found only in sea cucumbers — no sea star or urchin breathes this way. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_cucumber

question: To hide from a hungry fish, a sea cucumber pours its whole body like liquid into a narrow crack in the rock. Seconds later it locks that same body wall rigid as bone, and nothing can pull it out. What is its body wall made of?
answer: catch collagen the nerves stiffen and relax at will
choices: catch collagen the nerves stiffen and relax at will
muscle fibers that ratchet tighter and tighter
a fluid skeleton the animal pressurizes with water
waxy plates that slide and interlock like scales
context: The body wall is made of 'catch collagen' (mutable collagenous tissue), switched soft-to-stiff under nerve control rather than by muscle. A protein called 'tensilin' stiffens the tissue while 'softenin' relaxes it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catch_connective_tissue

question: A slender pearlfish leaves its home at night to hunt on a tropical reef. Home is the body of a living sea cucumber, which it enters tail-first through the rear opening. Coming back in murky, dark water, the fish must find that one small opening again. What cue guides it home?
answer: the current it pushes out as it breathes
choices: the current it pushes out as it breathes
the scent trail of the cucumber's mucus
the faint glow of the cucumber's skin
the beat of the cucumber's heart
context: The pearlfish follows the sea cucumber's breathing current to the rear opening, waits for the animal to exhale and dilate, then threads itself in tail-first, breath by breath. Not all are polite tenants — some species (genus Encheliophis) eat their host's gonads from the inside. Source: https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/blogs/creatura-blog/2014/08/pearlfish-lives-in-sea-cucumber-anus/

question: A small marine mammal floats on its back in a kelp bed off California, pounding open a clam on its chest with a stone. Unlike seals and whales, it has no thick blubber under its skin, yet it dives into near-freezing water day after day. Which animal is it?
answer: The sea otter
choices: The sea otter
The harbor seal
The manatee
The sea lion
context: The sea otter (Enhydra lutris) is the only one of these that lacks blubber entirely and habitually floats on its back to feed. Source: Seattle Aquarium, 'The densest fur of any animal on Earth' (seattleaquarium.org).

question: A sea otter floats on its back in the icy North Pacific off Alaska in winter, and no blubber lies under its skin. Only its fur stands between it and the freezing water, holding a thin layer of something against the skin. What does the fur hold there?
answer: A layer of air
choices: A layer of air
A layer of body oil
A layer of warm water
A layer of dead skin
context: The sea otter has no blubber. It survives on fur alone, which traps a layer of air against the skin for insulation. Source: Seattle Aquarium (seattleaquarium.org).

question: Only its fur keeps a sea otter warm as it dives into the icy North Pacific, and that fur holds a record no other animal comes near. In one square inch of its skin biologists have counted between 500,000 and a million of one thing, more than a whole human head has. What is packed so tightly into the coat?
answer: Hairs
choices: Hairs
Sweat glands
Scent pores
Tiny scales
context: The sea otter has the densest fur of any animal on Earth: up to a million hairs per square inch, versus about 100,000 hairs on an entire human head. Source: Seattle Aquarium (seattleaquarium.org).

question: In a California kelp bed, a sea otter's dense fur is the only thing keeping out the freezing water. If the coat mats down and starts to leak, the otter can chill and die. Biologists watching wild otters find one activity takes up about a tenth of their day. What is it?
answer: Grooming its fur
choices: Grooming its fur
Diving for shellfish
Sleeping in a raft
Chasing off rivals
context: Because insulation depends on the trapped air, a sea otter grooms almost constantly — about 10 percent of its day cleaning and fluffing its coat. Matted or oiled fur loses its insulation. Sources: Guinness World Records 'Densest fur'; iere.org.

question: With no blubber at all, a sea otter stays warm in the freezing North Pacific only by its dense fur and by the heat its body burns from food. To keep that little furnace running, it must eat almost nonstop. How much does it eat in a day, measured against its own weight?
answer: About a quarter of its own body weight
choices: About a quarter of its own body weight
About a tenth of its body weight
Roughly its full body weight
Barely a pound of food
context: A sea otter eats about a quarter of its body weight in food daily — the equivalent of a 160-pound person eating 40 pounds. Its high metabolism generates the heat that keeps it alive. Source: Seattle Aquarium (seattleaquarium.org).

question: A raft of sea otters settles onto the North Pacific to sleep, drifting on the current on their backs among the kelp. Out in open water the current could easily carry a sleeping otter far from the group by morning. What do the otters do with one another to keep from drifting apart?
answer: Hold each other's paws
choices: Hold each other's paws
Pile into a tight heap
Take turns as a night watch
Sing to stay in a group
context: Observed behavior: sleeping sea otters in a group — a 'raft' — hold each other's paws, hand in hand, so the current can't scatter them while they sleep. Source: mymodernmet.com; animalsaroundtheglobe.com.

question: Where sea otters vanish from a stretch of Pacific coast, the towering kelp forests collapse within a few years into a bare rubble field. The otters had been protecting the kelp all along just by eating one animal in great numbers, which makes them the classic keystone species. Which animal had they been eating?
answer: Sea urchins
choices: Sea urchins
Jellyfish
Starfish
Barnacles
context: By eating sea urchins that would otherwise devour kelp, sea otters keep entire underwater kelp forests alive — the classic keystone species. Where otters disappear, urchins strip the kelp to a barren. Source: Estes & Palmisano 1974, Science; USGS Jim Estes profile.

question: Before it can even swim, a sea otter pup bobbing in freezing water already makes body heat at full adult strength. Wright and colleagues found in 2021 that certain cells in the otter run their mitochondria inefficiently, leaking energy straight into body heat instead of useful work. Which part of the otter is doing all this heat-making?
answer: Its everyday swimming muscles
choices: Its everyday swimming muscles
A thick pad of brown fat
Its unusually large liver
The dense blood vessels in its paws
context: A 2021 study (Wright et al., Science 373:223-225) found sea otter skeletal muscle runs a 'leaky' metabolism: its mitochondria let protons short-circuit across the membrane to make pure heat rather than movement. This proton leak can reach about 40% of the muscle cells' total respiratory capacity, the highest measured in any mammal except tiny mice, and gives the otter a resting metabolic rate roughly three times higher than predicted for its size. Because pups generate this muscle heat at full adult rates before those muscles are strong enough to swim, the trait clearly evolved for staying warm, not for moving. Source: Wright T. et al., Science (2021); PMC9467568 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9467568/); Science News (https://www.sciencenews.org/article/sea-otter-warmth-mitochondria-muscle-metabolism-biology).

question: Surfacing in a kelp bed with a clam and its favorite rock, a sea otter hammers the shell open on its chest. The rock is the same one it has carried from dive to dive, and when it dives again it does not drop it: it tucks it into a spot on its own body, most often on the left side. Where does it keep its hammer between dives?
answer: A baggy pouch of loose skin under its foreleg
choices: A baggy pouch of loose skin under its foreleg
A gap between its rear paws while backstroking
A fold of thick fur just behind its rounded ear
A cheek pocket lined with stiff bristly whiskers
context: The sea otter (Enhydra lutris) has a loose pouch of skin that extends across the chest under each foreleg; in this pouch -- preferentially the LEFT one -- the animal stores food gathered on a dive and often a favorite rock used to break open shellfish and clams. Its use of rocks to hunt makes it one of the few mammal species to use tools, and it can hammer prey at ferocious rates (about 45 blows in 15 seconds against a tough abalone). Its 32 teeth, particularly the flattened, rounded ('bunodont') crushing molars, are built for smashing hard shells rather than shearing flesh -- unusual for a member of the weasel family. A note on lineage: the Enhydra line became isolated in the North Pacific about 2 million years ago (giving rise to the extinct Enhydra macrodonta and the modern otter), but the older textbook claim that it descends specifically from the fossil 'Enhydritherium' is now considered outdated -- the exact ancestor is still being worked out. Source: Wikipedia 'Sea otter' and 'Enhydra'; Grokipedia 'Sea otter' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Sea_otter).

question: A five-armed creature the size of a hand spreads across a wet rock in a tide pool, spiny on top and gripping the stone with hundreds of tiny tube feet. Everyone calls it a starfish, yet it is no fish at all. What group of animals does it truly belong to?
answer: An echinoderm, kin to sea urchins
choices: An echinoderm, kin to sea urchins
A mollusk, kin to clams
A crustacean, kin to crabs
A cnidarian, kin to jellyfish
context: A sea star (or starfish) is an echinoderm -- the spiny-skinned group that also includes sea urchins and sea cucumbers -- a marine invertebrate, not a fish. About 1,900 species live on the seabed in every ocean on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starfish

question: A sea star creeps across a tide-pool rock, all five arms working together. It has no head at all, no place where a brain could even sit, yet each of its hundreds of tube feet seems to know what the others are doing. With no brain, how is its nervous system built?
answer: A nerve ring circling its mouth, with a cord down each arm
choices: A nerve ring circling its mouth, with a cord down each arm
A knot of ganglia bundled at the base of each arm
A single thick nerve cord running along its back
A double chain of nerve knots along its underside
context: A sea star has no brain at all. Instead of one command center it runs on a ring of nerves around its mouth plus a nerve cord down each arm, so each arm can act somewhat on its own. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starfish

question: Rows of tiny suckered tube feet, hundreds of them under its arms, carry a sea star across the seabed. It has no legs and no fins, yet those feet grip hard enough to pry open a clam. What powers them?
answer: Seawater pumped through a plumbing system
choices: Seawater pumped through a plumbing system
Muscles anchored to an inner skeleton
Sticky mucus that grips and releases
Tiny beating hairs like an oar bank
context: A sea star walks on hundreds of suckered 'tube feet' powered by its water vascular system -- a built-in plumbing loop that pumps seawater to inflate and deflate each foot like a little hydraulic piston. There's no blood in it at all; the working fluid is essentially seawater. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starfish

question: In a rocky tide pool, a sea star humps its five arms over a fat clam, and its tube feet pull at the two halves of the shell for hours. Once the clam gapes even a sliver, the sea star feeds in a way that sounds impossible. How does it eat the clam inside?
answer: Pushes its own stomach out through its mouth
choices: Pushes its own stomach out through its mouth
Injects a venom that liquefies the meat
Grinds the meat with teeth ringing its mouth
Draws the meat up through a sucking throat
context: A sea star pushes its own stomach out through its mouth, slides it into the cracked shell and digests the clam outside its own body, turning the meal into a soupy broth that it then draws back in. Source: Wikipedia 'Starfish' (stomach eversion); https://iere.org/what-animal-turns-its-prey-inside-out/

question: A bright beam falls on a sea star in a tide pool, and slowly the animal creeps away toward the darker water. It has no head and no face, yet it can tell light from shadow. Where on its body is the part that senses light?
answer: At the very tip of each arm
choices: At the very tip of each arm
In a pair of pits beside its mouth
Along the underside of each arm
Scattered across its spiny upper skin
context: A sea star has an eyespot at the tip of each arm, so a five-armed star has five simple eyes -- one per arm tip. Each eyespot is built of roughly 80 to 200 tiny light-sensing units (ocelli) that read light and dark rather than sharp images. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starfish

question: A single arm of a bright blue Linckia sea star lies broken off on an Indo-Pacific reef, with none of the central disc attached. Like other sea stars, Linckia can regrow a lost arm, but over the following months this lone limb, nicknamed a 'comet', does something far stranger. What does the arm do?
answer: It grows an entire new star
choices: It grows an entire new star
It seals over and simply dies
It becomes food for the parent
It hardens into a defensive spine
context: A sea star can regrow a lost arm, and in a few species like the tropical Linckia a single severed arm with NO central disc can rebuild a mouth and disc and grow a whole new star. The lopsided one-long-four-short stage is nicknamed a 'comet' because it looks like a shooting star; the lone arm survives on stored nutrients until it can rebuild. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starfish_regeneration

question: Seawater flows into a sea star resting on a tide-pool rock, but it never just soaks in through the skin all over its body. It enters through a small sieve-plate called the madreporite. Where on the sea star does the water get in?
answer: Through one pale button on its top side
choices: Through one pale button on its top side
Through the suckers on every tube foot
Through gill slits along each arm
Through its mouth on the underside
context: That pale, off-centre button on top of a sea star is the madreporite -- the single intake valve where seawater enters the water vascular system to fill and power all those tube feet. Water gets drawn in at just this one spot, not through the skin all over. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starfish

question: In warm oceans around the world, an air-breathing reptile lives at sea, feeding and sleeping underwater and rising to breathe. Its legs are broad flippers under a smooth, streamlined shell, and only a female ever comes ashore, to lay eggs. What is it?
answer: a sea turtle
choices: a sea turtle
a sea otter
a sea lion
a sea snake
context: The sea turtle is a fully marine reptile: air-breathing lungs, flipper-limbs, and a low streamlined shell for gliding. Only nesting females come ashore. Otters, sea lions, and sea snakes are decoys that share the ocean but not the reptile-with-flippers-and-a-shell body plan. Source: NOAA Fisheries / Britannica (sea turtle overview).

question: A baby sea turtle no bigger than a cookie scrambles out of her sandy nest high on a beach at night. Her mother left months ago, and there is no parent to follow and no map, yet almost every hatchling heads straight for the surf. What does the little turtle steer toward?
answer: the brightest, lowest part of the horizon
choices: the brightest, lowest part of the horizon
the loudest crashing of the waves
the smell of salt on the wind
the warmest patch of sand
context: Hatchlings race toward the brightest, lowest horizon: moonlight and starlight reflecting off the water, plus the downward slope of the beach, both point to the sea. This is why beachfront lights can lure hatchlings the wrong way, inland. Source: oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/turtle-hatch.html.

question: On a moonlit beach, a hatchling sea turtle scrambles down the sand and disappears into the surf. She will not return to land for decades. When she is finally full grown and heavy with eggs of her own, she crosses whole oceans of open water to lay them. Where does she choose to nest?
answer: on the very beach where she hatched
choices: on the very beach where she hatched
on the nearest calm beach she can find
on a beach with the warmest sand
wherever her mother nested that year
context: This ocean-spanning homecoming is called natal homing: the female returns to nest on the very beach where she herself hatched decades earlier. Source: cell.com/current-biology (Brothers & Lohmann, Current Biology 2015).

question: A grown female sea turtle swims in from the open ocean after twenty or thirty years away and finds one particular stretch of beach among thousands of stretches of coast. She arrives to lay her eggs with pinpoint accuracy. What guides her there?
answer: Earth's magnetic field, which she imprinted on as a hatchling
choices: Earth's magnetic field, which she imprinted on as a hatchling
the taste of her home beach's own river water
the exact pattern of stars above her birthplace
a memory of the coastline she saw as a hatchling
context: As a hatchling she imprints on her home beach's unique magnetic signature, its field inclination angle and intensity, then reads Earth's magnetic field like a map and compass to steer back years later. This is geomagnetic imprinting. Source: cell.com/current-biology (geomagnetic imprinting, Lohmann lab).

question: A mother sea turtle drags herself up a warm beach at night, digs a pit with her flippers and lays about a hundred round eggs before heading back to the sea. In mammals, chromosomes fix a baby's sex the moment the egg is fertilized, but not in sea turtles. As the eggs lie buried for two months, what decides each hatchling's sex?
answer: the temperature of the sand
choices: the temperature of the sand
the depth the mother buried them
the order in which they hatch
the size of each individual egg
context: Warmer nests produce females and cooler nests produce males, with the 50/50 'pivotal' point near 29 degrees C (about 84 F). Source: oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/temperature-dependent.html ; SWOT (seaturtlestatus.org).

question: Scientists sampled young green turtles on Raine Island, a tiny sandy cay on the northern Great Barrier Reef and the world's largest green turtle rookery. Its beaches had grown very hot. What had that heat done to the young turtles there?
answer: over 99% hatched female
choices: over 99% hatched female
over 99% hatched male
almost none survived to hatch
the sexes stayed near 50/50
context: Warmer sand makes females, so hotter beaches skew nests female. At Raine Island over 99% of the young green sea turtles studied had hatched as females, leaving almost no males for the future. Source: fisheries.noaa.gov ; National Geographic 2018.

question: A leatherback sea turtle crosses whole oceans hunting jellyfish, its main food. Leatherbacks are endangered, partly because of a deadly mistake at sea: a common piece of trash drifts in the water looking almost exactly like a jellyfish, and the turtles swallow it. What is it?
answer: a floating plastic bag
choices: a floating plastic bag
a tangle of fishing line
an oil slick on the surface
a scrap of foam netting
context: A floating plastic bag looks just like a jellyfish to a leatherback, so the turtles swallow it by mistake, one reason they are critically endangered. Source: oceanicsociety.org ; SEE Turtles (seeturtles.org).

question: A green sea turtle grazes a seagrass meadow off the Great Barrier Reef. Of the seven kinds of sea turtle it is the only plant-eater, while its cousins hunt jellyfish, crabs and sponges. That diet is where its name comes from. How?
answer: the green diet tints its body fat green
choices: the green diet tints its body fat green
its shell turns green from the algae it eats
its skin greens as it grazes on seagrass
its eggs are stained green by the plants
context: The green sea turtle is the only plant-eating sea turtle, and its seagrass-and-algae diet tints its body fat green. That green fat, not the brownish shell, is what gave the turtle its name. Source: Wikipedia (green sea turtle) ; NOAA Fisheries (Green Turtle).

question: Archelon, the largest sea turtle that ever lived, swam a Cretaceous sea over the land that is now the Dakotas. It was as heavy as a rhino and wore a leathery, ridged back much like a modern leatherback's, yet the likeness is a coincidence: its family split off long before today's sea turtles arose. Which group of turtles does Archelon belong to?
answer: Protostegidae, an early branch outside the living sea-turtle line
choices: Protostegidae, an early branch outside the living sea-turtle line
Dermochelyidae, the same family as the modern leatherback
Cheloniidae, the family of green and loggerhead turtles
Chelydridae, the branch that leads to snapping turtles
context: The giant is Archelon, a Late Cretaceous sea turtle (Campanian, ~80-74 million years ago) from the Pierre Shale of the Dakotas. The biggest specimen, nicknamed 'Brigitta' (found 1992, now in the Natural History Museum Vienna), stretched ~4.6 m (15 ft) head-to-tail, spanned ~4 m (13 ft) flipper-to-flipper, and weighed an estimated 2,200+ kg -- roughly 3.5 times the biggest living leatherback. Like a leatherback it had a leathery, ridged carapace rather than a hard bony shell. But Archelon belongs to the Protostegidae, a basal lineage that does not share a marine ancestor with today's sea turtles -- so the leathery shell arose twice by convergent evolution, not by descent. Source: Wikipedia 'Archelon' (Brigitta 4.6 m / 4 m / 2.2-3.2 t, Campanian 80.21-74.21 Ma, Pierre Shale, leathery ridged carapace, Protostegidae basal lineage); Grokipedia 'Archelon'.

question: In near-freezing seas where almost any other reptile would turn cold and sluggish, a leatherback turtle hunts jellyfish, its core running up to 18 C warmer than the water around it. Its swimming muscles make the heat. What stops that heat from bleeding away through its flippers?
answer: countercurrent exchangers where warm and cold blood vessels run side by side
choices: countercurrent exchangers where warm and cold blood vessels run side by side
a dense coat of waterproof insulating fur beneath the tough outer skin
basking at the surface between dives to reheat the chilled flippers
pulling all blood back from the flippers into the body core while diving
context: This warm-bodied strategy is called gigantothermy (regional endothermy). Constantly swimming muscle generates heat; countercurrent heat exchangers in the flippers and around the windpipe -- where outgoing warm blood runs alongside incoming cold blood and hands off its heat -- plus a thick layer of insulating brown fat trap that warmth. The result is a core body temperature up to 18 C (32 F) above the surrounding water. That heat budget lets a leatherback forage where no other reptile can: one was recorded actively hunting jellyfish in water as cold as 0.4 C (near freezing), rewarming at the surface between dives. It is why a tropical-nesting turtle can feed off Canada and into sub-polar seas. Source: Wikipedia 'Leatherback sea turtle' (core up to 18 C above water; countercurrent exchangers in flippers and around the trachea; brown adipose tissue; hunting at 0.4 C); gigantothermy literature (Paladino et al.).

question: In a shallow seagrass meadow, a tiny creature drifts upright through the swaying blades. It stands vertical in the water, has skin without scales, a curled tail, and a horse-shaped head. Yet it also has gills, fins, a swim bladder, and a hard bony skull inside. What is this odd little animal, biologically?
answer: A true fish
choices: A true fish
A crustacean
A mollusk
A marine mammal
context: Despite swimming upright and having no scales, the seahorse is a true fish: it has gills, fins, a swim bladder, and a bony skull with no limbs or digits. Instead of scales, its skin is stretched over fused bony plates that form a suit of protective armor. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/fish/why-is-seahorse-a-fish

question: A storm surge sweeps over a coral reef, and a tiny seahorse anchors itself so the water cannot wash it away. Few fish have a tail like it: only its cousins the pipefish and pipehorses share the trick. What can that tail do?
answer: Coil around objects and grip like a monkey's
choices: Coil around objects and grip like a monkey's
Fan open into a broad paddle for a burst of speed
Glow to lure copepods within snout range
Snap off cleanly and grow back within days
context: The seahorse's curled tail is prehensile — it grips. It wraps around a blade of seagrass or a coral branch to anchor itself so the current can't sweep it away. Along with its relatives the pipefish and pipehorses, it is the only fish with a gripping tail. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/fish/why-is-seahorse-a-fish

question: A seahorse with no teeth at all aims its tube-shaped snout at a copepod, a jumpy little sea bug the size of a pinhead that can dart away in a blink. The strike is over in about three thousandths of a second, faster than a human eye can follow. What does the snout do to catch it?
answer: Sucks the prey up whole in a burst of suction
choices: Sucks the prey up whole in a burst of suction
Crushes the prey against hard throat plates
Wraps around the prey like a coiling lasso
Spears the prey on a sharp bony tip
context: The seahorse has no teeth and no stomach. Its tubular snout works like an eyedropper: it snaps its head upward and sucks tiny prey such as copepods in whole with a burst of suction — striking in just 2 to 4 thousandths of a second, faster than the prey can flee. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms3840

question: A pair of seahorses spirals together through the water in courtship, tails linked, and the female presses a tube called an ovipositor against her mate, passing her eggs across to him. Weeks later the brood is born. Who actually gives birth to the live young?
answer: The father, who carries and delivers them himself
choices: The father, who carries and delivers them himself
The mother, once he returns the eggs to her
Neither one — they hatch alone on the seafloor
Both parents, each releasing half the brood
context: In seahorses the MALE gets pregnant. The female uses a tube to deposit her eggs into a brood pouch on the male's belly; he fertilizes them inside and carries them himself. When it is time, he pumps and contracts the pouch with muscles, ejecting the fully-formed young — a brood of as few as 5 to as many as roughly 2,000 at once. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/how-do-seahorses-give-birth-the-male-pregnancy-explained/

question: A dwarf seahorse off Florida, about two centimeters long and no bigger than a fingernail, beats its dorsal fin between 30 and 70 times every second, a furious blur fit to rocket a fish forward like a torpedo. Yet no fish ever measured moves more slowly. After an hour of that frantic beating, how far does it get?
answer: About 1.5 metres
choices: About 1.5 metres
About 15 metres
About 150 metres
About 1.5 kilometres
context: The dwarf seahorse is the slowest-moving fish ever recorded, with a top speed of about 1.5 metres (5 feet) PER HOUR — yet the dorsal fin driving it beats roughly 30 to 70 times every second, a furious blur pushing a fish that barely moves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seahorse

question: Fertilized seahorse eggs settle inside a brood pouch, a sealed sac on the belly, and stay there for weeks. Yet the pouch is far more than a shelter: research revealed a role once thought to belong only to pregnant mammals. What is it?
answer: Feeds the embryos oxygen and nutrients like a placenta
choices: Feeds the embryos oxygen and nutrients like a placenta
Keeps the eggs warm above the sea temperature
Coats each egg in a hardening protective shell
Signals the embryos when to hatch using sound
context: The male truly nourishes the young. The wall of his brood pouch fills with blood capillaries like a placenta, feeds the embryos oxygen and energy-rich nutrients (lipids and calcium), and slowly adjusts the salt level of the pouch fluid to match the sea before the babies are born. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/how-do-seahorses-give-birth-the-male-pregnancy-explained/

question: A bird of prey nearly as tall as a child strides through the grass of the African savanna on long, stork-like legs. It corners a spitting cobra, stamps it dead with its feet, and never once takes to the air. Which African raptor is it?
answer: Secretarybird
choices: Secretarybird
Golden eagle
Peregrine falcon
Great horned owl
context: The secretarybird (Sagittarius serpentarius) is a tall African eagle that hunts on foot and kills snakes by stomping them to death with its feet, rather than catching prey in flight like other birds of prey. It stands over four feet (about 1.3 m) tall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretarybird

question: A secretarybird kills a striking snake with a downward kick of its foot, then walks away unbitten. When Steve Portugal's team put a trained bird on a force plate, they measured how long the foot actually touches the snake. How long does one killing-kick contact last?
answer: About 15 milliseconds
choices: About 15 milliseconds
About half a second
About two seconds
About five seconds
context: The killing kick lands in only about 10-15 milliseconds of contact - faster than a human blink - so the strike is over before a snake can turn and bite back. Measured on a trained captive secretarybird named Madeleine at the Hawk Conservancy Trust in Hampshire, England, who was taught to attack a rubber snake on a force plate. Source: Portugal et al., 'The fast and forceful kicking strike of the secretary bird,' Current Biology (2016), https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(15)01483-9

question: Striding through the grass on long legs, a secretarybird spends the whole day on the move across the African savanna, hunting on foot though it could fly instead. A researcher who tracked one clocked the total for its daily hike. About how far does it walk in a single day?
answer: About 30 kilometers
choices: About 30 kilometers
About 3 kilometers
About 100 kilometers
About 300 kilometers
context: Instead of soaring, the secretarybird walks up to about 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) a day striding through grassland to hunt, pacing at about 2.5-3 km/h. It has the longest legs of any bird of prey. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretarybird ; https://animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/secretary-bird

question: A female orange sulphur butterfly always picks a mate of her own kind, though to human eyes he looks almost identical to a male clouded sulphur. One gene, bric a brac, decides whether a male's wings carry her cue. What does it switch on or off across his wings?
answer: An iridescent ultraviolet flash
choices: An iridescent ultraviolet flash
A ring of poison scales
A louder wingbeat pulse
A sweeter courtship scent
context: The male orange sulphur butterfly's wings flash iridescent ultraviolet that the near-identical clouded sulphur males don't have — females use that hidden UV flash to pick out a male of their own species. A single gene (bric a brac) switches the UV nanostructures on or off. Source: Rutowski et al. 2005, Proc. R. Soc. B, doi:10.1098/rspb.2005.3216; Ficarrotta et al. 2022, PNAS, doi:10.1073/pnas.2109255118.

question: A garden robin and a European starling both look a plain dusty brown to human eyes. Like most songbirds, they carry not three but four kinds of color cone in their eyes, and the extra one opens a channel of light that human eyes cannot detect. What light is that fourth cone tuned to?
answer: Near-ultraviolet light
choices: Near-ultraviolet light
Far-infrared heat glow
The plane of polarised light
The magnetic field lines
context: Most birds are tetrachromats — they have a fourth cone sensitive to near-ultraviolet (about 300–400 nm) that humans lack entirely, so plumage that looks plain to us can carry a whole extra dimension of UV signal. It is a colour cone, not a heat, polarisation, or magnetic sensor. Source: Andersson et al. 1998, Proc. R. Soc. B, doi:10.1098/rspb.1998.0316; Hunt et al. on avian UV cones.

question: A reindeer scans the bright winter snow of Lapland for wolves. Its lenses let ultraviolet light through to the retina, as human eyes do not. Glen Jeffery, who studied its eyes, thinks this helps it spot a wolf on the snow, and even the marks one leaves. Which mark would stand out most sharply to that ultraviolet sight?
answer: The wolf's urine, dark where it stained
choices: The wolf's urine, dark where it stained
Paw prints pressed into the snow
Claw scratches on the icy crust
Frost from its breath on the twigs
context: Arctic reindeer see into the ultraviolet: their lens and cornea let UV through instead of blocking it as human eyes do. Snow reflects most ultraviolet, so to a reindeer anything that soaks it up looks black against the bright snow. Glen Jeffery, who worked on the study, points to urine, a sign of predators or rivals, and to wolf fur; paw prints, scratches and frost are only snow and ice, and shine as brightly as the rest. Source: Hogg et al. 2011, 'Arctic reindeer extend their visual range into the ultraviolet', J. Exp. Biol., PubMed 21613517; phys.org 2011, quoting Glen Jeffery.

question: A mantis shrimp, a fist-sized hunter of coral reefs, carries some of the most complex eyes on Earth. They hold as many as six kinds of ultraviolet receptor, each tuned by stacked colored filters, the most elaborate ultraviolet setup known in any animal. What advantage do biologists think all that filtering buys it?
answer: Splitting UV into several colors
choices: Splitting UV into several colors
Seeing UV in near-total darkness
Aiming at a UV point of light
Seeing UV through murky water
context: The mantis shrimp has up to six separate ultraviolet photoreceptors, tuned by 'biological sunscreen' filters (mycosporine-like amino acids, the same UV-absorbing compounds many animals use to protect their DNA) layered over the eye, which split the ultraviolet into several separate color channels. Whether the shrimp uses them to tell fine shades of UV apart has not been tested; other work found its color vision built for quick recognition rather than fine discrimination. Source: Bok et al. 2014, 'Biological Sunscreens Tune Polychromatic Ultraviolet Vision in Mantis Shrimp', Current Biology, PubMed 24998530; Thoen et al. 2014, Science.

question: Two birds perch on one branch, one seeing with a cone tuned to violet light, the other with a cone that catches true ultraviolet, a different band of the spectrum. Yet across the family tree of birds, evolution has flipped between those two designs at least fourteen separate times. What actually changes at each of those crossings?
answer: One amino acid swapped inside the cone's opsin
choices: One amino acid swapped inside the cone's opsin
A fresh cone type wired into the crowded retina
An extra opsin gene copied beside the old one
The cone's colored oil droplet bleached to clear
context: The flip is a single amino-acid substitution — Ser90Cys (S90C) — in the second transmembrane helix of the SWS1 cone-opsin protein, which shifts that cone's peak sensitivity below about 380 nm, from violet into the ultraviolet (sites 86, 90 and 93 fine-tune the exact peak). Because so radical a sensory change rides on just one swapped residue, it is cheaply reversible, and bird lineages have crossed back and forth between violet- and UV-sensitive eyes at least fourteen separate times. Source: Ödeen & Håstad 2013, 'The phylogenetic distribution of ultraviolet sensitivity in birds,' BMC Evol Biol 13:36 (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1471-2148-13-36); related origin work keying the avian UV pigment to a single SWS1 substitution: Yokoyama, Radlwimmer & Blow 2000, PNAS 97:7366-7371 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC16551/).

question: A rattlesnake lies coiled in a pitch-black rodent burrow in the American desert, its eyes useless in the dark. Yet a mouse creeping past in the tunnel has almost no chance. Between each of the snake's eyes and its nostril sits a small pit. What does that pit let the snake detect?
answer: The body heat glowing off a warm animal
choices: The body heat glowing off a warm animal
The faint scent trail the mouse leaves
The tiny vibrations of the mouse's feet
The high squeaks the mouse makes
context: Pit vipers (rattlesnakes, copperheads) have a heat-detecting pit on each side of the head, between the eye and the nostril, that senses the infrared glow of a warm animal's body heat. Source: Wikipedia, Infrared sensing in snakes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared_sensing_in_snakes).

question: Researchers blindfolded a rattlesnake so its eyes were completely covered, then loosed a mouse in total darkness. The snake still struck fast and true, and the spot where its fangs landed most often was the same on mouse after mouse. Where did the strikes land most often?
answer: On the chest
choices: On the chest
On the tail
On the head
On the belly
context: Blindfolded, a rattlesnake still strikes a mouse dead-on in total darkness, hitting the chest -- the hottest-glowing part -- about 99% of the time, because it 'sees' the animal purely by heat. Legendary-level feat. Source: A-Z Animals research summary (https://a-z-animals.com/blog/viper-pits-infrared/).

question: A fer-de-lance hunts in the dark, guided by two pits on its face, one on each side. Inside each pit there is no eye and no lens at all, only a tiny air-filled chamber with one ultra-thin sheet stretched across it. What is that sheet, and what does a warm mouse's body heat do to it?
answer: A membrane that warms where the heat lands
choices: A membrane that warms where the heat lands
A crystal that glows where the heat lands
A mirror that reflects the heat inward
A fluid that boils where the heat lands
context: The pit is a tiny air-filled chamber with an ultra-thin membrane stretched inside; it acts as a passive antenna for radiant heat, physically warming where the prey's infrared lands. Heat-sensing nerve endings off the trigeminal nerve then fire, building a crude heat-picture -- not a sharp lens image. Source: Gracheva et al. 2010 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2855400/).

question: Scientists measured the smallest temperature change that the nerves inside a rattlesnake's face pit can still register, and the number stunned them. It ranks the pit among the finest heat detectors ever built by evolution. How small a temperature change can the pit catch?
answer: Less than a thousandth of a degree
choices: Less than a thousandth of a degree
About a tenth of a degree
Roughly a whole degree
About five degrees at once
context: The pit's nerve fibers respond to temperature changes smaller than 0.001 C -- less than a millikelvin -- among the most sensitive heat detectors known in any animal. The pit acts as a biological bolometer, a warmth-measuring instrument. Source: Wikipedia, Infrared sensing in snakes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared_sensing_in_snakes).

question: A pit viper carries one heat pit on the left of its head and one on the right. A single pit could tell the snake a warm animal is out there, but two of them working together unlock something a single pit never could. What does having two pits give the snake?
answer: A sense of how far away the prey is
choices: A sense of how far away the prey is
A way to smell the prey through the pit
A brighter, sharper heat picture
A memory of where prey passed before
context: With a pit on each side of the head, the two overlapping heat-images give stereoscopic thermal vision -- a rough depth-map -- so the snake can triangulate how far away the prey is and aim a strike it cannot see with its eyes. Source: SnakeSnuggles / Wikipedia paired-organ depth perception (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared_sensing_in_snakes).

question: Elena Gracheva's team traced the molecule that turns warmth into a nerve signal inside a pit viper's heat organ in 2010. The very same channel lives in human bodies, where it fires on certain harsh foods rather than on gentle heat. What everyday sensation does that channel produce in people?
answer: The searing burn of wasabi up the nose
choices: The searing burn of wasabi up the nose
The icy tingle of fresh peppermint
The sour pucker of a lemon
The watering sting of chopped onion
context: The molecular trigger in the pit is TRPA1 -- the 'wasabi receptor' channel that in mammals makes us feel the painful burn of wasabi and mustard oil. In pit vipers it is retuned to fire on heat, becoming the most heat-sensitive vertebrate ion channel known. Source: Gracheva et al. 2010, Nature 464:1006-1011 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2855400/). Legendary-level surprise: our wasabi-pain channel is the snake's night-vision.

question: A python can hunt in pitch darkness by sensing a warm animal's body heat, and so can a boa and a pit viper. Yet on the snake family tree the three groups sit far apart, with many heat-blind snakes scattered between them. How did all three end up with heat vision?
answer: Each group evolved it separately
choices: Each group evolved it separately
One ancient ancestor passed it to all three
It jumped between them by interbreeding
One group taught the trick to the others
context: Pit vipers, pythons, and boas each invented heat-sensing pits SEPARATELY -- infrared sense arose by convergent evolution, with snakes adapting the TRPA1 channel into a heat sensor more than once. On the snake family tree these groups sit only distantly apart, with many pit-less snakes between them, so a single shared ancestor cannot explain it. The anatomy differs too: one large pit per side in vipers versus rows of smaller lip pits in boas and pythons. Source: Gracheva et al. 2010 discussion (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2855400/).

question: An angler on a wooden pier on the Florida coast reels in a silvery fish that flops on the boards and seems to grin at him, showing flat white front teeth that look eerily like a person's. Which coastal fish wears that human-looking smile?
answer: The sheepshead
choices: The sheepshead
The barracuda
The lookdown
The pinfish
context: The sheepshead (Archosargus probatocephalus) really does carry flat white incisors up front and rows of grinding molars behind. A 2021 catch off North Carolina went viral because the fish seemed to be smiling with human teeth. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History - Discover Fishes: Sheepshead; Smithsonian Magazine.

question: A sheepshead hangs around a pier piling on the Atlantic coast, five or six bold black bars running down its silver sides like the stripes on an old prison uniform. Anglers gave the fish a second nickname for those bars. What do they call it?
answer: The convict fish
choices: The convict fish
The tiger fish
The zebra perch
The ladder wrasse
context: Those bold vertical black crossbars on a silver body give the sheepshead its nickname, the 'convict fish', because the stripes look like an old prison uniform. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History; Wikipedia: Archosargus probatocephalus.

question: A young sheepshead starts life eating only soft food, drifting zooplankton and marine worms, nothing it has to break into. A grown one cruises the pilings of a pier crunching barnacles, oysters and small crabs that most reef fish will not touch. What grows in its mouth to make that switch possible?
answer: Broad shell-crushing molars
choices: Broad shell-crushing molars
Rows of needle-thin fangs
A single hooked beak
A rough rasping tongue
context: The sheepshead carries rows of blunt, flat molars at the back of its jaws, purpose-built to grind through armor. It eats barnacles, oysters, clams, and crabs, crushing shells the way our molars grind food. Juvenile sheepshead eat soft prey like zooplankton, marine worms, and insect larvae, and only develop the strong shell-crushing molars and switch to barnacles, crabs, and oysters as they grow.

question: A predator lunges at a shingleback skink in the dry Australian scrub and clamps onto completely the wrong end of the slow, tank-bodied lizard, which escapes the other way. What is the shingleback's short, blunt tail shaped like?
answer: Its own head
choices: Its own head
A coiled snake
A clump of leaves
A pinecone tip
context: The shingleback skink (Tiliqua rugosa) has a stumpy tail so like its head that one of its common names is the "two-headed skink." A predator aims at the wrong end and the lizard escapes the other way. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiliqua_rugosa

question: Cornered by a predator in the Australian outback, a shingleback skink wheels around to face it, gapes to show a shocking-pink mouth and hisses hard. Then it flashes one startling color inside that gape to scare the hunter off. What color is it?
answer: Bright blue
choices: Bright blue
Deep black
Pale yellow
Blood red
context: The shingleback flashes a broad bright-blue tongue against a pink mouth while hissing — a bluff meant to scare a predator off before any biting happens. Source: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/shingleback-lizard/

question: Each spring a male and a female shingleback skink find each other again at the very same spot in the Australian scrub, the same couple season after season. Most lizards mate briefly and never meet the partner again. In one documented case, how long had a single couple kept coming back to each other?
answer: Over 27 years
choices: Over 27 years
About one season
Around 3 years
Roughly 10 years
context: The shingleback is the only known monogamous reptile; some documented pairs stayed together over 20 years, and one couple in a long-term study was still reuniting after 27 years. Marked legend for its extraordinary duration. Source: https://blog.nature.org/2021/09/20/the-love-stories-of-sleepy-lizards/

question: A mother shingleback skink gives birth on the red desert dirt of Australia to between one and four live young, not a clutch of small eggs as most lizards lay. Each newborn is startling for a baby lizard. In what way?
answer: Nearly as long as a ruler
choices: Nearly as long as a ruler
Blind and hairless
Covered in soft down
No bigger than a coin
context: The shingleback gives live birth to one to four huge, fully-formed babies (usually two or three), each up to 220 mm long — a giant compared to most newly-hatched lizards. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiliqua_rugosa

question: A slow, tank-bodied shingleback skink faces danger in the Australian scrub without one of the classic tricks that its own lizard relatives still rely on. Somewhere in its evolution it lost that trick for good. Which classic lizard trick can it no longer do?
answer: Shedding and regrowing the tail
choices: Shedding and regrowing the tail
Playing dead until released
Squirting blood from its eyes
Inflating its body with air
context: Unlike most lizards, the shingleback has no autotomy — it cannot drop and regrow its tail — so the head-shaped decoy is a permanent, one-and-only piece of equipment it must protect. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiliqua_rugosa

question: A five-foot grey bird stands frozen at the edge of a papyrus swamp along the White Nile, barely blinking. Its enormous bill, nine inches long and wide as a shoe, ends in a sharp hook. It holds that bill over the shallow water for hours, waiting for a lungfish to surface. Which bird is it?
answer: shoebill
choices: shoebill
secretary bird
marabou stork
great blue heron
context: The shoebill fixes its swamp with a golden-eyed 'death stare,' waiting motionless until prey surfaces to breathe. Its scientific name Balaeniceps rex means 'whale-head king.' Source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, '7 Revealing Facts about Shoebills.'

question: A shoebill stands so still in a papyrus swamp of South Sudan that dragonflies land on its head, waiting for a big fish to surface for air. The instant a fish breaks the water, the bird 'collapses', as its keepers say. What does it pitch forward all at once?
answer: all five feet of itself, bill wide open
choices: all five feet of itself, bill wide open
only its long neck and head
a single grabbing foot
its outstretched wings
context: The shoebill hurls its whole body forward, engulfing the target along with water, mud, and vegetation in a couple of seconds. Source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance; Audubon, 'The Shoebill: Or, the Most Terrifying Bird in the World.'

question: Hauling a lungfish out of the swamp, too big to gulp down whole, a shoebill must deal with it before swallowing. Its enormous bill, shaped like a Dutch clog, has a sharp hook at the tip and razor edges along the sides. Using those blade-like edges, what does it do to its catch?
answer: decapitates it
choices: decapitates it
sucks it dry of blood
swallows it slowly tail-first
shakes it against a branch
context: The hooked tip stabs slippery prey and the razor-edged sides let the shoebill behead a fish before swallowing it. The bill runs about nine inches long and four inches wide. Source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance; Audubon.

question: A male shoebill in an African papyrus swamp warns off a rival by snapping the two halves of his massive bill together, like a pair of wooden shoes clapping shut. Shoebills have no true voice, no croak, no honk, no whistle, and males and females clap in different tones. What does the bill-snapping sound like?
answer: hollow machine-gun clattering
choices: hollow machine-gun clattering
a single deep bill-clap
a slow wooden knocking like castanets
a soft rattle like dice in a cup
context: This bill-clattering is loud and rapid, the shoebill's main way of communicating. Source: Audubon, 'The Shoebill'; San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance.

question: Reared up on its hind legs, Arctodus simus, the giant short-faced bear of ice-age North America, stood about 11 or 12 feet tall, twice the height of a tall adult human and the tallest bear that ever lived. Its head would have been level with what everyday thing?
answer: the rim of a basketball hoop
choices: the rim of a basketball hoop
the top of a school-bus roof
the crossbar of a soccer goal
the seat of a tall barstool
context: Reared up, the giant short-faced bear stood about 11-12 feet (3.4-3.7 m) - tall enough to look a person square in the eye over the rim of a basketball hoop, which sits at 10 feet. It is the tallest bear known to have ever lived. Source: University of Iowa Museum of Natural History (mnh.uiowa.edu/giant-short-faced-bear); North American Bear Center (bear.org).

question: Borja Figueirido's team studied the teeth of the short-faced bear Arctodus simus in 2010. For years it had been pictured as a fast super-predator, a bully that muscled saber-tooths away from their kills, and the team argued against that legend. What did they say the tooth wear pointed to?
answer: a giant opportunistic omnivore
choices: a giant opportunistic omnivore
a mostly plant-eating browser
a lean long-distance pursuit hunter
a seasonal salmon specialist
context: What Arctodus ate is still debated. Older chemistry studies read it as a pure meat-eater, but Figueirido et al. (2010), 'Demythologizing Arctodus simus... the predaceous bear that never was,' argued it was really a giant opportunistic omnivore: its teeth show plant-eating wear and lack the meat-shearing shape of a true super-predator, with no strong evidence it was a specialized scavenger either. Source: Figueirido et al. 2010, Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology (tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02724630903416027); National Geographic, 'The Fearsome Short-Faced Bear Gets a Makeover.'

question: Arctodus simus prowled ice-age North America with a blunt, cat-like muzzle, the very feature that named it the short-faced bear. Yet when Borja Figueirido measured the skull in 2010, he concluded the famous name is essentially a mistake. What did the measurements show the 'short' face really was?
answer: no shorter at all, only deeper and broader, so it merely looked stubby
choices: no shorter at all, only deeper and broader, so it merely looked stubby
shortened by a childhood injury that healed into a crushed snout
an illusion caused by worn canines that had snapped near the gumline
genuinely the shortest muzzle of any bear, exactly as the name claims
context: The stubby look comes from a deep snout and short nasal bones typical of tremarctine (short-faced) bears; the face is actually taller and wider than most living bears', not shorter. So the trait that gave Arctodus its name turns out to be a trick of proportion. Source: Figueirido et al. 2010, 'Demythologizing Arctodus simus,' Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology 30(1):262-275.

question: A hospital was going up in La Plata, Argentina, when the skeleton of a bear about a million years old came out of the ground, later estimated at around 1,588 kilograms. Arctodus simus of North America is the tallest bear that ever lived, but this skeleton outweighs it. Which giant is the heaviest bear known to science?
answer: Arctotherium angustidens, a cousin of the short-faced bears
choices: Arctotherium angustidens, a cousin of the short-faced bears
Ursus spelaeus, the cave bear of Ice Age Europe
Agriotherium africanum, a bear-dog of the open plains
Ursus maritimus tyrannus, a supposed giant polar bear
context: Soibelzon and Schubert (2011) estimated this old male at about 1,588 kg (~3,500 lb), possibly over 1,750 kg — roughly double a large Arctodus and heavier than any bear alive. Its remains turned up in La Plata during hospital construction in 1935. So the short-faced bears hold the height record with Arctodus, but the mass crown sits on the South American branch. Source: Soibelzon & Schubert 2011, 'The Largest Known Bear, Arctotherium angustidens,' Journal of Paleontology 85(1):69-75.

question: A male peacock struts into a clearing in an Indian forest and throws up a shimmering fan of feathers nearly a meter and a half long, each tipped with a jewel-like eyespot. People call it his tail, but a biologist would say that is wrong. What is the fan really made of?
answer: Elongated feathers that grow above his true tail, called the train
choices: Elongated feathers that grow above his true tail, called the train
Extra-long flight feathers spread out from his folded wings
Stiffened tail-bones fanned open like the ribs of an umbrella
A skin flap he inflates with air and stretches between his legs
context: The fan is the peacock's TRAIN -- about 140 to 170 elongated upper-tail-covert feathers that grow just above the short true tail, each tipped with an ocellus (eyespot) of blue, copper, green and bronze around a heart-shaped black center. At roughly 1.5 metres it makes up about 60% of the whole bird's length. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_peafowl; earthlife.net peacock feathers.

question: In a forest clearing in India, a male peacock lifts his huge fan of shimmering, eyespotted feathers and quivers it. He does not charge rival males or grab a female; he rustles the feathers into a shimmer and then waits. What is he waiting for?
answer: The peahen to inspect him and decide whether to choose him
choices: The peahen to inspect him and decide whether to choose him
A rival male to back down and surrender the clearing
The morning sun to rise behind him and light up the colors
The rest of his flock to gather and defend the display ground
context: In peafowl the female does the choosing. The male's job is to advertise; the peahen inspects and decides. That flips the usual expectation -- the showy sex is performing FOR the plainer sex, who holds all the power in the transaction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handicap_principle.

question: A peacock hauls his giant fan wherever he goes. It is heavy, it slows his flight, and its glitter makes him easy for a fox to spot, a plain burden for survival. Biologists say that burden is exactly the point. How can hauling around such a handicap possibly help him?
answer: Only a truly fit male can afford to survive while carrying it
choices: Only a truly fit male can afford to survive while carrying it
It frightens predators away by making him look far larger
It stores fat reserves he lives off during the breeding season
It lets him glide farther and escape predators he can't outrun
context: A costly, useless-for-survival ornament is honest precisely because it is costly. A weak male could not survive dragging one around; a male who thrives despite it is proving he is fit enough to pay the price and live. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handicap_principle; letstalkacademy.com Zahavi handicap.

question: Marion Petrie snipped some of the eyespots off certain peacocks' fans at Whipsnade and left their rivals untouched, to find out what peahens actually judge. The trimmed males still shimmered much the same. What happened when the peahens compared them?
answer: The peahens lost interest and chose the males with intact eyespots
choices: The peahens lost interest and chose the males with intact eyespots
The peahens preferred the trimmed males, whose lighter trains danced faster
The peahens ignored the trains and chose by the loudness of each male's call
The peahens picked the same males as before, unbothered by the change
context: Petrie's snipping test showed peahens judge the eyespots themselves, not just the overall shimmer -- take eyespots away and a male's ranking with the females drops. It was direct proof of what the females are reading in the display. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_peafowl; birdspot.co.uk 'How the Peacock Got Its Tail'.

question: A peahen that picks the showiest peacock may be choosing empty vanity or an honest billboard for good genes. Marion Petrie bred peacocks with fans both plain and elaborate, then raised the chicks in near-wild conditions to settle it. What became of the chicks of the most elaborate-fanned fathers?
answer: They grew bigger and survived better than the chicks of plainer fathers
choices: They grew bigger and survived better than the chicks of plainer fathers
They grew the fanciest trains but died younger than their plainer cousins
They fared no differently, showing the train advertised nothing real
They stayed smaller, having spent their energy growing early ornaments
context: Petrie's 1994 breeding study found chicks fathered by the most elaborate-trained peacocks grew bigger and survived better -- so the fan genuinely signals good genes a peahen is wise to choose. The vanity really is an honest advertisement. Source: nature.com/articles/371598a0 (Petrie 1994).

question: A male satin bowerbird weaves two parallel walls of twigs into a little avenue on the floor of an eastern Australian forest. In front of it he heaps a hoard of blue treasures: feathers, berries, even bottle caps. When a female flies down to inspect his work, what is she judging?
answer: The stage he has built and decorated, not his own plumage
choices: The stage he has built and decorated, not his own plumage
The brightness of the blue feathers growing on his own body
The height he can leap while hovering over his blue pile
The distance he carries each blue object back to the nest
context: The satin bowerbird builds an 'avenue' -- two parallel woven walls of twigs -- then collects a hoard of blue objects: parrot feathers, berries, flowers, cicada wings, even blue caps and pegs. Unusually, the female judges the architecture and the decorating rather than the male's own plumage. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satin_bowerbird; acp.eugraph.com Bowerbirds.

question: Beside the twig avenue he has built and decorated, a male satin bowerbird chews berries or charcoal into a colored pulp, sometimes grabbing a wad of bark to hold in his beak first. What are the pulp and the bark for?
answer: Painting the walls of his bower, using the bark as a tool
choices: Painting the walls of his bower, using the bark as a tool
Gluing loose twigs together so the walls don't collapse
Masking his own scent so rivals can't track the bower
Feeding the female a bright treat to keep her at the stage
context: He daubs the chewed pigment onto the twigs with his beak, sometimes holding a wad of bark as a crude paintbrush-tool -- a rare example of a bird using a tool to decorate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satin_bowerbird; utne.com 'The Art of the Bowerbird'.

question: When a male satin bowerbird flies off from his stage, he leaves his hoard of blue treasures behind on a forest floor where blue things are rare. His rivals have found a shortcut that is not exactly honest work. What does a rival do once he is gone?
answer: Raids the empty bower and steals its prize blue feathers
choices: Raids the empty bower and steals its prize blue feathers
Tramples the twig walls flat so the owner must rebuild
Copies the exact layout to build a matching bower nearby
Sings from the stolen bower to trick the female into landing
context: Because blue is so scarce, males raid rivals' bowers to swipe their blue treasures. Gerald Borgia found that older, more experienced males build neater bowers and amass more blue loot -- partly by out-thieving the competition. Source: pbs.org bower-bird-blues; Borgia bowerbird research.

question: The male great bowerbird (Ptilonorhynchus nuchalis) paves his court with grey stones, bones and shells, but not at random: he sets the smallest pieces near the female's viewing spot and the largest at the far back. Laura Kelley and John Endler found the males who arrange this best win the most mates. What does that careful size-gradient create?
answer: A forced-perspective illusion that alters how the scene looks
choices: A forced-perspective illusion that alters how the scene looks
A drainage slope so rain never floods the display court
A hidden count that lets the female judge how long he's worked
A ramp the male struts up to appear taller as he approaches
context: Small-to-large from front to back is forced perspective -- the same trick stage designers use. Kelley and Endler (2012) found males who build the strongest illusion win the most mates, meaning the female is responding to a visual trick, not just a pile of stones. Source: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1208350109 (Kelley & Endler 2012). (legend)

question: Courting a female, a superb bird-of-paradise snaps his cape into a jet-black oval crowned with a glowing blue 'smiley face' of two eyespots, then bounces around her. Before any of that, he does one careful piece of preparation. What is it?
