question: Kenneth Catania filmed a star-nosed mole hunting fully under water on a muddy pond floor, where no mammal was thought able to smell, and saw it working with tiny air bubbles. Once a fine grid sat between its nose and a scent trail, its success fell to a coin-flip 50 percent. What does the mole do with the bubbles?
answer: It blows bubbles onto an object, then re-inhales them to smell it
choices: It blows bubbles onto an object, then re-inhales them to smell it
It releases bubbles to scare prey out of hiding
It uses rising bubbles to steer back toward the surface
It stores bubbles in its cheeks as an oxygen supply
context: Catania showed the mole exhales tiny bubbles onto an object underwater and re-inhales them, letting the air pick up scent molecules, sniffing about 5 to 10 times a second. It and the water shrew, tested in the same 2006 study, were the first mammals shown to smell underwater. With the bubbles kept from reaching the scent, the mole's underwater smelling was disabled and its choices dropped to pure chance, proving the bubble-sniffing mechanism was doing the work. Source: Catania 2006, Nature, 'Underwater sniffing by semi-aquatic mammals'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star-nosed_mole

question: A fish shovels itself down into the seabed with its side fins until only its eyes and mouth are left showing on top, then bursts upward to swallow a passing fish whole. Which fish?
answer: A stargazer
choices: A stargazer
A flounder
An anglerfish
A stonefish
context: The stargazer (family Uranoscopidae) is a true ambush-from-below specialist. It uses its pectoral (side) fins as shovels to bury itself, leaving only its upward-facing eyes and mouth exposed at the surface of the sand, then rises and gulps a passing fish whole in an instant. Flounders bury too and stonefish ambush from the bottom, but only the stargazer aims straight up. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History, Northern Stargazer species profile (https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/discover-fish/species-profiles/northern-stargazer/).

question: A baby stargazer hatches as an ordinary larva with an eye on each side of its head, like most fish. The adult it grows into hides on the seafloor with only its face poking up, ambushing prey from below. As it grows toward that ambusher form, what happens to its eyes?
answer: They migrate to the top of the head
choices: They migrate to the top of the head
They stay put on the sides
They shrink down to tiny dots
They fuse into a single central eye
context: A stargazer is not born looking upward. It hatches as an ordinary side-eyed larva, and only as it develops do the eyes travel up to the top of the head, ending in the sky-watching position that gave the family its name. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History, Northern Stargazer species profile (https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/discover-fish/species-profiles/northern-stargazer/).

question: Buried in the sandy sea floor, a northern stargazer carries a 50-volt electric organ of its own. Electric eels, electric rays and other electric fish sense the faint fields of nearby animals to hunt and find their way in dark water, but among electric-organ fish the stargazer stands apart in one strange way. What is it?
answer: It cannot sense electricity at all
choices: It cannot sense electricity at all
It jams the fields that rivals give off
It reads prey heartbeats through the sand
It stores charge for one huge final blast
context: Electric stargazers (genus Astroscopus) carry an electric organ just behind the eyes that discharges up to 50 volts of direct current. Strangely, unlike eels and other electric fish, stargazers have no electroreceptors at all, so they cannot sense electricity to find prey. The organ is purely a weapon, for stunning a meal or driving off an attacker. Source: Britannica, Electric stargazer (https://www.britannica.com/animal/electric-stargazer); Wikipedia, Stargazer (fish) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stargazer_(fish)).

question: A stargazer lying in ambush on the seafloor shocks prey and rivals with a working electric organ, a rare weapon among fish. An electric eel's organ is made of spare swimming muscle, but the stargazer's was rebuilt from a different body part. Which one?
answer: Muscle that once moved its eyes
choices: Muscle that once moved its eyes
Muscle from its beating heart
Muscle that works its jaws
Muscle at the base of its fins
context: The stargazer's battery is a repurposed body part: the electric organ is built from modified extraocular muscle, the tissue that normally moves the eyes, rather than from ordinary swimming muscle. In the northern stargazer it is packed from roughly 200 thin stacked layers of electric tissue, like the plates in a battery. Source: Wikipedia, Astroscopus guttatus (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astroscopus_guttatus).

question: A stargazer buries itself in the sand so that only its upturned face shows on the seafloor. Its mouth gapes wide open, aimed straight up at the water above. Then, right inside its own jaws, it dangles a bit of living-looking bait to draw curious fish in close. What does that bait look like?
answer: A wriggling worm-shaped flap
choices: A wriggling worm-shaped flap
A glowing round bulb
A bright shrimp-like claw
A feathery fanned frill
context: Some stargazers grow a worm-shaped lure on the floor of the mouth and wiggle it, tricking prey into swimming right between the open jaws. Combined with the sand ambush, the electric shock, and venomous spines above the pectoral fins, it stacks several separate weapons into one buried face. Source: Wikipedia, Stargazer (fish); Discover Wildlife, Stargazer fish (https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/marine-animals/stargazer-fish).

question: A perch hangs perfectly still in the middle of a lake — not sinking to the bottom, not rising to the surface, its fins barely twitching. Most bony fish can do this, hovering weightless at any chosen depth without swimming. What organ inside their body makes it possible?
answer: A gas-filled swim bladder
choices: A gas-filled swim bladder
A ring of stomach muscle
A pair of extra gills
A layer of belly fat
context: The swim bladder is a gas pocket the fish inflates to take up more space and displace more water (floating it up) or shrinks to sink. Puffed to the right size, the fish neither rises nor falls -- it just hangs. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/the-fish-swim-bladder-function-form-and-problems/

question: A deep-sea shark cruises a dark slope far below the sunlit water, held up by a huge liver that can make up a quarter of its body weight. In sharks like it, as much as four-fifths of that liver oil is one light molecule. What is the molecule?
answer: Squalene
choices: Squalene
Lecithin
Triglyceride
Omega-3
context: In some deep-water sharks, squalene makes up 50 to 80 percent of the liver oil. It is a light molecule, less dense than seawater, that the body makes on the way to building cholesterol, and it gives these sharks lift. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squalene ; https://www.wildlifeonline.me.uk/questions/answer/how-do-sharks-and-rays-control-their-buoyancy-without-a-swim-bladder

question: A shortfin mako, the fastest shark in the ocean, races through the open Pacific and Atlantic, and unlike a bony fish it cannot simply hover in place. It makes its lift by swimming forward, the same way an airplane's wings only work while the plane is moving. If the mako stopped swimming and went limp, what would happen to it?
answer: It would slowly sink
choices: It would slowly sink
It would pop to the surface
It would hold its exact depth
It would roll onto its back
context: Most sharks are slightly heavier than water and use forward motion over their fins for extra lift, so many sink if they stop swimming. A few deep-sea species, like the sixgill, carry livers so large they actually float. Source: https://www.submon.org/en/sharks-and-rays-buoyancy/

question: A cuttlefish holds its depth with a stiff internal shell divided into chambers, not a soft balloon like a fish's swim bladder. It is the same flat white oval that washes up on beaches and ends up clipped into budgie cages. What is that rigid cuttlebone mostly made of?
answer: Calcium carbonate
choices: Calcium carbonate
Hardened cartilage
Packed keratin
Silicon dioxide
context: The porous cuttlebone is the ballast tank, and it is about 95-97% aragonite, a crystal form of calcium carbonate, the compound that also makes chalk and seashells. The cuttlefish floods its hundreds of tiny chambers with fluid to sink and lets gas back in to rise. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuttlebone

question: Three or four hundred feet down along the Pacific coast, a rockfish holds its depth with a gas-filled sac inside its body. An angler hooks one and cranks the reel too fast, and in under a minute the fish rises from the crushing dark to the sunny surface with its stomach pushed up into its mouth. What went wrong inside it as the pressure fell?
answer: Its swim bladder swelled up like a balloon
choices: Its swim bladder swelled up like a balloon
Its blood boiled into froth
Its gills fused shut
Its heart burst from the cold
context: A rockfish's swim bladder, only thumb-sized at depth, swells to the size of a party balloon at the surface as the pressure falls -- barotrauma. Sending the fish back down re-compresses the bladder, and the injuries actually reverse. Source: https://www.mercurymarine.com/us/en/lifestyle/dockline/best-practices-for-releasing-deep-water-rockfish

question: A herring hangs at its chosen depth on a gas-filled bladder, and a small open pipe, the pneumatic duct, runs from that bladder straight to its gut. Carp and eels have the same pipe; a perch or a bass has none, its bladder sealed shut. What can the open-pipe fish do that a sealed-bladder fish cannot risk?
answer: Burp gas out and rise fast without bursting
choices: Burp gas out and rise fast without bursting
Breathe underwater through the stomach
Store food inside the bladder
Change color to hide from predators
context: These 'physostome' fish gulp air at the surface to inflate the bladder and can burp gas back out to descend, so they rise quickly without rupturing it. A fish with a sealed bladder cannot ascend fast or it would burst. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physostome

question: Thousands of metres down in the crushing pressure of the deep sea, where a gas-filled bladder would collapse, an orange roughy swims on steady lift. Like the coelacanth, it packs its bladder with light oil or wax instead of gas. What property of oil makes it work where gas cannot?
answer: It stays the same size no matter the pressure
choices: It stays the same size no matter the pressure
It expands to give more lift as pressure rises
It absorbs gas from the surrounding water
It grows lighter the deeper the fish goes
context: A lipid is essentially incompressible -- the crushing pressure barely shrinks it -- so a fat- or wax-filled bladder holds steady lift at depths where a gas bladder would be squeezed away and fail. Source: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-marine-biological-association-of-the-united-kingdom/article/abs/swimbladder-of-deepsea-fish-the-swimbladder-wall-is-a-lipidrich-barrier-to-oxygen-diffusion/52C7BC88C21569BF765FD3D597B2F2B1

question: Out in the open sea, a mackerel releases its tiny eggs, and they drift near the sunlit surface, where plankton is thickest and the newly hatched young will find food. Each egg carries one small thing inside that keeps it riding the currents up top instead of sinking. What is inside each egg?
answer: A droplet of oil
choices: A droplet of oil
A pocket of gas
A jelly float ring
A cluster of salt grains
context: About 70% of ocean fish spawn floating (pelagic) eggs, and many carry an oil droplet that both nourishes the embryo and keeps the egg buoyant near the surface. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4605736/

question: A glass squid drifts in the dim middle depths of the ocean, so transparent that its dark eyes and gut show straight through its body. It hangs perfectly still without sinking and never beats a fin to hold its depth. What fills the one huge chamber that takes up most of its body?
answer: A body-filling tank of ammonium-chloride solution
choices: A body-filling tank of ammonium-chloride solution
A rigid internal shell of gas-filled chambers
A bulky reserve of lightweight waxy oil
A soft body of near-weightless watery jelly
context: Beyond the fish's gas bladder and the shark's oily liver lies a third answer to sinking: pure chemistry. Glass squid (family Cranchiidae) and many other deep midwater squid flood a huge coelomic chamber with a watery ammonium-chloride solution. It is nearly iso-osmotic with seawater, so it does not osmotically flood the animal, yet it is distinctly less dense -- steady lift with no gas and no swimming. The scale is the shock: this low-density fluid can make up roughly 50-60% of the animal's body mass, with ammonium concentrations near 500 mM. It is also why the colossal squid's flesh is famously flabby and gelatinous. Sources: landmark discovery Denton, Gilpin-Brown & Shaw, 'A buoyancy mechanism found in cranchid squid,' Proc. R. Soc. Lond. B 174:271 (1969), royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspb.1969.0093; body-mass and concentration figures from Seibel, Goffredi et al., 'Ammonium content and buoyancy in midwater cephalopods,' J. Exp. Mar. Biol. Ecol. (2004); corroborated by Wikipedia 'Teuthowenia megalops.'

question: A plant-eating dinosaur some 7 meters long lumbered past a stand of ferns on a North American floodplain in the Late Jurassic. Two rows of tall, diamond-shaped bony plates lined its back, and its long tail ended in four sharp spikes. Which dinosaur was it?
answer: Stegosaurus
choices: Stegosaurus
Velociraptor
Pteranodon
Ankylosaurus
context: Stegosaurus was about 6.5 to 7 meters long (over 20 feet) and weighed around 3.5 metric tons, with two rows of tall bony plates down its back, a spiked tail, and a plant-eater's diet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegosaurus

question: A Stegosaurus plodded across a warm floodplain in what is now Colorado, its head hanging low, only about a meter off the ground, swinging over the plants. The Late Jurassic Earth had no grass yet and no flowering plants of any kind; those would not appear for tens of millions of years. What did it eat?
answer: Soft, low-growing ferns and mosses
choices: Soft, low-growing ferns and mosses
Wide meadows of tall grass
Ripe fallen fruit and berries
Broad flowering shrubs and blossoms
context: Stegosaurus browsed within about a meter of the ground on soft, low-growing plants like ferns and mosses; one 2010 computer model put its bite at less than half a modern Labrador retriever's, though a 2016 model found it stronger. (Grasses had not yet spread in the Late Jurassic.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegosaurus

question: Paleontologists cleaned out the braincase of a full-grown Stegosaurus, a plant-eater of some 3.5 tonnes whose long, narrow skull ended in a beak for cropping plants. The organ that ran that huge body turned out to be startlingly small. What was its whole brain closest in size to?
answer: A walnut
choices: A walnut
A basketball
A house cat
A grapefruit
context: Stegosaurus had a brain of no more than about 80 grams, about the size of a walnut, and a braincase no bigger than a dog's, despite a body of some 3.5 tonnes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegosaurus

question: A Stegosaurus carried four long, sharp spikes at the tip of its tail, its main weapon against Jurassic hunters such as Allosaurus. For decades the spikes had no formal name, until Gary Larson drew a 1982 Far Side cartoon of a caveman lecturing on the tail spikes of 'the late Thag Simmons.' Paleontologists loved the joke and took up his word. What do they call that spiked tail now?
answer: The thagomizer
choices: The thagomizer
The tail club
The spike battery
The tail flail
context: The spikes each ran about 60 to 90 cm long (2 to 3 feet). The 'thagomizer' nickname was coined in a 1982 Gary Larson 'Far Side' cartoon and adopted scientifically by paleontologist Kenneth Carpenter starting in 1993. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thagomizer

question: Othniel Marsh named the first Stegosaurus in 1877, and scientists have argued ever since over what the two rows of tall plates on its back were for. Some said armor, some said radiators, some said signal boards. Recent scans show the plates were laced with blood vessels and far too thin to stop a predator's teeth. What do most scientists now think was their main job?
answer: Display and heat control
choices: Display and heat control
Blocking predator bites
Storing fat for lean seasons
Digging up buried roots
context: The plates did not cover the animal's vulnerable sides or belly and were laced with blood vessels, so most scientists think they served for display and thermoregulation, warming the animal in the sun or shedding heat. Source: https://dino-world.com/the-100-year-debate-about-stegosaurus-plates-display-or-thermoregulation-2-23614/

question: Museums once mounted Stegosaurus skeletons with the plates in matching pairs, one left and one right, running down the back like the buttons on a coat. Then paleontologists studied skeletons found with the plates still in place in the rock and saw that the 17 to 22 plates lined up differently on the two sides. How were they really arranged?
answer: In two staggered, alternating rows
choices: In two staggered, alternating rows
In a single row along the spine
In four tight bundles near the hips
Scattered randomly across the hide
context: A Stegosaurus carried somewhere between 17 and 22 plates, and they ran in two staggered (alternating) rows down the back rather than as a mirrored pair. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegosaurus

question: An Allosaurus tail bone dug from fossil beds in the American West has a perfectly round hole punched clean through it, a hole that a Stegosaurus tail spike fits exactly. When paleontologists looked closely at the bone around the wound, what did they see?
answer: Healed, remodeled edges: the Allosaurus survived the stab
choices: Healed, remodeled edges: the Allosaurus survived the stab
A fresh, ragged break: a killing blow
No bone reaction at all: the wound came after death
Open rot that never closed: fatal infection
context: The puncture in Allosaurus specimen UMNH 10781 matches a Stegosaurus tail spike, and the edges show healed, remodeled bone, meaning the Allosaurus was stabbed but lived. Nearly 1 in 10 Stegosaurus specimens show battle damage on their tail spikes. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/watch-out-for-that-thagomizer-98891562/

question: Miriam Reichel built a computer model of the Stegosaurus jaw in 2010 and found a mouth so feeble it could barely snip a twig about a centimeter thick. Stephan Lautenschlager's team digitally rebuilt the skull and jaw muscles of the famous 'Sophie' specimen in 2016, and both models still stand. What did Lautenschlager's reconstruction find?
answer: It bit as hard as a living sheep or cow, able to browse tougher plants
choices: It bit as hard as a living sheep or cow, able to browse tougher plants
It bit as hard as a hyena, powerful enough to crack and splinter bone
It bit even more weakly than the twig-snapping estimate had suggested
It bit hard enough to shear through wood like a beaver felling a tree
context: This is a genuine, still-unsettled scientific argument. Miriam Reichel's 2010 finite-element model of the teeth (Swiss Journal of Geosciences 103:235-240) found a very weak bite: about 140 N at the front teeth and only ~275 N at the back, enough to snip branches barely a centimeter thick. But Stephan Lautenschlager and colleagues' 2016 digital reconstruction of the whole skull (Scientific Reports, Univ. of Bristol) put the force squarely in the range of living plant-eating mammals like sheep and cows, meaning Stegosaurus could have browsed a far wider menu than just the softest ferns. Both models stand; the debate is unresolved. Sources: Reichel 2010 (link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00015-010-0025-1); Lautenschlager et al. 2016 (bristol.ac.uk/news/2016/may/stegosaurs-bite.html).

question: A Stegosaurus browsing low to the ground carried tall plates along its back but none over its throat and the underside of its neck, the very spot a low-slung predator would lunge for. Yet fossils show the throat was not defenseless. What guarded it?
answer: A mosaic of small bony studs set right into the skin of its throat
choices: A mosaic of small bony studs set right into the skin of its throat
A curtain of overlapping horny scales, much like a pangolin's armor
A single broad shield of solid bone plated across its windpipe
A thick pad of leathery, blubber-like fat cushioning the lower jaw
context: Paleontologists call these throat studs gular ossicles: small dermal bones ('ossicles') embedded in the skin of the gula, or throat. This cobbled soft-tissue armor guarded the one soft target the showy dorsal plates could not cover, exactly where a low browser was most exposed. It is a diagnostic feature described from Stegosaurus stenops armor specimens (Kenneth Carpenter, 'Armor of Stegosaurus stenops,' Garden Park, Colorado; researchgate.net/profile/Kenneth-Carpenter-2/publication/284097770), with plate and dermal-bone histology corroborated in Hayashi et al. 2012, Palaeontology 55(1):145-161.

question: A gecko dashes straight up a pane of smooth window glass and hangs there upside down by its dry toes, leaving no glue, no wet mark and no scratch. No suction cups or claws are helping it. Something working at a scale far too small to see holds it there. What grips a gecko to smooth glass?
answer: the faint pull between molecules that touch
choices: the faint pull between molecules that touch
static electricity built up in its skin
microscopic hooks snagging the glass
a ring of suction cups on each toe
context: A gecko uses no glue at all. The bottom of each toe is packed with millions of tiny hairs (setae) that grip by van der Waals force — the faint attraction any two molecules feel when they are touching. So many hairs touch at once that the faint pulls add up to hold the whole lizard. Source: Autumn et al. 2000, Nature 405:681; Kellar Autumn 2002 review.

question: A red-eyed tree frog crouches on a slick leaf in a Costa Rican rainforest at night while a downpour hammers around it. Its round toe pads press flat against the leaf, and even as water sheets across the surface the frog never slips. A gecko grips best on a bone-dry wall, but this frog uses the opposite trick. What holds it fast?
answer: a thin film of water pulling by surface tension
choices: a thin film of water pulling by surface tension
tiny claws hooking into the leaf veins
a sticky glue it makes in special glands
curling its round toes around the leaf edge
context: The tree frog uses the opposite trick from a gecko: it sticks with WATER. Its round toe-discs stay damp, and a super-thin film of fluid between the pad and the leaf grips by surface tension — the same clingy pull that makes a wet glass stick to a coaster. Dry gecko, wet frog. Source: Hanna & Barnes 1991, J. Exp. Biol. 155:103; Barnes et al. 2019 biomimetics review.

question: An octopus reaches one arm into a pounding tidal current and presses its round suckers against a bare, slippery rock, clinging so firmly that a strong wave cannot tear it loose. Each sucker is a small muscular cup it can squeeze and release on its own. How does a sucker grip the smooth stone?
answer: it lowers the water pressure trapped inside the cup
choices: it lowers the water pressure trapped inside the cup
it oozes a fast-drying natural cement
it drives tiny barbs from the rim into the stone
it grows thin roots into cracks in the rock
context: An octopus grips by pure suction, not stickiness. Muscles inside each sucker pull the middle of the cup back, dropping the water pressure trapped inside; the higher pressure of the surrounding sea then presses the sucker onto the rock. Each of its hundreds of suckers works on its own. Source: Kier & Smith 1990, Biological Bulletin 178:126.

question: On a vertical pane of glass, a Tokay gecko from Southeast Asia grips with millions of microscopic hairs, called setae, packed under its toes. With so many tiny hairs gripping at once, it can pull off a startling feat on the glass. What can it do?
answer: hang from the glass by a single toe
choices: hang from the glass by a single toe
leave a trail of glue footprints behind
walk upside down on glass underwater
pull each toe free with a loud pop
context: A Tokay gecko carries more than three million setae on its two front feet alone, so many that those feet can hold roughly 40 times the gecko's own body weight, which is why a gecko can hang from a pane of glass by just one toe. Source: Wikipedia 'Synthetic setae' (about 3.27 million setae on the two front feet; about 40 times body weight); Lewis & Clark Magazine (Kellar Autumn lab).

question: A housefly walks calmly upside down across a kitchen ceiling without falling. At the end of each of its six legs it carries two soft pads called pulvilli, each covered in thousands of fine hairs, and those hairs do something specific to keep it stuck to the plaster overhead. What do they do?
answer: each oozes a droplet of gluey fluid
choices: each oozes a droplet of gluey fluid
each spins a thread of silk to the ceiling
each inflates like a balloon against the plaster
each sparks a tiny jolt of static charge
context: On the last segment of each leg sit soft pads (pulvilli) covered in tiny hairs, and each hair oozes a droplet of gluey fluid so thin — less than a millionth of a millimeter — that the fly clings by the same molecule-touching pull the gecko uses, plus the stickiness of the fluid itself. Source: Bullock & Federle on fly pulvilli; Nature Communications 2013 (contact film <10–20 nm).

question: A rainforest tree frog clings to a rain-soaked leaf. Under a microscope its toe pad looks tiled like a tiny honeycomb, flat six-sided cells packed side by side and split by deep, straight grooves, and too much water under the pad would spoil its grip. What job do the grooves do?
answer: drain excess water out to the edges
choices: drain excess water out to the edges
store a reserve of glue for later
sharpen into tiny teeth that bite the leaf
trap air bubbles to work like suckers
context: The channels are drainage grooves — they let the water squeeze out to the edges so the pad can press close to the surface instead of just skidding on a puddle. Counterintuitively, the wet-gripping frog still needs to shed water so its pad can make close contact. Source: Hanna & Barnes 1991, J. Exp. Biol. 155:103; Federle/Barnes tree-frog pad microstructure.

question: A gecko sprints up a pane of glass, its toes gripping with hundreds of thousands of tiny hairs, yet it never gets stuck fast. The pull that holds each hair cannot be switched off the way a hand lets go of a rope. To peel each foot free in an instant, what does the lizard change about its gripping hairs?
answer: the angle it tilts the hairs to the surface
choices: the angle it tilts the hairs to the surface
the temperature of its toe pads
the amount of fluid it pumps into the hairs
the electric charge stored in the hairs
context: Van der Waals force can't be switched off — so the gecko changes the angle instead. When it tilts the hair's shaft to about 30 degrees from the surface, the tips peel free at the trailing edge and the grip releases instantly. That's how a gecko can run up glass without getting stuck. Source: Wikipedia 'Synthetic setae' (detach at ~30°); Autumn et al. peeling studies.

question: A limpet, a small sea snail under a low cone of shell, clamps to a wave-swept rock so hard that crashing surf cannot tear it off. To scrape algae from the stone it grinds with tiny teeth reinforced by fibers of an iron mineral called goethite. When scientists at the University of Portsmouth measured those teeth in 2015, what record did the teeth set?
answer: the strongest natural material ever measured
choices: the strongest natural material ever measured
the sharpest edge found in any animal
the fastest-growing tissue known in nature
the hardest shell of any sea creature
context: The limpet's teeth are reinforced with goethite fibers ten thousand times thinner than a human hair, giving a strength up to 6.5 gigapascals — beating even spider silk, and the strongest natural material ever measured. Source: Barber, Lu & Pugno 2015, J. Royal Society Interface, 'Extreme strength observed in limpet teeth' (University of Portsmouth; 3.0–6.5 GPa).

question: A barefoot wader on a warm Indo-Pacific reef steps toward a lumpy 'rock' that is really a fish, so still and so perfectly disguised that swimmers tread on it by accident. Venom-loaded spines lie hidden in the mottled skin of its back. Which fish is the most venomous in the world?
answer: The stonefish
choices: The stonefish
The great white shark
The electric eel
The lionfish
context: The reef stonefish (Synanceia verrucosa) is the most venomous fish in the world. Source: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish.

question: Hour after hour a stonefish waits in one spot on an Indo-Pacific reef to ambush any small fish that drifts too close. A wrasse or a shark keeps its scales scrubbed clean, but the stonefish never grooms its lumpy, warty skin at all, and something slowly builds up on it that makes its rock disguise even better. What builds up?
answer: Algae and sediment
choices: Algae and sediment
A coat of slippery slime
Bright warning stripes
A shell of tiny barnacles
context: The stonefish does not clean itself, so algae and sediment accumulate on its skin, improving the camouflage the longer it sits. It ends up looking exactly like an encrusted rock or lump of coral. Sources: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish; Oceana — Stonefish.

question: A bass or a grouper darts away in a flash when a diver drifts close, but a stonefish camouflaged as a lump of coral on an Indo-Pacific reef floor does the opposite. It holds its ground and readies its defense, trusting the venom-loaded spines along its back. What does a disturbed stonefish do instead of fleeing?
answer: Erects its row of dorsal spines
choices: Erects its row of dorsal spines
Puffs up into a spiny ball
Squirts a cloud of black ink
Buries itself deeper in the sand
context: When disturbed, a stonefish stays put and raises its poisonous dorsal spines. Press down on it — as a bare foot does — and the pressure squeezes the venom glands so the spines inject automatically, harder the harder they are pressed. Source: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish.

question: A stonefish keeps its weapons along the ridge of its back, not in its jaws: 13 stiff spikes hidden under thick, warty skin, each grooved and tucked into a sheath until a bare foot or a snorkeler's hand presses down. Then the spike punches through and drives venom deep into the wound. What everyday medical tool are these spikes most often compared to?
answer: A row of hypodermic needles
choices: A row of hypodermic needles
A set of surgeon's scalpels
A string of stitching sutures
A row of dental drills
context: A stonefish carries 13 stout dorsal spines, each grooved and fed by a venom gland at its base and wrapped in a sheath of skin — like a row of hypodermic needles lying flat until pressed. Source: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish.

question: Two barefoot swimmers step on the very same stonefish, yet one ends up with a far worse sting than the other. The fish injects no fixed dose — the amount of venom that enters a wound changes from one victim to the next. What controls how much venom gets pumped in?
answer: How hard the spines are pressed down
choices: How hard the spines are pressed down
The temperature of the surrounding water
The overall body size of the stonefish
The time since the fish last stung something
context: The venom is purely defensive — never used to feed — and injects automatically when the spines are pressed, in proportion to how hard they are pressed. Bear down harder and the glands deliver more venom. Sources: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish; Fact Animal — Stonefish; NCBI PMC7232307 — Defensive Venoms.

question: Disguised as a lump of coral, a stonefish lies statue-still on the Indo-Pacific sea floor, sometimes not moving for days at a time. When a small fish or shrimp finally drifts within reach, it launches its ambush. What is remarkable about the lunge it uses to snatch that prey?
answer: It is one of the fastest strikes in the fish world
choices: It is one of the fastest strikes in the fish world
It swallows prey twice its own length
It can be aimed from several feet away
It works only at night in total darkness
context: Instead of venom, the stonefish feeds with an ambush lunge that engulfs prey in roughly 15 milliseconds — so fast that high-speed cameras are needed to film it, one of the fastest strikes among fish. Sources: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish; TheSea.org — Stonefish Synanceia.

question: The tide goes out and leaves a stony beach behind. Hours later a barefoot walker steps on one of the 'stones' and is stung, because a stonefish stranded out of water can live on for a long while, breathing through its moist skin. Roughly how long can it last?
answer: About 24 hours
choices: About 24 hours
About 10 minutes
About three days
About one hour
context: A stonefish can survive out of water for up to about 24 hours by absorbing oxygen through its skin as long as it stays moist — so a 'rock' left by a retreating tide can still be alive and still sting. Source: Culture Trip — 7 Facts About Stonefish; Biology Insights — How Venomous Are Stonefish.

question: A bloodhound, a big, droopy-eared hound bred over centuries to track the faintest trail of a person or animal, puts its nose to the ground. A human nose carries about 6 million scent receptors and can still pick out a bakery a whole block away. Roughly how many scent receptors line the bloodhound's nose?
answer: About 300 million
choices: About 300 million
About 30 million
About 12 million
About 800,000
context: A dog's nose carries up to 300 million scent receptors, with bloodhounds at that top end, against only about 6 million in a human nose. It doesn't just smell more, it smells in far finer detail. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_sense_of_smell (PBS NOVA, 'Dogs' Dazzling Sense of Smell').

question: A dog casts its head back and forth over a trail, and it is not searching at random. Its two nostrils take in odor separately, each sampling its own patch of air. What does that let the dog do?
answer: Tell which side a scent is coming from
choices: Tell which side a scent is coming from
Detect a scent a mile off
Shut out every smell but one
Store a smell to recall it later
context: A dog smells in stereo: its two nostrils sample independently, so it can tell which side a scent came from and use its nose like a compass to point toward the source. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_sense_of_smell (PBS NOVA, PetMD).

question: A dog buries its nose in a scent trail and keeps breathing steadily, sniffing in and puffing out about five times a second. When it exhales, the spent air does not leave the way a person breathes out; it takes an exit a human nose never uses. Where does the used air leave the dog's nose?
answer: Through the side slits of its nose
choices: Through the side slits of its nose
Straight out the front of the nostrils
Down through the back of the throat
Out through tiny pores on the muzzle
context: When a dog exhales, the used-up air blows out through the side slits of its nose, not straight out the front, so the outgoing breath doesn't scatter the scent it's still sniffing in. This lets the dog smell continuously even while breathing out. Source: https://www.petmd.com/dog/behavior/5-dog-nose-facts-you-probably-didnt-know (PBS NOVA).

question: Alexandra Horowitz, who studies how dogs experience the world, wanted to show just how faint a smell a trained scent dog can still catch. She chose an everyday comparison: a single teaspoon of sugar dissolved in a huge amount of water. How much water?
answer: Two Olympic-sized swimming pools
choices: Two Olympic-sized swimming pools
A backyard garden pond
A single kitchen sink
A large rainwater barrel
context: A trained medical-alert dog can pick out an odor as dilute as one teaspoon of sugar dissolved in two Olympic-sized swimming pools of water, a comparison from dog-cognition researcher Alexandra Horowitz. Source: Alexandra Horowitz, 'Inside of a Dog'; med.news.am.

question: A shark closes on prey from open water, sniffing with two nostrils at once. Gardiner and Atema found out in 2010 how it picks a direction, feeding squid odor through a separate tube into each nostril of a smooth dogfish. What does the shark compare between its nostrils to steer?
answer: The timing of when the smell reaches each nostril
choices: The timing of when the smell reaches each nostril
How concentrated the smell is at each nostril
The temperature of the water at each nostril
The saltiness of the water on each side
context: Sharks steer toward prey by comparing the timing of when a smell reaches each nostril, turning toward whichever nostril the odor hits first, even when the other senses a stronger concentration. The gap can be as small as a tenth of a second. Legend/landmark study: Gardiner & Atema 2010, Current Biology; whoi.edu. Done on the smooth dogfish (Mustelus canis) with tubes feeding squid odor to each nostril separately.

question: An African elephant sweeps its trunk over the ground and through the air, sorting scents in fine detail. Its edge is written in its DNA: no animal is known to carry more genes for smell receptors, roughly double a dog's. About how many does it have?
answer: Nearly 2,000
choices: Nearly 2,000
About 400
About 90
Around 25
context: The African elephant has the largest known set of olfactory-receptor genes of any animal, nearly 2,000, more than twice a dog's and about five times a human's, letting it sort scents in astonishing detail with its trunk. Legend/landmark finding: Niimura, Matsui & Touhara 2014, Genome Research. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4158756/.

question: In the rainforest of New Guinea, a small black male bird does a strange dance. He snaps a fan of feathers open around his head into a perfect oval. The glowing blue-green marks look exactly like a floating smiley face. Which bird pulls off this trick?
answer: The superb bird-of-paradise
choices: The superb bird-of-paradise
The greater roadrunner
The Andean cock-of-the-rock
The king vulture
context: The courting male superb bird-of-paradise (Lophorina) snaps his black feather cape and iridescent blue-green breast shield open into a perfect oval that reads as a bright smiley face floating in a void. Source: birdsofparadiseproject.org (New Vogelkop superb bird-of-paradise changes up the old song and dance).

question: A male superb bird-of-paradise opens his feathers into a smiley-face oval for a female watching on the floor of a New Guinea mountain forest. He bobs and hops around her in tight circles, and the whole time he keeps one part of himself pointed straight at her. Which part?
answer: His electric-blue breast shield
choices: His electric-blue breast shield
His long tail streamers
His hooked beak
His feathered crest
context: As he bounces around her, the male always keeps his glowing blue-green breast shield squarely aimed at the female, so she sees the full floating face throughout the dance. Source: audubon.org (New bird of paradise slides around sporting a bright blue frown).

question: A courting male superb bird-of-paradise spreads his bright blue-green feathers against a velvet-black cape, and the cape is extreme: measured head-on, it reflects as little as 0.05 percent of the light that strikes it, one of the darkest surfaces known in nature. Why would evolution favor so black a cape?
answer: It makes the blue face seem to glow and float in empty space
choices: It makes the blue face seem to glow and float in empty space
The dark cape soaks up sunlight and keeps the male warm
The blackness hides the male from hawks hunting the canopy above
A wider patch of black makes the male look larger to his rivals
context: The 'super-black' cape absorbs about 99.95 percent of light striking it head-on (reflecting only 0.05-0.31 percent, versus 3-5 percent for an ordinary black feather). With almost no light returning off the cape, the eye has no reference against which to place the blue face, so it appears to float and glow against pure nothingness. Source: McCoy et al. 2018, Nature Communications, 'Structural absorption by barbule microstructures of super black bird of paradise feathers' (PMC5760687).

question: Researchers found no special dark pigment in the super-black cape of a male superb bird-of-paradise, though it is darker than any black a bird's pigment can make. How do those feathers swallow so much of the light that hits them?
answer: The barbs tilt to form deep pits that trap the light
choices: The barbs tilt to form deep pits that trap the light
A layer of black oil coats each feather and soaks up the light
The feathers are packed so densely no light can slip between them
The feathers chemically convert the light into heat
context: The super-black comes from structure, not pigment: the feather barbules bend upward into tilted arrays with deep cavities (200-400 micrometers deep), so light that enters bounces around inside and gets trapped instead of reflecting back out. Source: McCoy et al. 2018, Nature Communications (PMC5760687).

question: A flat, brown, wide-headed frog lies still on the bottom of a muddy, sluggish Amazon river, so hard to spot that even a keeper who knows one is in the aquarium can miss it. How does the Surinam toad stay hidden from prey and predators?
answer: It looks exactly like a dead, rotting leaf lying in the litter
choices: It looks exactly like a dead, rotting leaf lying in the litter
It buries itself completely beneath the mud
It glows faintly to blend into the dim water
It clings to the underside of floating logs
context: The Surinam toad (Pipa pipa) is almost entirely flat, like a mottled brown leaf, with a broad flat triangular head. This leaf-lump shape hides it as a piece of dead leaf litter on the muddy riverbed of warm, murky, slow-moving tropical waters. Source: Wikipedia 'Common Surinam toad' + San Diego Zoo.

question: A Surinam toad hunts the muddy rivers of the Amazon with no tongue at all, though most frogs snap up insects with a long, sticky one. Yet it still catches minnows, shrimp and worms in open water. When prey drifts close to its huge flat mouth, how does the tongueless toad seize it?
answer: It suddenly expands its throat and vacuums in a rush of water, swallowing the prey whole
choices: It suddenly expands its throat and vacuums in a rush of water, swallowing the prey whole
It fires a jet of sticky mucus to glue the prey and reel it back
It clamps down with rows of tiny needle teeth
It lassoes the prey with its star-tipped fingers
context: The Surinam toad has no tongue and no teeth. Instead of flicking a tongue, it is a suction feeder: it rapidly expands its throat cavity to inhale a rush of water that vacuums prey whole into its large mouth. Source: San Diego Zoo + Wikipedia 'Common Surinam toad'.

question: Down on the bottom of a muddy Amazon river, the water is so murky that a Surinam toad can barely see its own fingers. Each finger on its front feet ends in a tiny star-shaped tip, which gives the animal another name, the star-fingered toad. What do those star tips do?
answer: Feel out hidden prey the toad cannot see and guide it to the mouth
choices: Feel out hidden prey the toad cannot see and guide it to the mouth
Anchor the toad firmly against the river current
Sift edible scraps from the mud it takes in
Churn up the riverbed to flush prey out of hiding
context: Each front finger ends in tiny star-shaped tips (four star-like appendages), the source of the alternate name 'star-fingered toad.' These sensory fingertips feel and probe through leaf litter and murky water to detect prey the toad cannot see. Source: San Diego Zoo + Wikipedia 'Common Surinam toad'.

question: A female Surinam toad releases her eggs during mating, and the male presses them onto her back. Over the next day her skin swells and grows up around each egg until they sink in and become sealed inside pockets. Three to four months later, what happens on the mother toad's back?
answer: Dozens of fully-formed baby toads erupt out through her skin and swim away
choices: Dozens of fully-formed baby toads erupt out through her skin and swim away
The eggs loosen and float up to the surface to hatch
Tadpoles wriggle free and cling to her belly to grow
She sheds her whole back skin in one piece with the eggs still attached
context: The mother's back becomes a honeycomb of skin pockets, one egg sealed in each chamber. The young develop entirely inside, skipping the free-swimming tadpole stage and transforming directly into miniature toadlets. After 3-4 months they push and squirm to loosen the skin, the pockets open, and dozens of tiny toads (about 25 mm each) erupt out through her back and swim away. Source: San Diego Zoo + Wikipedia 'Common Surinam toad'.

question: Five or six orange-and-white clownfish live among the tentacles of a stinging sea anemone on a warm reef, ranked by size from largest to smallest, and they never wander far from home. When it is time to lay eggs, the job always falls to one member of that pecking order. Which fish lays the eggs?
answer: The biggest fish
choices: The biggest fish
The smallest fish
A middle-sized fish
Whichever one guards the eggs
context: Clownfish (genus Amphiprion) live in a strict size-ranked order inside one anemone: the biggest is the female, the second-biggest the breeding male, and the rest are smaller non-breeders that don't reproduce. Source: Emperor Divers (emperordivers.com/clownfish-male-female); Sequential hermaphroditism, Wikipedia.

question: On a warm damp night in the garden, two common earthworms surface partway from their burrows to mate. They line up belly-to-belly for a long, slippery exchange of sperm, but their soft, slimy bodies have nothing obvious to grip with. How does each worm keep the pair from sliding apart mid-mating?
answer: It drives dozens of tiny bristles into its partner
choices: It drives dozens of tiny bristles into its partner
It wraps its tail tightly around the other
It glues them together with sticky mucus
It bites down on the other worm's skin
context: To keep from slipping apart during the long sperm exchange, each common earthworm (Lumbricus terrestris) drives roughly 30 of its 40 tiny bristle-hairs into its partner, locking the two bodies together belly-to-belly. Source: Science News (sciencenews.org/article/battle-hermaphrodites); Koene & Schulenburg study.

question: A clownfish family shares one stinging sea anemone. Only two of its fish breed, the one that lays the eggs and her partner, and the rest never breed at all. When she dies, what happens to her partner?
answer: He changes into the new egg-laying female
choices: He changes into the new egg-laying female
He fights off the anemone's other fish
He leaves to find a new anemone
He shrinks back to a non-breeder
context: When the female dies, the breeding male changes sex and becomes the new female — a one-way change that cannot reverse. The largest remaining non-breeder then grows into the new breeding male. This male-first switch is called protandry, and clownfish are the classic example. Source: Emperor Divers (emperordivers.com/clownfish-male-female); Sequential hermaphroditism, Wikipedia.

question: Little Nemo ends the film Finding Nemo still a small fish, safe at home in his sea anemone with his father, Marlin. Real clownfish live in ranked groups where only one female breeds, and when she dies her partner changes sex to become the new female. In that real family, what becomes of a small non-breeder like Nemo?
answer: He grows into the new breeding male
choices: He grows into the new breeding male
He is driven out of the anemone
He stays a non-breeder for life
He splits off to find his own anemone
context: In real clownfish the death of the female triggers the whole rank to shift up: the breeding male turns female, and the largest remaining non-breeder — Nemo's role — grows into the new breeding male and mates with her. The film's tidy father-and-son ending isn't how the family really works. Source: Emperor Divers (emperordivers.com/clownfish-male-female); Reader's Digest (rd.com/article/scientifically-accurate-finding-nemo).

question: When the top female of its group dies, a common clownfish, the orange-and-white species of Finding Nemo, can change sex. One part of its body reshapes itself for its new sex within about six months, long before the rest catches up, and in some fish the gap lasts more than three years. Which part leads the way?
answer: The brain
choices: The brain
The gonads
The skin
The fins
context: The change starts in the brain, not the gonads: the preoptic area grows to female size within about six months while the gonads are still male. Professor Justin Rhodes put it, 'It's got a female brain, but its gonads are male.' Some fish hold that state for over three years before the gonads finish converting. Source: news.scubatravel.co.uk (reporting on Rhodes et al., Univ. of Illinois).

question: A big male California sheephead patrols a Pacific kelp forest with his harem gathered around him, easy to spot by his bulging forehead. Every fish in that group was born female. When the male dies or vanishes, what does the dominant female do?
answer: Turns into the male
choices: Turns into the male
Stops feeding to guard eggs
Splits off to start a new harem
Grows a protective shell
context: The California sheephead, a wrasse, is born a pink female and turns male at about four to six years old, developing a black head and tail with a bright red band across the middle. This female-first switch is called protogyny. If the male dies, a female's ovaries degenerate and sperm develops, completing the switch in as little as five days to two weeks. Source: Catalina Island Marine Institute (cimi.org/blog/sheephead-are-protogynous-hermaphrodies).

question: A drab yellow-brown wrasse on a Caribbean reef starts life as a female. When the dominant one turns into a 'terminal-phase' male, its body goes green with black-and-white bands and its head takes on one bold color, the color that gives the species its common name. Which color?
answer: Bright blue
choices: Bright blue
Solid black
Pale silver
Deep red
context: The terminal-phase male has a blue head, black-and-white bars, and a green body — the blue head gives the bluehead wrasse (Thalassoma bifasciatum) its name. When the dominant male is removed, a female begins acting male within minutes to hours and completes the full change in only about eight days. Source: Thalassoma bifasciatum, Wikipedia; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24036013.

question: Just before two garden snails mate, each stabs the other with a sharp, chalky 'love dart.' Each snail is both male and female, and the dart is no weapon of defense: its chemical coating does something that helps the snail that fired it. What does the coating do?
answer: Boosts its chances of fathering the eggs
choices: Boosts its chances of fathering the eggs
Numbs the partner's stinging cells
Dissolves the other snail's shell
Warns off rival snails nearby
context: The 'love dart' is loaded with chemicals that boost the shooter's chances of fathering the partner's eggs — and both snails are trying to do it to each other. Source: BMC blog (blogs.biomedcentral.com/bmcseriesblog/2016/05/13/love-dart-heart-sexual-conflict-snails).

question: A strange hummingbird darts through the foggy cloud forests of Ecuador, Colombia and Peru, high in the Andes. One part of its body has grown so long that it holds a record no other bird can match. What is special about the sword-billed hummingbird?
answer: Its bill is longer than the rest of its body
choices: Its bill is longer than the rest of its body
Its wings beat slower than any other bird's
It is the only hummingbird that cannot fly backward
Its heart stops completely every night to save energy
context: The sword-billed hummingbird (Ensifera ensifera) is the only bird in the world whose bill is longer than the rest of its body. The straight, sword-like bill runs 8 to 12 cm on a bird whose body (not counting the tail) is only about 13 to 14 cm long. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird

question: A sword-billed hummingbird flits through an Andean cloud forest with a bill so absurdly long that it cannot reach back over its own feathers, the way other birds preen with their beaks. How does it keep its plumage clean?
answer: It scratches itself clean with its feet
choices: It scratches itself clean with its feet
It rubs its back against rough bark
It lets rain and mist wash the feathers
It waits for smaller birds to groom it
context: Because its bill is far too long to reach its own feathers, the sword-billed hummingbird cannot preen with its beak like other birds. Instead it grooms itself using its feet, scratching its plumage clean. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird

question: Weighing only 10 to 15 grams, about as much as three small coins, a sword-billed hummingbird carries an enormous needle-like bill on its slim neck, and holding it up is tiring work. When the bird lands on a twig to rest, what does it do to ease the strain?
answer: Tilts the bill almost straight up toward the sky
choices: Tilts the bill almost straight up toward the sky
Rests the bill flat along a branch
Tucks the bill under one wing
Props the bill against its own chest
context: When it lands to rest, the sword-bill tilts its heavy bill almost straight up toward the sky, leaning its head back to balance the weight and ease the strain on its neck. A perched sword-bill points its beak at the heavens. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird

question: Dozens of hummingbird species swarm the high cloud forests of the Andes, all chasing the same sweet nectar, and squabbles over flowers are common. Yet the sword-billed hummingbird, with its outrageously long bill, almost never has to fight a rival for a meal. How does it feed while sidestepping the crowd of shorter-billed cousins?
answer: It drinks from deep tubular flowers no other bird can empty
choices: It drinks from deep tubular flowers no other bird can empty
It feeds only at dawn, before rival hummingbirds wake
It guards a patch of blossoms, chasing all other birds off
It follows blooming trees uphill as the seasons shift
context: By owning a food source no rival can reach, the sword-bill sidesteps competition entirely. Short-billed hummingbirds simply cannot get at the deep tubular flowers it drains, such as the long trumpet-shaped corolla of Passiflora mixta, so it feeds on nectar unavailable to any other bird. The bird and the flower are a matched pair. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird ; https://www.zmescience.com/feature-post/natural-sciences/animals/birds/the-sword-billed-hummingbird-long-beak/

question: A big blue-black wasp with bright orange wings hunts the deserts of the American Southwest, armed with one of the most painful stings of any insect. Each female stings a live animal far bigger than herself into paralysis and drags it home as living food for her young. What creature does she hunt?
answer: Tarantulas
choices: Tarantulas
Scorpions
Centipedes
Praying mantises
context: The tarantula hawk (genus Pepsis) is named for its prey. A female stings a live tarantula, and her venom freezes the spider without killing it, because she needs it alive. Source: Britannica, 'Tarantula hawk'; Discover Wildlife.

question: A female tarantula hawk paralyzes a tarantula with one sting, hauls it into a burrow and lays one egg on its belly before sealing the tomb. The grub that hatches eats the still-living spider from the inside for about three weeks, saving one group of body parts for last so its meal stays alive and fresh. Which parts does it eat last?
answer: The vital organs
choices: The vital organs
The eight legs
The venom glands
The silk spinnerets
context: By saving the vital organs for last, the larva keeps the paralyzed spider alive and fresh as long as possible. The tarantula only dies when the larva finally reaches those organs. Source: Discover Wildlife; Wikipedia, 'Tarantula hawk'.

question: Justin Schmidt let insects sting him on purpose to build a pain scale, and he scored the tarantula hawk a 4.0, behind only the bullet ant, calling the pain 'blinding, fierce, shockingly electric.' How long does that searing pain last?
answer: About five minutes
choices: About five minutes
About two hours
About six hours
About a full day
context: Schmidt rated the sting 4.0, second only to the bullet ant, yet the searing pain fades in about five minutes, and the sting is not dangerous unless the person is allergic. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarantula_hawk ; Grokipedia 'Tarantula hawk' (pain subsides within 5 minutes).

question: A mother tarantula hawk can paralyze a spider several times her own size, yet she never hunts for her own dinner; the spider is food for her young alone. On her own she is a gentle sipper, and so is every male. What does the adult wasp live on, day to day?
answer: Flower nectar
choices: Flower nectar
Tree sap
Aphid honeydew
Carrion juices
context: Adults are nectar-drinkers, both males and females sipping from milkweed, mesquite and western soapberry blossoms. The spider-hunting is done only by females, and only to feed the young. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarantula_hawk ; BeesWiki.

question: A naturalist squeezes the water out of a damp green clump from an old wall, catches the drips in a dish and looks at them under a microscope. Across the slide, on four pairs of stubby legs, a tiny animal waddles slowly along. What two-word nickname did that clumsy waddle earn it?
answer: The water bear
choices: The water bear
The mud minnow
The bark beetle
The sand flea
context: The German naturalist Goeze coined the name 'Kleiner Wasserbaer' (little water bear) in 1773 for the way it lumbers along like a bear. Its other nickname is 'moss piglet.' Source: Wikipedia, Tardigrade.

question: A tardigrade clambers through a drop of water on a microscope slide, waving its eight plump little legs as it goes. About how long is a typical one?
answer: About the size of a grain of sand
choices: About the size of a grain of sand
About the size of a small ant
About the width of a small coin
Longer than a whole fingernail
context: Most tardigrades are 0.05 to 0.5 millimetres long, about the size of a grain of sand or smaller; the largest reach about 1.3 mm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tardigrade

question: A biologist hunting for tardigrades needs no faraway trip: she soaks one ordinary clump of the right green plant in tap water for a few hours, squeezes it out and looks at the drops under a microscope. A single square metre of that plant can hold more than two million tardigrades. What plant does she soak?
answer: Moss
choices: Moss
Seaweed
Grass clippings
Fallen leaves
context: A square metre of moss can hold over 2 million tardigrades. They also live on Himalayan mountaintops, in the deep sea, and across Antarctica. Source: Wikipedia, Tardigrade.

question: A tardigrade barely half a millimeter long lives in the droplets of water that cling between plant strands, and to an animal that small every patch is a tangled jungle. It must grip and clamber over each strand as it goes. What does the end of each of its eight stubby legs carry, so it can hook on and hold?
answer: A cluster of tiny claws
choices: A cluster of tiny claws
A single suction cup
A sticky pad of glue
A tuft of bristles
context: Each of a tardigrade's eight legs ends in a set of tiny claws, usually four to eight per foot, which it uses to grip and clamber through the moss it lives in. Source: Wikipedia, Tardigrade.

question: A tardigrade on the hunt clamps onto a plant cell or a rotifer, an animal even smaller than itself, and settles in to feed. What does it do to get its meal?
answer: Sucks out the juices inside
choices: Sucks out the juices inside
Grinds it into paste
Wraps it in sticky silk
Filters scraps from the water
context: The tardigrade stabs prey with paired stylets made of the hard mineral aragonite, then pumps out the fluids inside. Source: Wikipedia, Tardigrade.

question: When its world freezes or dries out, a tardigrade can shut its body down, its metabolism all but stopped. Two tardigrades and an egg were once found in an Antarctic moss sample that had been kept frozen since 1983. Once thawed, how long a sleep had they survived?
answer: More than thirty years
choices: More than thirty years
A few weeks
About one winter
Roughly three years
context: Moss collected in Antarctica in 1983 and kept frozen at -20 C was thawed in 2014; two tardigrades and an egg revived after more than 30 years, crawled, ate, and one laid 19 eggs. Source: Tsujimoto et al., Cryobiology 2016.

question: A dried tardigrade, curled into its barrel-shaped tun, has survived a short spell at about 150 C and still woken when soaked in water again. Scientists have also chilled one in the laboratory and brought it back to life. How cold has a tardigrade been chilled and lived through?
answer: To about -272 C, one degree above absolute zero
choices: To about -272 C, one degree above absolute zero
To about -40 C, a deep winter freeze
To about -90 C, the coldest Antarctic air
To about -180 C, the cold of liquid nitrogen
context: A dried tardigrade has survived short spells at roughly -272 C, a single degree above absolute zero, the coldest anything can ever be, and at about 149 C, though only for short periods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tardigrade ('at least for short periods of time').

question: A tardigrade shrugs off a blast of about 5,000 gray of radiation, though just 5 to 10 gray kills a person. Scientists traced its trick to a protein they nicknamed 'damage suppressor.' What does this protein do inside the tardigrade's cells?
answer: Wraps around its DNA like a shield
choices: Wraps around its DNA like a shield
Rebuilds cells faster than they break
Flushes the radiation out as heat
Turns the radiation into food
context: The protein Dsup ('damage suppressor') shrouds the DNA and soaks up damage; added to human cells in the lab it made them about 40% more resistant to X-rays. Source: MIT News 2025 / Dsup, Wikipedia. (Legend-tier.)

question: European scientists strapped dried tardigrades to the outside of a satellite in 2007 for an experiment called Tardigrades In Space. For ten days the animals faced the raw vacuum of space and its cosmic rays. Back on Earth, what did the survivors go on to do?
answer: Revived and had healthy babies
choices: Revived and had healthy babies
Glowed faintly for weeks
Never moved again
Doubled in size
context: Most survived vacuum plus cosmic radiation and some even survived direct solar UV, making the tardigrade the first animal ever shown to survive open space; revived, they bred normally. Source: Jonsson et al., Current Biology 2008. (Legend-tier.)

question: A tardigrade can wait out years curled in its dried tun while making almost none of the sugar trehalose, which brine shrimp and some roundworms pack into their cells so nothing collapses without water. Its cells still pull through unharmed. What does it flood them with instead?
answer: Its own tangled proteins, which set into glass
choices: Its own tangled proteins, which set into glass
Sticky glycerol that clings on to water
Waxy fats that seal each cell from the air
A different sugar it stockpiles in bulk
context: Those proteins are the tardigrade's own CAHS proteins — short for Cytoplasmic Abundant Heat Soluble. While the animal is wet they are 'intrinsically disordered,' floppy and shapeless, but as the water drains away they pass through a glass transition and harden into a glass-like matrix, locking the cell's membranes and enzymes in place so nothing can unfold or clump apart. When Thomas Boothby's team silenced these proteins, the tardigrades lost the ability to survive drying; the purified proteins alone shielded other creatures' enzymes right through desiccation. Brine shrimp and many roundworms lean on the sugar trehalose instead — water bears run mostly on their own protein glass. Source: Boothby et al., 'Tardigrades Use Intrinsically Disordered Proteins to Survive Desiccation,' Molecular Cell 65(6), 16 March 2017.

question: A tardigrade waddling through its damp little world belongs to a line that goes back to before the first dinosaurs, and an animal that tough might be expected to turn up all through the rocks. The fossil record shows almost the opposite. How many tardigrade bodies have ever been found as fossils, and how were they preserved?
answer: Only a handful, each locked inside amber
choices: Only a handful, each locked inside amber
Many thousands, pressed flat in shale
Several hundred, turned to stone in limestone
A few dozen, frozen deep in permafrost
context: Only a handful of unmistakable tardigrade bodies have ever been found as fossils, four named kinds by 2024, and every one was sealed in amber, fossilised tree resin. The oldest, Milnesium swolenskyi, comes from New Jersey amber about 90 million years old; Beorn leggi and Aerobius dactylus share one piece of Canadian amber about 72 million years old. The youngest, Paradoryphoribius chronocaribbeus, was described in 2021 from 16-million-year-old Dominican amber; at just 559 micrometres it sat unnoticed beside three trapped ants for months before anyone spotted it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tardigrade ; Mapalo et al., Proc. R. Soc. B 2021; Mapalo et al., Communications Biology 2024.

question: A primate so tiny it could sit in a child's hand leaps between tree trunks at night in the rainforests of Borneo and the Philippines, hunting insects, small lizards and even birds. Each of its eyeballs is as big as, or even bigger than, its whole brain. Which night hunter is this?
answer: The tarsier
choices: The tarsier
The slow loris
The fennec fox
The sugar glider
context: Each tarsier eyeball is about 16 mm across and equals or exceeds the size of its entire brain. No other mammal has eyes so large relative to its body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarsier

question: A tarsier freezes on a dark branch in a Southeast Asian rainforest and tracks a moth flitting through the canopy behind it, its perched body never shifting a muscle. How far can the little hunter crank its head around to keep the moth in view?
answer: Nearly 180 degrees each way, like an owl
choices: Nearly 180 degrees each way, like an owl
About 90 degrees, a quarter turn to each shoulder
Roughly 45 degrees, a small glance either side
A full 360 degrees in one continuous spin
context: A tarsier's giant eyeballs are locked in their sockets, so it turns its head roughly 180 degrees in either direction, owl-like, giving it a full 360-degree field of view without moving its body. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/tarsier

question: A palm-sized tarsier clings upright to a tree trunk in a Sulawesi rainforest, a big-eyed night hunter. Almost every other primate, from gorillas to lemurs to chimpanzees, fills its belly with fruit, leaves and other plants, but the tarsier stands alone among them for one thing about its diet. What sets it apart?
answer: It is the only primate that eats nothing but meat, no plants at all
choices: It is the only primate that eats nothing but meat, no plants at all
It is the only primate that survives entirely on tree sap and gum
It is the only primate that will not drink water, only dew
It is the only primate that eats one single species of fruit
context: The tarsier is the only entirely carnivorous primate known, eating insects like beetles, cicadas, and grasshoppers, and even snatching lizards, snakes, small birds, and bats. It eats no fruit or leaves at all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarsier

question: A Philippine tarsier on a forest branch gapes its mouth open as though crying out, yet human ears hear nothing at all. Marissa Ramsier's team pointed bat-detector microphones at the little animals in 2012 and solved the mystery. What was the tarsier really doing when it 'silent-screamed'?
answer: It was calling in ultrasound, around 70 kHz, far above what we can hear
choices: It was calling in ultrasound, around 70 kHz, far above what we can hear
It was yawning as a threat display, not vocalizing at all
It was pushing air through its nose too softly to detect
It was clicking its teeth at a pitch our ears cannot register
context: The Philippine tarsier calls with a dominant pitch near 70 kHz and can hear up to about 91 kHz, far beyond the roughly 20 kHz ceiling of human hearing, so it can 'talk' in a channel we cannot detect. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarsier

question: A stocky black meat-eater the size of a dog screeches in the forests of Tasmania at night, and it carries its babies in a pouch. No meat-eating marsupial left on Earth is bigger. What is it?
answer: The Tasmanian devil
choices: The Tasmanian devil
The red kangaroo
The koala
The wombat
context: The Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii) is the largest surviving carnivorous marsupial in the world. Kangaroos, koalas, and wombats are all marsupials too, but they are plant-eaters. Source: Wikipedia 'Tasmanian devil' ('largest surviving carnivorous marsupial').

question: A Tasmanian devil arrives at a dead wallaby long after the foxes and birds have taken the easy meat and gone. Instead of nibbling at what is left, the dog-sized marsupial does something no bird or fox can. What does it do with the leftover carcass?
answer: It crunches up and swallows the whole thing — bones, fur, and teeth
choices: It crunches up and swallows the whole thing — bones, fur, and teeth
It caches the scraps in a den to eat over several days
It picks out only the rich organs and abandons the rest
It strips the last shreds of muscle and leaves the frame standing
context: Tasmanian devils consume all traces of a carcass, including bones and fur, leaving nothing for other scavengers. Source: Wikipedia 'Tasmanian devil' ('consume all traces of a carcass, including bones and fur').

question: Clucking softly while it feeds and screaming in a fight, a Tasmanian devil no bigger than a small dog is one of the noisiest animals alive. About how many distinct noises can one devil make?
answer: At least eleven different sounds
choices: At least eleven different sounds
Just two — a growl and a scream
Around fifty separate calls
Only one, repeated at different pitches
context: Despite being small, the Tasmanian devil has one of the loudest and most complex voices of any animal, using at least eleven different sound types, from gentle clucking while feeding to screams during a fight. Source: Currumbin Sanctuary; Wikipedia 'Tasmanian devil' (eleven sound types).

question: A mother Tasmanian devil gives birth to 20 to 30 young at once, each no bigger than a grain of rice. But inside her backward-opening pouch there are only four teats to feed them all. What decides which of those newborns actually lives?
answer: Only the first four to crawl into the pouch and grab a teat survive
choices: Only the first four to crawl into the pouch and grab a teat survive
The mother carries the four strongest and abandons the rest outside
The four largest at birth push the smaller ones away from her
She feeds all of them in shifts until the weakest give out
context: A devil bears 20-30 rice-grain-sized young but has only four nipples, so the newborns race to the pouch and only the first four to latch on survive. Source: Wikipedia 'Tasmanian devil' (20-30 young, four nipples); WWF-Australia '8 Fun Facts About Tasmanian Devils'. The rice-grain newborn detail is a widely retold wonder.

question: Two Tasmanian devils bite at each other's faces in a scuffle over a carcass, and a disease jumps from one to the other. It has wiped out roughly 80 percent of the wild population since 1996, and it spreads in a way almost unheard of in nature. What kind of disease behaves like that?
answer: A cancer whose living tumor cells pass directly from animal to animal
choices: A cancer whose living tumor cells pass directly from animal to animal
A virus carried in the saliva of infected devils
A bacterial infection picked up from rotting carcasses
A parasite that burrows in through bite wounds
context: Devil Facial Tumour Disease is a transmissible cancer — one of only a tiny handful ever found — in which living tumor cells themselves move between animals through facial bites, unlike a virus or bacterium. Source: Wikipedia 'Devil facial tumour disease'; The Conversation 'Tassie devil facial tumour is a transmissible cancer'; Transmissible Cancer Group, University of Cambridge.

question: A channel catfish glides along the silty bottom of an American river, where the water is far too dark and cloudy for eyes to be much use. The moment a food pellet brushes its long whiskers, or even its side or belly, the catfish turns and grabs it. What lets it find its food by touch in the dark?
answer: Its whole skin is packed with taste buds
choices: Its whole skin is packed with taste buds
It hears the pellet strike the water
It stuns the pellet with a weak electric jolt
It traps the pellet in a sticky mucus net
context: The channel catfish is essentially a swimming tongue: its entire skin, and especially the barbel 'whiskers,' is coated in taste buds, so it tastes food the moment food brushes any part of its body. Source: AskNature, 'Fish Body Is a Swimming Tongue'; Caprio, 'The taste system of the channel catfish' (Trends in Neurosciences, 1993).

question: A big channel catfish hunts the muddy bottom of a North American river with taste buds spread over its whole body, from its flanks to its long chin whiskers. A person has about 10,000, all of them on the tongue. Roughly how many does the catfish carry?
answer: About 175,000
choices: About 175,000
About 15,000
About 2,000
About 500
context: A large catfish can carry over 100,000 taste buds — as many as 175,000 — scattered across its whole external body, versus about 10,000 crammed onto the human tongue. It tastes with its skin. Source: LiveScience, 'What Animal Has the Best Sense of Taste?'; Atema 1971 on external taste-bud distribution.

question: A female butterfly lands on a leaf and, before laying a single egg, rapidly taps the leaf with her forelegs — 'tarsal drumming.' Why does she drum the leaf with her feet before egg-laying?
answer: Her feet taste the plant to confirm it is safe for caterpillars
choices: Her feet taste the plant to confirm it is safe for caterpillars
Her feet warm the leaf so eggs will stick
Her feet scrape off rival butterflies' eggs
Her feet drum a signal to attract a mate
context: Butterflies taste with their feet: chemoreceptors on the tarsi let her read the leaf's chemistry by drumming on it, confirming the right, non-toxic host plant before she trusts it with her eggs. Source: ScienceABC, 'Do Butterflies Taste With Their Feet?'; Animals Around The Globe, 'Butterflies Taste With Their Feet.'

question: Vincent Dethier sat down to lunch one day in the 1950s, and a blowfly kept landing on his liverwurst sandwich. Curious, he began touching drops of sugar water to the fly's tiny feet and watching what happened. The moment a hungry fly's foot touches sugar, he found, it does one thing at once, by reflex. What does the fly do?
answer: It unrolls its tongue to drink
choices: It unrolls its tongue to drink
It rubs its front legs together
It buzzes its wings in a burst
It curls its abdomen upward
context: A fly tastes with its feet too. When its foot pads touch sugar, the 'proboscis extension reflex' fires and it unrolls its tongue to feed — the reflex Dethier discovered from a blowfly on his lab-window sandwich. Source: The Wire Science, 'To Know a Fly: Vincent Dethier'; eNeuro on the gustatory system in feeding.

question: A snake flicks its forked tongue, catching scent particles from the air, then pulls it back inside. The tongue does not carry those particles to the nose. Where inside the snake does the flicking tongue deliver its scent load?
answer: To a paired sensor in the roof of its mouth
choices: To a paired sensor in the roof of its mouth
To glands behind its fangs
To sacs deep in its throat
To pits below its eyes
context: A snake 'smells with its mouth': flicking collects scent particles and delivers them to the two-pronged vomeronasal (Jacobson's) organ in the palate. Source: ScienceTimes, 'Snakes Use Their Forked Tongues to Smell'; on the Jacobson's organ.

question: A zoologist pulls back the lips of a wolf and a cow to compare the big cheek teeth well back in their jaws. The wolf's are thin, blade-shaped edges; the cow's are broad, flat slabs with hard ridges across the top. What do those teeth tell about what each animal eats?
answer: The wolf slices meat; the cow grinds tough plants
choices: The wolf slices meat; the cow grinds tough plants
The wolf grinds plants; the cow slices meat
Both slice meat, but the wolf's blades are simply larger
Both grind plants, but the cow's slabs are simply harder
context: A carnivore has bladelike shearing teeth for slicing meat; a herbivore has broad, flat, ridged molars for grinding tough plants. You can read the diet from the shape: a slicer versus a grinder. Source: Britannica, Carnivore (Form and function); Berkeley Morphology of the Vertebrate Skeleton.

question: A horse crops grass with its wide front teeth and grinds it with big flat cheek teeth farther back. Between the two sets runs a long, bare stretch of gum, the diastema, and the horse's tongue shoves grass along it toward the grinders. What fills that same spot in the jaw of a wolf or a lion?
answer: Long stabbing canines for seizing prey
choices: Long stabbing canines for seizing prey
A second row of grinding molars
A bony ridge that anchors the jaw muscle
An extra pair of biting front teeth
context: The toothless gap in a horse or cow is called a diastema, the empty space where a meat-eater's slashing canines would be. The tongue uses that gap to shuffle grass back to the grinding molars. Source: Berkeley Morphology of the Vertebrate Skeleton; BW Equine Vets, Equine Dentistry.

question: A cat works clean through hide, tendon and bone with back cheek teeth that have no flat grinding surface at all, their uppers and lowers never quite meeting. What everyday tool do these teeth work like?
answer: A pair of scissors
choices: A pair of scissors
A hammer driven onto an anvil
A pestle crushing in a bowl
A rasp dragged across a surface
context: These specialized cheek teeth are called carnassials (the upper fourth premolar and lower first molar). Their blade edges slide past each other like scissor blades, shearing meat and cracking bone. Cats, wolves, and hyenas have them. Source: Wikipedia, Carnassial; Britannica.

question: An elephant chews rough vegetation all day, and each grinding molar can be a foot long and weigh about eleven pounds. Rather than losing a tooth here and there, how does an elephant's jaw handle the constant wear?
