answer: Worn molars ride forward and crumble off the front as new ones push in from behind
choices: Worn molars ride forward and crumble off the front as new ones push in from behind
A single molar keeps growing taller from its root all life long
The elephant swallows worn teeth and grows softer replacements
Both jaws rotate the same four molars end over end to spread the wear
context: An elephant carries only four huge molars at a time, riding forward on a conveyor belt: worn ones crumble off the front in wafer-like sheets as new ones push in from the back. Source: globalelephants.org, EleFact Friday: Elephant Molars are Unique.

question: Biologists documented one woodchuck whose upper incisor had no opposing tooth to grind against. Like any rodent's incisor it grew without stop, and with nothing to wear it down it kept curving. What did the tooth finally do?
answer: Grew up through the roof of its mouth into its own brain
choices: Grew up through the roof of its mouth into its own brain
Locked its jaw permanently shut so it could not eat
Split down the middle and fell harmlessly out
Curled outward into a useless spiral past its lips
context: If a rodent can't gnaw, the tooth keeps growing in a curve until it spirals into the animal's own skull. A woodchuck's upper incisor once grew through its palate and into its brain, killing it. Source: Naturally Curious with Mary Holland, Rodent Incisors (documented case).

question: An old elephant cuts its last set of molars in its early forties, and once that set wears smooth it can no longer grind plants and slowly starves. How many sets of molars does one elephant get in its whole life?
answer: Six sets in all, and no more
choices: Six sets in all, and no more
About forty, one each year
Two sets, like most mammals
Twelve sets, two at a time
context: An elephant gets only six sets of molars in its whole life; the last erupt around its early 40s. When that final set wears smooth, the elephant can no longer grind plants and slowly starves. Its own teeth are its life clock. Source: globalelephants.org; Save the Elephants.

question: A beaver spends its life gnawing down hardwood trees along North American streams, felling trunks as thick as a person's leg for its dams and lodges. Its chisel-shaped front teeth take a beating every day for years, yet they stay razor-sharp without a whetstone, thanks less to new growth than to how each tooth is built. How does gnawing keep them sharp?
answer: Hard enamel coats the front and softer dentine the back, so wear leaves a chisel edge
choices: Hard enamel coats the front and softer dentine the back, so wear leaves a chisel edge
A wax coating slides down the tooth and re-hones it each night
New enamel grows only along the cutting edge as the tip wears
The two front teeth grind against each other like a strop
context: A rodent's incisor sharpens itself: the front face is hard enamel and the back is softer dentine, so gnawing wears the back away faster and leaves a chisel edge, like a self-honing knife. Source: Naturally Curious with Mary Holland; ACS PressPac.

question: The incisors a beaver bares at a tree trunk are faced in a striking rusty orange, not white like a person's. Recent chemistry credits the hardness and acid resistance of that orange face to one ingredient locked inside the enamel. What is it?
answer: Iron, worked into the enamel
choices: Iron, worked into the enamel
Fluoride, absorbed from river water
Silica, ground in from chewing sand
Calcium, layered on far thicker than normal
context: The orange front is iron-toughened enamel; the iron makes it hard and acid-resistant so the tooth can gnaw wood without wearing to a nub. 2024 research found the iron gives the strength, while the orange color likely comes from amino acids in the enamel, not the iron itself. Source: American Chemical Society PressPac, April 2024; Chemistry World.

question: The saber-toothed cat Smilodon carried upper fangs up to 11 inches long, the kind of weapon that seems to call for a crushing bite. Yet biomechanical models put its jaw force at only about a third of a lion's, feeble for a cat its size. With so weak a jaw, how did it force those long blades deep into pinned prey?
answer: Powerful neck muscles hauled its skull down to sink them in
choices: Powerful neck muscles hauled its skull down to sink them in
The full weight of its pouncing body dropped onto the fangs
A fast side-to-side sawing of its whole head worked them in
The prey drove itself onto the fixed fangs as it thrashed
context: Its sabers looked built for a monstrous bite, but the opposite was true. Biomechanical modeling estimates a canine bite force around 1,283 N, roughly a third of a modern lion's and close to the much smaller jaguar. So Smilodon used a 'canine shear-bite': the forelimbs pinned the prey motionless first, then the massive neck muscles pulled the skull downward to drive the blades home, doing the work the jaw could not. The killing power came from the neck, not the jaw. Source: Wikipedia 'Smilodon' (bite force ~1/3 of a lion, ~1,283.74 N at the canine; 'canine shear-bite' via neck flexion / skull rotation), from biomechanical modeling by Wroe et al. 2007/2008, corroborated by a 2018 comparative skull study.

question: An Edmontosaurus, a duck-billed dinosaur, chewed gritty plants year after year with the best grinding teeth ever, hundreds of them cemented together into one slab called a dental battery. Each tooth wove six kinds of tissue, where a horse molar uses four. What did the wear keep doing to its grinding surface?
answer: It kept re-cutting fresh, self-sharpening ridges
choices: It kept re-cutting fresh, self-sharpening ridges
It wore the surface flat and glassy, like a tile
It cracked and pitted the surface under the grit
It buffed the surface smoother and harder each bite
context: Duck-billed dinosaurs had the most sophisticated grinding teeth ever evolved. Each tooth was built from six distinct dental tissues, versus four in a horse or bison molar and just two in most other dinosaurs. Because those six tissues wore away at different rates, ordinary chewing constantly re-carved fresh ridges and hollows into the surface, so the teeth kept sharpening themselves as they wore. Source: Erickson, Krick, Hamilton, Bourne, Norell, Lilleodden et al., 'Complex Dental Structure and Wear Biomechanics in Hadrosaurid Dinosaurs,' Science 2012;338:98-101 (six tissue types vs four in mammals, two in most dinosaurs), corroborated by a 2017 Scientific Reports dynamic-dental-battery histology study.

question: A flightless bird nearly 10 feet tall ran down its prey over the pampas of South America on long, powerful legs, armed with a massive hooked beak. Back then the land held almost no large mammal hunters, and this bird ruled it. Its fossils turn up across Argentina. What are these vanished hunters called?
answer: a terror bird
choices: a terror bird
a thunderbird
a war eagle
a dread crane
context: The 'terror birds' (phorusrhacids) stood up to about 3 meters (nearly 10 feet) tall and reigned as the top land predators of South America for millions of years, long before and into the ice age. Source: Wikipedia, Phorusrhacidae (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phorusrhacidae).

question: Running down a smaller mammal on the pampas of South America, a terror bird closed in with its huge beak, shaped like a hatchet and hooked at the tip. It did not kill the way a lion's or a wolf's jaws do. How did the terror bird use that beak?
answer: it struck straight down like a swinging pickaxe
choices: it struck straight down like a swinging pickaxe
it clamped shut and dragged prey underwater
it sprayed venom through a groove in the tip
it filtered small prey from mud like a spoon
context: Its most fearsome weapon was a huge hatchet-shaped beak with a hooked tip; instead of biting and shaking, it struck straight DOWN at prey like swinging a pickaxe to break the neck or skull. Source: PMC 2923598, Mechanical Analysis of Feeding Behavior in Andalgalornis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2923598/).

question: A terror bird stood nearly 10 feet tall on long, muscular legs and chased its prey on foot across the open pampas of South America, never taking to the air as an eagle or a hawk does. What were its wings like?
answer: tiny and nearly useless
choices: tiny and nearly useless
large and clawed for grappling
tucked spurs it used to slash
paddle-shaped for pushing through brush
context: Terror birds had almost useless tiny wings but long, powerful running legs, and were built to chase prey down on foot rather than fly. Source: Wikipedia, Phorusrhacidae (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phorusrhacidae).

question: Guillermo Aguirre-Zabala dug the biggest bird skull ever found out of the fossil-rich cliffs of Patagonia in 2006. The 28-inch skull belonged to Kelenken, a terror bird about 10 feet tall that hunted mammals across ancient South America. The finder was no seasoned professor. Who was Guillermo Aguirre-Zabala?
answer: a high-school student
choices: a high-school student
a retired sea captain
a museum night guard
a visiting oil surveyor
context: The largest terror bird skull known belongs to Kelenken, found in Patagonia in 2006 by high-school student Guillermo Aguirre-Zabala; at about 71 cm (28 inches) it is the biggest bird skull known, with a hooked beak roughly 46 cm long. Source: Wikipedia, Kelenken (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelenken).

question: Scientists loaded a fossil terror bird's skull into a computer and ran stress tests on it, to see how it stood up to the forces of a hunt. Its bones were fused rigid. The skull held up well under some blows, but one motion of the head could have snapped it. Which motion was its weak point?
answer: twisting prey side to side
choices: twisting prey side to side
a hard downward blow
a forward jab at prey
a straight backward pull
context: Finite element analysis showed the skull was strong for straight downward strikes but weak against side-to-side twisting, so the bird could NOT thrash prey like a mammal; its skull bones were fused rigid (loss of cranial kinesis), turning the head into a solid pickaxe built to survive a hard downward blow. Source: PMC 2923598, Mechanical Analysis of Feeding Behavior in Andalgalornis steulleti (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2923598/).

question: Paleontologists in 2024 described one shin bone, twelve million years old, from the Tatacoa Desert of Colombia. It came from what may be the biggest terror bird ever found, a top land hunter of its day. Yet the bone is scarred with deep bite marks, so even this giant became prey. Whose bite left them?
answer: a giant caiman as long as a bus
choices: a giant caiman as long as a bus
a saber-toothed marsupial as big as a bear
a pack of wolf-sized marsupial hunters
a rival terror bird ten feet tall
context: This is the 2024 La Venta discovery from Colombia's Tatacoa Desert (Degrange et al., Papers in Palaeontology). The bird -- the northernmost terror bird known and possibly the biggest, roughly 5-20% larger than any before it -- survives as a single left shin bone (tibiotarsus) about 12 million years old. The bite marks on it match Purussaurus, an extinct caiman that grew to about 10 m (30 ft), longer than a school bus. So even the age's ultimate land hunter could be dragged down by a colossal crocodilian at the water's edge. Source: Degrange et al. 2024, Papers in Palaeontology 10(6):e1601, DOI 10.1002/spp2.1601; reported by Sci.News and Johns Hopkins Medicine, November 2024.

question: Researchers ran CT scans through the ear of Llallawavis, a terror bird whose skeleton, found in Argentina, is the most complete of its kind, down to the fragile coiled bones deep inside the ear. The ear's shape showed what kind of sound this hunter was tuned to catch. What was its hearing built for?
answer: deep, low sounds that carry for miles, like an elephant
choices: deep, low sounds that carry for miles, like an elephant
faint, high squeaks up close, like an owl hunting mice
its own echoes bouncing back, like a cave-nesting bird
a wide band of chirps and trills, like a songbird
context: This is Llallawavis scagliai, described in 2015 from Argentina -- about 95% complete, the finest terror bird fossil known (Degrange et al., Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology). CT scans of its inner ear showed its hearing was tuned unusually low for a bird, with mean sensitivity around 2,300 Hz, below the average for living birds. Low-pitched sound fades slowly and travels far, so the bird could likely hear prey moving out of sight -- footsteps in the grass -- and probably answered with its own deep, booming calls over long distances. Source: Degrange et al. 2015, Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology; reported via National Geographic ('The Call of the Terror Bird') and the Florida Museum (FLMNH) fossil-project research page.

question: A little crab scuttles over the rocks of a tide pool on legs that each bend at a joint like a knee. A hard shell, worn on the outside, covers its whole body. Which big invertebrate group does it belong to?
answer: Arthropods
choices: Arthropods
Cnidarians
Echinoderms
Sponges
context: Jointed legs plus a hard external skeleton (an exoskeleton made of chitin) is the give-away trait of the arthropods — insects, spiders, scorpions, crabs, lobsters, centipedes and millipedes all share this one body plan. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/arthropod

question: A see-through jellyfish drifts through the sea trailing its tentacles, and any small fish that brushes them is stung and paralyzed. Jellyfish, corals and sea anemones all fight with stinging cells like these. Which big invertebrate group do they belong to?
answer: Cnidarians
choices: Cnidarians
Arthropods
Annelids
Mollusks
context: Cnidarians are the stingers: they carry stinging cells (cnidocytes holding harpoon-like nematocysts), have radial bodies, and a single opening that serves as both mouth and anus. Jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones are all cnidarians. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/cnidarian

question: A biologist sorts every animal on Earth, from worms to birds, into a handful of big groups by body plan. One group outnumbers all the others together: about four in five known animal species belong to it. Which group is it?
answer: Arthropods
choices: Arthropods
Mollusks
Cnidarians
Annelids
context: Arthropods are the biggest animal group by far: roughly 80–84% of all known animal species are arthropods (insects, spiders, crabs). Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/anatomy-and-physiology/arthropods

question: An earthworm pushes through the garden soil, its body one long tube made of rings, each ring a segment stacked behind the next. Leeches are built on the same ringed plan. Which big invertebrate group does the earthworm belong to?
answer: Annelids
choices: Annelids
Echinoderms
Cnidarians
Arthropods
context: Annelids are the segmented (ringed) worms: their bodies are divided into repeating segments by transverse rings, and most bear tiny bristles called setae. Earthworms and leeches are annelids. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/annelid

question: A garden snail creeps across a wet leaf carrying a hard spiral shell it grew itself, though there is not a single bone anywhere in its soft body. With no inner skeleton to build from, how does a snail make that shell?
answer: A sheet of tissue over its body lays down shell material layer by layer
choices: A sheet of tissue over its body lays down shell material layer by layer
Tiny bristles along its foot weave the shell like a basket
It hardens a patch of its skin into bone from the inside out
It glues sand grains together with slime into a crust
context: Mollusks have a soft body, often a shell, and a muscular 'foot' plus a tissue fold called the mantle that secretes the shell layer by layer. Snails, clams, and octopuses are all mollusks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusca

question: A bright, blob-like animal clings to a coral reef, with seawater flowing in through the holes all over its body. It has no head, no gut, no nerves and no muscles, and it never forms true tissues or organs. Which big invertebrate group does it belong to?
answer: Sponges
choices: Sponges
Cnidarians
Annelids
Echinoderms
context: Sponges (Porifera, 'pore-bearers') are the simplest animals: no true tissues, no organs — just a body full of pores. Collar cells (choanocytes) beat tiny whips to pump water through and strain out food. Source: https://shapeoflife.org/phylum-porifera

question: A biologist lays an earthworm from the garden beside a leech from a pond and counts the rings on each. The earthworm has well over a hundred segments, sometimes 150 or more. Every leech, big or small, stops at the same tidy number. How many segments does a leech have?
answer: 34 segments
choices: 34 segments
12 segments
100 segments
6 segments
context: Segment-counting sorts the worms: an earthworm has over a hundred segments (8 tiny bristles each), while every leech has exactly 34 segments and no bristles at all. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/annelid/Form-and-function

question: A big-brained octopus jets across the reef and seizes a crab in eight sucker-tipped arms. A garden snail creeps along on one slimy foot under a coiled shell. Yet biologists file the two in the same enormous invertebrate group, along with clams, oysters and slugs. Which group's soft body plan do they share?
answer: Mollusks
choices: Mollusks
Cnidarians
Arthropods
Echinoderms
context: An octopus and a snail are cousins — both mollusks. The snail's muscular foot creeps along rocks; in the octopus that same 'foot' is divided into the arms that catch prey. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusca

question: H. V. Wilson pushed a whole living sponge through a fine mesh in 1907 and mashed it into a soup of loose, separate cells, a fate that would kill almost any animal. A sponge has no true tissues binding its cells together. What did the scattered cells do next?
answer: Crawled back together and rebuilt the sponge
choices: Crawled back together and rebuilt the sponge
Died apart as separated single cells
Grew into many tiny new sponges
Turned into free-swimming larvae
context: In H.V. Wilson's 1907 experiment the cells crawled back together and rebuilt themselves into a working sponge — possible because a sponge's cells are loners with no true tissues. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Van_Peters_Wilson

question: A biologist watching animal embryos grow sees the first opening of most of them become the mouth. In one camp of animals, fish, frogs and people among them, that first opening becomes the anus instead, and the mouth forms afterward. Which of these tide-pool animals grows the same back-to-front way?
answer: A sea urchin
choices: A sea urchin
A giant octopus
A horseshoe crab
A blue mussel
context: Biologists split most animals into two great camps by this embryo tell. Protostomes ('mouth first') build the mouth from the embryo's first opening: arthropods (insects, crabs, horseshoe crabs), mollusks like the octopus, mussel and snail, and segmented worms all belong here. Deuterostomes ('mouth second') form the anus first and the mouth later; the echinoderms, sea urchins, sea stars and their kin, sit in this camp alongside the chordates, the group that includes fish, frogs and people. So in how it develops, the spiny sea urchin in a tide pool is closer to a person than the sharp-eyed octopus beside it, even though the octopus carries the big brain and the urchin has none. (The protostome/deuterostome split is textbook-solid, but a 2021 genomic study questioned exactly how tight the echinoderm-chordate grouping is.) Source: OpenStax Biology 2e, 'Superphylum Deuterostomia' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/28-7-superphylum-deuterostomia); UCL News 2021 (https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2021/mar/analysis-are-we-more-closely-related-starfish-or-insects).

question: A lean dog with long legs, a deep chest and a whip-thin body tears down a racetrack. Trainers have clocked dogs of its breed running close to 45 miles an hour, faster than any other dog on Earth. Which breed holds the canine speed record?
answer: The greyhound
choices: The greyhound
The Doberman
The Dalmatian
The husky
context: The greyhound is the domestic echo of the cheetah's build: it runs the same double-suspension gallop, with two airborne phases per stride, powered by a flexible spine and a disproportionately large heart. Source: Greyhound, Wikipedia; RevealingPaws, Double Suspension Gallop.

question: A cheetah sprinting after a gazelle across the African plains flings its shoulders far forward through the air on every stride. In one bound it covers a startling stretch of ground before its paws touch down again. About how far does a single bound carry it?
answer: 6-7 meters (about 21-23 feet)
choices: 6-7 meters (about 21-23 feet)
1-2 meters (about 3-6 feet)
10-12 meters (about 33-39 feet)
Just under 1 meter (about 2 feet)
context: The cheetah's spring-spine throws the shoulder blades so far forward that a single bound covers 6-7 meters, roughly the length of a small car and a half. Source: SeaWorld cheetah adaptations; Cheetah Conservation Fund.

question: Running down a gazelle on the African savanna, a cheetah stretches its legs out long and then bunches them tight beneath its body, over and over. Twice in every stride, its feet do something almost no other running animal manages. What happens to its paws at those moments?
answer: All four paws leave the ground at once
choices: All four paws leave the ground at once
One paw always stays planted
Only the front paws touch down
The paws never fully leave the ground
context: This is the double-suspension gallop: once with the legs stretched fully out and once with them bunched under the body, all four paws are airborne twice per stride. The greyhound runs the same way. Source: Cheetah Conservation Fund; Biology Insights, How Can a Cheetah Run So Fast.

question: Sarah the cheetah, eleven years old, tore along a certified 100-meter track built just for her in 2012, at 61 miles an hour. Usain Bolt's human world record of 9.58 seconds looked slow beside her. What was Sarah's time for the 100 meters?
answer: 5.95 seconds
choices: 5.95 seconds
8.10 seconds
3.20 seconds
9.40 seconds
context: Sarah ran the fastest 100 meters ever recorded by anything on Earth: 5.95 seconds, more than three and a half seconds quicker than Usain Bolt's human world record. Source: National Geographic 2012, Cheetah Breaks Speed Record.

question: A pronghorn tears across the plains of the American West with far more speed than the wolves and coyotes that hunt it could ever demand. John Byers set out to explain all that spare speed. What does he think the pronghorn evolved to escape?
answer: A cheetah-like cat that no longer exists
choices: A cheetah-like cat that no longer exists
Grass fires that once raced over the plains
Golden eagles that swoop down on its fawns
Swarms of biting flies on its summer range
context: John Byers argues that the pronghorn's speed, far beyond anything its living predators demand, was shaped by Miracinonyx, the American cheetah, a sprinting cat that died out at the end of the last ice age; he calls such vanished hunters the ghosts of predators past. The idea is disputed: other researchers argue that the pronghorn's family was built for speed before such hunters reached North America. Source: John A. Byers, American Pronghorn: Social Adaptations and the Ghosts of Predators Past (1997); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pronghorn

question: An ostrich sprints about twice as fast as a person yet burns only about half the energy per step, a bargain no human runner can match. When biologists compared ostrich and human running, they found what makes it so fast and so cheap at once. What is it?
answer: Long tendons that recoil like springs each stride
choices: Long tendons that recoil like springs each stride
Oversized lungs that flood the muscles with oxygen
Hollow bird bones that lighten every single step
Big wings that beat to drive it on each stride
context: Studies led by Jonas Rubenson (around 2010-2011) compared mass-matched ostriches and humans and found the ostrich stores and returns roughly DOUBLE the elastic strain energy per step that a person does. Long tendons running down the leg and foot stretch as the foot lands and snap back on push-off, recycling much of each stride's energy instead of burning it in muscle, a biological pogo stick. The payoff: an ostrich runs about twice as fast as a human while spending only about half the metabolic energy. Source: Rubenson et al., 'Adaptations for economical bipedal running,' J. R. Soc. Interface / PMC3061092 (2011); phys.org, 'Ostriches run fast because of springy tendons' (2010).

question: A snake wriggles out of its old skin like a foot pulling out of a sock, leaving the whole hide behind in one inside-out tube. It has dry scales all over and lays its eggs on land. Which class of animals does it belong to?
answer: A reptile
choices: A reptile
An amphibian
A mammal
A fish
context: A reptile's tell is dry keratin scales or scutes - snakes, lizards, turtles and crocodiles all wear them, and the skin is dry rather than slimy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptile

question: A brook trout hovers in a cold mountain stream, opening and closing its mouth as water flows past. Feathery gills behind its head draw its oxygen from that water, and lifted into the air it would suffocate. Which class of animals is the trout?
answer: A fish
choices: A fish
An amphibian
A reptile
A bird
context: A fish's tell is gills - comb-like filaments on the sides of the throat that pull oxygen straight out of the water - plus fins and a life lived underwater. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish

question: A hunter at a woodland pond sees something wriggle in the weeds and swears it is a small lizard. It is a newt, with damp skin rather than dry scales, and it began life underwater as a gilled larva before growing legs and crawling onto land. What class of animals is it?
answer: An amphibian
choices: An amphibian
A reptile
A fish
A bird
context: A newt is an amphibian, not a lizard: newts are salamanders (family Salamandridae), with wet skin and a water-bound youth. The dry-scaled lizard only looks similar. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphibian

question: A blue whale glides like a fish, yet it keeps rising to breathe air through its blowhole. A few scattered hairs grow on its skin, its blood runs warm, and a mother feeds her calf rich milk. Which class of animals is it?
answer: A mammal
choices: A mammal
A fish
A reptile
An amphibian
context: A whale is a mammal, not a fish: cetaceans breathe air, have hair, and nurse their offspring with milk rather than laying eggs the way fish do. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal

question: A frog must hop back to a pond every spring, because its soft eggs would dry out on land. A desert lizard can lay its eggs on baking sand and walk away, and the young still grow fully inside their shells. What structure inside the lizard's eggshell lets its embryo develop so far from any pond?
answer: A sealed amniotic sac around the embryo
choices: A sealed amniotic sac around the embryo
A soft jelly coating
A yolk twice the usual size
A pocket of stored air
context: The shelled amniotic egg freed vertebrates from water: its membranes retain water, so reptiles could reproduce on dry land even in extreme, arid habitats. Amphibians still must lay their shell-less eggs in water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptile

question: Under a microscope, a biologist sets a bird's feather beside a scrap of a lizard's dry, overlapping body covering. They look nothing alike, yet both are built from the same tough protein, beta-keratin, just folded into different shapes. Which part of the lizard's body is a feather a reshaped form of?
answer: A scale
choices: A scale
A claw
A tooth
A belly scute
context: Feathers are made of the very same beta-keratin as reptile claws, scales and shells - a bird's feather and a lizard's scale are the same protein, reshaped. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feather

question: Small, feathered theropods, the dinosaur group that includes Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor, left descendants that live on today as one whole class of animals. That class is the last surviving branch of the dinosaurs. Which class is really a living dinosaur?
answer: The birds
choices: The birds
The reptiles
The mammals
The amphibians
context: Birds ARE living dinosaurs: Aves is the only surviving group of Dinosauria, descended from theropod dinosaurs - so the 'five classes' is hiding a dinosaur among them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird

question: A crocodile basking on a riverbank is closer kin to a sparrow than to any lizard, by the evidence of shared traits and DNA. The crocodile and the sparrow sit together on one branch of the family tree, the archosaurs, or 'ruling reptiles.' Where does that place the sparrow and its feathered kin on the tree of life?
answer: Deep inside the reptile branch, as one twig of it
choices: Deep inside the reptile branch, as one twig of it
As the reptiles' nearest outside cousins
As a fresh branch grown from the mammal line
As a lone trunk with no living relatives
context: Cladistically a crocodile is closer kin to a sparrow than to a lizard: birds are more closely related to crocodilians than to other living reptiles, both nested in the clade Archosauria - so birds sit inside the reptiles. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptile

question: Fresh air sweeps one way through a bird's lungs in a continuous loop, so oxygen keeps flowing even as the bird breathes out. Biologists long thought this was special equipment for flight, until Colleen Farmer and Kent Sanders turned up the same one-way flow in 2010 in a living animal with no air sacs at all. Which animal was it?
answer: The American alligator
choices: The American alligator
The fruit bat
The bottlenose dolphin
The giant tortoise
context: Birds move air one direction through their lungs - a continuous fresh stream even during exhale - and this was long assumed to be a specialization for the huge oxygen demand of flight. In 2010, Colleen Farmer and Kent Sanders of the University of Utah reported in Science that American alligators, which have no air sacs at all, also route air unidirectionally through their lungs, steered by aerodynamic 'valve' branch-points. Because crocodilians and birds sit on opposite sides of the archosaur family tree, the shared one-way lung is most simply explained as ancestral to all Archosauria - meaning the non-avian dinosaurs were already breathing this way. A 2013-14 follow-up found similar one-way flow in monitor lizards, hinting the trait may reach back roughly 270 million years. Source: Farmer & Sanders 2010, Science 327:338 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1180219); peerj.com/articles/60/.

question: Four sail-backed beasts loom out of the deep past, and their sails invite one easy guess: dinosaur. One of them is no dinosaur at all. Behind each eye socket it carries a single opening, the synapsid mark, which puts it on the branch that led to mammals. Which sail-back is a stem-mammal, nearer kin to cows than to lizards?
answer: Dimetrodon
choices: Dimetrodon
Spinosaurus
Ouranosaurus
Amargasaurus
context: Around 320-315 million years ago, in the late Carboniferous, the amniotes (backboned animals that lay waterproof eggs on land) split into two sister branches: Synapsida, which led to mammals, and Sauropsida, which led to every reptile and bird. Mammals never descended from reptiles - the two lines are cousins. The give-away is in the skull: synapsids carry a single opening (one temporal fenestra) behind each eye socket. Dimetrodon, the sail-backed Permian predator forever shelved with the dinosaurs, has that single hole, which makes it a synapsid - more closely related to you and to a cow than to any living lizard or crocodile. The other three sails all belong to genuine dinosaurs on the reptile (sauropsid) side: Spinosaurus, a spinosaurid theropod with a tall dorsal sail; Ouranosaurus, an iguanodontian ornithopod whose long back spines are usually restored as a sail; and Amargasaurus, a dicraeosaurid sauropod whose neck bore tall paired spines that may have carried sails. It is the mirror-image of the bird twist: just as a dinosaur hides among the 'reptiles,' a stem-mammal hides among the 'prehistoric reptiles.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synapsida; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauropsida; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimetrodon; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinosaurus; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouranosaurus; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amargasaurus.

question: A shaggy brown animal plods with its herd across the tundra of Alaska and northern Canada, crossing frozen rivers and mountains to find lichen and fresh grass. Its yearly loop of about 3,000 miles is the longest land migration on Earth. Which animal is it?
answer: The caribou
choices: The caribou
The bison
The gray wolf
The moose
context: Caribou hold the record for the longest land migration of any animal, with some Arctic herds traveling on the order of 3,000 miles a year across the tundra. Source: NPS, 'Confirmed! Caribou have the longest land migration in the world'; Earth.com, 'Largest On Earth: Caribou Migration'.

question: A vast herd of hoofed grazers, by long-standing counts over a million strong, sweeps around the Serengeti each year, joined by roughly 250,000 zebras. Each walks 800 to 1,000 km after fresh grass. Which African animal is it?
answer: The wildebeest
choices: The wildebeest
The impala
The Cape buffalo
The springbok
context: Each year a vast herd of wildebeest, long put at 1.3 million or more by aerial surveys (Wikipedia gives about 1.7 million), joined by some 200,000 to 300,000 zebras, moves around the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem, each animal covering 800 to 1,000 km as it follows the rains. A 2025 satellite survey led by Isla Duporge counted fewer than 600,000 wildebeest, so the true size of the herd is now debated. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Serengeti; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serengeti; Duporge et al. 2025, PNAS Nexus (https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2025-09-10-ai-satellite-survey-challenges-long-standing-estimates-serengeti-wildebeest-numbers).

question: At the Mara River, where Kenya meets Tanzania, a vast herd of hoofed grazers crowds the bank, with fresh grass waiting on the far side. They plunge into the deep, muddy water, the herd panics and splashes, and hundreds are seized. More than 3,000 hunters lie in wait below the surface. What are they?
answer: Crocodiles
choices: Crocodiles
Hippos
Piranhas
Snapping turtles
context: At the Mara River crossing, more than 3,000 crocodiles wait in the water while big cats wait on the far bank, together picking off the weakest of the herd - the deadliest stretch of the whole migration. Source: masaimara.com, 'The Great Migration in Masai Mara'; Discover Wildlife.

question: A young salmon hatches in a small mountain stream, swims down the rivers to the sea and spends years hunting in the open Pacific. Then it turns for home and swims all the way back to spawn in the same small stream it hatched in. How does it pick out that one stream from thousands?
answer: By smelling the unique odor of its home water
choices: By smelling the unique odor of its home water
By following the position of the sun overhead
By listening for the rush of its home stream
By memorizing landmarks along the coastline
context: As juveniles, salmon imprint on the specific smell of their home water - the dissolved amino acids that give it a unique odor - and follow that memory back to the exact stream years later. Source: NOAA Fisheries, 'Fish Olfaction and Homing Research'; Nature Scientific Reports srep36393.

question: Sockeye salmon fatten for years in the open Pacific, then swim thousands of miles back to the stream they hatched in. They fight upstream against the current, leaping waterfalls and dodging bears, to reach the gravel where their lives began. Within days of spawning there, what happens to them?
answer: They all die, spent by that one single breeding effort
choices: They all die, spent by that one single breeding effort
They rest for weeks, then drift back downstream to the sea
They stay behind to guard the eggs until the young hatch
They lose their bright colors and quietly return to feed
context: Pacific salmon pour everything into one breeding effort - a strategy called semelparity. A surge of reproductive and stress hormones triggers rapid aging and organ failure, and the fish die within days of spawning. Source: Britannica, 'Why Do Salmon Die After Spawning?'; Bay Nature.

question: Biologists in Alaska fitted a young bar-tailed godwit, a long-legged shorebird, with a tiny satellite tag labeled B6 in 2022. That autumn B6 lifted off, flew south across the open Pacific and did not touch down until it reached land on the far side of the ocean. It never stopped to eat or drink on the way. How long was that nonstop flight?
answer: 11 days straight
choices: 11 days straight
About 30 hours
About 3 days
Nearly 6 weeks
context: B6 flew about 13,560 km (8,425 miles) in 11 days and 1 hour without a single stop, the farthest nonstop flight yet recorded for a bird that cannot feed on the wing (common swifts stay aloft for months, but they eat as they fly). Before the crossing, a godwit fattens until more than half its weight is fat. Source: USGS Alaska Science Center, 'Juvenile bar-tailed godwit B6 Sets World Record'; Hedenstrom et al. 2016, Current Biology (common swift).

question: A mottled, barnacle-crusted whale feeds in icy waters off Alaska, then swims down the Pacific coast to the warm, shallow lagoons of Baja California in Mexico, where its calves are born. There and back, the trip covers about 16,000 to 20,000 km, the longest migration of any mammal. Which whale is it?
answer: The gray whale
choices: The gray whale
The blue whale
The orca
The sperm whale
context: The gray whale holds the mammal migration record at roughly 16,000-20,000 km round trip; one tracked female, Varvara, logged about 22,500 km (nearly 14,000 miles) in a single round trip. Source: NOAA Ocean Today, 'Gray Whale Migration'; Mate et al., Biology Letters (2015).

question: An autumn monarch butterfly sets off south for the high fir forests of central Mexico, where it must live through the whole winter before starting back north. Its parents lived only about a month. It manages its long life by holding off on one thing. What does it delay?
answer: Making the hormone that ages its body
choices: Making the hormone that ages its body
Growing its full-sized wings
Feeding on milkweed as a caterpillar
Developing its sense of direction
context: The southbound 'super generation' (sometimes called the Methuselah generation) lives about eight times longer than its parents because it holds off producing an aging hormone - letting it survive the whole winter and start the trip back north. Source: Green Bay Botanical Garden, 'The Magnificent Migration of Monarch Butterflies'.

question: A bar-tailed godwit about to fly nonstop across the Pacific piles on fat until fat is more than half its body weight, since it will not eat a bite on the way. In the days before takeoff, so that it is not too heavy to leave the ground, its body destroys part of itself. Which part?
answer: Its digestive organs, shrunk down and absorbed into the body
choices: Its digestive organs, shrunk down and absorbed into the body
Its tail feathers, molted away to trim weight and drag
Its leg muscles, wasted away over the long ocean crossing
Its blood, thinned into a lighter and more watery plasma
context: The classic study is literally titled 'Guts Don't Fly: Small Digestive Organs in Obese Bar-tailed Godwits' (Piersma & Gill 1998). Before the nonstop crossing the godwit shrinks its gut, liver, kidneys, and gizzard - organs useless in the air - and reabsorbs the tissue, while fat swells to about 55% of body mass (among the highest fat loads ever recorded in a bird) and the flight muscles and heart enlarge. The record juvenile, tagged B6, flew roughly 13,560 km from Alaska to Tasmania. Sources: Piersma & Gill 1998, 'Guts Don't Fly'; Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 2021 physiomorphic review (fevo.2021.685764); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar-tailed_godwit.

question: A salmon roams for two years across thousands of kilometers of the open Gulf of Alaska, far from any trace of its home river, and still returns to the right river. The leading explanation, still debated, is that as a young smolt it memorized one feature of the spot where its river reaches the sea. Which feature?
answer: The magnetic field's strength and tilt at its river mouth
choices: The magnetic field's strength and tilt at its river mouth
The star patterns above the coast on the night it swam out
The temperature and saltiness of the water at the river mouth
The arc the sun traces across the sky at that latitude
context: Homing looks like a two-stage act: a magnetic map for the open ocean, then smell for the final stream. As smolts, salmon appear to imprint on the geomagnetic 'signature' - field intensity and inclination angle - at their river mouth, then years later seek that same value across the featureless sea. The landmark evidence is Putman et al. 2013 (Current Biology), which mined a 56-year Fraser River sockeye fishery record: as Earth's field slowly drifted, the fish shifted which side of Vancouver Island they used, and the more a passage's field diverged from the river-mouth value, the fewer fish chose it. The magnetic-map role remains an active scientific debate. Source: Putman et al. 2013, 'Evidence for Geomagnetic Imprinting as a Homing Mechanism in Pacific Salmon,' cell.com/current-biology; follow-up PMC4233730.

question: A goldfish drifts in its tank with a faint dotted line along each flank, from behind the gills to the tail. It could pass for a painted stripe, but the dots are tiny pores in the skin, opening onto a sense organ called the lateral line. What does that line let the fish do?
answer: Feel the water moving against its body
choices: Feel the water moving against its body
Taste chemicals dissolved in the water
Glow faintly to signal other fish
Filter oxygen straight from the current
context: That line is the lateral line — a row of sense organs, not a stripe of pigment. It gives a fish a kind of touch that works at a distance, feeling currents and ripples push against its skin. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lateral line' (faint lines of pores running along each side; pored scales visible on a goldfish).

question: A fish noses through muddy pond water where its eyes are no use, yet it still senses a wall, a hidden hunter or a passing neighbor. Its lateral line, the row of tiny pores along each side, answers to some movements far better than others. Which kind is it tuned to feel?
answer: Slow, large ripples in the water
choices: Slow, large ripples in the water
Fast, tiny high-pitched vibrations
Sudden sharp jolts like a slammed door
A steady one-way current, nothing else
context: The lateral line answers to slow, large water movements — currents, ripples, and the push of an object gliding by (below about 100 cycles per second). Faster pressure wiggles get picked up by the ear instead. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lateral line' (detects frequencies below 100 Hz; determines direction and rate of water movement).

question: A current slides past a fish and pushes on thousands of tiny sensors along its lateral line. Each one, a neuromast, holds a tuft of hair-like bristles in a soft blob of clear jelly, and the push bends the hairs sideways. What happens next, turning that moving water into a feeling the brain can read?
answer: The bent hairs fire a nerve signal
choices: The bent hairs fire a nerve signal
The jelly changes color to warn the brain
The scales lift to catch more current
A muscle squeezes water back out
context: Flowing water shoves the jelly blob (the cupula), the jelly bends the hair bundles, and the bent hairs fire nerve signals — that's how moving water becomes a sensation. Source: scienceinsights.org and Wikipedia, 'Lateral line' (neuromast = hair cells capped by a gelatinous cupula).

question: Scientists blinded a predatory fish and it still struck its prey dead-on in the dark. Then they switched off its lateral line with cobalt ions — and the same blind hunter suddenly couldn't find a thing. What had the predator really been 'seeing' all along?
answer: The water the prey disturbed
choices: The water the prey disturbed
The prey's faint body heat
A scent cloud trailing the prey
The prey's shadow on the bottom
context: Blinded predators hunted fine, but not once cobalt ions shut down the lateral line — proof they were tracking the water their prey stirred up, not any image of it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lateral line' (blinded predatory fishes remain able to hunt, but not when lateral line function is inhibited by cobalt ions).

question: Tony Pitcher and Brian Partridge blindfolded a school of saithe, and the fish still held their places, turning as one. Only when the researchers also cut the lateral line nerve did the school fall apart. How does the school hold together in the dark?
answer: Each fish feels its neighbors' pressure waves
choices: Each fish feels its neighbors' pressure waves
One elder fish calls the turns with sound
They follow a scent the leader releases
They lock onto the seabed's magnetic field
context: Every fish feels the pressure waves its neighbors push against its flank and matches them — vision alone or the lateral line alone is enough, but knocking out both breaks the school. Source: Partridge & Pitcher 1980; journals.biologists.com/jeb (blinded saithe still school; both senses must be ablated for schooling to cease).

question: The blind Mexican cave fish, Astyanax mexicanus, spends its whole life in lightless caves — yet it swims straight toward a tiny food-vibration in total darkness. Its river-dwelling cousins can't. What did evolution give the cave fish to pull that off?
answer: Neuromasts crowding its empty eye sockets
choices: Neuromasts crowding its empty eye sockets
A second lateral line down its belly
Neuromasts that fire only in the dark
A ring of stiff whiskers on its snout
context: Living in the dark, the cave fish evolved more and larger neuromasts — even in the empty sockets where its useless eyes shrank away — and homes in on faint vibrations (peak sensitivity around 35 cycles per second), a behavior called vibration attraction. Source: Yoshizawa et al., Current Biology 2010.

question: A goldfish feels a ripple along its lateral line, and a girl hears a bell, with the same kind of sensor: a tiny hair cell. Evolution sealed that sensor inside the head and built from it one organ in every backboned animal, from fish and frogs to birds and people. What did it build?
answer: The inner ear
choices: The inner ear
The eye's lens
The taste buds
The sense of smell
context: That same hair-cell sensor, moved inside the head, became the inner ear of every vertebrate — so both your hearing AND your balance descend from a fish's lateral line. Scientists even group the two systems together as the 'octavolateralis' system. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lateral line'; Springer, 'Functional Evolution of Lateral Line and Inner Ear Sensory Systems' (homologous hair cells).

question: A ray glides over the sand and feels the faint electric field of prey buried beneath it, using pits called the ampullae of Lorenzini. They grow from the very tissue in the embryo that forms the lateral line, its electric twin. Biologists tracing that electric sense through fish history found a puzzle. What does the fossil-and-gene trail show?
answer: It was lost in the bony-fish line, then re-evolved more than once
choices: It was lost in the bony-fish line, then re-evolved more than once
It has run unbroken from the earliest jawed fishes to today
It arose late and stayed unique to sharks and their kin
It passed into bony fish from one shared ancestor, just once
context: Both senses belong to one embryonic system, the octavolateralis system, and both grow from the same lateral-line placodes (thickenings of embryonic skin). Ancestral jawed vertebrates had both the mechanical line and the electric one. The electric sense was then lost in the lineage leading to the neopterygian bony fish -- gars, bowfin, and the teleosts -- and in frogs, and then independently re-evolved at least twice within teleosts, most likely by re-tuning ordinary neuromast hair cells into electroreceptors. So electroreception is an old lateral-line trick that has been dropped and reinvented across fish history -- a genuine, still-debated pattern of repeated loss and convergent regain. Source: Wikipedia 'Lateral line' and 'Ampullae of Lorenzini'; Baker, Modrell & Gillis, 'The evolution and development of vertebrate lateral line electroreceptors', J. Exp. Biol. (PMC4988487); eLife 2016, 'Insights into electrosensory organ development... from a lateral line-enriched transcriptome' (elifesciences.org/articles/24197).

question: Scientists at Queensland trained mantis shrimp to pick a colored light for a food reward. Then they slid two colors closer and closer until the shrimp could not tell them apart. A trained human can still tell colors just 1 to 5 nanometers apart. How close could the mantis shrimp still tell them apart?
answer: Down to about 12 to 25 nanometers apart
choices: Down to about 1 to 2 nanometers apart
Down to about 4 to 6 nanometers apart
Down to about 12 to 25 nanometers apart
Down to less than 1 nanometer apart
context: The shrimp fell apart when two colors sat only about 12 to 25 nanometers apart; a human can split colors as close as 1 to 5 nanometers. The animal with twelve color channels is actually worse at telling similar hues apart than a human with three — the opposite of the legend. Source: Thoen, How, Chiou & Marshall 2014, Science 343:411; sci-news.com/biology/science-color-vision-mantis-shrimp-01719.html.

question: A mantis shrimp peering from its reef burrow sorts ultraviolet light, invisible to people, with six kinds of UV receptor built from only two UV pigments. Its eye makes up the difference by stacking colored filters ahead of the pigments, each trimming a slice off the band. What are those filters made of?
answer: The same sunscreen molecules that other reef animals grow to guard their bodies from the sun
choices: The same sunscreen molecules that other reef animals grow to guard their bodies from the sun
The red carotenoid pigments that flamingos and salmon pull straight out of their daily food
The clear crystal proteins that shape the transparent lens set at the very front of the eye
The dark melanin grains that line the back of a human retina and soak up the stray glare
context: The mantis shrimp builds six distinct ultraviolet receptor classes from only two UV visual pigments by placing four different colored filters in front of them. Those filters are made of mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs) — the same 'biological sunscreen' compounds many reef animals use to shield their tissues from UV damage — here repurposed to carve the ultraviolet band into six channels instead of blocking it out. Bok, Porter, Place & Cronin, 'Biological Sunscreens Tune Polychromatic Ultraviolet Vision in Mantis Shrimp,' Current Biology 24 (2014).

question: Jonathan, a Seychelles giant tortoise, grazes slowly across the governor's lawn on Saint Helena, a remote island in the South Atlantic. He is the oldest known living animal on land anywhere on Earth. Roughly how old is Jonathan?
answer: Over 190 years
choices: Over 190 years
About 40 years
Over 500 years
About 90 years
context: Jonathan, a Seychelles giant tortoise on Saint Helena, is over 190 years old — the oldest known living land animal, hatched around 1832, before the camera or the telephone was invented. Source: Wikipedia; Smithsonian (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_(tortoise)).

question: A slow, sluggish Greenland shark cruises the freezing black water beneath the Arctic sea ice. No animal with a backbone is proven to outlive it: scientists estimate the biggest live around 250 to 400 years, and possibly longer. What does that make true of a big Greenland shark swimming today?
answer: It may have been born in the 1600s
choices: It may have been born in the 1600s
It stops growing after age fifty
It must return to shore to breed
It glows to lure deep-sea prey
context: Age estimates run roughly 250–400+ years; the two largest studied sharks were estimated at about 335 and 392 years — so one alive today may have been born before the United States existed. Source: ScienceDaily, on Nielsen et al. 2016 (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/08/160811143218.htm).

question: Marine biologists hauled a little ocean quahog clam up from the seabed off Iceland in 2006. It turned out to have been living since around 1499, when the Ming dynasty ruled China, so they nicknamed it Ming. At about 507 years old, what record did Ming set?
answer: Oldest single animal ever aged precisely
choices: Oldest single animal ever aged precisely
Largest clam ever pulled from the sea
Deepest-dwelling shellfish ever found
First clam ever raised in a laboratory
context: Ming lived about 507 years, the oldest individual animal ever found whose age could be precisely worked out, by counting the yearly growth lines in its shell. It was dredged up off Iceland in 2006 and died when researchers, not yet knowing its age, froze it. (Deep-sea glass sponges have been estimated at over 10,000 years, but those ages are rough.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_(clam); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest-living_organisms

question: Ming, the clam dredged up off Iceland, had no bones, no teeth and no skeleton to give away its age. Yet marine biologists worked out that the little ocean quahog was about 507 years old by studying one part of its body under a microscope. What did they count?
answer: Growth rings layered in its shell
choices: Growth rings layered in its shell
Chemicals dissolved in its blood
The length of its muscular foot
Barnacles clustered on its outside
context: Ming's age was counted from growth rings in its shell, just like counting rings in a tree trunk. Source: National Museum Wales; Wikipedia (https://museum.wales/blog/2122/Meet-Ming-the-clam---the-oldest-animal-in-the-world/).

question: A Greenland shark prowls the icy depths of the North Atlantic, growing so slowly that it stays a youngster for an enormously long time before it can breed. At about what age does it first become an adult able to have young?
answer: Around 150 years old
choices: Around 150 years old
Around 15 years old
Around 40 years old
Around 300 years old
context: A Greenland shark doesn't become an adult able to reproduce until it is at least about 150 years old — older than most countries. Source: ScienceDaily, on Nielsen et al. 2016 (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/08/160811143218.htm).

question: Alaskan hunters landed a living bowhead whale in 2007, one of the huge, thick-blubbered whales of the Arctic ice, and found a rusty fragment of an old exploding harpoon lodged in its shoulder. Researchers traced the weapon to New Bedford, Massachusetts, where it was made around 1879. What did the fragment prove about the whale?
answer: The whale had swum for over 100 years
choices: The whale had swum for over 100 years
The whale had been raised in captivity
The harpoon had been fired that season
The whale was younger than first believed
context: The New Bedford harpoon fragment, made around 1879–80, meant that whale had been swimming for well over 100 years — the kind of embedded old harpoon tip that first revealed how long bowheads live. Source: Forbes (https://www.forbes.com/sites/scotttravers/2024/09/19/meet-the-longest-living-mammal-hint-its-been-found-alive-with-an-1880s-era-harpoon-in-its-side/).

question: An enormous rockfish came up from deep Alaskan water in 2013, and judging by its size alone, biologists at first guessed it might be about 200 years old, close to a record for its kind. Then they split open the tiny ear stones in its skull and counted the growth rings under a microscope. How old was the fish really?
answer: Only 64 years
choices: Only 64 years
Exactly 200 years
Over 400 years
Just 12 years
context: Otolith testing showed the record rockfish was really only 64 — a reminder that scientists must measure age carefully, not just eyeball a big animal. Source: The Spokesman-Review (https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2013/jul/06/record-rockfish-was-64-years-old-not-200-tests-sho/).

question: Off Hawaii, scientists radiocarbon-dated a slow-growing animal of the deep seafloor at about 4,265 years old, eight times the age of Ming, the 507-year-old clam. It was already alive when Egypt's pyramids were new. What kind of animal was it?
answer: A deep-sea black coral
choices: A deep-sea black coral
A deep-sea tube worm
A deep-sea sea anemone
A deep-sea feather star
context: A single colony of the deep-sea black coral Leiopathes glaberrima, collected off Hawaii, was radiocarbon-dated along its growth axis to about 4,265 years old, roughly eight times the age of Ming the clam and more than ten times a Greenland shark's. A black coral is not one creature but a colony of tiny cnidarian polyps that slowly build a shared protein skeleton. A companion gold coral (Gerardia) from the same waters came in near 2,700 years. Only some deep-sea glass sponges, estimated at more than 10,000 years, are thought to be older. Source: Roark, Guilderson, Dunbar, Fallon & Mucciarone (2009), 'Extreme longevity in proteinaceous deep-sea corals,' PNAS; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest-living_organisms

question: A bowhead whale's huge body holds more than a thousand times the cells of a person's. With that many cells dividing, cancer ought to be almost certain, yet bowheads almost never get it. When scientists read the whale's genome, what did they find protecting it?
answer: A knack for repairing its own DNA
choices: A knack for repairing its own DNA
A body kept too cold for tumors
Blood that hunts down cancer cells
An immune system that never sleeps
context: A bowhead's huge, long-lived body should be riddled with cancer (the puzzle biologists call Peto's paradox), yet the whales almost never get it despite carrying over a thousand times as many cells as a human. When the bowhead genome was sequenced in 2015, researchers found distinctive variants in DNA-repair and cell-cycle genes, notably ERCC1 (which helps fix damaged DNA) and PCNA (a hub of DNA replication and repair). Better damage repair is thought to head off the cancers that should overwhelm so many cells. Source: Keane, de Magalhaes et al. (2015), 'Insights into the Evolution of Longevity from the Bowhead Whale Genome,' Cell Reports; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhead_whale

question: A platypus finds hidden prey on muddy river bottoms with about 40,000 tiny sensors packed into its bill. Its egg-laying cousin the echidna, nosing through leaf litter, carries the same kind of sensor in the tip of its beak, but the two are not equipped alike. Roughly how many does the echidna have?
answer: Only about 400 to 2,000
choices: Only about 400 to 2,000
Roughly 30,000
About 15,000
Around 8,000
context: A baby echidna is called a puggle, and the echidna does have electroreceptors in its beak, but only 400 to 2,000 of them compared with the platypus's 40,000. Source: Discover Wildlife (discoverwildlife.com echidna).

question: An echidna mother keeps her one leathery egg in a temporary pouch on her belly. The tiny, hairless baby that hatches rides there until it grows something that forces her to move it out and dig it a burrow instead. What makes her evict it?
answer: It grows spines and becomes too prickly to carry
choices: It grows spines and becomes too prickly to carry
It grows too heavy for her to walk
It starts trying to eat her own food
It grows a long tail that won't fit
context: Once the puggle develops spines and becomes too prickly, the mother removes it from her pouch and builds a burrow for it, where it keeps suckling for about six months. Source: Australian Museum, Short-beaked Echidna.

question: Attenborough's long-beaked echidna, an egg-laying mammal, had gone 62 years without a single record by science when a team set camera traps deep in the Cyclops Mountains in 2023. When they checked the footage, what had the cameras caught?
answer: The living animal itself, snuffling past on camera
choices: The living animal itself, snuffling past on camera
Only a set of fresh claw-marks in the mud
A distant call recorded but never seen
A single blurry shape too dark to identify
context: Attenborough's long-beaked echidna (Zaglossus attenboroughi) was rediscovered alive in 2023 after 62 years unrecorded by science, filmed on camera traps in the Cyclops Mountains. Source: npj Biodiversity (nature.com/articles/s44185-025-00086-6); Sci.News.

question: A wombat marks its ground by placing its droppings on top of rocks and logs. They sit there without rolling away, because they come out as neat, flat-faced cubes, a shape unknown in the dung of any other animal. How does a wombat shape its droppings into cubes?
answer: Its intestine wall alternates stiff and stretchy zones that mould them.
choices: Its intestine wall alternates stiff and stretchy zones that mould them.
The dry outback heat bakes each soft pellet until it cracks into blocks.
It tamps each one flat against a rock with its broad, stumpy tail.
A ring of bony plates just inside its rear stamps square corners in.
context: When researchers inflated preserved wombat intestines, they found the wall wasn't uniform — it had alternating stiff and stretchy regions. In the final roughly 8% of the intestine, those uneven contractions slowly mould the drying droppings into flat-faced cubes. The wombat then stacks the cubes to scent-mark its territory, and because they're square they resist rolling off rocks. The work won the 2019 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics. Source: Yang, Lee, Chan, Martin, Edwards, Carver & Hu — 2019 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics (improbable.com/2019/09/12); Soft Matter / APS study on wombat cube feces; Georgia Tech Quantitative Biosciences (qbios.gatech.edu).

question: Paleontologists at an opal field near Lightning Ridge, in New South Wales, dig out fossils about 100 million years old, some of the bones turned to solid opal. Only the platypus and a few echidnas survive among the egg-laying mammals today. What did that one site hold?
answer: At least six egg-laying mammal species living there side by side.
choices: At least six egg-laying mammal species living there side by side.
Two platypus lineages already split between river and seashore.
Three egg-laying species that each dwarfed any alive today.
A dozen individuals of one burrowing species denning together.
context: The site is Lightning Ridge in New South Wales, famous for opal — and here the monotreme bones themselves survive as gem opal, so rare they're described as roughly one monotreme fragment per million opal pieces. Dated to the Cenomanian, about 100 million years ago, the deposit held at least six egg-laying-mammal species at once, more monotreme diversity in one place than exists on the whole planet today. The 2024 star is a creature nicknamed the 'echidnapus,' Opalios splendens, whose skull blends platypus and echidna features. Source: Flannery, Helgen, McCurry et al. 2024, Alcheringa: An Australasian Journal of Palaeontology (sci.news/paleontology/lightning-ridge-monotremes-12964.html; ScienceDaily 2024-05-27); Opalios, Wikipedia.

question: A scallop, a shellfish kin to clams and oysters, rests on the sandy seabed with its fan-ridged shells cracked open to filter the water. Along the frilly edge between the two halves glints a row of tiny blue dots. What are they?
answer: Up to 200 tiny eyes
choices: Up to 200 tiny eyes
Filter-feeding gills
Rows of stinging cells
Grip pads for the sand
context: A scallop can have up to 200 tiny blue eyes lining the edge of its mantle, peering out between the two halves of its shell. Source: C&EN, 'Reflective guanine crystals lend sight to scallops' (cen.acs.org/articles/95/i48); Palmer et al., Science 2017.

question: A scallop sits on the seabed with its shell agape, watching the water through tiny blue eyes along its rim. A human eye focuses with a curved lens at the front, but a scallop's eye has no such lens. How does it focus the light?
answer: It bounces light off a curved mirror
choices: It bounces light off a curved mirror
It funnels light down a narrow tube
It splits light through a crystal prism
It soaks up light with a dark pit
context: Instead of a lens, each scallop eye focuses light using a curved mirror built from tiles of guanine crystal behind the retina. Source: Palmer et al., 'The image-forming mirror in the eye of the scallop', Science 2017 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aam9506).

question: Behind the retina of each tiny scallop eye lie thousands of guanine crystals, stacked 20 to 30 layers deep. For the eye's picture to stay sharp rather than blurred, every one of those crystals must have one particular shape. What shape are they?
answer: Perfectly square, flat plates
choices: Perfectly square, flat plates
Round like tiny marbles
Long and needle-like
Six-sided like honeycomb
context: The scallop's mirror is made of 20-30 stacked layers of tiny square guanine plates, fitted edge-to-edge like bathroom tiles so the reflected image stays sharp. Source: C&EN (cen.acs.org/articles/95/i48); Science News, 'Scallops' amazing eyes use millions of tiny, square crystals to see'.

question: Anableps, the four-eyed fish, swims the rivers and shallow lagoons of Central America, yet it has only two eyes. It hangs at the surface, the top of the water slicing across the middle of each eye and cutting it into an upper half and a lower half. Why does that matter to the fish?
answer: Each eye's top half sees in air while its bottom half sees underwater
choices: Each eye's top half sees in air while its bottom half sees underwater
Each eye stores sunlight above and releases the glow below
The line marks where the eye must be kept wet to survive
The upper half is blind and only the lower half truly sees
context: The four-eyed fish (Anableps) has only two eyes, but each eye is split by a band of tissue into an upper half that sees in air and a lower half that sees in water at the same time. Source: Four-eyed fish, Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-eyed_fish); California Academy of Sciences.

question: Inside each eye of the four-eyed fish Anableps sit two pupils and two retinas, yet only one lens. That one lens must form sharp pictures from the air and from the water at once, and the two call for very different focusing. How does the single lens cope?
answer: The lens is egg-shaped, so its two directions bend light differently
choices: The lens is egg-shaped, so its two directions bend light differently
The lens flips rapidly between two focal settings
A second clear lens slides in only underwater
The lens is filled with two liquids of different density
context: Each Anableps eye has two pupils but only one lens, and that single egg-shaped lens bends light from both air and water correctly onto its two retinas. Source: Four-eyed fish, Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-eyed_fish).

question: A team from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute filmed the tube-shaped eyes of a live barreleye in 2008, inside the clear dome on the deep-sea fish's head. For 70 years scientists had thought those eyes were fixed in place. What did the film show them doing?
answer: They swivelled forward to aim at food
choices: They swivelled forward to aim at food
They blinked shut and reopened
They glowed brighter to signal
They retracted deeper into the skull
context: The barreleye's tubular green eyes rotate up to watch for prey overhead, then swivel forward to aim at food as it eats; MBARI first filmed this in 2008 after decades of assuming the eyes were fixed. Source: MBARI, Robison & Reisenbichler 2008; ScienceDaily 2009.

question: The brownsnout spookfish hunts thousands of feet down in the deep sea, where sunlight has almost run out. Each of its eyes is split into two halves. One half focuses light with an ordinary curved lens, like ours. How does the other half focus its image?
answer: With a curved mirror of stacked crystals
choices: With a curved mirror of stacked crystals
With an extra-thick bulging lens
By glowing to light up its own prey
With a heat-sensing pit instead of light
context: The brownsnout spookfish was the first vertebrate found to focus an image with a mirror of stacked guanine crystals (Wagner et al. 2009), doing so in one half of its divided eye while the other half still uses a lens. In 2014 Partridge and colleagues found a mirror-focusing eye in a second deep-sea fish, the glasshead barreleye Rhynchohyalus. Source: University of Bristol news 2009 (bristol.ac.uk/news/2009/6086.html); Wagner et al., Current Biology 2009; Partridge et al. 2014, Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

question: The ogre-faced spider hunts by night in warm forests, staring out of two enormous eyes, some 2,000 times as sensitive to light as a human's. To squeeze every last photon from the dark, it does something drastic to those eyes on a strict daily cycle. What does it do?
answer: It grows a fresh light-catching membrane each night and destroys it by dawn
choices: It grows a fresh light-catching membrane each night and destroys it by dawn
It seals the lenses shut through the bright daylight hours
It coats the lenses in reflective silk before hunting
It regrows entirely new lenses after every kill
context: The ogre-faced spider's eyes are so light-hungry that it builds a fresh light-sensitive membrane inside them every night and chemically destroys it again at dawn. A legend among spiders. Source: Smithsonian Magazine; Gil Wizen, 'Little Transformers: Deinopis'; biologyinsights.com.

question: A bluefin tuna, a mako shark and a bottlenose dolphin all chase prey fast through the open ocean, yet one is a bony fish, one a cartilage fish and one an air-breathing mammal. Evolution built them separately, from different ancestors, and still they ended up with almost the same body shape. What shape is it?
answer: A stiff, torpedo-shaped body that knifes through the water
choices: A stiff, torpedo-shaped body that knifes through the water
A flat, wide body that flaps through the water like wings
A long, eel-like body that wriggles head to tail
A tall, thin body pressed flat from side to side
context: This is the thunniform (tuna-like) body plan: a stiff, streamlined torso, a narrow tail-base, and a crescent tail. Fast open-ocean swimmers keep re-inventing it. Source: Nature Scientific Reports, 'Skeletal convergence in thunniform sharks, ichthyosaurs, whales, and tunas' (2023), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-41812-z

question: A tuna and a dolphin flash past a diver in the open ocean, two sleek swimmers built alike for speed, though the tuna is a fish and the dolphin a mammal. One clue in the way each one swims marks the dolphin as a mammal. What is the clue?
answer: Its tail beats up and down, not side to side
choices: Its tail beats up and down, not side to side
Its tail beats side to side, not up and down
It rows itself along with its front flippers
It steers by twisting its tall back fin
context: A fish's or shark's tail sweeps side to side; a dolphin's or whale's tail beats up and down, so the direction of the tail-beat gives a mammal away at a glance. Source: Whale and Dolphin Conservation, 'Why do whale and dolphin tails go up and down?', https://uk.whales.org/whales-dolphins/why-do-whale-and-dolphin-tails-go-up-and-down/

question: A bluefin tuna cruises the open ocean for days without stopping, its silvery body held almost stiff, with barely a wiggle from head to shoulder. Yet nearly all the power that drives it forward comes from one small part of its body. Where does nearly all of its swimming motion happen?
answer: At the narrow tail-base and the crescent tail
choices: At the narrow tail-base and the crescent tail
Along its whole body, rippling head to tail
In its wide, fanned-out pectoral fins
In its puffed-out gill covers on each side
context: A tuna's body barely bends when it swims. The stiff front knifes through the water while almost all the movement is isolated to the very tip. Source: American Scientist, 'How Tunas and Lamnid Sharks Swim: An Evolutionary Convergence', https://www.americanscientist.org/article/how-tunas-and-lamnid-sharks-swim-an-evolutionary-convergence

question: A bluefin tuna sprints after its prey at faster than 40 miles an hour. As it speeds up, the tall fin on its back and the wide fins on its sides seem to vanish, until its outline looks as smooth as a torpedo. What has become of those fins?
answer: They folded flat into grooves and slots in its body
choices: They folded flat into grooves and slots in its body
They turned as clear as glass so prey could not see them
They beat so fast that they blurred out of sight
They turned silver to blend with the shine of its skin
context: The first dorsal fin drops flush into a groove along the back and the pectoral fins tuck into slots on the sides, cutting drag. The tuna pops the fins back up for tight turns. Source: ResearchGate, 'Slot for storage of dorsal fin in a Pacific bluefin tuna (Thunnus orientalis)', https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Slot-for-storage-of-dorsal-fin-in-a-Pacific-bluefin-tuna_fig1_321700630; AskNature, 'Fins Provide Streamlined Shape', https://asknature.org/strategy/fins-provide-streamlined-shape/

question: A tuna sweeps a stiff, thin crescent of a tail, held out like a scythe blade behind a narrow ankle of muscle, nothing like a goldfish's flat paddle. Seen in cross-section, that crescent has a shape that explains why so little of the tuna's effort is wasted in swirl and drag. What shape is it?
answer: A curved airplane wing, an airfoil
choices: A curved airplane wing, an airfoil
A flat, thin blade like a butter knife
A round tube like a drinking straw
A jagged saw-edge for cutting water
context: The tuna's crescent tail is taller, narrower, and stiffer than an ordinary fish tail. Shaped like an airfoil, it makes thrust the same way a wing makes lift, turning each tail-beat into forward push instead of wasted motion. Source: American Scientist, 'How Tunas and Lamnid Sharks Swim'; Nature/PMC thunniform convergence review, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10550938/

question: A bluefin tuna races across the open ocean after schools of smaller fish, its deep red swimming muscle running far warmer than the sea around it, though most fish are as cold as the water they swim in. What does that warm muscle do for the tuna?
answer: It fires faster and harder, driving the tuna's blazing speed
choices: It fires faster and harder, driving the tuna's blazing speed
It makes the muscle glow to attract mates in the dark
It lets the tuna survive on almost no oxygen
It replaces the swim bladder and keeps the tuna afloat
context: A big Pacific bluefin tuna holds its red swimming muscle about 11 C (roughly 20 F) hotter than the water. Warm muscles fire faster and harder, part of why tuna are so fast. It only warms certain regions, not the whole body, so it is called 'regional endothermy,' not fully warm-blooded. Source: Springer, 'Ontogeny of regional endothermy in Pacific bluefin tuna (Thunnus orientalis)', https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00227-020-03753-3

question: Biologists comparing the skeletons of bluefin tuna, mako sharks, ichthyosaurs and dolphins, four groups with the same sleek outline and crescent tail, find that the likeness goes deeper than skin: all four groups evolved the same hidden engineering inside their bodies. What did they build?
answer: A thick, reinforced backbone and a stiffened tail-stem
choices: A thick, reinforced backbone and a stiffened tail-stem
A see-through skull to let in more light
Hollow, air-filled bones like a bird's
A second spine running along the belly
context: Shared skeletons show the convergence is real, not skin-deep: an unusually thick, reinforced backbone and a stiffened tail-stem are the internal engineering needed to concentrate the swimming motion at the very back of the body. (The vertebral analysis behind this is rated medium-confidence in the source.) Source: Nature Scientific Reports (2023), vertebral analysis, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-41812-z

question: A tuna's deep red swimming muscle lies buried beside its backbone in the middle of its body, and unlike the swimming muscle of most fish, it leaves the flank beside it unbent. Yet it powers the tail. How does that muscle move a tail it does not even touch?
answer: It hauls on long tendons that reach all the way back to the tail
choices: It hauls on long tendons that reach all the way back to the tail
It squeezes fluid through a channel that stiffens the whole tail-stem
It fires nerve signals to a second muscle packed inside the tail
It winds up the backbone like a spring that recoils at the tail
context: A tuna's red aerobic muscle is decoupled from the body wall beside it. Sitting deep against the backbone, it doesn't bend the nearby flank; instead it pulls on long tendons -- the posterior oblique and great lateral tendons -- that thread backward through the white muscle to the tail-base, driving the tail remotely. Because of this, the muscle's shortening and the body's local bending are out of phase, which is the mechanical secret behind the stiff-torso, all-the-motion-at-the-tail thunniform style. Source: Cromie Lear, Millard, Gleiss, Dale, Block et al., 'Biomechanical Analysis of the Slow-Twitch (Red) Muscle Force Transmission Pathways in Tunas,' Physiological & Biochemical Zoology 93(3):185-198, 2020 -- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32196408/

question: Lindgren and colleagues examined an ichthyosaur fossil from the Early Jurassic in 2018, a Stenopterygius so finely preserved that its skin was still in place. Under that skin they found what they took as direct evidence that this sea reptile ran warm, not cold like a lizard. What did they find?
answer: A thick, smooth layer of blubber packed under the skin
choices: A thick, smooth layer of blubber packed under the skin
A dense net of blood vessels coiled around the muscle
A honeycomb of tiny air pockets sealed below the skin
A pad of packed brown fat that burns to make heat
context: Lindgren et al. (2018, Nature) chemically analyzed a superbly preserved Stenopterygius and found flexible skin over a layer of blubber, which they read as the first direct evidence that an ichthyosaur was warm-blooded (homeothermic), the same insulating solution whales and dolphins would arrive at much later; warm-bloodedness itself stays an inference from that blubber. Preserved melanophores even revealed countershading: a dark back and pale belly, the classic open-ocean camouflage of living dolphins and sharks. Source: Lindgren et al., 'Soft-tissue evidence for homeothermy and crypsis in a Jurassic ichthyosaur,' Nature 564:359-365, 2018 (https://news.ncsu.edu/2018/12/ichthyosaur-blubber/).

question: On a cold morning a small lizard climbs onto a sunny rock and flattens itself against the warm stone. When it grows too hot it slips into the shade, then creeps back into the sun. Where does the warmth its body runs on come from?
answer: From the sun and hot rock outside its body
