choices: From the sun and hot rock outside its body
From burning the food in its stomach
From shivering its leg muscles
From a warm nest it built overnight
context: This shuttling between sun and shade is called behavioral thermoregulation: a cold-blooded animal takes its heat from the world around it rather than making its own, so it steers its body toward warmth or shade like moving between rooms. Source: https://southernxreptiles.com/how-do-lizards-regulate-body-temperature/

question: A pet mouse and a pet lizard sit in the same cool room, both doing nothing at all. The mouse must keep finding food, squeaking and scrabbling in its cage, while the lizard can sit still and eat nothing for weeks. What is the mouse paying for that the lizard is not?
answer: Keeping its inner furnace lit at a steady temperature
choices: Keeping its inner furnace lit at a steady temperature
Growing a new coat of winter fur
Storing fat for a coming hibernation
Rebuilding muscle worn out by shivering
context: Warm-blooded is the more expensive engine: size for size a mammal or bird must eat far more than a same-sized reptile because so much of its food is burned just to keep its temperature steady. That is exactly why a lizard can rest quietly for weeks while a mouse hunts for food almost constantly. Source: https://www.open.edu/openlearn/nature-environment/natural-history/studying-mammals-the-insect-hunters/content-section-5.2

question: A ball python hunts small rodents by night in the grasslands of West Africa, and as a cold-blooded snake it never spends food on keeping itself warm. That lets it go a remarkably long time between meals without wasting away. For a healthy adult ball python, how long can a fast last?
answer: At least six months without a single meal
choices: At least six months without a single meal
About two weeks before it weakens
Three or four days at most
Right through a whole decade
context: A healthy adult ball python can survive at least six months without eating, and the longest fast ever recorded in any snake was 21 months, also by a ball python. A big African rock python can be kept going for up to two years on one very large kill. Not paying to heat yourself is what makes such long fasting possible. Source: https://www.terrariumquest.com/ball-python/how-long-without-eating/

question: An Etruscan shrew, the smallest mammal on Earth by weight and lighter than a paperclip, hunts insects and worms almost nonstop, day and night. Warm-blooded and tiny, it leaks body heat into the air at an alarming rate. If it stops finding food, how fast can it starve?
answer: In as little as two to three hours
choices: In as little as two to three hours
In about two or three days
In roughly a week
In a month, like most small mammals
context: The Etruscan shrew, the world's smallest mammal by weight, must eat 1.5 to 2 times its own body weight in food every single day, and its heart beats up to about 1,500 times a minute, the fastest of any mammal. That runaway furnace means it can starve in as little as two to three hours. Source: https://smart.columbus.gov/columbus-news/meet-the-worlds-smallest-mammal-the-etruscan-shrew-1764805785 ; https://www.mpg.de/14755962/shrews-metabolism-winter

question: Snow piles up outside a beehive, but inside, thousands of honeybees pack into a tight ball, a winter cluster, and hold its center near 85 degrees Fahrenheit all winter. Insects usually cannot heat themselves the way a mammal can. How do the bees make that warmth?
answer: They contract their flight muscles hard without flapping their wings
choices: They contract their flight muscles hard without flapping their wings
They burn stored honey inside special heating glands
They pant warm air over the cluster in shifts
They press against the sun-warmed hive walls
context: When it turns cold the colony packs into a tight cluster and the bees shiver, contracting their big flight muscles against each other without flapping, generating heat instead of motion. They rotate from the warm center to the chilly edge and back, like huddling penguins, keeping the core near 85°F and rising toward 95°F when the queen starts laying. Source: https://www.betterbee.com/instructions-and-resources/what-your-honey-bees-do-in-the-winter.asp

question: A bluefin tuna swims through cold seawater that should chill its blood at the gills, as it does in other fish. Instead a mesh of vessels, the rete mirabile, runs warm outgoing blood right beside cold incoming blood and hangs on to the muscle's heat. How much warmer than the sea can that keep its swimming muscles?
answer: As much as around 20°C warmer
choices: As much as around 20°C warmer
About 3 to 4°C warmer
Around 50°C warmer
Just under 1°C warmer
context: This is called regional endothermy. The rete mirabile captures the muscle's own heat instead of losing it at the gills, up to 99 percent efficiently, so a bluefin tuna can hold its swimming muscles as much as around 20°C warmer than the water it swims in. Warm muscle is faster, more powerful muscle. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/are-tuna-warm-blooded-the-science-of-regional-endothermy/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rete_mirabile

question: A leatherback, the largest sea turtle alive, swims from the warm tropics to near the Arctic Circle, into seas as cold as 7.5 degrees Celsius, and still stays far warmer than the water around it. It has no inner furnace and it never shivers. What keeps a leatherback that warm?
answer: Its sheer enormous size holding heat in
choices: Its sheer enormous size holding heat in
A thick layer of blubber like a whale's
Warm blood pumped from a special gland
Basking at the surface between dives
context: This trick is called gigantothermy. As one of the largest living reptiles, over 900 kg, the leatherback's huge body, insulating outer tissues, and heat-exchanger flippers let it hold heat that a smaller reptile would lose, giving it the widest temperature range of any reptile. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/344858a0 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2978089/

question: John Grady's team studied how fast giant dinosaurs grew as they matured, and in 2014 argued from those growth rates for a startling verdict about the animals' inner engine. Other researchers quickly disputed the statistics, and the question is still open. What did Grady's team say the giants were?
answer: An in-between engine that could raise its heat but not hold it steady, like a tuna
choices: An in-between engine that could raise its heat but not hold it steady, like a tuna
Fully warm-blooded, running as hot and steady as any living bird
Fully cold-blooded, no warmer than the swamps they waded in
Cold-blooded as hatchlings but turning warm-blooded once grown
context: The 2014 study (Grady et al., Science) argued from growth rates that big dinosaurs were mesothermic, neither warm- nor cold-blooded but able to raise their body heat without holding it at a fixed level, like tuna and the echidna today. Other scientists soon published formal comments challenging the statistics, so the debate is far from closed. This is honestly unsettled science, not a settled fact. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1253143 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26023130/

question: A Burmese python goes months without eating, then swallows one large meal, and its body bursts into a violent stretch of work that lasts until about the tenth day. How much faster than at rest does its metabolism run to power that meal?
answer: Ten to forty-four times its resting rate
choices: Ten to forty-four times its resting rate
About double its resting rate
Roughly a quarter faster
Around a hundred times its resting rate
context: Within days of a big meal a Burmese python's metabolism runs 10 to 44 times faster, and its organs balloon in size, then shrink back to normal once the meal is digested by about the tenth day. The digestive burst is so extreme that sitting still and fasting for months is cheap by comparison, which is the whole cold-blooded bargain. Source: https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/211/24/3767/18007/Digestive-physiology-of-the-Burmese-python-broad

question: Ricardo Araújo's team set out in 2022 to take the temperature of long-dead mammal ancestors, though a fossil skeleton keeps no soft tissue to show its body heat. Working from bone alone, they traced the start of mammal warm blood to the Late Triassic. Which fossil clue let them do it?
answer: The shape of the fluid-filled canals of the inner ear
choices: The shape of the fluid-filled canals of the inner ear
The scroll-like nasal bones that warm each breath drawn in
The dense growth rings banded through the limb bones
The slope of the long leg bones set beneath the hips
context: Warm blood thins the fluid inside the ear's looping semicircular canals — the organ of balance — the way heat loosens honey, so a hot-running animal needs narrower ducts to keep that fluid reading motion sharply. Reading canal shape across the mammal lineage, Ricardo Araújo's team (Nature, 2022) found endothermy appeared abruptly in the Late Triassic, about 233 million years ago — before true mammals arose (~200 Ma) — alongside a sharp 5–9°C jump in body temperature. Exactly when the warm engine first switched on remains an open, active research question. Source: Araújo et al. 2022, Nature, 'Inner ear biomechanics reveals a Late Triassic origin for mammalian endothermy.'

question: A ground squirrel ends its winter hibernation chilled almost to freezing, then floods itself with heat to wake without a single shiver or twitch of muscle. All that warmth wells up from a special tissue, brown fat, whose cells are crammed with mitochondria. How does brown fat make heat with no movement at all?
answer: Its cells let their fuel's energy leak out as heat instead of banking it as usable power
choices: Its cells let their fuel's energy leak out as heat instead of banking it as usable power
Its cells pack in far more mitochondria and drive them to burn their fuel much faster
Its cells release a hormone that speeds every reaction inside the tissue at once
Its cells snap their stored fat apart in a rapid, self-feeding chemical cascade
context: Normally a cell's mitochondria pump protons across a membrane, then let them flow back through a turbine that banks the energy as ATP, the cell's usable fuel. Brown fat carries a protein called UCP1 (thermogenin) that punches an open hole in that membrane, so the protons rush back with no turbine and no ATP — the fuel's energy escapes purely as heat. This 'non-shivering thermogenesis,' switched on by the sympathetic nervous system, lets hibernating mammals (and brown-fat-rich newborns) rewarm without the muscular shivering that a winter honeybee cluster relies on. Source: 'Thermogenin (UCP1)'; Nicholls & Locke on brown adipose tissue.

question: A honeybee scout comes home from a patch of flowers under about 50 meters from the hive, roughly a school hallway away. For far-off flowers she would run her long figure-eight dance on the comb, but for food this close she skips it and does a much simpler routine. What does that near-food dance look like?
answer: Just circling one way, then the other
choices: Just circling one way, then the other
A single sharp jab toward the door
Trembling in place without moving
Climbing straight up and freezing
context: For food closer than about 50 metres a bee does the 'round dance' - simply circling one direction then reversing - instead of the full waggle dance with its angle and duration code. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_dance_(honey_bee)

question: A honeybee scout dances on the dark comb for a long stretch, and the angle of her run points her sisters toward the flowers by where they lie from the sun. But the sun creeps across the sky as she dances, so the flowers keep shifting against it. How does she keep her dance pointing true?
answer: An internal clock slowly shifts her dance angle
choices: An internal clock slowly shifts her dance angle
She stops and re-scouts the flowers
Other bees correct her by touch
She waits for the sun to hold still
context: A bee dancing for a while gradually changes her dance angle to track the moving sun - her internal biological clock corrects for it, so the instruction stays accurate as the sun travels. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/frisch-discovers-bees-communicate-through-body-movements

question: Karl von Frisch, working in the 1940s to crack how honeybees tell each other where flowers are, wanted to follow one single bee through a crowd of thousands that all looked alike. He built a hive with glass walls to watch them work, but he still needed a way to pick out one forager. What simple trick marked her?
answer: Tiny dots of red paint on the thorax
choices: Tiny dots of red paint on the thorax
A numbered tag glued to each wing
Clipping one antenna short
A dab of scent only he could smell
context: Von Frisch marked his foragers with tiny dots of red paint on the thorax and watched them in a glass-walled observation hive by a window, so he could track individual bees through the crowd. He later shared the 1973 Nobel Prize for decoding the dance. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/frisch-discovers-bees-communicate-through-body-movements

question: A scout bee dances her coded run on the upright comb inside a hive so dark that no light gets through the wax. Her sisters still read her directions, though none of them can see her move. How does each follower pick up the message?
answer: She reaches out with her antennae and keeps touching the dancer
choices: She reaches out with her antennae and keeps touching the dancer
She feels the comb shudder under her feet
She tracks the heat rising off the dancer's body
She listens for the rhythm of the dancer's buzz
context: Follower bees crowd the dancer and keep in contact with her body using their antennae, reading the coded run by touch in the hive's total darkness. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/frisch-discovers-bees-communicate-through-body-movements

question: A thorny devil, a small spiky lizard of the Australian desert, never bends its head down to drink. It just stands still on damp sand, and the water climbs up its legs and body to its mouth. Which part of it pulls the water in?
answer: Its skin
choices: Its skin
Its tail
Its eyes
Its front feet
context: Tiny grooves between the thorny devil's spines wick water up to its mouth by capillary action -- so it can drink just by standing in a puddle or damp sand, the water crawling uphill against gravity across its whole body to its jaws. Source: Animal Diversity Web (animaldiversity.org/accounts/Moloch_horridus/); JEB 2016 'Cutaneous water collection by a moisture-harvesting lizard'.

question: A hawk swoops toward a thorny devil, the spiky little lizard of the Australian desert. Instead of running, the lizard tucks its real head down low between its front legs and holds still, and something on its body fools the hunter into striking the wrong target. What is it?
answer: A knobby fake head
choices: A knobby fake head
A cloud of foul spray
A rattling tail
A pair of glowing eyespots
context: The thorny devil has a decoy 'false head' -- a knobby, spiny lump on the back of its neck. When threatened it hides its real head between its front legs and shows the soft decoy, which can heal if it gets bitten. Source: Animal Diversity Web (animaldiversity.org/accounts/Moloch_horridus/); Wikipedia 'Thorny devil'.

question: A thorny devil, an Australian desert lizard covered in hard spikes like a walking pincushion, sits beside a busy trail and flicks its dinner up with a sticky tongue, as fast as one a second. It eats only one kind of tiny creature. What is it?
answer: Ants
choices: Ants
Beetles
Termites
Small spiders
context: The thorny devil eats nothing but ants, taking them one tiny ant at a time off ant trails: feeding averages about three ants a minute, with bursts of up to one a second, and an estimated 750 ants a day. Source: Animal Diversity Web (animaldiversity.org/accounts/Moloch_horridus/); Bush Heritage Australia.

question: A thorny devil crosses open desert in broad daylight while hawks circle overhead. Instead of bolting for cover, it walks in an odd way that probably keeps a bird of prey from locking onto it. How does the thorny devil move across the open?
answer: Rocks and freezes like a wind-blown leaf
choices: Rocks and freezes like a wind-blown leaf
In a fast zig-zag sprint
By burrowing forward under the sand
In long bounding hops
context: The thorny devil walks with a slow, jerky, rocking motion -- freezing and rocking back and forth as it goes -- thought to make it look like a wind-blown leaf and confuse birds of prey watching from above. Source: Animal Diversity Web (animaldiversity.org); Parks Australia / Uluru-Kata Tjuta (uluru.gov.au).

question: A thorny devil wanders the deep desert, where water often lies hidden in barely damp sand rather than in open pools. With no puddle to stand in, it still finds a way to draw that hidden moisture up to its mouth. What does it do?
answer: Shovels moist sand onto its own back
choices: Shovels moist sand onto its own back
Digs a deep well and waits
Presses its belly flat against wet clay
Kicks sand into a rain-catching pit
context: In the desert the thorny devil shovels moist sand up onto its back with its legs, pressing damp grains against its skin so the grooves can wick even more water out of the sand and up to its mouth. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology 219:3473 (2016); asknature.org 'Grooves Gather Water'.

question: A thresher shark cuts through the open sea trailing a huge, curved upper tail behind it like a scythe. No other shark has a tail quite like it. Next to the rest of the thresher's body, how long is that upper tail?
answer: As long as its entire body
choices: As long as its entire body
About the length of one fin
Barely longer than its head
Roughly a third of its length
context: The upper lobe of a thresher shark's tail can equal the length of the shark's entire body, extending in a long sickle-like arc — no other shark has a tail like it. Source: Britannica Kids / Florida Museum of Natural History (thresher shark species profile).

question: Out in the open ocean, a thresher shark goes after a school of sardines, but unlike most sharks it does not chase down a fish and bite it first. It strikes with a body part that almost no other predator hunts with. Which part?
answer: Its tail
choices: Its tail
Its jaws
Its snout
Its fins
context: The thresher is one of the only sharks that hunts with its tail: it whips the giant upper tail lobe overhead like a bullwhip to stun and kill fish, rather than biting them first. Researchers called it 'extraordinarily rare in the animal kingdom to see animals hunt with their tails.' Source: National Geographic, 'Thresher Sharks Hunt With Huge Weaponised Tails' (quoting Simon Oliver).

question: A thresher shark charges straight into a swirling ball of sardines and, just before it reaches them, snaps its wide side fins inward to brake hard. The sudden stop tips its back end upward. What does that lift let it do with its enormous tail?
answer: Fling it overhead like a trebuchet
choices: Fling it overhead like a trebuchet
Curl it beneath its belly for balance
Lock it stiff to glide silently
Fan it sideways to change direction
context: To wind up the strike, the thresher charges a ball of sardines, then snaps its pectoral fins inward to brake hard — lifting its back end and slinging its tail forward 'over its head like a trebuchet.' Source: National Geographic, 'Thresher Sharks Hunt With Huge Weaponised Tails.'

question: Marine biologists off the Philippines filmed thresher sharks hunting a packed shoal of sardines, cracking their whip-like tails overhead. They slowed the film down to see what one overhead tail-slap did to the fish. What did a single slap do?
answer: Killed several fish at once
choices: Killed several fish at once
Herded the shoal into a cave
Startled the fish into scattering
Stripped scales off one fish
context: A single overhead tail-slap can kill several fish at once without a chase: successful strikes averaged 3.6 sardines each, and one strike killed 7 sardines in one blow. Source: Oliver et al. 2013, PLOS ONE 8(7):e67380 (via PMC3707734).

question: Filming a thresher shark as it whipped its huge tail through the sea, researchers caught tiny plumes of bubbles fizzing off the tip on high-speed film, a burst they suspect could even stun small fish. What makes those plumes appear?
answer: The tail-tip moving fast enough to boil the water
choices: The tail-tip moving fast enough to boil the water
A gland releasing ink to hide the strike
Trapped air escaping the shark's gills
Salt crystallizing in the cold water
context: The tail moves so fast it makes the water boil: filmmakers caught bubble plumes (cavitation) at the tail tip — the same shockwave trick the mantis shrimp uses. Oliver: 'I think the shark's causing a shockwave that's strong enough to debilitate small prey.' Source: National Geographic (quoting Simon Oliver); Oliver et al. 2013 PLOS ONE.

question: A scuba diver drifting along a reef off the Philippines comes face to face with a big thresher shark, its long tail sweeping behind it. How does the thresher behave toward a person it meets underwater?
answer: It stays shy, with no unprovoked attack on record
choices: It stays shy, with no unprovoked attack on record
It circles in tight and rams the diver's flank
It lashes its tail toward the diver as a warning
It charges the moment the diver comes near
context: Despite being a fearsome hunter, the thresher is shy with people: the International Shark Attack File lists no unprovoked attack and no fatal attack by a thresher, only a single provoked attack and a handful of incidents with boats, probably from sharks fighting capture. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History / International Shark Attack File; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_thresher

question: A common thresher shark swims the same seas as its two cousins, the bigeye and the pelagic thresher, and all three trail the same scythe-like tail. Yet only the common thresher's swimming muscle runs a few degrees warmer than the sea, while theirs stays at water temperature. What sets it apart inside?
answer: Its red muscle sits deep by the spine, wrapped in heat-trapping vessel nets
choices: Its red muscle sits deep by the spine, wrapped in heat-trapping vessel nets
Its oily liver slowly ferments as it swims, shedding warmth into the core
Its gills reclaim heat from outgoing blood before it meets the open sea
It basks belly-up at the surface between deep dives to soak up the sun
context: This is regional endothermy, the same trick tunas and makos use to power fast, sustained swimming. In the common thresher (Alopias vulpinus) the red swimming muscle is shifted deep and forward, right against the backbone, and sheathed in retia mirabilia: dense 'wonder nets' of blood vessels that work as a counter-current heat exchanger, catching warmth from outgoing blood before it can bleed away at the gills. The muscle averages about 2.3 C above the sea (measured up to 5.4 C above ambient, and as much as 7.6 C above the shark's own white muscle). In the bigeye (A. superciliosus) and pelagic (A. pelagicus) threshers the red muscle has no such nets and stays at water temperature, though the bigeye has a separate vessel net that guards its brain and eyes. Source: Sepulveda & Bernal, 'The vascular morphology and in vivo muscle temperatures of thresher sharks (Alopiidae)' (PubMed 21688299); Bernal & Sepulveda, 'The red muscle morphology of the thresher sharks,' J. Exp. Biol. 208:4255 (2005); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bigeye_thresher

question: Giant sharks the size of a great white prowled the sea off what is now Maryland about 15 million years ago, known today only from teeth that wash out of the Calvert Cliffs. When scientists named one of them in 2018 as a new giant thresher, Alopias palatasi, one feature of its teeth stunned them. What was it?
answer: They were serrated - steak-knife edges, unheard of in a thresher
choices: They were serrated - steak-knife edges, unheard of in a thresher
They were grooved to inject venom, unmatched in any living shark
They curved back into hooks like a deep-sea viperfish's fangs
They fused edge to edge into one long continuous sawing plate
context: Almost every thresher tooth ever found, living species or fossil, has a smooth cutting edge, which is exactly why the serrations on Alopias palatasi (nicknamed the 'serrated giant thresher') were such a shock; its close relative A. grandis lacks them. It reached about great-white size, with teeth topping 4 cm, and lived in the Miocene, roughly 20 to 14 million years ago. Bretton Kent and David Ward named it in 2018 from teeth collected at the Calvert Cliffs of Maryland, a giant shark known entirely from its teeth. A 2025 monograph by Tanaka and Kohno lists it, with A. grandis, in a separate genus, Trigonotodus, whose place among the sharks is debated, so whether these giants were true threshers is now an open question. Source: Kent & Ward 2018, Smithsonian Contributions to Paleobiology 100; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alopias_palatasi; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonotodus; https://shark-references.com/species/view/17582

question: Neil Shubin and his team chipped a strange 375-million-year-old creature out of the rock in 2004. It was half fish and half four-legged animal, with scales and fins at one end and the start of a land body at the other. What nickname did Shubin give it?
answer: Fishapod
choices: Fishapod
Fishosaur
Amphifish
Finwalker
context: Tiktaalik lived in the Late Devonian, roughly 375 million years ago. Because it mixes fish traits and land-animal traits in one body, Shubin coined the nickname 'fishapod', fish plus tetrapod. It sits right on the road from water to land. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik

question: Tiktaalik, a fish well on its way to life on land, swam warm swampy shallows about 375 million years ago and grew 4 to 9 feet long. Yet its body still carried a very fishy holdover from its water-only ancestors. What covered it?
answer: diamond-shaped scales
choices: diamond-shaped scales
feathery down
armored plates
slimy bare skin
context: Tiktaalik reached about 4 to 9 feet (1.25–2.75 meters) long, and its body was still covered in diamond-shaped fish scales — a reminder that this in-between animal was still very much a fish in many ways. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik

question: Prowling a plant-choked Devonian swamp about 375 million years ago, Tiktaalik, a fish partway to life on land, carried a low, flat head unlike any modern fish's rounded snout. Its two eyes sat in a spot strange for a fish. Where were they?
answer: on top of its head
choices: on top of its head
wide-set to the sides
close to the snout tip
on short stalks
context: Tiktaalik's flat, crocodile-like head carried its eyes on TOP — perfect for peering up above the water's surface while the rest of its body stayed hidden below, exactly like a crocodile lurking at the waterline. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik

question: Snapping at prey in a Devonian swamp 375 million years ago, Tiktaalik had none of the bony gill plates that bolt an ordinary fish's skull to its shoulders and lock head and body into one stiff block. In their place it gained something no earlier known fish had. What was it?
answer: a neck
choices: a neck
a hinged jaw joint
a rotating eye socket
a flexible spine
context: By losing the bony gill plates that fasten a normal fish's head to its body, Tiktaalik gained a real neck, which makes it the earliest known fish that could turn its head to snap at prey. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik; https://evolution.berkeley.edu/evo-news/what-has-the-head-of-a-crocodile-and-the-gills-of-a-fish/

question: Tiktaalik lived at the surface of warm, shallow swamps where the water often held little oxygen. It could take in oxygen in two different ways, one of them closed to any fish that lives only in water. Besides its ordinary gills, what else did it have?
answer: lungs to gulp air
choices: lungs to gulp air
a spare set of gills
a blowhole
gill-filtering barbels
context: Tiktaalik carried BOTH gills and lungs, so it could breathe water and also gulp air at the surface — a body caught right between two worlds. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik

question: Tiktaalik paddled through its swamp on front fins with thin fish fin-rays along the outside. Inside each fin, past a shoulder and an elbow, lay bones that people still use today to bend a hand. What were they?
answer: a wrist
choices: a wrist
finger bones
a collarbone
a thumb
context: Inside Tiktaalik's front fins were the bones of a shoulder, an elbow, and a wrist — the very bones that would become our arms — while the outside still carried thin fish fin-rays for paddling. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04637

question: Before anyone had ever seen a Tiktaalik, Neil Shubin's team went looking for one. Working out when fish must have first crawled ashore, they picked out rock of just the right age to search, and after years of digging, in 2004, they found the fossil. Where did they dig?
answer: the Canadian High Arctic
choices: the Canadian High Arctic
the Australian outback
a Gobi Desert cliff
a South African cave
context: Reasoning about when fish moved onto land, Shubin's team deliberately searched rocks of the right age in the Canadian Arctic — and found Tiktaalik on Ellesmere Island in 2004, a rare case of paleontology 'calling its shot.' Tetrapod expert Jennifer Clack said of it: 'It's one of those things you can point to and say, I told you this would exist, and there it is.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik

question: Shubin's team finally described Tiktaalik's back half in 2014, long after its famous front fins, and got a shock. In most fish the pelvis is a small, simple bone, but Tiktaalik's was huge, nearly the size of its shoulder girdle, and its hind fin was as long and complex as the front one. In that powerful back end sat a joint expected only in a four-legged walker. Which one?
answer: a ball-and-socket hip
choices: a ball-and-socket hip
a hinge-jointed knee
a pivoting, rolling ankle
a socketed, clawed toe
context: The 2014 description of Tiktaalik's pelvis overturned the old 'front-wheel drive fish becomes four-wheel drive tetrapod' story. Its pelvis was nearly as large as its shoulder girdle and carried a true ball-and-socket hip joint with a mobile femur, and its hind fin was at least as long and complex as the celebrated front one. The upshot: powerful, weight-bearing hind limbs began evolving while the animal was still a fish — before anything walked on land. Source: Shubin, Daeschler & Jenkins, 'Pelvic girdle and fin of Tiktaalik roseae,' PNAS 111:893-899 (2014), pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3903263; sciencedaily.com/releases/2014/01/140113154211.htm; Grokipedia (grokipedia.com/page/Tiktaalik).

question: On top of Tiktaalik's flat skull sat a pair of large openings, spiracles left from an old gill slit. In its land-living descendants, the passage was never abandoned but remade into a different organ entirely. Which one?
answer: the middle ear
choices: the middle ear
the voice box
the tear ducts
the nasal passage
context: On top of Tiktaalik's flat skull sat enlarged spiracles — relics of a gill slit. Devonian swamp water was warm, and warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, so these top-of-head openings likely helped it gulp air at the surface. In more derived, land-living descendants that same spiracular passage was not lost but repurposed: the space and bones once used to breathe became the machinery of the middle ear, the apparatus of hearing on land. Source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com/page/Tiktaalik) — spiracle/otic notch 'that in more derived animals became an ear'; corroborated by general Devonian tetrapod evo-devo (spiracle to stapes/middle ear).

question: A sea otter floats on its back in the North Pacific and smashes clams and mussels open on a rock resting on its chest. It does not grab just any pebble: it searches the seafloor for one particular kind of rock and keeps a good one for meal after meal. What makes a rock a keeper?
answer: A flat side and a weight of about half a pound
choices: A flat side and a weight of about half a pound
A jagged edge sharp enough to pierce shell
A hollow center it can grip with one paw
A porous surface that traps and holds bait
context: The sea otter becomes picky about a rock's exact shape and weight — roughly half a pound to a pound, with a flat side that works as a good anvil. It tucks that favorite into a pouch of loose skin under its forearm to carry between dives. Source: Silicon Canals; Animals Around The Globe.

question: An Egyptian vulture, a small white scavenger of the African savanna, comes across an ostrich egg lying in the grass, its shell thick as the rim of a coffee mug. The vulture's beak is nowhere near strong enough to crack it. To get at the meal inside, what does the vulture do?
answer: Picks up a stone in its bill and hurls it down at the shell
choices: Picks up a stone in its bill and hurls it down at the shell
Rolls the egg off a cliff onto the rocks below
Sits on the egg until the heat cracks it open
Pecks a single weak spot for hours until it caves
context: The Egyptian vulture holds a stone in its bill and throws it down at the egg by swinging its neck, repeating until the shell cracks. An ostrich shell is too tough for the vulture's beak, so the thrown stone does what the beak cannot. Source: Wikipedia, 'Egyptian vulture'; National Geographic.

question: Gripping a stone in its bill, an Egyptian vulture with a bare yellow face stands over an ostrich egg whose shell is so thick a lion cannot bite through it. A bird has no arm to wind up a real throw, and its neck is short. Where does the force to crack that shell come from?
answer: It swings its whole neck to drive the stone down
choices: It swings its whole neck to drive the stone down
It flaps hard and dives, adding its body weight
It jerks the stone with a snap of its beak alone
It drops the stone from as high as it can jump
context: With no arm to throw, the Egyptian vulture generates its force by swinging its whole neck, hurling the held stone down at the egg and repeating until the shell cracks. This stone-throwing was famously filmed in 1966 near Olduvai Gorge and reported in the journal Nature. Source: Wikipedia, 'Egyptian vulture'; Thouless et al. 1989, Ibis.

question: Jane Goodall, a young English researcher at Gombe Stream in Tanzania in 1960, watched a wild chimpanzee she had named David Greybeard strip the leaves off a grass stem and poke it into a termite mound to fish out termites. Why did this quiet moment shake the scientific world?
answer: It was the first time a wild animal was seen making a tool
choices: It was the first time a wild animal was seen making a tool
It proved chimpanzees eat insects for most of their diet
It showed chimps teaching each other by imitation
It was the first chimp ever seen standing fully upright
context: Stripping the leaves off the stem turned it into a tool: manufacture, not just use, and the first time anyone had seen a wild animal make a tool. Until then, toolmaking was thought to be a defining mark of humans. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Greybeard; History.com; Leakey Foundation.

question: A wild chimpanzee in the Tai Forest of Ivory Coast sets a rock-hard Panda nut on a tree root that serves as an anvil. Then it swings a stone hammer down on the nut with both hands, over and over, until the shell splits. How heavy can a Tai chimp's hammer stone get?
answer: Up to about 15 kilograms
choices: Up to about 15 kilograms
About the weight of a golf ball
No more than a single kilogram
Around 50 kilograms, needing two chimps
context: Tai Forest chimpanzees use stone hammers weighing from 3 up to 15 kilograms — a heavy rock swung with real force — to smash the very hard Panda nut against a tree-root anvil. Source: Boesch & Boesch 1984; Royal Society Open Science.

question: Archaeologists dug beneath a spot in the Tai Forest of Ivory Coast where wild chimpanzees crack nuts with stones today. Below it they uncovered ancient chimpanzee stone hammers and nut fragments, far older than anyone expected: a true chimpanzee Stone Age. About how old were they?
answer: About 4,300 years old
choices: About 4,300 years old
About 200 years old
About 500 years old
About 40,000 years old
context: Excavators found a 4,300-year-old chimpanzee nut-cracking site in the Tai Forest, evidence that chimps have used stone tools for thousands of years. Source: Mercader et al. 2007, PNAS 104:3043, '4,300-year-old chimpanzee sites and the origins of percussive stone technology'; National Geographic.

question: A small brown finch on the Galapagos Islands, off the coast of Ecuador, does a woodpecker's job: it digs insect grubs out from under tree bark, for no true woodpeckers live on the islands. How does this woodpecker finch pry the grubs out?
answer: It holds a cactus spine in its beak to pry them out
choices: It holds a cactus spine in its beak to pry them out
It hammers the bark loose with a reinforced skull
It licks them up with an extra-long barbed tongue
It waits for the grubs to crawl out at dusk
context: The woodpecker finch holds a cactus spine or twig in its beak to pry grubs out of bark — and will even snap the spine shorter to make it easier to handle. With no woodpecker to compete with, it took over that job using a tool. Source: Wikipedia, 'Woodpecker finch'; Earth Life.

question: A New Caledonian crow rips a blade-like tool from the long, spiny edge of a Pandanus leaf, cut in one of three set designs: wide, narrow or stepped. Across the whole species, which edge of the leaf do most of these crows tear their tools from?
answer: The left edge
choices: The left edge
The right edge
The pointed tip
The base near the stem
context: When making stepped Pandanus tools, most New Caledonian crows tear from the LEFT edge of the leaf — a population-wide 'handedness,' or laterality, seen across the species. The stepped design also takes the most steps to make of the three. Source: Hunt et al., Nature 414:707.

question: Researchers handed a New Caledonian crow named 007 a puzzle with eight linked stages, each one locking away the tool needed for the next, with a piece of meat at the end. The crow had to use each tool in turn to open the stage after it. Roughly how long did 007 take to work through all eight?
answer: About two and a half minutes
choices: About two and a half minutes
About half a second
About two full hours
About three days of attempts
context: The crow named 007 solved the eight-stage puzzle in about two and a half minutes, using tools in sequence — one tool to fetch the next — to reach the meat. Source: Alex Taylor, University of Auckland, via BBC 'Inside the Animal Mind'; Gizmodo.

question: Divers off Indonesia filmed a small veined octopus hauling two matching halves of an old coconut shell, thrown overboard by people, across the open sandy seafloor. She walked stiffly on her arms like a creature on stilts, for as far as 20 meters. Why would an octopus go to all that trouble?
answer: To reassemble them later as a hideout
choices: To reassemble them later as a hideout
To trap small fish between the shells as bait
To use the shells as paddles for faster swimming
To scrape algae off the shells for food
context: The veined (coconut) octopus carries shell halves — sometimes as far as about 20 meters — to reassemble later as a shelter. Carrying a tool for FUTURE use, when it gives no benefit in the moment, is a rare sign of planning. This was a documented observation by Julian Finn and Mark Norman off Sulawesi and Bali, not a legend. Source: Finn & Norman 2009, Current Biology, via CBC News; National Geographic.

question: In Shark Bay, a bottlenose dolphin tears a cone-shaped sponge loose and wedges it over her beak before jabbing into the rocky seafloor to flush out fish. Other dolphins share the same bay but do not hunt this way. What do biologists think puts these fish beyond the others' reach?
answer: The fish have no swim bladder, so the dolphin's sonar can't spot them
choices: The fish have no swim bladder, so the dolphin's sonar can't spot them
The fish burrow so deep in sand that sonar echoes never reach them
The fish dart off far too fast for any dolphin to chase down
The fish carry sharp spines that only a padded beak can brave
context: In Shark Bay, Western Australia, a subgroup of Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops aduncus) called 'spongers' break off a cone-shaped marine sponge and wear it like a glove over the rostrum, then plough the rocky seabed to root out bottom-dwelling fish. Those prey lack a gas-filled swim bladder, the structure a dolphin's echolocation normally pings off, so biologists think they are hard to find by sonar and must be flushed out by probing; the sponge saves the beak from the sharp rocks. Krutzen and colleagues (PNAS, 2005) sequenced mitochondrial DNA and found the skill passes almost entirely down the female line, mother to daughter, making it a learned tradition, not a gene or a quirk of habitat, and they called it the first case of material culture in a marine mammal. Source: Krutzen et al., 'Cultural transmission of tool use in bottlenose dolphins,' PNAS 2005 (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0500232102); Patterson & Mann 2011, PLoS ONE 6(7):e22243.

question: Wild bearded capuchins in Brazil's Serra da Capivara hammer quartzite cobbles against stone, and sharp flakes fly off that look nearly identical to the cutting tools of early humans. Yet the monkeys never cut anything with them. What are they after?
answer: The quartz dust they lick off the shattered stone
choices: The quartz dust they lick off the shattered stone
Insects the hammering flushes out of the rocks
Nuts they have wedged against the anvil to crack
A hammer stone they will carry off and reuse
context: At Serra da Capivara, Brazil, bearded capuchins (Sapajus libidinosus) pound rounded quartzite cobbles against embedded anvil stones. Proffitt and colleagues (Nature, 2016) analysed 111 of the resulting artefacts and found sharp-edged flakes bearing conchoidal (shell-like) fractures nearly indistinguishable from the Oldowan cutting flakes long treated as a hallmark of early hominins. The twist: the capuchins ignore the cutting edges entirely -- they pound to lick the quartz dust and grit off the smashed cobble (likely for minerals, or to scrape away lichen). Because a wild monkey mass-produces 'stone tools' with no interest in a blade, the find complicates how archaeologists read the earliest human stone record -- as the Oxford team put it, humans may be 'not unique after all.' Source: Proffitt et al., 'Wild monkeys flake stone tools,' Nature 2016 (nature.com/articles/nature20112).

question: A big black-and-white bird perches on a mossy branch deep in a South American rainforest. Its bright orange-and-yellow beak, up to four times as big as its head, stretches nearly as long as the rest of its body. Which bird is it?
answer: Toucan
choices: Toucan
Flamingo
Pelican
Ostrich
context: The toucan is famous for a bill that can run up to four times the size of its own head and nearly as long as the rest of its body. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants — Toucan (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/toucan).

question: A toucan in a Central American rainforest plucks a berry with the very tip of its huge bill, far out past its mouth, with no way to swallow the fruit from there. How does it get the berry down its throat?
answer: It jerks its head back and tosses the berry up, then catches it dropping straight down its throat
choices: It jerks its head back and tosses the berry up, then catches it dropping straight down its throat
It works the berry inward along the bill, then rolls it back to the mouth with its tongue
It clamps down to crush the berry open, then laps the sweet juice off the bill
It grips the berry against a branch, then shears off bites small enough to swallow
context: A toucan grabs fruit at the tip of its bill, then jerks its head back and flicks the food into the air so it drops straight down the throat — it eats by throwing its food and catching it. Source: HowStuffWorks — The Toucan (animals.howstuffworks.com/birds/toucan.htm); San Diego Zoo — Toucan.

question: A toucan flaps through the rainforest of Central and South America carrying a bill nearly as long as the rest of its body, a huge orange banana jutting from a small black bird. Such a beak ought to weigh the bird down and tire it in flight, yet it flies with ease. What keeps that enormous bill so light?
answer: A foam of thin bony struts and air inside keratin
choices: A foam of thin bony struts and air inside keratin
Solid bone that grows lighter as the bird ages
A core of soft cartilage like a shark's skeleton
Air sacs the bird inflates before takeoff
context: The bill is a natural foam sandwich — an outer sheath of keratin (the stuff of hair and fingernails) over an airy inner core of bony struts and closed air-filled cells, so it weighs only a tiny fraction of the bird's body. Source: SeaWorld — Toco Toucan Facts (seaworld.org/animals/facts/birds/toco-toucan/); San Diego Zoo — Toucan.

question: A toucan sits out sweltering afternoons and chilly spells in the South American rainforest, its enormous bill bare to the air through both. Scientists filming it with thermal cameras found that the bird uses that bill to manage its body heat both ways. How does it do it?
answer: It floods the bill with blood when hot, then cuts the flow when cold
choices: It floods the bill with blood when hot, then cuts the flow when cold
It points the bill into the breeze when hot and into the sun when cold
It grows a thicker keratin layer for winter and molts it thinner for summer
It pants with the bill wide open to cool, then clamps it shut to stay warm
context: The bill is a controllable radiator: the toucan adjusts blood flow to dump 30–60% of its total heat loss through the beak, one of the largest heat-exchange 'thermal windows' relative to body size of any animal, rivaling an elephant's ears. Source: Tattersall, Andrade & Abe (2009), 'Heat Exchange from the Toucan Bill Reveals a Controllable Vascular Thermal Radiator,' Science 325:468–470.

question: A tiny hunter stalks the leaf litter of a tropical forest, its two long, straight jaws held open like a cocked mousetrap. When prey brushes them, they snap shut faster than almost any other move an animal makes. Which creature is it?
answer: The trap-jaw ant
choices: The trap-jaw ant
The bombardier beetle
The tiger beetle
The whip spider
context: The trap-jaw ant (genus Odontomachus) cocks its huge straight mandibles wide open at a full 180 degrees, then snaps them shut in about 0.13 milliseconds -- roughly 35 to 64 m/s, over 60 m/s at the top end, one of the fastest movements known in any animal. Source: Patek, Baio, Fisher & Suarez 2006, PNAS 'Ballistic jaw propulsion in trap-jaw ants'; Patek Lab, Duke.

question: A bigger predator corners a trap-jaw ant on the forest floor, and the ant turns its lightning-fast hunting jaws to a second use. It points them straight down at the ground and fires them shut. What does that do for the ant?
answer: The recoil flips it backward into the air
choices: The recoil flips it backward into the air
It burrows into the soil to hide
It sprays a jet of stinging acid
It clamps onto the predator and holds on
context: The trap-jaw ant uses one structure two ways: a lethal snap-trap on prey and an ejector seat for itself. Firing the jaws against the ground, the recoil flings the ant about 8.3 cm (3.3 inches) up and backward, like a five-foot-six adult leaping 44 feet with a snap of the jaw. Source: Patek et al. 2006, PNAS; Larabee & Suarez, PLOS ONE 2015; National Geographic Kids 'Fastest jaw on the draw'.

question: A trap-jaw ant creeps forward with its jaws locked open at 180 degrees. The instant a prey insect wanders between them, the jaws fire on their own, and the ant never has to aim. What lines the inside of each open jaw to tell the ant that prey has arrived?
answer: Rows of sensitive trigger hairs
choices: Rows of sensitive trigger hairs
A ring of tiny suction cups
A patch of light-sensing cells
A coating of sticky glue
context: Fine sensory hairs line the inside face of each open mandible and wire directly to the nerves that release the catch -- so the jaws fire the moment prey brushes them, no aiming required. Source: Wikipedia 'Odontomachus'; Patek Lab, Duke.

question: A trap-jaw ant slams its jaws shut in about a tenth of a millisecond, one of the fastest movements ever measured in an animal and far quicker than any muscle in its body could pull them. How does the ant move its jaws so fast?
answer: It pre-loads spring energy behind a latch, then releases it all at once
choices: It pre-loads spring energy behind a latch, then releases it all at once
It grows the jaws lighter so they fall shut on their own
It uses jets of pressurized fluid to fling them
It relies on a whip-like flick of its antennae
context: The trap-jaw ant works like a loaded crossbow: it locks the open jaws with an internal latch, builds up spring energy in advance, and releases it in an instant. That stored-and-released spring energy lets the strike accelerate at roughly 100,000 times gravity -- a snap no muscle could ever match. Source: Patek Lab, Duke; Sheila Patek in NBC News 'Trap-jaw ant has world's fastest bite'.

question: A tiny sap-sucking insect, a cousin of the cicadas, clings to a plant stem in a tropical forest. Over its back it wears a bizarre helmet, sculpted into thorns, horns or a crown of spikes, a different costume for each kind. What is this insect?
answer: A treehopper
choices: A treehopper
A leafhopper
A planthopper
A shield bug
context: Treehoppers (family Membracidae) are tiny sap-sucking relatives of the cicadas. The helmet is the pronotum, normally a small plate on top of an insect's thorax, which in treehoppers balloons into thorns, antlers, horns or spikes, giving each species its own alien-looking headgear. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treehopper

question: A hungry songbird patrols a plant stem, hunting for the soft, juicy insects it likes to eat. Right in the open on that stem sits a whole cluster of treehoppers -- tiny sap-sucking bugs with strange bumpy shells. Yet the bird's gaze slides straight over them. What is it about how these treehoppers hold themselves that lets a bird look right past them?
answer: they line up in a row so they resemble the plant's own thorns
choices: they line up in a row so they resemble the plant's own thorns
their bodies are transparent, letting the green stem show through
they flatten against the bark and match its mottled brown color
they hang motionless underneath leaves like tiny curled buds
context: Many treehoppers are thorn mimics: lined up along a stem, a row of them looks exactly like the plant's own spines, hiding the insects in plain sight from birds. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/membracidae-a-look-at-bizarre-thorn-mimicking-insects/

question: Ants swarm over a colony of treehoppers clinging to a plant stem, biting and chasing off ladybird beetles and other hunters like hired bodyguards. The ants are not doing it for nothing. What do the treehoppers give them in return?
answer: honeydew, a sweet liquid waste they dribble out
choices: honeydew, a sweet liquid waste they dribble out
tiny eggs the ants carry back to feed their grubs
shed skins the ants use to line their nest
a scent trail that guides the ants to new plants
context: Treehoppers suck sugary sap and excrete a sweet waste called honeydew. Ants farm them for it -- guarding the treehoppers from predators in exchange for the sugar, a classic mutualism. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2627810/ and https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982208007409

question: Cera Fisher studied how a treehopper grows its spiky helmet, which is part of the thorax, and expected thorax-building genes to switch on. Instead hundreds of genes lit up, matching the set that builds a quite different body part. Which one?
answer: the wings
choices: the wings
the legs
the eyes
the antennae
context: The treehopper's helmet is part of the thorax, but researcher Cera Fisher found hundreds of genes giving off a wing-like pattern as it grows, prompting her reaction: 'Oh my god, how did something like that evolve?' Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/treehoppers-bizarre-wondrous-helmets-use-wing-genes-grow-180973713/

question: A rhino-sized plant-eater roamed the plains of what is now North America about 68 million years ago. It carried a short horn on its nose, two long horns above its eyes and a huge bony frill fanning out behind its head. Which dinosaur was it?
answer: Triceratops
choices: Triceratops
Stegosaurus
Ankylosaurus
Iguanodon
context: Triceratops means 'three-horned face' -- a short nose horn plus two long brow horns on a big bony frill. Source: AMNH (amnh.org/exhibitions/permanent/ornithischian-dinosaurs/triceratops).

question: A hulking, four-legged Triceratops roamed North America about 68 million years ago, 26 to 30 feet long from beak to tail, on stout, elephant-like legs built low and broad. Roughly how heavy did the biggest ones get?
answer: 6 to 10 tons
choices: 6 to 10 tons
1 to 2 tons
20 to 30 tons
40 to 50 tons
context: Triceratops was rhino-shaped and built low and heavy, weighing 6-10 tons in Late Cretaceous North America. Source: National Geographic (nationalgeographic.com/animals/facts/triceratops-horridus).

question: Triceratops lived in North America until the age of dinosaurs closed 66 million years ago, and its bones turn up in the very last layer of rock before the worldwide die-off. Scientists blame a single catastrophe for ending its world. What was it?
answer: A city-sized asteroid slammed into what is now Mexico
choices: A city-sized asteroid slammed into what is now Mexico
A slow ice age froze the plains over ten thousand years
Rising seas drowned the continents in one vast flood
A supernova exploded a few light-years from Earth
context: Triceratops lived right up to 66 million years ago, one of the very last dinosaurs, wiped out in the extinction after the Chicxulub asteroid struck what is now Mexico. Source: Wikipedia Triceratops; NatGeo.

question: With a sharp, parrot-like beak, Triceratops snipped tough leaves off, then ground each mouthful down on columns of teeth stacked one behind another inside its jaws. Whenever a top tooth wore out, a fresh one was already rising from below to replace it. How many teeth did this grinding system hold at once?
answer: Up to 800
choices: Up to 800
About 60
Exactly 32
About a dozen
context: These stacked columns are called 'dental batteries' -- roughly 36-40 columns of 3-5 teeth each, up to 800 total, for grinding tough plants. Source: Wikipedia Triceratops; Animalia.bio.

question: Triceratops carried the biggest skull of any land animal that has ever lived. Its bony frill fanned out behind the head, and the whole heavy skull, horns, beak and frill together, made up nearly a third of the animal from beak-tip to tail. About how long was that famous skull?
answer: About 8 feet
choices: About 8 feet
About 8 inches
About 30 feet
About 2 feet
context: The Triceratops skull reached about 8 feet, the largest of any land animal ever, nearly a third of its body length. Source: Wikipedia Triceratops; AMNH.

question: Paleontologists compared the healed scars on the skulls of two horned dinosaurs of Late Cretaceous North America: Triceratops, with its pair of long brow horns, and its cousin Centrosaurus, with only a single nose horn. The Triceratops skulls carried far more frill wounds. What best explains the difference?
answer: Triceratops regularly fought each other with their horns
choices: Triceratops regularly fought each other with their horns
The scars were T. rex bites, not horn wounds
The frill marks were birth deformities, not injuries
Triceratops horns were too soft to wound anything
context: Two-horned Triceratops racked up far more squamosal wounds than one-horned Centrosaurus -- the tell-tale sign of Triceratops jousting rivals of their own kind. Source: Farke, Wolff & Tanke 2009, PLoS ONE (PMC2617760).

question: Erickson and colleagues ran a microprobe across a fossil Triceratops tooth in 2015 and mapped five different tissues. One was a soft dentine riddled with blood vessels, an odd thing to find in a grinding tooth, and that soft strip turned out to be the whole trick. What did it do as tough plants ground the tooth away?
answer: It wore down faster than the rest, carving a groove that kept the tooth self-sharpening
choices: It wore down faster than the rest, carving a groove that kept the tooth self-sharpening
It flexed under the load, cushioning the tooth against gritty sand and stone
It funneled fresh blood to the crown to sense which plants were the toughest
It swelled with fluid to shove the next replacement tooth up into place
context: Erickson and colleagues (2015, Science Advances) dragged a diamond-tipped microprobe across Triceratops teeth and found FIVE distinct tissues -- enamel, hard mantle dentine, orthodentine, soft vasodentine, and coronal cementum -- one more than the four-tissue teeth of horses and bison, until then thought the most complex teeth evolution had ever produced. The blood-vessel-filled vasodentine wore about 1.6 times faster than the orthodentine beside it, so grinding gritty Cretaceous plants hollowed a recessed central channel -- a 'fuller,' the very same blood-groove ground into a sword or knife blade -- that kept a sharp slicing edge instead of grinding to a blunt nub. It is an actual mechanism for how the tooth batteries stayed sharp. Source: Erickson et al. 2015, Science Advances (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4640618/); Live Science summary (https://www.livescience.com/51108-triceratops-teeth.html).

question: A grown Triceratops carried two long brow horns that swept forward over its beak. When paleontologists set its skulls side by side in order of age, the smallest a 38-centimeter hatchling and the largest two-meter adults, they found the horns had rebuilt themselves as the animal aged. On a young juvenile, which way did those brow horns point?
answer: Backward toward the frill, only recurving forward once it reached adulthood
choices: Backward toward the frill, only recurving forward once it reached adulthood
Straight upward at first, then folding flat against the skull with age
Forward already, just shorter and blunter than the adult pair
Downward past the beak, then lifting and lengthening as it grew
context: Horner and Goodwin (2006, Proceedings of the Royal Society B) assembled a growth series of ten skulls, from a 38-cm baby to roughly 2-m adults, and traced how the head remodeled through life. The postorbital (brow) horns began as straight little stubs, curved BACKWARD in juveniles, straightened out in subadults, then recurved FORWARD in adults. Meanwhile the frill margin, deeply scalloped in babies, sprouted 17-19 delta-shaped triangular bones (epoccipitals) that later flattened, elongated, and fused smoothly into its edge -- so a juvenile Triceratops looked strikingly unlike the forward-horned adult everyone pictures. Source: Horner & Goodwin 2006, Proc. R. Soc. B (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1635501/).

question: A trilobite crawled across the Cambrian ocean floor 500 million years ago, when the seas were first filling with animal life. Jointed armor covered its soft body, and it walked on many legs, much as a modern woodlouse does. To which great group of animals did it belong?
answer: Arthropods
choices: Arthropods
Mollusks
Corals
Sponges
context: Trilobites were arthropods — the same great group as today's insects, crabs, and spiders. Hard-shelled, jointed-limbed sea creatures, they crawled, burrowed, and swam across the ancient ocean floor for hundreds of millions of years. Source: Natural History Museum, London — 'How trilobites conquered prehistoric oceans' (nhm.ac.uk).

question: Many trilobites scuttling over the ancient seafloor were no smooth, armored ovals. Their shells grew strange features that may have kept predators from biting them, or kept them from sinking into the soft sea mud. What did these trilobites grow all over their shells?
answer: Long, sharp spines
choices: Long, sharp spines
A thick coat of fur
Rows of suction cups
A pair of grasping claws
context: Many trilobites, especially in the Ordovician, grew elaborate spines all over their shells — long spikes for defense, or possibly to keep from sinking into soft mud — turning the armored crawler into a walking pincushion. Source: Wikipedia 'Trilobite' (Lichida and spinose forms, Ordovician–Devonian).

question: A trilobite was scuttling across the ancient seafloor when a predator loomed above it. Its back was hard, armored shell, but its belly and jointed legs were soft and exposed underneath. With no hope of outrunning the attacker, what did many kinds of trilobite do when threatened?
answer: Curled into a tight armored ball
choices: Curled into a tight armored ball
Buried straight down into the sand
Squirted a cloud of ink
Shed its legs to escape
context: When threatened, many trilobites rolled up into a tight ball — bending the thorax and tucking the tail beneath the head — exactly like a modern pillbug or woodlouse, hiding the soft underside behind the armored shell. Source: Natural History Museum, London (nhm.ac.uk); Oxford UMNH.

question: Isotelus rex, the biggest trilobite known, crawled the ancient seafloor at over two feet from head to tail. The tiniest trilobite ever found, Acanthopleurella stipulae, sat at the far opposite end of that scale. About how big was it?
answer: About 1.5 millimeters, smaller than a grain of rice
choices: About 1.5 millimeters, smaller than a grain of rice
About 2 centimeters, like a coin
About 10 centimeters, like a hand
About 30 centimeters, like a ruler
context: Trilobites ranged from giant to tiny: the largest known, Isotelus rex, reached about 72 cm (over 2 feet), while the smallest, Acanthopleurella stipulae, was just 1.5 mm — smaller than a grain of rice. Source: Wikipedia 'Trilobite' (Isotelus rex; Acanthopleurella stipulae).

question: Paleontologists have named more than 22,000 kinds of trilobite from the fossils they left behind, and they warn that those fossils are far more common than the animals themselves ever were. Why do so many trilobite fossils exist for each trilobite that lived?
answer: Each one shed many empty shells while alive
choices: Each one shed many empty shells while alive
They laid thousands of hard-shelled eggs
Their shells split into pieces after death
They lived crowded together in vast reefs
context: Like all arthropods, a trilobite grew by molting — splitting its old shell open along built-in weak lines (facial sutures) and crawling out. Because one animal shed many times in a lifetime, a huge number of trilobite 'fossils' are actually just empty cast-off shells, not dead animals. Source: NHM London; Oxford UMNH; PMC review on trilobite moulting.

question: A trilobite peered over the ancient seafloor through some of the earliest true compound eyes, the same many-lensed mosaic a bee or a dragonfly uses today. Yet its lenses were made of something no animal alive builds an eye from. What were they made of?
answer: Calcite — clear crystal, actual stone
choices: Calcite — clear crystal, actual stone
A soft transparent jelly
Thin sheets of chitin shell
A ring of tiny water droplets
context: Astonishingly, trilobite eye lenses were made of the mineral calcite — actual clear crystal, a stone lens set right in the head. They are the only animals known to have made their eyes out of rock. Their compound eyes stitched many separate lens units, called ommatidia, into a mosaic picture. Source: Beaty Biodiversity Museum, UBC — 'Trilobite Eyes Are Hard'; ScienceAlert.

question: Trilobites crawled the seas from deep in the Cambrian to the end of the Permian, a run so long that our own genus Homo, barely 2 million years old, is a blink beside it. Roughly how long did trilobites rule the seas?
answer: Almost 270 million years
choices: Almost 270 million years
About 40 million years
About 90 million years
About 900 million years
context: Trilobites ruled the seas for almost 270 million years — from about 521 million years ago in the Cambrian until roughly 251 million years ago. For comparison, our own genus Homo is only about 2 million years old. Source: Wikipedia 'Trilobite'; Oxford University Museum of Natural History.

question: Erbenochile, a Devonian trilobite, carried a towering eye packed with hundreds of lenses in dozens of vertical rows, which gave it a near-360-degree view of its surroundings. Perched right on top of that eye-tower sat one more small structure. What was it?
answer: A shell rim shading the eye from above
choices: A shell rim shading the eye from above
A second eye facing backward
A pair of long feeler-antennae
A hollow snorkel-like tube
context: Erbenochile's tall eye held roughly 560 calcite lenses in 33-36 vertical rows, giving it a nearly 360-degree view at eye level — and a rim of shell projected over the top to block glare from light overhead. It was a fossil animal wearing its own visor. Source: Fortey & Chatterton, 'A Devonian Trilobite with an Eyeshade,' Science (2003).

question: Every last trilobite died out about 251 million years ago in the end-Permian catastrophe known as the Great Dying. It was no ordinary die-off. Of every kind of living thing in the sea and on land, how much did that single event erase?
answer: More than 90% of all species
choices: More than 90% of all species
About 10% of all species
About one-third of all species
About half of all species
context: After 270 million years, trilobites vanished completely in the end-Permian 'Great Dying' — the largest mass extinction in Earth's history, which killed more than 90% of all species on the planet. Not a single trilobite survived it. Source: Oxford University Museum of Natural History; Wikipedia 'Trilobite' (end-Permian extinction).

question: A phacopid trilobite looked out through eye lenses that each seem a single clear blob. Modeling showed every lens was really two stacked pieces meeting along a curved inner surface, the very shape Descartes and Huygens would work out on paper some 400 million years later. What did that surface do to the light?
answer: Focused every ray to one crisp point
choices: Focused every ray to one crisp point
Split white light into rainbow bands
Filtered out the sea's dim blue glow
Polarized the light to cut the glare
context: Those two designs are the only aberration-correcting lens shapes humans ever derived on paper — René Descartes in 1637 and Christiaan Huygens in 1690 — yet a phacopid grew the same aspherical calcite interface some 400 million years earlier, cancelling the blur (spherical aberration) that plagues a simple lens and driving light to a single sharp focus. Clarkson & Levi-Setti first matched the geometry (Nature 261:130, 1975, 'Trilobite eyes and the optics of Des Cartes and Huygens'); Lee, Torney & Owen later measured a real magnesium-concentration contrast between the two calcite units, chemical proof the doublet was genuine (Palaeontology 50:1031, 2007).

question: Paleontologists hold millions of trilobite shells in their collections, yet none had ever seen what a trilobite ate, because the soft gut never survives. Then in 2023 a synchrotron scan looked inside a 465-million-year-old Bohemolichas and found its gut packed solid. What was crammed in there?
answer: Crushed shells of clams, ostracods, and shelled seafloor prey
choices: Crushed shells of clams, ostracods, and shelled seafloor prey
A soupy mush of filtered plankton and free-drifting algae
Soft marine worms tugged live from their muddy burrows
Films of bacteria scraped off the muddy seafloor bottom
context: It was the first trilobite ever found with its gut contents preserved — 3-D imaged by high-resolution synchrotron microtomography at the ESRF — despite the millions of trilobite fossils already known. The crushed shells mark Bohemolichas incola as an opportunistic durophage: a shell-crusher and scavenger that bolted small seafloor animals whole or in fragments. Tellingly, the swallowed shells were not etched by acid, so the team inferred a neutral-to-alkaline gut like a modern horseshoe crab or crustacean, not the acidic stomach of a vertebrate. Kraft, Vaškaninová, Mergl, Budil, Fatka & Ahlberg, Nature 622:545 (2023), 'Uniquely preserved gut contents illuminate trilobite palaeophysiology'.

question: The tuatara's spiny relatives once scurried among the dinosaurs on nearly every continent, back in the Jurassic over 150 million years ago. Then the whole group vanished except the tuatara itself, which survives today only on a few small islands off New Zealand. What nickname has that long survival earned it?
answer: A living fossil, its lineage older than lizards
choices: A living fossil, its lineage older than lizards
A missing link, caught mid-change to a snake
A living rainbow, for its shifting colors
A living compass, for its unerring homing
context: The tuatara is the sole surviving member of an order that flourished 200 million years ago. Its lineage split off before lizards and snakes even existed. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); NZ Geographic, 'Tuatara — A survivor from the dinosaur age'.

question: On one of New Zealand's small islands, a male tuatara squares off against a rival on his patch of rock. A ridge of tall, pointed spines called the crest runs down his back, and it stands tallest on males. What does he do with that crest?
answer: Flares it and inflates his body dark
choices: Flares it and inflates his body dark
Sheds it in a startling spray of spines
Snaps it flat and plays dead
Lights it up with glowing tips
context: The Māori name 'tuatara' means 'peaks on the back', describing the spiny crest down its spine — largest in males, who erect the crest and darken as they inflate the body during territorial display. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara).

question: A tuatara hatchling, just out of its egg on a small island off New Zealand, carries a small pale patch on the crown of its head. Scales slowly grow over the patch as the animal matures. Almost no other living reptile has anything like the organ beneath it. What is that organ?
answer: A working third eye, with its own lens and retina
choices: A working third eye, with its own lens and retina
A heat-sensing pit that maps warm prey
A pressure gland that reads coming storms
A scent organ that tastes the air
context: The tuatara's parietal eye is a genuine third eye, complete with lens and light-sensitive retina, visible in hatchlings before scales cover it. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); Animal Diversity Web (Sphenodon punctatus).

question: Under the scales on the crown of a tuatara's head lies an organ that cannot form a picture of the world, yet it earns its keep. Researchers suspect it serves as a kind of natural compass, setting the animal's inner clock and body temperature through the changing seasons. What kind of compass is it?
answer: A sun-compass, reading daylight
choices: A sun-compass, reading daylight
A magnetic compass, reading Earth's field
A star-compass, reading the night sky
A wind-compass, reading the breeze
context: The parietal eye is thought to act as a light sensor and sun-compass, tracking daylight to regulate the tuatara's circadian rhythms and temperature rather than forming images. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); 'The lonely eye', PMC/NIH.

question: A tuatara stays active on its New Zealand island in near-freezing cold and can barely tolerate a warm afternoon, while most reptiles bask in the sun and thrive in real heat. Its preferred body temperature is lower than that of any other reptile. What is it?
context: The tuatara prefers a body temperature of about 16–21°C — the lowest of any reptile — and stays active down to 5°C, overheating and dying above about 28°C. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); Animal Diversity Web (Sphenodon punctatus).

question: A tuatara grows slowly for its first 35 years, then keeps going for decade after decade. At the Southland Museum, a captive male named Henry stunned his keepers not merely by surviving to a great age, but by doing something no one expects of so ancient an animal. What was Henry still doing past the age of 100?
answer: Fathering new offspring
choices: Fathering new offspring
Growing a fresh set of teeth
Regrowing a lost tail
Shedding his skin whole
context: Tuatara can live past 100. Henry, a captive male at the Southland Museum, was reported still breeding — fathering offspring — at age 111. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); Animal Diversity Web (Sphenodon punctatus).

question: A two-legged meat-eater about 40 feet long stalked western North America in the last days of the dinosaurs, right up until an asteroid struck 66 million years ago. It stood 13 feet tall at the hip and weighed up to 8 tons. Which famous dinosaur was it?
answer: Tyrannosaurus rex
choices: Tyrannosaurus rex
Triceratops horridus
Stegosaurus ungulatus
Brachiosaurus altithorax
context: Tyrannosaurus rex means 'tyrant lizard king.' It stood roughly 13 feet tall at the hip and could weigh up to about 8 tons, living at the very end of the age of dinosaurs, 68 to 66 million years ago. Source: Australian Museum fact sheet, https://australian.museum/learn/dinosaurs/fact-sheets/tyrannosaurus-rex/

question: A Tyrannosaurus rex crushed bone with a huge, boxy skull that held roughly 60 curved teeth and the massive jaw muscles that powered its bite. Roughly how long was that skull, from the tip of the snout to the back of the head?
answer: About 5 feet (1.5 m)
choices: About 5 feet (1.5 m)
About 1 foot (0.3 m)
About 15 feet (4.5 m)
About 2 inches (5 cm)
context: A T. rex skull was about 1.5 meters (5 feet) long, roughly as long as a grown person is tall, and carried around 60 teeth. A head that size gave the animal room for the bone-crushing jaw muscles that made it such a fearsome predator. Source: Australian Museum fact sheet, https://australian.museum/learn/dinosaurs/fact-sheets/tyrannosaurus-rex/

question: Tyrannosaurus rex hunted through the swamps and forests of North America about 68 million years ago, and the movies give it thin, knife-like teeth for slicing flesh, like a shark's. Its real back teeth were built for a very different job. What were they shaped like?
answer: Thick and banana-shaped
choices: Thick and banana-shaped
Flat and shovel-shaped
Long and needle-thin
Curved like a comb
context: The back teeth of T. rex were thick and banana-shaped, not thin blades. The largest reached about 20 to 30 cm (8 to 12 inches) long including the root, and were built to withstand struggling prey and crush bone. Source: Extinct Atlas T. rex skull guide, https://extinctatlas.org/species-guide/tyrannosaurus-rex-skull-and-teeth/

question: Whenever a Tyrannosaurus rex bit down hard on a struggling Triceratops or duck-billed hadrosaur, one of its curved teeth might snap off deep in the wound. Unlike a human, T. rex did not lose that tooth for life. What happened to the gap left behind in its jaw?
answer: A fresh tooth grew in to replace it
choices: A fresh tooth grew in to replace it
The jaw sealed the socket shut for good
A neighboring tooth slid over to fill it
The gum hardened into a bony ridge
context: T. rex replaced its teeth throughout its life. If a tooth broke off while feeding, a new tooth grew in to take its place, so the animal never ran short of weapons. Source: Australian Museum / Extinct Atlas, https://extinctatlas.org/species-guide/tyrannosaurus-rex-skull-and-teeth/

question: The jaws of a Tyrannosaurus rex clamped around a Triceratops with tremendous force. Scientists worked out how strong that bite was by measuring the marks its teeth left in fossil bones and modeling the massive muscles packed into the back of its skull. Roughly how much force did those jaws deliver?
answer: About 8,000 pounds
choices: About 8,000 pounds
About 3,000 pounds
About 5,500 pounds
About 12,000 pounds
context: T. rex bit with a force of about 8,000 pounds, nearly 3.6 tonnes, the strongest bite of any known land animal. The pointed tips of its teeth could focus pressures up to about 431,000 pounds per square inch, enough to pulverize bone. Source: Gignac & Erickson, Scientific Reports 2017, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-017-02161-w

question: Karen Chin, a paleontologist who studies the fossils many of her colleagues walk right past, described a strange 15-pound lump of rock from Saskatchewan in 1998. A Tyrannosaurus rex had left it behind more than 65 million years ago, and it was the largest specimen of its kind ever found. What was this famous find?
answer: Fossilized dung packed with crushed bone
choices: Fossilized dung packed with crushed bone
A jawbone with a tooth still lodged in it
A footprint pressed deep into old mud
A nest of eggs with unhatched young
context: The 15-pound (7 kg) T. rex coprolite, or fossilized dung, from Saskatchewan was packed with crushed fragments of a young plant-eating dinosaur's bones, proving T. rex swallowed bone. It is the largest meat-eater dropping ever found. Source: Karen Chin et al., Nature 1998, 'A king-sized theropod coprolite', https://www.nature.com/articles/31461

question: Paleontologists poured latex or plaster into the empty inside of Tyrannosaurus rex skulls to make casts of the brain that once sat there. Those casts revealed that one region devoted to a single sense was proportionally among the largest of any known dinosaur -- larger than the parts for sight or hearing. Which sense was T. rex especially built for?
answer: Smell
choices: Smell
Hearing
Touch
Taste
context: The olfactory bulbs, the part of the brain handling smell, were proportionally enormous in T. rex, among the largest of any known dinosaur. It likely could detect carcasses or blood from far away. Source: AMNH, 'How Superior Senses Helped T. rex Hunt', https://www.amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/t-rex-super-senses

question: Heavy as a school bus and over a dozen feet tall at the hip, Tyrannosaurus rex carried front arms barely three feet long, a wild mismatch for so huge a body. Each stubby arm ended in an unusual number of clawed fingers. How many fingers did each arm have?
answer: Two
choices: Two
Three
Five
Four
context: Each T. rex arm ended in just two fingers, while most of its relatives had three. The arm bones show the limbs were thick and muscular, but what T. rex actually used them for, pushing up off the ground, gripping prey, or mating, is still debated. Source: Natural History Museum, https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/how-did-tyrannosaurus-use-its-arms.html

question: Inside the leg bones of a young Tyrannosaurus rex, growth rings stack up like a tree's, one for every year it lived. When paleontologists sliced those bones open, the rings laid down from about age 14 to age 18 showed something dramatic. What did those years record?
answer: A teenage growth spurt packing on pounds daily
choices: A teenage growth spurt packing on pounds daily
A long stretch of near-starvation and shrinking
A slow, steady gain across its whole lifespan
A sudden stop in growth in its earliest years
