context: Growth rings show T. rex bulked up in a teenage growth spurt from about age 14 to 18, packing on roughly 4.6 pounds (about 2 kg) a day at its peak and adding most of its adult weight in just a few years. Source: Erickson et al.; Science News 'Growth Spurt', https://www.sciencenews.org/article/growth-spurt-teenage-tyrannosaurs-packed-pounds

question: Yutyrannus, a tyrannosaur cousin of T. rex some 30 feet long, left fossils that kept a soft-tissue feature, and scientists announced the find in 2012. It hints that parts of T. rex may not have been the bare-scaled giant people usually picture. What did Yutyrannus preserve?
answer: Down-like feathery filaments
choices: Down-like feathery filaments
A fleshy throat pouch
A brightly color-banded skin patch
A dangling skin wattle
context: Yutyrannus, a roughly 30-foot feathered tyrannosaur, was found with down-like filaments, which is why scientists suspect parts of T. rex may have had a sparse feathery covering. Direct T. rex skin impressions found so far show scales, so full feathering is not settled. Source: AMNH Yutyrannus, https://www.amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/yutyrannus-huali-feathered-tyrannosaur

question: Sue Hendrickson, a fossil hunter, spotted bones sticking out of a cliff near Faith, South Dakota, in 1990. She had found a Tyrannosaurus rex, and the find was nicknamed Sue in her honor; the skeleton now towers in the Field Museum in Chicago, one of the most-studied dinosaurs in the world. What makes Sue so prized by scientists?
answer: It is about 90 percent complete
choices: It is about 90 percent complete
It is the smallest T. rex on record
It was the first ever dug up
It still had skin covering the bones
context: SUE, nicknamed after fossil hunter Sue Hendrickson, is about 90 percent complete and over 40 feet long, one of the most complete T. rex skeletons ever found. SUE sold at auction in 1997 for $8.3 million and is now displayed at the Field Museum in Chicago. Source: Field Museum, https://www.fieldmuseum.org/blog/sue-t-rex

question: Mary Schweitzer found soft, still-bendy tissue inside a 68-million-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex thigh bone in 2005. Two years later she and John Asara pulled collagen protein from it and compared it with the proteins of living animals. Which creature's protein turned out to be the closest match?
answer: A chicken
choices: A chicken
A crocodile
An ostrich
An iguana
context: That 2007 result, published in Science, was the first time anyone had read a dinosaur's actual protein rather than just its bone shape -- and the recovered amino-acid sequence lined up with birds, matching chicken most closely of all. It was molecular confirmation of what the skeletons already suggested: birds are living theropod dinosaurs, so T. rex is far nearer kin to a barnyard hen than to any crocodile or lizard. The femur was specimen MOR 1125, nicknamed 'B-rex.' Sources: Schweitzer, Asara et al., Science 316:277-280 (2007), https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1138709 ; summary https://phys.org/news/2007-04-soft-tissue-million-year-old-tyrannosaurus-rex.html

question: A small bat flies out over the cattle country of Latin America on dark nights to find the only food it eats in its whole life. It is one of just three mammals on Earth that live on that one food and nothing else. What is that food?
answer: Blood
choices: Blood
Fruit
Insects
Nectar
context: The common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus) is one of just three mammal species that live entirely on blood. It doesn't suck it like the movies show -- it presses its grooved lower lip and tongue to a small cut and laps, like a cat at a bowl of milk. Source: Wikipedia, Vampire bat; HowStuffWorks 'Meet the Real Vampires of the Animal Kingdom'.

question: A common vampire bat lands beside a sleeping cow in the Latin American night. In total darkness it must find the one spot where its meal runs closest under the skin, and three tiny pits set around its nose find it without the bat ever seeing it. What do those pits sense?
answer: The heat radiating off the animal
choices: The heat radiating off the animal
The animal's heartbeat vibrations
The smell of the blood vessels
The faint sound of blood flowing
context: Three pit organs around the nose, called leaf pits, sense warmth radiating off a warm-blooded animal from as far as 20 centimeters away, letting the bat aim for the exact spot where blood runs closest to the surface. Source: Nature news 2011; National Geographic 'Vampire Bats Have Vein Sensors'; Wikipedia, Infrared sensing in vampire bats.

question: On a sleeping tapir in a Latin American forest, a common vampire bat slices a small nick in the animal's shoulder, and the tapir never stirs. The bat's two upper front teeth cut so cleanly because of an odd feature of their make-up. What makes them so keen?
answer: They lack enamel and stay razor-sharp
choices: They lack enamel and stay razor-sharp
They inject a numbing venom first
They are coated in a slick oil
They vibrate rapidly like a saw
context: The upper incisors are so sharp and lack enamel that they slice a tiny cut without waking the animal, and they're self-sharpening. Museum workers have cut themselves just handling vampire-bat skulls. Source: Wikipedia, Vampire bat; DentisX 'The Specialized Teeth of Vampire Bats for Blood Feeding'.

question: For a full 20 minutes a common vampire bat laps at the tiny nick it has cut in a sleeping cow's leg. An ordinary scratch would soon stop bleeding, but this little wound refuses to seal. What in the bat lets a single meal last that long?
answer: A chemical in its saliva that blocks the blood from clotting
choices: A chemical in its saliva that blocks the blood from clotting
A grip that keeps the two teeth wedged in the skin
A tongue that scrapes away each new clot
A body heat that keeps the blood warm and thin
context: The bat's saliva holds an anticoagulant nicknamed 'draculin' that blocks clotting, so the little cut keeps bleeding while the bat laps for up to 20 minutes. Source: Wikipedia, Draculin; MDPI Toxins 'Vampire Venom' (PMC6356263).

question: A bat that falls from a cave ceiling can only crawl awkwardly over the ground, dragging its wings, until it climbs up and takes off again. Nearly every one of the more than 1,300 kinds of bat in the world is that helpless on the ground, but the common vampire bat of Latin America is the great exception. What can it do there that no other bat can?
answer: Run, galloping along the ground
choices: Run, galloping along the ground
Swim across small streams
Dig burrows to hide in
Leap straight up ten times its height
context: Out of more than 1,300 bat species, only the common vampire bat can run. It gallops with a bounding gait that uses its powerful wings, not its legs, to push off the ground -- one scientist called it 'kind of like running push-ups.' On a treadmill vampire bats walk on all fours at slow speeds, but at about 1.8 km/h they break into a true run, leaving the ground completely between strides. Cornell researchers filmed them in a plexiglass cage to prove it. Source: Riskin & Hermanson, Nature (2005); Science 'Vampires Run'; Cornell Daily Sun (2005).

question: A 40-gram vampire bat can drink more than 20 grams of blood from a sleeping cow in a single meal, which would leave it too heavy to fly back to its roost. Yet only two minutes into the meal, it is already lightening itself. How does it shed the extra load so fast?
answer: It pees out the watery part right at the wound
choices: It pees out the watery part right at the wound
It dribbles the extra blood back out of its mouth
It pants the water away as warm, damp breath
It packs the blood into a pouch to drop later
context: A gorged bat would be too heavy to fly, so it starts peeing out the watery part of the blood within two minutes of feeding, right there at the wound. Source: Wikipedia, Vampire bat; Bohn et al., kidney physiology (PMC/PubMed 12010738).

question: Back at the cave roost, a common vampire bat returns hungry, having found no animal to feed on, and three missed nights in a row would starve it to death. A well-fed bat in the group can save its life. How does the full bat keep the hungry one alive?
answer: Throwing up part of its own blood meal into the hungry bat's mouth
choices: Throwing up part of its own blood meal into the hungry bat's mouth
Leading the hungry bat back to a fresh wound
Wrapping its wings around it to keep it warm
Sharing the warmest sleeping spot in the roost
context: A vampire bat dies after about 70 hours without a meal -- roughly three missed nights. A bat that fed well will regurgitate part of its meal into the mouth of a hungry roost-mate, giving up a little to save a friend's life. Source: Wilkinson (1984); Scientific American 'Blood Sisters'; Carter & Wilkinson (PMC3574350).

question: Gerald Carter and Gerald Wilkinson watched a captive colony of common vampire bats share blood with hungry roost-mates, logging 950 sharing bouts to learn what decides whom a full bat will help. One factor stood far above the rest. Which one?
answer: Whether the hungry bat had fed it before
choices: Whether the hungry bat had fed it before
How closely the two bats were related
Which bat was physically largest
How loudly the hungry bat begged
context: Across 950 sharing bouts in a captive colony, the best predictor of whether a full bat fed a hungry one was whether the hungry bat had fed it before, 8.5 times more important than relatedness. Vampire bats keep score, remembering who shared and paying it back. Source: Carter & Wilkinson 2013, Proceedings of the Royal Society B (PMC3574350).

question: A small, dark vampire squid drifts through the deep ocean. Its scientific name, Vampyroteuthis infernalis, means 'vampire squid from hell,' and it sounds like the name of a fierce hunter. What does this creature really feed on?
answer: Drifting flakes of dead matter it collects while floating
choices: Drifting flakes of dead matter it collects while floating
Live fish it chases down and drains of blood
Warm mammal blood, like the bat it is named for
Coral polyps it scrapes off the reef with its beak
context: The vampire squid (Vampyroteuthis infernalis) is the only cephalopod that does not chase living prey. It drifts in the deep and collects 'marine snow' — drifting flakes of dead matter. The scary name comes from its blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing, not its gentle habits. Source: Hoving & Robison 2012, MBARI news release (mbari.org).

question: A vampire squid only about 15 centimeters long, roughly the length of a kid's hand, drifts through the dark deep sea. One part of its body sets a world record: for its size, that part is the biggest of any animal on Earth. Which body part is it?
answer: Its globe-shaped eyes, each about 2.5 cm across
choices: Its globe-shaped eyes, each about 2.5 cm across
Its beak, sharp enough to crack open shellfish
Its brain, unusually large for a sea creature
Its webbed cloak, which can span a full meter
context: In a squid only about 6 inches long, the globe-shaped eyes are roughly 2.5 cm (1 inch) across — proportionately the largest eyes in the animal kingdom. They are huge to catch the faintest glimmer of deep-sea light. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid.

question: When a predator closes in, a vampire squid flips its arms up and back over its own head, turning almost inside out into a spiny ball that hides its soft body and points fleshy spines at the attacker. What do scientists call this defensive shape?
answer: The 'pineapple posture'
choices: The 'pineapple posture'
The 'artichoke fold'
The 'acorn ball'
The 'walnut curl'
context: Turning inside out into this spiny defensive shape — also called the 'pumpkin posture' — hides the vampire squid's vulnerable body and points its fleshy spines (cirri) outward at the attacker. It is the animal's signature move. Source: MBARI Animals of the Deep; Wikipedia: Vampire squid.

question: Somewhere between 600 and 900 meters down, where daylight never reaches, a hungry predator lunges at a vampire squid. Squids of the sunlit shallows hide behind a squirt of dark ink, but down here dark ink would disappear into dark water. What does the vampire squid shoot out instead?
answer: A glowing cloud of bioluminescent mucus
choices: A glowing cloud of bioluminescent mucus
A jet of icy water to numb the attacker
A spray of stinging venom from its arm tips
A burst of bubbles that blinds the hunter
context: The vampire squid has no ink sac at all — ink is useless in its lightless world. Instead it squirts a glowing cloud of bioluminescent mucus full of blue light orbs to dazzle predators, a dazzling display that can last nearly 10 minutes. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; MBARI.

question: A vampire squid hangs motionless in the deep and pays out two thin, sticky fishing threads. A diver might expect each one to reach an arm's length or so, but each unspools far past that. How far can a single feeding thread stretch?
answer: Up to eight times the length of its own body
choices: Up to eight times the length of its own body
About half the length of its own body
Roughly the same length as its own body
Up to twice the length of its own body
context: It catches food on two long, sticky, retractable filaments that can stretch up to eight times its body length, then wipes the loaded thread back through its arms to eat. Source: MBARI news release on Hoving & Robison 2012 (mbari.org).

question: A slow rain of specks drifts down past a vampire squid in the deep, and scientists call it marine snow. The name sounds pretty, but the flakes are the leftovers of everything living in the water above. Biologists describe the mix, bluntly, as three things. Which three?
answer: Dead bodies, poop, and snot
choices: Dead bodies, poop, and snot
Salt crystals, sand, and foam
Live plankton, eggs, and larvae
Seaweed, shells, and pebbles
context: Marine snow is remains of tiny algae and animals, fecal pellets from copepods and krill, and mucus debris from gelatinous larvaceans — dead bodies, poop, and snot. Source: MBARI / Hoving & Robison 2012 (mbari.org).

question: Carl Chun, a German zoologist leading the first deep-sea expedition to trawl the Atlantic, hauled a strange, soft creature up from thousands of feet down in 1903. He named it Vampyroteuthis infernalis, 'the vampire squid from hell.' Which features of the animal inspired that dramatic name?
answer: Its blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing
choices: Its blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing
Its habit of draining blood from fish
The bat-shaped fins on its head
The way it shrieks when pulled from the water
context: Vampyroteuthis infernalis literally means 'vampire squid from hell.' The teuthologist Carl Chun named it in 1903 for its dark blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing — not for its habits, which are gentle. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid.

question: A vampire squid makes its home in a strange band of the deep ocean, 600 to 900 meters down, where almost no other predator can follow it. It is not the cold or the crushing pressure that keeps other predators out; a chemistry problem suffocates most animals there. What deadly condition does the vampire squid tolerate?
answer: Oxygen drops as low as 3 percent saturation
choices: Oxygen drops as low as 3 percent saturation
The water pressure crushes bone instantly
Freezing temperatures turn the water to slush
Toxic gas bubbles up from vents on the seafloor
context: This band is called the 'oxygen minimum zone.' The vampire squid lives there permanently, surviving where oxygen saturation drops as low as 3 percent — an environment so hostile that few predators can follow it there. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; MBARI (Hoving).

question: In the black deep, a predator bites the glowing tip off one of a vampire squid's arms. The attacker turns on the flashing morsel as if it had caught a meal, and the squid glides away nearly unhurt. Why is the bitten-off arm tip such a clever loss?
answer: It keeps flashing as a decoy while the tip regrows
choices: It keeps flashing as a decoy while the tip regrows
It releases venom into the predator's mouth
It was already dead tissue the squid was shedding
It signals nearby squid to swarm the attacker
context: The vampire squid's body is dotted with light organs (photophores). If a predator bites off a glowing arm tip, the tip keeps flashing as a decoy while the squid escapes — and the arm tip grows back. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; Animal Diversity Web.

question: A vampire squid drifts through the deep midwater, a soft, dark body no bigger than a football, the only survivor of Vampyromorphida, an ancient order whose other species vanished millions of years ago. Biologists call it a 'living fossil.' What makes its place on the cephalopod family tree so strange?
answer: It shares traits with octopuses and squids but is neither
choices: It shares traits with octopuses and squids but is neither
It is the direct ancestor of the modern octopus
It is the only cephalopod without a beak or arms
It evolved from a fish that lost its bones
context: The vampire squid is the only surviving member of the order Vampyromorphida, an ancient cephalopod lineage. It shares traits with both octopuses and squids while being neither — a true living fossil. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; marine-biology sources.

question: Scientists put a Jurassic relative of the vampire squid, 164 million years old, through a synchrotron X-ray scanner, and the fine detail of its two long arms showed a way of life far from the modern squid's. What did those arms carry?
answer: Rows of muscular suckers for gripping live prey
choices: Rows of muscular suckers for gripping live prey
Sticky threads for gathering drifting flakes of food
Rows of glowing organs to lure prey closer
Curved hooks for snagging small passing fish
context: The fossil is Vampyronassa rhodanica, a roughly 10-cm cephalopod from the 164-million-year-old La Voulte-sur-Rhône deposit in France. Rowe and colleagues (Scientific Reports, 2022) used synchrotron X-ray microtomography on its exceptionally 3D-preserved soft tissue, revealing robust muscular suckers on two elongated dorsal arms — forming a watertight suction seal — plus sensory appendages for detecting prey. That marks it as an active hunter, in sharp contrast to the modern vampire squid's low-energy life scavenging marine snow. Source: Rowe et al., Scientific Reports (2022), nature.com/articles/s41598-022-12269-3; via Sci.News (sci.news/paleontology/vampyronassa-rhodanica-10934.html) and ScienceDaily.

question: Early naturalists who netted young vampire squid at different ages were so confused by the way the animals changed shape that they catalogued the same species several times over. A young one steers with a single pair of fins on its mantle. Once that mantle grows past about two centimeters, how do its fins change?
answer: A new pair sprouts up front and the old pair is absorbed
choices: A new pair sprouts up front and the old pair is absorbed
The single pair splits lengthwise, leaving it with four
The fins fuse into one broad fin ringing the mantle
The fins are pulled inside and it jets like a young squid
context: Juvenile vampire squid have a single pair of fins and swim by jet propulsion. When the mantle reaches about 15–25 mm long, a second pair of fins develops farther forward (anterior); once the new pair matures, the original pair is reabsorbed, and the animal switches to swimming by flapping its fins. Because it looks so different at each stage, early naturalists mistakenly described the life stages as separate species. Source: Animal Diversity Web (animaldiversity.org/accounts/Vampyroteuthis_infernalis); corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Vampire squid'.

question: A long, thin, brown stick insect hides in plain sight among the twigs of a bush, and birds and lizards walk right past without spotting it. It adds one extra trick, copying something a real twig does on a gentle, breezy day. What does it do?
answer: It rocks and sways gently from side to side
choices: It rocks and sways gently from side to side
It curls up tightly into a hard ball
It buries itself in the loose soil below
It spins a sticky web between two leaves
context: Many stick insects sway as they walk or rest, mimicking a real twig or leaf trembling in the breeze — so even their MOVEMENT doesn't give them away. Source: Wikipedia, Phasmatodea ('swaying' behavioural crypsis).

question: A ptarmigan, a plump grouse of snowy mountains, sits pure white against the winter drifts and turns mottled brown each summer. The ground where it lives lies buried in deep snow for half the year. What flips the switch between the two coats, right on schedule?
answer: The number of daylight hours
choices: The number of daylight hours
The temperature of the air
The first snowfall of the season
The food it finds to eat
context: The change is triggered by DAY LENGTH, not temperature — so the timing is the same every year even when snow comes early or late, which can leave a half-turned bird briefly mismatched. Source: Audubon Field Guide, Rock Ptarmigan; Alaska Dept. Fish & Game.

question: A leaf insect clings among the foliage of a Southeast Asian rainforest, its flat green body laced with fake veins and ragged brown edges, so a bird gliding past sees only a leaf. It even wears one extra detail that makes its 'leaf' look old and used rather than fresh. What is that finishing touch?
answer: Fake chewed-out bite marks and blemishes
choices: Fake chewed-out bite marks and blemishes
A row of bright warning eyespots
A dusting of glittering silver scales
A pair of long trailing feelers
context: The insect mimics a leaf a caterpillar already chewed on — a perfect, unblemished leaf would actually look MORE suspicious than a battered one. Source: Australian Museum, Leaf and Stick Insects (Phasmatodea).

question: An octopus resting on a coral reef can make its smooth skin suddenly erupt into a bumpy, ragged surface that copies the seaweed, sponges and coral nearby, and flatten it again when it wants to swim off. Biologists call these muscle bumps papillae. Roughly how fast can the octopus throw them up?
answer: In about a fifth of a second
choices: In about a fifth of a second
In about ten minutes
Over the course of a full day
Only once, permanently, as it grows up
context: The bumps are muscle-driven skin projections called papillae; the octopus pushes them up in about 0.2 seconds and can hold them or drop them at will. Source: Scientific American, octopus 3-D camouflage; PMC6059360, Neural Control of Dynamic 3-D Skin Papillae.

question: A decorator crab walks a coral reef wearing a living garden it planted on its own back. Its shell bristles with tiny hooked hairs that grab like Velcro, and instead of hiding under things, it builds its disguise onto those hooks. What does it stick there?
answer: Living sponges, algae, and stinging anemones
choices: Living sponges, algae, and stinging anemones
Flat pebbles it glues down with mucus
Shed scales borrowed from passing fish
A hard crust of dried salt and sand
context: The crab plucks bits of the reef and presses them onto its hooked bristles — anemones even add stinging defense — and can swap the decorations out as it moves to new ground. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, Decorator Crab; Wikipedia, Decorator crab.

question: A cuttlefish paints patterns across its skin with tiny pigment sacs, and each sac is a miniature machine: a ring of muscles pulls it wide, and its own nerve runs straight back to the brain. With all that equipment per sac, how many fit in one square millimeter of skin?
answer: Around 200 of them
choices: Around 200 of them
Around 5 of them
Around 20 of them
Just a single large one
context: These pigment sacs are called chromatophores, and they're packed up to about 200 per square millimeter — each with its own muscles and its own nerve line — which is how a cuttlefish can 'paint' finely detailed patterns across its skin. Source: Roger Hanlon, National Geographic; PMC3403426, chromatophore density.

question: A flounder lies flat on the seabed, changing its skin to match the sand or gravel beneath it. In one famous test, scientists laid a checkerboard of black and white squares under one, a pattern found nowhere in nature, and cameras watched its skin. About a minute later, what had happened to the flounder?
answer: It broke into dark and light blotches copying the squares
choices: It broke into dark and light blotches copying the squares
It settled on a single grey average of the whole board
It flashed rippling stripes across its back
It darkened uniformly to a flat solid tone
context: The flounder's skin broke into dark and light blotches roughly matching the checkerboard — a striking demonstration of background-matching against an unnatural pattern, rather than just averaging or flashing. Source: American Museum of Natural History; Royal Society Open Science, flounder background-matching study.

question: A shark, a deer and a penguin all wear the same two tones: dark on the back, pale on the belly. Sunlight pours down from above, so a rounded animal casts a shadow across its own underside that gives away its solid shape. How does the light underside defeat that shadow?
answer: The paler belly reflects light back to fill the shadow to an even tone
choices: The paler belly reflects light back to fill the shadow to an even tone
The dark back soaks up the sunlight before it can cast a shadow
The dark-pale boundary sits where a predator's eye locks, pulling the gaze off
The pale belly matches the bright surface above, erasing it from below
context: This is countershading: the naturally-shaded belly is painted paler so it reflects light back and fills in its own shadow, leaving the body one even tone that reads as flat and un-solid instead of a spottable 3-D shape. The other options are real tricks other animals use — heat-absorbing dark backs, disruptive edge patterns, mirror-belly matching the surface from below — but none is how countershading works. Source: Wikipedia, Countershading ('Thayer's law'); The Conversation, dark backs and pale bellies.

question: A satanic leaf-tailed gecko clings to a branch in Madagascar looking like a dead leaf come to life, its flat tail notched, fake-veined and ragged as if half-rotted. One more feature erases the tell-tale line where its body meets the bark. What blurs the gecko's outline?
answer: Fringes of skin along its edges
choices: Fringes of skin along its edges
A coat of loose downy fur
A shell of overlapping hard plates
A trailing cloud of fine bubbles
context: Skin fringes break up the gecko's silhouette against the forest floor, so predators can't find the crisp edge that would betray an animal. Source: Wikipedia, Uroplatus phantasticus; Smithsonian National Zoo, Phantastic Leaf-tailed Gecko.

question: A mimic octopus on the sandy Indo-Pacific seafloor does more than blend in: it impersonates other animals to scare predators away. In one famous trick it sinks six arms into a burrow and stretches out only two, one to each side, waving them. Which deadly, banded reef animal does that striped, wavy shape copy?
answer: A banded sea snake
choices: A banded sea snake
A stinging box jellyfish
A bristling stonefish
A venomous cone snail
context: By tucking six arms and trailing two, the octopus mimics a banded sea snake — all four choices name genuinely venomous reef animals, but the two-armed, striped display copies the snake. It also splays its arms to imitate a spiny lionfish and flattens all eight to glide like a flatfish, swapping impersonations to match whatever predator is near. Source: Wikipedia, Mimic octopus; ScienceDaily, flatfish mimicry study.

question: A cuttlefish meets shades its pigment sacs simply cannot mix, yet it matches them anyway, using a hidden second layer of skin beneath the pigment. What trick does that under-layer use to fill in the missing shades?
answer: Mirror-like cells bounce back whatever light is around
choices: Mirror-like cells bounce back whatever light is around
It slowly grows fresh pigment to order over minutes
It borrows dye absorbed from the food it eats
It bends its whole body to catch a different angle
context: By pulling the top pigment sacs aside, the cuttlefish lets reflective under-layer cells — iridophores and white leucophores — throw back the surrounding light, filling in colors the pigments alone can't produce, and matching a shade it may not even be able to see. Source: Nature Scitable, Cephalopod Camouflage.

question: Velociraptor stalks the kids through a kitchen in the movie Jurassic Park as a scaly monster taller than a grown-up. The real one, dug from Mongolia's Gobi Desert in the 1920s, was about the size of which farm bird?
answer: A turkey
choices: A turkey
An ostrich
A chicken
A goose
context: The real Velociraptor stood only about 0.5 m (1.6 ft) at the hip and ran 1.5–2 m long — turkey-sized, far smaller than the man-sized monsters of the films. Source: Natural History Museum, nhm.ac.uk/discover/velociraptor-facts.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor.

question: A Velociraptor hunted small prey across what is now Mongolia around 75 million years ago. Its fossil braincases, the bony shells that once held its brain, show paleontologists what its head was really like. What did its skull give it?
answer: A relatively large brain for its size
choices: A relatively large brain for its size
Heat-sensing pits like a pit viper
A second jaw joint for a wider gape
A bony crest for booming calls
context: For its size Velociraptor was smart and sharp-sensed, with a relatively large brain, keen eyes and a good sense of smell — a small, clever hunter that chased small prey, not the giant creatures of the films. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor; ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7542195/ (endocranium and trophic ecology of Velociraptor).

question: The makers of Jurassic Park wanted raptors scarier than the real Velociraptor of Mongolia, which was far too small for the part. They modeled their monsters on a bigger North American cousin, a 10-foot meat-eater named for the huge curved killing claw on each of its feet. Which cousin was it?
answer: Deinonychus
choices: Deinonychus
Tyrannosaurus
Spinosaurus
Allosaurus
context: The film's 'Velociraptors' were sized after Deinonychus, a larger raptor cousin — which is why the movie monsters dwarf the real turkey-sized, feathered Velociraptor of Mongolia. Source: nhm.ac.uk/discover/velociraptor-facts.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor.

question: On the second toe of each foot, Velociraptor carried a huge, curved sickle claw, bigger than the toe claws around it. Yet fossil footprints of raptors like it show no drag mark from that claw at all: only the two outer toes ever touched the ground. Why did Velociraptor keep the big claw raised?
answer: To keep it sharp like a switchblade
choices: To keep it sharp like a switchblade
To grip slippery rocks
To signal to other raptors
Because it was broken
context: The sickle claw curved over 6.5 cm (2.6 in) around its arc. Held up off the ground, it stayed unworn and razor-sharp — raised and ready like a switchblade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor; nhm.ac.uk/discover/velociraptor-facts.html.

question: Alan Turner's team examined a well-preserved Velociraptor forearm bone in 2007. The Jurassic Park movies drew the dinosaur as a bare, scaly killer, but along the bone's rear edge ran a neat row of six evenly spaced bumps, a pattern with a well-known meaning on modern birds. What were the bumps?
answer: Quill knobs where feathers anchored
choices: Quill knobs where feathers anchored
Scars from an old bite wound
Growth rings marking its age
Attachment points for venom glands
context: The six 'quill knobs' on specimen IGM 100/981 are the same anchor points where wing feathers attach in living birds — direct proof of feathered arms, even though Velociraptor could not fly. Velociraptor was a feathered dinosaur; feathers on non-flying dinosaurs likely helped with warmth and display before flight ever evolved. Source: Turner et al. 2007, Science, science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1145076; nationalgeographic.com/science/article/evidence-that-velociraptor-had-feathers.

question: Sprinting after lizards and baby dinosaurs across ancient Mongolia, a Velociraptor held its long tail out stiff behind it. Bundles of hardened, bony tendons ran through that tail and turned it into a rigid rod, almost like a broomstick. What did the rigid tail let the running hunter do?
answer: Turn on a dime while chasing prey
choices: Turn on a dime while chasing prey
Whip it like a club in defense
Prop itself upright to rest
Rattle it to warn rivals
context: Ossified tendons — bundles of bony rods — stiffened the long tail into a counterbalance, helping Velociraptor turn and change direction quickly at a run. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor.

question: Paleontologists who built the 'raptor prey restraint' model see Velociraptor hunting much like a modern eagle: it leapt onto smaller prey, pinned it under its body weight and hooked the big sickle claw in to hold it fast. In their model, what actually killed the pinned prey?
answer: Its jaws
choices: Its jaws
The sickle claw
Its stiff tail
Its front arms
context: This is the 'raptor prey restraint' model: the sickle claw gripped and pinned rather than slashed, while the jaws did the killing — just as a hawk or eagle holds prey with its talons and dispatches it with the beak. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor; livescience.com/deinonychus-dinosaur-claw-pin-grasp.

question: A Velociraptor and a plant-eating Protoceratops fought in the Mongolian desert, the raptor's sickle claw at the plant-eater's throat and the Protoceratops biting down on its arm. Scientists found the pair still locked in mid-battle in 1971, and they believe both were suddenly buried alive together. What killed them?
answer: A collapsing sand dune
choices: A collapsing sand dune
A rising flood
A lava flow
A tar pit
context: The 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen froze a real dinosaur fight in stone, the raptor's claw at the Protoceratops's throat and its right arm trapped in the plant-eater's jaws, when a collapsing dune or a sudden sandstorm buried them mid-struggle. It is now a national treasure of Mongolia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Dinosaurs; amnh.org/explore/ology/ology-cards/038-fighting-dinosaurs.

question: David Hone and his team peered inside the rib cage of a beautifully preserved Velociraptor fossil in 2012, at the spot where its last meal would have been. Tucked in there lay a long, thin limb bone from another animal, the leftovers of dinner. What kind of creature did that bone belong to?
answer: A large flying reptile.
choices: A large flying reptile.
A young horned dinosaur.
A small burrowing mammal.
A slow shelled turtle.
context: The bone came from an azhdarchid pterosaur, a flying reptile with a wingspan near two metres, an animal far too large and formidable for a turkey-sized raptor to have pulled from the air alive. David Hone's team read it instead as a scavenged meal: the raptor fed on the carcass after the pterosaur was already dead. A second clue points the same way. In 2010 Hone described shed Velociraptor teeth scattered beside a tooth-marked Protoceratops jaw, read as late-stage carcass consumption, the raptor gnawing bony scraps from a head after the good meat was gone. Together they show an opportunistic carnivore that took carrion as readily as it took live prey. (Hone et al. 2012, azhdarchid gut content; Hone et al. 2010, Protoceratops jaw. https://www.ucd.ie/news/2012/03MAR12/080312-Preserved-bone-of-Pterosaur-in--stomach-of-Velociraptor.html ; https://archosaurmusings.wordpress.com/2012/03/04/velociraptor-scavenging-azhdarchid/ )

question: Schmitz and Motani measured the bony ring that sits inside Velociraptor's eye socket in 2011. In living animals the size of that ring matches the hours they keep, whether they are out by day or by night. What did the ring say about Velociraptor's active hours?
answer: It prowled through the dark of night.
choices: It prowled through the dark of night.
It hunted under the bright midday sun.
It stirred only at dawn and dusk.
It stayed active around the clock.
context: Schmitz and Motani measured the scleral ring, a bony circlet inside the eye socket, across 164 living species and found its shape tracks activity: a wide opening gathers faint light in night-active animals, while a thick narrow ring suits daylight hunters. Applied to fossils, Velociraptor came out nocturnal, while the plant-eater Protoceratops looked cathemeral (active by day or night), hinting the famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' clash may have happened at twilight. It remains a genuine debate: later work questioned whether eye shape alone can cleanly separate day-active from night-active animals. (Schmitz & Motani 2011, 'Nocturnality in Dinosaurs Inferred from Scleral Ring and Orbit Morphology.' https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21493820/ ; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/dinosaurs-around-the-clock-or-how-we-know-velociraptor-hunted-by-night )

question: A gardener in Georgia is weeding a flower bed when a fuzzy bug the size of a fingernail scurries across the bare dirt, bright orange and black and covered in soft, velvety hair. Locals call it a velvet ant, but it has no bent antennae and no ant waist. What is it really?
answer: A wingless female wasp
choices: A wingless female wasp
A furry moth caterpillar
A flightless beetle
A ground-dwelling spider
context: The velvet ant belongs to the wasp family Mutillidae. Every female is flightless and fuzzy, while the males have dark translucent wings — they look so unlike each other that the two sexes are easily mistaken for different species. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: Farmers call the fuzzy orange-and-black velvet ant the cow killer, because its sting hurts so badly that a grown adult can scream. But pain and poison are not the same thing. Measured side by side with an ordinary honeybee's venom, how does the velvet ant's compare?
answer: Far less toxic than a honeybee's
choices: Far less toxic than a honeybee's
More toxic than any other insect
Roughly ten times as toxic
About the same as a honeybee's
context: The screaming pain comes from overwhelming the nerves, not from poisoning the body: the venom is actually far less toxic than a honeybee's. No cow — and no human — has ever died from the sting; the 'cow killer' name is pure pain-reputation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: A collector picks up a velvet ant between two fingers, and it does something no true ant would ever do: it rubs a pair of rough ridges on its abdomen together, the way a cricket rubs its wings, and fires off a rapid, high-pitched chirp loud enough to hear. What is the squeak for?
answer: To warn a predator to let go
choices: To warn a predator to let go
To call a mate over
To echolocate in the dark
To cool its body by vibrating
context: This chirping is called stridulation, made by scraping ridged patches on the abdominal segments together. Both males and females do it — a sound warning to back up the insect's other defenses when it is grabbed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: An insect collector pins an ordinary honeybee to his display board with ease, but when he presses the steel pin against a velvet ant, the pin will not go in. Sometimes he must take up a small hand drill and bore a hole first. Why is this little insect so hard to pin?
answer: Its exoskeleton is armored many times harder to crush
choices: Its exoskeleton is armored many times harder to crush
Its body is coated in a slippery wax
It curls into a spiny defensive ball
Its shell is hollow and shatters the pin
context: A velvet ant's exoskeleton takes roughly eleven times more crushing force to break than a honeybee's. This tank-like armor is also what lets a female raid another wasp's nest and stay 'impervious to the stings' of the furious owners. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: A female velvet ant roams sunny fields in search of a nursery to raid, for she never builds a nest of her own. She creeps down into the underground burrow of a ground-nesting bee, hunting for the owner's helpless young. When she finds a bee larva, what does she do to it?
answer: Lays an egg on it so her own young can devour it
choices: Lays an egg on it so her own young can devour it
Carries it back to her own burrow
Stings it to store as paralyzed food
Eats it whole on the spot
context: The velvet ant is an ectoparasitoid: her larva feeds on the host from the OUTSIDE. Eastern cow killers (Dasymutilla occidentalis) target big diggers like cicada killers, laying an egg in the pupal case of the host's young. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: In the dark leaf litter of the forest floor, a velvet worm creeps up on a cricket far too fast to catch by chasing. From a few centimetres away it launches a surprise attack that pins the cricket to the ground before it can hop. What does the velvet worm fire at its prey?
answer: Two jets of sticky glue from nozzles beside its mouth
choices: Two jets of sticky glue from nozzles beside its mouth
A cloud of choking gas from vents along its back
A cluster of barbed harpoons from its clawed feet
A jolt of electricity through the damp soil
context: The velvet worm has a pair of nozzles (oral papillae) on either side of its mouth. It sprays two jets of slime that fling a net of glue over prey from a short distance, sticking the animal to the ground before the velvet worm moves in to eat it. Source: eartharchives.org/articles/velvet-worms-the-voracious-snipers-of-the-undergrowth/

question: A velvet worm's two slime nozzles are tiny, yet a single squirt lays down a wide zig-zag net of glue that covers far more ground than a straight shot could. As the slime fires, the nozzles blur back and forth 30 to 60 times a second, though the animal has no muscle anywhere near fast enough to wave them. What makes them whip so fast?
answer: The force of the fluid firing through the floppy nozzle whips it on its own
choices: The force of the fluid firing through the floppy nozzle whips it on its own
A ring of super-fast muscle unique to the mouth region
A spinning valve that flicks the stream side to side
Rapid puffs of air that buffet the jet mid-flight
context: This is an elastohydrodynamic instability: the fast fluid passing through the flexible nozzle makes it flail on its own, with no fast muscle involved. The worm's quickest real muscle is about 25 times too slow to move the nozzle that fast. Source: Concha et al., Nature Communications 2015, PMC4382676.

question: A velvet worm oozes through the leaf litter like a soft, stubby-legged worm, but its body plan is over 500 million years old, tracing back to the Cambrian seas. It is not a true worm, and it is not an insect. Where does biology place it?
answer: In its own phylum, Onychophora, the 'claw-bearers'
choices: In its own phylum, Onychophora, the 'claw-bearers'
Among the segmented annelid worms, like earthworms
Among the myriapods, alongside centipedes
Among the soft-bodied molluscs, like slugs
context: The velvet worm is its own phylum, Onychophora ('claw-bearers') - a soft-bodied survivor of a Cambrian-era body plan over 500 million years old. Its closest living relatives are the tiny tardigrades (water bears). Source: Burgess Shale (Royal Ontario Museum); bmcecolevol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12862-014-0222-z.

question: In Australia, families of up to fifteen velvet worms of the species Euperipatoides rowelli hunt together to bring down prey too big for one alone. When the prey is stuck fast in glue, the family does not share it evenly: one member feeds for up to an hour and bites any that try to sneak in early. Who eats first?
answer: The dominant female, usually the largest and most aggressive
choices: The dominant female, usually the largest and most aggressive
The oldest male, who leads the group on the hunt
Whichever animal landed the first slime shot
The smallest youngsters, fed before the adults
context: These velvet worm families are ruled by a single dominant 'alpha female,' usually the biggest and most aggressive, who keeps order by biting and shoving. She feeds first and alone for up to an hour before the other females, then the males and young, take their turn. Source: Reinhard & Rowell, Journal of Zoology 2005; eartharchives.org.

question: A poison-dart frog in a Central American rainforest oozes poison from its skin, and one lick can kill a person. A desert rattlesnake carries a toxin just as deadly in its head, yet a person could drink it from a cup and live. The difference is delivery. Which of the two injects its toxin through a wound, as venom?
answer: The rattlesnake
choices: The rattlesnake
The poison-dart frog
Both of them
Neither of them
context: Venom must be INJECTED through a bite, sting, or spine; poison harms on eating, touching, or inhaling. The rattlesnake injects venom through its bite, which is why swallowing that venom is harmless — it is made of proteins too large to cross the gut wall into your blood. The poison-dart frog's toxin sits on its skin and harms on contact or if eaten. Source: Natural History Museum, 'Bite or be bitten' (nhm.ac.uk/discover/bite-or-be-bitten.html).

question: A viper strikes a leg, and its haemotoxic venom breaks down the tissue: the leg swells, bruises purple and bleeds under the skin. A cobra's neurotoxic venom works differently, blocking the signals that travel from nerve to muscle, and that is why a cobra bite can kill faster. Which part of the body does it quietly shut down?
answer: The breathing muscles
choices: The breathing muscles
The blood-clotting system
The heart's valves
The digestive tract
context: Neurotoxic venom (typical of cobras) blocks the nerve signals that command the muscles, so the breathing muscles fail and the victim cannot draw breath. Hemotoxic venom (typical of vipers) instead destroys blood cells, prevents clotting, and rots tissue — hence the swelling and bruising. Real venoms usually mix both; the clean cobra-vs-viper split is a teaching simplification. Source: Zoo Atlanta, 'Snake venoms and myths'; Snake venom, Wikipedia.

question: A spitting cobra in Africa rears up when a threat comes close and sprays venom through tiny holes in its fangs, aiming a fine stream as far as 3 meters. It tracks the threat's movements as it spits, and about 90 percent of the time the venom hits one particular part of the body. Which part?
answer: The eyes
choices: The eyes
The mouth
The nose
The hands
context: A 'spitting' cobra sprays venom out of forward-facing holes in its fangs, aiming for the eyes of a threat up to about 3 metres away; roughly 90% of spits hit the eyes, and the snake predicts where the threat's head will move. This is defense, not hunting. Source: Live Science, 'Secret to Spitting Cobra's Deadly Accurate Aim Revealed'; Britannica, 'Spitting cobra.'

question: A tiny octopus no bigger than a golf ball lives on the shallow reefs of the Pacific and Indian Oceans. Cornered by a curious diver, it suddenly lights up with about 60 electric-blue rings across its yellow skin, and if the diver keeps pressing in, it bites with a beak loaded with tetrodotoxin, one of the most powerful nerve poisons known. Which animal is it?
answer: The blue-ringed octopus
choices: The blue-ringed octopus
The mimic octopus
The vampire squid
The reef cuttlefish
context: The blue-ringed octopus flashes roughly 60 iridescent blue rings as an aposematic (warning) display before biting. Its tetrodotoxin is one of the deadliest nerve toxins known — far more potent than cyanide — and there is no antivenom. Source: Britannica, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Natural History Museum (nhm.ac.uk). LEGEND.

question: A slow, thumb-sized cone snail on a tropical coral reef hunts fast little fish. It stretches a fleshy tube from its shell, fires a single hollow harpoon on a tether, stabs a fish, injects venom and reels the paralyzed meal back in. What is that harpoon made from?
answer: A modified tooth
choices: A modified tooth
A sharpened claw
A hardened tentacle
A stinging hair
context: The geography cone snail (Conus geographus) fires a single hollow, barbed radular TOOTH — a modified tooth on a tether — from an extendable proboscis, then reels the speared fish back to swallow it. Source: Conus geographus, Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conus_geographus).

question: A fish brushes a jellyfish's trailing tentacle, and one of thousands of microscopic sting-capsules called nematocysts fires: a tightly coiled tube unrolls and drives a barb into the fish in about 3 milliseconds, injecting venom before the fish even feels the touch. How does that speed rank among all the movements biologists have measured in living things?
answer: One of the fastest movements known
choices: One of the fastest movements known
About as fast as a human blink
A typical nerve-reflex speed
The fastest a muscle can contract
context: On contact a nematocyst fires in roughly 3 milliseconds, driving a spined tube into the skin to inject venom — one of the fastest movements known in all of biology, far quicker than a reflex, a blink, or a muscle twitch. Each is a pre-loaded microscopic harpoon. Source: University of Melbourne AVRU, 'Venomous marine animals — jellyfish'; Firing the Sting, PMC4379534.

question: A slow cone snail hunting fast-swimming fish skips the harpoon its relatives use. It releases a cloud of a chemical the fish's own body already makes; the cloud drifts in through the fish's gills and drops it into a helpless stupor, and the snail swallows it whole. Which of the fish's own hormones has the snail turned into a weapon?
answer: Insulin
choices: Insulin
Adrenaline
Melatonin
Testosterone
context: Certain cone snails release a specialized INSULIN into the water; through the gills it drives the fish into hypoglycemic shock, sedating it — chemistry out-drugging a faster animal. Researchers nicknamed this sedating blend the 'nirvana cabal.' Source: PNAS 2015, 'Specialized insulin is used for chemical warfare by fish-hunting cone snails.' LEGEND.

question: A golf-ball-sized octopus of Pacific tide pools bites with tetrodotoxin, one of the deadliest poisons on Earth, enough to kill a person in minutes. Yet when biologists read its DNA looking for the recipe, they found no gene anywhere that could build the toxin: the octopus is not making it. Where does the toxin come from?
answer: Bacteria living in its salivary glands
choices: Bacteria living in its salivary glands
A gland behind each blue ring
The venom of prey it eats
Sunlight stored in its skin
context: The octopus does not make its own toxin — symbiotic bacteria in its salivary glands produce the tetrodotoxin. That also makes it BOTH venomous (its bite injects the toxin) and poisonous (harmful if eaten). Source: Britannica, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Natural History Museum, 'Bite or be bitten' (nhm.ac.uk).

question: A box jellyfish carries one of the deadliest venoms in the sea, yet for decades nobody knew how it wrecked a cell. Raymond Lau and Greg Neely's team ran a gene-editing screen in 2019 and found the venom can harm a cell only when the cell offers it one particular molecule; a drug that strips that molecule away works as an antidote. What does the venom depend on?
answer: Cholesterol built into the cell membrane
choices: Cholesterol built into the cell membrane
Iron carried in the red blood cells
Calcium stored inside the muscle fibers
Sugar coating the cell's outer surface
context: Chironex fleckeri is often called the most venomous animal in the sea: a single individual carries roughly enough venom to kill about 60 adults, and a severe sting can stop the heart in 2-5 minutes. The venom works through pore-forming proteins (porins) that punch holes in cell membranes; potassium floods out, and the resulting spike in blood potassium (hyperkalemia) drives cardiovascular collapse. In 2019 a University of Sydney team (Greg Neely and Raymond Lau) ran a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen and found the venom requires membrane cholesterol to act. Common cholesterol-stripping drugs called cyclodextrins block the damage and, in mice, still worked as an antidote up to about 15 minutes after the sting. Sources: Nature Communications 2019, 'Molecular dissection of box jellyfish venom cytotoxicity highlights an effective venom antidote' (s41467-019-09681-1); University of Sydney news, 1 May 2019; Wikipedia, 'Chironex fleckeri'.

question: Long before any snake existed, a Late Triassic reptile on the crocodile-and-dinosaur branch already delivered venom. Today it survives only as fossilized teeth in the rock. Laid out in order, those teeth are prized because they preserve which rare record?
answer: A step-by-step shift from an open surface groove to a fully enclosed internal tube
choices: A step-by-step shift from an open surface groove to a fully enclosed internal tube
A step-by-step shift from a crushing molar into a sharp slicing blade
The earliest known bite marks left by one predator upon another
A single fang regrown and resharpened dozens of times in one lifetime
context: The animal is Uatchitodon, a Late Triassic archosauriform (a reptile on the crocodile-and-dinosaur branch, roughly 220-237 million years ago), known only from its teeth. Those teeth are extraordinary because, across different specimens, they capture a complete transition series: from a shallow open groove on the tooth surface to a fully enclosed, tube-like internal canal for conducting venom, with some teeth carrying two canals apiece. This 'grooves to tubes' sequence shows the very pathway by which a venom-delivery system evolves, it predates venomous snakes by well over 100 million years, and it happened on a completely separate reptile lineage. Sources: Mitchell, Heckert & Sues 2010, Naturwissenschaften (The Science of Nature), 'Grooves to tubes: evolution of the venom delivery system in a Late Triassic reptile' (doi 10.1007/s00114-010-0729-0); Wikipedia, 'Uatchitodon'.

question: Deep in the western Pacific Ocean, about a kilometer down in the cold black water, a slender white vase sits on the muddy seafloor. It is a Venus flower basket, a kind of sponge, and its whole cage-like skeleton is woven from a lattice of long, thin spikes called spicules. What are those spikes made of?
answer: Silica — the same stuff as glass
choices: Silica — the same stuff as glass
Coral limestone
Woven seaweed fiber
Hardened tree resin
context: The Venus's flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a deep-sea glass sponge whose entire skeleton is woven from silica, the same material as glass, built into a delicate white latticework cage shaped like a vase or basket, roughly 10 to 30 cm (4 to 12 inches) tall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus'_flower_basket

question: A pair of baby shrimp squeeze in through the tiny openings in the walls of a Venus flower basket, a deep-sea sponge shaped like a slender vase. They settle inside, feed on scraps that drift in and keep the inner walls clean. As they keep growing, something happens that they never planned for. What is it?
answer: They grow too big to ever get back out
choices: They grow too big to ever get back out
They eat their way through the glass
They turn transparent like the sponge
They stop growing to stay small
context: A breeding pair of tiny shrimp (Spongicola venusta) swims into the sponge as babies, then grows too big to ever get back out through the glass lattice — so the pair spends its whole life imprisoned together inside the glass cage, cleaning it in exchange for food and shelter. Their own babies are born small enough to slip out through the lattice and swim off to find a sponge of their own, so only the parents stay imprisoned, and each new sponge gets its own captive couple. Source: https://schmidtocean.org/cruise-log-post/a-deep-sea-love-story/

question: A Venus flower basket stands upright about a kilometer down, its open top facing into a slow, steady current that brings it food. It must stay upright to feed, but the seafloor there is soft mud with no rock or reef to grip. How does it hold itself up?
answer: A tuft of hair-thin glass threads driven into the mud
choices: A tuft of hair-thin glass threads driven into the mud
Suckers that clamp onto passing fish
A heavy stone it swallows for ballast
Long muscular roots that dig downward
context: The sponge anchors to the muddy deep seafloor with a tuft of glass threads — spun-glass fibers about 5 to 20 cm long and as thin as a human hair — that hold it upright in the current like a base of spun glass. Source: https://www.pnas.org/content/101/10/3358.full

question: Some of the thin strands of a Venus flower basket stunned materials researchers. Grown in cold seawater with no furnace, they already pull off a high-tech trick that the researchers' own factories struggle to match. What do these strands do?
answer: Pipe light along their length like fiber-optic cables
choices: Pipe light along their length like fiber-optic cables
Spin a trickle of electricity from the passing current
Flex toward drifting food and grip it like tiny fingers
Ring with sound to scare off circling deep-sea hunters
context: Each thread is a natural fibre-optic cable: a core of pure silica about two micrometres across, wrapped around a central organic filament and sheathed in a finely layered shell that works just like the optical cladding of a telecom cable -- and it carries light just as well. Because the sponge grows the thread in cold seawater instead of a furnace, it can lace the glass with impurities such as sodium that IMPROVE light transmission but get destroyed in high-temperature factory glass. And unlike brittle manufactured fibre, you can tie the sponge's thread in a knot without snapping it. Source: Sundar, Yablon, Grazul, Ilan & Aizenberg, 'Fibre-optical features of a glass sponge,' Nature vol. 424, pp. 899-900 (2003), https://www.nature.com/articles/424899a ; Scientific American, 'Sea Sponge Inspires Better Fiber-Optic Cables.'

question: Katia Bertoldi, James Weaver and Matheus Fernandes, engineers at Harvard, 3D-printed the lattice of a Venus flower basket's skeleton beside the criss-cross bracing that has held up bridges since the 1820s. Then they loaded both, built from the same amount of material, until they buckled. How did the sponge's design do?
answer: It carried over 20% more load before buckling
choices: It carried over 20% more load before buckling
It matched the human grid almost exactly
It gave way first but sprang back unharmed
It held less, though it bent much further
context: The sponge's cage is no plain grid: a square lattice is overlaid with a DOUBLE set of parallel diagonal struts fused across it in a checkerboard pattern. Harvard engineers Matheus Fernandes, James Weaver and Katia Bertoldi 3D-printed rival lattice shapes and ran finite-element buckling tests, and found the paired-diagonal design is over 20% stronger -- higher buckling resistance for the same amount of material -- than the criss-cross lattice humans have braced bridges and towers with since Ithiel Town patented it in the 1820s. The sponge quietly solved a load-bearing problem better than 200 years of human engineering. Source: Fernandes, Weaver, Bertoldi et al., 'Mechanically robust lattices inspired by deep-sea glass sponges,' Nature Materials vol. 20 (2021), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41563-020-0798-1 ; Harvard SEAS news, https://seas.harvard.edu/news/marine-sponges-inspire-next-generation-skyscrapers-and-bridges.

question: A lizard lunges at a vinegaroon, a small desert arachnid of the American Southwest also called a whip scorpion, which has no stinger and no venom anywhere in its body. The vinegaroon swings its rear end up toward the attacker's face and fires a fine spray. What ordinary kitchen smell does the spray give off?
answer: Vinegar
choices: Vinegar
Rotten eggs
Bitter almonds
Ammonia
context: That sharp vinegar smell is how the animal earned its common name: the vinegaroon. The spray is mostly acetic acid, the very acid that makes vinegar sour, and the vinegaroon can aim it from a few inches out to about a foot away. Source: Oakland Zoo, Giant Vinegaroon (oaklandzoo.org/animals/giant-vinegaroon).

question: A vinegaroon of the American Southwest drags a long, thin, whip-like tail behind it that looks, from a distance, just like a scorpion's stinger. Yet the whip has no point and no venom, and it cannot hurt anything. What does the vinegaroon really use it for?
answer: Feeling its way through the dark
choices: Feeling its way through the dark
Storing fat for the winter
Signaling to a mate
Anchoring it in its burrow
context: The whip is called the flagellum, and it works like a rear antenna. The vinegaroon waves it around to sense its surroundings in the pitch dark. True scorpions sting with their tails, but the vinegaroon's tail can only feel. Source: UF/IFAS EENY493, Giant Whip Scorpion (ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN890).

question: A cricket blunders past a hunting vinegaroon in the dark of a desert night. In a blink the vinegaroon, an arachnid with no venom and no stinger, seizes it in its heavy front pincers, and within seconds the cricket is dead. How does the vinegaroon kill its prey so fast?
answer: Crushes it whole in its pincers
choices: Crushes it whole in its pincers
Drains its blood through a fang
Suffocates it in a burrow
Dissolves it with acid spray
context: Those front arms are pincers called pedipalps, lined with spiny teeth. Lacking any venom, the vinegaroon simply seizes prey and crushes it, then chews it up. The same pincers can deliver a hard pinch to a careless human hand. Source: UF/IFAS EENY493 (ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN890); Oakland Zoo.

question: A vinegaroon's spray is mostly one sharp acid, and on its own that acid does almost nothing to a cockroach: the roach walks away unharmed. But the vinegaroon blends a second, oily acid into the mix, and now the spray turns lethal. Researchers propose that the oily acid breaks through one particular barrier. What does it break through?
answer: The waxy coating on the roach's shell
choices: The waxy coating on the roach's shell
The tough plates over the roach's back
The breathing holes along the roach's sides
The nerve cord running down the roach
context: The oily ingredient is caprylic acid. A roach's shell is coated in wax that repels the watery vinegar-acid, so even 85% acetic acid beads up and rolls off. Researchers propose the caprylic acid dissolves that waxy cuticle, letting the acid soak in and become lethal to insects like fly larvae. This penetration mechanism is a proposed finding, not fully settled. Source: The Transient Biologist, citing Eisner/Meinwald defensive-secretion research (thetransientbiologist.wordpress.com).

question: A viperfish, a hand-sized hunter with a huge head, lurks in the pitch-black midwater of the deep ocean. Its needle teeth are too long for its closed mouth to hold, and its jaws gape in a fixed, toothy grin. Where do the tips of those fangs end up?
answer: Curving back until the tips reach almost to its own eyes
choices: Curving back until the tips reach almost to its own eyes
Folding flat into grooves along the roof of its mouth
Sliding sideways into pouches inside its cheeks
Retracting into the base of its throat between bites
context: The viperfish's fangs are so long they don't fit inside its mouth; the needle teeth curve back very close to the fish's own eyes, so its jaws hang permanently agape around them. This is the animal's signature image. (Source: seasky.org/deep-sea/viperfish.html)

question: A viperfish hunts the pitch-dark deep ocean, more than a kilometer below the surface, with two long front fangs jutting straight up from its lower jaw. When a smaller fish drifts by, it lunges and its jaws slam shut. What do those upthrust fangs form around the prey as they close?
answer: A cage of teeth the prey cannot escape from
choices: A cage of teeth the prey cannot escape from
A funnel that flushes the prey deeper down its throat
A pair of pincers that crush the prey before swallowing
A saw that slices the prey into bite-sized pieces
context: Two prominent front fangs jut up from the viperfish's bottom jaw past its own eyes, and when it strikes, the teeth close into a cage that keeps prey from escaping. (Source: mbari.org/animal/pacific-viperfish)

question: A viperfish can barely see anything more than a few centimeters away in the black midwater, but it carries a tiny bead of living light, a photophore, at the tip of a long spine curving up over its back. Everything down there is drawn to a glimmer. How does the viperfish turn that one glow into a full belly?
answer: It waves the spine like a fishing pole and flashes the light to lure prey onto its fangs
choices: It waves the spine like a fishing pole and flashes the light to lure prey onto its fangs
It sweeps the spine across the seafloor to flush hidden prey out of the mud
It beams the light into prey eyes to blind them while it charges
It holds the light steady as a warning that keeps rival hunters away
context: The viperfish dangles a glowing photophore on the tip of a long dorsal spine and waves it over its own head like a fishing pole, flashing the light on and off to lure smaller fish right onto its fangs. (Source: seasky.org/deep-sea/viperfish.html)

question: A viperfish glows along its belly, where two rows of tiny light organs run its whole length. In the pitch dark that glow seems suicidal, a beacon for every hunter around, yet the belly lights are a survival trick. How do they keep the viperfish hidden?
answer: They match the dim glow drifting down from the surface so the fish casts no dark silhouette
choices: They match the dim glow drifting down from the surface so the fish casts no dark silhouette
They flash a sudden burst that startles the attacker into fleeing
They paint fake glowing eyes to make the fish look far larger
They leave a cloud of glowing particles for the fish to escape behind
context: Photophores line the viperfish's belly, glowing to mask its silhouette from predators looking up from below; this is called counter-illumination. So the fish uses light two ways at once: a lure above to attract prey, belly-lights below to hide. (Source: whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/ocean-facts/sloanes-viperfish)

question: A slender viperfish, only about 30 centimeters long, hunts a mile down, where food is scarce and days can pass between meals. It swallows whatever it catches, sometimes prey 20 to over 50 percent bigger than itself. What lets so small a fish gulp down a meal larger than it is?
answer: It unhinges its skull and jaw and expands its whole stomach
choices: It unhinges its skull and jaw and expands its whole stomach
It slowly dissolves the prey with acid before pulling it inward
It drags the prey in whole, working it down tail-first
It stores the prey in an inflatable pouch beneath its chin
context: The viperfish unhinges its skull and opens its jaw up to 90 degrees, expanding its stomach to swallow prey 20% to over 50% larger than itself. (Source: whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/ocean-facts/sloanes-viperfish)

question: Striking blind in the deep-sea dark, a viperfish sometimes locks its teeth into a fish far too big for it to swallow. Its long fangs point inward and cannot easily let go, so its greatest weapon becomes its doom. What happens to a viperfish that bites off more than it can chew?
answer: The trapped meal jams on its teeth and it slowly starves to death
choices: The trapped meal jams on its teeth and it slowly starves to death
It coughs the prey back up and swims off unharmed
Its fangs snap off and slowly regrow over several weeks
It swells up and floats helplessly to the surface
context: If a viperfish miscalculates and catches prey too big, its giant teeth trap the meal so it can neither swallow it nor spit it out, and it starves. (Source: usa.oceana.org/blog/freaky-fish-2-pacific-viperfish)

question: Flora, a Komodo dragon kept at Chester Zoo in England, had never once shared her home with a male. In 2006 she laid a full clutch of eggs anyway. It was a virgin birth, a mother's egg growing into a baby with no father at all. When incubation ended, how many of her eggs hatched into healthy baby dragons?
answer: Seven
choices: Seven
One
Twenty-three
Four
context: Seven of Flora's eggs hatched into healthy baby dragons, all with no father at all, a true virgin birth. Source: Nature News, 'Dragon virgin births startle zoo keepers' (2006) (https://www.nature.com/news/2006/061218/full/news061218-7.html); Watts et al. 2006, Nature 444:1021-1022.

question: At London Zoo, a female Komodo dragon named Sungai laid a clutch of fertile eggs, and the timing was the shock — it had been more than two years since she had shared space with any male. When keepers ran DNA tests on the eggs, what did the results show?
answer: Sungai was the only parent
choices: Sungai was the only parent
A distant male had somehow fathered them
The eggs were another female's
Two dragons had shared the clutch
context: Over two years past her last contact with a male, Sungai still produced fertile eggs -- and the DNA proved she alone was the parent. A second confirmed Komodo virgin birth. Source: Nature News (2006) (https://www.nature.com/news/2006/061218/full/news061218-7.html); Watts et al. 2006, Nature 444:1021-1022.

question: A herpetologist spends a whole season catching desert grassland whiptails, quick striped lizards of the American Southwest, and marking every one she finds. By autumn her notebook shows that the species breaks the most basic rule of lizard families. What is so unusual about it?
answer: The species has no males -- every one is female
choices: The species has no males -- every one is female
The lizards change sex when they need to
Each must pair with a related species
Its young are born live instead of hatching
context: The desert grassland whiptail (Aspidoscelis uniparens) is an all-female species: every individual is female and reproduces by parthenogenesis, essentially cloning herself. Source: Wikipedia, 'Desert grassland whiptail lizard' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_grassland_whiptail_lizard).

question: A biologist watching desert grassland whiptails can catch two females going through the full motions of mating: one climbs onto the other, wraps her tail under her partner's and wriggles just as a mating pair of ordinary lizards would. Far from pointless, what does this pretend mating accomplish?
answer: Triggers the other female to make eggs
choices: Triggers the other female to make eggs
Marks which lizard owns the burrow
Cools the pair down in the heat
Warns off a circling hawk
context: The mating-like behavior helps stimulate the mounted female's body to produce eggs, a courtship ritual kept alive in a species that has no males. Source: Desert Museum, 'Whiptails (Aspidoscelis spp.)' (https://www.desertmuseum.org/books/nhsd_whiptails.php).

question: Aphids, the tiny greenfly on garden plants, and water fleas in a pond run all-female lines through the warm months, each mother giving virgin birth to more daughters, generation after generation. Then the weather turns cold and harsh. What change do they suddenly make?
answer: They start producing males
choices: They start producing males
They stop breeding entirely
They shrink to survive
They abandon the plant
context: When conditions sour, these insects and crustaceans finally make males and switch to fertilized eggs -- tougher eggs that can ride out the bad season. This on-off strategy is called cyclical parthenogenesis. Source: Britannica, 'Parthenogenesis' (cyclical parthenogenesis) (https://www.britannica.com/science/parthenogenesis).

question: Combing the studbook DNA of 911 California condors, San Diego Zoo scientists discovered two males whose genes held no trace of a father. What stunned the team was not the virgin births themselves, but the circumstances of the two mothers who produced them. What was surprising about these mothers?
answer: Each was penned with a fertile mate she had bred with
choices: Each was penned with a fertile mate she had bred with
Each had been hand-raised by human keepers since hatching
Each was among the very last females left alive
Each had been dosed with drugs to boost fertility
context: This broke a rule biologists had trusted for decades -- that vertebrate parthenogenesis only kicks in when a female has no mate available. Both condor mothers had fertile partners on hand and had bred with them normally before. The two fatherless chicks were ZZ males, fully homozygous (inbreeding coefficient 1.0), and they were the first parthenogenesis ever confirmed in the species. Source: Ryder et al. 2021, 'Facultative Parthenogenesis in California Condors,' Journal of Heredity 112(7):569.

question: A big dark bird glides high over open country on a warm afternoon without a single wingbeat, its wings held in a shallow V. It rocks gently from side to side as it circles a rising column of warm air. Which bird is it?
answer: Turkey vulture
choices: Turkey vulture
Great blue heron
Snowy owl
Mallard duck
context: The turkey vulture soars on rising columns of warm air called thermals, wings held in a shallow V and spanning up to about 6 feet (1.8 m). Riding thermals lets it circle for hours without flapping, saving energy while it searches the ground below. Source: Wikipedia, 'Turkey vulture' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey_vulture).

question: A turkey vulture soars over highways and open country across the Americas, its body cloaked in dark feathers like any other bird's. But one part of it is bare, wrinkled skin, where other birds stay fully feathered. Which part of the turkey vulture is naked skin?
answer: Its head and neck
choices: Its head and neck
Its legs and feet
Its wingtips
Its tail
context: The vulture's bald head is an adaptation, not ugliness. To reach meat it plunges its head deep inside a carcass, and a feathery head would trap rotting scraps and bacteria; bare skin stays clean and washes off, and it can bake sterile in the sun. Source: Cornell Lab Bird Academy / Natural Connections, 'Spring cleaning with turkey vultures'.

question: A carcass rots under a thick forest canopy, hidden from any bird that hunts by sight, as almost every bird does. Yet a turkey vulture circling far above drops straight down onto it. How does it find a meal it cannot see?
answer: It smells it — homing in on the faint gas of early decay
choices: It smells it — homing in on the faint gas of early decay
It hears the buzz of the flies already swarming the body
It feels the warmth the decaying body gives off from far above
It follows the crows and ravens that spotted the body first
context: The turkey vulture is one of the very few birds that hunt by SMELL, a rare skill in the bird world. It homes in on ethyl mercaptan, the sulfurous gas of early decay, at just a few parts per trillion, and its olfactory brain lobe is enormous compared to other birds'. Legend-tier wonder. Source: Wikipedia, 'Turkey vulture'; Cornell Lab Bird Academy.

question: A vulture tears into flesh that has been rotting for days, a meal crawling with germs that would poison almost any other animal, and simply digests it unharmed. The secret sits in its gizzard. What is that stomach fluid like?
answer: Roughly as corrosive as battery acid, near the very bottom of the acid scale
choices: Roughly as corrosive as battery acid, near the very bottom of the acid scale
A thick alkaline slime that coats and neutralizes the meat
No sharper than a house cat's stomach, just paired with a fast gut
A cocktail of antibiotics the bird's own body brews up
context: A vulture's gizzard has a pH of slightly above 0 — about as corrosive as battery acid — while a human stomach sits around pH 2. This acid bath is the vulture's headline superpower, letting it eat rotten flesh that would sicken almost anything else. Legend-tier wonder. Source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, 'Vultures: The Gastronic Marvel'.

question: A cow dies of anthrax, its carcass loaded with hardy spores that can survive in soil for decades and sicken almost anything that touches them. A turkey vulture arrives and eats its fill, then flies off to roost miles away, perfectly healthy. Where do the anthrax spores end up?
answer: Broken apart inside the vulture, never leaving its body alive
choices: Broken apart inside the vulture, never leaving its body alive
Riding in its gut to the roost, seeded across fresh ground in its droppings
Wiped harmlessly onto its bare legs, then dried in the sun
Coughed back up in a pellet the vulture leaves at the carcass
context: The vulture's stomach acid is so corrosive it dissolves and destroys the microbes that cause anthrax, botulism, cholera, rabies and tuberculosis — diseases that would kill other scavengers. By eating diseased carcasses and destroying the germs inside its own gut, the vulture works as a walking disease-disposal unit that stops outbreaks from spreading. Legend-tier wonder. Source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, 'Vultures: The Gastronic Marvel'; Cornell Lab Bird Academy.

question: A vulture on a scorching day cannot sweat, and panting only does so much. So it soaks its own bare legs with its liquid waste on purpose, streaking them white. What two jobs does the waste do for it?
answer: The waste evaporates to chill its blood, and its acidity kills the bacteria on its feet
choices: The waste evaporates to chill its blood, and its acidity kills the bacteria on its feet
It signals other vultures to a carcass, and warns off rival birds
It waterproofs the skin, and masks the bird's scent from predators
It hardens into a protective crust, and stores water for later
context: This behavior is called urohidrosis. A vulture urinates and defecates on its own legs; the evaporating liquid chills the blood in its bare legs and feet, and the acidic waste also kills bacteria picked up from walking on carcasses, streaking the legs white. Legend-tier wonder. Source: Wikipedia, 'Turkey vulture'.

question: Wallace's flying frog, a big green tree frog, leaps from a high branch in the rainforest of Borneo and sails as far as fifty feet through the air to the next trunk, instead of climbing down and hopping across the ground. What lets it ride the air across such a gap?
answer: Its toes are fully webbed to the tips, so the four outspread feet open like parachutes
choices: Its toes are fully webbed to the tips, so the four outspread feet open like parachutes
It beats its front legs like stubby wings to stay aloft
It puffs its lungs full of air and floats like a balloon
It flicks a long tail to steer and catch an updraft
context: Wallace's flying frog (Rhacophorus nigropalmatus) of Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula glides tree to tree by spreading all four feet, whose toes are fully webbed right to the tips so the outspread feet act like parachutes. Catching air with its feet and loose skin flaps along its limbs, it can glide 50 feet (15 m) or more. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace's_flying_frog ; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/amphibians/facts/wallaces-flying-frog

question: A Wallace's flying frog glides up to fifty feet from a high branch toward the next tree in the rainforest of Borneo. At the end of the glide it must stop dead on a slick, wet leaf or a smooth trunk without bouncing off and falling to the forest floor. What lets it grab hold and land softly?
answer: Oversized sticky pads on its toe tips that cling to smooth surfaces
