choices: Oversized sticky pads on its toe tips that cling to smooth surfaces
Tiny hooked claws that dig into the bark
A ring of suction cups around its belly
Sticky mucus it sprays ahead of itself before touchdown
context: Oversized, sticky toe pads (adhesive discs) let the frog grip and land softly, sticking to smooth leaves and tree trunks at the end of a glide. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace's_flying_frog

question: Wallace's flying frog lives nearly all its life up in the canopy of the Southeast Asian rainforest, coming down only to breed over a rainforest pool. Instead of laying her eggs in the pool, what does the female build on a branch above it?
answer: A whipped-up foam nest, so the hatched tadpoles drop straight into the water below
choices: A whipped-up foam nest, so the hatched tadpoles drop straight into the water below
A cup of chewed leaves glued to the branch with tree sap
A cluster of eggs stuck under a broad leaf so rain drips them down
A ball of leaves she folds shut around the eggs on the twig
context: It is a canopy frog that lives almost exclusively in the trees, descending only to breed at pools and wallows below, where the female whips up a foam bubble-nest on a branch overhanging water so the hatched tadpoles drop in. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace's_flying_frog

question: Out on the Arctic ice lies a walrus, wrinkled and brown, with a bristly moustache and two enormous ivory tusks curving down from its upper jaw, each as long as a grown man's arm. Where the tusks meet the skull, they turn out to be a very familiar body part, hugely overgrown. What are they?
answer: Enormously overgrown canine teeth
choices: Enormously overgrown canine teeth
Twin horns of solid keratin
A pair of fused nose bones
Stiffened cartilage antlers
context: A walrus's tusks are two hugely elongated canine teeth, growing up to about 3 feet long, and BOTH males and females grow them. Source: https://www.pbs.org/wnet/nature/blog/walrus-fact-sheet/

question: Walruses climb out of the freezing Arctic sea onto beaches and floating slabs of ice to rest side by side between dives for clams on the seafloor. Roughly how many of them pile into a single one of these resting herds?
answer: Thousands, packed shoulder to shoulder
choices: A dozen or so
A hundred at most
A family of four or five
Thousands, packed shoulder to shoulder
context: Walruses haul out onto beaches and ice in enormous crowds packed shoulder to shoulder that can number in the thousands, and some Arctic haulouts reach tens of thousands of animals. Source: https://www.worldwildlife.org/resources/explainers/what-is-a-walrus-haulout-and-what-does-it-mean-for-the-planet/

question: A walrus dives to the pitch-dark Arctic seafloor for clams hidden in soft mud, where even its big eyes are useless. Yet it finds and plucks out a shellfish faster than any human diver could. What does it use to feel out each hidden shell and tell it from the sand?
answer: Hundreds of stiff, super-sensitive whiskers
choices: Hundreds of stiff, super-sensitive whiskers
Faint electric pulses from its tusks
A glowing lure dangled from its chin
Sonar clicks bounced off the mud
context: A walrus's snout carries roughly 400 to 700 stiff vibrissae that it sweeps across the dark seafloor mud to feel out buried clams, telling shell from sand by touch alone. Source: https://marinesanctuary.org/blog/sea-wonder-walrus/

question: A walrus at the edge of the pack ice tries to heave its huge, blubbery body up out of the freezing water, and the way it does so earned it the Latin name Odobenus, 'tooth-walker.' It uses its two long ivory tusks as no other animal does. What does it do with them?
answer: Hooks its tusks over ice and hauls itself up
choices: Hooks its tusks over ice and hauls itself up
Chatters its teeth to echo-locate prey
Walks the seabed on its two long tusks
Grinds its molars to grip slick rocks
context: Odobenus means 'tooth-walker' — a walrus hooks its tusks over the edge of an ice floe and hauls its huge body up out of the water, in effect walking on its teeth. Source: https://www.pbs.org/wnet/nature/blog/walrus-fact-sheet/

question: Down on the muddy Arctic seafloor, a walrus clamps its rubbery lips over a closed clam shell. A second or two later the soft meat slides into its mouth, and the empty shell drops away, uncracked and unchewed. Its mouth works more like a kitchen gadget than a jaw. How does it empty the shell?
answer: A piston-like pull of the tongue vacuums it out
choices: A piston-like pull of the tongue vacuums it out
A crushing bite that shatters the shell
Grinding molars mash the shell to bits
A jet of water blasted in to flush the meat
context: A walrus clamps its lips over the shell and pulls its tongue back like a piston, creating powerful suction that sucks the soft clam meat straight out. Source: https://www.pbs.org/wnet/nature/the-weird-way-walruses-eat-with-their-tongue/33419/

question: Swimming in the icy Arctic sea, a walrus keeps a mesh of tiny blood-vessel shortcuts in its tough grey skin clamped shut, so its warm blood stays deep in its body. Then it hauls out onto the pack ice to bake in the sun, and the shortcuts snap wide open, sending a huge rush of blood through them. Where does that blood suddenly go?
answer: Straight to the skin's surface
choices: Straight to the skin's surface
Pooled deep around the heart
Rerouted to the swimming muscles
Shunted into the blubber layer
context: The pink flush works through blood-vessel shortcuts called arterio-venous anastomoses (AVAs); when they open, blood floods the skin's surface to dump body heat like a radiator, turning the walrus pink. Source: https://www.gi.alaska.edu/alaska-science-forum/why-does-walrus-blush

question: Amazon hunters have tipped blowgun darts with curare, the classic dart poison, for centuries. The golden poison frog of Colombia carries a skin toxin of its own. How does the frog's toxin measure up against curare?
answer: Chemically stronger
choices: Chemically stronger
About the same strength
Weaker but faster-acting
Only dangerous when eaten
context: Batrachotoxin from the golden poison frog is chemically stronger than curare, the classic dart poison — and terribilis carries roughly twenty times more toxin than any other poison-dart frog, which is why it alone can arm a dart with a single living touch. Source: American Museum of Natural History Bulletin v.161 art.2 (Myers, Daly & Malkin, 1978), digitallibrary.amnh.org/items/d82fffd4-13a8-4bc0-97df-40e96e7e6f14

question: Emberá Chocó hunters of western Colombia arm their blowgun darts by wiping them along a living golden poison frog's back, and the frog survives the job. So little poison arms so many darts. About how many can one frog tip?
answer: 30 to 50 darts
choices: 30 to 50 darts
2 or 3 darts
A single dart
Several hundred darts
context: The frog is so toxic the darts are simply rubbed across its back while it lives; one frog tips 30 to 50 darts, which stay lethal for about a year. Only terribilis carries enough — roughly twenty times more toxin than other dart frogs — to arm a dart with a single living touch. Source: American Museum of Natural History Bulletin v.161 art.2 (Myers, Daly & Malkin, 1978), digitallibrary.amnh.org/items/d82fffd4-13a8-4bc0-97df-40e96e7e6f14

question: A bird snaps up a bright red-and-black ladybug and drops it at once. The beetle has neither bitten nor run; it has oozed a yellow fluid straight from the joints of its legs. What is that fluid loaded with?
answer: Alkaloids like coccinelline
choices: Alkaloids like coccinelline
Sticky tree sap
A cloud of stinging acid
Sugary nectar to distract
context: Ladybugs 'reflex-bleed' — when grabbed they squeeze bitter yellow fluid from the knee-like joints of their legs. The fluid carries alkaloids like coccinelline, so the beetle tastes foul and a bird spits it out. The bright red-and-black is the honest warning label. Source: colorado.edu/asmagazine/2020/07/21/ladybugs-bright-colors-advertise-toxic-chemical-defenses

question: A striped skunk, about the size of a house cat and common across North America, wears two thick white stripes from its head to its hindquarters. They work like an arrow drawn on its body, pointing at the very tool it is about to use on any coyote or dog that scares it. Where do the stripes point?
answer: Back toward the glands that fire its spray
choices: Back toward the glands that fire its spray
Toward its face and sharp teeth
Down at its digging claws
Up at a raised, bushy tail alone
context: The skunk's stripe is an honest warning that points, arrow-like, back toward the glands that fire its spray. Predators mostly aren't born fearing it — they learn by trial and error to avoid the pattern after one bad encounter. Source: nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/skunks-stripes-warning-colors-predators

question: Researchers compared striped skunks in 2023 across regions with very different numbers of predators, expecting one fixed coat everywhere, and found the black-and-white pattern shifting from place to place. Where mammal predators were plentiful, what were the skunks' stripes like?
answer: Bolder and more symmetrical
choices: Bolder and more symmetrical
Fainter and messier
Wider but grayer
Exactly the same everywhere
context: The 2023 study found skunks have bolder, more symmetrical stripes where mammal predators are many, and fainter, messier stripes where predators are sparse. A warning only pays off if there's an audience to teach: no predators, no reason to pay for a loud advertisement — proof that warning color is only worth its cost where predators exist. Source: phys.org/news/2023-11-skunks-stripes-prominent-predators-sparse.html

question: A big brown bat hunts by echo through the night, where warning colors are useless. Yet a dogbane tiger moth can still warn it off, and teach it to skip moths of its kind next time. How does the moth do it?
answer: It clicks back at the bat with bursts of ultrasound
choices: It clicks back at the bat with bursts of ultrasound
It puffs out a bitter, throat-catching scent
It coats itself in an oil the bat tastes on contact
It hums a low buzz the bat feels in the air
context: This is acoustic aposematism — a warning broadcast as sound, not color. Naive big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus) quickly learn that clicking moths are noxious and stop hunting them (Hristov & Conner 2005, Naturwissenschaften 92:164-169). The moth makes the clicks with paired thoracic organs called tymbals. A close relative, Bertholdia trigona, pushes the same trick from warning into active defense, firing up to roughly 4,500 ultrasonic clicks per second to JAM the bat's sonar outright (Corcoran, Barber & Conner 2009, Science 325:325-327). Grokipedia; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19608920.

question: A golden poison frog carries deadly toxin on its own skin but does not die of it. Scientists once thought the frog's cell channels carried a mutation that blocked the poison, but a study in 2021 showed the poison still acts on those channels. What do scientists now think saves the frog?
answer: A protein that soaks up the toxin before it hits the channels
choices: A protein that soaks up the toxin before it hits the channels
A skin layer too dense for the toxin to pass inward
An enzyme that splits the toxin into harmless pieces
Gut microbes that neutralize the poison as it forms
context: The old story — that toxic frogs and birds evolved batrachotoxin-resistant channels — collapsed when Abderemane-Ali et al. found the sodium channels of poison frogs AND toxic pitohui birds are still sensitive to the toxin (2021, J. Gen. Physiol. 153(9):e202112872). Their proposed 'toxin sponge' — a protein that binds and sequesters batrachotoxin before it reaches the channels — is a hypothesis, not a settled answer; how these animals resist their own poison is still an open question. rupress.org/jgp/article/153/9/e202112872; UCSF news 2021.

question: Pakicetus, a wolf-sized hunter with long jaws and sharp meat-eating teeth, ran on four legs beside ancient rivers 50 million years ago. Nothing about it looked like a whale, yet one hidden clue in its skull places it among the whales. What was the clue?
answer: A whale-only structure in its ear
choices: A whale-only structure in its ear
Blubber preserved under its skin
A blowhole opening on its head
Fins where its front legs should be
context: Pakicetus was a wolf-sized, four-legged land animal (1 to 2 m long) that lived in and around water, yet its ear already carried the whale involucrum, the clue linking this running land beast to modern whales. Source: UC Berkeley Evolution 101; Thewissen et al. 2001, Pakicetus attocki.

question: Basilosaurus, a whale shaped like a sea serpent and 15 to 18 meters long, cruised the oceans some 40 million years ago without ever coming ashore. Far down its long body, scientists found something startling for such a creature. What did they find?
answer: A pair of tiny back legs with knees and toes
choices: A pair of tiny back legs with knees and toes
A set of gills tucked behind its ribs
A row of bony plates along its spine
A second smaller mouth near its tail
context: Basilosaurus still had tiny back legs, complete with a working knee joint and little three-toed feet, far too small to walk or help it swim, a leftover from its land-walking past. LEGEND-level fossil. Source: Gingerich et al. 1990, 'Hind Limbs of Eocene Basilosaurus'; Wikipedia: Basilosaurus.

question: Whalers off Vancouver Island caught a humpback in July 1919 with something no whale should have: real limbs sticking four feet out of its body. Roy Chapman Andrews, an explorer, took a close look at the bones. What did he say they were?
answer: A leg, with shin and foot bones
choices: A leg, with shin and foot bones
An extra flipper, with fin rays
A twin calf, partly formed
A giant tumor, full of teeth
context: Very rarely a whale's genetic 'off switch' fails and it is born with real hind legs. Andrews identified a shin bone and foot bone, a throwback to the whale's land-walking ancestors. LEGEND-level. Source: Andrews 1921, AMNH, 'A Remarkable Case of External Hind Limbs in a Humpback Whale'.

question: A whale embryo about a month old sprouts tiny buds that in most mammals would grow into back legs. Then the buds shrink and vanish, and the whale is born legless. What halts them is a single developmental signal going missing. Which signal is it?
answer: The Sonic hedgehog signal
choices: The Sonic hedgehog signal
The insulin growth signal
The melanin color signal
The keratin scale signal
context: A whale embryo sprouts hind-limb buds about a month in, then a genetic 'off switch' — the Sonic hedgehog signal going missing — halts them and the buds shrink away. Source: Thewissen et al. 2006, PNAS, 'Developmental basis for hind-limb loss in dolphins'.

question: Buried deep inside a living whale's body float a pair of small hip bones, left over from its walking ancestors, with no leg attached. A 2014 study found these bones are far from useless. What job do they still perform?
answer: Anchoring the muscles that control the penis
choices: Anchoring the muscles that control the penis
Storing extra oxygen for long dives
Filtering salt out of the bloodstream
Balancing the whale as it rolls and turns
context: The 2014 study showed these vestigial pelvic bones anchor the muscles controlling the penis, and grow larger in species where males compete hardest to mate. Source: Dines et al. 2014, 'Sexual selection targets cetacean pelvic bones', Evolution.

question: Indohyus, a deer-like plant-eater the size of a raccoon, lived about 48 million years ago, an unlikely relative at the very root of the whale line. Its bones were strangely dense and heavy. What did those heavy bones let this little animal do?
answer: Wade and hide underwater from predators
choices: Wade and hide underwater from predators
Burrow deep tunnels through hard clay
Butt heads in fierce mating contests
Glide between trees on stretched skin
context: Indohyus had unusually dense, heavy bones that let it wade and hide underwater from predators, much as a hippo does today, plus the whale ear bone that gave away its place at the root of the whale line. LEGEND-level fossil. Source: Thewissen et al. 2007, Nature; ScienceDaily.

question: Philip Gingerich's team studied Maiacetus, a 47.5-million-year-old whale from Pakistan fossilized as a female with a small skeleton curled head-first inside her pelvis. A modern whale calf comes out tail-first, which keeps it from drowning during the slow underwater delivery. What bold, still-debated conclusion did the team draw?
answer: The mother had hauled out onto land to give birth
choices: The mother had hauled out onto land to give birth
The birth happened in shallows, head held clear
The tiny skeleton is swallowed prey, not a calf
The head-first pose is a fluke of decay, not birth
context: Philip Gingerich's team described Maiacetus inuus in 2009 (PLoS ONE) from a fossil pregnant female whose calf lay head-first, the way land mammals are delivered. Because a head-down birth underwater would drown the calf, they read this as a sign that these early whales still came ashore to give birth, a halfway stage in the move from land to sea. The find is genuinely contested: Hans Thewissen argued the small skeleton might be scattered or swallowed bones rather than a true fetus, and Gingerich's team countered that the tiny skull bears no tooth marks, so it was never eaten. Sources: Wikipedia 'Maiacetus'; ScienceDaily / University of Michigan 2009 release on Gingerich et al., PLoS ONE 2009; grokipedia.com/page/Maiacetus.

question: A whale shark glides slowly past a group of scuba divers in a warm tropical sea, longer than a school bus and spotted with pale polka dots. The divers like to point out that, despite its size and its name, it is no whale at all. What is it?
answer: The largest fish alive on Earth today
choices: The largest fish alive on Earth today
The largest ray gliding in the open sea
The heaviest bony fish swimming today
A giant grouper of the deep coral reefs
context: The whale shark (Rhincodon typus) is a shark — specifically a carpet shark — and the biggest fish alive. It breathes through gills and never surfaces for air the way a whale, a mammal, must. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale_shark

question: A swimmer can drift right beside a spotted whale shark as long as a school bus without any danger. Where a great white snaps its jaws shut on seals and fish, the whale shark cruises slowly with its huge mouth held wide open the whole time. What does it hold its mouth open to do?
answer: Strain tiny plankton, krill, and fish eggs from the water
choices: Strain tiny plankton, krill, and fish eggs from the water
Gulp seals and large fish whole
Suck in air to fill a swim bladder
Wash sand and grit out over its gills
context: The whale shark is a gentle filter-feeder. It glides with its mouth open and sieves out plankton, krill, and fish eggs, harmless to the swimmers drifting beside it. Source: https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/discover-fish/species-profiles/whale-shark/

question: A whale shark pushes more than 6,000 liters of seawater through its mouth every hour, a flood of food that would clog an ordinary sieve within minutes. Yet its filter pads seldom jam. How does it keep them clear?
answer: The water sweeps along the pads, not straight through
choices: The water sweeps along the pads, not straight through
Its rows of tiny teeth chop the clumps into crumbs
It swims backward now and then to wash them out
The pads shiver to shake loose any trapped food
context: The whale shark's mouth uses what engineers call cross-flow filtration: the water flows along the filter surface rather than straight through it, sweeping particles past the pads toward the throat instead of packing them into the mesh, so the sieve seldom clogs (now and then the shark seems to 'cough' to clear it). Its 300-odd rows of tiny teeth play no part in feeding, and like other sharks it cannot swim backward. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale_shark

question: A whale shark cruises the warm sea with its eyes low on the sides of its huge head and no eyelids to close, wide open to scraping coral, drifting jellyfish stingers and curious little hangers-on. When something threatens an eye, the shark still has a way to shield it. What does it do?
answer: It pulls the whole eyeball partway back into the socket
choices: It pulls the whole eyeball partway back into the socket
It clouds the eye with a burst of dark ink
It rolls belly-up so the eye faces the seafloor
It seals the eye behind a bony sliding plate
context: Lacking eyelids, the whale shark can retract the eyeball into its head — drawing it back like a snail pulling into its shell — to protect the exposed eye. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/whale-sharks-have-tiny-teeth-their-eyeballs-180975240/

question: Scientists studying a whale shark's eye up close in 2020 found something no one had expected: clustered around the iris sat nearly 3,000 tiny structures, each one shaped like a tiny oak leaf under the microscope. What are those structures?
answer: Tooth-like scales — the shark has teeth on its eyes
choices: Tooth-like scales — the shark has teeth on its eyes
Light-sensing dimples that glow in the dark
Salt glands that squeeze seawater out of the eye
Suckers that grip prey drifting too close
context: The whale shark's eyeball is armored with about 2,900 dermal denticles, the same tooth-like scales that cover a shark's skin, clustered around the iris. Each looks like an oak leaf under magnification. The whale shark literally has teeth on its eyes. Source: Tomita et al. 2020, PLOS ONE (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0235342).

question: A researcher meets a whale shark, snaps a clear photo of the patch of white spots just behind its gills, and drops the shot into a database of thousands. What can that one photo do that a photo of the shark's fin or tail cannot?
answer: Match it to a specific individual seen years earlier and oceans away
choices: Match it to a specific individual seen years earlier and oceans away
Estimate the shark's total body length
Reveal whether the shark is male or female
Show which regional population it belongs to
context: No two whale sharks share the same spot pattern, so the spots behind the gills serve as a natural fingerprint. A single clear photo of that patch lets scientists re-identify one specific individual against databases of thousands, even years later and oceans apart. Source: https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/whale-shark-identification-catalog-telescope-algorithm

question: Researchers fixed a tag to a female whale shark named Anne near Coiba Island, off Panama, in 2011 and followed her on what was, by 2018, the longest whale-shark journey on record, more than 20,000 kilometers. Where did that epic swim finally take her?
answer: To the Mariana Trench near Guam
choices: To the Mariana Trench near Guam
To the Galapagos Islands off Ecuador
To the reefs of the Maldives
To Australia's Ningaloo Reef
context: Anne, tagged off Panama's Coiba Island, swam 20,142 km clear across the Pacific to the Mariana Trench near Guam, the longest whale-shark migration on record when it was reported in 2018. The Galapagos, Maldives, and Ningaloo are all real whale-shark hotspots, but Anne's track ended at Guam. Source: https://stri.si.edu/story/mystery-migration

question: A whale shark sees in the black water nearly two kilometers down with a dim-light eye pigment that carries a single mutation, the very change that causes night blindness in a person. The mutation also leaves the pigment fragile, and that fragility is the whole trick. What switches this deep-sea vision on?
answer: The cold of the deep, where the fragile pigment holds together only when chilled and dissolves in warmth
choices: The cold of the deep, where the fragile pigment holds together only when chilled and dissolves in warmth
The crushing pressure of the deep, which forces the loose pigment down into its working form
The utter darkness of the deep, which shields the delicate pigment from light that would bleach it
The thin oxygen of the deep, which keeps the fragile pigment from slowly oxidizing itself away
context: Osaka Metropolitan University researchers Koyanagi and Terakita reported this in PNAS in March 2023. The whale shark's rhodopsin — the pigment that lets any vertebrate see in dim light — carries an amino-acid swap at a known spectral-tuning site (position 94) that shifts its peak sensitivity toward blue, the one color of light that still reaches the deep sea. The very same substitution in humans causes congenital stationary night blindness. What makes it work for the shark is that the altered pigment is thermally unstable: it degrades in warm surface water but functions perfectly in the cold of the deep, so the animal's own body temperature acts as an on/off switch for deep vision — blue-tuned sight that literally would not survive at the surface. Source: Koyanagi & Terakita et al., PNAS, 2023 (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2220728120); Science/AAAS coverage ('Mutation behind night blindness in humans helps whale sharks see in the dark') and Osaka Metropolitan University via EurekAlert.

question: An ostrich sprints across an African plain, unable to fly. A penguin dives and 'flies' through Antarctic seas instead of the sky, and an emu jogs across the Australian outback. All three wear one body covering that marks each, at a glance, as a bird. What is it?
answer: Feathers
choices: Feathers
Scales
Fur
Slime
context: Feathers are the single feature unique to birds — NO other living animal grows them. Not flight, not eggs, not nests — plenty of other animals do those. But feathers belong to birds alone, so a flightless ostrich or penguin is still unmistakably a bird. Penguins even use their feathers for waterproofing and warmth in freezing water. Source: Audubon Magazine, 'The Multiple Miracles of Bird Feathers'; Cornell Lab of Ornithology.

question: A farmyard bird pecks grain and snatches a beetle. A dog has teeth, a snake has fangs and a shark has row after row of them, but the bird has none at all. Its mouth is capped instead with a hard structure. What is it?
answer: A toothless keratin beak
choices: A toothless keratin beak
A leathery grinding gizzard plate
A forked flicking tongue
A pouch of stinging spines
context: Birds have no teeth at all. A beak (bill) of keratin — the same stuff as your fingernails — replaces the toothy jaws their dinosaur ancestors carried. Source: Britannica, 'Why Don't Birds Have Teeth?'; Forbes/GrrlScientist.

question: A pigeon lifts off the ground into flight, and to do that it has to be light. Its skeleton is built for that in a way a running mammal's dense, heavy bones are not: a pigeon's leg bone snapped in half feels startlingly light for its size, almost empty. What lies inside a bird's bones?
answer: Hollow air spaces linked to the lungs
choices: Hollow air spaces linked to the lungs
Solid heavy marrow like ours
A core of stored body fat
A rod of springy cartilage
context: A bird's bones are 'pneumatic' — hollow and air-filled, laced with extensions of the lungs' air sacs. This lightens the skeleton so the bird weighs less in the air. Source: UCMP Berkeley, 'Morphology of the Aves'; Biology LibreTexts 29.5 Birds.

question: A tiny ruby-throated hummingbird gets by with just 940 feathers. One bird of the cold, wet northern waters wears more than 25,000, the most ever counted. Which of these cold-water birds is it?
answer: The tundra swan
choices: The tundra swan
The common loon
The Canada goose
The mallard
context: The tundra (whistling) swan holds the record at over 25,000 feathers — a cold, watery life demands dense insulation. A robin sits in the middle around 2,500, and the ruby-throated hummingbird has the fewest counted, just 940. Source: Audubon, 'The Multiple Miracles of Bird Feathers'; Bird Watcher's General Store.

question: Kids snap the dried wishbone off a Thanksgiving turkey and make a wish. In a living bird, from a turkey to a hawk, that Y-shaped brace at the top of the chest is a spring: each wingbeat bends it a little, and it snaps back, storing and releasing power. Which bones is the wishbone made of?
answer: The fused collarbones
choices: The fused collarbones
The fused shoulder blades
The fused breast plates
The fused tail bones
context: The wishbone is the furcula — a pair of fused collarbones. It acts as a spring and brace during the wing's downstroke, storing and releasing energy with each beat. Source: UCMP Berkeley, 'Morphology of the Aves'.

question: A biologist studying a mouse and a blue whale looks for the one thing that makes both of them mammals, a trait no other animal shares. What does every mammal mother, and only a mammal mother, do?
answer: Feed her babies milk from her own body
choices: Feed her babies milk from her own body
Lay eggs in a warm nest
Carry her young inside a pouch
Breathe air through her skin
context: Milk from mammary glands is THE defining mammal trait — no other animal group makes milk. Carl Linnaeus named the whole class 'Mammalia' in 1758 after these milk-making glands. Source: Britannica 'Mammal'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal.

question: A bat clings under a cave roof and a cat curls up on a couch. Both are mammals, and both wear one body covering that every mammal grows at some point in life; even a whale is born with a few strands of it. What is it?
answer: Hair or fur
choices: Hair or fur
Feathers
Scales
Slime
context: All mammals grow hair or fur at some point in life — it helps trap body heat. Linnaeus could have named the class 'Pilosa,' meaning 'the hairy ones,' but chose milk instead. Source: ScienceInsights 'What Makes a Mammal'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal.

question: A zoologist sorting a drawer of skulls can tell a mammal's from a reptile's by counting the tiny bones inside the middle ear. A snake and a chicken each carry just one there, passing sound along to the inner ear, while a mammal packs more into the same small space. How many middle-ear bones does a mammal have?
answer: Three
choices: Three
One
Six
Zero
context: A mammal's middle ear holds three tiny bones — the malleus, incus, and stapes (hammer, anvil, and stirrup). No other animal has all three; reptiles and birds have only one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossicles; evolution.berkeley.edu 'Jaws to ears'.

question: Deep inside a person's ear sits a bone shaped like a riding stirrup, called the stapes, one of the little middle-ear bones that let a mammal hear. Of all the bones in the human body, from the thighbone to the skull, the stapes holds one record no other bone can claim. What is remarkable about the stapes?
answer: It is the smallest bone in the whole body
choices: It is the smallest bone in the whole body
It is the hardest bone in the whole body
It is the only bone that keeps growing forever
It is the only bone with no blood supply
context: The stapes is the smallest bone in the human body — only 2 to 3 millimeters long, about the size of a grain of rice. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stapes; my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/ossicles.

question: Paleontologists dug up the skull of Morganucodon, a shrew-sized creature of some 200 million years ago, and found two separate jaw hinges working side by side. A reptile's jaw hinges on several bones and a mammal's on just one, while a mammal's middle ear holds two bones, the hammer and the anvil, that a reptile's does not. What did the double hinge reveal?
answer: One hinge's bones were turning into ear bones
choices: One hinge's bones were turning into ear bones
Mammals and reptiles once interbred
The jaw evolved only after the ear was finished
The double hinge let it chew and swallow at once
context: Morganucodon had a double jaw joint — the new mammal joint and the old reptile joint together, one still working the jaw while the other was becoming ear bones. It is one of the most iconic transitional fossils known. The malleus and incus (hammer and anvil) began as the articular and quadrate, bones at the back of a reptile's jaw; over evolution they shrank and migrated into the ear, one of the clearest transitions in the whole fossil record. Source: AMNH; Britannica 'Morganucodon'; evolution.berkeley.edu 'Jaws to ears'; PMC3552421.

question: A lizard and a salamander sit side by side on a riverbank, the same size and the same color. The lizard is a reptile and the salamander an amphibian, a cousin of the frogs, and a single touch tells them apart. What does a hand feel?
answer: The lizard is dry and scaly; the salamander is smooth and moist
choices: The lizard is dry and scaly; the salamander is smooth and moist
The lizard is warm; the salamander is icy cold
The lizard is soft; the salamander is hard and bony
The lizard is sticky; the salamander is dry and dusty
context: A reptile's skin is dry and scaly (that's the lizard); an amphibian's is smooth, moist, and slimy (that's the salamander). Even when a dry lizard and a wet salamander look almost alike, the feel gives it away at once. Source: Forest Preserve District of Will County / National Aquarium  -  'A lizard's skin is dry and scaly, while a salamander's is usually smooth and moist.'

question: A frog climbs out of its pond. It is an amphibian, from the Greek for 'double life,' and it earns the name not by living in water and on land at once but by living two lives in turn, its first body rebuilt into another. What is that double life?
answer: A water-breathing tadpole that transforms into an air-breathing adult
choices: A water-breathing tadpole that transforms into an air-breathing adult
A creature that can survive equally in salt water and fresh water
An animal that is awake by night and asleep by day
A body that switches between male and female as it ages
context: 'Amphibian' loosely translates from the Greek as 'dual life,' a nod to the two-stage cycle: it begins as a gilled, water-breathing larva (a tadpole), then transforms through metamorphosis into an air-breathing adult with lungs and legs. Source: Wikipedia, Amphibian.

question: A small, tail-dragging creature creeps on four legs along a woodland pond, and visitors keep calling it a lizard. It is a newt, an amphibian and a cousin of the frogs, born in water; a real lizard is a reptile. What two things does a real lizard have that a newt never does?
answer: Clawed toes and external ear holes
choices: Clawed toes and external ear holes
A forked tongue and a rattling tail
Webbed feet and a fin along its back
A hard shell and a beak
context: Lizards are reptiles with dry, tough scales, clawed toes, and external ear openings; newts and salamanders are amphibians with no scales, no claws, and moist slimy skin. Wet and clawless means amphibian. Source: Discover Wildlife / Forest Preserve.

question: A frog can hop far from the pond to hunt bugs, but come breeding season it is chained straight back to the water's edge and cannot lay anywhere else. A desert lizard is under no such rule. What is it about the frog's eggs that ties its whole life to water?
answer: The eggs have no shell, so in dry air they would shrivel up
choices: The eggs have no shell, so in dry air they would shrivel up
The eggs must be kept warm by the parent's body heat
The eggs are too heavy for the frog to carry overland
The eggs will only hatch in complete darkness
context: An amphibian's egg has no shell, so it dries out in air  -  which is why frogs and salamanders must lay their jelly-covered eggs in water. That single fact chains their whole life to ponds and streams. Source: Encyclopedia.com / Biology LibreTexts.

question: A lizard bakes all day on a hot desert rock, then skitters off across the open sand. A salamander, an amphibian that can look nearly identical from a few feet away, would shrivel dry within an hour in the same spot. What does the lizard's skin do that the salamander's cannot?
answer: Seals water inside the body with a thick, waxy, keratin-packed layer
choices: Seals water inside the body with a thick, waxy, keratin-packed layer
Reflects the sun's heat with a mirror-like silvery sheen
Stores a hidden reservoir of water in pockets under the scales
Sweats to cool the body down like a running animal
context: A reptile's main problem is preventing water loss through the skin, solved by a thick stratum corneum with waxes layered between keratinized cells. That waterproof seal is exactly why a reptile can bake on a rock or cross a desert while an amphibian, whose skin must stay wet, cannot. Source: Britannica, Integument  -  Reptiles.

question: A plethodontid salamander thrives in a cool, wet forest with no lungs at all, and its family is the biggest of all the salamanders on Earth. Even a frog, which has working lungs, dies within hours if it dries out in clean, open air. Where does the plethodontid get its oxygen?
answer: Through the skin and the moist lining of the mouth
choices: Through the skin and the moist lining of the mouth
Through a pair of gills kept hidden under the throat
Through tiny air tubes running along the spine
Through swallowed air stored in a balloon-like gut
context: An amphibian's moist skin is a major organ of respiration: oxygen passes straight through the thin, wet skin into blood vessels just beneath  -  cutaneous respiration. That's the real reason the skin must stay damp, and why an amphibian can't survive in the salty sea. The Plethodontidae are the largest group of salamanders despite having no lungs whatsoever  -  they breathe entirely through their skin and the lining of their mouths, a stunning proof of how well skin-breathing works. Source: Wikipedia, Cutaneous respiration & Amphibian.

question: A grasshopper in a summer meadow has no lungs anywhere in its body, yet every cell deep inside it gets a steady supply of fresh air. Tiny round openings dot its sides. How does the air reach the cells inside?
answer: Air seeps in through tiny holes along its sides and runs through branching tubes to the cells
choices: Air seeps in through tiny holes along its sides and runs through branching tubes to the cells
Its heart pumps oxygen-rich blood to the tissues like a mammal's
It absorbs oxygen through its wings while gliding
It swallows air and digests the oxygen in its gut
context: Those side-holes are called spiracles, and the branching tubes are the tracheae; together they pipe outside air directly to nearly every cell, skipping blood entirely. Source: Duke University Library Exhibit, Insect Sizes & Oxygen; Wikipedia, Respiratory system of insects.

question: A gnat, a flea and a fruit fly do no work at all to breathe: fresh air drifts down the tiny tubes inside each one and reaches every cell on its own. What is it about being so small that lets them skip the pumping?
answer: The air only has to travel a hair-short distance, so it arrives fast enough
choices: The air only has to travel a hair-short distance, so it arrives fast enough
Their extra-wide breathing holes let far more air rush in at once
Their thin outer shell soaks up oxygen straight from the surrounding air
Their cells burn so little oxygen that a trickle is plenty
context: Oxygen moves through the air tubes on its own, drifting from where it is plentiful to where it is scarce. That drift is fast over the hair-thin distances inside a small insect, so no pump is needed at all; the catch is that it only stays fast over short distances. Source: Duke University Library Exhibit, Insect Sizes & Oxygen.

question: A small beetle breathes with no effort, letting oxygen drift in through tiny holes along its sides and down air tubes to every cell. Suppose you could inflate it to the size of a golden retriever, holes and tubes unchanged. It would suffocate within minutes. Why?
answer: The oxygen drifts too slowly to reach the core, so the innermost cells suffocate
choices: The oxygen drifts too slowly to reach the core, so the innermost cells suffocate
The air tubes grow so long the bug can't push the stale air back out
The extra weight crushes the soft breathing holes shut
The blood grows too thick to carry the oxygen inward
context: Diffusion is fast over short distances but painfully slow over long ones. In a huge insect, core cells would starve for oxygen before it ever arrived. Source: Duke University Library Exhibit; eLife, insect respiratory literature.

question: Scientists raised young fruit flies and grasshoppers in sealed chambers kept low in oxygen, then compared the grown adults with insects raised in ordinary air. They suspected that adult size depends on how much oxygen an insect can take in. How do insects raised in low oxygen turn out?
answer: They grow up markedly smaller than normal
choices: They grow up markedly smaller than normal
They grow up markedly larger to grab more air
They grow at exactly the normal size
They stop growing wings but keep their body size
context: Insects reared in low-oxygen air end up much smaller than usual, direct evidence that the oxygen a body can supply, not appetite or genes alone, sets the ceiling on insect size. Source: Duke University Library Exhibit, Insect Sizes & Oxygen; PNAS related work on oxygen and insect body size.

question: A ground beetle, filmed by synchrotron X-ray video, works over and over to drive air through its body instead of waiting for it to drift down its breathing tubes on its own. What does it do to push the air along?
answer: Squeezes its air tubes flat, then lets them spring back
choices: Squeezes its air tubes flat, then lets them spring back
Reverses the flow so air is pulled out through its mouth
Floods the tubes with fluid to carry oxygen inward
Swallows air and forces it into the tubes from its gut
context: Synchrotron X-ray video caught ground beetles, carpenter ants and crickets collapsing and reinflating their main air tubes every second or two, working them like tiny bellows to push air along. Source: Westneat et al. 2003, 'Tracheal respiration in insects visualized with synchrotron X-ray imaging', Science 299:558.

question: Alexander Kaiser's team X-rayed beetles of several sizes and measured the air tubes running through the narrow opening where each leg joins the body. The bigger the beetle, the bigger the share of that opening the tubes took up. What would that trend mean for a beetle much larger than any alive?
answer: Its legs would be crammed too full to hold muscle
choices: Its legs would be crammed too full to hold muscle
Its legs would snap under the weight of its heavy shell
Its leg joints would grow too stiff to bend at all
Its heart could not pump air down so many tubes
context: Kaiser and colleagues (PNAS 2007) X-rayed beetles of different sizes and found that the air tubes passing into the legs take up a growing share of the leg opening as beetles get bigger. Extrapolate the trend and, in a beetle much larger than the biggest alive, the tubes would fill the leg, leaving no space for the muscle that moves it. Source: Kaiser et al. 2007, PNAS, 'Increase in tracheal investment with beetle size supports hypothesis of oxygen limitation on insect gigantism'.

question: Giant griffenflies, huge dragonfly-like insects, flew over the swamp forests of the Carboniferous some 300 million years ago. A tidy story credits their size to the extra oxygen in the air of that time, and says giant insects became impossible once oxygen dropped. Which fossil fact spoils that story?
answer: Giant griffenflies lived on into the Late Permian, long after oxygen had fallen
choices: Giant griffenflies lived on into the Late Permian, long after oxygen had fallen
The very largest griffenflies come from the lowest-oxygen Permian rock beds
Some later times with air just as oxygen-rich produced no insect giants at all
Giant griffenflies shrank steadily even while oxygen was still climbing toward its peak
context: The giant griffenflies (Meganisoptera) persisted into the Late Permian, after oxygen had already dropped well below its Carboniferous peak, so rich air can't be the sole cause of insect gigantism; other factors likely mattered too. Source: Wikipedia, Meganeura, oxygen hypothesis caveat; Wikipedia, Meganisoptera.

question: A resting insect can open and shut the tiny air holes along its sides. Many insects at rest work them in one odd pattern that scientists have argued over for decades, with no winner yet. What does an insect using that pattern do with its air holes?
answer: Keeps them clamped shut for long stretches, then cracks them open in one quick burst
choices: Keeps them clamped shut for long stretches, then cracks them open in one quick burst
Holds them all wide open so fresh air streams steadily to every inner cell
Opens the holes along one side while sealing the other, sweeping air across the body
Squeezes and releases its whole body nonstop, driving a constant current through the tubes
context: Many resting insects don't breathe steadily at all -- they run a 'discontinuous gas exchange cycle': spiracles clamped shut for long stretches, then a brief flutter phase, then one open burst that dumps the built-up CO2. WHY they do it is a genuine, decades-old unsettled debate with three rival explanations, and no consensus has been reached. The hygric hypothesis says sealed air-holes save precious body water from evaporating out. The chthonic hypothesis says the pattern aids gas exchange in low-oxygen, high-CO2 spots like burrows and soil. The oxidative-damage hypothesis says keeping internal oxygen low shields tissues from being 'rusted' by the raw O2 the tracheae deliver straight to the cells. Tests keep partly supporting and partly undercutting each. It sharpens the core idea of these questions: direct tracheal oxygen delivery is a double-edged tool, so insects must actively throttle their air-holes rather than drink air freely. Sources: 'Discontinuous gas exchange' overview (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discontinuous_gas_exchange); Chown et al., PNAS 2007 (pnas.org/content/104/20/8357); review, Physiological & Biochemical Zoology 79(2), 2006.

question: Matthew Clapham and Jered Karr gathered the wing lengths of more than 10,500 fossil insects in 2012. Through most of that long record, the largest insects grew and shrank alongside the oxygen in the air. Then, around 150 million years ago, insect size stopped tracking oxygen, though oxygen stayed high. What took over as the new limit on insect size?
answer: Nimble birds became airborne hunters, and a bigger insect is a clumsier, easier-to-catch flier
choices: Nimble birds became airborne hunters, and a bigger insect is a clumsier, easier-to-catch flier
Flowering plants spread and reshaped insect diets, favoring smaller, quicker-feeding bodies
A warming climate raised their energy needs, so smaller bodies that shed heat faster won out
Crowded skies full of early flying reptiles squeezed insects into smaller, hidden lives
context: In 2012, paleobiologists Matthew Clapham and Jered Karr compiled the wing lengths of more than 10,500 fossil insects across the entire fossil record. For most of insect history, maximum body size closely tracked atmospheric oxygen -- strong support for the oxygen-limitation idea. But around 150 million years ago, in the Late Jurassic, size stopped following oxygen even though oxygen remained high. That decoupling coincides with the radiation of birds: agile, size-selective aerial predators. Because a flying insect's maneuverability drops as it grows, larger insects became easier to catch -- so predation, not air chemistry, set the new limit. This is the concrete 'what else besides oxygen' behind the older observation that giant griffenflies outlived peak Carboniferous oxygen. (Exact ancient oxygen levels are themselves estimated from geological proxies.) Source: Clapham & Karr, 'Environmental and biotic controls on the evolutionary history of insect body size,' PNAS 2012 (doi:10.1073/pnas.1204026109; PubMed 22665762).

question: Saber-toothed cats and one big pack hunter prowled the marshy ground where Los Angeles stands today, some 13,000 years ago. More than 4,000 of the pack hunters have come out of the sticky La Brea Tar Pits, more than of any other mammal. Which ice-age predator was it?
answer: The dire wolf
choices: The dire wolf
The gray wolf
The coyote
The American cheetah
context: Aenocyon dirus (renamed from Canis dirus in 2021) is the most common mammal recovered from La Brea - over 4,000 individuals. Dire wolves and sabre-tooth cats vanished from the site roughly 13,000 years ago. Source: tarpits.org (La Brea Tar Pits official); Scientific American, 'Fossils Buried in LA Tar Pit Show Why Saber-Toothed Cats Blinked Out of Existence'.

question: Haury, an archaeologist digging at Naco in Arizona in 1952, uncovered a Columbian mammoth with Clovis stone spear points still stuck in its bones. One lucky throw might drop a smaller beast, but this giant took a barrage. How many Clovis points did the dig find in it?
answer: Eight points
choices: Eight points
One point
Two points
Twenty-six points
context: At Naco (1952), Haury found a Columbian mammoth with eight Clovis fluted points in it; at the nearby Lehner site he later found mammoth bones with 13 points beside ancient fire hearths. These kill sites are cornerstone evidence for the overkill case. Source: Wikipedia, 'Naco Mammoth Kill Site' and 'Lehner Mammoth-Kill Site'.

question: Polynesian settlers reached New Zealand, where the moa, giant flightless birds, were not in decline. Within 150 years people had hunted every kind of moa to extinction, a pace that sounds like the work of a crowd of hunters. How thinly spread were the people who did it?
answer: About one person per 100 square km
choices: About one person per 100 square km
About one person per 10 square km
About one person per square km
About ten people per square km
context: Moa were not in decline before Polynesian arrival, yet all species were hunted out within about 150 years by an extremely sparse human population, about one person per 100 square km and only some 2,500 people in all when the last moa died. That tiny population still exterminated them, the clearest overkill case. Source: Holdaway et al. 2014, Nature Communications 5:5436, 'An extremely low-density human population exterminated New Zealand moa' (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2014/11/141107091656.htm); PNAS, 'Extinct New Zealand megafauna were not in decline before human colonization'.

question: Climate researchers reading the ancient DNA locked in Yukon soil argue that the ice-age giants starved as their world melted. From about 14,500 years ago, rapid warming broke apart the mammoth steppe, the vast, dry grassland of the far north, and the DNA records what replaced its rich grasses. What took over the mammoths' feeding grounds?
answer: Mosses, shrubs and tundra
choices: Mosses, shrubs and tundra
Dense evergreen conifer forest
Bare gravel and permanent ice
Flower-rich meadows even lusher than before
context: Rising moisture turned the nutritious mammoth-steppe grasses into mosses, shrubs and tundra as the ice sheets retreated; ancient environmental DNA from Yukon soil records the turnover directly. This habitat-collapse evidence anchors the climate case. Source: Nature Communications, 'Collapse of the mammoth-steppe in central Yukon as revealed by ancient environmental DNA' (2021); Wikipedia, 'Mammoth steppe'.

question: Researchers working at the La Brea Tar Pits propose a one-two punch that joins the two sides of the extinction debate. In their account, people wiped out the big grazers and browsers just as the land dried out, and something dangerous piled up across the landscape. What built up once the plant-eaters were gone?
answer: Unbrowsed brush that fed raging wildfires
choices: Unbrowsed brush that fed raging wildfires
A boom in small burrowing rodents
Erosion as grass roots died back
Weedy plants crowding out the last grasses
context: Many scientists now favor a synergy: climate change shrank and shifted habitats while human hunting pushed already-strained populations over the edge. At La Brea, researchers propose that killing off plant-eaters let wildfire-fuel vegetation build up just as the climate was drying - a one-two punch. Which factor mattered more is genuinely still debated. Source: Scientific American, La Brea study; History.com, 'What Killed Off Giant Animals of the Ice Age?'; PNAS, 'Explaining the Pleistocene megafaunal extinctions'.

question: Genyornis, a flightless two-meter thunder bird, stalked Australia until about 47,000 years ago, just as the first people arrived. Charred shell from its eggs lies at more than 200 sites, but a wildfire could char a shell too. Gifford Miller's team read one clue as the mark of human cooks. What was it?
answer: Each shard is seared at one end and raw at the other, the pinpoint burn of an egg on campfire embers
choices: Each shard is seared at one end and raw at the other, the pinpoint burn of an egg on campfire embers
Each shard is scored on the inside with stone-tool cut-marks where a blade cracked the shell apart
The shards lie heaped in rings around fire-cracked hearth-stones dragged into the camp
The shards were crammed into ash-lined roasting pits packed with charred animal bone
context: A wildfire racing across the land would bake a buried shell fairly evenly, but embers heaped under a single egg scorch one side toward 1,000 F while the far side stays raw - the pattern Gifford Miller's team read as human cooking. The charred shell shows up at more than 200 sites dating to about 47,000 years ago, right as people spread across Australia - the same window the rhino-sized Diprotodon, the marsupial lion Thylacoleo, and the giant short-faced kangaroo Procoptodon disappeared. Miller called it the first secure evidence that humans preyed directly on Australia's giant animals, by raiding Genyornis nests. That is overkill-side evidence; how much of the killing was people versus a shifting climate stays an open question. Source: Miller et al. 2016, 'Human predation contributed to the extinction of the Australian megafaunal bird Genyornis newtoni ~47 ka,' Nature Communications 7:10496; University of Colorado Boulder news, 29 Jan 2016.

question: The last woolly mammoths on St. Paul Island, in the Bering Sea, died about 5,600 years ago, and no person set foot there until 1787. Five separate lines of evidence, dung-fungus spores among them, pin that date. With no hunter anywhere near, what finished the last mammoths?
answer: Their one freshwater lake silted up until there was nothing left to drink
choices: Their one freshwater lake silted up until there was nothing left to drink
A string of savage winters buried the last of their grazing under deep snow
The rising sea drowned the low-lying island out from under their feet
A creeping epidemic ran through the small, inbred herd until none were left
context: As the ice age ended, St. Paul shrank from part of the Bering land bridge to a scrap of about 110 square kilometres holding a single freshwater lake. Radiocarbon on 14 mammoth bones, three species of dung-fungus spore, sediment DNA, pollen, and lake-core chemistry all land on roughly 5,600 years ago (sediment DNA: 5,650 +/- 80 years), making it one of the most precisely dated prehistoric extinctions known. Russell Graham's team argued the mammoths hastened their own end: penned on shrinking ground, they stripped the plants and trampled the shoreline, speeding the erosion that choked the lake with silt until the drinking water gave out. Because no person reached the island until 1787 CE, it is a rare clean test - environment alone, with no hunter in sight, erasing a mammoth population. It pulls against the mainland kill-sites, and the overkill-versus-climate debate stays unresolved. Source: Graham et al. 2016, PNAS 113(33):9310-9314; Penn State University news.

question: A flat, blotchy shark lies draped over an Australian reef, so still that divers swim right past it. Branching skin flaps fringe its wide mouth like a shaggy beard. What kind of shark is it?
answer: A wobbegong
choices: A wobbegong
A nurse shark
A zebra shark
A horn shark
context: Wobbegongs are the bearded carpet sharks of the family Orectolobidae. The branching skin flaps around the jaw help hide the shark's outline and also work as sensory barbels, and the name 'wobbegong' is thought to come from an Aboriginal word for 'shaggy beard'. Nurse, zebra and horn sharks also rest on the seafloor, but none wears the fringed beard. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wobbegong

question: A tasselled wobbegong rests dead still on an Australian coral reef for hours, its edges fringed with flaps of skin like seaweed. Only one thing about it moves: slowly, over and over, it waves the tip of its tail back and forth. Why would a hidden ambush hunter move its tail at all?
answer: Its tail fin mimics a small fish, drawing prey close
choices: Its tail fin mimics a small fish, drawing prey close
It fans oxygen-rich water over its gills to breathe
It sweeps loose sand off its back to stay hidden
It signals to rival wobbegongs to keep their distance
context: The tasselled wobbegong's caudal (tail) fin resembles a small fish, complete with a dark eyespot near its base. By waving it slowly, the motionless shark lures curious fish straight into striking range — its beard hides it while its tail baits the trap. Source: https://saveourseas.com/worldofsharks/species/tasselled-wobbegong

question: A small fish drifts within inches of a wobbegong's flat, whiskered face as the shark rests on an Australian reef. The wobbegong has lain frozen there for hours and cannot give chase, yet in a single instant it seizes the fish. How does a shark that can barely move grab its prey?
answer: It gapes its jaws and vacuums the fish straight in
choices: It gapes its jaws and vacuums the fish straight in
It flares its gill flaps to trap the fish in a rush of water
It stuns the fish with a sharp electric pulse
It pins the fish against the reef with its broad fins
context: When prey comes close the wobbegong flings its jaws open at lightning speed; the sudden drop in pressure creates powerful suction that vacuums the fish in and swallows it whole. It doesn't chase — it waits, then inhales. Source: https://oceana.org/marine-life/tasselled-wobbegong/; https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/discover-fish/species-profiles/tasselled-wobbegong/

question: Divers surveying a reef off Great Keppel Island, Australia, in 2011 came on a tasselled wobbegong, some 1.25 meters from snout to tail, with a meal jammed in its wide jaws: prey roughly 80 percent as long as itself, going down whole. What was it swallowing?
answer: A brownbanded bamboo shark
choices: A brownbanded bamboo shark
A basking sea turtle
A giant reef octopus
A giant moray eel
context: Daniela Ceccarelli and David Williamson, counting fish on a reef off Great Keppel Island in August 2011, photographed a tasselled wobbegong about 1.25 m long with a dead brownbanded bamboo shark about 1 m long jammed in its mouth; they did not see the meal end, but the wobbegong presumably finished it. Stomach studies had already shown that wobbegongs eat other sharks. Source: Ceccarelli & Williamson 2012, Coral Reefs, 'Sharks that eat sharks: opportunistic predation by wobbegongs' (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00338-012-0878-z); National Geographic 2012 (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/120213-sharks-swallows-whole-great-barrier-reef-animals-science).

question: A buried wobbegong lies motionless for hours, so it cannot swim water through its mouth the way cruising sharks do -- and drawing water in through its mouth would only suck in a cloud of sand. How does it keep breathing without giving its hiding spot away?
answer: It snorkels clean water down through spiracles set behind its eyes
choices: It snorkels clean water down through spiracles set behind its eyes
It absorbs dissolved oxygen straight through its thin, patterned skin
It reverses the current, pulling water in through its five gill slits
It rises for a quick gulp of air, then sinks back into the sand
context: A resting shark cannot ram-ventilate by swimming, and inhaling through its mouth on the seabed would pack its gills with sediment. Wobbegongs breathe instead through a pair of large crescent-shaped spiracles -- openings just behind each eye. The spiracle draws clean water from above like a snorkel, and the shark buccal-pumps it back over the gills, so it can lie buried and motionless for hours without stirring up the cover that hides it. Source: Catalina Island Marine Institute, 'Spiracles: The Secret of the Benthic Shark,' and the Georgia Aquarium spotted-wobbegong profile -- https://cimi.org/blog/spiracles-the-secret-of-the-benthic-shark/

question: Corrigan and Beheregaray read the DNA of wobbegongs, the flat, frilly sharks draped across reefs from Australia to Japan, and dated the branches of their family tree in 2009. The sharks look like shaggy relics that might have crept over the reefs since the age of dinosaurs. What did the dated tree reveal?
answer: The living species radiated only recently, within the last 20 million years
choices: The living species radiated only recently, within the last 20 million years
They are unchanged living fossils dating back to the age of the dinosaurs
They descend from a deep-water ancestor that only later colonised the reefs
Their carpet camouflage arose separately in several unrelated shark lineages
context: Despite the living-fossil look, the DNA says the opposite. Corrigan and Beheregaray's molecular phylogeny ('A recent shark radiation,' Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution, 2009) found the whole family Orectolobidae only began splitting into today's species in the Miocene, within roughly the last 20 million years, inside the Indo-Australian region. The burst was driven by the Miocene collision of the Indo-Australian and Eurasian tectonic plates, which reshaped the shallow reefs these ambush sharks depend on -- so the 'ancient carpet' is really a recent evolutionary flowering. Source: Corrigan & Beheregaray 2009, Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution 52 -- https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1055790309000736

question: A stocky, short-legged hunter roams the far northern forests. It is shaped like a small bear, dark brown with pale side stripes, and about the size of a medium dog. Even with that bear-like build, it is the largest land member of one animal family. Which one?
answer: The weasel family (mustelids)
choices: The weasel family (mustelids)
The bear family (ursids)
The dog family (canids)
The raccoon family (procyonids)
context: The wolverine (Gulo gulo) is the largest terrestrial mustelid — the same family as weasels, otters, and badgers. Males run about 25–40 lb, roughly medium-dog sized, but the low-slung, muscular, bear-like shape fools people into guessing a small bear. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolverine

question: Deep, soft snow blankets the north. A wolverine glides across the top of it, barely sinking, while a deer or elk many times its weight breaks through the crust and flounders belly-deep. What lets the wolverine stay up on powder that swallows heavier animals?
answer: Huge, fur-soled paws that spread its weight like snowshoes
choices: Huge, fur-soled paws that spread its weight like snowshoes
Hollow, air-filled bones that make it float
A layer of trapped body gas that buoys it up
Long claws that hook onto an icy under-layer
context: The wolverine's oversized, five-toed, fur-soled paws spread its weight so it skims over deep powder while heavier prey post-hole through. Using the snow itself as a weapon, it can run down and kill animals more than ten times its size. Source: https://www.vitalground.org/winters-warrior-wolverine-fragile-fierce/

question: A wolverine tears into a carcass frozen rock-solid in the Arctic winter — food most predators simply can't get their teeth into. Its secret is in the back of its jaw: the upper molars aren't aimed straight back like most mammals'. How are they set instead?
answer: Rotated roughly 90 degrees sideways, turned inward
choices: Rotated roughly 90 degrees sideways, turned inward
Fused into a single flat grinding plate
Curved forward into small tusks
Replaced by a hard toothless ridge of bone
context: A weasel-family trait taken to an extreme: the wolverine's upper molars are rotated about 90 degrees inward, turning the back teeth into a shearing-and-crushing tool that rips meat and bone off carcasses frozen solid. Source: https://wolverinefoundation.org/dentition-of-the-wolverine

question: A small brown creature of the North American forests wears a dark band from its snout back across each eye, like a bandit's mask. Which animal wears that mask?
answer: the wood frog
choices: the wood frog
the spotted salamander
the pine marten
the ringtail cat
context: The wood frog (Lithobates sylvaticus) is a small brown frog of North American forests, marked by a dark 'robber's mask' band running from the snout back over each eye; it survives winter by freezing solid. Source: Discover Wildlife (discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/amphibians/wood-frog).

question: The little brown wood frog breeds in shallow forest ponds each spring, and no other frog in North America lives as far north. How far north does its range reach?
answer: north of the Arctic Circle
choices: north of the Arctic Circle
only into southern Canada
only to the Great Lakes
no farther than the northern Rockies
context: The wood frog ranges farther north than any other North American frog: it is the only one on the continent found north of the Arctic Circle, up past Alaska's Brooks Range. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_frog; University of Alaska Fairbanks (uaf.edu/news/wood-frogs-farthest-north-amphibian-cannibals.php).

question: Winter settles over a northern forest, cold enough to kill almost any frog. The wood frog lives through it by doing something that looks, to anyone watching, exactly like dying, for weeks or even months at a stretch. What does the wood frog do to get through winter?
answer: it freezes solid, heart stopped
choices: it freezes solid, heart stopped
it burrows below the frost line
it slows its heart to one beat an hour
it drains its blood into its bladder
context: To survive winter the wood frog lets itself freeze solid: its heart stops, it stops breathing, its kidneys shut down, and it lies stiff and frozen, appearing completely dead, for weeks or months. In Alaska, wood frogs have been recorded staying frozen for more than six months at a stretch. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_frog; National Geographic 'Antifreeze-Like Blood Lets Frogs Freeze'.

question: A wood frog lies stiff through the depth of a northern winter. Anyone might expect a thin skin of frost on it and nothing more, yet a startling share of the water inside its whole body has turned to solid ice. About how much of it?
answer: around two-thirds of it
choices: around two-thirds of it
around a tenth of it
only the skin and toes
just the fluid in its gut
context: When the wood frog freezes, as much as roughly 65% — about two-thirds — of the water in its body turns to solid ice, yet it revives when it thaws. Source: National Wildlife Federation / Discover Wildlife roundup, search-verified across multiple wood-frog freeze sources.

question: The first hard freeze of winter reaches a wood frog, and ice begins to form outside its cells. That ice pulls water out of the cells, which are in danger of shriveling. The frog's liver answers by flooding its body with one substance that works as an antifreeze inside every cell. What does the liver pour in?
answer: a flood of glucose
choices: a flood of glucose
a rush of adrenaline
a wash of salt brine
a surge of alcohol
context: As freezing starts, the wood frog's liver dumps a flood of glucose (sugar) into its cells as natural antifreeze; the syrupy sugar keeps the cells from losing all their water and collapsing. Far-north Alaskan frogs add a second cryoprotectant, urea. Source: National Geographic; PMC PMC4331536.

question: Spring warms a wood frog that has lain frozen for weeks under the leaf litter. It does not thaw all at once, like a chicken breast left on a kitchen counter; it thaws in a set order that gives it the best chance of coming back to life. Which parts of the frog revive first?
answer: the heart and brain
choices: the heart and brain
the legs and feet
the outer skin
the eyes alone
context: The wood frog thaws from the inside out — heart and brain come back first. The ice melts in about 20 minutes; the heart takes another 20-30 minutes to restart before the frog gulps, breathes, and hops away. Source: National Geographic 'Antifreeze-Like Blood Lets Frogs Freeze'.

question: A wood frog spends the winter frozen under the leaf litter right beside the shallow woodland pool where it will breed, and it thaws the moment snowmelt fills that pool. Among the frogs of its forest, what does that let the wood frog do?
answer: wake and mate earliest
choices: wake and mate earliest
breed twice each spring
lay the most eggs of all
live the longest lives
context: Because it overwinters right beside its breeding site and thaws as the vernal pools fill with snowmelt, the wood frog wakes and mates earlier than rival frogs that must wait for open water to thaw. Source: Discover Wildlife; Vermont Center for Ecostudies vernal-pool page.

question: Beetles and grubs hide beneath the bark of an oak, and a woodpecker clinging to the trunk drills for them, slamming its beak into the wood again and again in a machine-gun blur. Over one busy day of chiseling, roughly how many times does its beak strike the tree?
answer: 8,000 to 12,000 strikes
choices: 8,000 to 12,000 strikes
about 200 strikes
about 800 strikes
about 40 strikes
context: A woodpecker can hammer up to about 20 times every second and lands 8,000 to 12,000 strikes in a single day. Source: ScienceABC / BirdWatchingDaily, https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/animals/how-woodpeckers-dont-get-concussions

question: A woodpecker lands hard on the upright trunk of an oak, with no branch to perch on. To hammer the bark without sliding down, it grips like a pair of pliers: the four toes on each foot clamp the wood in a pattern most other birds do not share. How are those toes arranged?
answer: Two toes forward and two toes backward
choices: Two toes forward and two toes backward
All four toes pointing forward
Three forward and one tiny backward
Two fused into a hoof-like pad
context: This two-forward, two-backward arrangement is called a zygodactyl foot, and it gives the bird a firm four-point clamp on the bark. Source: Avian Report 'Woodpecker Feet', https://avianreport.com/woodpecker-feet/

question: A downy woodpecker climbs a smooth beech trunk and stops halfway up to hammer at the bark. Its two feet alone would let its body sag away from the wood, so it braces itself like a tripod, pressing a third point against the trunk just below its feet. What does it press into the bark?
answer: Its stiff, spiny tail feathers
choices: Its stiff, spiny tail feathers
Its folded wingtips
Its long hooked claws
The underside of its beak
context: The stiff, spiny tail feathers push against the trunk and, together with the two feet, form a stable three-point brace. Source: Avian Report / Animal Kingdom, https://avianreport.com/woodpecker-feet/

question: A long, loud drumroll rings out across a New England forest on a cold spring morning: a downy woodpecker is pounding a hollow dead tree, and the sound carries for hundreds of feet. Anyone hearing the rattle might think it was digging for insects, but fast, echoing hammering like this usually is not feeding at all. The noise itself is the point. What is the woodpecker doing?
answer: Claiming territory and calling a mate
choices: Claiming territory and calling a mate
Sharpening its worn-down beak
Warning the flock of a hawk overhead
Loosening sap to drink from the wood
context: A long, loud burst of hammering is a drummed message that stakes out territory and calls for a mate, the way a songbird sings. Source: All About Birds (Cornell Lab), https://www.allaboutbirds.org/news/how-to-recognize-woodpeckers-by-their-drumming-sounds/

question: Sometimes a woodpecker hammers at a surface that holds no insects at all, choosing it only because it rings louder than any tree could. When it drums like this, the farther the sound carries, the better. Which surface does it seek out?
answer: A metal gutter or street sign
choices: A metal gutter or street sign
A hollow dead snag
A wooden fence rail
A house's plastic downspout
context: Because a drum's job is to carry, woodpeckers pound loud man-made things like metal gutters, chimney caps, and street signs to broadcast as far as possible. Source: Cornell Lab / Sialis.org drumming, https://www.sialis.org/drumming/

question: A northern flicker jabs its short bill into an anthill; this brown woodpecker of the Americas spends more time on the ground than in trees. The ants live in deep, twisting tunnels that its beak alone could never reach, yet the flicker empties whole nests without cracking the mound open. How does it get the ants out?
answer: It shoots its tongue inches out past the beak tip
choices: It shoots its tongue inches out past the beak tip
It floods the tunnels with sticky spit
It cracks the mound open with its feet
It waits for the ants to march up on their own
context: The Northern Flicker's tongue extends about two inches beyond its beak to snake deep into anthills; woodpecker tongues in general can reach several inches past the bill. Source: American Bird Conservancy, https://abcbirds.org/news/woodpecker-tongues/

question: A woodpecker punches a hole into rotting oak and finds a tunnel full of pale, slippery beetle grubs. The tip of its tongue has to grab and hold a wet, squirming grub that the bird can barely feel. What lets the tongue tip snag such slippery prey?
answer: Backward-facing barbs and sticky saliva
choices: Backward-facing barbs and sticky saliva
A hard bony hook
A ring of tiny suction cups
A mild numbing venom
context: The tongue tip carries tiny backward-facing barbs and glue-like saliva that snag and hold insects probed from deep inside a tunnel. Source: Avian Report, https://avianreport.com/woodpecker-tongue/

question: In the oak forests of California, a family of acorn woodpeckers, black-and-white birds with clown-red caps, drills thousands of small round holes into a single granary tree. Instead of hiding acorns one by one, the birds wedge an acorn into each hole. The biggest granary tree ever found held a staggering hoard. About how many acorns?
answer: Around 50,000 acorns
choices: Around 50,000 acorns
Around 50 acorns
Around 500 acorns
Around 5,000 acorns
context: The acorn woodpecker builds a 'granary' tree drilled with thousands of holes; the largest known granary held around 50,000 acorns. As the acorns dry and shrink, the birds move each one to a snugger hole. Source: Atlas Obscura / Cornell Bird Academy, https://academy.allaboutbirds.org/storing-food-the-granaries-of-acorn-woodpeckers/

question: Its probe of a grub tunnel finished, a woodpecker draws its tongue back in. The tongue rides on a slender, forked support bone called the hyoid, and it is far too long simply to sit inside the mouth. Where does the hyoid run once the tongue is pulled all the way in?
answer: Up over the top and around the back of the skull
choices: Up over the top and around the back of the skull
Coiled inside the throat like a spring
Folded flat under the lower beak
Stored in a pouch below the eye
context: The tongue's bony support starts near the nostril, splits into a V between the eyes, loops over the top and around the back of the skull, then meets again at the base of the lower beak. Source: American Bird Conservancy, https://abcbirds.org/news/woodpecker-tongues/

question: Sam Van Wassenbergh's team filmed woodpeckers pecking in slow motion in 2022 to test an idea people had long assumed: that a spongy skull cushions the bird's brain like a bike helmet. What did the films show the skull really does?
answer: Acts as a stiff hammer for a harder hit
choices: Acts as a stiff hammer for a harder hit
Bends like rubber to absorb shock
Redirects the shock down the neck and out the tail
Splits the impact between the two jaws
context: 2022 research found the skull is no cushion; it works as a stiff hammer that makes pecking more powerful, and the brain stays safe for other reasons. Source: Current Biology 2022 'Woodpeckers minimize cranial absorption of shocks', https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(22)00855-7

question: Every peck stops a woodpecker's head at nearly 1,000 g, thousands of times a day. A jolt like that would rattle a person's brain against the inside of the skull and bruise it, yet the woodpecker's brain comes through unharmed. Why doesn't all that hammering rattle it?
answer: It's small and packed too snugly to slosh
choices: It's small and packed too snugly to slosh
A cushion of fluid floats it in place
It shuts down blood flow on impact
It's wrapped in a thick fatty pad
context: The brain is small and held so snugly inside the skull that it barely moves, so it can't slosh and bruise the way a loose brain would, even at decelerations near 1,000 g. Source: ScienceABC, https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/animals/how-woodpeckers-dont-get-concussions

question: A woodpecker's head whips to a dead stop 20 times a second - hard enough that an eyeball could jolt forward out of its socket or shake the retina loose. About a millisecond before each blow, what comes to the eye's rescue?
answer: A see-through third eyelid snaps shut and pins the eye
choices: A see-through third eyelid snaps shut and pins the eye
A shelf of bone slides up from the cheek to cap the eye
A ring of muscle behind it hauls the eyeball deeper in
A pad of dense fat swells forward to wedge it firmly still
context: This is the nictitating membrane, a tough translucent 'third eyelid' many birds have but which the woodpecker puts to extreme use. Firing about one millisecond before each hammer blow, it does double duty: it shields the eyeball from flying wood chips AND physically clamps the eye in its socket, so the ~1,000+ g deceleration can't shake the retina loose or pop the eye forward. None of the bird's famous headgear helps here - the eye needs its own seatbelt. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nictitating_membrane; corroborated by ophthalmologist Ivan Schwab's award-winning work and The Naturalist's Notebook (thenaturalistsnotebook.com) pileated-woodpecker anatomy.

question: George Farah's group at Boston University took the preserved brains of ten woodpeckers in 2018, stained them, and set them beside the brains of blackbirds, which do not drum. Woodpeckers had long been called immune to head injury, all that hammering and no harm done. What turned up in the woodpecker brains?
answer: Clumps of tau protein, the marker seen in concussed athletes
choices: Clumps of tau protein, the marker seen in concussed athletes
Torn axon fibers, the damage seen in whiplash victims
Rusty microbleeds, the staining seen in blast survivors
Shrunken dead neurons, the loss seen in stroke patients
context: The study, led by George Farah (PLOS ONE, Feb 2018), used Gallyas silver staining and anti-phospho-tau immunohistochemistry on museum brains of 10 woodpeckers versus 5 red-winged blackbird controls. Most woodpeckers showed build-ups of tau - the very protein tied to CTE in concussed football players - while the controls had none.
