It punctured the tidy 'immune to injury' story, but the debate is genuinely unsettled: whether that tau is a protective adaptation or a sign of real damage remains unresolved. Source: journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0191526 (PubMed 29394252); coverage: CBC News, 'woodpecker-brain-damage-protein.'

question: A shaggy, cold-loving relative of today's elephants trudged through the last ice age across a vast frozen grassland that stretched from Spain all the way across Siberia to the Yukon. It is one of the most famous ice-age giants of all. Which one?
answer: The woolly mammoth
choices: The woolly mammoth
The woolly rhinoceros
The giant ground sloth
The Irish elk
context: The woolly mammoth (Mammuthus primigenius) grazed the vast, dry 'mammoth steppe' that stretched across ice-age Eurasia and North America, browsing on grasses, sedges, and forbs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth

question: An elephant on the hot African savanna flaps its huge, flat ears like fans to dump heat. A woolly mammoth on the frozen tundra had the opposite problem: it had to hold on to every scrap of warmth. What were its ears like next to an elephant's?
answer: Tiny, only about a foot long
choices: Tiny, only about a foot long
Even bigger and floppier
Feathered for extra warmth
Folded flat and hairless
context: A woolly mammoth's ears were only about 38 cm long and its tail just 36 cm, so it lost far less body heat and avoided frostbite in the deep cold. Small extremities are a classic cold adaptation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth

question: A woolly mammoth wore long, coarse guard hairs, some nearly three feet long, draped over its flanks like a shaggy brown skirt to shed snow and rain. Beneath them, pressed against the skin, a second layer did the real work of trapping warmth against the cold. What was that inner layer made of?
answer: A dense underfur of fine hair
choices: A dense underfur of fine hair
A layer of loose feathers
A coat of oily scales
Bare wrinkled skin
context: The outer guard hairs ran up to about 90 cm long, while the soft underwool beneath, up to about 8 cm long, trapped a warm layer of air against the skin. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth

question: A woolly mammoth trudged through the freezing winters of the last ice age with more protection than its coat alone. Beneath its skin lay a layer nearly four inches thick, and a shoulder hump stored more of the same stuff as fuel for lean winters. What was it?
answer: Insulating fat
choices: Insulating fat
Extra muscle
Stored water
Hollow air pockets
context: The fat layer reached about 10 cm thick, and the fatty shoulder hump acted as a fuel and water reserve to carry the animal through hungry winters. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth

question: A woolly mammoth's tusks weren't straight spears like an African elephant's — they curved and spiraled inward until they sometimes crossed in front of its face. When scientists study preserved tusks pulled from the Siberian permafrost, they notice worn-flat patches on one side of each tusk, showing a daily chore the mammoth did over and over on the ice-age plains. What was the mammoth using its tusks for?
answer: Sweeping snow off buried grass
choices: Sweeping snow off buried grass
Digging burrows to sleep in
Cracking open frozen rivers
Stripping bark from tall trees
context: Preserved tusks show flat polished wear patches up to 30 cm long from sweeping snow off the grass the mammoth wanted to eat, and from fighting. The biggest male tusk ever measured ran 4.05 m along the curve. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth

question: Whole woolly mammoths thaw out of the frozen ground of Siberia tens of thousands of years after they died, some so complete that scientists can study what no bone could ever save. What has the frozen ground kept?
answer: Skin, hair, and stomach contents
choices: Skin, hair, and stomach contents
Only the outline in the ice
Just the tusks and teeth
A hollow shell of dried hide
context: Frozen mammoths have been recovered from Siberian permafrost with skin, hair, and even stomach contents intact after tens of thousands of years; named specimens include Berezovka, Yukagir, Dima, and Lyuba. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth

question: A mammoth calf about a month old died some 42,000 years ago, and her body is now the best-preserved mammoth ever found. Close study of that body finally showed how such a healthy calf had died. What killed her?
answer: She inhaled mud and choked
choices: She inhaled mud and choked
A cave lion ambushed her
She froze in a blizzard
She starved after losing her herd
context: Bogged down in a muddy river, Lyuba inhaled fine mud that suffocated her; afterward lactic-acid bacteria 'pickled' her body, sealing it against decay for 42,000 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyuba_(mammoth)

question: Scientists examining the stomach of a frozen mammoth calf, about four weeks old when she died, found her mother's milk and, stranger still, some of her mother's dung. Baby elephants still eat their mothers' dung today. Why would a mammoth calf swallow it?
answer: To seed her gut with plant-digesting bacteria
choices: To seed her gut with plant-digesting bacteria
To ease the pain of a sore belly
To mark herself with the herd's scent
To fill up when milk ran short
context: Calf mammoths, like baby elephants, ate some of their mother's dung to stock their bellies with the gut bacteria needed to digest tough plants. Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S104061821100173X

question: On Russia's Wrangel Island, out in the Arctic Ocean, a small, stranded herd of woolly mammoths outlived the mainland herds, which had died out around 10,000 years ago. How late did the last of them survive, measured against Egypt's pyramids?
answer: Still alive well after the Great Pyramid was built
choices: Still alive well after the Great Pyramid was built
Died out a thousand years before the first pyramid
Gone some 5,000 years before the first pyramid
Lasted until Roman times, long after the pyramids
context: A small, isolated population survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean until only about 4,000 years ago, later than the Great Pyramid of Giza, built about 4,500 years ago. This last line was inbred and descended from a single maternal lineage, and studies point to defects such as a weakened sense of smell and a coat that no longer insulated well. Mammoths also outlasted the mainland on St. Paul Island (Alaska), to about 5,600 years ago, where fresh water dried up; island refuges like these are a key point for the climate side of the extinction debate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth; PNAS, 'Timing and causes of mid-Holocene mammoth extinction on St. Paul Island, Alaska' (2016).

question: A woolly mammoth saved precious body heat by letting its legs, ears and trunk run bitterly cold, yet tissue that cold normally cannot wring enough oxygen from the blood passing through. Kevin Campbell's team rebuilt the mammoth's blood protein from 43,000-year-old DNA in 2010 and put it to the test. What set it apart?
answer: Its hemoglobin released oxygen even in near-freezing blood
choices: Its hemoglobin released oxygen even in near-freezing blood
It flushed the cold limbs with warm blood in bursts
Its chilled muscles ran on fuel that needs no oxygen
Its blood stockpiled spare oxygen in extra red cells
context: In a 2010 study led by Kevin Campbell, scientists spliced a ~43,000-year-old mammoth hemoglobin gene into E. coli and brewed the actual protein, 'like taking a blood sample from a living mammoth.' Normally hemoglobin grips oxygen more tightly as it cools, so chilled blood struggles to hand it off; three unusual amino-acid changes lowered that energy cost, letting mammoth blood keep unloading oxygen to near-freezing legs, ears, and trunk, something a modern elephant's blood cannot do. That let the mammoth run its extremities cold to save heat without starving them. The 'built for cold' story reached all the way down into the blood chemistry itself. Source: Campbell et al. 2010, Nature Genetics, 'Substitutions in woolly mammoth hemoglobin confer biochemical properties adaptive for cold tolerance' (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20436470; nature.com/articles/ng.574).

question: A woolly mammoth grazed the frozen mammoth steppe of the ice age, but it was not the only heavyweight on that cold grassland. A neighbor plodded the same ground beside it, crowned with a single great horn instead of tusks. Which ice-age beast was it?
answer: The woolly rhinoceros
choices: The woolly rhinoceros
The steppe bison
The saiga antelope
The reindeer
context: The woolly rhinoceros shared the cold, grassy mammoth steppe with woolly mammoths, reindeer, bison, and saiga antelope -- an ice-age crew scientists call the Mammuthus-Coelodonta Faunal Complex. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_rhinoceros

question: A woolly rhinoceros carried a front horn unlike the rounded one of any living rhino: flattened side-to-side, almost blade-like, and worn smooth near the tip. That scuffed horn hints at what it probably did with its head all winter to keep feeding. What was it?
answer: Swept it across the ground to brush snow off the frozen grass
choices: Swept it across the ground to brush snow off the frozen grass
Locked it against rivals in shoving matches over territory
Levered it under frozen trees to strip away edible bark
Drove it into hardened soil to hook up buried roots
context: The flattened blade-like horn and the abrasion on it suggest the woolly rhino swept its head to-and-fro to clear snow off the frozen steppe grass it grazed; Wikipedia calls this a possible use the wear patterns indicate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_rhinoceros

question: A baby woolly rhinoceros nicknamed Sasha thawed out of the Siberian ice in Yakutia in 2014, its woolly coat still on, the first intact calf of its kind ever found. Its body came out gray and muddy. What did scientists find when they cleaned it?
answer: Its original fur was a light strawberry-blond
choices: Its original fur was a light strawberry-blond
Its horn had already grown longer than its legs
It still had its mother's milk in its stomach
Its skin was patterned with dark stripes
context: Sasha (Yakutia, 2014) was the first intact woolly rhino baby ever found; cleaning the remains revealed the calf's fur had been a light strawberry-blond, not the dull gray it looked at first. A second young rhino, three or four years old, thawed out near the same spot in 2020. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/sasha-woolly-rhino-mummy-siberia-ice-age-spd; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_rhinoceros

question: Love Dalen's group read the DNA of woolly rhinos frozen in the Siberian permafrost in 2020, tracking the population across thousands of years. One idea held that ice-age hunters had slowly picked the rhinos off until none were left. What did the genomes show about the rhinos' last stretch of time?
answer: They stayed numerous and genetically healthy, with no long decline
choices: They stayed numerous and genetically healthy, with no long decline
They had been inbreeding and dwindling for tens of thousands of years
They had boomed to record numbers in the centuries before vanishing
Their numbers had already collapsed long before people reached Siberia
context: In Lord et al. (Current Biology, 13 Aug 2020), Dalen's group sequenced one complete nuclear genome and 14 mitochondrial genomes from frozen woolly rhinos. The DNA showed the population stayed large, diverse, and not inbred from about 29,000 years ago until at least ~18,500 years ago -- meaning the rhinos thrived in northeast Siberia alongside humans for over 13,000 years without declining. The rapid crash to extinction around 14,000 years ago instead lines up with the sudden Bolling-Allerod warming. This remains a genuine, still-open scientific debate: the 'overkill' hypothesis (Paul Martin, 1967) blames human hunting, while studies like this one point to abrupt climate change -- the evidence does not yet settle it either way. Source: Wikipedia, 'Woolly rhinoceros'; Lord et al. 2020, Current Biology (via sci.news and sciencedirect.com). Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403).

question: A ghost-white crab clings beside a hot vent on the dark Pacific seafloor, its legs thick with silky, hair-like bristles. Scientists first hauled one up in 2005, and its shaggy look gave it a famous nickname. What is this crab called?
answer: The yeti crab
choices: The yeti crab
The spider crab
The king crab
The mitten crab
context: Kiwa hirsuta, the first yeti crab, was found in 2005 at hydrothermal vents on the South Pacific seafloor. Its pale, hair-covered legs earned it the name of the Yeti, the abominable snowman of the Himalayas. Source: MBARI, 'Discovery of the Yeti Crab' (mbari.org/news/discovery-of-the-yeti-crab).

question: A yeti crab crouches beside a scalding vent on the dark Pacific seafloor. What looks like fur on its arms is really dense rows of tiny bristles, and on them the crab does something few animals do: it raises a living crop there, and then eats it. What is the crop?
answer: Bacteria it farms on its bristles
choices: Bacteria it farms on its bristles
Tiny shrimp it snares in the hairs
Algae that photosynthesizes there
Coral polyps that bud on it
context: The bristles (setae) carry a living crop of bacteria that the crab grows and later eats, using comb-like mouthparts to scrape it off. National Geographic hailed it in 2011 as the first animal seen deliberately farming bacteria on its own body. Source: National Geographic, 'Yeti Crabs Farm Food on Own Claws, A First'; Thurber, Jones & Schnabel 2011, PLOS ONE.

question: Andrew Thurber, a biologist, filmed a yeti crab crouched at a cold methane seep off Costa Rica, slowly swaying its bristly claws back and forth through the seeping, chemical-rich water, the same motion over and over. It was not swimming, and it was not fighting. Why the rhythmic waving?
answer: To wash nutrients over its crop
choices: To wash nutrients over its crop
To shake off silt settling on it
To signal a mate in the dark
To sift the mud for buried worms
context: The slow 'dance' washes chemical-rich seep water over the bacteria growing on the crab's bristles, helping them grow, like fanning a garden. Andrew Thurber filmed a dancing Kiwa puravida at methane seeps off Costa Rica and described it in 2011. Source: Thurber, Jones & Schnabel 2011, PLOS ONE, 'Dancing for Food in the Deep Sea' (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3227565/); National Geographic.

question: Kiwa tyleri, a yeti crab of the Antarctic seafloor, spends its life crammed onto a band of seabed only a few meters wide around a hot deep-sea vent. Any closer to the vent and the water would cook it. What hems it in on the outer side of that strip?
answer: The near-freezing Antarctic seawater
choices: The near-freezing Antarctic seawater
Fish that hunt the open seabed beyond
Water too poor in minerals for its shell
A steep cliff of glassy, bare lava rock
context: The diffuse vent fluid the crab huddles in is only about 3.5-20 C, while the surrounding Antarctic seawater is near freezing (about 0 to -1.3 C). Too close to the vent and the crab cooks; too far and the cold hems it in, so its world is just a few meters wide. Source: Thatje et al. 2015, PLOS ONE (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4480985/).

question: A yeti crab grows its dinner as a living fuzz matted along its bristly claws, but bristles are not a mouth, and the crop still has to travel from arm to stomach. Filmed feeding at a methane seep off Costa Rica, the crab keeps drawing one mouthpart back across those claws. How does the crop get from claw to mouth?
answer: The appendage is a fine comb that rakes the bacteria loose.
choices: The appendage is a fine comb that rakes the bacteria loose.
The appendage is a hollow straw that sucks the bacteria up.
The appendage is a sticky pad that traps the bacteria fast.
The appendage is a sharp blade that shaves the bristles off.
context: The comb is a row of highly modified, comb-like setae on the crab's third maxilliped — a mouthpart. In Kiwa puravida, the crab draws it across the bacteria-coated bristles on its claws to scrape the crop free and into its mouth, in effect eating from a fork it grew on its own face. Source: Thurber, Jones & Schnabel 2011, PLOS ONE, 'Dancing for Food in the Deep Sea' — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3227565/

question: Kiwa tyleri crabs crowd together in the warm water of an Antarctic vent. Yet a female carrying eggs crawls the opposite way, out onto bare rock far from the vent's warmth, and fasts there for months on her stored fat. Her eggs leave her no choice. What drives her off the warm vent?
answer: Vent warmth would cook her developing eggs before they hatch.
choices: Vent warmth would cook her developing eggs before they hatch.
Only the cold water carries the oxygen her eggs must have.
Rival crabs raid the crowded vent and devour exposed eggs.
The packed vent leaves no bare surface to anchor her clutch.
context: In Kiwa tyleri, the Hoff crab, egg-carrying females migrate off the warm diffuse flow (about 3.5-20 C, where adults feed) out into 0 to -1.3 C Southern Ocean water, because the embryos cannot survive the vent's heat. Cut off from their bacterial crop, the mothers stop feeding entirely and burn stored fat while their yolk-fueled (lecithotrophic) larvae slowly develop — a stark tradeoff between reproducing and eating. Source: Thatje, Marsh, Roterman, Mavrogordato & Linse 2015, PLOS ONE, 'Adaptations to Hydrothermal Vent Life in Kiwa tyleri' — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4480985/

question: A carpenter ant on a rainforest trail brushes against something too small to see, and it sticks. Days later it has grown right through the ant's body and is steering it toward its death. What kind of living thing is at the controls?
answer: A fungus
choices: A fungus
A virus
A worm
A bacterium
context: The carpenter ant (genus Camponotus) is taken over by the fungus Ophiocordyceps unilateralis. It is a fungus, not a virus or a 'zombie disease' — the fungus itself grows through the ant's body and drives its final acts. Source: Britannica, 'Zombie-ant fungus'; Penn State News, 'Getting to the bottom of the zombie ant phenomenon.'

question: A carpenter ant, its body taken over by a parasite, leaves its trail and climbs down into the low leafy plants near the rainforest floor. There it does one last thing that will keep its body fixed to the spot once it is dead. What does it do?
answer: Bites down and locks its jaws onto a leaf
choices: Bites down and locks its jaws onto a leaf
Digs a burrow into the soil
Wraps itself in a silk cocoon
Curls up under a fallen log
context: The fungus drives the ant into a 'death grip' — it clamps its mandibles onto a leaf and dies there. This locked bite holds the corpse in exactly the spot the fungus needs. Source: Britannica, 'Zombie-ant fungus'; Penn State News, 'Getting to the bottom of the zombie ant phenomenon.'

question: In a Thai rainforest, carpenter ants steered by the parasite Ophiocordyceps end their lives in a death grip on the underside of a leaf. When one field study tracked hundreds of them, 98 percent had clamped onto the same kind of spot on the leaf. Where did the death grip land?
answer: On a major vein
choices: On a major vein
On the flat middle of the blade
On the pointed leaf tip
On the leaf's stem
context: The ants bite onto a major primary or secondary vein on the underside (abaxial surface) of the leaf, not the flat blade. The tough vein is thick and sturdy enough to anchor the corpse for weeks while the fungus finishes growing. Source: Hughes et al. 2011, 'Behavioral mechanisms and morphological symptoms of zombie ants,' BMC Ecology (PMC3118224).

question: David Hughes and his team measured hundreds of dead carpenter ants, all killed by the parasite Ophiocordyceps and clamped to leaves in a Thai rainforest. Nearly all hung at the same height, give or take a few centimeters: about 25 centimeters above the forest floor. Why does the parasite drive its hosts to that narrow band?
answer: It has the temperature and humidity the fungus needs to grow
choices: It has the temperature and humidity the fungus needs to grow
It is the exact height the fungus can no longer climb
It keeps the corpse away from ants on the ground trail
It is where leaves are widest for a strong bite
context: The bites cluster at about 25 cm (roughly 10 inches) up — measured at 25 ± 3 cm. That low, cool, humid understory has the precise temperature and moisture the fungus requires to grow and make spores. Source: Hughes et al. 2011, BMC Ecology (PMC3118224); Penn State News, 'Getting to the bottom of the zombie ant phenomenon.'

question: Scientists watching a population of carpenter ants taken over by the parasite Ophiocordyceps saw that they did not bite down at random moments. The doomed ants clamped onto their leaves together, abruptly, at nearly the same time each day. What time of day sets off the bite?
answer: Around noon, sun high overhead
choices: Around noon, sun high overhead
At first light, just after dawn
At nightfall, in full darkness
Late afternoon, as the heat fades
context: Across the population the bites came abruptly and together around noon: the sun stood about 80 degrees up when the ants clamped down, close to its highest point. The trigger is tied to the daily cycle of the sun. Source: Hughes et al. 2011, BMC Ecology (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3118224/).

question: A carpenter ant killed by the parasite Ophiocordyceps hangs dead beneath a rainforest leaf. Days later a long, thin stalk pushes out of the body and showers spores down onto the trail beneath, where the next ants to pass will pick them up. Which part of the dead ant does the stalk grow from?
answer: The head
choices: The head
The abdomen
A leg joint
The jaws
context: The spore-bearing stalk grows out through a hole in the dead ant's head, then showers spores down onto the foraging trail below to catch the next ants. Source: Penn State News, 'Getting to the bottom of the zombie ant phenomenon'; Britannica, 'Zombie-ant fungus.'

question: Maridel Fredericksen and David Hughes rebuilt an infected carpenter ant in 3-D in 2017, expecting to find the parasite packed into one command center, since people call what it does mind control. Instead they found it threaded through tissue all over the body, yet one organ, the one anyone would bet on for mind control, held none of its cells. Which organ was it?
answer: The brain
choices: The brain
The gut
The antennae
The compound eyes
context: The fungus surrounded and invaded the ant's muscle fibers throughout the body, forming an interconnected network — but no fungal cells were found inside the brain. It is a body-hijack working the muscles directly, not a puppeteer reading the mind from inside the skull. Source: Fredericksen et al. 2017, PNAS (doi:10.1073/pnas.1711673114); Penn State News, "'Zombie ant' brains left intact by fungal parasite."
